GREAT GAME!  This blows other open-"world" space games (Evochron Merc, X: Rebirth, etc.) out of the water as far as fun and dynamics go.  You don't have to grind too much to make geat profits.  Want a new ship?  Find one you can beat, board it, capture it, captain it, then work your way up the food chain.  Environments beautifully done, as well as artwork on the ships and weapons effects.  Combat is very tactical and lgical, taking into account where your weapons are placed and requiring you be at a certain azimuth to fire from them (left side, right side, front, back), so it takes some thought and power management during battles, especially when against tough ships.  I definitely recommend!

Starpoint Gemini 2(Just Released into Beta) is exactly what you want from this genre.
Compared to other space games in its genre, this game has more of an arcade style of gameplay.  If you are expecting the depth and simulation of something such as the X-Universe then you will probably want to avoid this game.   However if you want to just fly around in a beautiful world, and combat enemies with responsive and fuild controls then this game is for you.
The ship designs are very beautiful and unique. The enviornments are very good and beautiful to look at as you go through the game.
There are many different factions within the game that will end up fighting each other.  As well as many you can gain or lose rep with that will effect your standing with them.
The controls are easy to understand and reponsive.
Combat can be fought in several ways, you can hire a crew to improve stats of your ship such as accuracy, dodge, shields, etc.  However you can also tell the gunner to shoot for you, so either you can fly and have the A.I. shoot for you or you can Shoot and fly yourself.  This provides a nice change of pace for when you are wanting the A.I. to focus on defense or attack while you just maneuver the ship.

I bought Mad Max feeling a bit skeptical, considering I'm not typically a violent roleplay type person. That being said, my love for the movies pushed me into it, and it turns out I was not remotely disappointed. The game is fast, beautiful, and the cars are just cool. I found the various landscapes made even routine scavenging fairly interesting, and the characters are at least not total cliches. The storyline was definitely not one of its stronger suits, but it pulls you along well enough. I leveled out too early - before reaching the final area - and would have appreciated either a steeper slope or a higher one. If there was anything I would have absolutely changed - and this is a stupid nitpick, I know, but it was driving me crazy and no pun intended - is that Max cannot jump to save his life. Literally. I got stuck in a two foot crevasse thing while some guy was shanking me, and because I couldn't get out, he killed me. Aggravating. But don't jump to conclusions, because that one fact certainly doesn't ruin the game. I would definitely recommend.

Obviously I'm in the minority here...
I've experienced no lag what so ever. Game runs at a constant 45-55fps al throughout the Paris level on medium/high settings (I don't really care about graphics so whether or not I go ultra is quite irrelevant to me). For that I run a 6600 i5, 960 4gb (OC) and 8gig ddr4 RAM.
Now the game itself is really cool so far. It's a lot more akin to Blood money or Silent Assasin where you have tons of ways to complete a mission. I would go so far as to say that the Paris map is by far the largest map in a hitman game to date and it is loaded with possibilities and challenges.
The Mastery system is a nice addition and adds to the already great replayability (you unlock weapons, starting points and gadges as you progress in a mission). I've yet to try contracts but that should add even more replayability.
I've heard that a lot of people have horrible FPS (although again, I certainly don't) so that is definatley something to be aware of if you purchase, though it will get patched out. =)
Another issue to A LOT of people is the episodic release. This is individual of course, I have absolutely no problem with it. To me it allows them (given budget constraints and deadlines) to create ever larger and better maps compared to if they hadn't done it like this. IF you hate this release system, kindly wait until the full game is released early next year. It's really as simple as that, no?
I'd definatley recommend this game, it's so far cheaper than a ticket to the cinema and you get a whole lot for the €13 you spend.

If you're old enough to remember the days of Advance Wars on the GBA then this game is worth your time. While not exactly turn based it's also not as hectic as RTS can be. Each unit is on a transmission speed, the higher the transmission speed, the faster you can make each move with it,
Now I love humor just as much as the next guy and this game has that quirky humor in every cutscene and theres no voice overs so you don't have to worry about bad voice acting. The only sounds you will hear is in the tranisitions and when you use units to fire or when they're destroyed.
I got the hang of this game fully but the 4th level simply because it doesn't overwelm you with infomation. In the first tutorial level it tells you the basics and thats it, after that it explains each unit including new ones that you use and the ones you face. Just be careful not to shoot your own units. (Although it's hilarious when the Enemy AI does it)
Each unit is unique and well balanced. You've got Assault, Shock (Self destructing or Melee), Artillery, Scouts and Interceptors. My personal favourite is the interceptor when it's fully researched and with +3's on both range and area coverage, never worry about artillery with one of those babies. It's really rewarding to research and if you're in need of some extra supplies, simply grind out some free battles and you're set.
Another feature is the line of sights, very similar to the Fog of War from Advance Wars. If you scout an area, that area will be seen until your scout that you used can be used again so you can watch for incoming enemy tanks. Giving your scout that extra range and area coverage though modules can really help. Hell, if you have good enough units you'll never need to hit the max capacity for tanks on any given level.
My only downside that I've found is the campain. It's only 13 missions long (Excluding the few side ones and the free battles) but still tells a moving story within that time. It doesn't feel too rushed considering you're gonna be doing some grinding before some of them. You get the chance to go back and redo the campain which is not that bad when your units carry on as does your research. So it gives you plenty of time to obtain everything, plus it becomes easier with each pass of the campain rather then the opposite. (Be warned, the 13th mission is nightmare fuel, it gave me a jump when I first saw this thing)
Final score leaves me with a 9.5/10

Having played the (pre)-(se)quel, my expectations for this game were high. I also knew that, this game having just 3 episodes compared to the 5 in the original game, it would be over way too quickly.
The story in this game is really good. I would compare it to a good book; Once you start reading, you can't stop until you reach the end. Having played the first Life is Strange game, and this being a prequel, I knew where the story would go. Nevertheless, the game surprised me multiple times. The characters are very well thought out.
As I had expected, the game didn't take me a long time to complete (24 hours for two playthroughs), but it was quality time.
The game gives you the impression that 'Choices matter'. However, after the second playthrough, i was dissapointed in this. I made other choices wherever i could. And sure, there was some other dialogue here and there, but this never really made a big difference in how things played out.
Bottom line; A gem of a story, my expectations came true.
Pro's:
+ Hella story
+ Got me emotional
Con's:
- Too short
- Choices don't do a lot

(Note: Even though I only got about a half-hour on the PC version, I completed the game on the Wii U.)
Shantae is back and just as good as she was before! Though is this a definitive version to play? Let's get Ret-2-Go!
Story: In a dream, Shantae saw herself go into a cave underneath (or she thinks) Uncle Mimic's house. A voice explains that she's their only hope to the one that'll doom them all. The next morning, after getting a sneak peak of the Dynamo, Risky starts her attack immediately after a Tinkerbat stole the Dynamo Blueprints! As far as story goes, it's pretty simplistic by its accord and there are a lot of movie-quality cliches in this game. 7.5/10
Controls: Very much like Pirate's Curse, this relies on the arrow keys and zxcasd for the main controls. Still plays pretty solidly even on a keyboard, but it still pays to have a controller on hand. Back is the "dreaded" dancing and it's incorporated in a way similar to Risky's Revenge, though it was supposed to be like the original game's dancing mechanic in that enemies can interrupt you. Each creature plays relatively unique from one another and they control pretty great. 8.5/10
Graphics: Out with the pixel-work and in with the chibi Flash style! To be fair, the graphics are still great even if they're relatively old, the characters still are themselves, the levels have their feel and beauty, and it's not hard to understand why they wanted to use this style in contrast to the pixelart style. 9/10
Sound: Music and Audio go here. As per usual, Jake Kaufman has done fantastic work in his music, and really, my only complaint has to be that he had to add in an electric guitar riff in an otherwise mostly techno-inspired music. (9.5/10) As well, there are more voice lines in the game, though those do vary in quality and volume, especially near the beginning. And as usual, the sounds connected to objects are still satisfying enough that it's a pleasure to continue. (8/10) Overall: 8.8/10
Overall and mentions: This game, while good, is also close to unforgivingbly short, with side-quests placed in to make this otherwise short game feel much longer. However, while I do say that, I argue that it works in its own accord, especially when we have time sinks like Skyrim and Fallout in the area. The bosses are satisfactory enough, and it's challenging, though not impossible to get all the keys to the local Art Gallery. This game will get an 8.5/10, since while this game is not THE best of the Shantae series, it's far from being the worst, hell, every Shantae game is at or above an 8/10 for me and should get a little more attention, just not so much Capcom buys it out and ♥♥♥♥♥s it out. Otherwise, this is SoupCanMafia, age 20 and this is the badly drawn review.

(I'll try to avoid spoilers, because it's better to go in knowing nothing about the game, but there might/will be some hinted stuff..)
Spec Ops: The Line. What can be said about it? Well quite a lot actually. You start the game off as Captain Martin Walker, leading a three-man team into an almost post-apocalyptic Dubai. What starts off as exactly the kind of game you'd THINK yourself getting into, is a third-person cover shooter with plenty of brown to spare, designed the lure in the exact kinds of people who play such games. From a gameplay standpoint, Spec Ops fails to break any new ground, playing like how you'd expect a game to play from ten years ago, but the shine isn't from the game itself surprisingly enough, but from the story. As you progress through the game, traversing the ruins of Dubai fighting various baddies, the story really picks up. You go from fighting the locals for the first few missions to actually fighting rogue US soldiers.
Every encounter leaves you a little more worn, both physically and mentally, as well as your own soldiers, degrading as the game drags on. Dealing with the more serious, personal aspects of war such as PTSD to the very morality of what you're doing, a subject not often touched in war games where you kill five or six dozen people in a level and don't give it a second thought. Your two comrades begin to question your every choice and action, voicing their (sometimes conflicting) opinions after firefights and during decision making periods. The choices don't often matter, sometimes forcing you into situations where there's only one choice to pick, but still lays the burden of its actions on your shoulders as in the end, you are the one who did it.
The game degrades further as you play, at times breaking the fourth wall and speaking directly to YOU; the player, often through the almost subliminal nature of the environment, even to the very loading screens, where the gameplay tips often found at the bottom begin to say such things as "Can you even remember why you came here?" and "You're still a good person." to the later "If you were a better person, you wouldn't be here." making every level dredge up regret from the more sound-minded players.
Overall, Spec Ops has grown to be one of my favorite games, having already beaten it several times on another system and twice now on PC. I rather enjoyed the bitter-
story, the simple (and sometimes annoying) gameplay, and down-right misery and regret my first playthrough brought me… I don’t know, maybe I’m just a masochist. But then again, if I was a better person, I wouldn’t be here.

Almost 3 years now, but finally I'm out, i'm done with Maia for good now.

MAIA is clearly a labour of love for an indie developer. I have a lot of sympathy for that, and viewing it through that prism helps me see past some of the more glaring issues.
The game is essentially a Dungeon Keeper-style simulator set in space, where you are a administrator rather than an evil wizard overlord. You carve out rooms, place objects in said rooms, and the colonists do their thing with what you provide. The strategy is in when and where you place rooms and objects, and it's good fun.
The game is not easy at the start, particularly as the tutorial doesn't linger long on some key elements. It took me several plays just to realise some core gameplay elements, too, like the importance of having the smelter and the robot manufacturer early, as well as power and space heaters, but that may just be me. (I lost many a colonist to hypothermia. Good times.)
To my mind, given I haven't found any major game-ending bugs, the issues are with the UIX and the colonist AI.
The UI feels sluggish, which is irritating to begin with, but you do get used to it. That's not a big issue.
The colonist AI, however, is more problematic. Because there's no way of directing individual colonists, you are completely at the mercy of the AI. And it has no mercy. It will send your colonists off to do things you would consider very low priority over things that are litterally life-saving. That's a much bigger issue, as several hours of game can be ruined by a colonist taking a stroll outside while fires rage and fellow colonists suffocate.
Having said that, I still give MAIA a thumbs-up. It's a worthy endeavour that needs your support. If you like Dungeon Keeper-style games, pick it up.

I find it hard to say that I recommend this game, or even that I do not.
I was a huge fan of Freelancer, and I have spent years looking for something that could fill the hole that Freelancer left behind. While Starpoint Gemini 2 comes close, it's not... quite... there yet. This game is still in development (just recently in beta), so bear that in mind.
All of the pieces are there - free roaming, trading, space battles - however, SG2 seems to fall flat a key area - ship movement. The starting vessel, a frigate, I believe, looks like a fish, moves like a fish, but steers like a cow. Most combat is spent circling around trying to get a bead on your enemy for about 1/2 a second before they move out of view once more. By that point, his buddy has been firing lasers up your butt. I'm a space combat noob with this game, but even Freelancer felt like it had more "zip" to ship movement. I had to crank the mouse sensitivity just to feel like there was some kind of response to the controls.
Graphically, it's quite nice. Ships, planets, stations and space "stuff" is lovely to look at.
The game requires some optimization. When you are in a serious furball with many other ships, I find that the game really chugs and slows down - even if you are not involved in the combat, and it's just nearby.
The game is not multiplayer, and I am not clear on whether or not it is ever going to be multiplayer. That is also a major wall for a lot of people. Freelancer was great. Freelancer with friends was amazing.
This is not a Freelancer replacement, though it comes close. If you're not concerned about a multiplayer experience, you're not going to find a game that delivers what this one does at this price point. However, I would wait for later in the beta cycle or even for wide release. It's not quite ready for prime time.

I love Maia. I've played the game through at least 30 builds.
The good.
The game is fully playable.  Rare crashes - and for those that experience - a dev who is extremely responsive / quick to fix if it's something on his end.
It's hard.  Not least because the AI is; on occasion, still a bit screwey - but it's basically 90% baked now so it's totally workable.  The hardness is just that.  It's a hard game.  Building a colony on a remote planet with only 4 people probably would be right.
You'll die.  You'll die again.  Sometimes it will be bad luck. Sometimes it will be a gameplay mechanic you need to learn.  Sometimes it'll just be a bad spawn (you'll soon learn to recognise the good ones!)
The bad
Very little.  it's a one man dev but the progress is steady if not light speed.  But updates come regularly.  Are properly tested. There is a dev / experimental branch for those inclined.  The dev Simon is very responsive - there is a good community of loyal players who have played multiple builds and provide constructive feedback.   Why is that bad.  Well it's small and it's slow.  And like everyone of course I'm impatient.  So the bad isn't too bad at all.
Overall.
It's an early access game with a committed developer; a clear and achievable roadmap and steady progress towards a fully baked game.  At the moment it's fully playable across multiple plarforms and configs and for those rare ocassions where a new player has a hardware issue - the dev is quick to work to resolve.
A game that only got made becaues of Kickstarter and Early Access and which will benefit from your investment.  It's not 100% - I'd say a good 70% though and very playable and enjoyable.
(Steam says I've played 150 odd hours but that's a significant undeestimate. Some builds don't seem to trigger Steam's clock and streaming locally - which I do all the time - never counts towards play time.  It's probably more like 400 hours and therefore worth every penny of what I paid !)

If you are expecting Sid Meier's Pirates! you will be disappointed. While the game was inspired by it, it's nothing like the golden classic, except that it has ships. There is no Spanish Main to explore, no letters of marque to get, no treasure maps to collect, no relatives to free, no mutinies, no boarding of vessels and no swordfights.
Instead, there is nicely rendered random territories to explore. You will join a couple of factions to choose from, none of which resemble any actual states, but rather traders, warriors, etc. Choosing a faction gives you bonuses to your stats, which you can level up through experience gained from (simple and repetitious) quests and equipment you will find or buy. Since you cannot capture enemy vessels for yourself, you need to unlock and buy stronger ships as you play. You can or rather must conquer territories for your faction, either by capturing cities or colonizing land. All of this takes very very very long. If it wasn't for the fun combat, the game would be a total bore. However, the combat is solid and entertaining; even in Single Player, but you can also play it online with friends.
I don't regret buying this game, but it could have been much more. It was cheap enough though and I could idle away one hour here and one hour there, which fits my time current time budget. Plus, it plays totally fine on my Ubuntu with just an Intel HD 5000.

These games are great. The first Life is Strange is amazing. It sucked me in with it's story and developed an almost emotional bond with the characters. Playing Before the Storm was the same way, maybe not to the same degree, but very close. The first game had more disaster, emotional situations, and in general, just more touching and involved moments. This was a great sequal, but if I could go back and do it all again for the first time, I would take a day off work, turn off all the lights and block the windows, and start with Before the Storm and then play the original Life is Strange. Damn I wish I could play these for the first time again. If you're reading this and haven't played either, do what I described above. Yes it's true that no matter what you do, you always get the same ending, but this game isn't about Starting at A and how it Ends at B. This game is about all the parts inbetween A and B, how they differ with each choice you make, how they affect you and not just your character, and they all come together to the same story ending. You may not get a completely different ending based on every choice you make, but if you let yourself get sucked in, those choices you make along the way and the story that developes with it, when it ends, you're reactions and feelings and emotions are going to be completely different each time and different from any other persons. There should be more games like this, that doesn't mean just more choices matter genre games, but more story rich, heartwrenching, emotional rollercoaster games. Together, these two games are my favorite story. This is the first Shantae I played to completion. I've played a little bit of Risky's Revenge but otherwise I was going into this blind. It's a very short game, six levels in total with some goodies to find in each one. However, I do remember that two of those levels were Kickstarter stretch goals. DLC. So that would put the main game at four levels discounting those two "episodes" that may be part of the main progression but honestly they just come out of nowhere in the storyline without any semblance of transition and once they're wrapped up that's it no one mentions them again. Story was nothing to write home about either. It's your standard Goody Two Shoes vs Supreme Badness black and white plot. Shantae learns of a great threat to the Genie Realm, promptly forgets as she helps her uncle build a machine, does some other hero stuff, then oh no Genie Realm is now in danger because the villain is trying to destroy everything for some unexplained reason.
I found all the collectibles in this game, explored all the hidden areas, found all the dances, spells, items, etc. A big issue though is that the forms are either useless or only needed for one or two areas in the game then shove them in the box. There's 16 total dances (there's a damn BLOBFISH dance that does nothing) and you make use of three or four on a regular basis, mostly Monkey. There's also two that break the game open completely: Bat and Harpy. Bat lets you move horizontally as long as you don't have any obstacle. Harpy is free flight. In a platforming game this pretty much lets you cheese entire levels with some creative positioning.
My playtime clocked in at a little over 7 hours and I was taking my time. For a $20 game, though I did Kickstart it. This is a very, very, VERY short game and I honestly cannot recommend it at this price point. It doesn't feel cohesive in gameplay, story, or anything really. I'm actually disappointed I backed it. Supposedly it will eventually have a story where you play through as Risky Boots and others but they're not in yet so, what you see is what you get.

A great game for strategists. You are a commander of an army in the totally not Japan country called Japon, where they use Amasson to carry parts around.
The gameplay is simply complicated. In that I mean that it's simple that you can either send your units to attack a spot, move them, get them to reveal some map space, or do nothing. However, as simple as that looks there are a lot of factors. Different tanks excel in different areas.
The main types are "Commander", of which you need a minimum one, and if you lose all of you lose.
"Shock", which can be divided, but generally hit an area around them, but also blowing themselves up in the process.
"Recon", which can reveal large areas of map, move far but are generally bad at combat.
"Assault" which usually are destructive, but otherwise all around.
And "Artillery" which have insane range, at the cost of low mobility and speed.
Now, at the start of a round you can use any mix of tanks you've made, all of which are made to be human-like, but usually without questioning orders. As you do missions, you get resources to make more. However, if a tank dies, it's permanently dead, excluding your default tank Hishiko, as well as a few select specialty tanks (Which is an important part of the plot. Unless you're Mr. Cat. Then it's just the embodiment of evil). So managing your tanks in a way to prevent them from going down as much as possible pays off. (Ie. Better strategy always pays off more than trying to brute force things with kamikazes.)
The game itself isn't too hard, as long as you take the time to plan things out. In fact, it seems most people beat the story without a loss 99% of the time on their first playthrough. However, there are more stories to be told based on how you do missions (If you fail certain ones, specifically), so it's worth a second playthrough to find these. The characters are also very interesting, as they make you question your character's motives. Is he a good guy? Or is he right in his name of "General From Hell"?
A lack of multiplayer is a let down, especially in a game like this. Granted, it could obviously tip the scales towards a player who has more time in the game, but all the same they could have had a type of draft you could do, or had ___ resources to use to make your army.
In summary, it's a great strategy game with a great story. A lack of multiplayer is a let down, but it's easily overlooked.

Edit: Played entire series (1-8) before Steam release.
Umineko is, and always will be, the perfect mystery story to me. Don't let the fact that it's a visual novel from Japan put you off; it's not a tiddie tale. It's an undeniably thrilling magical murder mystery that, like its predecessor Higurashi, poses several questions over 4 arcs and then explains them in 4 answer arcs (known as Umineko Chiru). Compared to Higurashi though, Umineko is on a whole other league.
The story deals with mystery, murder, life & death, the occult, magic, choice, love, and even delves so deep as to deal with issues of identity amongst other things I can't mention due to spoilers. It also has some really fantastic music ranging from classical pieces to pussi-poppin' EDM(-ish) tracks.
I can't do this story justice with my words; let its own words explain why this story altered my life from the moment I first read it.
P.S. If the artstyle puts you off, try searching around for the PS3 patch (when it comes out for the Steam release), or play it with the original Ryukishi sprites.

I've been playing this game for a long time now, over the years. It's getting better, but I enjoy it for more than the gameplay. If you want to know about gameplay and the genre, etc. You may be better served reading a different review. Know that the game is early access. It is improving, with bugs being squashed, game mechanics being tweaked, and new aspects being introduced.
I became aware of slow TV via Norwegian programming. Slow TV programs run for hours sometimes even tens of hours, showing a task in its entirety, like the preparation and burning of a log fire. The programming shows the actual effort that goes into creating things. There's no montage to steal that appreciation for the real effort, which yields the result and how that effort contributes to the satisfaction in the well done job.
Maia has held my interest in a similar way. On the other hand, Maia sometimes feels like an Advent calendar. I open it up, get a treat and go away, returning when it's time to open the next box.
Observing the steady progress and effort put out by Simon Roth has made the game rich for me. I watch the pathing today and know that Simon spent significant effort to improve it. At the start of each game, I wonder how food consumption will proceed, because it's been tweaked over and over in the effort to find the right balance. I take direct control of the utility robot with its laser welder then head off to the livestock room for some culling, and anticipate the day that the oxygen draining chicken parades are no more.
Simon is a responsive developer, but is firmly set on his vision of Maia. He interacts with the community, taking ideas, offering explanations, and generally demonstrating his interest in what people have to say. If a developer version of the game goes south, I'm used to his quick action to restore the game to a playable state.
Owning Maia is contributing to a Work. What kind of Work might be up for debate, but that Simon Roth has set out to create a Work is unquestionable. Indie gaming has seen its share of failures. Developers throwing up their hands and calling whatever was in front of them "good enough". For years Simon has steadily plodded along, singlehandedly developing his concept. I applaud that effort. From the outside it's like watching concert music being composed with various movements being created in a fit of inspiration and then being worked over to complement each other. Frankly, I can't wait to see this Opus finished.
The fact is that this game has held my attention more than any other purchase I've made. Heck, I've almost invested 3 working months of time in gameplay.

This could have been the next "Sid Meier's Pirates", but you will be VERY disappointed if that's what you're looking for.  Here's just some of the problems with that expectation, as far as I can tell:
Pros:
-Linux support: The only reason (other than price) that I gave this a try at all.
-Moddable?  Supposedly this is moddable, (but it looks like nobody's actually taking advantage of it).
-Procedural world: This is actually pretty great, it'd be tiring going around the same Caribbean (which isn't terribly interesting in the first place) over and over.
Cons:
-WAY too "gamey".  Unlike Pirates, this game is full of the standard awful copy-paste MMO gimmicks.  Upgrading, "leveling", and a numbers/stats game are favored over skill and experience.  (Not saying skill is a non-factor, maybe it is to a small degree.)
-Scale: ships are just WAY too big, towns are WAY too big to the point that it's just annoying.  Pirates was stretching things here big time but this game's scale is so far off, any sense of realistic immersion is destroyed.  It sounds silly but the biggest pain so far was that due to the sheer size of ships, you're actually spending much of your time avoiding collisions with other ships!  Pretty sure that wasn't a real problem, other than during busy port navigation.
-Instances: oh god, please stop it with the MMO feature cloning.  This ties into the next issue.
-Transitions and "fast travel": By far the biggest design failure this game has to offer.  Probably due to the multiplayer requirements, but nevertheless, moving to other regions has a load screen.  Not the huge world feeling you get from Pirates or other older explorer games.  Even worse, the the transitions are almost more like "levels" than true world transitions.  A major problem with "fast travel" is that you can't just turn around and go back across the "edge" of the map, obviously, so it's another big immersion killer.
-No realism whatsoever: Does wind even matter? Not that it was truly realistic, but wind and weather mattered in Pirates, how did they screw this one up?  It doesn't seem like this was given any thought at all.
-"Casual" feel - don't know if it can be or not, but it feels dumbed down enough that it'd be playable on a tablet.  If I had realized this I would have moved on.
If you're a stupid millennial with no attention span looking for yet another MMO-like casual game with a built in treadmill, you'll love this.  But if you're looking for a modern "Sid Meier's Pirates" game with added depth and realism (as should be expected of a remake), you're going to be seriously disappointed.

Let's go ahead and get the negative stuff out of the way. Trackmania 2 had the misfortune of being split into several games, each containing only one enviornment. I can see how that might have seemed like a good move on paper (rather than buying a full-priced game, you can simply pay only for the enviornments you care for) but a lot of people in the fanbase will probably tell you that it ended up fracturing the community quite a bit. Another negative thing about the game, in my opinion, is the fact that on the singleplayer maps there's a 5 minute cooldown period in between official race attempts. TM United didn't have that; you'd just pay 10 coppers per attempt and you could do it as many times as you wanted. I'm sure the cooldown timer was introduced to stop people from spamming official attempts, but it sucks to have to wait 5 minutes to try an official race again just because you nicked the wall. This only affects the singleplayer maps though, and it only matters if you care about official races.
But this is a positive review, SO...
Hello, new racer! TrackMania is a game about getting your car to the finish line as fast as possible. Which seems kind of..."duh", because it's a racing game, but hear me out. Trackmania doesn't have car upgrades, boost meters, moving obstacles, or collision detection between you and other players. It's entirely you vs the clock, and you can't blame any of your mistakes on not having a fast enough car or getting punted into a wall by another racer. This game is entirely skill-based because everybody has an identical car with no handicaps or advantages, and there's no random or variable elements. If you didn't win that gold medal, it is purely because you didn't control your car well enough to get to the finish line in time. This alone makes TrackMania one of the most well-designed, perfectly fair, violently rage-inducing,
-tier games you'll ever play. It's great, trust me.
Coming from somebody that's put almost 100 hours into TrackMania United in less than 2 months (on a crappy laptop) I can confirm that TrackMania 2 on it's lowest settings will not only
better but also
better. The performance is buttery smooth and very consistent. There's plenty of singleplayer tracks, tons of mods for custom tracks, car models, skins, and total conversions (check out the F1 mod). There's also the super-popular multiplayer mode. Even if this game only has one enviornment and less game modes than TrackMania United, TrackMania 2 Stadium still has a wealth of content. Of all the enviornments, Stadium is probably the best-feeling one anyway (although Canyon is a lot of fun too). For the current price of $9.99, this game is a ♥♥♥♥ing great buy. If you like it, check out some of the other enviornments too. Hopefully once Lagoon releases, we'll see a TrackMania 2 United. Until then, TM2 Staduim is a great introduction to the new generation of TrackMania.

This is one of the best games I have ever played. I didn't expect to like it when I got it, but I adore it. It's probably the combination of great performance, a lively community of map makers, and great time attack multiplayer servers. Plus, since it's so cheap, I have no qualms recommending it to friends who might not have a large budget for games.
Gameplay. Let's start out with the car. There's only one car in Trackmania. There's a gas button and a brake button. You can also steer with the arrow keys or on a controller. There's not much to car mechanics, but the main variety in gameplay comes from the maps. The maps have a multitude of various doodads that switch up gameplay. There are booster pads that boost you in a certain direction, there are twisty tracks where you turn... and stuff. You can boost and ride on walls, you drive off ramps and make jumps at high speeds. There are fullspeed maps where you never let go of the gas until you make it past the finish line.
Gameplay Continued. There are LOL maps which are puzzle maps that have to be figured out. You have to learn about the more quirky mechanics of the game and utilize them to get to the finish line in the shortest time, or maybe there's just a skip that most people don't notice until it's too late. These maps are often really janky but still really fun on multiplayer servers because you can see everyone else is failing as bad as you are.
Multiplayer/Maps. Speaking of multiplayer servers, there are lots of great multiplayer servers which run custom maps made by the community. There's no need to download a giant map pack since it automatically streams it to your computer along with some custom music. There are many different kinds of multiplayer servers, but almost all of them are Time Attack. Within Time Attack, there are Fullspeed and LOL maps. There's probably others too, but I mainly play Fullspeed.
Ranking System. There's a really nice ladder points system in Trackmania that shows you your ranking worldwide and nationwide and statewide after each Time Attack map you finish. If you beat a player who is waaay ahead of you in rank, then you get a crap load of Ladder Points. It can be fun to see how much you climb. You can't ever lose points so the only way to lose ranking is by not playing. This means that every time you
play, you'll likely be a little further down in rank, but you'll also have the chance of getting more points.
Game Client. Maniaplanet is a really handy client that allows you to instantly do things conveniently with your mouse that wouldn't be otherwise possible in a normal game. For example, you can pan the cursor up to the top edge of the screen and instantly turn down the ingame volume and turn up the music volume. It's intuitive and easy. No need to alt-tab out and go into the volume mixer in Windows. Also, I know Maniaplanet looks and sounds like the evil Uplay, but I promise, it's not that bad. Whatever disadvantages it may seem to impose, it more than makes up for it by adding to the game's convenience.
Do I recommend this game? Heck yes I do. Buy this game. At base price it's only $10, and when it's on sale, it's even cheaper. It's definitely worth the price. Why? It's got tons and tons of fun, high quality community made maps, and it runs really well and is only like 1GB of space.

Over the last couple of years, the Shantae-games have become one of my favorite 2D-plattformer games. Not only did they make great use of the Metroidvania-style gameplay, but they also had very charming and memorable characters, interesting oriental-themed levels and great music. Half-Genie Hero is no exception here, I had a blast from beginning to end.
One of the problems of the older games was that the animal-transformations, one of Shantae's signature moves, take way too long and therefore hurt the pacing of the game. That problem has been totally fixed here, so playing through each of the very well designed levels feels totally fluid.
I was a bit worried about the new graphic-style of the game, but after playing it for a while, it became totally natural to the point where it was actually hard to go back to the older games with their pixel-graphic. The soundtrack is also amazing, there's a lot of catchy tunes that fit the theme of the levels perfectly.
However, there's still a few minor things I didn't enjoy. Firstly, the game got rid of any dungeons, which makes each level feel much more linear. Secondly, the story felt very disconnected. Each level basically had a mini-arc, but they weren't really connected in any way so the overall arc felt way too basic and undeveloped. And thirdly, there's really not a lot of levels here, namely 6 in total. And 2 out of these 6 levels were only included because certain Kickstarter-stretchgoals were met, which means the game was originally planned to only have 4 levels. Granted, all these levels are very big and you visit them multiple times to unlock new areas, but still. I hope the upcoming DLC will expand these levels in some way.
Despite all these minor gripes, I still had a lot of fun with the game, and I can encourage everyone to try it. All the Shantae-games are underrated gems that should really get more love.

Okay, there is already tons of reviews out there for this game. Most good, others...not so good and unhelpful.
When I first played this game, I was pretty much confused at first as I assumed (incorrectly) that it was turn based or something. That thought went away the moment I lost my first unit when I was trying to figure out what I was supposed to do from a shock-unit blowing her up.

I'm a long time fan of the Fire Emblem series, as well as the Final Fantasy Tactics series. I'm one of those people who'll get mad and reset whenever someone dies. In my fantasy wars, my army destroys it's enemies mercilessly without any casualties.
This game did some bad things to me.
One of the first units they gave me blew herself up all in the hopes of taking a few enemies with her. I reached out, a soft no escaping my lips before her final warcry, a deafening explosion, and a heavy silence.
War of the Human Tanks is a comedy game of give and take, managing your expendable human pawns in an effort to make sure the enemy loses more expendable human pawns. It's brilliant. I expected this game to start preaching at me about war and death and the value of life and it never did, because the game recognized that those things are probably common sense, and instead we could have light-hearted, yet dark humor develop interesting characters. I got the game to slake my thirst for grid based tactical combat, and also received a surprisingly deep narrative along with it.
The most notable feature of the combat is that it takes place in real time, with your light, kamikaze units often being the quickest, and your heavy, blow them up from a distance units being a bit more sluggish. The game uses fog of war to keep you on your feet and a wrong step into enemy territory is certain death. Not for you, but sometimes you feel pretty bad when your terrible decision making gets your innocently little scout shot to pieces.
Most units die with only one hit, but units that are larger-and thus also easier targets- must be hit in each of their segments before they die.
If I had to complain about anything, it's that once you get certain units you're basically an untouchable god of death. When you can literally bombard an entire half of the map with just one unit, you're probably not going to lose any fights. But then getting to that point is rewarding the first time you actually get to do it, but that said, the challenge maps usually laugh at simplistic strategies like that and send you straight to hell. Well, not you, so much as your pawn tanks, but still.
Pros- Hillarious, surprisingly interesting narrative, combat is simple enough to pick up quickly and deep enough to stay interesting for the long haul.
Cons- Some of the sound effects (mostly death cries) get annoying pretty quickly, not too hard to get over-powered, and I wish there was a competitive multiplayer mode, even if it was just local.
5/5
As a final note, this game has a demo, so there's no reason not to at least give it a try.

I am the General from Hell, Shanon'ei or something. Even though I am pretty uninteresting except for being very good at anime, games and being lazy, my ability to be serious for a few minutes and not act careless to my soldiers has made me the perfect anime protagonist for every girl I come across to either want me or to pretend not to want me.

The game becomes a game of hide and seek where the first people to find the other gets the kill. It's turned based, but also works in real time, so you wander out and hang about for a few minutes while people walk up to you and shoot you in the face. If you're lucky, the person next to you may decide to shoot them first, or they may just watch you die in an explosion with joy.
Basically, stick your Command Tank in the back of the field, and then begin a thorough carpet bombing of the area with your insanely overpowered tanks. If you're not quite over-powered enough, you can grind, but honestly, the game throws resources at you that you'll not fall behind the power curve. Occasionally, the game will mix it up, but eventually you'll discover that nothing is as good as area of effect attacks, since they have all the benefits of a single shot but all the benefits of levelling a quarter of the stage in a single shot, killing everything that you may or may not have known is there.
You have suicide units... in a game which limits how many tanks you can take. A one-use unit, or a tank which can flatten a street is your choice. I think I may have the suicide unit twice in the game. As they ran up the enemy, they were shot. Huh.
It's a pretty fun game, you can run it in a window and listen to a podcast (I like to think this was the equivalent of me in the game basically saying "Time to win this war... Satou, have the entire army bomb the crap out of the enemy. I'll be here fiddling with my iPod and listening to Queen. Let me know if something happens). This is not a bad side; it's engaging enough and quick enough that you can fit it in between sessions or a lunch break or during a Skype conversation where the Internet keeps breaking.
As for the story, well, there is a Royal Army and an Imperial Army in a land of Japon, not Japan, Japon. The two armies are effectively indistinguishable, you fight them because... well, they're on the other side of the battlefield and that's the point of the game. There seems to be some kind of underlying conversation about whether or not a Human Tank is actually worth treating well, but it's hard to tell a deep conversation while you're also have a little power fantasy and then your Command Tank walks in and it's funny because she is stupid or something.
Oh, the whole Human Tanks thing? Basically, tanks don't work anymore, so they decided to make anime girls fight each other with weapons and call them tanks, a slight lobotomy to reduce initiative and then a tendency to explode if someone looks at them; later you can get tanks that require to be hit in four places to die, and as long as you bomb the enemy first, most of them should make it through.
It's a nice little game, and I had fun, and that's enough. I'd say £5 or whatever heathen money you use is definitely worth getting it. It has a New Game Plus and alternative endings, but the gameplay isn't THAT good and neither is the story. But it is solid and the anime is nice, and it doesn't have any bloody panty-shots, so it's the good kind of anime, not the kind that governments seem to be trying to outlaw recently.

This game is now quite complex and avanced and I'd recommend it to anyone enjoying administering a colony on a foreign planet. Nevetheless, I'd like to point out that I used the world "administering" and not "ruling", for example.
Indeed, it's not a "god game", your role is to give the priorities of the station through make/build/repair/expand/research commands. However, the game has a built-in life simulation, which means your colonist need to eat/sleep/socialise and also to take care of your base (repairing, handling food growth, food making, dealing with water supplies, etc.). An excellent and original idea that completely fails in execution.
Unfortunately, I can only give limited gameplay reviews, as the engine and various other failings have hindered my access to the actual game.
First and foremost: Fullscreen mode scaled to screen size! How can I emphasize this enough? Every game scales the screen size to the edges of the monitor, and adjusts its resolution within these limits. But not Maia... Heaven help you if you toggle fullscreen, as the menu, along with 75% of the game's interface, will be shoved out of your view, leaving you to desperately try to find a way to get it back. But why would you need fullscreen in the first place? It is a convenience, truly, but I enjoy being able to scroll my view down in the game, a luxury that is denied for those of you who cannot properly scale the game's interface on full screen.
NOTE: I may retract this portion of my review in the event that I purchase a 5 foot screen.
Second, optomization. For the love of all that is holy, optomize this game! My top-of-the-line computer should not be choking or lagging the instant I activate 2X antialiasing. And to add on to that thought, why am I forced to ramp up the graphics settings in order to get back to "none"? Another seemingly nit-picky feature that has ended me in a CTD because I had to go up to maximum antialiasing to get to none. The game panicked at what appeared to be a demand for unreasonable graphics and immediately jumped off of a bridge. So perhaps the ability to simply select lower graphics settings without testing the strain on your engine?
Third, and I know I'm going to get crapped on for this, fix the OS X port! Yes, I became so frustrated trying to make this game work on windows that I resorted to an iMac to come from another angle. I know the saying "nobody games on a mac" and apparently, the development team here has taken that to heart. Their OS X version of this game doesn't even finish loading the main screen before crashing into a heaping pile of wasted code. If you're going to sell a product for a different platform, so help me God, it is on you to make sure that it at least works! Anything less, is theft, plain and simple.
Fourth, the AI needs some serious love. For the time I was able to play, my colonists watched as two atmosphere generators broke down and a third caught on fire. They started crying instead of worrying that the air was going to run out if they didn't jump to action. Two of them chose to starve to death instead of going to eat, and a second one kept sleeping, rather than do her job. Yes, I'm talking about you, K. Smith, you lazy freeloader! Nobody wanted you in this colony anyway!
TL;DR,
Don't buy this game until they fix their graphical interface to something actually usable. Don't buy this game until the AI is less pathetic. And DON'T BUY THIS GAME IF YOU OWN A MAC!! (Unless you don't like having money and want someone to take it from you. And even then, there's better ways than to give to these people.)

This racing game has been around for nearly a decade, connecting racing fans from all around the world in a giant competition. There's not much to say, as the game is self explanatory. Prove yourself to be worthy and out race your opponents as they eat your dust, but watch out for that wall, or that hole in the floor, and that jump, and OH CRA-

The graphics in this game also hold up pretty well from 2013 to 2016 with good lighting effects and nice looking cars. The multiplayer in this game is also addicting while you continue to race many community maps to become the number 1 racer in your area. So over all this game is great fun, and you can expect to get many hours of racing out of this cheap 10 dollar game.

Ordinarily, i am not one for games taking place in the age of sails, let alone, shipgames. The Total War series had it somewhat right, but they lack the singular control which i savor a lot.
Those who know me, knows that I am quite fond of vehicular engagement in games. But for this once, I made the exception, mainly because I have a past with roleplaying and doing combat in SL, specifically in the same era as this game. So I thought; why not give it a shot?
I've been playing it on and off, and I've come to realize that Windward not only is a game reminding me about my old days where I played Overboard (The game is ancient and has graphics on the level of pre-FF7), but it struck me as being a highly amusing and semiinteractive game, both with the AI and if you invite friends along.
It is a defining game of its kind. Throw at me whatever you like of remarks about other games of this era or style, but it most likely wont get more than a snicker from me. It's hard to get me hooked on a game to this extent, and windward performed to a most satisfying degree.
The music is amazingly fitting (Albeit a bit repetitive when you've been junking the game for about five to six hours straight), the graphics are wonderful. The lighting, the shading, the details, the way the effects look with weapons firing, all adds up to create a nostalgic, entertaining mood.
The way the game handles, is simple; and even more simple when adding macros (Which are disgustingly simple to set up in-game). A brief introduction to basic naval tactics and you're set for combat. Navigation is amusing in the procedually created world. Want to do trading? Go for it! Wanna do diplomacy? Go for it! Fight pirates because you're a pirate! Ship customization for colors, crews, accessories, weapons, various sizes of ships, each with their perks for speed, defense and capacity.
If you want an entertaining game which is simple to get into, amusing to play and most efficient at Co-op, Windward is the game for you. It's a real hook.
... Oh did I forget you get to throw barrels at the enemy? ... well you can!

I don't typically write reviews, but Rogue Legacy for me is going to be an exception. Ill start off with the pros and cons and then give some of my final thoughts.
But first, I just logged into the game to play one run through and HOLY CRAP I BEAT THE GAME! Finally!!
Pros:
+Fast paced, hack and slash, dungeon crawl
+Simple mob combat
+Very fun spells
+Strategic and challenging boss fights
+After you defeat a boss, the door unlocks so you can do a unique challenge fight
+RPG elements (item upgrades, rune upgrades, castle upgrades)
+Very wide character variety
+Deaths bring you a selection from three random characters
+Randomized character traits
+Randomized levels after each death
+Quirky and a fun story line
+Weight - Yes, weight. It brings a special element and challenge. You can't just unlock the best gear and wear it. You have to make sure your character upgrades accordingly.
+Difficulty starts at a standard. You can control it by adding runes, which I've found also gives you new and unseen levels to the dungeon
+168 hours played and I just beat the final boss. I still have so many upgrades and blue prints to find.
+In that, extremely high replay value
Cons:
-Finding later tier (tier 4 and 5) gear is very difficult
-Once you unlock enough upgrades to your castle, the grind can feel tedious. This doesn't happen for a very long time, though.
-There are very annoying occurances at times due to bridge placement. I.E. when trying to escape a level by jumping up to a bridge and activating it, only to have the hit cause your character to fly into the upper room and then back to the lower room. Causing it to reset. I'm not sure if this is meant to be a challenge to the player or just poor placement.
This game will always be a favorite of mine. The control you have to either farm for gold or challenge yourself to get blueprints for gear, is amazing. I find it really fun to have a choice of random characters and I love all of the unique traits they can come with. Whether you are looking for a dungeon crawl to play casually, or challenge yourself with hardcore settings, this game can fit anyone's arsenal of games.
5/5

I really wanted to like this game, but it has been an incredibly buggy experience. Ignorning the fact that the game can sometimes quit without warning (everytime you agree to listen to the music your colonist has created.), the game isn't really in a stage where it is actually playable - as far as I can tell - the colonists will just stop collecting the smelted metal and you won't have any building materials to build anything, or they just won't build. So your colonists are pretty much doomed to starvation, or hypothermia or death due to fatigue as they won't do any of the things you want them to do.
You also can't really react to all the emergencies and warnings that you are given because they will simply keep warning you of low temperatures at a certain room but since the colonists won't build the heaters you asked them to, they will freeze to death.
It's an interesting simulation but pretty repetitive. I see that the creator has been working on a ton of new features but I think he should probably work on polishing the AI till the game doesn't just end in failure each time. I haven't actually gotten far enough to enjoy the new features (or even the research lab) because the colonists just keep dying and refusing to build anything.

I ended up reversing my first review. My initial complaint was about the lack of feedback. This still holds true at the start of the game! If you can keep your colony alive past the first few desperate days the game does become more intuitive. At that point I found the game much more entertaining. You now must play a balancing game, "Do I risk sending colonists outside during a meteor swarm to build more power generation, or can I risk a loss of power?" I do like the unique feedback system that comes in hints in the Emails sent by your colonists. I see a lot of potential for this game.
But! The reason why I originally did not recommend this game is still there. The first few days of the game are still a black box, with only one path forward to survive. I hypothesize that the difference between life or death can measured in how many steps the colonists must take to get between rooms. That’s harsh for the first few minutes of the game! In the end I never did solve this initial hurdle, but had to watch and copy the developer’s video blog.
So, welcome to Maia, a death world where the Reaper is breathing down your neck!
P.S. And, remember it is still in Alpha.

Fantastic fun, interesting story with many twists and several endings, engaging gameplay that demands strategic thinking and an incredible soundtrack throughout.
The game's story is told through visual novel format, which sets the state of affairs and the stage for the battle to follow. Battles are fought in real-time, but with a sort of turn-based system that runs on ticks, for example after giving a unit orders to move you must then wait for it to radio in asking for new orders before it can be moved again. Battlefields are presented as a grid of octagons, and before the round commences you must first place your units as in Battleships. Each unit has it's own special properties and characteristics similar to chess, for example some may move 2 spaces at a time whereas others may only move 1, or one unit might only be able to attack horizontally whereas others must attack at least 2 spaces ahead of itself. The aim of each battle is to eliminate the opponent's 'Command Tank' before they destroy yours which, regardless of how many units they have remaining, wins you the battle. The battlefield is covered by a shroud as seen in most real-time strategies with sight range varying between your different units, so early game tactics may usually consist of Battleships-esque artillery strikes into the dark hoping you'll hit something, as your units gradually advance closer to the enemy, thinning out their ranks until their command tank is within firing range.
Very nice little strategy game, with several challenging achievements to really push your tactical prowess.
I also throughly recommend purchasing the unbelievably extensive soundtrack, 91 tracks with a runtime of exactly 3:32:23. Three and a half hours of various funk, electronica, pop, rock and other genre-bending music that's really worth a listen if you're a true connoisseur of music.

No. There's no humans inside tanks in this game. Instead tanks in this game are just a term for...erm...female robots? That's all I can gather on what tanks are XD
Being serious now, the game itself is a fun little strategy game which concepts from (from my experience) Risk, Battleship, bit of Checkers, and a bit of Chess. Just to recap so you're not reading paragraph after paragraph of rambling, here's the good bits:
- The game board itself relies on a mix of RTS mapstyle, Tetris, and a bit of turned base gameplay. For the RTS style everything on the map except your spawn point is hidden and won't be revealed unless if your ally gets shot by a nearby enemy or you recon the area revealing that bit for a little while (this goes same with the AI in the game, don't mistaken them shooting randomly as an AI fault, they're just as blind as you). Your units also have a timer on them in which they can CONNECT and start moving, so the board does rely on real time to get things going. Usually the heaviest armed unit moves last, and the most mobile unit moves first. This goes same with the enemy, and make sure you plan your moves carefully because if you switch out of an unused unit, it does count as your turn. As for the Tetris bit I mentioned, without spoiling anything in the game, some units take up more space than others, which restricts the number of units you can place on the battlefield. The bigger the better, but that means less tanks to spare, so plan wisely.
- The AI is suprisingly good. More than often I find myself being shot by an unknown assailant on the map which forces me to plan more strategically and carefully. They will use their recon units to scope you out, which won't show up on your map as being spotted. Same goes with the AI, if you recon them, chances are you have the upperhand and they can't see you. AIs will use their units as they are meant to be, usually sending fast units in first to cushion up your army for their heavier units in the back.
- Unit development, assembly, and earning money for units to develop and build is great. Every upgrade has a better trait than the last. Small complaint: I do find myself grinding a bit for better units to beat the next chapter. Losing doesn't affect you for most of the game but I'd rather keep winning ^^
- The storyline is great. Not expecting golden novel material here since I'm just a casual gamer, but I find the dialogue to be pretty well done. It looks as if the writing was edited after translation so I appreciate the effort put into this.
- The music is great. I'm loving the variety of songs available in this game.
- Controls are really simple. It's mostly a point and click kinda game so you won't need to bind lots of keys to make the game work.
- Preformance of the game is great, since this is an indie game based on board game-like mechanics it doesn't require the highest build out there to run. I would argue that this could run on any computer just fine :D
Just a few bits I wanna discuss about:
- I find the noise of gunfire and explosions to be too excessively used in the dialogue sections of the game as well as the screen shaking effect. Expect lots of shaking and loud noises when you're going through these scenes.
- This game will deter people who just wanna play the game and enjoy the story but on a limited time. The dialogue sections themselves are worth a full chapter of a novel (if you take your time) in real time to read and understand for most of the time. Just a head warning: if you get the game, hope you like reading because there is lots of it.
- Music can get pretty obnoxious at times especially during the cutscenes, thankfully there's a full on custom sound tool that allows you to turn it off when it needs to be off.
- This game has an ongoing morbid humour of treating tanks (I wanna call them androids) like expendibles. If you're not into that kind of thing then you can just skip the cutscenes if you want (the game has that option).
- The AI can be predictable since spawns are set and not randomized. If you're the type to play this game for hours on the same map, expect to see a pattern on how the AI behaves and where they spawn. No this doesn't mean they become ENTIRELY predictable, I had that mistake happen to me once on the same map on the 11th playthrough and had three of my tanks destroyed by a sniper, which never happened in the past games.
All in all, it's a fun little game to play. Looking forward to seeing what they'll add in the future (on their site they said they're planning to add more content). Have fun!

*WOW*
Space sims have almost disappeared as a genre over the last 15 years or so, but this is the most promising one I've play since X-3.  Having been disappointed by the original Starpoint Gemini, this mere Alpha of Starpoint Gemini 2 really blew me away.  The dev comment "hugely improved sequel" is very much an understatement.  I barely got my feet wet, but this game is literally a decade ahead of its amateurish predecessor.
Forget all the wrongs of the original Starpoint Gemini (or just forget that game entirely), SG2 fixes all the terrible compromises it made:
1. No longer locked a 2-D plane, you have full six degrees of freedom.  As the developer blurb says "everything now is in 3D!"  *shock, horror*
2. No wierd incremental steering. (I guess you have to play the original to understand this one.)  As I said earlier, full six degrees of freedom.  Pitch, yaw, and roll to your heart's delight.  There's even a toggle to steer with you mouse for more precision dogfighting.
3. No amateur voice actors reading non-native English scripts.  Not a lot of voice acting in the alpha, but what it did have was professionally polished.
4. No hideous 2002-era low poly character renders.  Hand-drawn 2D portraits FTW!
In general, the production values are up to what you'd expect from a modern game.  Those screeenshots don't lie, it really does look that good in-game.  The soundtrack and sound design is also very well done.  The UI is beautiful, handles well, and very user friendly.
It's still alpha, so there some key content missing (mainly the campaign, and the the trade system is very under-developed), but so far this looks like the first promising successor to the Elite/Privateer/Freelancer legacy in years.

I originally downloaded this game as a meme to pass the time while waiting for something else to download. Turns out I liked this game way more and it even made me go and buy the previous installment "Shantae and the Pirates Curse" as well
Pros:
-Fun, satisfying combat
-Genuinely likeable characters and funny dialogue
-Excellent HD Graphics
-All the levels and enemies associated with them are unique, no reskin & repeat mobs
-With the upcoming DLC, you can play as Risky Boots, the main antagonist as well as all of Shantae's friends
-Plenty of collectibles to keep you busy, there's always something you need to do and you rarely, if ever, get lost
-Several combat options ranging from Shantae's signature hair whip, to powerful magic spells
-The transformations are all really cool, even the bat has it's uses especially if you're speed running
-Absolute god-tier soundtrack
Cons:
-The game is short, like, 6-9 hours short
-You have to backtrack frequently to previous levels after acquiring new abilities in order to get stuff you couldn't before
Things You Need To Decide For Yourself Whether Or Not They Are Pros Or Cons:
-Unless you play Hardcore mode, the game is pretty easy and healing items are abundant
-There's a near end game item that gives you infinite magic which you can pair with an invincibility spell and become literally unkillable
-Similar to The Pirate's Curse, there's a somewhat large jump in difficulty between the rest of the game and the final platforming level.
-Some people complained about backer exclusive kickstarter rewards, however I personally found that they weren't that special and missing out on them doesn't detract from the game in the slightest
-All you miss out on are two color palette swaps, one for Shantae and one for Risky, a sword reskin for Risky Boots, and the tinker bat transformation, which honestly, isn't all that useful
Verdict?
Great, low stress game with good replay value, entertaining characters and interactions as well as fun combat. 9/10 would recommend

pros

cons

game could have similar length and greater depth by combining usage of multiple powers in puzzles and removing
the more useless powers

slide perfectly or start it completely over. These segments strip away the core mechanics of the game for a
lackluster spectacle segment

Now is this game good? Absolutely, but you know what else is good? Pirate's curse and compared to that game, half-genie hero Is a pretty big downgrade. Quickly stating the positive, the gameplay is still relatively nice, the writing is still dumb in a good way and the new visuals are beautiful. After that it's just a downhill slide, mostly because after the pirate equipment in pirate's curse this game returns to the animal transformations. (Spoilers: they still suck) not only are the transformations slower and pace breaking compared to the pirate equipment they're also useless for the most part. Apart from the Harpy, mermaid, monkey and maybe the elephant the transformations are either trophy fodder or just plain worthless and it feels so boring and sluggish when you have to constantly alter between different forms. The game also has the usual problem of unnecessary backtracking which is an issue in every game in the series but in here it's worse. The game is also pretty damn easy and you can quickly get pretty OP items, only for the game to give you a large difficulty spike in the final level because that's fun. And the final boss...jeez. the pirate master was an amazing final boss and was very challenging. This games final boss is a joke if anything, just like every other boss in this game.
Now I'll say this again, half-genie hero is a good game. Nothing special but I enjoyed it a little bit. It's better than the first game and Risky's revenge (not saying that's exactly impressive) but Pirate's curse is pretty much the only truly great game in the series. I wanted to be part of the early access for ONI and see it evolve but the game is already quite fun, deep and fulfilling for dozens of hours. You have to manage some dumb and clumsy inhabitants that are more like big babies, and create life-support systems for them.
It's really interesting the way you can interlock these systems and manage elements of physics and chemistry. Liquids have surface tension (so for example shallow water trickles down along tiles rather than freefall, gases have thermodynamics, CO2 falls in the basement pockets, oxygen floats above it, lots of resources can be transformed in a chain of recycling waste from one system into another. ONI keeps throwing problems and each solution creates a new problem in the long term (in atmosphere balance, in resource or power consumption or infrastructural risk).
For what it's worth, ONI also made me appreciate more some basic life commodities like clean water or food, and think about how many systems must run behind them.

Original Review(0.61):
It's not often I write reviews, particularly negative ones, generally speaking it's not worth the effort but for Maia I will make an exception. I bought Maia a number of years ago and no, I'm not upset by the lack of progress, the issue here is I have yet to get to find out how much is even possible within the game. I cant get past the first few days, despite following the quick-start guide to the letter. Everyone that makes suggestions as to what to do to progress makes the assumption that if I issue an order to my colonists, they will actually do it. Unfortunately they are so abominably stupid that nothing ever gets done. The first few things take an incredibly long time but do eventually get done. My first workshop, Table, Drill and so on. I build a smelter and an atmosphere generator and mine minerals and what have you but that's about as far as I get. I'll write the issues I have in a list format.
Colonists stop building stuff. I'll have building materials lining the walls in the storage room and they will do nothing at all. Occasionally they may fiddle with the table for a bit before continuing their exercise in inadequacy.
Colonists are stupid to the point of having four rooms to stand in, three of which are a comfortable temperature with a dedicated atmosphere generator in each one, they will choose to stand in the empty room that is cold enough to give them hypothermia even though it is unfurnished and has a construction order in it for stuff that they will not build.
Certain objects the colonists never build. I've tried queueing up vents, space heaters etc, which never get done even if there is only a single order given at that moment, there is plenty of material and they are all walking around faffing about.
On the rare occasion where a colonist decides to actually do something (it's generally not what I wanted them to do) it takes so abominably long for them to get it done that it's barely worth doing at all.
I tried extremely hard to like Maia, I really did but my god, I've never had a game make me so damn angry at the idiocy on display by the colonists.
I'll delete this review if the issues are fixed or I am proven wrong.
Edit: I've given it another few hours and frankly I think I was too generous the first time around. People just start dying within the first two days for stupid reasons. Starving with plenty of food, dehydration despite hundreds of litres of water, freezing to death despite having warm rooms to stand in. Broken and buggy mess. I still want to like it but there are some ridiculous design decisions here even past the extremely "early access" colonist AI. Why do walls not connect with the stone? That's just needlessly wasted space. Why do colonists run two steps then stop then run two steps then stop?

It seems this game doesn't do a good job of showing what it is/is not.
Maia *is not* a game where you can micro-manage people, fiddle with spreadsheets and build queues.
Maia *is* a game where you try to build a base with (and for) a bunch of colonists that will allow them to survive on a hostile alien world. The colonists handle (most) prioritisation of tasks, they handle what they will and will not build, they handle most of their needs; the game is working out what rooms or equipment they need to fulfill those needs and explore the world they have landed on, without dying.
The lack of build queues is not a bug, the lack of spreadsheets containing task prioritisations and other ways to fiddle is not a bug. The developer has (rightly) decided these things exist in other games to patch over bad AI and we have just normalised them. In software development these things are called 'leaky abstractions' and are not desirable.
It's been a long, hard slog to get the AI to the point where it works properly (AI is hard, BTW) and doesn't eventually do something dumb and kill itself, but with 0.61 I think we're at the point where it works pretty well.
The one big minus with this game seems to be usability: the game doesn't show the player what it is (note: I don't use the word 'explain' here), meaning users have the expectation of spreadsheets and tweaking, and the build menus are cumbersome and slow to use.
Maia is also working great for me on Linux (AMD/Mesa drivers). Simon Roth also is an alright bloke who's genuinely dedicated to finishing his game.

I want to recommend this game but right now it has a few fundamental problems that need to be addressed. The good thing is that they are all problems that can be fixed.
The main issues are kind of tied together, the lack of visual feedback and the clunky interface.
To give you a basic example, when you start a game there are a few tasks that need to be dealt with right way, get a power supply going and get heat and atmosphere generating up and running. So you go to slap down some wind turbines outside and a atmosphere generator inside. The first problem comes when you have to actually pick those things from the menu, instead of having menus that you pick things from you instead have to cycle through every buildable object(a list which changes depending on what room the mouse cursor is over.) to get to the one you need. It is clunky and is the kind of design choice that seems super streamlines and easy on paper but in actual fact is far less efficient than just having a menu of items. Take Prison Architect, if I want to build something it is only two clicks away (One to open the menu, another to select the object) but here it can be anywhere between 1 to 10 clicks to get the thing I want.
The other problem is the lack of visual feedback on things. I like that you get emails from the people on base, they are well written and honestly help to bring the game to life. The main problem again comes back to building things, if we continue that previous example we have placed down all the things that need to be built. Now all I can do is wait for the stuff to get built. I cannot set priorities on things and there is not a job list so I can see what is going to be getting done next. This could be solved with some kind of way to tell if a job is quede, someone is moving to work on it or they are actually working on it.
It is hard to explain how frustrating it is to watch people wander around, freezing to death because none of them will just go outside and build the bloody wind turbine so they have some power. It may be that there is a reason they are not going outside but I am not seeing it. If it is something that is buried in the emails that they send then that is a problem. the emails are fun but they are also too long, you cannot just skim them to get the gist of something, you have to stop and spend time reading them and when there are other things pressing on you that is really not something you should be doing.
I really want this game to get better, as I said at the top, none of the problems the game has are beyond saving. Unlike other EA games there are no fundamental problems with the game that could only be fixed by starting from scratch. The foundations of the game are solid and it has a charming sense of humour that makes me want to stick with it but it needs some basic work.
I hope to revisit this review down the road and change my verdict.
