Although I never actually got to play the original TrackMania or its successor "Sunrise" for any part, I regard Stadium as one of the best TrackMania games in the series. Essentially, this game is an arcade racer where you compete against the clock to see who can get the fastest time around the track. However there is a twist, if you're playing online, then be prepared to compete against 50 other people who are trying to do the same thing as you!
Not really... You'll need a Maniaplanet account to play online, unless you're just interested in playing the game offline, then you won't need an account at all, but I highly recommend that you make an account.
Absolutely limitless! So you can create tracks in the track builder and then share them to the Steam Workshop, or share them to the ManiaExchange website which is the biggest collective of user-created tracks. As well as this, you can create skins for your cars, which includes colours and paint-jobs for the stadium car, as well as entirely different models for your car.
Nope. There are a lot of user-implemented modes in this game. Some great examples are NASCAR, (you drive around ovals at break-neck speeds) RPG (which is essentially a very large track that can take from 5 minutes to an hour to complete) and the likes of other fantastic modes!
In my opinion, the online community is the best part of the game. Back in the day, I used to play this game religiously and made loads of friends on the LOLMAPS server. (if you play on there a lot, what up it's Mumbles!) There's also an e-Gaming community behind this game, so if you think you're pretty good at this game, you can crank it up a notch and compete against the REAL good players.
Yes I do! If you manage to pick it up on the cheap, then even better! I also recommend trying out Canyon, Valley, Turbo and United Forever if you liked this game.

The game is about to enter Beta.  As it stands, the game is not only playable, it's stable and fun!
Everyone compares the game to Freelancer, which makes a lot of sense.  The input for flying is similiar with mouse and keyboard.  But I like the fact that you captain a capital ship instead of flying a starfighter.  Even smaller ships (like the Destroyer you start out with in the Alpha) have a sense of weight and inertia in their movements.
It's a fun game, with a slower, more deliberate pacing than a starfighter game.  There's time to decide your own fate while being pounded on by your opponents.  You end up feeling like the captain of a tall ship at sea.  Which means they must have done something right.
There's no campaign yet, but sandbox offers a complete game in and of itself.  It's a career mode, so there is persistent progression, kind of like a campaign might have.  There are tons of ships to buy, and plenty of missions to run.  Or you can run around getting into trouble, and you'll progress just as fast.
So far, I haven't needed anything that isn't implemented yet.  In fact, the only things I've actually missed up till now are the jumpdrive (T-drive) and cloak.  Other than that, nothing
like it's missing.
It's well polished at this stage, which makes sense since it's one week from Beta.  The graphics and UI look slick.  Anything that's actually implemented at this stage is almost always bug-free.  The game is very stable, too.  I don't think it's crashed once on me.
This is March of 2014, and as it stands the game provides a satisfying experience to play repeatedly.  It is on sale till the 17th, but will have a price hike immediately afterwards as it goes into Beta.  Also, buying it before Beta will give you 1 free copy of the original game.  A fun tide-me-over till this game is complete.

An odd but great doujin game by Yakiniku Banzai! or Yakiniku Oh! Yeah!
Basically, a full scale war breaks out in Japon between the Imperial Army of the Empire and the Royal Army of the Kingdom. The primary weapons of war are artificially created beings called Human Tanks who are designed for the sole purpose of dying and combat. They are treated as weapons and have no humane rights whatsoever. You play as the laid back general of the Empire, Shoutaro Daihon'ei, as you push the overwhelming Royal Army away and strike back.
The game flows and plays very similar to the Super Robot Taisen series and most of the Strategic RPGs (SRPG) out there including Fire Emblem, Advance Wars and FFTactics. That is, you start with the story full of dialogues then you get into gameplay then the aftermath with more dialogues then finally an intermission; rinse and repeat. Unlike such Strategic RPGs however, its gameplay is in Real-Time. You can only move your tanks if you have established a connection with them or when "Connect" shows up. This means that you'll need to be on high alert AT ALL TIMES, making the game feel intense than other SRPGs. The game does tell you what you can do in the game and what to do, but certain crucial tips such as modules don't happen until slightly later so I highly recommend doing trial and error as you play. Futher, almost every tank dies in one hit; The only tanks that take a few hits are the "big ones" that take up more than one square; much like battleship. The object of the game is to either take out the enemy's command tanks, much like the king in chess, or achieve dominace on the battlefield, forcing them to retreat.
During Intermission, you may develop stronger tanks, purchase new ones, or enter a free battle on maps you've fought on. Playing through free battles for funding or crates is somewhat a grindfest and the enemy does little to change its tatics. However, I encourage you to play the free battles a lot it allows you to try many combinations of tanks that you should've used, experiment with new tanks, and find the most effective tactics that nets you a strong victory without casualties. It feels very rewarding when farming enough crates to start building tanks that are equipped with ridiculously powerful weapons enough to annihilate half of the playfield or tanks with a beacon that allows satellite cannons to fire and wipe out everything in its sight. Try not to point these to your allies though!
The graphics in this game are between decent to quite good, depending on people's tastes. Nevertheless, its charm is undeniable. However, there is a heavy lack of diversity between tank models. Asahi and Tsubasa for example have identical appearance but one hits a single square while the other does a twin rifle salvo hitting 1 square further around. Tanks that have large equipments on their backs are an exception. It would be slightly better if they were given different hair color or accessories.
The music in this game are mostly techno, funk, rock, and hip-hop. However, they are very catchy and fit incredibly well in every situation in the game; The custom theme heard while deploying your tanks sums up the overall themes and oddities of the Human Tanks in general. Unique to this game from other SRPGs and even most visual novels is the anime openings and endings between each chapter in the story or episode. Not many may like these videos however due to its seemingly bland vocals and animation. I feel that its presentation is intentional however and the vocals reminds me of the vocals of most anime openings and jpop of the mid 80's to the early 90's which I am quite fond of.
War on the Human Tanks is a simple yet addictive game but first impressions on the game and its overall presentation depends on people's niche and taste.  That aside, I dare you to beat the first map in free battle with just Heshiko or only shock tanks!
What else? Oh yeah! When playing this game, beware the Cat!

The latest, and second-best, entry into the Shantae series. A competent platformer full of fun characters, humor, and music along with an absolutely adorable art style, I can definitely recommend Half-Genie Hero, along with the rest of the series... especially Pirate's Curse.
The gameplay is a level-based platformer with some seemingly token Metroidvania aspects, but continues the Shantae series's trend of moving away from a "true" Metroidvania style. Instead of complex levels as seen in previous titles, levels are now standard left-to-right platforming stages where you move through 2-3 areas and end with a boss. Metroidvania aspects come in when you have to repeat levels with new lock-and-key transformations (and unlockable powers for them) to find 'hidden' areas to collect collectibles for various NPCs or new abilities. This leads to the gameplay "loop" of doing a few new levels, getting to a plot roadblock, and backtracking to solve it.
The world of Shantae does, however, make up its merely good-but-not-great gameplay. It's hard to not have fun in the colorful world filled with its genuinely likeable characters, humor, and music. As a entry-point into the series, you meet most, if not all, of the series's cast of characters and the humor isn't too reliant on referential in-jokes.
Perhaps the most disappointing thing I can say about the game was the fact it was a Kickstarter game with more ideas than they hit stretch goals for, and it shows. This game is pretty amazing, defining of the rogue-like genre and packed with hours of fun. Raiding the castle is its strong suite, and you'll go through the randomly generated castle rooms time and time again and have a blast doing so. The main bosses are fun, excluding the final battle, and the optional end-game bosses. The issue with the final bosses final form and the end-game optional bosses is that they mainly utilize pseudo difficulty. They're meant to feel super hard, but in reality are not. By the time you defeat them, rather than feeling like you're overcome an obstacle, you're thinking "thank goodness I did not get too many undodgeable knife cycles", or that you didn't take a hit you couldn't have possibly avoided. The RNG makes the fight, it can be very easy with good RNG, or a nightmare with stacks of attacks you cannot dodge(Unless you're the right class).All in all, still a great game, but the last 5 bosses(excluding the final brothers fight) all leave much to be desired. If anything, you can learn how RNG can turn a fight that's supposed to be difficult, into a grind for the right RNG. Another con is that in the late game (NG++ and on) which class you are determines whether or not you'll be able to achomplish anything. And the gold collecting class becomes completely useless. You can also unlock a dragon class, but in NG+, it's completely useless and just wastes your roster slots and increases the odds you get a useless class.
I know I mostly sang the flaws of this game, but I still highly suggest it. It's because I enjoy the game so much that I harp so heavily on the flaws that it does have. If these issues were resolved, it'd go from a good game to a great game. But I still reccomend this game to those who are a fan of the genre.

When this was announced, my initial reaction was that it seemed like a mistake to go back to any of these characters. I have to admit that I was wrong. Deck Nine has created a prequel that not only respects the first game but actually makes it better by fleshing out the character of Rachel Amber and the depth of her relationship with Chloe. Before the Storm may in fact be a better game overall.
The only real criticism I have is that I'm not a huge fan of the Backtalk system. It's not awful, but it feels like attempt to "gamify" things - like something inserted to try to give the game its own unique hook in the absense of Max's time bending powers. That said, they're pretty easy to get through for the most part, and you'll probably make the choice to skip a few anyway.
It's also worth noting that the changes in the voice cast are a bit disappointing but mostly good to adequate. It's also far less than ideal that the developer chose to (or was forced to due to time/budget constraints or publisher pressure) employ scabs that didn't honor the voice actor strike.
The game has great storytelling and character development though, and that's what truly matters here. Even under a new developer, Life is Strange continues to excel - Telltale should really take note of the care put into these titles and stop shoveling out new games with as many licensed properties as they can sign.

Think StarTrek meets Cowboy Bebop. Yes, that good.
At this stage in development only two things can be suitably inferred from this game. Its tone and core mechanics. And I am exceptionally pleased with both. Even as an early alpha it is successfully scratching a difficuly itch to reach.
I wanted a game where I could zoom around the solar system getting into fights with phasers and torpedos, having to jockey for position all the while balancing my shields, engines, and weapons. SG2 gave me exactly that. The combat is very nice. In its current state the missions are randomly generated, MMO style, filler quests, but this does not prevent the encounters from being very fulfilling, if for no other reason then the solid underlying mechanics. This game will really cause you to think strategically. Will you perform the risky gambit of dumping all power to the shields and weapons to try and pick off a weakened enemy in one pass or will I shift that power into the engines and hope for a second chance to strike at that exposed hole in their shields. As the game progresses you will be making that decision and others as you have to contend with swarms of fighters and imposing warships. It requires just enough of the player to be extremely fulfilling when a risky maneuver works without being unduely frustrating when it fails. And you will fail alot. But the game is at its best when it is challenging. That is when the flexibile thinking and fast micromanagment that characterizes its combat will bring out your inner Jean-Luc Picard. And when it does you will feel great.
The tone is harder to express then the mechanics, but is a perfect compliment to them. If you have ever watched Cowboy Bebop then this game will be like putting on a pair of comfortable shoes. Two things drive this feeling. First, the music distinctly reminds me of some of the tracks from the show. There are no jazzy interludes, but the background music reminds me of some prog songs accompanying the space scenes. The music is seamlessly woven into the background noise of your lasers, phasers, engines, and missles. Most of the time it is barely noticeable above the ruckus but it is a soothing distraction during a long sprint across the map. It simply suits the game, perfectly conveying the mystery and the solitude of space. The more obvious callout to the tone of Bebop is the types of missions available so far. Most are bounty type missions and trading runs. All taking place in fantasitic locals with cool space stations. The game has a very awesome setting. And the scale of which really makes you feel like a plucky captain trying to scrape by in a much larger universe.
All in all I was looking for a game that would let me feel like I was flying a spaces ship. This did that and more! Not only did it have the gameplay I desired but it did so in a very cool way. As such SG2 has exceeded my expectations. It is perfectly filling a niche in my gaming library which I have been searching to fill. I would highly recomend the game to anyone who has got the space captain itch. Star Citizen is a far way away. But even in Alpha SG2 rocks! And its future looks so promising. All things considered, 9/10.
The only downside is a slightly difficult camera. You will get used to it but I feel like it doesn't need to be something that we should have to get used to. An autolock feature which would keep the camera centered on a target and  making the turret mode more responsive with less 'momentum' would be sufficient. But this is just nitpicking. SG2 looks to be a great niche game. And if you are interested it deserves your money and attention.

An amusing mix of real-time strategy and japanese visual novel. The story part is presented as an episodic anime with lots of light-hearted humor, but also deep topics such as humanity, loyalty, sacrifice and betrayal. It has two very different plot branches and four endings, inviting you to do additional New Game+ runs. And then there's small things, like varying company logo animation / voice acting, the intro video getting more revealling as you progress through the game, and 8+ unique chapter outro videos.
The strategy part has combat, resource management, a long research tree, various unit types and lots of equippable upgrades. It is really well done. There's also a lot of bonus levels of varying difficulty that you can play during intermission between chapters. Things can get repetitive when farming resources for R&D to get 100% completion, but there is a good guide on how to deal with that. (Don't attempt to do the $99,999,999 bonus upgrades without a memory editor cheat, you'll go insane =D)
Finally, there's a ridiculous amount of music in this game. Almost every map has its own fast-paced soundtrack, each consisting of 3 tracks depending on your state on the battlefield (cornered, balanced, dominant). And the story sequences also received their share of tracks, so enjoy.

Let's journey back to the year 2012. Barack Obama was president,  console gamer were buzzing about the upcoming Playstation 4, and a young Brit started a Kickstarter project inspired by Dungeon Keeper called Maia. It was a promising pitch - a game about controlling a colony with a 1970s British "real" sci-fi aesthetic. It seemed mighty ambitious for a solo developer, but I was younger, more idealistic and believed in Maia enough to pledge USD $11 on Kickstarter.
Fast-forward to 2017. Barack Obama is no longer president. Playstation 4 dominates the console market, Rimworld has show gamers how a procedurally generated storytelling, colony building game can work, and Maia is still a glorifed tech demo with no signs of becoming a real game most people would want to play.  The graphics are even more outdated than they were in 2012. The game is stil buggy and lack focus. More than any of that, there's just not much to it. At the rate the developer is moving, my as of yet unborn children will be starting university before this "game" become anything remotely fun.
I have to hand it to Simon Roth. Most indie developers would have realized by now that their plans were not going to come to fruition, given up and faded quietly into the night with whatever Kickstarter funds were left, but Simon continues to s-l-o-w-l-y build his quixotic masterpiece (?) I personally gave up any hope on this game at least 2 years ago, but for anyone thinking about buying, only do so if you're cool with buying games that are unlikely to ever be finished and even less likely to ever be good.

First things first, this is an ALFA version of the game (0.60 at the writing of this review), that means they are still developing it and will improve it in the future.
Now the review.
Maia basically is a base building game set on another planet where you have to make the rooms, provide food and water to your colonists, power to the machines so they can work and so on. With science fiction elements like green text everywhere, modern mechanics and fun messages from the scientifics (and some silly ones) combined with the good aesthetics, looks like it will be a good base/colony building game.
The game mechanics are easy, you select the terrain where you want to make space for the new rooms and a robot will go and demolish the walls and clean the space. Then you select the new room type and "paint" it on the floor and the colonists will go and build it and the last step it is to put the objets in the room and the walls (remember this) and let your humans work.
Also the game has natural disasters, strange alien lifeforms, robots, humans and some earth lifeforms like cats and dogs too. And chickens, be ware of them, they look suspicious.
Right now there are two game modes aside the tutorial, one it's  Missions whith objectives you have to meet and the other is an open/free base building mode called Exploration where you simply construct the base and try to survive.
Been a multiplatform game, I did not see any major bugs, just some missing game features like some sound efects or strange npc behaviors, but since it's an ongoin development and I'm sure they will implement them in the future.
One of thing I did not like was the UI but the next version comes with improvements on this area so lets see what they will do.
Overall, you can see what they are doing and where this game is aiming to be and personally I like it, that's why I recommend it, because the game looks good, the basic mechanics are there and it should be a good game when they finish it. Of course been an Alpha version they still have work to do, but they seem able to do so.

Initially I was a little worried. Would it be possible to replicate and improve upon the genius that was Life is Strange? Would it be possible to give us the same feeling the original did? It's easy to copy the mechanics, but it's another thing entirely to convey the feelings and a similar atmosphere that the original one had. And the story. How will they create an interesting, engaging story for Chloe and Rachel, when we already know what the future has in store?
I should not have worried. The mechanics are solid, I'm not going to talk about them more than to say that they work. The second question was answered pretty quickly during the first episode. Chloe and Max are very different people. The atmosphere reflects this perfectly. There are still quiet moments of reflection with beautiful, soft tunes but occasionally Chloes anger brings about frantic rock and punk. The themes discussed in the game are still heavy, still meaningful and still current. And it still makes you think.
The third question can only be answered now that I finished the third episode. But I'm not going to spoil anything. I'll just say that now that it's over, I miss it. I could have played one or two more episodes just to have some more time with these characters. The story was like Chloes mind. Occasionally frantic, fast, exciting, explosive. Occasionally quiet, sweet, sad and so touching. And the ending was perfect. Of course our knowledge of the future affects the way we see the ending, but that did not matter.
5/5, anxiously waiting for the bonus episode.

What is Oxygen: Not Included? Is it for you? Will it be abandonware in a few months?
The short answer to that spiel: Fun. Yes. No.
If you've ever played Don't Starve (or its MP version) you'll recognize the artstyle. Beautifully cartoony yet not white washed RGBs. Graphically speaking even in Early Access, O:NI runs beautifully. You little dupes run around crazily and act wonderfully. There's not a whole slew of differences between male or female or specific personalities. Other than casual renames (I personally use Youtubers) you won't fall in love with an individual dupes actions (Though having a narcoleptic Ohmwrecker falling asleep at his computer gave me a few chuckles ;) ) but you will see them run around trying to get stuff done and hopefully survive.
Sadly there's currently no tutorial so if you've never watched a youtube video you will be grossly uninformed about what this game does and how it acts. So here's a quick coles notes:
1) There are liquid and gas physics. You DO have to manage where various good and bad gasses travel through your base while being careful not to flood your basement.
2) Dupes, like you and I, are filthy things. Insert food and oxygen, out comes all sorts of harmful gases and by products. You have to manage where this waste goes early or they'll be swimming in their own literal manure.
3) Food is hard to come by. As is water and power. Do NOT try to get as many people into your base as you can until you are sure that extra mouth can be supported. As a general heads up: Avoid all duplicates that have destructive stress or have gross over eating habits unless you are completely comfortable with setting up a self sufficent base.
There is no 'end game' at the moment. Your poor dupes will not get rescued after X cycles pass. The main purpose of this game (at the time of this writing) is to develop a self sustaining home and last as long as you can before you eventually run out of resources. Think early builds of Rimworld, the difficulty of surviving was a gradual progression to where its a contest of how far you can get before all hell breaks loose and everyone dies.
The big question though, is it for you?
Quite possible. Like Rimworld, like Don't Starve. The true guts of the game is to test your own experimental builds and live as long as possible. If you enjoy that sort of gameplay without a set 'You are Weiner!' goal, GET THIS GAME NOW. If you need to be hand held where everything is explained? Wait a bit. Watch some lets plays. Blitzgrieger for example has multiple play throughs of a few builds which show alot of what can and will happen to you.
Still in short, yes its early access and this might shade you opinion to be less than stellar. But with fairly regular updates and an already fun existing game layout its worth its price.

This is a nice and pretty laid-back strategy game with a (to me, atleast) fun storyline.
The units are easy to understand and master, making it quick to pick up.
Resource gathering is also pretty simple: depending on how many enemy units you destroyed, you get resources (called supplies) awarded at the of of a mission (even one you lost!).
The game starts off simple, with missions that can be won with little or no casualties. But after the third mission it starts to increase in difficulty (albeit slowly) so be sure to research new units and equip power-ups to your tanks.
There are three main methods of attack: fast close-quarters "kamikaze" units, medium speed short-range assault, and slow but long-ranged artillery (Personally, I feel that attacking with the kamikaze tanks is basically trolling the enemy, so I only do that for sh*ts and giggles).
Scouts and anti-artillery units add depth to the gameplay due to their early warning and defensive capabilities, respectively.

If you like anime, grid-based tactics remniscent of Battleship, and a fun mixture of humor + cuteness, you will really enjoy this game.
There is quite a bit of text to provide the story in between battles, but I - admittedly - have skipped through it because I always want to get right into the next battle. The voice acting is in Japanese and the music and aesthetics provide a nice anime-feel with the cute, cartoonish character models and backgrounds.
The learning curve is fairly marginal for this game, as the tutorial helps you understand the fundamentals of the game very quickly. It is important to remember that every unit dies with one hit from any other unit (think Battleship, and all your ships cover only one grid point).
During the preloadout screen, you can deploy your troops in the allotted grid space. To field troops, you have to pay credits (at a very reasonable price compared to your post-battle loot, which means grinding is very balanced) to train them. In order to unlock the next tier of troops, you must research them, and they will be available to train after the next battle. There are also modules, which are either persistent or one-use equipments, and you can also research new modules and build them in the pre-battle setup. Some examples are permanent modules that allow your equipped character to move +1 extra grid space or have +1 improved range for their attack, and and example of a one-use module is a long-range scanner that reveals a large chunk of the grid map (also with a vast range).
The troops you can deploy include a commander/general unit (killing these units end the game in victory or defeat, so fielding more may be beneficial) that also provides a "connection" mechanic to every human tank. A general's connection speed determines how fast or slow it will take for your units to be "connected," which makes them active and allows you to issue commands to them.
There is a shock trooper unit that self-destructs to do damage to all grid points directly above, below, and to the right/left.
A recon unit can scan an area, revealing any enemy troops on those particular grid points. You reveal grid points on the map by scanning with the recon (other units can recon, but at significantly less efficiency [ex: artillery can only reveal 1 grid point, at a very short distance]). Your units also reveal a small radius around them, so moving them will provide holes in the fog of war.
There are general soldiers that will be the stormtroopers of your army, advancing rapidly and attacking at a short-medium distance.
Artillery provide long range support and are very useful when synchronized with careful recon scouting.
As you research and unlock higher tiers of each unit, you will notice numerous things improving like total movement points, attack range, and ability range.
You have the option of replaying free battles or continuing with the main story. Grinding is very quick and easy in this game.
The game has a lot of charm and humor, and it does a great job and making you feel like you are in an anime. In between battles, there is even a short intro/theme song sequence that is pretty funny. There are also those ad-style pictures that come before and after commercials in an actual anime. The voice acting is very anime-style, and characters will express themselves when they attack or die.
If you are a fan of grid-based strategy and/or like anime, then you should definitely give this game a try.

I bought this on a whim after hovering over the "Buy" button two or three times previously. I wasn't expecting much, but War of the Human Tanks absolutely hurdled the low bar I set. Then it started doing backflips over the bar, while thumbing its nose at me for not believing. Then a Samurai Tank beat me to death with the bar.
The strategy is deep enough to be enjoyable while being light enough that it never feels overwhelming. It resembles Advance Wars in terms of strategic depth, although not in actual gameplay--it resembles the ATB systems in certain RPGs, where a bar fills in real time for each unit, with the unit able to take its turn when the bar reaches maximum. Killing enemy tanks and winning victories gets you supplies, which you use to build Human Tanks to send into the meat grinder. Using your tanks and spending supplies lets you develop new tanks, as well as equipping your better tanks with stat-boosting modules.
The story is pretty engaging, although it took a while for me to warm up to it. The writing seemed a bit stiff at first, even a bit hackneyed, but it came into its own later--its clear the writer was playing with certain anime cliches, though whether it can be called a parody is up for debate. In short: Alpha build frustrations cloud what seems like a very promising colony builder & sim. Support now to increase its chances of reaching its very tangible potential.
First things first: it's an alpha build. Not a very early alpha - it already looks very good, the base game has a bunch of systems in it already - but not a polished and certainly not a balanced end-product.
The game is basically a dystopic, older vision of science fiction colony-building on an alien planet with cheekily British tones. To sell this game by its emotional air is mainly noting it's hilariously depressive tone. Everything is terrible: setting up a colony is not easy, and the human condition has so many requirements to retain the spark of life - your people will complain about being sad, tired, hurt, lonely, cold, hungry and thirsty, and then they will break down and die. Unless of course you manage to do your job.
Which, at the current time is more than just midly difficult. Here's where the alpha-ishness comes off heaviest. The balance is not just there yet, and the building-up-to-something-great is still coming up with bugs as games tend to when they're in their growing youth. Sometimes the game may deal you a foul hand by simply ruining the crucial piece of your initial setup, like caving in on your starter construction IMP robot just as you have spent your last building materials, leaving you to wonder who's doing the digging to get up some material production necessitated by your workshop attempting to construct the air processor to stop your folks from the good old freeze-and-choke of having no warmth and breathable air. Fair amount of my plays have been 10-20 minutes in to notice some calamity or unexplained AI non-co-operation to decide I'd rather start over than deal with the fresh hell that just ruined the current colonists' lives. And people dying off when colonizing a strange place is still OK, mind you, but some of these scenarios just flip over too many of the crucial pieces you need to have stuff progressing sensibly.
User-friendliness is not terrible, even at this alpha stage - having played some Dungeon Keeper or imitators will do you no harm to get the generic idea of how digging areas, building rooms and filling them with operational equipment works -  but the main mechanics are succinct and simple. You'll experiment a bit and learn a few things, browsing your available rooms and items and seeing through the mouse-over descriptions explain a couple things more. The tutorial is not a heavy chore, save for a few bugs at the time of writing this, that may confuse you when you are for instance ordered to build a room, but the tutorial step might not get checked and carry on if you didn't build a large enough room; something which will surely be corrected in improved instruction and polish soon enough.
All in all I got some bugs, some frustration out of confusion when I could not identify when colonists were not doing their tasks (were it an intermittent alpha AI bug, or was the colonist just too far gone in hunger and depression?), but for someone who looks up to building and growing an operation, nostalgizes about dungeonkeeper-alikes or maybe enjoys these sordid little histories that the game generates with these sorry folks trying to survive, there is a lot of promise in this one.
I'll be logging in a few feedbacks and a bug report soon and am looking forward to the day when I agree with the level of challenge as entertaining rather than frustrating when a few of my issues are being fixed in the coming versions - so far the developer communication and reactivity has given me nothing but trust for matters to proceed just so. Also, for whatever reason I keep getting pulled back in for a new try even though I feel the current build is just prone to quick failures with unclear or unfair situations in play. I'd love to get to the first play where I'll actually manage to ripen and harvest something from my hydroponics room before people starve to death or my mining robot collapses a lava flow onto itself and the colony.

I was given a Steam Review Copy of Shantae: Half-Genie Hero by WayForward themselves, so I felt obligated to finish this game and review it.
Note that this is the first time I'm actually trying to review something for realz, so I'm as unproffesional as you can get. LOL
At the time of this review, I only finished the Shantae Main Mode on Steam.
ABOUT:
Shantae embarks on her first full HD adventure! When a mysterious crime wave sweeps Sequin Land, it’s up to Half-Genie Hero Shantae to save the day! Use Shantae’s devastating Hair-Whip Attack to send monsters flying, or Belly Dance to transform her into more powerful forms! Topple the masterminds behind each criminal caper and prepare for the ultimate showdown against Shantae’s arch nemesis - the bodacious buccaneer Risky Boots!
VISUAL:
The visuals are strikingly beautiful and the animations are amazingly smooth! No one can shake their booty as smoothly as Shantae can! EVERYTHING is so beautifully designed, I actually tried to Google Image search to see if there's any other side scroller games that can even match this game visually. There are none. Seriously, the way this game look, it can make Nintendo jealous.
Even though it looks visually nice, I'm surprised by how much they lack fanservices. Shantae games are known to be very fanservice-y.
I really wish the KickStarter reach the Animated Cutscenes stretch goal. It would've been really amazing seeing all these wonderful to see and hear characters act, rather than them standing around and talking in text boxes.
AUDIO:
Aside from Dance Through The Danger
which is an absolutely amazing song by the awesome Cristina Vee, the other soundtracks range from catchy to just okay. They range from what sounds like an elevator music, to something that sounds like it belongs in the first level of a current gen Donkey Kong game, and service their purpose really well. You'll be able to recognize where those tracks are from, but they not good enough to get stuck in your head for hours.
Due to not reaching the specific stretch goal, the game isn't fully voice acted. Like Shantae And The Pirate's Curse, only a handful of lines are voice acted, and most of them belong to Shantae and Riskyboots. It's actually quite sad, really. All those quietness could've been filled with Cristina Vee's amazing voice-acting.
GAMEPLAY:
A 2D side-scroller game where you use various magic and items to help you solve puzzels and find hiddle treasures.
There's also a couple of fast-travel features that help the player travel from area to another with relative ease. It was a welcomed innovation for the series because helps so much with the back-tracking, and you get them very early and very easily! Screw collecting warp squids! Give me the Bird Whistle and the Warp Dance!
There's a couple of magic/items felt like they exist for only like one or two uses, and they won't be used ever again. They're almost pointless.
DIFFICULTY:
Out of all the Shantae games, this is easily the easiest one of the bunch. Unlike other Shantae games, it very forgiving. I only used like 3 potions through the entire game, and it was because I ran out of Magic, not Health. This caused me to max out the amount of gems I can carry, after purchasing every item in game, at around the half-way point. But it's not to say that this game is completely easy. The last area can really make you rage if you haven't mastered all of Shantae's animal forms.
GAMEPLAY LENGTH:
It took me around almost 12 hours to complete the Shantae Main Mode with 100% Completion, and that includes the times I spent revisiting areas and looked all over the places for hidden treasures to achieve 100% Completion. It'd be a lot shorter if it was a speed run.
There's also Shantae Hero Mode that unlocks after playing Shantae Main Mode, and possibly a Riskyboots Mode that I haven't unlock yet.
The player can also replay the game as Rottytops, Bolo or Sky in their own storyline!
So yeah, lots of gameplay value in this game.
VERDICT
Shantae: Half-Genie Hero is actually a really good and fun game. Yes, it does feel like it is lacking a few things that could've make it perfect, but I honestly can't blame WayForward for that since those missing things are the stretch goals that they never reach. Their KickStarter campaign was up around the same time as Mighty No. 9, and most people either just support MN9 only, and/or being really hateful towards Shantae for some reason, maybe because they're being pro-MN9 at the time. For what Shantae: Half-Genie Hero turned out to be with what WayForward got from crowdfunding, unlike Comcept, WayForward delivered in spades, and for only USD19.99 too! I can say that it's better than Shovel Knight, I highly recommend this game to anyone!

First of all, I'm going to start off by saying, that this review is merely based on my opinion.
I'm going to be honest with whomever is reading this review, and admit that the first Life Is Strange, wasn't of my liking. Despite that being said, I wanted to keep an open mind, and try out the prequel, thinking that perhaps some of the things I didn't like from the first Life is Strange, have been amended in the prequel. I was wrong. The differences between the two games are extremely minor.
So, what I liked about this game:
- Beautiful art style (same as the first one, so no difference there, as one would anticipate)
- Realistic, to a certain extent
- I have personally enjoyed the music in this game more than in the first one, but the music in the other Life is Strange perhaps fit the atmosphere more (but hey, still not complainin')
- Questions your morality, at certain points
What I didn't really like about this game:
- Didn't really enjoy the language used throughout the game, sometimes it's almost cringy (same issue as the first one)
- Some voice acting wasn't that good
- The animations STILL look stiff, just like in the first one, and I had even pointed that aspect out in the review I made on the other game. The movements just look SO unnatural

Spec Ops: The Line are not a shooter game, it's a story game that use shooter as it's gameplay and to define itself in the ever-growing list of game-genre.
It's the masterpiece of Yager Development, that Spec Ops: The Line can come with such a story that no other shooter game can rival.
Spec Ops: The Line gameplay is standard or mediocre for a third-person shooter game, you'll find shooter game with better gameplay out there, but that's not what Spec Ops: The Line is trying to sell.
It's the story.
Most shooter game have a linear story, or non-linear story but centered on a larger view of the conflict.
Spec Ops: The Line have a large story centered on how our character will define himself during all his 'brutal' mission in Dubai.
Surprisingly the larger story of how the conflict in Spec Ops: The Line happen are told only by collected Intel that are miss-able.
Upon playing to a certain degree, you'll be faced with a choice, that will make effect on your squad impression on you as their leader and your sanity that tread the thin line of soldier that obey order or a human being trying to survive on Dubai's Apocalyptic vision of hell.
A minus factor is that all the choices you made will not result in a different ending. Ending will be determined only by 2 choices, and all the choices you made previously will be presented in a flasback momentarily at the ending choice.
All in all, why should you get Spec Ops: The Line?
Because of the deep story, and how the main character develop it's character. In the end of the story 1 likely thought that the main character will have, is the recurring loading screen message: "Do you feel like a hero yet?" after all you have done in Spec Ops: The Line.
Getting this for the gameplay, and you will have a bad time.
8/10, if only it has a unique or a little deep gameplay style. But 1 can't ask too many.
Forget the multiplayer aspect of this game. Spec Ops: The Line is intended for a single-player game. (Even Yager says the MP mode initially aren't in the game scope, and it's been worked by another Studio)
Though you can try the co-op mode if you have friend who also buy this game and playing it.

Let me start by saying that i am a huge fan of
work. I count
and
among my favorite games and i have yearned for
since i first heard of it.
And despite my unreasonably high expectations i was sill very impressed.
Here is why:

is essentially a game about building a habitable base and micro managing a small bunch of adorable little guys and girls
to prevent them from starving and/or suffocating horribly, and maybe even keeping them mentally stable in the process.

You do this by ordering them to dig tunnels into the rock around them and letting them use the minerals and metals they gather in the process to build rooms, ladders, mashies and furniture, and the seeds and plants they find in caves to create simple farms
.

These base game mechanics are in and of themselves, while well executed, nothing special. The real meat of the game lies in understanding and utilizing the
behavior of the gasses and to a lesser extent liquids your guys are surrounded by and submerged in.
In
Oxygen and other gasses are not just statically present or not, but rather move around dynamically and constantly have to be accounted for. You can not just plop your air scrubber or photosynthesizing algae wherever you want, you have to carefully consider the flow of air in your base
. You also have to take care to design your base in a way to allow for good ventilation and exchange of gasses or your people will soon asphyxiate in their own dorm. These systems only gain depth and complexity as you move to later stages of the game and suddenly the quick rising Hydrogen, the breathable but toxic gasses from your sewage system and
the deadly chlorine enter the mix.

But managing the air in your base is only one of many challenges. Creating a functioning power grid, constructing a sewage system so your guys and girls don't pee themselves
taking care of your plants and later even temperature control while at the same time managing the stress of your people by keeping the environment nice and clean, so they wont break and stress eat all the stored food, go berserk on the machines that keep them alive or vomit in the water tank, all while dealing with inherently limited and constantly dwindling recourses can be quite a daunting task at first.

Luckily the game gives you an array of simple but versatile tools ranging from gas and liquids pumps and filters over Different generators, batteries and wires, heaters and sensors to pipes, vents and even gas permeable walls and floors, as well as an excellent and easily controllable interface with many different overlays and settings.

This is a game that rewards creativity, unconventional thinking and learning from your own mistakes.
Most of the time there are innovative ways to work around problems and lack of recourses and i found the constant tinkering with your own systems highly addictive and rewarding especially when you finally manage to create a stable base
. And you can really go crazy while playing with the physics, you could even conceivably melt and subsequently vaporize solid materials and pump them around or cool down gasses like hydrogen or oxygen to liquid or even solid forms.
Provided you have the power and recourses.

All that said, the game is at this point still lacking in content, the research tree is ridiculously short, and when you finally reach a stable and self sufficient state, there is not much left to doo.
However i bought this game because i wanted to support it and I'm confident that
will provide frequent updates as they have with

I bought this game because Don't Starve is one of my favorites out there. I am not disappointed. It's a very good game with a lot of potential, very original and it's different from Don't Starve but you still get that don't-starve vibe.
It's a game where you have to manage your colony in space. Now, it may seem simple enough, but it's really not. You have to take several things into account and just like it happens with Don't Starve, you have to gradually learn from trial and error! Also, know how in starve you don't die from hunger? Well, Oxygen isn't the only thing that's not included.
The art is very pretty and it never feels repetitive. Each time you start a game you get a random set up, just like it happens in Don't Starve. This makes every new map an adventure. You might get a very difficult map, with a lot of polluted air and no water nearby, or you might get the best map (and still manage to screw up).
Plus, the little guys are very cute. Just sayin'. They end up being your babies. Your messed up babies. The little sounds they make when they're eating happily make my days better.
I really recommend this game, however, bear with it. It's early access, so there are stressful moments that make you wonder why on earth it's that hard. It's simply because they're working on it, so if you're not a patient person, don't buy it yet. If you are patient and you like Don't Starve, then absolutely get this game!

So, this isn't ready. What's there is polished and well made- the basic "solve emergent problems" gameplay loop that's the purpose of this genre is in place, but really short in this instance. Expect to spend your whole time chasing oxygen- to be expected for sure given the title of the game, but I found all the other problems trivial while the oxygen problem never stabilized.
There's a tech tree, but it's laughably short right now. There's Intermediate research (which you can pursue immediately) but no Advanced, so this is clearly planned to change, but the game might be better right now if there wasn't a tech tree at all.
There's very little to work towards for your colony, just digging to different quickly exhausted resources to turn into oxygen. People have said there's no late game yet, but I'd say there's no real midgame either. No trading, nothing to upgrade, nothing interesting to craft.
Worst for me was that the game is designed against making you care about your colonists.
They're called duplicants, flavor text says they have no memories from before their arrival, you literally 3d print them. The game stops just short of saying outright "these aren't really people, you don't have to care about them." There's very little you can do to make their lives better, with only one tier of furniture and decoration, no leisure needs. I never had problems with stressed colonists until my colonies were dying of something else.
Basically, right now it's a short frustrating gameplay loop that provides no meaningful goals.
Klei has a good record, so they'll probably fix most of the problems I had with the game. It's not worth paying for yet though.

On the surface, this is a base building survival game. Somewhat like Terraria, where you mine blocks and build you base with it. You build living quarters, research labs, water reservoirs, farm etc. When I first bought it, I was expecting it somewhat fallout shelter.
But it is so much more! This is one of the few games where you have to plan for both short and long term (a couple other being Factorio, Minecraft with industrial mods etc). Want short term gain by placing your toilet closer to your base? Your base will smell like♥♥♥♥♥♥after a couple cycles in. Forgot to build ventilation in the rooms? You'll have CO2 build up and your duplicate (the game's residences) will choke. Did not build insulation around your batteries? You base will heat up and make all your plants die.
Everything you do will have short term, mid term and long term effect on the survival of your base. In fact, it's fairly hard to lose short term (unless you trap everyone in a room full of chlorine), but it's also very hard to fix problems if you let it manifest and become a long term problem other than to start over.
tl;dr If you are looking for a great macro management strategy game, this is the game for you!

There are a lot of really good space sims out there, this is one of them.  But one thing that sets this game apart from those other games is this:  Noob friendliness.  This games UI and setup is so easy/simple that even someone who has never played any space sims before can get the hang of within an hour or so, and that's FAST.  The UI may be simple, but it's still got the same flexibility to let you do what you want.  Every time I start a new space sim, I always think 'oh god, i gotta relearn the whole system again.'  but not for this one.  Also, that map UI reminds me soo much of google chrome.
Currently, the gameplay is extremely fun even for not being complete.  One could hardly tell, except for the fact that skill, equipment, and fighter keybinds don't work--but that's okay, they're all just a mouseclick away via the easy to use UI.
I haven't played long enough though to figure out how deep this game is, whether or not the trading system is static or dynamic, or whether or not what you do affects prices.  I haven't played long enough to see whether or not the universe is 'alive' like in other games, but this is good enough for someone who wants to pick up their first space sim and not be overwhelmed.

Love this! Have not stopped playing it since I downloaded it. Shows a huge amount of promise in terms of gameplay; the visuals of the spaceflight scenery, ships, asteroid belts, stations and nebulae are brilliant and very atmospheric. Even the icons and equipment images are polished and impressive.
There are the inevitable comparisons to games like Elite and X, but even in this early incarnation I feel that Starpoint Gemini has the capacity to surpass them; I haven't seen much of the trade mechanic yet, but have enjoyed myself immensely with the freelance missions and grappling enemy ships before boarding, capturing and selling them.
Some other memorable moments so far are the sound of the engines powering up when you leave a station, or slicing up asteroids to mine ores.
I also really like the dimensions in the game - the stations are big, but the planets are massive and I like that you can land on them. I'm about 20 hours in and have covered maybe a quarter of the map (and most of that was a fleeting visit).
The gameplay gets sticky on my machine moving between sectors but  this is only the Alpha build and I imagine there is still a lot of coding spit-and-polish to come.
My wishlist for the finished game would be to be able to reduce the number of turrets as well as increase them (have been a bit overly-optimistic with power management for my Myrmydon weaponry) and for alliance ships to stop shooting at my captured enemy vessels while I'm trying to drag them back to port.
Highly recommended if you like space exploration/combat/trade games.

After 200+ hours, I decided to uninstall FreeStyle2: Street Basketball after asking myself, am I really having fun playing this game? My answer was no.
Community [3/10]
The community is horrible. It seems like no one is out to really have fun, but more to win. I've meet a few cool people who seemed genuine, but the vast majority are just ♥♥♥♥ wagons who talk constant smack and make the games drag on.
Gameplay [8/10]
One of the only reasons I continued playing this game was because of the gameplay, which seems to be the only thing the developers got right. It's difficult to master, and difficult to pick-up. However, getting better is satisfying enough to promote continued progress.
Developers	[2/10]
No developer interaction with players. The store is filled to the brim with items that make the game P2W. Translation to English in this game is a hot mess, with constant spelling errors. A complete and utter lack of professionalism.
Server [3/10]
The server for FS2SB is stable enough, but operates off of Peer to peer connectivity, which is completely dated technology. Not to mention, several key elements of this game operate off of this, such as the rebounds, blocks, shots, etc. The person with the lower ping will likely end up succeeding in this game, although I wouldn't discount skill entirely. However, if you intend on playing and have 60 + ping, dont plan on playing a PF, CT, or C. You'll never get a single rebound.
Conclusion [4/10]
There are many other aspects to this game, but the ones I covered were due the most coverage. Overall, FS2SB is a good game, but is completely veiled by poor developer choices and a terrible community.

Just to make things clear I am partially biased in this review.
The DayZ mod gave me some of my most heart-pounding moments ever and I'm eagerly waiting for 0.63 beta to bring the gameplay of DayZ to a whole new standard. Though I think that 0.63 will be a make it or break it situation.
The bitternes people have had over DayZ's slow development is understandable. But we also have to undestand that DayZ was kicked into Early Access way too early, due to the whole genre and all the derivatives that DayZ mod created.
And then there is the whole slew of people calling the developers lazy and incompetent in the wake of the drawn out development, although all of DayZ rivals still also being in early access indicates that the genre is not easy to develop.
But in the defense of DayZ's early access it has always been here with disclaimers, both on the store page and every time the game is booted. Along with DayZ teams decency to not monetize the game through lootboxes or DLC whilst still in Early Access.
Unlike some devs.
I for one bought the game to support its eventual release and haven't been mad at its slow release due to my realistic expectations and patient nature.
So! To the big question:
Do I recommend DayZ?
I'm cautiously optimistic and hyped for the next version. If it's as good as what I've seen and head the HELL YES I do recommend. And will update this review to reflect on it.
As a disclaimer though I will say that DayZ is definitely not everyones cup of tea.
It involves a lot of learning. As a matter in fact it taught me navigation and gave me my first touch of learning the cyrillic alphabet.
DayZ involves a lot of down-time of looting and sneaking around zombies. Until you make contact with another player and the stakes are terrifyingly high as all the gear you've worked on gathering is on the line.
The magic of DayZ is that due to how unforgiving it is you can feel a real sense of mortality.
And the way DayZ has been and how it's only going to get more depth to its survival mechanics it'll just mean that the game will get more venues for creating organic player driven narratives.
Ever talk with your friends about what you'd do in a zombie apocalypse?
At it's best, DayZ is like a simulation of your friends zombie apocalypse scenario survival.
Or solo survival.
Can't really say that I've had any worst moments linked directly to gameplay. Only due to past and present technical limitations tied to it's unfinished state.
Jogging
But next year looks promising for DayZ and if 0.63 fails to deliver I'll never forget the amazing situations I've experienced in DayZ.

DayZ is not only a game. It's also a symbol of growth, development, and the ability to overcome whatever gets in the way. DayZ is... Hope. I have to say, I really find joy reading the funny reviews, good and bad. At least those people took the time to be creative rather than just spew misguided opinions about the game. One thing that everyone really has to understand is that the developers are trying. I can see where some are coming from when they argue that enough has changed over the 4 years this game has been in Early Access. Nonetheless, the devs have been trying all along and they have been making big moves since 2013. And now, with 2018 being called "the Year of DayZ," many people are skeptical, hopeless, and completely unimaginative. I believe that 2018 will be DayZ's year. I have enjoyed sticking with this game through thick and thin. DayZ is really just like a kid going through school. You think that in the early stages of elementary school that big things are going to happen. Most kids enjoy going to school in their early years. Then, they enter middle school and they realize how monotonous school can be, and this was DayZ about two and a half years after Early Access release. Now, everyone's here is high school. Senior year to be exact. Everyone's just ready to get out of high school. Many people are just done with school in general. Well, for DayZ, Senior year is almost over. It's about to enter the real world with all the other big games. And, again, it's just like a student in that it needs support, hope, and trust that it will make it. Needless to say, it has my trust. I urge all of the naysayers to really step back and see DayZ in the bigger picture. It's been 4 years of growth and development and when all had seemed lost and hopeless, here we are, about to be out of Early Access.
So, don't look at DayZ for how long it's been in Early Access of how long it's taken the developers to make big leaps. Judge DayZ for all the hard work, late nights, and lost sleep that has gone into the production of a truly extensive, amazing game. Remember that DayZ is open world and open survival. Remember how much content the game and the entire map has. Maybe you too will start to see how hard it may have been to turn a game mod into a full game with the quality of DayZ. Nothing comes fast, nor easy in life, especially the best things.
Simply put, just have an open mind. Have hope, have trust, and have faith. We're about to enter the year of DayZ, why not come along for the ride?

After a few hours I am a bit disappointed. The game premise is nice, but I can definitely say what it lacks. The generic simple "game hygiene" things are missing. For example, you cannot find a key bindings menu at all. It's just not made. Saving the game is unintuitive and unclear - automatic, but resuming the exact save you want is based on just creating a new game with same skipper name, and same world - and lo and behold it is the save game not a new world. A simple load game menu would be clearer. Also, you cannot without mods zoom in or out, so you cannot look around at all, but you are forcefully looking too close all the time.
The game is in the beginning at least incredibly slow. There is no go to command like in say Colonization, where you know you want your cargo in Jamestown so you just put go to and wait or fast travel. There is fast travel only between map zones, but the zone itself is kind of big, which is nice. The speed however is low and the distances long so to just make a 100 gold profit you might have to sail for 5-10 minutes. So you can maybe make over a 1000 gold in an hour of trading or questing. But the better boats and the improvements cost up to hundreds of thousands in the end, so you would play a hundred hours of waiting to get to your destination. And all this without story, no taverns, swordfights, no boarding, no governors.. The game needs the depth that was in pirates. The factions feel kind of bland and non-interesting. They have no common leader or cause. They could have been made more like pseudo Hansa union, pseudo British etc, and give them faces and campaigns they rally. This is of course a lot of work for a small company.
I also didn't like the combat. Firing a volley makes you choose by mouse on who to fire. In pirates you would just try to aim with your broadside and then hit spacebar when you think the lead was enough. This actually made you position yourself for firing and trying to hit the sweet spot. Now it is just circle strafing around and clicking on your enemy for volley hits, while the autofiring happens between the volleys anyway.
Also the sailing was kind of dorky. At least in Pirates you couldn't sail straight upwind, but then the wind was unrealistically set always from east, which was annoying to get back to then. But at least you moved fast in general around the map so it was no issue to circle the caribbean. I think this type of game would benefit from having straight upwind impossible, and having to go 35 degree angle to wind at minimum, and get the highest speed at around 30-45 degrees off tailwind like in reality, not straight downwind (which is poison for sail vessels). Couple this with slowly changing prevalent winds, and you would have an excellent fun game with regards to travel and combat. Also more stormy raging seas and vast ocean expanses would be nice.
The game has huge potential and I am looking forward to its development. Right now I would recommend the cheaper Sid Meier's Pirates still.

If you like god games, hard sci-fi, hyper-realistic sims, and dark, British humour, then you'll like Maia.
I've played Maia for about 20 hours now, more than enough to have built myself a fully self-sustaining colony with all the bells and whistles, including the rooms that require certain levels of research, so I've seen pretty much all of the permutataions of gameplay you can get within the game.
It took me a while to get that Maia is a delicate balance between active user input (build orders, smelting stuff, etc) and watching the formidable AI systems run. However, once I understood this, my colony ran a lot better, was more productive, and I got a lot more out of gameplay. Another challenge is balancing the amount of activity. Unlike other sims, your colonists get tired and sick and dehydrated if you work them too hard, so you can't just set 4892438 build orders and go make some tea. On that note, I LOVE the level of detail - from temperatures reactive to whether an air vent system is on or off, to body heat of chickens altering room temperatures, to the relative humidity being affected by water condensing systems, to atmosphere quality being augmented by potted plants, to plants *literally* getting species-specific diseases like fungal rot and black spot... there is phenomenal detail in here that I struggle to understand at the best of times, but massively appreciate.
Another thing is that dev Roth is quite literally the King of the Easter Egg. Most people probably don't notice or read the descriptions and names of objects, but there are some real 'laugh out loud' examples of punning names that play very well within the cultural nexus of dry, dark British humour. There's also a brilliant sense of British understatement to the emails - instead of saying 'we're literally starving here, half-wit, build some food prep stations', they say wonderfully passive aggressive things like "I hope this lack of X isn't another bureaucratic oversight." Ah, the art of the strongly worded letter is strong in this game.
In terms of practical playability, the game is pretty easy to get the hang of; controls are intuitive, and the 'tabbing through' range of objects based on context rather than having to go through a sims-style full-scale menu system is great.
The fact that the game is still under development shouldn't put you off - it's fully fledged already, and the updates (like 0.60 adding colonist relationships... again, how the heck was this coded in?!) just add more levels of detail and interest to an already fully formed and extremely well-thought-out idea. I paid full price for the game and don't mind as it's an indie dev, but it seems like it has frequent sales, so definitely pick this up right now.
Overall 9/10, definitely reccommend.

This is an update to my March 11th review. That seems very long ago and it was. Now that hitman world of assasination has wrapped up its first season ( Which is odd that was never stated at the start when I first purchased the game.) I can comment on the final product. All in all I couldn't ask more from a hitman game. I would say this game deserves a 10 out of 10 if it wasn't for a couple of things.
Firstly the need to be connected and online at all times to get the benefit of your unlocks. That said I get the reason they did it. To prevent piracy! However it does little to make it less annoying for people who payed for the game. My only other complaint is the fact it wasn't revealed until after the fact this games story is going to be on going in seasonal installments. So for that I knock a couple points off and give hitman an 8 out of ten. But then they gave us two bonus level and now with Christmas they added more free content. So being mildly surprised I bump my score to a 9. Solid game.
Hitman has great replay value with its Elusive targets and esculation modes. At first I felt there was little reason to do these as you didn't get much reward or incentive. But the developers did a good job adding the ability to unlock suits for taking out the elusive targets. They are worth going after!!!
Also for those that don't know you unlock much better equipment for 47 to use in all missions by completing level challenges. This is another reason to replay levels! And while you don't get the break down sniper rifle in a briefcase ( at least not this season ) you do have the abilty to earn 47's awesome silenced 3x scope sniper rifle.
So in summing up about this version of a hitman game in my humble opinion it hits on much or what a hitman game should be. The only thing I wish it had was the bullet time of absolution. I enjoyed that, but then again I imagine it was left out for balance. Same with the briefcase sniper rifle. It could be a game breaker. I've enjoyed the story of this hitman but didn't care for the way the first season ended. But only because I'm eager to learn more!

When this game came out, I gave it a good review. But in retrospective, I can't. This game is not good.
Being a kind of fanboy of the series, I was SO excited for this game, which might be the reason why I hate it, but I will
try to explain why, and give context compared to the previous games in the series. I'm probably gonna be really harsh here, but these are my honest feelings, K?
(I AM ONLY REVIEWING THE BASE GAME, NO DLC)
Story:
The story in this game, is BLOODY ATROCIOUS. It mostly consists of random chores Shantae has to do, fighting some evil
while at it. There is no more character development, and in fact it throws the charming character development of the main villain, Risky Boots, out of the bloody window. In fact, this game has so little refferences to the previous games, that it is pretty much a reboot of the series. Each area that Shantae goes to has pretty much NOTHING to do with the overarching story, and is pretty much pointless padding. So the story sucks, but what about the gameplay?
Gameplay: Its average... The fighting and spells are pretty cool, and the dancing works, but I do prefer the dancing from the GBC original. Instead of the world being linked, it goes for the Pirates Curse style of having a hubworld and some form of transportation to get from level to level (A feature which I was iffy about in TPC). Unlike the cool Zelda-type dungeons from the first 3 games, this game THROWS that out the window, and we just have.. A level.. A level with a boss at the end. Pretty much not even a Metroidvania anymore. Also the game relies on insta-death spikes more than ever, So that sucks.
Graphics: They are great! It's the best part of the game. The has the whole hand drawn on 3d environments look, and it is really charming and adorable. The character portraits are adorable, and the reward pictures are my favourite in the series.
Music: Its good. There are about 4 or 5 really catchy songs IMO, and the rest is ok music and like, Item get or level complete jingles, ect. My favourites are:
Counterfeit Mermaids
Dance through the Danger.
Other notes:

If you're looking for a deep story, great levels and a big world, this is not your game. Half-Genie Hero has more in common with Megaman than it does with its previous entries in the Shantae Series, while trying to hold to its original roots, and somewhat failing at it.
Where HGH succeeds the most at is in its fidelity. This game is really colourful, the animations are bouncy and lively, it's just very pleasant to look at. The soundtrack is really good too, however, I do find it to sound REALLY flat due to its really high volume. After downloading several soundtracks from the composer, Jake Kaufman, that seems to be an ongoing issue with his masterings. So if the game sounds too loud when you first start it up, it might catch you off guard and I defnitely recommend lowering your volume.
When it comes to being a sequel, the game improves a few things from it's closer sibling, Risky's Revenge, is the dancing system and overall powerups. The new system implemented in this one works better as you only have to press the dance button and then choose which transformation you want by pressing a direction. It works well and if you think it's too slow, you can even get a powerup to make the dance faster. In fact, HGH is probably the fastest feeling entry so far thanks to its responsiveness.
Probably my personal favorite part of the game when it comes to gameplay are the first four stages... when played linearly. They are quick, action-packed and are quite fun to traverse with fun bosses (Except for the last two...).
The first part where game falls apart to me when they want you to backtrack to stages to get specific items. It wouldn't be a huge issue if the stages introduced new things but they just don't. The ''new paths'' are usually one or two rooms, which more often than not, will either be coursed through in less than a minute, or are big and open with nothing in them, just to pad things out. It gets really monotous to since you have to do exactly that, several times in a row to even progress to the next stage.
The second part is actualy the final third of the game. The stages feel unfinished, with even less original set pieces, hazards, especially when two key characters are haphazardly placed in the second to last stage, with no introduction. In fact, a lot of characters in HGH are completely forgetable and have barely to no development at all and when the game ends, it really feels unsatisfying. Now if you factor the rather dull design, and combine what is essentially the game breaking transformation, the Harpie, you get a final stage that is insultingly easy. Why? The stage was designed for you to take advantage of a couple of transformations. The Issue? The harpy can fly over the majority of them. There were only two counts where I switched to the monkey. This makes some rather elaborate traps completely useless.
The final boss and endings are not much better. First, my game crashed once when I defeated the first phase of the boss. Second, I skipped the cutscene as the fade to black was still on the screen, leaving it black and making the fight impossible (I've encountered several glitches so far, some worse than others). Third, if I am either regular Shantae, Mermaid Shantae or Harpie Shantae, the background of the second phase will never rotate like it should and screw with the movement of the boss' attacks. FOURTH, the final phase has an attack that circles the whole arena, and it makes no sound effects. If it does, I can't hear it. It also blends with all the other assets during the fight due to their colours. FIFTH, the endings are almost identical, regardless if you get the ''best'' or ''regular'' ending. It's  just not satisfying at all and feels slapped together.
The final slap in the face to me from this game, is the fact the DLC will have to be paid for non-backers. Considering how barebones the game felt, along with the lackluster two final stages AND the full price of this game, I flatout cannot consider even getting the DLC. I feel like they should have been part of the game ''and the price'' from the very start.
If Shantae Half Genie Hero was not forcing mandatory exploration and padding and was more like Megaman, as its stages are clearly focused on being much more linear than the areas from the previous entries of the series, this would be so much better. However, as it stands, and WITHOUT THE DLC AND AT FULL price. I can't really recommend this game unless you're a die hard fan. If you want a significantly better experience, go get Shantae and The Pirate's Curse.
If the DLC releases and they have a bundle for the launch price of the game and cut the standalone game's price, then it might be worth checking out. Maybe....

Definitely not the game I thought it was. I knew it was whacky but found out there was a bit of seriousness behind the scenes. Watching the previews I got the sense it would be similar to HotWheels Turbo Racing in which players were able to maneuver the cars in mid-air. This is not the case here; you'll need to time and calculate your speed, angle and take-off.
The
within this game is pretty rock solid. Although simplistic in nature, the game delivers a solid driving experience. The steering is tight but feels closely to the stiffness of an F1 car. The acceleration feels like you're speeding up and gaining momentum. Complete the former two with outlandish tracks with extremely tight and fun turns makes it almost into a complete game. The career mode in this is a bit odd. It seems as though the game was meant to be played online but can provide just as much fun offline. The only catch here is you're not really racing. You are, but you're not. Most of the career races involve time attacks. There are races which are lapped but for the most part it's time attack. Some gamers may find racing by yourself is a bit of a nuisance, even for single player mode. Again, online there can be multiple people on the track at the same time but in time attack, you'll be racing a ghost. Completing each race challenge results in attaining either a bronze, silver or gold card depending on your performance. The game is good enough that single player does not feel like a grind (in my opinion). Record breaking times are kept for each individual track and gives the player a ghost to play against.
To maximize time and acceleration, it's best to try and keep straight and avoid jumps. This will be unavoidable as the tracks go from a linear build to some extremely crazy turns and loops. The race starts in a straight line. Then some turns will be thrown in. Next thing you know you're driving sideways then into a loop-to-loop. One thing to note is that when you drive through a loop, it switches to first person view. This may drive some nuts as a quick view switch is sort of unexpected. The tracks themselves can change from concrete, to grass or to gravel/dirt (which significantly effects turning controls). I find for most turns simply letting go of acceleration can work but there are cases where you'll need to specify which brake type to use. The hard brake slide/stop will bring your car quickly to a halt for sharp turns while the hand brake will allow you to maintain speed while sliding. Additionally, being in the air can cause quite some complications. If taking off isn't done right, sometimes the car won't land properly or spin out of control. There is an "air-brake" sort of feature in which you need to hold acceleration but tap the brake button in the air. Doing this tries to halt your movement. If you take a jump poorly, most likely you'll end up with poor results.
What isn't advertised is the fact that (I'm assuming all) Trackmania is
. There is an option for local play which can include up to four players. The players are sort of limited in choice regarding game mode. The only mode available is "round" in which the first player across the finish line wins. On top of this, if you do manage to complete all the courses and do get tired of local and multiplayer, the devs have been kind enough to include a solid track editor into the game. Want an entire track full of loops? Go ahead and go nuts. Just be aware that the cars need enough acceleration to make it through certain points! Adding a speed boost can definitely help reduce free-falls. A helpful tip to a possible future game would be to not fight against the games physics. The "A" button on a 360 controller holds the car steady in mid-air. Don't get your landing angle right and face the consequences. Also, drift is sort of possible in dirt.
The
are pretty good for a game with a bit of age. Everything seems to have a nice polish and colors mesh nicely together. Not to mention, the back drop of being in a giant stadium is neat. The only thing that's extremely bothersome for me is not being able to see the nose of the F1 car in first person view.
are generic and are decent. There isn't much to talk about here either than the sounds play/change at the right times (when you change track from concrete to grass) and the engine sounds are decent.
Overall, it's a decent game for what it is, an outlandish track game. It's not exactly a racing game per se, but it will give any racing fan something to play.
