Everyone has a game to which he/she comes back again and again to have some fun. This is that game for me, a bit surprising as I'm a casual player so rogue-lite's are not usually my cup of tea.
Rogue legacy is an action-platformer dungeon crawler.
The levels and enemies are randomized (from a pool) but there are always 4 main sections (in order or increasing challenge): main castle (centre), forest (right), tower (top) and dungeon (bottom).
Every time the hero dies, a new heir needs to be selected from 3 randomly generated characters (again, from a pool of classes, but with random characteristics from dwarfinism/gigantism to IBS).
All the money is passed to the next generation, but you'll need to forfeit it before starting a new game. This basically means that you're encouraged to spend all the money possible in the castle (opening new or upgraded classes, upgrading energy, mana, power, armour, etc), in the blacksmith (upgrades to the armour and sword) or the enchantress (upgrades like double jump, speed, easier or harder enemies).
Basically, the objective is to go to the castle and get as much money as possible to upgrade our hero.
Once the hero is strong enough, you can battle 4 bosses (1 in each section) to open up the last battle. And then, a +1 harder version of the game opens. And then a +2. And as many +N as you want to keep the challenge going.
I had way more fun with this than with more expensive AAA games. Given that it is frequently on sale, there is no excuse not to buy it!

This game is definitely worth picking up on a sale.  I've logged ~20 hours, and I'll probably log many more.
Windward is a very casual game that plays like Sid Meier's Pirates, but with multiplayer and a few tweaks in mechanics.  The game starts with you declaring loyalty to one of several factions, which carry different in-game bonuses that advantage you in offense, defense, etc.  From there, you take quests from cities that vary from A->B quests (take passangers from one city to another) to hunting down Pirate Captains.  As you advance, you acquire skills and conquer new territories (from pirates or other factions).  The game has a skill tree, you can improve your ship and crew, and ultimately you can link up with other players in specific instances (for questing, PVP, or fighting pirates) and whole worlds you can conquer together.
The multiplayer is a little slow (~100 people at this writing, not a few thousand).  That being said, every time I've logged onlne hours I've found 1-2 people to play with (which makes it easier to conquer new territory).
My best description of the game is that it is relaxing.  It is something you can play casually, while you're watching TV on the couch.  That is my style of gaming and so, this game appeals to me.  I think if you prefer fast paced games this isn't for you, because even at its best the game moves slowly and can feel like you are grinding a bit (running quests, killing pirates, etc).
Overall, it is absolutely worth it.

The game is promising.  It looks lovely, its systems look to be interesting, and its sense of humor is enjoyable.  But at this point it's simply too unpolished to really be worth buying.
---
The most obvious problem is that there are no (reasonably functional) speed controls.  The game, as far as its UI will inform me, has exactly one speed, sloth.  People move like molasses and completing basic tasks takes ages.  And despite this pokey pace, you can't sit back and relax as you strategize as you would with other games in the genre because there's no real-time pause fuction - sure, there's an undocumented pause function if you hit the Pause Break key, but this can often crash the game.  The result is that you need to quickly queue up your commands, almost a bit like Starcraft but without the immediately obedient underlings or any of the good UI design that went into that game.
This is made worse by the awful controls - the game's framerate is still not as good as it should be so it's already not quite responsive enough on reasonable hardware, but inconsistent controls make planning out your base maddening.  When placing items, right click both returns you back to your regular cursor/interact mode
removes items under your cursor, either queuing placed items for destruction or immediately removing what you just placed.  The result is a lot of frustration as you have to swipe away to an empty part of the map to safely right-click your way out, or risk misclicking with the flakey FPS when trying to click the menu item to swap out of item placement.
Placing rooms of course breaks this convention - right click will remove placed floors, but it does so immediately without any queuing so you can very easily cause messy problems that you'll then need your minions to slowly fix, and if you right click in an empty area you don't go back to Interact mode like you'd expect.
And Interact mode, where you can click on stuff and see information or view the station from the point of view of your colonists in first person (which is neat and even has a low-res camera feed filter), also doubles as your mining tool, so you'll frequently be mining things when you're just trying to click on a moving colonist.
Oh, and you have to do all this when it shakes the screen due to eathquakes, meteorites, and cave-ins, which are annoyingly frequent and make it hard to just control the game.
Then there's just the bizzare key placement.  Y and N are something you need to frequently hit, and I mean
, which is rather uncomfortatble since the game expects you to have a constant WASD grip.  The three main building tools - the aforementioned Interaction, Room, and Item modes - are bound to J, K, and L respectively.  These keys are nowhere near WASD where your fingers will be resting most of the time, while Z, X, and C right underneath remain unbound.  Why?  The keys are at least rebindable, though you'll have to spend a good amount of time figuring out what keys are important and which are pointless from experience.  The tutorial doesn't even bother telling you want the keys are, and the UI doesn't bother listing the keybind either on its icons.
These may seem like small nitpicks, but bad controls combined with time pressure in what's usually a more methodical genre make for an incredibly frustrating experience.
---
And then we get into the typical EA problems.
The game provides very little feedback on why your colonists aren't doing what they need to do.  I can have three full barrels of water and water fountains everywhere, yet my colonists will mysteriously die of dehydration regardless.  Hopefully this eventually changes, but for now it's complete guesswork as to what's wrong.  In a good Dwarf Fortress-like game you don't always know immediately what little cog in your operation is causing a holdup, but at the very least you have tools at your disposal to figure out what's going on.  Those tools apparently don't exist yet, mousing over a colonist gives some physical information but you can't get useful stuff like the last letter they wrote or recent complaints or anything like that, instead forcing you to dig through the often busy feed (while the game is still running in real time, mind you).  And since the game is buggy, you can't ever feel confident that you're losing because you messed up, you're always wondering if the AI is just being bad and not doing obvious things like eating when it's hungry.
Then there's the lack of content, bugs, and general unfinished state of the game that you'd expect out of an EA title.  Yeah, it's nothing shocking, but it's nothing special either that really demands your money now like Kerbal Space Program or Darkest Dungeons or Space Engineers.  Updates happen, but they sure as hell take their time.  This game's been in EA for a long time and it still feels like it has a long way to go.
~~~
The game simply isn't ready for your money.  I want to love the game so much and it feels like in two years maybe there will be a game worth playing, but as it is now it's just a really pretty piece of junk compared to other Dorflikes like Dwarf Fortress, Prison Architect, or even other EA games like Stonehearth.  It's not Spacebase-DF9 levels of terrible, there aren't unexplainable oxygen leaks that eventually kill everyone with no further promises to improve, but it just gets so many little things wrong that it can't hold a candle to a game like Banished.
Wait and see, the game has the potential to be great.

I enjoy games where you can build a base, upgrade your stuff, dig and explore, solve problems, and generally try to avoid the impending chaos of the universe.  So far, I haven't been able to avoid the chaos for very long, but the failure has been fun.

NOTE: The game has only been out on Steam for 3 days at the time of this review.
OxyNotIn is a great game already, but needs much more content before it heads to release. The existing systems work well and I look forward to seeing how they develop over the next several months. I anticipate that the variety of buildables and researchable technology will expand greatly, as we have seen in Klei's other titles already.
This is an easy game to grasp, but very difficult to master or even keep balanced at times. The complex, interwoven systems play off one another in sometimes diabolical ways: Think you have lots of food stored? Oops, your binge-eater got stressed and just polished off the entire stock of mush bars and lice cakes. Think you have plenty of oxygen production? That slime you tunneled through is now giving off poisonous gas and needs to be scrubbed from the atmosphere before everybody gets sick and starts vomiting spores. Or the electrolyzer is putting out a lot of hydrogen you didn't plan for, and the lightweight gas is flooding those tunnels up above and keeping your colonists from building that water pump you so desperately need.
Things to know: Research should be your top priority after you build your first outhouse. The weight and pressure of gasses matters. (Liquids, not so much yet.) There are only basic tools available to meet your colonists needs at this time, but they can be combined in some suprisingly clever ways. The load on your electrical systems should be planned carefully, or you will find your colonists constantly running around, spending all of their time fixing blown wiring until you run out of metals altogether. Look for Natural Gas and Steam vents and start building toward them as soon as you practically can. You'll probably start to feel the need for those resources before you can get there anyway.
In-game object models, while polished and well-animated, lack in much variety. (One painting, one sculpture, one floor light, one ceiling light, one station for reducing stress, etc.) Certain tools can be a bit clunky to use at times, and don't always work reliably. I am sure these issues will be addressed by the developer, however, so patience is called for. So far, they haven't broken the game for me, only made it slightly tedious to manipulate at times. Saving and restarting the game seems to fix these problems. In-game alerts and notifications are very unobtrusive, but frequently have a specific sound associated with them. You'll need to be paying close attention if you don't want dead colonists.
Overall, I have felt continually challenged at every step of the way by OxyNotIn's play mechanics. But after surviving with 7 colonists for 100 days with no deaths, I feel like I have a solid grounding in the basics. I can also tell from the tools I haven't made use of that there is a lot of complexity I haven't uncovered yet. ('Hot' showers, anyone?) I look forward to seeing what challlenges the game will throw at me next.
Incidentally, this games shares some close ties with Dwarf Fortress, Rimworld, Starbound and Factorio. Having said that, the developer has taken a different approach to many of the mechanics that have made those titles popular, and it works well to form a cohesive whole.

If someone reading this is concerned about the game due to the voice acting change/gameplay, I'll
remedy your worries. I've read reviews in which people claim this game does not stack up to the original Life is Strange and I must wholeheartedly disagree with them 100%. I love this game probably more than the original and I did not think that was possible.
I pre-ordered this and waited to play it until all three of the main episodes were released. This review will not include anything on the Bonus episode which is expected to be out early 2018. With that saaiiiiidddd--
1. Chloe VA changes:
Ashly Burch (who played Chloe in original LiS) will always be Chloe to me. No one can really replace that. However, I'd like to point out that BTS takes place in May 2010 while OG LiS takes place October 2013. Rhianna DeVries (BTS Chloe) does a FANTASTIC job, truly. She is not Burch so that little hint of spunky fire isn't present in BTS however, I think DeVries has her own charm that is really nice in a younger Chloe (albeit only three years). People complaining that they cannot tolerate the difference, in my opinion, are just close minded about it all.
2. Gameplay mechanics:
I've read concerns about what the game would be like without Max and without her time-rewinding power. I was rather skeptical about this too but I assumed the devs would throw something together. They did..sorta? There is a mechanic called Backtalk. It's...very appropriate for Chloe, honestly. I suppose the downside is that I was afraid to use it half the time as I did not want to make some situations worse (I plan on going back with a second playthrough to explore said options). You may have read that this is not so much a video game but more of an interactive novel? I would have to agree. Don't get me wrong, I enjoyed the story and cutscenes but I feel like the player should have had a bit more exploration available to them.
3. Spoilers! I'm slapping a tag over this so don't hover over or w/e unless you want to see!
cough cough
TLDR: it's a lot better than you think it will be. truly.
I can't wait to see what happens with the bonus episode and while part of me is glad Ashly Burch will be returning, it sort of ruins my whole "young chloe=DeVries, older chloe=Burch" thing. that's assuming "Farewell" is really the last moments between Chloe and Max before Max moves.
anyway, please give this game a shot if you have doubts! It's worth the money. ♥

There are 2 simple components that could make the game much more manageable.
1: Make tracks easier to download, and save them to the game's files without the need to take a tutorial to do so. This can be accomplished by simply the server owner ticking a "allow download" box, and giving us a simple "download this track" option.
2. Make the physics engine more forgiving of mistakes committed that happen 9 times out of 10 by complete accident. Give us options to correct our angle midair, point the nose of the car downward so as to prevent bouncing off of the side of the track. The option to turn your car in midair and to correct your positioning midair would prevent SO MUCH frustration and allow the player to make more percise jumps much more easily than if they were flung off of a ramp, with the correct angle expected to be taken before gaining altitude. Excuse me if I didn't have the split-second reaction time needed to correct my angle before flying off of a ramp. It really is not my fault when I cannot correct a mistake that was made by accident.
Overall, the game needs to let us download tracks easier, so we can better learn it in our off time when we are not playing multiplayer where the time limit for learning a track is not nearly long enough 90% of the time. Some of us require hours of constant practice in order to make sure that we are familiarized with a track's layout before we can start aiming for shorter and shorter completion times. Or, even better, have a practice server option so players can judge your track, practice it, and familiarize themselves with it. Secondly, all I want is to be able to correct my angle in midair. That's it. Being able to steer your car in mid air would correct so many mistakes, and would make even the toughest track layouts just a BIT more fair and manageable.
Now, given my gripes so far, there are really only two issues I have with this game, despite them in my opinion, being major flaws. Everything else about this game, from the track editor, the car editor, mod support, and the sheer intensity and adrenaline rush you get when you go full speed is absolutely stunning. All I want is easier track downloads for practice, and midair correction. LITERALLY nothing else needs to be fixed.

I wanted to like this game pretty badly, as the reviews and description for it had me kinda hyped. Unfortunately, I just couldn't get into it enough that I would recommend it to anyone.
The main issue is that you spend more time clicking though dialogue than fighting, and where that may work for Mass Effect and similar games, this one has nowhere near a strong enough storyline to support that. I felt like I was trapped in a bad anime- everything was over-cliched (seemingly on purpose- I hope), and there was no interaction or input from the player at all. This is coming from someone who likes both anime and anime-based games, as well. I feel like some sort of dialogue options, main character customization, or ability to make decisions regarding the story might have done a lot to make me feel at least slightly invested, but as it was I felt like a passenger just along for the ride, and lost interest quickly.
I also feel the story is too silly and over the top to try to throw in existential questions about the humanity of your human tanks, or to make you try to feel bad for seeing them die in combat- it just ended up feeling so out of place, like they were trying to tell two different stories at the same time. Which is overall sad, because I think those things if better executed or embedded in a less silly story would have been great hooks for a player's interest.
The combat is okay, but it's not deep or complex enough to save you from the story. Directing your units in combat felt clunky in some way I can't quite put my finger on, but probably would have become familiar enough over time to not be a concern, had I been engaged enough to continue playing.
In short, I don't remember how much I paid for this game, but unless it was under 2$, I feel it was too much.

Best See-How-OP-You-Can-Make-Your-Units Simulator I've played this year! Not since Disgaea have I had so much fun modding out my units to insane levels. Assault Tanks that can nuke half the battlefield? Scout Tanks than can recon the entire map at once? You can do all that and more in WotHT.
I've sunk about 30 hours into the game so far and still haven't beaten it. I was a little hesitant to write a review early on since the game seemed rather simplistic and I was worried it would be too short or not have enough variety to last but the tank development and modding always keeps things fresh and if you like buffing your units up until they're crazy powerful, you'll get plenty out of this game. It may not be as pretty or complex as games like Disgaea or Advance Wars but it's still good in it's own right.
I do have some minor quibbles, though. 1) The UI is very unintuitive. I could make a long list of minor tweaks that would make it very much improved but after playing for a couple hours you get used to it. 2) The game is pretty easy. Part of this is due to the fact that you can develop your tanks at your own pace, regardless of the story progression but even then, they could have made the missions more difficult expecting you to develop strong tanks. 3) The game is a little grindy. If you want to keep up on tank development you tend to go through a cycle of: beat a new mission, replay that mission 3 more times to stack extra supplies, proceed to the next missions, beat the new mission, replay that mission 3 more times to stack extra supplies, repeat. It's not terrible since, like I said, the missions aren't that difficult but I feel something could have been done to make replaying missions a little more interesting.
Overall it's a fantastic game, though. I highly recommend it if you have any interest in strategy games like Disgaea or Advance Wars.

Giving this game a thumbs up based on Early Access status.
It's fun, 16+ hours in and looking forward to the next update.  If you are looking for a polished game, with no bugs this is not the game for you, but worth putting on  your follow list.

Cons: The build priority of the colonist is a bit wonkers, and the tools to set priority don't always work.  At times (without cheats) you're at the mercy of what ever the colonist think should be done first.  Often you will find a colonist build a new facility only to have the build the wrong door first, and without additional raw building materials they will dye of hypothermia.
That being said I like it, I like it a lot.  I have played several Early Access games and this is one that I will follow regularly.  Is it worth at buy, yes, especially since it is on sale this week.  But be aware it is underdevelopment and you will encounter bugs, and things that don't work as they should.  It's challenging, and entertaining!

As you advance in play, more tools become avalible and you need to adjust your systems to adapt to the new tools.
The learning curve is high. Not quite a much as DF, but more than most games of it's ilk.
If you like organizing systems and optimzing  them, I believe you will be satisfied with your purchase.  Plus the little guys are cute... with thier eye's full of tears... crying a river (no really).
I just wonder now, why I didn't buy this game way back when I saw it, but decided not to.

Once again WayForward have delivered a wonderful adventure. Though different in structure, Half-Genie Hero retains its predecessors' exploration-heavy gameplay, encouraging players to revisit and eke out every secret from its varied levels. The move to hand-drawn HD visuals worried me at first glance, but in motion it's utterly charming and the attention to detail is excellent. Music maintains the very high standard of the series, and our lovable cast of heroes and rogues drive the lighthearted story full steam ahead.
Though not a challenging game by any means, Half-Genie Hero keeps the player on their toes with its abundance of secrets and a dash of precision platforming. The highest recommendation.

The fourth game in the Shantae series is another instant classic. While not quite as good as Pirate's Curse, it offers snappy controls, plenty of movement and combat options, and a solid (if episodic) storyline with the series' trademark adorable pitch-dark humor.
Shantae herself controls as wonderfully as always. Once again possessed of her genie powers, she learns transformations from each stage or from hidden items. Most of them, such as the elephant (which can crush blocks) and the mermaid (which can swim freely underwater) are primarily movement-focused, and open up new areas of each stage.
Ah, yes ... stages. And therein lies the only problem with Shantae: Half-Genie Hero. In previous games of the series, Shantae would travel across the land, face a number of challenges, and then open up a dungeon for exploration. These dungeons were very much in the Metroidvania tradition, and navigating them successfully was the game's primary intellectual challenge.
In Half-Genie Hero, the dungeons have been removed entirely; at the point in each stage when you'd be unlocking them, you go directly to the boss fight instead. The stages are mostly slightly longer than before, but not really enough to make up for the loss. A couple of them -- Main Street and a late-game castle -- remain downright puny.
This makes the game's other negative more serious: the amount of BACKTRACKING. In the previous games, you mostly returned to old areas to seek out power-ups like life bar powerups or caches of treasure. While those are still here, some of the stages have little corners and nooks that contain MANDATORY items, including a transformation without which you can't even enter the last level! It honestly seems like you're intended to replay every stage to date whenever you get a new movement ability, or else take an amount of notes on obstacles that would put a JRPG to shame. (And even that wouldn't help in a couple of places -- I only found two crucial items by exhaustive searching.)
All of this shouldn't put you off the game, though. Shantae: Half-Genie Hero is linear, sure, but you'll still get many hours of sweet gameplay for your admission fee. It's absolutely worth the price, even if it doesn't quite live up to its immediate predecessor.

So this is my third time reviewing this game. This update includes the DLC Risky Mode and Firends Forever.
Pros of Orginal:
Good music
Good graphics and animations
When there is voice acting it sounds good
Levels have many secrets
Gameplay wasn't too hard or easy (for the most part)
Smooth controls
Cons of Orginal:
Story is very lacking and feels rushed at points
Risky is pure evil despite what happened in the last game (Pirate's curse)
Levels were short and linear
Difficulty spikes because of different mechanics (such as the slide or using transformations for difficult sections)
Overal fixes:
Underwater mines now show explosion effect (No longer causing confusion)
Hypno Baron's castle can no longer be flown over at the outside area (at least in hardcore mode, not sure about orginal)
and some other small fixes I can't think of at the moment
Hardcore Pros:
Enemies are actually a threat and take more damage while doing more damage (although some enemies do way too much in my opinion)
Enemy attacks are faster and aim more for Shantae
Deserves the name "Hardcore mode"
Hardcore Cons:
Enemy placement can feel just jerkish and annoying
The amount of enemies is way too high
Some enemies doing way too much damage for normal enemies
Bosses take too long at times or don't give you enough time to attack their weak points (Giga Mermaid is the worst in this case)
The first phase of the last boss has an instant kill attack (which is cheap not hard)
Risky takes even longer to defeat (doesn't help that if you die on the last boss you have to face her again)
The difficulty spikes from the orginal feel even worse and I hated them
It made this game a bad experiance for me (I loved the orginal story a lot and made me a Shantae fan but this made me feel like crap and I didn't enjoy playing it)
Overall I feel like people should play the orginal and should only play the hardcore if they're looking a for a big challenge, It's a shame that the hardcore mode changed my opnion of this game so much but it feels like it was made just to be hard, not to be fun or fair. I still like the game and I'm still looking forward to the other modes (like Risky mode or the other playable characters) but if they end up with that same difficulty I might take a pass.
My scores of this game are
Orginal : 78/100
Hardcore: 60/100
DLC Review
Risky Mode
Pros:
Stages are made different and use Risky's skills to get through them.
You can do any stage in any order, makes for replayabilty and a change of pace.
Risky is good to control and her abilites are fun and helpful.
Upgrades to abilities that make them more useful.
Hard but fair.
Cons:
Stages use the same music and have some of the same collectable locations.
The Kraken ball is useless to upgrade.
Too many buttons to press to do complex tricks needed to progress.
Some bosses like Giga Mermaid last too long.
Huge difficulty spike at the last level.
Friends to the end
Pros:
Three unique characters to play.
Level up system is cool and easy to handle.
The stages are changed up again.
Retro music is used in stages that make the stages feel more unique to this dlc.
Each character is fun and easy to control.
Less button clutter.
Cons:
Collectables are useless and just there for collection.
Bollo and Sky's dream magic abilites are almost useless.
There is no way to upgrade health or abilites making this debatably the hardest mode yet.
Bosses are very stressful as you only have three health.
Only one way to heal without finding hearts.
In the end I liked Shantae Half-Genie Hero. The DLC added to what I already loved about this game and the characters are all very likeable and funny. The graphics are top notch and gameplay is polished. The DLC didn't have any bullcrap moments like hardcore mode but Friends to the end definitely put me in the hot seat a lot. I'm a bit sad to say goodbye to the game but I'm glad I played it and don't regret my purchase.
Risky mode: 72/100
Friends to the end: 65/100

Like a level 1 fireball that shoots 1 fireball to a level 2 fireball that shoots 2. Some transformations are oddly specific and have no other use to them.
Dances is what Shantae does, yet she does only one dance for all the transformations. Which was sad to see.... I liked where she had many dance moves (animations) when she would transform.
It seems art styles change with each game, and I am a huge fan of the Pirate Curse art the most. It had personality. I would blame transformations for taking up production time on making the conversation art better.
Puzzles are nearly nonexistant, or way too easy. The game was fairly easy. I did not have to worry about dying due to lose of hearts, well, neither did I in the last game....
There is no map this time, and finding things was easy. Some items made the game too easy. You can turn them off if you think that would present a challenge. Then if thats the case, don't look for items.

The good part is that they made it easier for you to travel where you want faster with a travel dance and a whistle to travel from world to world. A Little.
I still recommend this game. I wished I got wind of the Kickstarter so I could support them. I want them to continue making more Shantae games, but I think they need to look back at Pirates Curse, which I think to be the best of the series.

Let's get something on the table: I normally never liked Call of Duty. Like many other people, I thought the series was a boring year after year rehash of the same tired shooter mechanics. However, Black Ops II blew me away. I originally rented this game for Xbox 360, and I liked it so much that I had to pick it up for PC.
Going into this game initally, I wasn't sure what to think. The first Black Ops, was the only Call of Duty that I really ever liked (World at War was okay, but I'm not a fan of any of the Modern Warfares). I thought Black Ops had a great story, very interesting characters, and very basic but fluent shooting gameplay.
Black Ops II took everything I liked about Black Ops, and made it even better. The story is extremely entertaining and well-written. For the first time in a Call of Duty game, there are multiple endings based on your choices during the campaign. Not just two or three, but six different endings, plus about a dozen different paths through the game. And each ending is sincerely different, and they all carry a unique feel and tone.
This is also the first Call of Duty to let you customize your loadout (including perks, attachments, grenades, and even weapon skins) before each level. Yes, there are perks in the campaign. This doesn't seem like much, but it's nice to be able to tailor your starting loadout to your personal style of play.
As far as multiplayer, I am thoroughly satisfied. I never really got into the CoD multiplayers on PC before this, so I don't have much to compare to, but overall I am very happy with the experience. The action is fast-paced (especially during hardcore modes) and very engaging.
In conclusion, this game, plus the first Black Ops, changed my opinion of the Call of Duty series (or at least Treyarch's additions to the series). If you're a CoD hater, then I highly recommend giving this game a try, as it may well change your perspective (play Black Ops first to understand the story). This really is a great game, and I feel that it would reach a broader spectrum of players on the PC if it didn't have the words “Call of Duty” slapped on it.

I have yet to try this game in multiplayer/Co-op. The comments below are for single-player only.
Visuals in the game are of above average quality. Music is excellent for the genera. Default factions are all quite unique and seem very balanced--something that is all too rare in most games. Gameplay is generally quite relaxed and has a very sandbox feel. There is no "pressure" to jump from A to B to C at a breakneck pace. Interface/controls have a decidely tablet feel, but work perfectly with mouse and keyboard.
As others have mentioned, both as a pro and a con, the game is very grindy. As someone who enjoys seeing everything and maxing out traits et al. this will take an exceedingly long time to achieve. There are situations required to unlock certain ships, the ability to upgrade crew/gear and level up your general character and traits. There is a significant degree of customisation available.
Windward, however, is no Pirates! and it does not try to be. It lacks some of the depth of that pinacle of swashbuckling games. There is no naval or ground combat to capture towns/cities. There are no duels, no armies and no capturing of enemy vessels. There is no flotilla/fleet and, thus far, there is not quite the same emmersiveness in diplomacy as was present in Pirates!.
Windward, however, is still very enjoyable and has vast room for customisation and growth, wrapped in an atmosphere which encourages a more relaxed gameplay.

Maia is an intelligent, engaging, darkly humourous game. The overall feel is an enjoyable blend of contemporary sci-fi and 70s retro. It's a base management/survival sim that takes healthy splashes of inspiration from games like The Sims, Dungeon Keeper and Evil Genius. It's rich in character; touches like colonist-created, programmatically generated music and haiku, and colonist skillsets like cat appeasement and lukewarm tea brewing, add an undeniably charming flavour to the game.
In action, it's a constant, remarkably challenging exercise in staving off disaster, whether caused by your colonists' stupidity, the environment's general malice, your own ineptitude at the sheer complexity of colony management - or, admittedly, the occasional bug, as the game is still very much a work in progress. That complexity is both one of the game's biggest selling points, and one of its biggest hurdles; the sheer intricacy of the simulation's modelling gives the game enormous depth - if you can navigate your way up the remarkably steep learning curve.
The game discards many of the usual crutches of simulation and management games. The inability to directly control your colonists certainly adds to the challenge, making the gameplay experience more one of orchestration than direct management; likewise the lack of a comprehensive, point-by-point UI - beyond the basics, the stats and status of your base and colonists are communicated more by visual and audio cues than direct notifications. The overall sensation is one of trying to conduct an orchestra comprised largely of simpletons, playing music utterly unfamiliar to you, where a quarter of the instruments are invisible, another inaudible, and nobody thought to bring any sheet music. It's unashamedly difficult, but deeply satisfying one you manage to get a handle on things.
The game is absolutely still a work in progress, but with enormous promise. The developer, Simon Roth, is active and engaged, and calling him deeply deeply invested would be an understatement. I look forward to watching it grow and flourish towards full release. Highly recommended for anyone who enjoys sci-fi, has a penchant for micro-management, and is perhaps just a bit of a masochist.

I didn't manage to get much time on this game due to study taking priority, but from the miniscle amount of time I did get I can say this; it's fun!
The game is a simulation of sorts of trying to colonise an inhospitable planet. There are many dangers present, such as colonist incompetence, your own incompetence (yep! My first play and everyone died of hypothermia), planetary dangers (earthquakes), equipment failures, solar flares/radiation. A bit like a Sim-something game, scaled down and focused on the premise of colonising - well okay, similar in scope to "The Sims", but Mars!
Colonists all have their own personalities and skillsets, and as such are more/less suited for particular tasks. Getting a random song or poem from one is a charming touch.
It is a very interesting game, and one that is gaining more depth and complexity as time goes on. It may be early-access alpha level, but the game already has more than enough in it to entertain for hours; I can see myself getting lost in it easily.
The developer is incredibly active, both on social media, as well as posting a game changelog on their website and in the games news section on Steam. Seriously, check out the news section! They are very passionate about their game, and this shows heavily in playing it.
If you like the idea or premise behind "The Sims" but didn't like the mundane setting of it, maybe this will tickle your fancy?
Oh and did I mention it has humour?

The story was a risk for the developer which definitely payed off but, while it was absolutely the best choice, I feel the intentionally bland marketing limited sales a bit and pushed the impact below the radar a bit. Please hold out through the end for this one, you owe it to yourself to dig into this story and let it impact you, however it touches you. Even if you find it hard to play. There is so much more I'd love to say and discuss about this game but I've already said too much. Just play this, as soon as possible.

PROS:
- Gameplay is classic Hitman, if you turn off the hints and instinct mode.
- Lots of different ways of completing a contract - rat poison, staging an accident, plain ol' fiber wire,   or a shot to the head-you name it the game has it.
- Paris mission is a proper sandbox - lots of opportunities, huge in size and scope.
- Mostly clean UI, though navigating the menu is kinda iffy.
- Doesn't take much to get killed, blow your cover and you're going to have to restart the mission.
- Challenges are fun, but the devs need to incentivize it to keep players interested. It might not be for everyone though -  repeating the same mission with different variations. But Hitman is about experimentation, and there is ample scope for that.
CONS.
- Questionable navigation in the menu. Default keyboard mapping is off-putting at first - middle mouse to holster?  Button remapping is also limited.
- AI can be pretty dumb. I poisoned the drink of the target right in front of his bodyguard and he didn't notice just because I was in disguise.
- Minor animation issues - like putting a body in a dumpster isnt preceded by an animation of picking the body up from the floor.
- Graphics options are somewhat limited. I cannot seem to increase texture settings from low.
- Weird scripting issues. Dragging a body requires you to move yourself depending on the limbs you are holding.
- Frequent autosaves can cause FPS drops. No way to disable autosaving at the moment.
Regarding performance, the first training area is very densely populated and players are complaining about that. But the next level runs without problems. Oh I have a 10-YR-OLD-POTATO-PC with an entry level GT 730 DDR5 and the second segment plays at near 30 FPS with low settings and medium shadows. I don't care what you think of my standards but that's fine by me. Even then the game looks great TBH.
BOTTOMLINE: Expect to take a performance hit in very heavily populated areas.

The first time I saw War of the Human Tanks, I was put off by how obviously low-budget it is; that was a huge mistake. Apparently, the art style just needed some getting used to, because once I got into it, I thought the graphics were actually pretty good. There's full voice acting, fun animations and even some really catchy music that makes me itch to buy the soundtrack.
But what about the meat of the game? That, for me, comes in two packages (or perhaps Amasson boxes): the story and the gameplay. Let's get this out of the way: The story is awesome. I loved it. This is definitely not a "skip-the-dialogue" kind of game; in fact, after a certain point, the story became the main appeal. It's simultaneously lighthearted and grim, with a really interesting setting that ends up being much more detailed than you might suspect at first. There are four endings (two main paths, with two endings each) that all end up being pretty radically different and are all fantastic in their own way. I'm really in love with the setting, and all the little things you can learn about the rather disenfranchised battle-androids they call Human Tanks; the story really exceeded my expectations in every way. The translation is great, and the writing is clever, funny and serious when it needs to be; some of the big twists were huge gut-punchers. I'd definitely say the story was maybe the best part for me, and it'll stick with me and inspire me for other personal projects for quite a while.
Finally, the gameplay itself: it's great. My first playthrough was fantastic. The active-time battles with a heavy focus on recon and fog of war really keep things interesting, and even after you've played a battle a bunch of times you might still find yourself having trouble. There are plenty of different unit types that can switch up the way you play (though I tended to shy away from the poor Shock tanks because they just break my heart when they yell "I DON'T WANT TO DIE!" before exploding) and the long and rewarding research lines kept me grinding away at the free battles for a long time. Even the grinding was fun, though! I found myself enjoying the battles no matter how many times I played them, even when I got them down to a science. The AI is fairly challenging, and even with heavily-upgraded units, the later battles can really surprise you with how they masterfully crank up the difficulty. Naturally, the New Game Plus makes you feel a bit overpowered, and once you get to the highest levels of tech, your units are laughably broken, but that's kind of part of the appeal, and at a certain point I was just using the beefed-up units to fly through battles and get to all the endings anyway, since the story was really compelling. There are incredibly, incredibly challenging extra free battles, and you can play any of the myriad different story missions any time you like. I think my only complaint with the battle system was the 'evade' mechanic; it's basically just a random chance that, for no real reason, your attack just didn't work. It was pretty frustrating having sound strategy and fully-upgraded units but still missing because of a roll of the dice, and the evade mechanic never seemed to do me any favors either, but maybe I was just unlucky with the RNG. Either way, seeing as I put 35 hours into the game over just a couple of days, it clearly didn't dampen my enthusiasm that much.
After all that, my opinion is pretty clear; as of now, this is the only game I've bothered writing a review for, and it's because I loved the gosh-darn heck out of it. The story is fantastic, the gameplay is both super unique and endlessly engaging, and even if it looks a little low-budget at first, the entire game is surprisingly polished and clearly has a lot of heart behind it. I'd heartily recommend this to anyone who's a fan of military strategy, Fire Emblem-type games with a compelling narrative. Please, give it a spin-- and for god's sake, be nice to Heshiko!

It's often a fact that the games you play before and after a game can color your experiences with them. At least, if you're the type that plays large numbers of games like myself. War of the Human Tanks entered my library at a time when I was also playing another Japanese tactical game, Fire Emblem: Awakening. Thus it's rather natural that there would be a comparison.
But I find it kind to warn prospective players: Many will compare this to Fire Emblem or Battleship, but it's definitely NOT. Honestly, while it IS a strategy game, it's actually a pseudo-real time strategy, not a turn based game. This caught me off guard at first, so I feel it's fair to warn people.
Now, for those experienced with these types of games, it follows the pretty typical formula: You're in charge of an army, and your job is to accomplish objectives and not lose your command tank(s) before the match ends. The first matches are actually quite challenging as you get used to the systems, but once you start being able to field certain units, the game can become laughably easy. Don't get me wrong, the challenge is still there, especially if you're averse to grinding missions, but if you like the challenge you'll probably find yourself cranking up the difficulty and/or springing for the bonus maps.
So if you like Japanese style indie games with a sense of humor and don't mind sending cute little tank-girls to their deaths (seriously, there's a unit whose specific existence is to suicide bomb the enemy. It's the cheapest unit, and screams that it doesn't want to die as it explodes.) this is the game for you.

TL;DR: A wonderus harmony of what could well be some of the best platforming, exploration, and FUN I've ever had! I'm a gamer of over 25 years, and this game is simply AMAZING! New features: More direct level designs, a fresh "2.5D" graphics engine with HD support (4k+), AMAZING animation,  fun and memorable soundtrack you'll be humming all day long, and 10+ hours of gameplay. Super cute characters, PG-13 animated boobies on nearly everything, and nearly everything dances! Oh, and it's NOT a frustrating roguelike!
Long review:
Graphics: 10/10. Supports 4k+ resoutions. Beautifully animated (hand-drawn, not "flash game" type), "2.5D" graphics. Everything is bouncy, round, wiggly, jiggly, and FULL OF LIFE! Such talent and effort! Even the backgrounds are animated, every enemy, all the widgets, everything! If I could give an 11, I would! Thank you for raising the bar on what a modern platformer should look like!
Sound/music: 10/10. Beautiful, level-matching, custom soundtrack with loop points, an energetic song with vocals, fresh and original. A TON of effort was put into this soundtrack! Quality over quantity, every song is unique and very memorable! I LOVE THE SNARE IN MERMAID FALLS (a'la Sonic 2)!
Controls: 10/10. Accurate, precise, fast and responsive movements. Flawless and natural feeling with a gamepad!
Gameplay: 10/10. Everything in the game "fits" and has a purpose. The level design is top-notch, reminiscent of games of old; nearly every level is like an onion, with multiple layers depending on your current abilities. They're not too mazey, not frustrating, yet they're challenging and clever. FUN BOSSES that aren't too frustrating or difficult! You never really get tired of revisitng a level and searching for treasures unfound. The only notch off a perfect score is the transformation selection system: it's NOT BAD, don't get me wrong, I didn't DISLIKE it, but it felt a bit out-of-place in this finely polished gem of a game. Noticeable when you need to change often in a level. I would have prefered a right-analog-stick menu, but I understand the choice that compromised between keyboard, non-stick gamepads, and xbox-style gamepads.
Story: 6/10. It's very fun and gives the game a way-better-than-most-platformers plot device. It's not going to bring you to tears or make you think about philosophy or anything beyond providing a fun plot device for the game to progress on.
Game Length: 8/10. I got about 10 hours out of my first playthrough, and managed 92% item completion. At the end, I was hoping for one last uber-boss to appear, becasue that would've been perfect. I haven't played the other modes as of this review (2/20/17), but I'll give them a try and see how long I can actually stretch this game out to.
Overall: 9/10. Buy this game, it's EASILY worth $20. You'd be hard-pressed to get a meal for two for that amount, a couple coffees, or a boquet of flowers. The developers put thousands of hours (cumulative) into this game, requiring decades of talent and learning; and it shows BIG time! EXCELLENT JOB!
Final thoughts: I've been playing platformers hardcore since the early 90's. I like some platformers, and I dislike others. I like my platformers to be challenging yet fun (like Mario 3 or Sonic 2), or deep and immersive Metroidvania 40+ hour games. This game filled my "challenging yet fun" bucket FULL of candy!  I dislike games like Megaman, I Wanna Be the Guy, or most "that's a game mechanic, not a glitch" type games.
I thoroughly enjoyed this game. Everything about it is fun, detailed and engaging. I love the new engine, and the animations stand out in the best way possible. I like the "like an onion" level designs, and I wish every level had the same depth that Mermaid Falls had, even if it were for some pointless loot and a completion percentage. I wanted to use the mouse (transformation) and spider a little more! I REALLY like how the levels are shorter, much less mazey, and don't require a minimap to navigate. Thanks for an immediately amazing, thoroughly fun and extremely well-produced game!

: It's simply overly beautiful. Cities are well crafted, just out of your reach. You can visit & admire the view, just that everything is treated like a 'back-drop'. Lots of detail & attention was put into everything.
-
: It's amazing when you're trucking while being able to haul goods. The feeling of having to be cautious, signaling, not hitting the curb, and having to turn on thel lights. Lots to pay attention to & get into habit-mode. Even being able to customize & such.
-
: Cabin shaking on bumps, the GPS, the horn, the way they sound, run, and operate. It's all interesting. Even the ability to buy & customize them.
: Previously cars & vehicles did not react to your signaling & presence. Thanks to one update they now do, and even honk when they see you as a pest. They give way when you signal, and they're aware of your presence.
: It's sweet how you have to stay at a red light. It get penalized when you don't, and you also are forced to kick that Grand Theft Auto habit of running lines to stay professional. Stay within the speed limit or get fined....There's speed traps.
: Even though there's no real damage, you do however have to repair from normal or AI stupidity. You have ot keep repairing from normal wear & tear, or else risk stalling & crippled on the side of the road needing to call a taxi.
: Love the whole photography bit of taking & saving images. It makes the game more fun with the fun side-things you're able to do. I was able to spam my gallery with them from my journies around Europe.
: The game is always updating, and something that keeps me drawn to the game. The more it updates the more willing I"m willign to stay to see what's new. I love seeing new "small" features being actual "big" ones to enjoy. It added the whole "AI interaction" when you blinker.
: The new heavy Cargo DLC adds to the game by adding nice new challenges as you truck around with heavier cargo. Things like heavy concrete slabs, cranes, transformers, trains, and etc. Backing it up also becomes a challenge when you reverse because of how the wheels assist you with turning that it feels like your trailer is skidding on ice. It's a nice challenge as you also squeeze by on certain roads.
- There's even more that I just want to list. That awesome feeling of exploring, seeing you & your drivers level, while also seeing the constant updates. Even the nice little features of monuments, war museums, planes flying, ships sailing, and guys cycling. Nice trains even coming & going at random.
-
: You're always penalized when the AI is at fault. Always finding myself cursing when I dent or get cut-off by these AI "greedy" drivers. They do react to you, just ignore everything else.
-
: It's a real shame that the cities in ETS2 behave simply like a place to go with landmarks being cut-off. Take Bratislava for example with how you can't go on the "UFO Bridge" (Novy Most), or with how Frankfurt & Paris both push you away from such. [Fixed in ATS, or so mentioned by devs].
-
: It's a real shame you can't see your own hired drivers with their own customized vehicles. Even if it's simulated, then pops up briefly for you to see. It bothered me how your hired drivers didn't bother to go trucking to a neighboring town or city to try and get a job back. This was a forced "low economic" feature that irritated me the most. They're intelligent & capable of improvising their way back since I was able to do the same.
-
: No official, though there is a nice 2nd party type. It's awesome when you finally do managed to play on there. ATS needs to make note of this to also find its way into ETS2.
Even so, this game is awesome. I love it, and still would play it with how much fun it is simply driving out accomplishing tasks. That feeling of detail alone is what is wanting me to come back in. European made games are so rewarding and so much fun. They know where the fun is at.

Welcome to the apocolypse!
Mad Max follows the format of Fury Road in a sense by immediately opening up with action.  Max's famous car, the Interceptor, is taken from him just before he is about to begin a periless journey across The Big Nothing.  Max's immediate goal becomes to find find a vehicle that can carry him through that journey.
You play the role of the titular character Max, road warrior and man on the run from his past.  Accompanied with the black finger hunchback mechanic, Chumbucket, you ride through the wastes that has become Australia (I'm assuming).
The main focus of the game is building your vehicle, The Magnum Opus, into the pinnacle of war machines.  Venture through the wastes collecting scrap (the currency of Mad max), fighting caravans of enemies, all while meeting new & intriguing characters.  Many opportunities lie out there in the Wastes!
You'll find this game to be well optimized to the point where it is shocking.  I never dropped below 60 FPS at any point in the game with maxed out settings.  Visual effects are impressive as well.
Gameplay is well balanced.  While you will do
of driving, you will enjoy it.  Only thing I bothersome was having to grind scrap to upgrade the Magnum Opus.
If you're looking for a new adventure in a ruined world then Mad Max is right for you.  So get out there and be witnessed!

It's Borderlands 2, the sequel to Borderlands (duh), a FPS in the typical cel shading look. It's bloody, violent, premature and doesn't take itself one bit seriously.
About the game itself:
Borderlands 2 is quite similar to Borderlands, at least in regards to it's mechanics and gameplay. It's got better graphics and overlays, a new HUD, new characters (without DLC 4, with 6) and a lot of new weapons. As you would expect from Borderlands, it's humour is rather "simple" and violent. Really not much to say as it is Borderlands in a nicer looking design and with other characters.
Pros:
-Randomly created weapons in enormous amounts
-Characters got individual Skill Trees with 3 paths
-One playthrough with one character can take 20-70 hours (depending on how much you explore the game and how many side quests, tasks etc. you absolve)
-Quite a bit of replayability
-One of the best villains in video game history
-Completely playable solo or with up to 3 friends in coop
-Giant, open world
-DLC add a lot of content
-Graphic style
-Humour
Cons:
-Quite buggy/glitchy
-Can be frustrating at times since dying grants you a short amount of time to kill an enemy in order to get back up, but enemies tend to run away from you and you may not be able to do anything at all if you die in a certain position or get completely annihilated
-Gameplay may not appeal to you as it is mainly the same despite different classes
-Player has no chance to interact in the story since you will always be told what to do
-Solution to challenges is almost all the time just running in guns-a-ablazing, no real other way to solve conflicts presented to you
-Tons of DLC are expensive
-Graphic style
-Humour
Personal opinion:
To my mind Borderlands 2 is better than Borderlands, which I already liked a big deal. While the game is definitely not of immense quality, I like it for what it is. I like the universe it creates and in which the story takes place, I like the way the story is presented (which is mostly a matter of taste, e.g. Do I like this graphic style? Do I like this heads up stupid humour?) and I like the gameplay. It's a silly FPS shooter that is supposed to be just that: silly and stupid. It's way more fun to play in coop, but such is the case in every game. I absolutely would recommend this to someone who likes to just play some casual games from time to time and to get a few good laughs out of them. If you're interested, you should pick it up when the Game of the Year version is for sale since the DLC offer quite some content but the casual price is not worth it in my opinion.

Welcome to Spec Ops: The Line. This game is set in a sandstorm ravaged Dubai, you are Captain Walker. You and your team of Delta Force Operators have been sent to recon the ruins of the "City of Gold" and report if there are any survivors. The gameplay is average, and the controls are pretty good but I did play this game with a controller so it might be worse or better with the good old keyboard and mouse. I recommend you buy this game at full price if you care more about a good story then great/good gameplay because like I already wrote it is just average gameplay. Even though it is average gameplay it does have some cool sand physics effects that make for a fun time and can really add to your overall tactics. If you care more about gameplay I recommend you pick this game up at a discount. If you just want to pwn some bad guys don't pick it up, this game is not for you. If you love the novel Heart of Darkness or the film Apocalypse Now, pick this game up now.

A decent and fairly well-made successor (or predecessor) to the original game. It doesn't quite capture the feeling of agency making your own decisions as well as the original game but with the limitations in the story it does well enough that your choices in this game affects its own world. Storytelling in this game is absolutely beautiful, quirky and sometimes solemn, the characters are well written and the story is a departure from the expectations of the previous game. If you're here to see the story of Chloe and Rachel up until her disappearance in LIS, this is not what you're getting. Instead, the game gives you a mere snippet of their relationship which makes Rachel all the more mysterious - a good thing for the character.
Unlike LIS, playing as Chloe doesn't give you time travelling superpowers, instead the novelty of the game is Chloe's ability to argue her way out of trouble or to get what she wants. Despite this however, there is an option to hold your tounge and let the story carry on without interference. A really silly addition to the game, but one I found very entertaining was the option to play two small D&D scenarios with Chloe's friends. They're not too short that they're a throwaway in the gameplay but not too boring or long enough that you would choose to skip them altogether (unless you think D&D is for nerds).
A story mechanic often used in the game is Chloe's very eerie dreams about her dad, they play much like the nightmare sequences from the original game though each being much shorter. During these dream sequences, Chloe reflects on her choices made in the story and what her dad might think of her. Another returning mechanic is the journal, photo (grafitti) collection and text messages all of which provide more insight to Chloe and the other characters. The game introduces several new characters into the story, all of which are unique to the game. Some old characters make appearances too, though not all of them can be interacted with and some are only mentioned, however some of them play a big part in the story.
The game's graphics are a minor improvement over the previous installment with better facial and character animations as well as a better interaction mechanic for the objects and people around the player. Despite the outcry before the game's release about the recasting of all returning characters, Rhianna DeVries does her very best job of emulating Ashly Burch's voice as Chloe. All that being said, I have only one gripe with the game which is it's lack of background noise and music. The game chooses to use most of its music from the band Daughter, hired to make the soundtrack for the game. The music isn't bad, but the most of the tracks don't loop and most scenes carry on much longer than the length of the track, which leads to a lot of moments where the only noises heard will be the dialogue. Besides the music from Daughter, there is also very little variety in the music featured in the game unlike the previous installment's massive collection of 145 tracks.
HOWEVER, my final verdict of the game is a positive one and to put it in numbers, the game scores an 8/10 in my book for its great storytelling and characters.

This game is one of the biggest pieces of♥♥♥♥♥♥I have ever played, quite the polished turd,  but still a complete disaster to play.
The game starts of strong  with an intriguing opening,  although you're not playing it it serves as a solid hook.  You're fed a lot of information about how mMax winds up in this game world,  and shown some stunning eye candy. This is an overly deceptive ploy as It's unique positive qualities come out here.    However after this point  you are bombarded with tedious side quests , mundane busywork, and tedious scrap grinding ( the curency of this game).   However, the game does not at all make you aware this is how the game is going to continue as.   I wound up playing through half of the game waiting for it to start only to realize THIS IS IT.
So lets start with a more concise list of the♥♥♥♥♥♥show that is this game.
-Melee combat is awkward and inconsistant:
It plays like a crappy version of arkham asylum,  the combos and skills are all fine.  The biggest failings however are in the camera and the parry counter moves.   Since the camera is often trying to be dynamic, sometimes slowing down for bulet time,  you'll often not see threats that are unblockable.  Have fun ruining your combo because you didn't see it!  Later in the game attacks you have to dodge and counterable attacks become the norm,  but if you're too far away from an enemy,  because of the buggy terrain or otherwise, you lose your combo.  Even timing things corretly  you CAN STILL MISS THE PARRY.  That's right,  thier reach  exceeds your parry range.  On top of that if you're in the middle of a combo there is no way to cancel out of certain moves so you will be hit without being able to counter. FUN
-Upgrading Max:
Remeber what I said about combos? THIS IS WHY.  You don't get exp,  instead you get mini achievments that are used to level you up.   Each level has 10 tiers and getting to 11 puts you at the next level at 1.  Sounds easy right?   NOPE,  see, later into the game THE ONLY WAY TO LEVEL IS TO GET 25 HIT COMBOS.   Which means you'll be locked out of  upgrades in the game till  you grind forever, because you didn't luck out with your combos.  Both this and the clunkiness of the combat could be fixed with some very minor tweaking but as is they are both MAJOR PROBLEMS as you spend most of this game in forts punching the homeless.
Vehicules:
For a game all about Mad Max the roadwarrior,  you'd think the game's car combat would be good,  right?  WRONG.  All the cars in this game control like they're made out of floaty hunks of♥♥♥♥♥♥butter.  Driving from point a to b is a nightmare and this isn't even including the random skirmishes you're forced into.  The cars do get better...at endgame.   No I'm not kidding, you need to get to endgame to have a car that is not complete♥♥♥♥♥♥to control. So you hit a rock  and your car will shoot into the air and then turn backwards every single time.   If an enemy car nudges you, you will either spin around completely or be magnetized to it and unable to move.  Picture that for the whole game.
Vehicular combat:
Now that you know about how bad the cars handle, lets move on to the combat,  don't even think about boarding a car roadwarrior style and blowing a guy's head off.   Instead use the fury road harpoon guns at varying effectiveness and rammming gently into the side of an enemy car for no damage for hours on end. The only consistently good weapons on the car are the explosive harpoons,  the shotgun , and the sniper.   The sniper can't be used while driving,  and the shotgun should be saved to slog through the melee sections,  so now you're left with a cannon that has 16 shots with limited ammo you need to scavenge. Sleeping dogs has FAR better car based combat than this and it wasn't even a big feature of that game. This game was focues around this ♥♥♥♥♥♥ combat.
Characters: There's like two,  and every npc that isn't them is voiced by the same guy.  I don't care about any of these people besides the mechanic and the dog.  The dog isn't even used in combat and stops being relevant a few minutes in,  while the mechanic is with you the whole time and his dailogue gets repetitive by midgame.
Bosses:  Or should I say boss.  What the ♥♥♥♥,  You get Stank gum,  and a guy who they cloned 10 times.  Enjoy.  And I guess the big bad who dies in the opening cutscene and is the guy from fury road for some reason.
Scrap:  Collecting thsi stuff is unrewarding as hell and you get most of your in-game cash by capturing scrap cars, and conquering forts.  Even scrap pallets and boss drops give you paltry sums of the stuff.  There's no point to looting locations other than for completionists sake.  Sometimes you can luck ouut and get 500 scrap from a tornado,  but normally you're only getting 2-6 pieces per drop with 50 for the bosses and pallets.  Abilities you unlock with levels cost about 80 scrap for the first level,  then the price shoots up to about 600 per level.  This is for around 20 seperate upgradable things
Weapons: You get a junk shotgun that turns into a quad shotgun.  That's it.   Sniper is used out fo your car only.  There's no revolver,  machine gun,  carbine rifle,  or handgun.  No,  not even his trademark doublebarrel.   Just a gun you fashion out of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t lying around.
Max customization/upgrades:
As you progress you will unlock cosmetic and utility upgrades for our hero Max.  However most of them make Max look unrecognizeable to the point that he looks like some war mongering homelsss biker from Texas.  Some of the best upgrades in the game are things Max would probably never even wear, let alone find in the wastes and completely break the immersion.
Random bugs:  Despite all it's polish, you will sometimes get out of your car only to be jetisoned across the wastes for no reason.  Or grab some scrap only to clip through the floor,  die,  and then have to restart an area.  Not to mention  Gpu  failing artifacts randomly appearing,  despite your hardware being fine.  THAT'S MAD MAX FOR YOU.  Please keep your hands and arms inside of the vehicle at all times while it shoots wildly into the sky and explodes FOR NO REASON.
Great,  now that that's all out of the way, lets move on to the good stuff:
Graphics and enviornments:  Graphically,  this is a beautiful game. Setpieces:  There's like none in the game, but the few there are are amazing.  I wish the game had more of these.
All in all,  don't buy this hunk of♥♥♥♥♥♥  I wish I'd pirated it first prior to buying it,  if I'd paid full price Idve been FURIOUS. Going to try to get a refund,  wish me luck.

Fight for survival by gathering everything you need to build and maintain your base, including food to eat, water to shower and run other equipment, power to keep it all working, oxygen to breath, and construction materials to expand (of which there are more than a few), all while maintaining important factors like air quality, by filtering out or pumping away bad gasses, stress levels, by keeping the place looking nice and not putting your inhabitants through too much hardship, and temperature, by any number of possible means.  Whether it's done by your inhabitants by digging out more material around you, or by pumps submerged in gas or liquid, operating all the equipment you need to keep these resources in balance will require a constant supply of resources, making you either continue expanding, or find ways to become "renewable" - something players of Klei's other big hit, "Don't Starve", should understand very well.  This is easier said than done, however, due to how interrelated everything is.
Be mindful how you go about this; there is a lot of complexity to this game, with many things indirectly affecting others, so you really have to keep an eye on all of it while you build up the base, because one problem can and will eventually lead to another if not dealt with.  Food, water, power, air quality, stress, temperature, and the resources you're consuming through one means or another to keep these in check will all have your full attention if you want to succeed.  That said, it seems to be done very fairly.  They could have gone for an unrealistic approach where nothing really has any ripple effects, or they could have gone for an approach I've seen in other games where very suddenly, and at any time, something will happen that was easy to miss and is unrecoverable from for some stupid reason, even though it shouldn't be, causing a downward spiral until it is truly hopeless, but they split the middle and made all the resources important, but not so critical that if missed momentarily cause the base to inevitably and unavoidably collapse.
And on that note, the AI seems to be very good under pressure.  Unlike some games where as soon as things start going badly the entire base just collapses due to the AI's inability to handle the situation, sometimes once things go bad, and sometimes even before then due to bugs, these little guys just can't be stopped.  They will continue doing just barely enough of everything needed to keep the base - and themselves - alive until the very last possible moment.  Only the most completely inept builder running the most hopeless base should find themselves with dead workers on their hands.  That said, as I mentioned earlier, there is a lot to keep track of, so don't let this make it sound like long term success is easy - it isn't.
The challenge of balancing everything as you grow, and the quest for a perfect base, all while being able to design the systems that keep it running make this a very fun game for me.  I played 30 actual hours in two days upon first getting this, seriously.  It was that addictive.  If that sounds like you, I'm sure it will be great fun.  That is to say it isn't without some bugs.  I've found the liquid plumbing system to have issues with all but the simplest of systems, but it can generally be worked around, and I assume it will be fixed eventually since this is still early access.
---
Here's a demo scenario, so you know what I mean about interconnected:
Start with basic food, made from dirt and water pressed together into a bar and deep fried (yes, they will eat that).  This requires power, just make a hamster wheel for now.  Make sure you've gathered enough metal for the electrical components.  Keep researching.  You need the other tech, but this takes time and electricity, time for while you must keep the base running on simple things.  Most people won't enjoy eating fried dirt and water forever, so you're going to need something to keep them calm.  You'll also need to make sure the air quality stays good, producing oxygen and containing pollutants, such as would be emitted from the outhouse.  Running the oxygen producers also requires electricity and a constant input of organic material you must dig out of the walls.  Fast forward now and you'll want to add a shower and proper washroom to replace the outhouse.  This requires pumping out water from somewhere, which requires more power.  You'll also want to make sure you don't use up all your water, so build a refiner to purify the used water back into fresh.  All of this electrical equipment is starting to get too demanding for hamster wheels; your inhabitants are spending nearly the whole day just running which doesn't leave them enough time for other important duties.  Build some power stations.  These require additional resources which you must find (coal or natural gas) or make (hydrogen).  They also require dealing with the polluted air, and pumping this gas around.  This additional equipment quickly significantly increases the load on your electrical system, causing a bit of a snowball effect, making you jump up from what you had to something "end game" in one move, more or less.  Oh, and those things that deal with the polluted air?  They also need plumbing tie-ins, so how much fresh water you consume and how much polluted water you produce could also really change here - make sure you have the equipment needed to deal with that.  You might want to use your polluted water to make fertilizer, especially since these units produce natural gas which you can burn for power, but they will pollute the surrounding area so keep it contained... oh, and don't run out of water.
My advise is to take it slow and careful, but be mindful of the resources you have on hand and don't go so slow you run out.  Also, be extremely picky about who you let into the base, and who you start with.  If you just pick any old person, it will make things harder.
That's just sort of the main points... you'll run into other little things along the way too, and each map is a bit different in the resources it has since they seem to be randomly generated.

Reviewed: Alpha 0.58 - 16th Oct 2016
TL;DR
Don't buy it until the AI/pathfinding got a lot better, or it's on sale for <10 USD.
It has a lot of potential, the core elements are there, and there are some interesting gimmicks but it needs to get better to be enjoyable IMHO.
---------
I WANT TO BELIEVE *insert X-files joke here*
I'm a sucker for survival/build-up games (logging ~1500 hrs in Space Enginners alone) and I've been watching & wishlisting this title for two years now.
Infrequently I've been visiting the store page of this title but was always repelled by the mixed reviews, their contents and reasons.
But this weekend was a 50% off special, so 'out of boredom' I finally picked it up, especially since in version Alpha 0.58 "AI has been tremendiously overhauled and improved".
I like the aspect that you do not directly control your crew in this game, you do have control over the IMP humanoid-bots and repair-bots, but you do not specifically tell your crew what they're doing when.
That's good in my books.
But it's not good if crew-members get stuck in the middle of a Workbench, or behind walls or in Atmosphere Generators. Also not good is when crewmembers infrequently dying of dehydration, even though there's like three half-full water-tanks to drink from.
What this game needs is an overhaul of the UIX; when every ~20 seconds a full-screen displayed warning been thrown into your face - stealing the focus - bcause your veggie-farms needing to be pitched, you're slowly turning into the infamous meme of fire-breathing Pepe, yelling at your monitor.
Frequently I had to abandon & restart my early-games, because of key crew-members being stuck, trapped or clipping into stuff. Like, remotely controlling a repair-bot. it's easily to drive it through walls, but you'll never get it back out of there, being stuck. you can't disassemble it because your crew-members can't reach it. When visual novel meets strategy game, the result is this game: War of the Human Tanks. Its simplistic art style compliments its simplistic gameplay, making a good game to pass time.
Like all visual novels the game has mulitple endings, however, here they are dictated through your performance rather than choices. The banter between the protagonists and his corp is that of slice-of-life anime, giving this war game a relaxed feel to it. As for the music, its quite good, most if not all of the tracks fitting the mood of the situation.
However, there are aspects of the game that gripe me. One is the level of grind that one has to do to even develop most of the tech. This is further compounded by the fact that you cannot cut out the animations to save time, so even if you are speed running to farm money, it still eats up a bit of time. Lastly, the game is a little too easy. I personally would have liked to have seen a "hard" mode that most Japanese games feature, where you get to start over against more difficult opponents.
All in all, a good game to pass time.

Shantae: Half-Genie Hero is an indie 2D Metroidvania platformer and the fourth installment in the series.
HGH boasts an enormous visual upgrade compared to its handheld predecessors, with smooth, fluid sprites popping against gorgeous 3D backgrounds. The sprites are lovingly animated and move with a bubbling energy, often, seemingly, in rhythm with the background music.  The game is a joy to the eyes and the ears, with an aesthetic integrity that's rare in indie titles.
These visuals compliment the story and characters of HGH. Shantae is surrounded by barely threatening antagonists and frequently obstructive friends, all of whom are charming and fun. Lacking a central antagonist for much of the narrative, the game is presented as a series of tangential episodes strung together by a vague goal, an undefined threat, and a series of humorous contrivances. As refreshing as this approach is, it often makes the game feel directionless. Further, whereas the previous installment gave Shantae a foil in the form of Risky Boots, HGH only casually touches upon the protagonist's relationship with her friends and enemies, making her feel unmoored in the setting.
As a platformer HGH gives a solid performance. Shantae controls with precision and grace in a world that makes her limitations clear; players won't struggle against false impressions of what obstacles Shantae is and isn't capable of surmounting. Puzzles are solved by transforming into various animal and monster shapes that are unlocked over the course of the game, most often at the expense of offensive capabilities. Combat is a fairly bare-bones affair, with Shantae being limited to a melee attack that's supplemented by underwhelming mana-dependent spells.
HGH is paced like a mad dash, with the game throwing power-ups and new abilities at players faster than they can find a use for them. Indeed, Shantae has a wide assortment of tools with too few obstacles to apply them to, and many of her more interesting powers go underused or are rendered superfluous by later acquisitions. Complicating this problem is all the backtracking that's required of a Metroidvania title; revisiting the game's small handful of areas quickly feels like padding, and makes replaying from the beginning feel unlikely. On the other hand, the dizzying volume of options available to Shantae by the end of the game will undoubtedly delight many players; for all of its backtracking, the sense of progress and growth is palpable.
While not without its flaws, it's difficult to not recommend HGH. The game is clearly a labor of love, with an emphasis on color and energy that's uncommon in today's industry.
