Windward starts out as a slow paced, calm and somewhat confusing game (what am I doing, what does all this stuff mean, what's my objective), but, once you start picking up quests and sailing around it becomes an enjoyable leisurely experience as you seek to upgrade your boat and your exploits grow the towns around you. The game could definitely benefit with some more content, and tweaks to some mechanics, but its quite a pretty sailing adventure capapable of entertaining you for a number of hours.
Windward's main lack, for me at least, was the way in which it handles the building of structures and the way the AI steals your exploration from you a bit. Whilst it is possible to create new towns (this isn't explained in the game but you'll encounter it as a quest) lighthouses and defensive structures (which mainly serve as distractions for pirates until they're destroyed, rather than actually being formidable), the ability to build these is restricted by the whims of the towns or finding a rare item (then it's great!) They are all picked up as 'quests' and to successfully complete the quest you're required to put it within a certain proximity of the town (I failed a number of these by apparently not putting them close enough...there's no indication of what's close and what's too far) you can however place them pretty much anywhere until you reach the limit for that section of map. It'd be nice if it was easier to obtain the item from a store for a hefty fee so at least you know you can do it.
As for exploring, your faction's AI will roam around finding towns and claiming enemies structures for you, and whilst this is a welcome feature when you go into contested territory and have pirates constantly claiming back stuff whilst you're trying to conquer the south, it takes away from the feeling of discovery and wonder a bit. That said if you go somewhere where your faction has no presence you get to discover however much you want until you establish a town (done so by taking a quest from a region you're in and then building it somewhere else).
Combat isn't explained but it essentially involves you positioning yourself to have your side facing your enemies and you'll automatically blast them. Additionally you get a number of abilities you can use, more of which can be unlocked through leveling up or by spending skill points. I found it enjoyable when I focused on speed and maneuverability with long range weapons, going circles around my opponents out of their range to keep my weak ship armour safe and sound. The nice part is that combat is, to an extent, largely optional. Players can choose to bribe or hire others to support them and you can always choose not to accept combat missions. Be warned, smuggling missions often make your faction start shooting you if you're doing something illegal, I didn't know this so I got a shock...
All in all Windward is a pleasing game, but it suffers from a lot of lacking conveyance. There's little to no tutorials or indications of simple things such as having new skill points available or that there's more you can do if you're just lucky enough to find an item. Introduction of more things to do (fishing, treasure hunting, town destruction and relocation) would be welcome features as it can be a bit repetitive after a couple of hours. With some more Age of Empire style mechanics this game could be a lot more enjoyable and long lasting (particularly with some more things to buy like more ships you can see from the start per faction, and sideways trees instead of mainly upwards ones). There's much more to this game than first seems, if they can improve their conveyance and let you buy more action enabling items (such as the building plans for towers and lighthouses) it'd be a much clearer and enjoyable experience.

One of the most overlooked games of last year, Mad Max is a truly fun game that is polished to perfection. While I have yet to complete the story, one of the most fun and exciting aspects of this game is the wasteland itself. The developers of this game created an environment and atmosphere unlike all other apocalytpic games, where the so called "wasteland" in Mad Max is very real feeling. While it's dead, in ways it also feels so alive. The driving is also an important factor in Mad Max, and this game hits the driving perfectly. The cars are well-balanced and actually feel as powerful as they look. Listening to the engine roar to life as Max gets in to drive is so satisfying. The final thing that really impresses me with this game is its optimization. I have very rarely, if ever, dropped below 60 frames per second. That says something about the developers and the time they put into this game, because most games now-a-days have awful launches and those first day patches just to optimize them. In conclusion, Mad Max is a fantastically designed game with beautiful graphics, realistic and fun driving, and a wasteland that's so dead but at the same time has never felt more alive.

Really fun cover shooter, it's worth every penny just to be able to complete the story of the game, played 12h out of it getting most of the achievements (all except the difficulty ones). If you are hesitant on paying $30 then just wait for a sale, this game is well worth $10-20 in my opinion.
There are a few choices that change a little bit the game, you can replay the chapters with such choices for the achievements and see the little nuances of the story. If you like some challenge you have 2 higher-than-Normal difficulties, personally I was satisfied enough with completing the main story and seeing the little twists that came when you made different choices in the 3 or 4 chapters that your choices mattered (you have up to 3  different endings too).

Nice shooting and good difficulty levels, good cover mechanics although sometimes it was slightly frustrating that some big structures haven't a cover area or that you instantly cover instead of keep running. The weapon selection is good and it adapts to your preferences (shotguns, ARs, SMGs, snipers, RPGs, grenades, etc).
Great visuals, the world is very polished and it truly shines in some mirage sequences and at the radio tower, you also have some pretty memorable moments, including a Lord of the Rings reference. Also a thing I loved is that you do notice the main characters wear and tear during the game, you see them bruised and you see them bleed, that makes them human and not Rambo-like.
The game is a masterpiece regarding story, what seemed like another military shooter takes quite some twists and turns and by the end of the game *SPOILERS ALERT*
which makes you question a little bit about the nature of war instead of just playing the same old "Freedom Police vs Terrorists".
I loved this game score, it did immerse me pretty well into it and also have great sounds, the gun shooting, bullet impacts and wind effects are remarkable. In a few chapters you listen to some pretty great funky music that blends really well with the story (yeah, I was surprised too), the voice acting is pretty solid and make the characters believable to the point you care about their fates.

The original game is an artistic masterpiece as I mention
Naturally to have the chance to deeply explore more of the characters we fell in love (or hated) from the original within
is an experience no one should miss.
Make no mistake. Before the Storm is true to the Life is Strange franchise. Well, it is kind
that this franchise has only two titles so far with a sequel in the works. The magic of the game comes from compelling storylines and storytelling,
characters and a sense of adventure, internal conflict, intra/interpersonal relationships, loss and sorrow, finding happiness in little things and other people. You cannot go wrong with Life is Strange. The game offers messages that reverberate across generations and you'll find all sorts of people enjoying and contemplating what this game is all about, regardless of their backgrounds. Sure, it might be more appealing to young adults, but that doesn't mean it's only for those people to enjoy, laugh and even cry about.
Before the Storm takes you back in terms of the game's lore. Chloe Price and Rachel Amber are the focal points of this story and with good reason. Theirs is a tragic/hopeful tale of coming of age, filled with many forks in their journey through adolescence. What messages you extract from your playthrough is up to you, be it with the choices you make... or better yet, the choices you
make.
To go deeply in depth with Lis:BtS story is counter-intuitive. You need to play and experience firsthand what the game has to offer. If you're familiar with the original, then you know what to expect in terms of gameplay. But for those who delve into the world of Arcadia Bay for the first time: You play as Chloe Price, a teenager student of Blackwell Academy in the fictional town of Arcadia Bay, Oregon. You're a delinquent as you skip school, smoke pot, attend punk rock concerts without ID and lots of other stuff you might expect from a person fitting that stereotype. But underneath all that teenage angst, lies a real broken girl who lost her father in a car accident and her best friend Max has abandoned her. You're all alone in a world which scares you, in a world which you hate, in a world which seems against you only to find a ray of sunshine, a beacon of hope in the eyes of Rachel Amber, a top of the class student at Blackwell Academy which behind that model exterior hides a world not unlike your own.
How you choose to play out the events between Chloe, Rachel and the family & friends surrounding them,
in fact the whole game. You'll make tough and easy choices, say stupid or nice things to other people and you actions will shape the in-game world. And therein, lies the magic of Life is Strange.
Gameplay wise, there's about of 8-10 hours to enjoy, a few very easy 'puzzles' here and there (I enjoyed the 'backtalk' mechanic that Chloe uses to get out of a sticky situation) and some graffiti to express your teenage acts of rebellion! There's also a collector mode so you can get the collectibles you missed.
Of course for players who have played the original, we are left with some of the lesser aspects of the game. Mainly how the story plays out and some glaring mistakes that tarnish an otherwise fantastic experience. HEAVY SPOILERS AHEAD.
From a technical point of view, the game runs extremely well and smooth. The facial animations which were an issue for me in the original are better but not really as good as you'd expect; to be fair I believe that's more of a limitation of the game's engine rather than poor work from the developers.
The soundtrack is fantastic, with many original tracks which create a very appropriate atmosphere for several key moments in the game. There's pretty good music layering and even a zen mix-tape mode for people who really enjoyed the very fitting music score of Before the Storm.
So where does that leaves us with Life is Strange: Before the Storm? While I did find the original more powerful, that doesn't mean that Before the Storm is any less inspiring or any less thought provoking. The emotion is still there to be felt and the story is still captivating with its many twisted turns and real characters to interact with. Fans of the original will be hella satisfied with the extended lore and if you're one of the lucky few who haven't experienced Arcadia Bay yet, Before the Storm is a brilliant way to start your journey and then moving on to the original. I got the game during the Xmas sale and it was more than worth it, an absolute recommendation.

The gameplay revolves entirely around gathering resources to expand and maintain your colony, while ensuring the survival of all the inhabitants or duplicants as they’re called. The duplicants are random, and have different stats, passive abilities, and stress responses.
Dig, dig, and dig some more. Gather resources to build to survive. Along with the initial crafting cost, some buildings will need to be resupplied regularly if you want to keep using them. I found that turning buildings on or off helped a lot to conserve precious resources. It takes a lot of building and expanding to gather enough resources to even come close to making the base self-sustainable (in my 32+ hours of playing, I still haven’t been able to achieve it yet)
Managing your population also plays a role. I’ve found that recruiting too many duplicants is way too much of a strain on resources, so I wound up declining new recruits very often. (So far, my most successful colony still has only 5 duplicants after 69 cycles.)
When things inside the base start to go wrong, it can trigger even more things in your base to go badly, and spiral out of control if you don’t pause the game, and address the issues quickly. There were many times where I felt like my colony was on a path to extinction, and I wasn’t sure if I could fix the problems. Fortunately, every cycle the game auto saves, which is really nice to have in case you completely screw up and kill everyone by mistake. I think the auto-saves eventually overwrite, but there are still plenty available to revert to.
Researching new technology in game is essential for progress, and you will be able to learn everything. You’ll need to set up a stable power grid to keep everything up and running. Things like gas and liquid filtration become very important as the colony grows. Filtering out toxic gases and carbon dioxide, while pumping in oxygen, but at the same time managing the gas pressure and temperature in each of the areas as well. Some structures consume one type of resource, and generate others, such as the scrubber that uses clean water and carbon dioxide, but produces polluted water as a byproduct.
Oxygen Not Included is a great game. Even in its early access state, the game is very fun and very addicting. There is plenty of stuff to build and manage with more updates being added, the game has a ton of potential. I recommend it to anyone who enjoys base building survival strategy games. Just keep in mind that the game is not finished yet, so if you’re turned off by early access titles, then you might want to just wishlist it for later.

The game's mechanics are enjoyable at some times, but can also make you rage the next time. For the most part the combat is great other than a few tiny things. The crafting in Rust seems perfect, in my opinion, I feel like it beats many other survival-based game's crafting systems. Rust's building situation seems kindve weird to me at some times but overall seems very good.
I feel like Rust sometimes has a lack of content making it boring or repetitive which is one of Rust's biggest cons in my opinion. But as I said earlier on, if you jump in with a friend or two it will spice up the game for a bit.
Overall, I think that Rust is worth the $20, the game may seem very frustrating or boring sometimes, but there is usually a way to mix it up. It has entertained (and made me rage) for 178 hours and is one of my favorite games!

I used to love DayZ standalone. I never played the mod, as I wasn't into PC games when it was popular, although I've seen plenty of gameplay, have played ArmA 2 OA a good amount, and have played Exile on ArmA 3. DayZ standalone has always been a buggy mess, but a lot of things have changed since launch, for better or for worse.
I'll start with the pros - the game looks beautiful, or at least a lot better than it did at launch, and it runs a lot better too. Really, that's about it. I can't think of anything else that has made the game significantly better since launch, except maybe vehicles, but I'm not a huge fan of how those have been handled.
Cons - I'll start with the biggest one; the game is pretty much dead. When the game launched, and for about a year and a half after that, there was usually at least 15,000 people playing. These days that number is around 2,000, which isn't a huge people, but it just means that most people have lost interest in the game, which can be attributed to the lack of care and bug fixes this game got.
Another big con is the fact that the mod for ArmA 2 offers a lot more to do, with missions, helicopters, base building, etc. The standalone version of the game really only has PvP which, although exhilerating (pardon my spelling if that is wrong) and high stakes, is really the only thing to do other than loot. It becomes stale.
I would like to go back to my first experience with this game, which was basically watching two British guys play both the mod, and, when it came out, standalone. It looked fun, but I didn't give it much thought. In the summer of 2014 I was playing Rust one day while sitting in a Steam Call (gross, I know) and listening to my friend be force fed spaghetti while he was afk by a couple of his buddies. My friend then told me to get the game, so I had a friend at the time get it for me.
I was bad, but I was hooked. I had a group of people that my friend and I ran around with, and I had a good time. After cutting ties with them for a while I put the game down almost entirely, then a year later, in around August 2015 I joined the guys again and we played again, and that was basically the last fun I had with it. Coincidientally, in about April of that year the game took the hardest hit in players, losing about 4.5 thousand average players. The months before and after weren't great either, losing a little over 1.16 thousand average players and  2.75 thousand average players respectively.
TL;DR: DayZ Standalone is a game that had a lot of potential but disappointed everyone. It hs been over 4 years since the game released and we still have yet to see a beta version, although it has been promised. This game is dead, and for good reason. These words are bitter coming out of my mouth, as I have made quite a few good memories playing this game, but if you need your fix of high stakes PvP play a game like PUBG or Rust, as you will get much more enjoyment.

A fun survival game, if you can find people to play with!
The game is coming to the end of early access; no hard dates have been given by the developers, however speculation says early 2018 (February-March) we will probably see beta. They're developing a brand new engine just for this game!
Like most online games, if you can find people to play with consistently it's great fun. If you can't, then it becomes a game of how much loot can you hoard to yourself. Public servers are crap, there's not much loot to be found because people server hop to get all the gear. Private servers have a great amount of loot. On DayZ Civilizations (private server), the server restarts every six hours so that's how often loot resets. When searching for a server, choose the "community" tab, and on the right hand side, hit the box for "public servers" until it becomes an X. Now you're looking at only private servers.
The only servers (I only look at private, so that's what I'm referring to) that have a population of "high" are servers listed as PvP servers, or ones that say "PvP coastal tents" in the title; which means they have tents on the coast that have a lot of military gear you can grab for PvP. You'll usually spawn on the coast. If you're ever unsure of how many other players are on the same server with you, press "shift + tab" to bring up the Steam Overlay, then press the "view players" button. That'll show you everyone else on the server with you.
I absolutely recommend this game. It's a great amount of fun and it's exhilarating when you get an inch from death only to survive, or when you have a scary encounter with someone. But honestly, if you want to make sure you're not playing with yourself all the time you need to reach out to people to play with. Join me on DayZ Civilizations!

I first became aware of Maia back in 2012 when Kickstarter was in full swing. The unusual sci-fi aesthetics and interesting vision are what initially attracted me, and I continue to be impressed by how driven the developer is.
This is a god game with subtle challenges underneath. Challenges which may even change the way you view game design in general afterwards.
Why even mention the HUD? Well, rather than take the approach of giving the player an easy categorised spreadsheet list of all the various variables/states in the game via large sprawling HUD panels, Maia chooses to integrate much of that as items/signals visually within the world itself. It is this world which you'll spend most of your time interacting with as you expand your base, build machinery, craft autonomous robots, and battle the various hardships that colonising a harsh alien landscape requires.
This difference in game design approach isn’t for everyone, and can force the more casual gamer to rage, but therein lies the treat for those who persevere. Creating a large self-sustaining tech-enabled
colony from a few desperate souls is really satisfying, and you’ll end up more attached to it than just about any other god/sim game out there.
Sure, it does take some time to understand how the world works, and there are some quirks which may be bugs (it is in Early Access currently), but it makes for such a refreshing change from the sea of clone and asset store created games currently on sale.
As a fan of both the 80’s culture and electronic music in general, the general model design and music/effects are really top notch for a small studio, and thus deserve a special mention. I had flashbacks of Vangelis’ Blade Runner combined with Space 1999 and it’s a perfect fit for this type of game in my opinion.
If we’re lucky, we’ll see a Maia soundtrack release at some point.
For a game initially Kickstarted in 2012/2013, you’d be quite right to question when the release would be, especially as we’re now approaching 2017.
Thankfully, unlike many other games that become abandonware, the Maia build is still being actively updated with fixes and new content.
To give an example, I've recently seen the developer having to put in extraordinary work to fix problems for Linux users which were not caused by the game, but GPU drivers. I also heard they spent a huge amount of time trying to make the game run on older Intel drivers. These particular issues are also somewhat to blame for the slip in release dates.
That's commitment you don't see from AAA devs, let alone an indie dev.
You can clearly tell that this is a passion project, which more than likely means that development will continue for some considerable time irrespective of version numbering. Not only that, but the developer is extremely technically skilled, having written the actual game engine itself that drives Maia.
If I had any critisim of the developer, it would be the heavy reliance on Steam Early Access, but then this is more a business issue rather than anything else, and hopefully the future will be a bit brighter after the recent Steam changes and tweaked business models from lessons learned.
If you're anything like me, and have an interest in what's under-the-hood, you may be surprised to hear that the developer seems very keen to engage in that kind of discussion.
I've watched a dev twitch stream where a crash occurred. The dev then took viewers through code explaining a sizable amount, making a change, recompiling the game source, and playing the new revision. I don't think I've ever seen that kind of open engagement from a developer before.
See for yourself:
On top of that, they’ve also provided a publicly accessible site showing the code changes committed to the project:
Again, which other developer does this?!
If you want a new experience and appreciate the different approach Maia takes, then you will, I’m sure, see the beauty behind this one-of-a-kind labour of love.
Edit (Feb 2017): The most recent version of the game, 0.60 has lava (seen in original kickstarter art), and many, many fixes. In fact, the game has been fixed/tweaked in a huge number of places over subsequent updates such that it's hard to find any glaring issues. Very happy to see this and very impressed at the continued commitment.

A rich and detailed interplanetary colonization game that is as difficult as it is enjoyable. Start a colony from scratch with just enough to survive. Manage expanding the base with the complex energy, water, and oxygen needs of both the colonists and base itself. Perform vasts amounts of research (that the colonists decide on, not the player, which actually makes the game more interesting and unpredictable) that improve every aspect of the base, colonists, and robotics that help around the colony. And that's barely scratching the surface!
Don't let the Early Access scare you, Simon Roth and Machine Studios are one of the few that actually get it right. They put out constant updates in content and are qutie open with the community across social media. It's not hard to find out what's new, what's coming next, and what they have planned for the future.
I would STRONGLY recommend this game and look forward to see everything that they add to it in the future.

I was really looking forward to playing MAIA as I have been following it for a long time now.  After reading some positive reviews I thought I would give it a shot.  Unfortunately there are still many issues with the game and I cannot recommend it to anyone, even if its on sale.  One major problem would be with the AI.  The workers and robots  are so slow to respond and complete tasks that I alsways died from freezing.  All I needed to stop freezing is to build a workshop, wind generator (outside) and some wall heaters but this is almost impossible to complete because the workers refuse to complete the tasks or are too slow to complete anything.  Another problem would be the UI, there is no icons or buttons to show you have much power/water/food you have.  Instead you get emails after each day to update you with the amounts??  I understand this game is Early Access but it has been here about three years now, so I was expecting further progress.

First, let me say, it does have great progress so far, and comming along.  I think more people should support it, that said ...
So I went on a mission, where the mission items were timed (I really hate to be pushed on timers, not fun at all). But ok, not a huge deal.  Built what I needed to, down to 5 mins, put some items down, including the main mission item – a communications antenna.  Some people were doing nothing, and eventually started building.  Seems they didn’t get the memo that communications was the next mission item, so they left it last.  1.5 minutes left, communications still pending, people are walking around, and hugging, etc., and the timer is ticking away.  It eventually reaches 0, mission failed, and the colonists don’t give a damn, lol.
Ok, I think I put down too many items at once, so I did it a bit more controlled. There’s very little room for error, as you have to think minutes ahead (not seconds). Made it to the next mission item – also timed (argh). Ok, so started to clear an area.  Colonists are now complaining about needing sleep, and food, but the medical center and beds is the top priority?  I guess it is in case they die from hunger while working as slaves to build while starving to death because the timer doesn't have any wiggle room. I also needed more power, built another wind generator, then started the medical building, laid out the door, and 3 medical beds.  After 1-2 minutes, a colonist finally shows up to build it, and the door, and leaves the beds and takes off.  Ok, no problem, 1.5 minutes left, let’s see if anyone comes to finish the beds.  Timer runs out, mission failed, colonists don’t give a damn (again – 3 beds was the mission item), lol.
Cool, you can control the robots in first person view. After clicking the mouse button, I thought the robot pooped/regurgitated something awful. Oh ok, just the rocks I guess it collected? Not a bad thing, just funny. ;)
You can right-click to de-select the active action under your cursor when building items. You can also right-click to destroy a building without warning (oops). Costs time and materials to rebuild what was destroyed in a fraction of a second.  Had to reload the game (on timers after all, no room for error).
In the middle of all this, while building, the game takes control and throws the camera over to the incoming colonists.  I DON’T CARE, I saw the message already, let me finish what I was doing.  Now I don’t even know where I was, must scroll back – yet, on the way, the camera pulls me to something else. :/
Keep getting a warning the storage room is getting cold.  You can now hover over rooms to see their temperatures. I built atmospheric generators to help (one per room), and it helps, but I found out from watching a video that you only need space heaters in other places.  How much do they output though, or how much power is required? Doesn’t say.  I can see the temperatures in rooms rising now.  Stats are getting better, but still a bit poor list of stats, still difficult to see what’s really going on around the base.
It also crashed a few times in a way that made the cursor disappear.  Make sure to save often.
Things it needs:
1. Much better AI (perhaps even mission focused). Enough hanky panky, get back to work!
2. A priority system, so you can better queue up what needs to get built first.
3. Much better stat reporting on the items (especially generator outputs for one). If there is a warning a room is cold, at least show room stats also.
4. Status icons you can click to quickly bring you to the events/issues. DONT FORCE MY CAMERA - I might be in the middle of something.
5. Automated smelter, or show an icon when it is waiting, or done. Don't turn this into a space focused Farmville game, lol.
6. Fix building bugs (see comments), random crashes (rare), and errors restarting missions (always have to restart the game).
7. Built hydroponics for food, but people are still dying from starvation? lol This needs to be fixed. If I'm missing something, then that should be in my notifications. ;)
8. No idea what anything does, or why I need it, nor how many I need to make.  There are details when selecting items to build, but no text describing what it is for.  Makes it a bit tedious to keep looking up what things are for, and why. For example, until I watched a video, I had no idea space heaters could be used instead of atmospheric generators.  I thought I needed a generator in every room.
I'll keep an eye on these issues and update the review as the game progresses.  I think it is a great game to support, but I had to give a thumbs down until a lot of issues are ironed out. I'm half afraid sometimes to play it in fear I forget to save and it crashes. ;) Perhaps Auto-save is needed at an internval I can specify.

Fantastic game despite not being playable for any prolonged period in its current state. The game is constantly improving with changes having positive impact and is responsive to player feedback. Can't really ask for more from a game in Alpha.
Maia is basically a base management game with survival elements and will be even better once more content is added and the bugs ironed out. At present there are actually a surprisingly low number of bugs but the main one that gets me everytime is the deaths from your colonists just deciding to stop moving and eventually dehydrate or starve (whichever comes first). This wouldn't be a problem if there wasn't a cap on the number of colonists meaning they don't get replaced. Eventually everyone will be dead and with nobody replaced the base can't get bigger as more people would be required.
For an early access game it's a good problem to have as it will be fixed eventually. General gameplay is still really fun and oddly stable. I would recommend this game to anybody that can overllok bugs at this stage and wants to try iterations of build orders etc to try to get a perfect base. Just be aware that you will fail regardless of how well you plan at this stage.

War of the Human Tanks is a charming grid-based tactical game. It features a set of colorful character archetypes (the strict Satou, the easygoing Choko, a shut-in genius, and a bunch of awesome 'Human Tanks'. After playing for over 30 hours, here's what I think..
Pros:
- upbeat soundtrack
- large unit strategic variation
- challenging bonus maps
- multiple routes
- easy to learn
- great character design
Cons (sort of):
- the campaign was too easy (common in a lot of games that emphasize difficulty in bonus content)
- the tutorial was a bit lacking
- there's a fair bit of farming involved (as with most Japanese games)
- there is no way to significantly speed up large actions (you can cut out animation but it still takes a while to do hit confirmation for a large target area radius attack)
**The game has a lot of dialogue in it. If you are solely interested in the tactical combat, there are several skip features implemented to aid in this.
Overall, the game was really enjoyable. It would have done just fine with a little less farming but that's not much of an issue. The campaign does not take long to complete in case you are interested in the story behind it all. I am definitely interested in playing the other titles in this series once they get on Steam!
Oh and for those of you who like achievements..

I'll give Mad Max 8.5/10
Buy it if: you like cars or games with cars, you're a fan of the (Mad Max) movies, you're looking for a good single player game, you liked the Arkham series of Batman games (on foot combat is quite similar)
The Good:
-impressive sounds and visuals (game seems to be optimized very well, runs very smoothly--3.5GHz intel i5, 16GB ram, GTX770 2GB, running at 1080p with everything on high or ultra)
-good car physics, intuitive handling (if you like arcade style handling, look elsewhere for real world simulation)
-fairly robust car customization system along with a wide variety of driveable npc vehicles
-good balance between in car and on foot combat
-well done default control layout (for xbox controller at least, which is how I chose to play the game)
-good story campaign (a nice change when compared to most other big titles launched recently)
-it has entertained me so far (~30 hours total gameplay at this point) and I still to want to play it more
The Bad:

The graphics are still very dated, though.. you can see it on models like cars, animations, lighting etc.. the game uses an old engine, nothing awesome (seems to me that Hitman Absolution had nicer graphics..) but now works and can be enjoyed.

Sure the missions are few, but the replayability is very high, as they are much less linear than Absolution.. so I think the monthly release schedule is a good idea as players are forced to replay the same level to discover all what's hidden, achievements, contracts etc.

Before you hate my review for being negative let me tell you my point of view.
I loved the first game - Life is Strange - that was so amazing and wonderful that it set standard so high it is almost impossible for a sequel or a spin-off such Before the Storm is to reach it.  I'm not holding it against this game and I try to evaluate it as a stand-alone game with no ties to the previous title, so before playing I had my expectations moderate and kept my hype in check.
Teen story about rebellion against parents, against society, cliche as usual but that is why we play this, nothing wrong about that. The game is set in a small town on the west coast of the USA (Arcadia Bay, Oregon), perfect place, you got everything you want to see there in a slow paced adveture like Life is Strange is. Chloe is attending high school, which she hates and has problems with due to lack of interest and even attendence, she rather hangs out in the junkyard or at home by herself. But something changes, and that is when she meets Rachel Amber.
Everyone percieves Rachel as an angel, but she's a devil inside with a lot of issues. The part of the game when Chloe and Rachel get to know each other was good, but for me there is an edge in the middle of the game, when characters started acting very irrationally, and there was no other option but to see their stupid and clueless acting and you know that every choice you have is a bad one.
From then on characters were babbling, conversations (which I see as the most important part of any story-based game) were so prolonged that I had a need to do something while I waited for them to be over. Overwhelming boredom, and Chloe, Rachel and even other people in the game were acting just plain stupid, talking nonsence and even the story was predictable.

I read a lot of reviews here, people poiting out the games heartbreaking ending, but I felt nothing. From my point of view the game is about two spoiled brats who made problems they never even had. Maybe its because I didn't like Chloe even in the first game, but this is just my opinion. Only thing I can say now is that

Life is Strange: Before the Storm is a prequel to the Life is Strange. The story focuses on Chloe and her life. You can try this game without playing the original series (Life is Strange), however it is recommended that you play the game before trying out this one.
I waited to bought this game until the 3 episodes are released and finished the 3 episodes in one sitting. As you can see I finishes this game in 8.5 hours. Was it fun? Do I enjoy the game? I will explain further below.
Being a visual novel, most of the time what you were doing was watching cutscenes. At some point you move from one place to another place and interacting with some objects to solve simple puzzle. Yes the puzzle is too simple that you do not even need to think about it. However, the focus on this game is the story development. Yet the simple puzzle is not even bothered me a bit and I just keep playing (and watching) and the story goes on.
There is a system here called 'back-talking' thingy, in which, you will try to do some persuading to another character to win over the argument (or goal whatever is it). It was.... uh, how do I say it? It was challening for the first time, but as the story goes on, it is never even be a challenge, It was kinda boring and I felt like I wish this back-talking is removed or even supposed to be made harder? I dont know. I felt like I will lose nothing if I failed, but it was too easy that I even made it out without even thinking about which choice should I choose.
Unlike LiS, where Max have superpower. Before the Storm focuses only on Chloe and her life, being a normal, rebelious girl. Thus, do not expect some kinda superpower thingy happened again. It focuses on her and only her life and her surrounding. Her, being a normal girl at her age, rebelling and stuff. However, it was still fun to watch and see.
The story in my opinion is good. At some point it kinda touch my feeling. Some makes me upset, sad, mad, etc. However, idk, it was just me, or perhaps you too?
Anyway there will be another episode (bonus episode) in which has not been released by now. However the 3 episodes have been released and you can finish it right now (hoilday sale). Oh it is discounted as well so why not buy it? :p
Do I recommend this game? Yes, especially if you like the original series.

The first LiS was art so I was vary of having to high expectations, turns out I worried for naught as this entry more than lives up to it's predecessor. If you didn't play the first game then go do that now, if you did - well then you should know there's no higher praise than saying that Life is Strange: Before the Storm lives up to it's name.
If I had to nitpick something I'd say I wish it was longer, I clocked out at slightly under 10 hours in my first playthrough which is not a whole lot of bang for my buck length wise, but the experience is powerful enough to make up for it.

Note: I backed this game on Kickstarter.
Shantae: Half-Genie Hero is very interesting platformer. Before playing Half-Genie Hero I have played Shantae: Risky's Revenge and Shantae and Pirate's Curse.
Shantae: Half-Genie Hero is much easier than previous games. I think I died only once while playing the game. The problem is that you can easily get Shantae overpowered for each stage. You get plenty of extra health, you get different methods of healing and you can power-up Shantae really fast. Also for last stage and bosses in it, I was able to be literally invincible. In other games I was never so overpowered. Good thing is that it's possible to turn off upgrades, so even if you try getting 100% everything, you don't have to be overpowered.  I believe that by turning of some of the upgrades, game gets much more challenging.
I'm also little sad, how little some transformations and their skills are used in the game. Some transformations I only needed once or twice and some of their skills I never needed. On the other hand other transformations and their skills you need little too much. Also I used some transformations to skip platforming sections.
I really love the new visuals. Every character and stage were visually very beautiful.  I think this game has best soundtrack of the franchise so far. Jake Kaufman truly nailed it with the soundtrack.
Game has pretty nice and very funny story. There are lots of jokes with the characters. There's even some fourth wall breaks. It's not very long game, but that is good for me. I finished the story in 100% in 11 hours. After that you unlock a new mode, which I haven't at the time of writing this review.
Even though I citicised some aspects of the game, I still loved it. It might be little too easy, if you make it too easy, but it's still very fun. Bosses are clever, though little easy. It is fun game. I'm not sure, if I liked this game more than Pirate's Curse, but I would recommend playing this one first of the franchise.

I have played other Shantae games and this is my fave. From its art style to its platforming, it just feels better over all then the previous entres. It is slightly less difficult but that is a strength in this case, as it makes the game more engaging without becomming overly frustrating.

The 4th game in the Shantae series (the GBC game counts damn it), Wayforward put a bunch of emphasis in revamping the presentation this time around: and the change definitely works. While I still enjoyed the more classical pixel style of the older series, this new art style brings colors that jump off the screen, while still keeping the animation quality at the series high standards. And while the sound design does leave a bit to be desired, the music is fantastic as you would expect when Jake Kaufman is involved (Shovel Knight, Shantae series fame). This game is just a pleasure to look at, and the character design is probably the best it has ever been in the series.
The gameplay on the other hand has taken a step back. While the platforming is still enjoyable, its difficulty in combat has taken a step back from Pirate's Curse, as some of the returning transformations such as the monkey form make dodging enemies a breeze. The emphasis on movement over combat still shows off the smart level design Wayforward is known for. And the boss fights do bring it a bit more this time around, as they are better designed then in Pirate's Curse. But a lack of length in gameplay and just a overall lack of difficulty plagues the game a bit.
Overall, the game still is an enjoyable romp that keeps with the Shantae style. If you've liked the previous games in the series, you'll love Half-Genie Hero. Just don't expect an evolution in the gameplay.

So what can I say about this little game that you've not already managed to read or find out for yourself? Well I have played it for a bit and have found myself enjoying it more with each playthrough. You start off with three Duplicants (People), much like RimWorld. More often than not you also have this miricle ore that produces Oxygen (Highly important for your people) while slowly it breaks itself up until it is depleated. You also start off with some food (less important than oxygen but still pretty high up on the list) and with this you can start to dig out a starting base. I found the animations of the Duplicants rather adorable and they seem to be done in a sort of 'Don't starve' meets 'Prison Architect' kind of style, they make little bleeps and hums while doing their day to day business though you do need to look after them as they have bad habbits too, I personally look for those with Narcolepsy as in my last game 'Stress induced vomiting' managed to stop my water pump. In turn that blocked my air scrubbers and by doing that it stopped my farms from working. I know what I should of done, worked earlier in the game to make sure that stress levels could be reduced.
This game has you planning, failing, restarting, planning differently, failing differently, restarting over and over until you get that perfect mix of the right people, the right start, the right planning and the right.. oh yeah.. restarting again thanks to some other thing you've not planned for. I recommend this game to any fan of resource management or base building or Indie supporting player as it has a whole lot of promise and I believe that it will meet it perfectly.
I've not mentioned what else happens in this game, the population does grow and that adds to the level of difficulty. You get the balance right for 3 people and the addition of the 4th throws it, by the time you've got it set up for 7 people you have 10. That is of course if you wish to have more people, you can always skip it.
This game keeps getting better, for each moment I think I have got hold of it a new release changes or tweaks the whole game, that base layout that you poured hours into? Yeah that needs a total overhaul. Those pipes? They work better like this. I love it and the game developers do seem to keep pouring love and good results into this game, I can't commend it high enough.

Out of all the Alpha/EarlyAccess games I have played, this one has been the most enjoyable. While there are many things that it can improve upon, it has only gotten better as time has gone on, and every major update has added much to the game.
Currently, the game is about guiding a group of 'duplicates' in creating a viable colony inside of an asteroid. In this creative survival game, you must manage not only food but also oxygen, stress, and the waste that your colonists produce. There isn't any built-in end goal, however the argument could be made that the goal is to create a completely self-sustaining colony.
It is to be noted that this game is NOT FOR EVERYONE. This game can be complex at times and it does not hold your hand as you learn how to play. While, personally, I feel it isn't very complicated, some of the more in-depth options could certainly confuse people. This isn't a game about being able to just build what you want without a care, but it also isn't about being extremely realistic and super challenging to play.
If you enjoy being creative but also like more of a challenge than, let’s say, Minecraft, then this might be the game for you. If you prefer to just create and dislike the idea of having to manage anything more than the aesthetics of your creations, then perhaps you should look elsewhere. Though keep a bookmark on this game, as the developers may decide to add a 'creative mode' in the future.

A game rushed to the steam store to cash in on the early hype. Sadly the game is floating dead in the water now that the initial hype has gone. I want it to succeed as it's the OG First Person Zombie sim, but due to poor handling of development and now a decreased flow of funds it'll likely never be released in a way which feels truly complete. The devs seem focused on adding pointless items and guns while refusing to fix gamebreaking bugs which are inherent to the Arma 2/Take On Helicopters engine. I'm fully aware of the new engine and work which is being put in to make the engine better but I'd say the game would have benefited from starting from scratch with an engine made to handle these sorts of games. Now folks will say I'm in no place to judge as I'm not a game dev. But this should be obvious enough to anyone, I recall at the announcement of the standalone how hyped I was as I thought servers wouldn't need to restart and the movement wouldn't be as janky as it is in Arma 2. But, the game ended up being less of its own game and more of a plus sized DLC/Expansion (Like Halo: ODST was to Halo 3 or  Fallout New Vegas was to Fallout 3) with all the issues and drawbacks of the original, just with slightly less fluff and slightly streamlined.
Now you might not care about the development process, cool. But how's the gamplay? Boring. With a dead fanbase you'll likely not run into too many people. If you do, they'll likely shoot you. The mod had a side chat which allowed folks to connect and possibly team up or challenge eachother. It made the world feel alive and dangerous. Now the world feels desolate and lonely and not in a fun way. You're not sure if you'll even bump into a player and that's where the real challenge was in the mod. Sneaking around worrying other players might see you, in this you'll find yourself sneaking from the zombies which isn't all that fun and when they spot you they run through objects and glitch around you. Killing a zombie now devolves into standing in front of eachother and swiping at one another until the zombie dies and you find yourself bleeding.
Looting is fairly basic and you'll find yourself with top tier loot after around 3 to 5 hours of looting once you learn the general layout of the map. After that point you'll likely find yourself looking for other players to kill or party up with and finding them is risky and often you won't even find one when you want to. This then leaves you to experience the atmosphere and that's the one thing this game does right but is it worth it?
This game nails the atmosphere, I still get the same vibe as I did the first time I spawned by Kamyshovo in 2012. You feel exposed and once you spawn your clock is already counting down, so you go and scavenge food. You then make a way along a path usually heading inland to the north west. For that journey you'll have a decent enough time but will likely find yourself bored at times or just frustrated to find the buildings you're looting have already been looted. But the more dire the circumstances, the more invested you get and the harder you fight to stay alive the more fun the game becomes. But after fully gearing up, which is quick you'll want to take risks and as I've stated before, that's hard to do and not guaranteed to result in finding anyone.
IF YOU WANT GAMES THAT DO WHAT DAYZ DOES BETTER, I suggest Project Zomboid if you enjoy a gritty zombie survival game. Project Zomboid is much more atmospheric and modular. With workshop mods, the possibilities are endless. If you enjoy combat similar to Arma 2, DayZ and Arma 3 in a much more rapid fire, high stakes way which will get your heart going every time, I suggest Player Unknown's Battlegrounds.
Overall I want DayZ to do well as I've got amazing memories from 2012 and 2013 playing the game and its offshoot mods. But this game missed its shot and was executed on in the worst way. After now 4 years in Early access, it's a true disappointment. Shout out to Dean Hall, The head project staff and Bohemia interactive for botching this. I also feel really bad for anyone who's left to salvage this who doesn't want to.
This is not okay. This needs to stop NOW. This is cancer. This is so much cancer, that I can feel the tumors growing on my back, and it's weighing down heavy on me and it's not okay.

Forget the bunch of military shooters out there, they only simulate the gun part of war. This rare gem right here shows you the moral, psychological, and ultimately dark side of conflict. And it will leave a mark on your mind.
Gameplay-wise, this game is extremely similar to Gears of War, including elements such as run-and-cover system, grenade lobbing, squad-based combat, and hell even the animations look similar. Just swap in a modern setting and there goes a "modern warfare" version of GoW. If GoW is fun, then this game should also be entertaining. So what's different here?
The story makes all the difference. As a player you will pass judgment on the "enemies" through various events, but as you carry on, you will begin to feel uneasy and doubt whether you are doing the right thing. This game then thrusts you into situations where hard decisions must be made. The character you play will also gradually change his tone from neutral to violent, adding to your feeling of frustration, anxiety, and, perhaps, madness. At the end when truth is revealed, I was dumbfounded and began questioning all my actions before. Replaying the campaign will make them all the clearer.
While the plot does lack certain explanations, the journey itself is a remarkable (or should I say horrifying?) experience. I highly recommend this game to anyone who plays shooters. Gives you something to think about next time you pull a trigger somewhere else.

On the surface Spec Ops: The Line appears to be just another Call of Duty clone. Once you get started, the story comes alive. It is very captivating and will hold your interest until the end, and quite possibly for another play through.

Every part of me wanted to enjoy THE LINE, and occasionnally, while blasting enemy defenses with rock'n'roll music in the apocalyptic Dubai I did, but mostly, playing through the game was a chore. A straight look at the horrors of war with horrendous gameplay mechanics (this one reminds why I hate third person shooters) and rather lousy controls (you use the same button to jump or melee, the spacebar to run or cover). It basically plays like 'Frontline commando', yes the free app, and although the scenery is beautiful and many levels feature a lot of verticality within the broken buildings, it's repetitive as hell, and the mac version is a little glitched with weird performance issues and mouse lag.
The game had great press and reviews, hailed as the mature alternative to 'Call of Duty', but besides one great moment around the middle of the game, SPEC OPS is totally streamlined and would play exactly like COD if it was first person (and it would probably be a better game thanks to more reactive controls). The game plays on rails and there are no important choices to be made as advertised. You will be forced to commit atrocities and deep down the story (although inspired by Apocalypse Now) doesn't make much sense and the soldiers are rather flat, with no specific characteristics. There are other games out there that bring criticism to the genre itself and a much more subtle mind♥♥♥♥ (like Bioshock Infinite) with better gameplay, so I suggest you only get this if it's on sell or just watch the youtube movie that compiles all the cinematics so that you know what the fuss is all about.
PS: Coop and MP are virtually unplayable thanks to the controls (the same button does several actions so half the time it won't work, you'll hit an obstacle when you want to jump or execute a soldier when you want to melee the one next to him) and almost no players are online. Also the game is very sentitive to the hot corners on the mac so you have to deactivate them with a script or work around by adding an extra input key if you don't want to force pause the game when aiming through the barrel, breaking down the action and causing many unnecessary deaths.

Windward is a fun and relaxing oceangoing RPG that can be played solo or with friends. If this isn't the most underrated game I've played in recent years, it's certainly high on the list.
What I like:
-- The game is customizable. I can build my own map and even redefine the factions.
-- The game is simple enough for a few minutes of pickup play, but engaging enough to keep me playing for hours if I let it.
-- There are multiple ways to gain experience and advance. The game doesn't penalize you if you'd rather trade or take commissions (quests) than fight.
What I dislike:
-- The factions are static. Even if you set your world to permanent war, the AI will not take territory or do anything else without direct intervention from the players. This is fine for a dedicated server perhaps, but tends to ruin my immersion a bit when playing solo.
-- Combat can seem a bit cheesy at times. Trying to push the pirates out of a high level area during solo play can seem nigh impossible. The game *does* warn you that the higher level areas are designed for group play, but I see no reason that a game like this can't be designed all the way through for both single and multiplayer.

UPDATED after full playthrough!  Yes it's short as of right now since the full game isn't released that is why there is $15 and $60 for the current version with tutorial and 1 mission while the $60 is based on the full 6 missions that it's supposed to have in the end.
TLDR:  I suggest this game since nothing I can find is game breaking or unexplainable.  Most PC games have a few issues with every GPU and CPU working flawlessly until a few patches are out.  Also there is probably a heavier load on their servers due to the release.
My Specs: 16 GB RAM, 2 x 1 TB HDD, GTX 660, AMD FX-8350
Overall  - 8.5/10
Gameplay - 9.5/10 - Balancing feels great
Graphics - 9/10
Controls - 8/10 - Based on default layout for PC keyboard+mouse
Story - 5/10 - Had to give low since not much of it so far but I am want to learn rest
Pricing - $15 is worth what you get but not sure on other price until rest of episodes release
Crashes - I have had a few problems with the game but have found a few fixes for them while playing.  I had two crashes one after another and found loading a previous save fixed the issue for me at least.
Settings Locked - There are some settings that are locked out based on your system.  I personally am only limited on Texture quality and it only allows Low.  Not sure of this limitation but the game looks good even with low texture quality.  There is another setting that I can max out called Level of Detail so not 100% sure of the difference between the two.  I can only imagine the developers don't want people maxing it all and complaining due to poor ports even though they still complain.
Must remain connected - Although the game will boot you out of a mission if you disconnect you can play offline.  The only reason for this is online leaderboards and such is my assumption.
Multiple choices - The game has many ways to do everything.  The only limitation is your imagination....well not quite.  The game gives you many different ways to reach a target and different ways to eliminate them.  The first level had plenty of witnesses and many disguise possibilities.
Gunplay - Feel nice and smooth.  You can't be a bullet sponge and neither can enemies.  It's hard to run and gun but it's a possibility if you so wish.
HUD/Menu - I see no visible health which the game SHOULD NOT have.  There needs to be no HUD except for what item you currently have which is what they give you.  You can easily pull out the item and put it away with a simple middle mouse click.  There is a ammo count for clip and total as well if you have a gun selected.  Enemies also appear with a dot above them now if they will go WHO ARE YOU if they spot you to give you a heads up on which guys to avoid.
Difficulty - Game is difficult if you want to run and gun but in a way it's kinda easy to take your target out and run away.  Not hard to sneak and remain hidden.  Game has instinct mode which makes it easier to detect enemies behind walls.
If there are any questions I will try to answer them and possibly add details about them to the review.  I will try to update this again in a day or so as I test out more of the game modes.

I'll give Mad Max 8.5/10
Buy it if: you like cars or games with cars, you're a fan of the (Mad Max) movies, you're looking for a good single player game, you liked the Arkham series of Batman games (on foot combat is quite similar)
The Good:
-impressive sounds and visuals (game seems to be optimized very well, runs very smoothly--3.5GHz intel i5, 16GB ram, GTX770 2GB, running at 1080p with everything on high or ultra)
-good car physics, intuitive handling (if you like arcade style handling, look elsewhere for real world simulation)
-fairly robust car customization system along with a wide variety of driveable npc vehicles
-good balance between in car and on foot combat
-well done default control layout (for xbox controller at least, which is how I chose to play the game)
-good story campaign (a nice change when compared to most other big titles launched recently)
-it has entertained me so far (~30 hours total gameplay at this point) and I still to want to play it more
The Bad:
-side objectives to reduce enemy influence in each map area start become grindy and repetitive by late game
(minor gripes)

Update:
With 0.59  Maia has had a lot of content , fixs and tweaks - really making it feel more and more like a decent budget AAA game rather then a indie. I mean, its not there yet, but Maia's pretty darn ambisious, so its amazing how far its come.
I think the key to if you will enjoy Maia or not is if your prepared to learn and replay a lot. While initially it feels like "scifi dungeon keeper", the game is a lot less forgiving. You have to balance life essentials like heat,power,atmosphere before you even get to food and drink. Each time you play - and your colonists all die horribly - you tend to learn a bit more for next time.
The game also, despite being early access, has a lot of content already, with various scenarios as well as free exploration. So with these too things in mind, its certainly not a game to be used up quickly.
The downloads/limitations of the current 0.59 state of the game are mostly UI related, as well as some AI issues with colonists build priority's. Its perfectly possible for them to build themselves into a room with no doors - so you better hope another colonist will decide to build a door before they die or starvation/dehydration.
Despite this, its a game I definitely recommend for sci-fi fans with patience, and a desire for a reasonably realistic "let me set up a base on a unexplored alien world" game.

Forget the bunch of military shooters out there, they only simulate the gun part of war. This rare gem right here shows you the moral, psychological, and ultimately dark side of conflict. And it will leave a mark on your mind.
Gameplay-wise, this game is extremely similar to Gears of War, including elements such as run-and-cover system, grenade lobbing, squad-based combat, and hell even the animations look similar. Just swap in a modern setting and there goes a "modern warfare" version of GoW. If GoW is fun, then this game should also be entertaining. So what's different here?
The story makes all the difference. As a player you will pass judgment on the "enemies" through various events, but as you carry on, you will begin to feel uneasy and doubt whether you are doing the right thing. This game then thrusts you into situations where hard decisions must be made. The character you play will also gradually change his tone from neutral to violent, adding to your feeling of frustration, anxiety, and, perhaps, madness. At the end when truth is revealed, I was dumbfounded and began questioning all my actions before. Replaying the campaign will make them all the clearer.
While the plot does lack certain explanations, the journey itself is a remarkable (or should I say horrifying?) experience. I highly recommend this game to anyone who plays shooters. Gives you something to think about next time you pull a trigger somewhere else.

On the surface Spec Ops: The Line appears to be just another Call of Duty clone. Once you get started, the story comes alive. It is very captivating and will hold your interest until the end, and quite possibly for another play through.

Every part of me wanted to enjoy THE LINE, and occasionnally, while blasting enemy defenses with rock'n'roll music in the apocalyptic Dubai I did, but mostly, playing through the game was a chore. A straight look at the horrors of war with horrendous gameplay mechanics (this one reminds why I hate third person shooters) and rather lousy controls (you use the same button to jump or melee, the spacebar to run or cover). It basically plays like 'Frontline commando', yes the free app, and although the scenery is beautiful and many levels feature a lot of verticality within the broken buildings, it's repetitive as hell, and the mac version is a little glitched with weird performance issues and mouse lag.
The game had great press and reviews, hailed as the mature alternative to 'Call of Duty', but besides one great moment around the middle of the game, SPEC OPS is totally streamlined and would play exactly like COD if it was first person (and it would probably be a better game thanks to more reactive controls). The game plays on rails and there are no important choices to be made as advertised. You will be forced to commit atrocities and deep down the story (although inspired by Apocalypse Now) doesn't make much sense and the soldiers are rather flat, with no specific characteristics. There are other games out there that bring criticism to the genre itself and a much more subtle mind♥♥♥♥ (like Bioshock Infinite) with better gameplay, so I suggest you only get this if it's on sell or just watch the youtube movie that compiles all the cinematics so that you know what the fuss is all about.
PS: Coop and MP are virtually unplayable thanks to the controls (the same button does several actions so half the time it won't work, you'll hit an obstacle when you want to jump or execute a soldier when you want to melee the one next to him) and almost no players are online. Also the game is very sentitive to the hot corners on the mac so you have to deactivate them with a script or work around by adding an extra input key if you don't want to force pause the game when aiming through the barrel, breaking down the action and causing many unnecessary deaths.

I came into this game with low expectations. I really didn't like Risky's Revenge, and never played Pirate's Curse. I was prepared to walk into another boring backtracking marathon.
And then The title screen came up and I changed my mind. You can tell a game is going to be great when the freaking title screen makes you excited. I made a new file and holy♥♥♥♥♥♥everything just blew me away. The animations are so fluent, the graphics are amazing, it controls really well, and that was just from the intro section.
I soon got into the game, surprised to see it's really more of a metroidvania hybrid of sorts. There are metroidvania elements, but for the most part it plays like a regular platformer. It's like your first time through the stage is normal, and once you clear it you can revisit it to get the stuff you couldn't before. Unlike in RR, the areas are all REALLY interesting. (Mermaid Falls is easily my favorite level in any platformer, actually!) And the backtracking doesn't get old. It'd be nice if there was a minimap of some sort, so you could easily check unexplored areas on the fly. But it's not that hard to figure out without it. I managed to 100% this game in 7 hours, and I enjoyed every minute of it.
A bit of a fair warning, though. This game suffers from "Help the enemy is too cute and I don't want to kill it" syndrome. Especially prevalent with Nagas, Mermaids, and Slimes. You may take lots of damage from ogling the things out for your head instead of fighting.
I don't usually mention music in my reviews, because there's not much to say about it usually, but this has a really great soundtrack. It's a real earworm that pumps you up. And what else could you ask for with a platformer?
The game isn't too challenging, as long as you keep yourself upgraded. If you get 99% before the last level, you are basically immortal, as you can infinitely use Invincibility or Total Restoration. And you'll NEED IT. Because WOW that last level is so freaking rough. It's incredibly challenging, much more than the rest of the game. But all that aside, the game is amazing in every other regard. Unless you really like frustration and lack of information as to why things aren't working, I'd steer clear of this for now.
Maia's concept basically takes Dwarf Fortress and puts it into space, on another planet.  That's both a good and a bad thing.
Like DF, you decide what needs to get done, and the colonists go off and do that on their own, with no direct control.  Unlike DF, if a colonist is unable to do something, you don't actually get any sort of message as to why — it just doesn't get done.
Like DF, it's being built by a solo developer, who is focusing way more on adding new features than on fixing bugs, even old or important ones.  Unlike DF, those bugs aren't things like "military training isn't working" — they're game-breaking things like "none of my colonists will go outside to make a wind turbine to generate power for the atmosphere generators, so they all die due to lack of oxygen".
Even once you get through the first few steps and get a real colony going, it's only a matter of time before colonists just up and decide they can't do some critical thing and they'd all prefer to die, and you don't get any indication why.
My suggestion to the developer would be: Even if it's not part of your vision on how the final game will look — for now, give us some debugging tools!  Even if they're off by default, we need some way to show us what our colonists are up to, what tasks need doing, why they aren't being done, how priorities work, etc.  For one, it's just too frustrating to play without those right now; and two, they would enable us to give you actually helpful bug reports, instead of just vague statements like "nobody would go outside so they all died".
Sadly, my experience playing Maia for several hours today was basically the same as my experience back in 2014.  A ton of stuff has been added, but the game feels exactly as inscrutable and unplayable now as it did back then.  I love the concept, I hope it becomes a great game someday, and I appreciate the difficulties a solo developer faces on a project of this size, but I can't base a review on hope and speculation.

UPDATED after full playthrough!  Yes it's short as of right now since the full game isn't released that is why there is $15 and $60 for the current version with tutorial and 1 mission while the $60 is based on the full 6 missions that it's supposed to have in the end.
TLDR:  I suggest this game since nothing I can find is game breaking or unexplainable.  Most PC games have a few issues with every GPU and CPU working flawlessly until a few patches are out.  Also there is probably a heavier load on their servers due to the release.
My Specs: 16 GB RAM, 2 x 1 TB HDD, GTX 660, AMD FX-8350
Overall  - 8.5/10
Gameplay - 9.5/10 - Balancing feels great
Graphics - 9/10
Controls - 8/10 - Based on default layout for PC keyboard+mouse
Story - 5/10 - Had to give low since not much of it so far but I am want to learn rest
Pricing - $15 is worth what you get but not sure on other price until rest of episodes release
Crashes - I have had a few problems with the game but have found a few fixes for them while playing.  I had two crashes one after another and found loading a previous save fixed the issue for me at least.
Settings Locked - There are some settings that are locked out based on your system.  I personally am only limited on Texture quality and it only allows Low.  Not sure of this limitation but the game looks good even with low texture quality.  There is another setting that I can max out called Level of Detail so not 100% sure of the difference between the two.  I can only imagine the developers don't want people maxing it all and complaining due to poor ports even though they still complain.
Must remain connected - Although the game will boot you out of a mission if you disconnect you can play offline.  The only reason for this is online leaderboards and such is my assumption.
Multiple choices - The game has many ways to do everything.  The only limitation is your imagination....well not quite.  The game gives you many different ways to reach a target and different ways to eliminate them.  The first level had plenty of witnesses and many disguise possibilities.
Gunplay - Feel nice and smooth.  You can't be a bullet sponge and neither can enemies.  It's hard to run and gun but it's a possibility if you so wish.
HUD/Menu - I see no visible health which the game SHOULD NOT have.  There needs to be no HUD except for what item you currently have which is what they give you.  You can easily pull out the item and put it away with a simple middle mouse click.  There is a ammo count for clip and total as well if you have a gun selected.  Enemies also appear with a dot above them now if they will go WHO ARE YOU if they spot you to give you a heads up on which guys to avoid.
Difficulty - Game is difficult if you want to run and gun but in a way it's kinda easy to take your target out and run away.  Not hard to sneak and remain hidden.  Game has instinct mode which makes it easier to detect enemies behind walls.
If there are any questions I will try to answer them and possibly add details about them to the review.  I will try to update this again in a day or so as I test out more of the game modes.

Control is ok, weapons ok, sand effect pretty good, general gfx rather middling, AI barely there, level design copy and paste, and overall end result bordering on total apathy. It commits the usual crimes of disabling run when it has something to tell you (which is very often), briefly giving control for something as pointless as climbing a set of stairs, and taking away control for some of the more exciting stuff.

Only 4 hours into this game and it is wonderfully stable thus far. If you feel a bit burnt by another recently released space game, give Starpoint Gemini 2 a try - I really think you'll like it. If you are a Star Wars fighter jock you'll have to get used to flying a heavier ship. The UI is both intuitive and beautiful. This feels like a sort of dystopian 29th century Star Trek.
Edit: Now 15 hours in and this game just keeps getting better all the time. I took down a "hero" a.k.a. a large ship with a threat level of "Impossible." The fight took 20 minutes and alternating between targeting the enemy's heavy batteries and subsystems. This ship jumped me and was not part of a mission.  My little ship a small Pegasus class gunship wore this bad boy down and the reward was 4 million credits! I decided to step up to a Corsair class rather than an even more powerful Frigate.
This is really a game to be savored and frankly, I am so happy with Starpoint Gemini 2 that I really couldn't care less for Elite: Dangerous especially with today's (18 Novemeber) announcement that Elite: Dangerous will require constant online even in single player.
You can play this game as you see fit and don't be fooled into thinking that the explorable area is small because there isn't a whole galaxy to explore. I've only seem a tiny part of this game. Somewhere in the Community Hub of this game someone had posted a complete map of the game and suffice to say it is M A S S I V E.
Limit Theory is now the only other space game that I think will force me to divide my time if it turns out to be as good as it looks. CNo Man's Sky is still a long way off and Star Citizen is so bloated that I believe it can't possibly live up to the hype nor the budget which I think equals  the budget for Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan.
Simply put, Starpoint Gemini recaptures the magic of the great space games of the past like Indepence War I and II, the Freespace series, and the legendary Tie Fighter and X-Wing and all from a small studio. If you love space games,  get this. Ignore it at your peril.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.
