Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is a First Person Shooter set in a comptetetive scene where two teams battle for an objective. It is a stand-alone follow-up to the famous Counter-Strike mod from Half-Life where terrorists battle the Counter-Terrorists on different locations.
The gameplay consists of buying weapons and shooting your opponents. Easier said than done actually, since your opponents are either human players sitting on the other side of the world wide web or some AI programmed to shoot you first. CS:GO is for a reason the biggest competetive shooter on the market for years, since it offers great weapon balance, tactical possibilities for teams to approach and a large player base that keeps growning each day. The story behind the game is based on the oldschool Counter-Strike game, where one side takes the approach as terrorists either trying to plant a bomb or protect the hostages and other being Counter-Terrorists either try to protect a bomb site or trying to rescue the hostages held at Terrorist base.
The combat is absolutely fluid in CS:GO and there are barely any moments, that you could blame the broken hitboxes or the bad netcode for dying. People tend to rage and blame the bad balance on maps, weapons or programming of the game, however the success of this title proves that it is the best competetive shooter on the market. The challenge in this game is definetely to be able to rise through the ranks in competetive matches, playing against hackers on opposite team or some players on your team that want to teach you some bad words in russian or french. I am always thankful for such opportunities to improve my language skills and consider it just a chance of becoming even better if I did not win the match no matter the team stacks. Reaching Global Elite rank after around 200 hours, I can safely say that it is possible to rise to the top even when the odds are stacking against you.
The graphic when set to higher settings is actually pretty good, sadly the competetive scene barely allows it since there are certain tricks like setting your resolution lower on purpose to be able to aim better, that crash the feeling of this game in graphical matters. Most of the maps contain some details that make them distinguishable, like certain grapphiti on some maps. The interface is kept simple and almost transparent so that it does not disturb the concentration.
It is possible to consider progress by rising up the account level that comes from simply playing CS:GO in any form, there are forms of rising up your ranking by playing competetive or gathering skins for the weapons you are using or want to sell. Some people actually make money by playing this game and selling the skins on the steam market, so different ways to progress in and outside of the game. The biggest progress for me was improving my hand-to-eye coordination by playing it competetively.
Each weapon sound is unique for itself, and since the sound plays a great role in this game it is really important to get to know the sounds and be able to distinguish where the shooting is coming from. CS:GO fulfills its task really well. The music is played only in menues and during the highlights. The game music is nothing special, but since you can get/buy music kits to fit your music taste, Valve found a good workaround for not creating amazing music by themselves.
CS:GO has its reasons to be the Number One FPS in the ESL Scene and its popularity is currently only rising. It is great to see that it has not been abandoned by the developers after reaching its peak state, but still keeps getting updated. I would recommend trying CS:GO to every game, just to know what this game is that defines the global FPS market so much and while FPS fans might love it, some might well get turned off by the hardcore players or the cursing and spitting wanna-bes.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying and installing this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.
~ForestWolf

Half Genie Hero is another excellent Shantae game.  I've played Risky's Revenge and Pirate's Curse as well and each game has it's own strengths and weaknesses despite them being similar overall.  I've enjoyed my time with each game enough that I'm not sure I could even rank them. It should suffice to say that Half Genie hero was not a disappointment for me, but I can't say it stands head and shoulders above the other games either.
First up, the game looks fantastic, maybe not quite up to par with something like Ori and Blind Forest, but it has a crisp cartoon style that's appealing and is definitely one of the best (if not *the* best) implementations of 2D sprites on 3D backgrounds I've ever seen in terms of making the two look like they belong together.
The music is also great.  It conveys the feeling of upbeat chiptunes from platformers of old while still using a modern full (synthesized) orchestration.
The game is still basically a Metroidvania, just with discrete levels instead of a contiguous world.  The animal transformations (which weren't in Pirate's Curse) make a return and are a welcome sight.  The level of challenge is still pretty light, with the exception of two sections in the last level which can get a tad frustrating, but aren't too bad.
The one downside - the game is a little content light. There are only 5 main levels and then an ending level.  The game is structured so that you will need revist those 5 levels multiple times as you get new powers.  There's a scripted dependency where you'll get a power in one level that lets you explore a singe new area of another level, where you'll find an item which unlocks the next power in a different level and so on, at some point wrapping back around to letting you explore the next hidden area in the original level.  I.e. this isn't a game where playing through all the levels once gets you all the powers you need to unlock everything and then you can just go back to the levels one more time, getting all hidden items in one shot.
That said, the game is very generous at giving you tools to warp around levels quickly and you can quit out of a level as soon as you get an item or powerup without losing it.  So despite the need to revisit the same levels, they do actually allow you to eliminate much of the tedium of retreading old ground.
I was still quite satisfied with the amount of play time and the game overall for the price, but if there was just a little more unique meat on those bones, I think this would easily be the best Shantae game.

With sturdy Opus and maximum Max's equipment and stats I got into a nasty storm in Dead Barrens. I've tracked the scrap box and pulled it to a safe shade of a cliff rubbing my hands from excitement of looting my preciuos treasure! I smashed the box and tried to grab the first loot piece when the lightning hit right under my feet igniting me like a christmas tree. After recovering I attempted to grab it one more time and got b.u.t.t.hit by a passing Buzzard enemy. But I didn't gave up. Half dead I rushed to my beloved Magnum Opus and got hammedred by a huge piece of scrap. "I AIN'T DEAD YET", - I shouted and rushed to my car again. I'm in! I'M IN!!! I blew enemy's car defences and ripped their wheels off. All 3 drivers rushed at me and in a matter of a few moments ended up on their shoulder blades. I dried all my water recovering from most of the damage when suddenly a sparkling blue light exploded next to me sendinging me ragadoll for a few meters. Good god I was lucky to heal up before it happened. I jumped into my severly damaged Deathmobile and rushed for the cover again. To my surprise I had another ferociuos Buzzard gang speeding my direction. The encounter  emerged into a "last man standing" carmaggedon. Two down, one to go. My four wheel Fury blazing in fires left me standing alone against enormous storm and a skink on his Spiky Hellmobile. 10/10! Would storm again!

Combat gets old too; I want a handful of bullets, like how Resident Evil lets you conserve bullets, but this feels like Resident Evil with 2 bullets. I am fighting 8 guys and even cars and can't even shoot half of them!?
Definitely not worth the full price, but glad I at least saw awesome cutscenes in the beginning wen I bought it off Humble Monthly in June; wait for a sale if you need to try it out, and be patient for that backtracking and traveling/scavenging for bullets/scrap.

Here is the original text of my review from last March, when the game had just been released:
"Dammit man. I really, really, really wanted to be able to write a good review about this game... because on the rare occasion that the game runs without crashing, it's REALLY FUN. I have a GTX 970, i7 4770, and an 850w Platinum rated power supply. I doubt my hardware is the issue. In this sorry state I cannot recommend this game, at least not until they hopefully patch it to where it is playable. PLEASE FIX THIS IO AND I WILL CHANGE MY REVIEW."
EDIT:
So, IO has long ago fixed the issue I was having (and actually it appears the issue was with Nvidia's drivers at the time) and I have had a year to dive in and enjoy this game... and I must say it is by far the best game in the Hitman series.
IO took a gamble with the episodic model but it has really paid dividends to the players with this particular game. I'm not sure that it could work with many other styles of games... but for a game like Hitman with a focus on open ended, choose your path, highly replayable setpiece levels, it really makes a lot of sense. Each level is it's own open world to explore, study, and master. Each time a new map is released, it feels like new expansion pack. Because outside of the main mission with it's gazillions of different ways of completing the objectives, there are even more game modes that challenge your sneaking skills to an insane level. I'm of course speaking of the vaunted "Escalation" mode and it's even trickier cousin, "Elusive Targets". I won't go into how they work, but needless to say they each pack hours and hours of extra enjoyment into already incredibly designed maps that you will WANT to explore every nook and cranny of.
In short, once the bugs were figured out, this game has cemented itself in my mind as a new classic in the stealth game genre. The fact that I get blessed with a new map practically every month that I'll probably spend minimum 20 hours in alone gets me pumped every time I hear news of a new map coming out...
... speaking of, Japan just released, I think I've got some assassinating to do!

I'd like to start off saying, I love the hell out of gang beasts and have put some hours into it with my friends.
Just not THIS gang beasts.
When I first played this game it was back in 2015 or so, the game was in Alpha (0.1.5), and it was a blast. Eight player, silly physics, a couple bugs that only enhanced the gameplay. The only problem was you needed a beefy computer to run certain maps like buoy, and that on the rare occasion a round would end prematurely when one but not all players died, but it didn't matter.
I'm thankful as hell that I got a new computer around that time and was moving files around, because I discovered that the alpha version of gang beasts could be run on its own outside of steam without being updated, so I can still play the 0.1.5 alpha with my friends when we get together.
Now you might be wondering, what could you do back in the alpha that you can't do now?
To start, even though the characters felt more jiggly and silly, you also felt a lot more strength in your actions. With one hand you could hold on to just about anything, like holding on to the side of a truck, or holding the side of a ferris wheel and holding seven people below you over the water no problem. With this, you could climb in all sorts of places too with a bit of practice. Up, down and along walls, under platforms like on Gondola, up ropes and wherever you could get a hold of an object.
Getting more to the jiggly and silly part of the characters, there was the ragdoll button or lay down button. Whatever it was supposed to be, it was hilarious. Holding it and moving around like a snake on the ground while your friends try to pick you off the floor before resorting to crawling like a snake as well, was fun. Being able to fall forward and do continuous front flips was hilarious, and managing to pull off a front flip between the two trucks on the trucks stage was so satsifying. Raising people hasn't changed too much I don't think, but it will always be great when you get a tower of people haphazardly perched over a cliff, or when you hold a pylon and lift it just right to super jump on the train stage.
And those bugs I mentioned? It was one bug in particular really, was on the Gondola stage. If you broke off a part of the support cables into a little section and grabbed a hold of it, you could hold A to keep going up and fly around like you're on a broomstick (Which me and my friends dubbed the "Hogwarts" glitch). The most we managed to get flying on the same broom at once was three people on a large cable, and it ended with someone holding Y and the three of us rocketing to the ground screaming.
The game now, although the physics of props and overall appearance are improved greatly, the gameplay itself feels worse. Basically, before you controlled characters that felt like they had a lot of muscle but no bones. Now it feels like you're controlling a wet pancake that can barely stand on its feet.
I could go on about how fun this game was, but I feel like I've made my point. And you have to understand that I have more than 11 hours playing this game, because I've been playing the Alpha version that isn't linked to steam anymore.
If you can get your hands on the old version, which is eight player, I say again, EIGHT PLAYER, get it.
And to the developers if you happen to read this, your game is fun now too, but it's just not the same. I trust that in time you'll bring this game back to what it used to be, or at least make it better than the Alpha ever could have been, but for now I can't recommend this game.
And for the love of god, bring back eight player multiplayer.

If you were disappointed by X:Rebirth, like I was, Starpoint Gemini seems to be more in the spirit of the previous games than their own successor. Frequent updates sometimes break saves, but it all seems quite polished thus far except for some balancing with missions.

Ok, first I want to say that overall, this is a fun game.  Even though it is in it's alpha phase, it still has a lot of fine points to keep me playing for the time being.  There is one point about this game that is going to kill it for me, but I'll get to that later.
The graphics are well done.  I have several hours into it, and have yet to experience a graphical glitch.  The ship models are well done and the stations aren't bad to look at.
The flight controls are a bit weird at first, but it really doesn't take much to get used to them.  The biggest gripe I have is that there is no first person view so you can't fly directly at something.  If you try, you actually fly over it.  Not that big of a deal and after you get used to it, it works out.  If you are flying mouse mode, there isn't enough dead space for level flight.  Your ship is always changing direction.  I ended up not utilizing the mouse mode and stuck with WASD.
As it is still in Alpha phase there are only a few different types of missions to work on.  These are called Freelances.  They are usually quick and easy.  It looks like there will be several different types of missions put in later on, so this isn't a slight, just an observation.
Also, the money doesn't keep up with your pilot level.  I'm currently level 25 and still can't afford to buy another version of the same ship I'm currently in.  I should have been able to upgrade ships a while ago.  I'm sure with the advent of other missions, the money thing will probably work itself out.
There needs to be more tutorials.  There needs to be something on Grappling and taking over ships.  Might be offered farther down the road.  Also on derelicts.  Try as I might, I can't figure them out.  I don't seem to get anything off of them.  I might not understand their mechanics, but since there is no tutorial on them, I don't know.
Now for the part that breaks this game for me personally.  I do enjoy combat and exploration.  I've never been huge into trading or diplomacy.  However, I love games where I can create things.  Crafting is huge for me.  Starpoint Gemini 2 has these huge asteroid fields that if I spent years playing, I wouldn't be able to empty them out.  However, all you can do with them is shoot them for ore and then vendor it...for a very small price I might add.  There is nothing else to do with all of this ore.  Now, your saying...wait, it is still alpha, they might add it in later.  Well, I've read up in their forums and one of the developers has already stated that they don't plan on adding in any kind of crafting utility to the game.
If I could put a station out in the fields, and have them manufacturing ship equipment, weapons & and ships themselves, this game would be one that I kept and played for years to come.  As it is, I'm going to get tired of shooting random encounters pretty quick.
As a single player game, I need something that is going on in the background while I'm out exploring and building for the economy would be great.  Without this ability, the game gets stale, at least for me.
For most people, this game will be great.  I know that a good majority of people don't care to craft anything.  For me, without it, it is a game breaker.

Been a year that I last wrote something about this game, and considering that the updates for the game come frequently, I think it's time to update the review as well.
Last year I called it "playable". This year I can actually call it entertaining. What's most entertaining, at least for me, is that the colonists are actually very human. Allow me to explain.
In most games, you have people that feel more like worker drones. They will go from place to place, build, mine, craft, sleep, get hurt, go to the medic bay, build, mine, craft... The "people" here feel actually like people. And they don't want to be treated like worker drones. They get stressed out if all they do is build and work.
Of course the idea that people do something aside working isn't new. But this is I think the first game that actually models "stress". I wonder why this isn't a sales argument, but I was actually happily surprised when I noticed this!
You start out with 4 colonists and you can of course make them work, work and work. But don't be surprised if they get really burned out very, very quickly. And that means that accidents will happen, that they get depressed, and that they will simply not really want to work anymore. They start making bad decisions, they start to mess up priorities. And they'll start to complain. Subtle at first, and eventually they'll be anything but subtle. Ever heard of "quitting on the inside"? That's what they do. If only because they can't actually quit, being stuck on an alien planet. They'll just get sick a lot, make snide comments in the emails they send you, complain about their coworkers and actually be hostile to them, work the bare minimum...
A bug? No, probably not. Because if I lower the work load, if I add "stress relievers", if I add more people to spread out the work, suddenly they start to behave "normal" again.
This is actually pretty amazing. I have never encountered this depth of AI in any other game.
Aside of this, yes, there's still a long, long road ahead of them. They now added "missions" to the already existing sandbox game where you get more or less easy tasks to fulfill within a given time. Still in need of some tweaking and balancing, IMO. The alien fauna still doesn't quite have as much of an impact as I'd have hoped it would (basically the alien animals are a backdrop and don't interact much with your base). The balancing in general still needs work, it's VERY hard to start out but if you survive the first 10 days it becomes pretty much a cakewalk, a slow, steady increase in "demand" from the colonists would be great here. And there's still not that much to "do", so to speak. Research now works pretty well, but after about a dozen or so research topcs have been checked off the list, you're done with that, too.
So we're still not looking at much of an "endgame" to to speak, and I still hope that we'll eventually see some sort of "campaign mode" or something that's more than the sandbox (plus the "guided sandbox" callsed missions).
It's not done yet. But with very frequents updates (about one large update per month), we're looking at a game that not only gets active development but one that actually improves with every update. Many Early Access games "break" at some point and start getting worse, losing or throwing away the reason you bought it for. So far, Maia avoided this fate. The things that get added make sense and add depth to the game.

Progress is being made on this game and the developer is putting a lot of care into this project. I wouldn't recommend buying it at this moment, but it does have a ton of potential. Add it to your wishlist and check back later.

I've been following this game for some time and when is came onto Early Access I was very excited by the concept. However since then I have become a bit disillusioned with it. But I will provide a fair judgement of it in its current state and the developers.
The game does have amazing charm, almost all the tech in the game is not far from what we have now and this gives the game a fantastic sense of realism. Even the charecters are dressed to match what you would expect and the game has a fantastic sense of humour in the little info pop ups. Base construction is intresting placing rooms and then decorating them freeform does give a great sense of personalisation (beware OCD people out there, trying to place things dead on is a nightmare, I suffered!). The world outside your underground home feels alive in the style it has been done in with various creatures who may pose a challenge to you. And they accompany the various events such as earthquakes that keep the game fresh and intresting. Managing the various resources is also given a sense of realism such as managing air production and flow, heat, food and such and the devices used are, as I've said, realistic in design the type of thing you would see in a building today. Futhermore the game's developers are fairly active and updates are common but nothing really seems to make serious progress forward.
However this sense of realism is compounded by the fact the game is buggy as hell. I cannot reason the A.I of your people who seeminly act at random if at all. They will often die standing in a room that has no heaters set up yet while the room next door is fully heated. Getting them do to anything is a chore and I have often had people die early on because they take so long constructing the basics. The tutorial is terrible, I thought that all you needed as the atmos gens to sort our heating and the like, but while the tutorial gets you to build one it does not get you build the heaters meaning by the time you realise you really really need to, coupled with the time it takes the A.I to do anything, it might be too late.
The U.I is not very helpful with nothing immediatly displayed on the screen meaning on your first go you wont even know how much elect, water and such you have until it runs out. I like where the developer is trying to take it however, being able to read your peoples E-mails is a great idea and again adds to the personalisation. But at the moment is fails to give the player what they need.
The colonists work independent of the player, but sometimes it is needed to force construction of an item or activity and if there is a way to do this I havn't found it. If you need to build a turbine for an emergency power drop, but have other actions already in place your a little screwed.
All in all the game has a great feel to it and that is why I am reccomending it, to keep and eye on it but not to buy. Previous versions of this game were more enjoyable and to me more stable and that is a shame but hopefully this is due to them implimenting the game proper and this is just a rough patch. As I said a game to follow not to wishlist.

Played the game for a bit and I think this game is pretty decent game. It's a bit overpriced, in my opinion. On the Steam store it's $10 but if your able to pick it up for a $1 either from other sites or on a Steam sale it's worth a play or two.
It's a bit long winded with it's dialogue and really didn't care for the cut scenes. I couldn't get in to that but maybe some people will enjoy it, as for my experience it was a bit odd to say the least. The art and battle animations are a bit different when you think of strategy games but I guess that it's suppose to have an Anime appeal. The actual gameplay though is some what satisfying. It's a very simplified grid based game but instead of turn based, each unit has a timer for when they'll be able to make a move. Which is a bit different from most grid based games.
Other then that, it's pretty straight foward pick between recon, assault, shock, battery  and command tanks to make up your army of human tanks. There's a fog of war which keeps thing interesting. There is no terrain modifiers, which was surprising for a grid based strategy game. The thing that I thought was most interesting was that you can upgrade your tanks with "modifiers" which give them certain augments in battle and also the fact that when your units are killed they don't come back. You have to replace them with parts which can only be gained in battles won, so you'd want to keep your human tanks alive. At least in the main campaign which progressing through so far, is similar to an RPG to an extend.

I like that they have a customizable deck that you change, RPG element and the abilty to lose units in battle as the campaign progresses. It would have been nice to see it more polished but for what it is, it's an alright game. If your looking for more a of a traditonal strategy games I'd suggest Unity of command instead. This is really a niche game and would suggest only pick it up if you really like Anime quirkness. Which appears to be the main selling point, in my opinion.

The latest Shantae is the 4th in the series and is a fully crowdfunded game.  The self destructive mayor fires  Shantae (again) and she must solve a series of problems and fetch quests to regain Scuttle Town's favor.
This game does a few new things.  First, the game is less like a metroidvania and more like Mega Man X.  The game no longer has a map, and instead has a sereis of levels with nooks and crannies that can only be accessed with new upgrades.
This game has the nicest production values of the franchise.  Characters are now fully 3d cel shaded, looking like Guilty Gear Xrd without the deliberate frame rate reduction, so all animations and movement are silky smooth.  The soundtrack is phenomenal, including electronic and funk beats.
The game starts off very strong, with wonderful humor, action and boss fights.  But as the game goes long, two things happen.  First, the action is bogged down between fetch quests.  For those who don't know, Shantae always has humorous fetch quests which depend on key items that you will not expect to need, recieve, or give.  In this game they are easily the most numerous.  You will run around in circles checking if your latest upgrade will work in "that one spot" you couldn't reach before.  If only you could remember where it was: you have no map!  Second, the difficulty of the game PLUMMETS.  This is easily the lowest difficulty game in the franchise.  In the time I spent running around in circles, I fully upgraded my attack and attack speed.  In the midgame, you will find heart containers like candy, to the point you can ignore enemies and damage to a silly degree.
This was the most tiresome and boring Shantae game I played.  Play Momodora or any other intense action game and just youtube the boss fights instead.

I've been greatly enjoying some of the most recent WayForward games lately and this one is definately on the peak of enjoyment. Ever since they made A Boy and His Blob for the Wii, they have had this asthetic of hand drawn animations and amazing backdrops. I feel that Ducktales Remastered helped them solidify their style. And they brought it to Shantae, their own IP. And this game shines for so many reasons. Their art style brings every little detail to life. The music is really catchy, especially the one with lyrics you encounter early on. The gameplay gives this sense of exploration that fits the Metroidvania style of coming back to places once you have new powers. It is fun to play.
Now, there are a couple gripes I've got. The game length is pretty short. Getting near 100% took me just about 6 hours to do. If the game had maybe a level or two more, I'd feel more satisified. There is also a huge issue in Mermaid Falls in the factory setting. At one point, you are jumping from hook to hook, but they are not in sync to always line up. I've spent a great deal of time just trying to get up the first time I played. It was frustrating.
But beyond the slight flaws, I have to say I love this game. This is one I'd suggest you pick up and normal price if you love exploring based side-scrolling games. If you're on the fence, maybe wait for a sale, but I don't regret getting this game.

I have been a fan of Shantae since Pirate's Curse, and Pirate's Curse is one of my favorite games of 2014. A new Shantae was very excited for me that the moment it went on sale and I had money I bought it and, long story short, I loved it. Now it's not as big as Pirate's Curse and 1/2 Genie Hero doesn't have dungeons like the last game but I still love 1/2 Genie Hero.
Let us start with the graphics... amazing. No joke, this is what HD sprites should look like, not just high color pixels. What made me like the graphics especially was the fact that the character portraits look like the models. Pirate's Curse had portraits similar to this game but the sprites were pixels, it created a discord between what the gameplay says characters look like and what the portraits and promo art says the characters look like.
The gameplay, on base level, is mostly the same as the previous game but with the added bonus of not having the well implemented pirate gear and replacing it with the well implemented animal transformations. The most useful to me was the monkey because of it's speed and jumping ability. Despite my previous statement on the animal transformations, there are many ways to cheat. Case in point, the bat. It is so easy and tempting to jump to the highest place on a horizontal scroll and transform into the bat and fly over every thing. Also the Harpie kinda makes the monkey and bat useless.
And now some quick thoughts on small points. The music is amazing in 1/2 Genie Hero, I recommend that you go get the soundtrack from Jake Kaufman's bandcamp page, seriously you don't have to play the game to like the soundtrack. Next, the story, it's okay. SomeCallMeJohnny put it best, it's more like a series of microstories with a big plot at the end.
I hope you found this review helpful and be kind this is my first review. Thank You!

Months after the release of the newest movie in the Mad Max franchise, Avalanche Studio brings us a new adventure in the form of a third person sandbox game featuring the road warrior.
Although it accompanies the movie in its release, we find a game that has received the required attention and establishes itself as a stand-alone product. The first proof of it is the story: An original scenario with a plot that feels much closer to the first movies.
The game starts in the middle of a thrilling cutscene where Max faces one of the wasteland’s warlords and ends up losing his means of transport, leaving him stranded in the desert.
This leads to an encounter with our companion for the rest of the game, Chumbucket, who promises to help us build a vehicle that will be even better than the one we lost. The plot is basically limited to this concept: finding the pieces to build the Magnum Opus, the ultimate car. To achieve this there is a variety of missions to fulfil and errands to run while facing the dangers of the wasteland. Unfortunately, as far as plot goes, there’s isn’t much more to it. The supporting characters are few and have little real substance or relevance and there are no subplots of importance.
The terrain where we will travel to fulfil those missions uses a considerably bigger map than the one we’ve seen previously in Just Cause 2 and offers us all the space we need to drive, explore and fight.
It’s precisely in the map where we will get to see the full magnificence of the graphics. The wasteland looks incredible on PC, offering a solid 60 fps at 1080p at all times. This allows us to focus on enjoying the level of detail of the textures. The landscapes are beautiful and the light during the different times the day only heightens it, it’s a shame that, true to the idea of a wasteland, there are few edifications to admire.
The physics, although not perfect, aids the immersion by offering moments like the feared sandstorms, where we will see debris flying in all directions.
With regards to gameplay, we find a mix of systems that works really well together. The combat system is the one we’ve already seen in the Arkham saga, less deep but with a more cinematic feel, which works perfectly for this game, as driving has more importance. Driving has been very well adjusted and vehicular combat feels addictive and diverse, offering us many different ways of destroying our enemies.
The survival mechanics don’t interrupt the fun but feel somewhat redundant. While upgrading the character and vehicle constantly reveals new resources, the same can’t be said from the secondary missions, which end up being repetitive.
Mad Max deserves the attention of gamers and promises hours of driving and fighting entertainment to those who give it a chance. However, the lack of variety in the missions and the absence of a memorable plot prevent it from standing out among other releases.

Here is the original text of my review from last March, when the game had just been released:
"Dammit man. I really, really, really wanted to be able to write a good review about this game... because on the rare occasion that the game runs without crashing, it's REALLY FUN. I have a GTX 970, i7 4770, and an 850w Platinum rated power supply. I doubt my hardware is the issue. In this sorry state I cannot recommend this game, at least not until they hopefully patch it to where it is playable. PLEASE FIX THIS IO AND I WILL CHANGE MY REVIEW."
EDIT:
So, IO has long ago fixed the issue I was having (and actually it appears the issue was with Nvidia's drivers at the time) and I have had a year to dive in and enjoy this game... and I must say it is by far the best game in the Hitman series.
IO took a gamble with the episodic model but it has really paid dividends to the players with this particular game. I'm not sure that it could work with many other styles of games... but for a game like Hitman with a focus on open ended, choose your path, highly replayable setpiece levels, it really makes a lot of sense. Each level is it's own open world to explore, study, and master. Each time a new map is released, it feels like new expansion pack. Because outside of the main mission with it's gazillions of different ways of completing the objectives, there are even more game modes that challenge your sneaking skills to an insane level. I'm of course speaking of the vaunted "Escalation" mode and it's even trickier cousin, "Elusive Targets". I won't go into how they work, but needless to say they each pack hours and hours of extra enjoyment into already incredibly designed maps that you will WANT to explore every nook and cranny of.
In short, once the bugs were figured out, this game has cemented itself in my mind as a new classic in the stealth game genre. The fact that I get blessed with a new map practically every month that I'll probably spend minimum 20 hours in alone gets me pumped every time I hear news of a new map coming out...
... speaking of, Japan just released, I think I've got some assassinating to do!

I have a lot of games, and most of the time can't decide which one to play.  But, this game kept my interest and I played all the way through without jumping to another game.
It has many of the same features as other games; go to a new territory, take out enemy structures, take over enemy strongholds, find hidden stuff, etc. But for whatever reason it didn't seem tedious. The fighting was fun with the finishing animations. And the driving/combat was really fun. Not a lot of unrealistic speed, spinning out, uncontrollable crashing all the time.

As some others have already written I really wanted to like the game. It was unfortunately not meant to be so, Mad Max is an incredibly pretty game, the car combat is a nice change of pace and definitely sets the game apart from others. The story is mostly interesting and well written. What in my opinion sinks the game is it's repetitiveness. Once you have completed first of the regions you have, outside of the main missions, seen everything the game has to offer.
All of the strongholds are upgraded in the same way, while it was nice to see them change visually getting the same parts for the same thing for the n-th time was just plain boring.
And don't get me started on clearing the regions to 0 threat, to achieve that you have to clear everything from the region (aside from scrap locations), minefields are especially annoying, requiring you to change the car, drive to the location, find 3 mines, get out of the car and dismantle each one. And you if you want some of the upgrades you have to do that.
TL;DR Overall I don’t think I can recommend Mad Max, completing the game felt like a chore due to its repetitiveness.

Finished Mad Max late last night. Being an open-world game, I neglected the main story for the most part and did all sorts of side activities. Usually not much of a completionist but this time around I did a lot of that. Cleared the Threat Level in each area to Zero, leveled up Max
and so on. Didn't do any races though, not a fan of races. Anyway, I think there is plenty good with the game but it definitely won't be a good time for everyone. The campaign itself is fairly standard in length but the world itself took centerpiece during my time. Probably one of my favorite post-apocalyptic wasteland worlds in all of gaming. The atmosphere is on point. Desolate, destroyed, almost alien. Inhabitants having lost all sense of mercy or ethics. So does Max, the protagonist. One of the few games where the players actions feel perfectly in line with the character and world. Characters and story are sadly passable at best. There's only very little to get you invested in them. An alright excuse to keep things moving. Besides the main story there are several major side stories which happen at the four friendly strongholds. Each has their own ideology and it was compelling to see how humans could make sense of living in an utterly destroyed world. These strongholds can also be upgraded by scavenging for special loot-crates in the world which open up permanent benefits for Max, health-refill, tank-refill, etc. These are very useful and make the tedious scavenging hunt worthwhile.
Most of your time will be spent doing other things though. The world is huge and it is daunting at how much there is to explore at the beginning. You slowly discover new areas but in the end it all goes the same way. You search for the hot air balloon at each area and by using it, the fog of war clears, enemy camps and other points of interest get marked on your map. These places are identical across the whole world, so it's easy to get in a repetitive motion very quick. Taking over enemy camps, clearing minefields, looting the many small loot locations, taking out convoys. The thing that makes this still fun and worthwhile is the constant change of activities. At one point you are brawling your way through enemy camps where you can spice things up by melee weapons, makeshift bombs and special finishing moves. On the surface the combat is not deep but the combination of ways you can fight makes it always fun and satisfying. It's a similar story with the second big pillar of combat, by car. This one starts of seriously under-powered and you will have a hard time tackling even smaller convoys. Upgrading your car - especially weaponry - will drastically turn the tides and soon you'll feel like an absolute bad♥♥♥♥♥of a one-man army ripping off tires during high-speed car battles, sending enemies flying through their windshields with your high-powered hook or straight up turn vehicles into fiery explosions of metal with your thunderpoon. It's as bad♥♥♥♥♥as it sounds really and does not get old.
This all, the actual gameplay and the beautiful and diverse areas help make the otherwise repetitive tasks a joy to fulfill for the tenth, twentieth time but in the end, they are repetitive tasks and if it is not fun the first time, I doubt things will change. For me it just clicked. I enjoyed clearing the world of enemy patrols and camps, upgrade my car, destroy huge enemy convoys and see how strongholds strived and prospered by my hand. After clearing the whole map of threats and doing all side missions, tackling the final third of the story became sort of a final pay-off to me. A nice and fitting end to a long road.

The first game I think about when starting this is of course Sid Meier's Pirates! Not that strange, since both is about ships in the West Indies during the Age of Sails. But they are quite different.
In Windward you start with a single small ship that you use for trading or running quests (or "missions"), earning money and XP. With money you can upgrade your ship and with XP you make your crew better. Earn enough and you can buy a bigger ship.
You fight pirates, make friends with the different factions and try to grow the cities dotted around the map.
Only 1.5 hours played sees me in the very first stage of the game, but it's a lot of grinding to earn money and XP to improve. I have no idea if the later game will be hugely different.
It is gorgeous looking but I'm not sure if the gameplay is varied and deep enough to keep me invested for longer periods of time but I might return for an hour or two sometimes.

This game. THIS GAME. OOH YEAH.
Prison Architect is an amazing game. I've been playing this game since 0.22 or so, and it has truly come a long way. It's awesome to see an early access game with developers who actually care about it and set a bar for themselves. That way, an update came out every month and never was it disapointing.
Now that the official Alpha is out, I can say that I and probably 99% of players are more than satisfied with the result. The game itself can call itself the best prison sim of it's time and now that they have added escape mode and story mode it really can't get much better.
Personally, I think the game is near perfection. There are still some bugs, but you I can live with those. I also think that in escape mode the prisoner is slightly overpowered. However, this can also be a fun experience as you completely demolish a prison with a gang of over 20 prisoners.
The difficulty of the game can be set to ones own preference, which is great. Experienced players can make it a lot more difficult for themselves and new players can discover the game without problems.
When you look at the community for the average player, it doesn't really stand out. You can share your prison on the workshop and download prisons from others, but that's really it for most people. Not that there's a lot more needed, it just is that way and I like to point that out.
Overall, Prison Architect has evolved over two years to be the best prison management sim yet, and I think that it's worth every penny. You're going to enjoy yourself for hours on end, and when you think you've discovered everything there is, the game gives you another challenge and more posibilities.

It always sad when a game looks promising on screenshots and trailers, but bland in terms of gameplay. RL is full of poor design decisions.
1. Player Character attacks with "wind up" frames. This leaves nothing more than a feeling of input lag and frustration from missed attack as a result. This is also true for Shield block.
2. While many enemies have signaling animations before they attack, some of them move on screen in wonky unpredictable pattens. Also there is a bug when in some situations ranged attacks from enemies could pass solid floor or wall when you already learned that some attacks are blocked by walls. Not a challenge for a player, but mere "screw you" from the game.
3. Player's hitbox is not what it should be judging by the looks of it's sprite on screen. It is slightly lower and wider.
4. You have to spend as much gold as possible, because there is no way to save any remainder of it. Just a way to give game some longevity, but it feels cheap and repulsive.
5. The only important player stats are health and mana. Getting more gold in single attempt is the real reason to play.
6. What is the point of whole random heir hero generation? If you got a bad hero just die in room 1 and respawn with another one and probably with more chances to mine more gold successfully.
7. Game is lacking in terms of variety of gameplay. There is no\not enough random artifacts that could change how you play every playthrough. Instead you buy one set of equipment and use it to go through many-many retries.
I will keep the game (1,5$ feels like fair price now when I played it) and will still play it from time to time.
If you looking for Rogue-like-lite that is actually fair to the player, fun and actually enjoyable to play, try Crypt of the Necrodancer, or Spelunky.

War of the Human tanks plays like a sort of grid-based strategy game in the vein of battleship, but with significantly more tactical options and threats than the board game classic. Unit abilities can light up fog of war, kill enemies at greater range, self-destruct your unit for a wide swathe of, well, destruction, and so on. Between missions, you spend supplies gained from previous sorties to upgrade and replenish your army, increasing their effectiveness, area of effect of attacks, range, and so on.
Its titular unit, the human tanks, are mass-produced military personnel who for some unknown reason look like cute young women and charge fearlessly to their doom at your command. If that sounds too weird for you, this game may not be for you. But if you can look past that strange outer layer and the (gasp!) DREADED ANIME AESTHETIC (the horror!) this game offers a lot of fun and deep tactical gameplay.
The plot is presented in a visual novel sort of style between missions, so you will have to do a lot of reading. But there is plenty of (dark) humor to be found, and some surprisingly deep themes for such a wacky game.
Also, its soundtrack is seriously catchy and unique.
I personally ADORE this game, and if you have any interest in tactical RPGs like advance wars or any other strategy title really, I think you could do a lot worse than War of the Human Tanks. If nothing else, try the demo - it gives five levels of playtime, plenty to decide on whether this game is for you.

Before going any further into this review, I must point out that besides maybe a few minutes of the Game Boy Color original, I had no experience with the Shantae series heading into Half-Genie Hero. I had heard some great things about the franchise, I just hadn't gotten around to it until now. And let me just say, this game has made me very interested in playing the others.
Right off the bat, the visuals in this game are absolutely gorgeous. When it comes to side scrollers, a 2D traditional animation style is my preferred choice. The game looks so alive and vibrant, and the 3D environments only serve to compliment the 2D sprites. Most of the characters also have fun and cute designs, so there's no complaints in the visual department from me.
The sound is also awesome, this game has one of the more rocking soundtracks I've heard in a platformer in quite a while. I was tapping my foot throughout it. The minimal amount of voice acting sounds great as well, although it is underused.
The control is spot on, Shantae moves perfectly with your imput and it delivers a smooth platforming experience.
As for the gameplay itself, it's quite solid. I love games that give us the ability to switch out character styles at a moment's notice, and Half-Genie Hero allows for a number of fun interchangeable forms to help further are exploration experience. It was always exciting getting a new ability to see how it would change the level, and overall they didn't dissapoint. I will admit that while cool, I do wish the air transformations didn't somewhat break certain platforming segments once you obtained them.
The only two complaints I really have about this game is the length and backtracking. The game only has a few levels, which was a bit dissapointing since I liked all of the ones offered. Also the game features some serious padding with having us have to revisit levels with our new abilities. While discovering new hidden areas with new spells is a good feeling, it ends up with us having to play a lot of sections multiple times with little new content. Although they at least didn't make us refight the bosses.
Overall I really enjoyed this game, it is a very solid entry to the platforming genre. I said I would change my review back if the final product is shiny and it was so I did. I now give this game a solid 10 out of frikken 10. Graphics? Done and Done. Mechanics? Smooth. Everything is there. DX12 is finally fixed. My only complaint is that I am still mad about how they lied about Elusive Targets and I refuse to alter my real life schedule over a video game. We were told different things that weren't delivered. I love escalations though, always have. Look when this game first launghed I was able to forgive bugs. But the bugs extended well into the 3rd episode when I left. THAT is what made me mad. This stuff should of been ironed out. We were told this was an episodic release, which I defended from DAY ONE, but it played out more like a messy Early Access. BUT they got it done. And whatever problems the game had in the past, they had and it's done. Elusive targets aside everything about this game is perfect. The cutscenes look like the best movie I've ever seen. You can't even tell it's animated. Actual gameplay is almost the same. You can tell it's animated but only if you look close. And being able to simply tell the difference between animation and real life isn't a bad thing, in fact this game borders on creepily intesnse graphics. It's only slightly better than the graphics from MGSV which I say are the second best graphics I've ever seen. Keep in mind it took IO a long time to get to this point, but they did it. I notice the game can get a little choppy still, IF you have a bad graphics card. I DONT. But i did notice on some youtube videos, so.. I gotta give it a 10, because they came back from a point where everything really did seem hopeless. Remember this is the follow up after Absolution, a truly terrible experience! This game outshined it, and dare I say it even outshined blood money? The ONLY THING that prevents me from saying "better than blood money" is that blood money was a little longer, had more targets and was more difficult. I still have trouble with the Mississippi River mission and the inbred wedding. Hitman's levels feel easy, BUT it has replayability. So the challenge is totally in your hands which I guess is accurate. It shouldn't be hard to kill people, but it should be hard to do it creatively and such. A few things are missing from blood money like accident mechanics. You can't push someone down the stairs and have it count as an "accident" and the rating system is soul less. I like the newspaper scheme but I can live without it. At least this rating system is competitive and ego crushing. So.. I do like the fact that I can use instinct WHEN I WANT to. Which isn't often. In other words you don't need it to complete a level. I love how they brought back cameras, this time in a digital fashion and on EVERY level. I love the pop culture references. The donald Trump reference had me cracking up! I strongly reccomend playing this game all the way through. Some people diss the story but I dont think they played previous games very much because the story is written the same way the story is always written. Very vague. BUT IT IS THERE. And it DOES answer TONS of questions and there is a HUGE cliff hanger for season 2 which has been confirmed. Anyways, thanks IO. I really wish we could have skipped the summer when things got bad, but you pulled through by November, like you promised so for that I give you credit. And I do think the series made a major comeback. In fact I think you are missing out if you haven't played this game yet. The only thing is I wish there was "advanced mastery" that is to say I wish mastery levels went on to level 40 or 60 instead of just 20, even without rewards, just having the thing on my record would be nice. I feel like some levels I should have a 40, not a 20 know what I mean? A lot of cool stuff you can do is not even listed in the "opportunities" which I think is a good thing. LEaves room for the true Silent Asassins to shine.

The description "bad or worse choices" may have you thinking you have choices in this game.  You do not.  It is a heavy handed moralizing storyline that forces you to make bad choices, then punishes you for them.
SPOILER
There is a point in the game where you are forced to use phospherous mortar shells on civilians.  It is so stark, I kept trying to figure out what the other "choice" was.  One of your squad actually says "there's always another way".  No, there really isn't.  They position snipers to halt your advance until you use the mortar against overwhelming numbers.  If you kill the snipers with gunfire, they get replaced immediately.  If you use the phospherous you cannot exit the interface until you have bombed both the enemies and civilians with it - as in target the group of civilians *specifically* and bomb them.  "Choices" were made by their "creative" team and are not something you find in this game.
As a shooter, it is mediocre.  You are effectively in a long tunnel of cover, killing successive waves of bad guys.  Your squadmates have unlimited ammo and can only be incapacitated.  There are a few near-scripted actions like shooting out windows but the game basically says "aim at that thing and shoot it", then plays the canned animation sequence.
End note: the developer implied the only way to win was to not play.  I disagree.  The only way to win is to not buy this game.

Dubai. An oasis of technology and lust in the middle of desert. Magnificent buildings in a developed city. But nature is always more ruthless than our ability to oppose. Destroyed by intense sandstorms, a city in ruins. The 33rd Battalion of the American army is sent to town for a rescue and extraction operation of the survivors. And then, they disappear from the map.
You are Captain Martin Walker, leader of an elite team of Delta Force of the Army of the United States of America, leading his fellow Lieutenant Alphanso Adams, heavy gunner and Sergeant John Lugo, sniper. Sent to Dubai after a transmission captured after six months without contact, his mission is to locate, reunite and rescue possible survivors.
Beautiful scenarios, even among ruins. The opulence of Dubai can be seen in the ruins and in few places that remained intact. Even the desert, displays an exotic beauty that brings a melancholy tone to the game.
Spec Ops is not just a shooting game in third person. It is a psychological plot. Every dialogue, every action, every event in this journey shows you more than bullets flying. Dubai is alive. Dubai is at war. And war... war never changes. The horrors of war are not shown as simple digital polygons falling to the ground with AI off. You will really feel them. You will hesitate. You will have anger and and will be thrilled. And maybe you even cry. You'll be confused. Do not stop. Go straight. Reflect, try to understand. Do not come to this game to play. Come to this story to live it. And so, you will not regret it.
Gentlemen, welcome to Dubai.
--
Dubai. Um oásis de tecnologia e luxuria em pleno deserto. Construções magníficas em uma cidade extremamente desenvolvida. Mas a natureza, é sempre mais impiedosa do que nossa capacidade de nos opor. Destruída por intensas tempestades de areia, uma cidade em ruínas. O 33º batalhão do exército americano é enviado a cidade para uma operação de resgate e extração dos sobreviventes. E então, eles desaparecem do mapa.
Você é o Capitão Martin Walker, líder de uma equipe de elite da Força Delta do Exército dos Estados Unidos da América, liderando seus companheiros Tenente Alphanso Adams, artilheiro pesado e Sargento John Lugo, franco-atirador. Enviados a Dubai após uma transmissão ser captada depois de 6 meses sem contato, sua missão é localizar, reunir e resgatar possíveis sobreviventes.
Belos cenários, mesmo entre ruínas. A opulência de Dubai se destaca em traços que podem ser percebidos nas ruínas e em poucos lugares sobreviventes. Mesmo o deserto, exibe uma exótica beleza que traz um tom melancólico ao jogo.
Spec Ops não é apenas um jogo de tiro em terceira pessoa. É uma trama psicológica. Cada diálogo, cada ação, cada acontecimento nesta jornada te mostra mais do que balas voando. Dubai está viva. Dubai está em guerra. E a guerra... a guerra nunca muda. Os horrores da guerra não são mostrados como simples polígonos digitais caindo ao chão com IA desligada. Você realmente irá sentí-los. Você irá hesitar. Você terá raiva e se emocionará. E talvez, você até mesmo chore. Você ficará confuso. Não pare. Siga em frente. Reflita, procure compreender. Não venha a este jogo para jogar. Venha a esta história para vivê-la. E assim, você não irá se arrepender.
Senhores, bem-vindos a Dubai.

Months after the release of the newest movie in the Mad Max franchise, Avalanche Studio brings us a new adventure in the form of a third person sandbox game featuring the road warrior.
Although it accompanies the movie in its release, we find a game that has received the required attention and establishes itself as a stand-alone product. The first proof of it is the story: An original scenario with a plot that feels much closer to the first movies.
The game starts in the middle of a thrilling cutscene where Max faces one of the wasteland’s warlords and ends up losing his means of transport, leaving him stranded in the desert.
This leads to an encounter with our companion for the rest of the game, Chumbucket, who promises to help us build a vehicle that will be even better than the one we lost. The plot is basically limited to this concept: finding the pieces to build the Magnum Opus, the ultimate car. To achieve this there is a variety of missions to fulfil and errands to run while facing the dangers of the wasteland. Unfortunately, as far as plot goes, there’s isn’t much more to it. The supporting characters are few and have little real substance or relevance and there are no subplots of importance.
The terrain where we will travel to fulfil those missions uses a considerably bigger map than the one we’ve seen previously in Just Cause 2 and offers us all the space we need to drive, explore and fight.
It’s precisely in the map where we will get to see the full magnificence of the graphics. The wasteland looks incredible on PC, offering a solid 60 fps at 1080p at all times. This allows us to focus on enjoying the level of detail of the textures. The landscapes are beautiful and the light during the different times the day only heightens it, it’s a shame that, true to the idea of a wasteland, there are few edifications to admire.
The physics, although not perfect, aids the immersion by offering moments like the feared sandstorms, where we will see debris flying in all directions.
With regards to gameplay, we find a mix of systems that works really well together. The combat system is the one we’ve already seen in the Arkham saga, less deep but with a more cinematic feel, which works perfectly for this game, as driving has more importance. Driving has been very well adjusted and vehicular combat feels addictive and diverse, offering us many different ways of destroying our enemies.
The survival mechanics don’t interrupt the fun but feel somewhat redundant. While upgrading the character and vehicle constantly reveals new resources, the same can’t be said from the secondary missions, which end up being repetitive.
Mad Max deserves the attention of gamers and promises hours of driving and fighting entertainment to those who give it a chance. However, the lack of variety in the missions and the absence of a memorable plot prevent it from standing out among other releases.

Described by many as 'Open World Game the open world game', Mad Max deals appropriately with the issue of inter-mission travel with few fast travel points but many ways to enjoy the travel between points.
Sometimes repetitive, the game struggles with its on-foot combat system, but this is made up for by it's vehicular combat system, the best I've really seen.
The games story does take a fair role of the reason I like it, and the side-characters range from decent to out-right enjoyable.
The game itself seems to get more into its own culture as you play it, as does Max, and it drags the player into it equivalently.

As some others have already written I really wanted to like the game. It was unfortunately not meant to be so, Mad Max is an incredibly pretty game, the car combat is a nice change of pace and definitely sets the game apart from others. The story is mostly interesting and well written. What in my opinion sinks the game is it's repetitiveness. Once you have completed first of the regions you have, outside of the main missions, seen everything the game has to offer.
All of the strongholds are upgraded in the same way, while it was nice to see them change visually getting the same parts for the same thing for the n-th time was just plain boring.
And don't get me started on clearing the regions to 0 threat, to achieve that you have to clear everything from the region (aside from scrap locations), minefields are especially annoying, requiring you to change the car, drive to the location, find 3 mines, get out of the car and dismantle each one. And you if you want some of the upgrades you have to do that.
TL;DR Overall I don’t think I can recommend Mad Max, completing the game felt like a chore due to its repetitiveness.

Finished Mad Max late last night. Being an open-world game, I neglected the main story for the most part and did all sorts of side activities. Usually not much of a completionist but this time around I did a lot of that. Cleared the Threat Level in each area to Zero, leveled up Max
and so on. Didn't do any races though, not a fan of races. Anyway, I think there is plenty good with the game but it definitely won't be a good time for everyone. The campaign itself is fairly standard in length but the world itself took centerpiece during my time. Probably one of my favorite post-apocalyptic wasteland worlds in all of gaming. The atmosphere is on point. Desolate, destroyed, almost alien. Inhabitants having lost all sense of mercy or ethics. So does Max, the protagonist. One of the few games where the players actions feel perfectly in line with the character and world. Characters and story are sadly passable at best. There's only very little to get you invested in them. An alright excuse to keep things moving. Besides the main story there are several major side stories which happen at the four friendly strongholds. Each has their own ideology and it was compelling to see how humans could make sense of living in an utterly destroyed world. These strongholds can also be upgraded by scavenging for special loot-crates in the world which open up permanent benefits for Max, health-refill, tank-refill, etc. These are very useful and make the tedious scavenging hunt worthwhile.
Most of your time will be spent doing other things though. The world is huge and it is daunting at how much there is to explore at the beginning. You slowly discover new areas but in the end it all goes the same way. You search for the hot air balloon at each area and by using it, the fog of war clears, enemy camps and other points of interest get marked on your map. These places are identical across the whole world, so it's easy to get in a repetitive motion very quick. Taking over enemy camps, clearing minefields, looting the many small loot locations, taking out convoys. The thing that makes this still fun and worthwhile is the constant change of activities. At one point you are brawling your way through enemy camps where you can spice things up by melee weapons, makeshift bombs and special finishing moves. On the surface the combat is not deep but the combination of ways you can fight makes it always fun and satisfying. It's a similar story with the second big pillar of combat, by car. This one starts of seriously under-powered and you will have a hard time tackling even smaller convoys. Upgrading your car - especially weaponry - will drastically turn the tides and soon you'll feel like an absolute bad♥♥♥♥♥of a one-man army ripping off tires during high-speed car battles, sending enemies flying through their windshields with your high-powered hook or straight up turn vehicles into fiery explosions of metal with your thunderpoon. It's as bad♥♥♥♥♥as it sounds really and does not get old.
This all, the actual gameplay and the beautiful and diverse areas help make the otherwise repetitive tasks a joy to fulfill for the tenth, twentieth time but in the end, they are repetitive tasks and if it is not fun the first time, I doubt things will change. For me it just clicked. I enjoyed clearing the world of enemy patrols and camps, upgrade my car, destroy huge enemy convoys and see how strongholds strived and prospered by my hand. After clearing the whole map of threats and doing all side missions, tackling the final third of the story became sort of a final pay-off to me. A nice and fitting end to a long road.

quick summary:
+ rather bug free
+ you get everything that you see in the trailer
+ the game can be played almost without any disturbances
+ no game-breaking bugs (at least none that i encountered)
- no autosave (at least not that i know of)
- game sometimes crashes (at least on win10)
so i'd say, if you don't mind running into small bugs occasionally or (seemingly) random game-crashes and you like the game's concept, go ahead and buy it, even if it's just to support the developer.
Edit: it has been more than a year since i played this game last time. Currently, it is definitely not "an entirely new game" (which is good, because i liked the game the way it was) but there are a lot of changes. as far as i could tell in the few hours that i have played now, pretty much all bugs that i mentioned have been fixed and i didn't experience any crashes. there are also a few new and interesting objects to work with. i still wasn't able to locate any option for autosaves, but now that the crashes seem to have been fixed, that is only a very minor issue and almost not worth mentioning. so, i'd say it has improved a lot since i wrote my initial review.
Edit2: and just about an hour after i finished the edit, the game crashed. but still, the game has definitely improved, even if the crashes are not fixed yet and there is still no autosave to use as some sort of workaround.

Have been following this game through development for a while now, both by playing each new increment, and also watching the dev streams.
Firstly, lets reiterate that this is an Early Access Game. This means that it's in development, some features aren't 100% correct, bugs 'may' be included (for now), and it's not a final product.
Maia isn't your everyday resource planning, create, build kind of affair. Yes, it has those elements, but the game is way more technical and scientific. You have to bear in mind breathable atmosphere for your people. You have to watch for the core temperature and air flow. Create correct conditions for plant and animal life to grow. And watch that your people don't go loco and start losing their minds.
Graphically the engine is quite well done. Visual representation of solar flares, and external radiation are well done. Of course these conditions affect your environment too.
Building and placing objects is pretty easy to do, after some practice you'll be placing and moving about freely. Personally I would like to be able to zoom out a little further, but that's personal preference.
Looking forward to more interaction with the wildlife - they are out in the wild, but I've yet to experience them attacking my crew, for example.
The addition of missions is a welcome one too. You have objectives to achieve and a time limit to do so. Once complete, you progress further on. I've not tried all of them but they certainly make you focus on the tasks in hand.
Just remember - early on - Crew need clean air, food, water. Nail that down quick and fast.
Looking forward to seeing what's coming next to this game - certainly a worthy purchase, in my opinion.

I just finished this game yesterday, after spending about 12 hours playing it and to be honest, I didn't think that they could make this game as emotional and thrilling as the first Life is Strange was. It is not the same, but they came pretty close!
In the first game we had a really emotional story with lots of heartbreaking moments as well as WTF-moments that led us to one of the most emotional endings in videogame history!
In this game we see the beginning of the relationship of Chloe and Rachel from their very first meeting in which we also witness very emotional scenes involving the two characters. They really get along really great frome the first time they meet, like they are meant to be together, either as BFFs or maybe as something more, because they are always there for each other and trying to help and save the other whenever they can!
What I love the most about this game it that it feels so familiar, cause they have the same art style and graphics, also the music is similar to Life is Strange 1, you see lots of locations from the first game as well as lots of characters, but also new locations and characters. And even though all characters have different voices now, it is not much of a difference, especially Chloe's new voice, since it is very close to the original voice of Ashly Burch, so you actually doesn't really feel that this is not Chloe, because that really sounds like the Chloe we all love!
Even though this game is also very thrilling and emotional, it is not as great as Life is Strange 1 imo, but like I said it's very, very close to it! And also this game is a great additon to the first story, since it reveals how close Chloe and Rachel really were and so makes it even more emotional playing the first game, cause you now know, what Rachel really meant to Chloe and why she is how she is!
Another point, that I have to criticize, is the fact that I felt something was missing, that we were rushed through the story, without really getting a sense of the deep relationship between Chloe and Rachel, it all plays out in just a few days, where they just have met and especially in the 3rd episode you don't have that much scenes with Rachel involved. And frankly they should've made at least 5 episodes to tell a deeper and emotional story between them and also for the sake of involving other characters more into the game, that we don't see that much, even though they deserve more scenes. But the whole Chloe and Rachel story should've been more deeply and longer telled, like from the moment they met, how their relationship evolved, until the day she disappeared! Of course not every single day, but just a bigger story that connects directly to the first Life is Strange! I know they showed some scenes in the epilogue, but that is not the same as personally experience it yourself and feel through that story!
Enclosing I can still say that was one of the most emotional games I've played since the original Life is Strange, even though it had not the same depth, it was still worth every penny and every second I heve spend with it and will spend over the next weeks and months probably!
I'm also really exited for the bonus episode to come out to see Max and Chloe reunite again, especially since they're bringing back the original voices from LiS 1! When it's out and I'm done, I will return and add a few more words to my review!

This is where everything falls off the table, and the game ceases being fun. Chances are the pirates controlling the region are going to wipe the floor with you. So back to the faction controlled areas to grind out quests and trading to purchase better gear and level up. Once the requisite treadmill activilties are complete, back to pirate controlled areas, where you can then proceed to play a game of whack'a'mole with infinite spawning pirates at unbalanced spawn rates.
If sixty to eighty hours of grinding to reach the fun is up your alley, then this title is for you. You'll be challenged relentlessly, without mercy or thought. If you're interested in a more casual experience then the title is something you should pass over.

I played this game directly after playing Shantae and The Pirates Curse, which I absolutly Reccomend. Honestly, Half-Genie Hero, while visually pleasing and mechanically sound, is not at good. Don't get me wrong, still a good game that I feel is worth the price tag. It is simply that the game did not do what The Pirates Curse did for me. One of my favorite things is that even the hardest levels of the game aren't too frustrating and I found myself wanting to complete the level no matter what. However, my main issue with the game is level design. There are 2-3 levels set up around the idea of you dying a handful of times before you learn the 'pattern' and make it to the goal. Unlike Pirates Curse, where the game would introduce you to new things individually before forcing you to deal with combinations, they made sure you had an idea of what you might be facing and then if you died, it was your fault because you didn't handle a puzzle or scenario correctly. This game makes the mistake of just throwing things at you and forcing you to find the best way while dying several times to do so. The other issue I have with level design is that the game has several animal forms that are essentally the same form just one of them is superior and the other one is required for one or two puzzles. For example, there are two water forms, one is large and lets you swim in any direction, the other is small and lets you walk under water. It can be said, oh you need the small form to get through the blocks of seaweed, but the large form gets an ability that lets it break through large blocks of stone, so the same puzzles for the small form could have been scaled to allow the large form in with the block breaking ability. Similarly you get two flying abilities, one that lets you fly left to right, and one that lets you fly freely, the left to right one also gets another ability that is only usefully for a single puzzle and most of the left to right flying power's puzzles could have been solved by the free flying one if they had simply changed the distance of spike walls or removed one entirely, the left to right form cannot go up or down, so you simply transform on a platform and float lazily left or right. My final two issues are with post game events. During the entire game you can travel back to each location with the boss fights and some hazards removed, ie. sand storms. Yet for some reason they give the option to start a new playthrough with all of the main transformations already unlocked, it seems pointless seeing as aside from the end game boss all the bosses were beaten without using transformations. The final issue is simply a continuity problem in my opinion that involves spoilers, but as you can guess from the title, Pirate's Curse, the previous game was about Shantae and Risky Boots.
****Spoilers Below****
At the end of Pirate's Curse they show not only does Risky Boots reguard Shantae as some semblance of a friend, but she is extremely smart and was able to plan the entire adventure ahead insuring Shantae's Victory. So why in this game is she so dumb she not only drops a map to her hide out, but several articles of clothing around town? The other issue is that at the end of Pirate's Curse the two part ways, Shantae returning to being the Guardian Genie and Risky saying she must forge her own path, as she cannot become a 'goody two shoes' like Shantae, they part with a seeminly mutual understanding and a few nice words that make Risky seem like she actually has grown to like Shantae as the adventure came to a conclusion. So why would Risky just leave a Shantae after she converts her magic to dark magic, wouldn't she want to take her friend with her? Which reminds me, when Shantae is converted to evil nothing happens, literally each of her friends says, hey snap out of it, and she does. It's very anticlimatic and it feels like a small mini-boss fight is missing.
If you actually read to the end, I'm amazed I know I went off on a tangent, but over all the game is good and a worth while buy, it just doesn't stack up to the standard that the previous game set for me.
