Alright, So my 45th review.
Well...second review. If you count reviews that have made it onto paper, or screen, or whatever.
So I'm a bit lazy.
Lets start off with the overview.
Overview
Prison Architect is really quite a solid game, a few bugs here and there, but it is still a alpha, a very very playable alpha. This is really one of the few games i've encountered in early access with a ideal level of developer involvement and actual work/content addition.
So you might be saying "I dont give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about your musings! The GAME man!
In Prison Architect( PA from here on out), you actually build prisons. I know, I know, never would have guessed on your own.
So the concept is straightforward, but the devil is in the details, and very likely also in all your future prison building endeavours.  PA is less about building a prison for me, and more about peering into the heart of simulated darkness.
You see, you as the god with questionable tenancy of your prison, are given the power to either help the downtrodden crims that will call your prison home.
Rehabilitate them, make sure they dont shank each other over the green jello, and provide opportunities to become better people!
Or... send these incoming degenerate heathens into an iron and concrete hell with♥♥♥♥♥♥meals once a day and a simple choice in the afternoon, get shanked by another hell-dweller, or face the shotgunny wrath of sadistic guards.
You see all the things that you can build and place are great and allow you to indulge your micromanaging OCD to highly satisfying levels.
But the real joy is watching your little ants run around the farm and overdose on bleach, or whatever it is they use to get high in prison.
Also, modding is not a criminal enterprise in the devs eyes, which is good for everyone.
So now for some actual points.
Pros
- Good level of items allow you to really customize your prison to be a reformists dream or a cold unlit hell.
- Prisoner AI makes it feel as if there are really personalities to each prisoner, sure, some are much like other prisoners, but a crim with the "Deadly","Fast",and "Volatile" modifiers is a sure candidate for supermax level after killing a guard, police dog, psychologist and a cook.
- Ability to separate individual inmates based on 5 security levels, from protective custody to supermax.
- Ability to build a death row for the allegedly worst of the worst.
- Dogs.
- Ability to put the squeeze on inmates with inmate level punishments.
- Allows for player to be either angel or devil, or incompetent fool trying not to starve everyone to death.
- More that I'm not bothering to list.
- Modding support and ease of mod use.
- Currently better put together in alpha than most AAA games on release day.
Cons.
- Not enough of some types of objects to place.
- Some bugs yet, nothing too game breaking for an alpha
- Can get to a point of feeling lost on what to do, somewhat like Banished, but not nearly as bad.
- Slower computers will have trouble on larger population levels.
- Can be tricky to understand all the mechanics properly.
- Prisoners tunnel too damn fast.
- Needs gun towers.
All in all, damn good quality game, should be enjoyable for anyone who likes god simulations / micromanaging / has OCD.

It's good, but it's not great. 10 hours in the curiosity will give way to tedium as each camp becomes a pattern of fight, loot, fight, loot, fight, loot, fight with nothing to stop one camp blending in to all the others. It's a shame because the developers have built a fantastic platform and sand-box filled with potential but didn't have the finesse to fill it with interesting things to do. Had they put the car-parts you needed in each camp or maybe had less of a reliance on collecting scrap it could have alleviated the tedium. The tedium reaches breaking point in having to methodically clear minefields one mine at a time. Infuriatingly mundane.
The combat is solid but uninspiring. The driving mechanics are decent but the lack of a hand-brake is mind-boggling given much of the game is vehicular combat relying on ramming.
The storyline is decent and includes some fairly brutal developments along the way that reflect the harsh world you find yourself in perfectly.
Despite the negatives outlined above, I still sank 70 odd hours into it which is a testament to the underlying world. Max himself is the strong silent type you'd expect and between him and the 'Magnum Opus' there's sufficient cool to make it interesting - just. With just a little more time spent in the ideas department this could have been a classic. As it stands, it's a good game and worth it if you can get it at a discount.

Other than that, I recommend it.

About halfway through Yager's third-person-shooter
, in one of the game's most controversial moments, I found myself disgusted and infuriated. Not at the scene I'd just witnessed, or at the game's statement as a whole, but rather that it even needs to be said at all. Two of the ten bestselling video games of all time are
and
. The "military shooter" is one of the most successful genres of the last ten years, and the objective of these games is to kill people.
of people. We eat it up non-stop, and always, always ask for
seconds. In order to keep the profit margins wide, we are encouraged to never think about it, to never stop and look at ourselves with a critical, compassionate, clear eye. Of course, it's not only Hollywood that benefits from the blinders we've all put on, since only the desperate and crazy would fight our wars for us if it weren't for the glorification of war peddled by the governments of this strange, sad world upon which we find ourselves spinning through the abyss.
In an ideal world, these things wouldn't need to be said and all of this would be a moot point. Games like
would be seen as a gratuitous miserywank, and people would rightly ask, "Why do we need something like this?" But we don't live in an ideal world, and as gamers, we inhabit a very flashy and seductive yet still a very small and confined space where, ever since John Carmack created
and
and ushered in the era of the ultraviolent shooter genre, there is an elephant in the room covered in blood and gore. As such,
is a game that needed to be made, its message one that we need to listen to.
The plot, involving a small group of elite U.S. soldiers sent to Dubai on a rescue mission in the midst of a freak sandstorm that all but destroys the city, is adapted from the novella
by Joseph Conrad, which also inspired the movie
. The themes of both are intact here -- the horrors of war, the darkness that lives in the soul, and the lengths to which the human mind will go to rationalize its own nature -- but I would argue that they are made much more effective by the vicarious immediacy of the video game medium, and because so much of gaming involves visiting death on whole populations of pixellated AI effigies. Here, the formula is largely unchanged; indeed, you mow down an impressive number of folks with a variety of well-represented handguns, rifles and heavy weapons, but unlike your regular military shooter,
invites and occasionally straight-up forces you to think about the enemy soldiers: who they are, what their motivations are, and of course, how they die. The writers at Yager accomplish this in several ways, some with all the subtlety of a sledgehammer to the face, but others which surprised the sheer hell out of me with their deft use of the medium's voyeuristic and user-participation elements. Spoiler: There's one such moment available in the demo after you use a zipline to reach a building where you sneak up on a pair of soldiers overlooking the ruined city. Their quiet, wistful conversation together is human, poignant, and, because you have no choice but to kill them to proceed with the mission, painfully affecting.
and I doubt I'm saying anything new. It is well-deserving of its praise. It's mature and uncompromising. The characters are believable, sometimes heartbreakingly so. At one point I questioned Yager's decision to use the third-person perspective instead of first-person; it seemed to me that the latter would have been much more powerful. But when you stop to wheel the camera around and look at your character, you don't see your typical hardcore BAMF with the obligatory, almost muscular, furrowed brow, the thin, tight, all-business lips, the hard eyes, etc. You see a soldier scared for his life, scared for his soul. His eyes dart everywhere like a cornered animal, he breathes unsteadily, he looks like he feels: horrified, nauseated and on the edge of tears.
The devs say that the story is open to interpretation, but for me, the game is at its heart an honest illustration of post-traumatic stress disorder, or as George Carlin would say, "shellshock":
If George were still around and had been a gamer, he probably would've approved of
. He was first and foremost an observer of life, a philosopher who just happened to be funny as hell. This is not a funny game. One of the characters starts off as the typical comic relief character that all shooters seem to require, but like Pvt. Joker in
, he sobers up fast and his wisecracks dry up completely during the events of the game. It's almost a shame the cover-based shooting mechanics are so well done, because I find myself torn between wanting to do another playthrough and not wanting to feel the way this game makes me feel. Because this is where
lives: the duality of our chosen brand of entertainment, where we "play" at the deadly game of simulated mortal conflict, and never stop to ask ourselves: what does my kill/death ratio mean for my soul? Does blood still stain if it only exists in my head? Should I even care?
is a game that needed to be made. It is a game that, in my opinion, needs to be (I hesitate to use the word "played") experienced. It is a powerful milestone in the ongoing evolution and maturation of gaming, and it asks hard questions that deserve to be heard. It's up to you whether or not to listen. To paraphrase Kenneth Jarecke, a Gulf War photojournalist
: if you're big enough to fight a war, you should be big enough to look at it.

This game is an example of how crowd-funded projects can turn out spectacularly well.  If you've played any of the Shantae games before, you already know what to expect.  If you haven't, you've clearly had a deprived, borderline abusive childhood, and I'm sorry for that.
Shantae: Half-Genie Hero is a 2D platformer that, despite the HD graphics, retains its indie-esque feel.  Mechanics of the game are simple enough to pick up quickly, yet with enough depth that the game remains enjoyable many hours later (I pause to note that Steam vastly underestimates how many hours I've put into this game.  At time of writing, it's close to 20 hours).
Having mentioned it earlier, I should mention that the graphics of this game are simply gorgeous.  It's an upgrade from the classic style without disrespecting its roots.
Soundtrack is absolutely amazing.  Plenty of allusions to previous Shantae games that carry over with distinctive sequencing, and virtually guaranteed to be stuck in your head for hours to come.  Not that I'm complaining.
With regards to the plot/story, Shantae isn't known for its compelling storytelling.  The plot is best described as 'cute' or 'quirky' and mostly serves as a vehicle by which the gameplay is delivered. Overall thoughts:  This game is absolutely amazing and everybody should be playing it.

Over 500 hours in it, every single minute was worth it. Easy to learn, hard to master. Way better than 2k games IMO.
PROS:
+Great community
+Highly skill based
+Spamming moves is not a thing! You become extremely predictable and easy to block.
+Very fun, despite the not-2k17-graphics
+Teamwork and communication is key
+Not pay to win! I've seen many people complain about it being pay to win, but really, special characters are only better in the early levels. When you get to lv 40-50 you can't tell the difference, apart from different looks, voice and animations.
+New events almost every week, giving you items that you would have to buy with real money for free, if you do simple tasks such as daily login, play 10 matches, which take 5-10 mins each, and such.
CONS:
-Of course, in every game that has a great community, there is the toxic side
-There is a card system, which can give players who are lucky and/or invest a couple bucks a small edge over the ones who don't, as they give bonus attribues. Don't get discouraged though. I've seen people who didn't pay a cent have the best deck in the game for their position, and the ones who spent over $100 who don't have it. It is RNG.
-This game isn't pay to win. It isn't quite skill to win either. It is PING TO WIN. Depending on your position, you can do very poorly if you have a certain ping. If your ping is anywhere between 0-50, you'll do great in Center, Power Forward, Control Tower (The big positions). If it's higher than that, I don't recommend it. Ping doesn't affect any other positions so don't trouble yourself too much. In fact high ping can help the small positions.
TIPS FOR STARTERS:
*In the early stage, you will be placed in the Rookie channel. Here you will mostly play with and against people with your skill, novices. But you will also come across people who have played this game for a long time, with over 500 hours in it like me, who created a different character and have to play in Rookie to level up. If you see rooms named 50,50+,50 main and such, don't enter unless you already have one character that is max lv, lv 50 in your account. You will get kicked out of it. If you do, and they ask "main?", they mean "what is your main character level", so you say 50 and you stay unless they can tell you're lying.
*Many people who start, including myself, get very confused by the attribute system which doesn't explain itself fully. As you level up, starting from lv3, you gain +2 attribute points on every level. You can use those attribute points to level up your attributes. When you get in the attributes menu, you will see different skills. There are 4 sections in each row. 1st section requires 1 attribute points for 1 square. 2nd section requires 3 attribute points for 1 square. 3rd section requires 5 attribute points for 1 square. 4th section requires 7 attribute points for 1 square. Here is a tip, use it. Attributes only really make the difference at every number that ends with 0. For example, 189 3pt stat is the same as 180. Only 190 will make the difference.
*With toys, for scorers, get 3pt success, not 3pt attribute. Try to get at least 12, because it only counts for 12, 24, 36. If you have 23, it is the same as if you were to have 12. For PG's, instead of steal, get steal motion. Same, 12, 24, 36. For rebounders, you can get either tussle, block or rebound. I prefer rebound but you do you. These, however, stack on top of your attriubtes. For example, if you had 200 rebound stat, and your toy has +10 rebound, when the toy activates, you will have 210 rebound. Toys won't activate every time. Every toy has it's own % chance of activation, usually its 20%-30%.
Good luck! Be free to create your own style, freestyle!

If you enjoyed Life is Strange, you're going to love Before the Storm. And you're going to hate Before the Storm.
Why will you love it? It's more of the world of Arcadia Bay with cynical, no-ahems-given Chloe Price. Despite the different team working on the game, they've kept the characterisations pretty well, with Chloe, David, Joyce and Frank returning from the original. The story focuses on the relationship between Chloe and Rachel Amber (and if you want them to be 'just friends' well...it's definitely more than that, sorry), and it's quite well done here. The way the two girls are portrayed here is really the star attraction. You also find that Chloe's character is more fleshed out compared to the first game - the interactions with her deceased father are really well done, and definitely show her in a more vulnerable light. We also get to see a lot more about Rachel, who was talked about a lot in the first game, but we only got our impression of her from Chloe's own memories. Here, she is front and centre, and it's interesting to see her influence on Chloe, and how that continued to the events of the first game.
The music, provided mainly by British band Daughter, is just as atmospheric and emotional as from the original and - without giving too much away - the song (not by Daughter) that plays as the game ends is just perfect. And talking of the game ending, Before the Storm is much shorter than Life is Strange, clocking up three episodes which are (at least in my view), a little shorter than the episodes from the original. For me, that's neither good or bad, but you may think differently. The other interesting thing to note is that it's much more reality-based than the first one - no magic time powers or weird storms here. I found this a nice thing, but it did limit the game somewhat.
Now onto the bad stuff. Firstly, in comparison to the first game, there's much less to do. There are far fewer physical puzzles (maybe one or two per episode), and the main bulk of the game is about what you say to people. The addition of the 'backtalk' mechanic goes a little way to counteracting this, but this game is much more watching rather than doing. I also found the game world a lot more limiting - areas like the Price house and Blackwell academy are constrained in what you do (you can't wander round nearly as much) and places like the Diner and the lighthouse are completely absent.
Then there's the tone and pace of the story, which is all over the place. Episodes one and two are fairly light and gentle, then episode three suddenly wraps the whole thing up and gets a bit darker. It's very much off-balance, and could either have been stretched to a couple more episodes at the same place or (better) spread more evenly over two. I was also somewhat disappointed that the game ended where it did. I had formed the impression that the game would cover the events leading up to and around Rachel's disappearance, seeing as it was an important plot point in Life is Strange. It does not. This resulted in my feeling a little unsatisfied and unfinished.
Don't get me wrong, Before the Storm is not bad. It's just not as good as the original game. If you expect something that's more of a movie about Rachel and Chloe meeting each other, with choices you can make, then you won't be disappointed. But if you want more of the first game, this isn't where you'll find it. I'd recommend it for those who want more story about Arcadia Bay (and Chloe), but if you're not too bothered about the story of Chloe and Rachel, you can give it a miss.

Honestly, is it amazing and perfect? Of course not. It has glitches, some of the character models look like they could have been in a good PS1/bad PS2 game, the voice acting is sometimes cringe-y, and the game has some slow points.
Regardless of all of that I still loved the game. I'm not sure I would have liked this game without playing the first LIS though. There was never a complete, isolated feeling I felt in Before the Storm in and of its own game.  If it was grinding my heart into the dirt, it was because of what I learned and know from the first game. Just playing the prequel probably would not replicate the same emotional responses as someone who had played the games in order.
My recommendation is to play the first LIS game then buckle into the feels train for some more pain when you play Before the Storm.

Spec Ops is a third-person shooter with a run-and-cover mechanic.
While there is nothing new about this, I couldn't help but love this game, because this is so much more than your average TPS. It's also really, really well optimized.
The gameplay is nicely done, and you handle it pretty fast, being immersed into the universe and the action really quickly. But what really makes it a unique game, is its story.
In this game, you are not just an almighty stereotypical soldier, you are also just a man, with his weaknesses.
The story features some choices; and while you're playing, I'd like you to think twice about everything that happens. Is everything justified? Can anything be justified at all?
I won't spoil the story for you, but this game is much more than an action game. The scenario reminded me a bit of Shutter Island, and this is a good thing.
TL;DR - If you want a game with a lot of action, this is for you. But if you also want an interesting and deep enough storyline, by all means, PLAY THIS GAME.

Premise of this game is a rogue-lite platformer, metroidvania style, where you need to traverse different environments, collect gold and defeat the big bad.  When the game starts, the player is woefully unprepared to fight much of anything. You don't hit much, can't take much damage, etcetera you'll die a lot. Then you start upgrading, buy more health, get better gear, attach ruins to your items, slowly bit by bit you get better. You unlock new classes with new abilities and now you can one shot the enemies.
Just one problem. As you get better, the challenge increases.  You'll encounter new enemies, rooms with mini bosses, more and more challenging environments until finally you discover that you're pretty much treading water.  Worse than that, any gold you accumulate in one run is lost before the next so unless you accumulate enough to actually buy something, say goodbye to the gold. This will become more frequent as you progress through the game as items become more and more expensive.  You can reduce how much gold you lose but either way you're left with a pittance that is not worthy of note.
At most I found I could unlock one or two upgrades, and when you look at the stat upgrades, about 6-8 of them have either 50 or 75 levels! So I need to play the game about 600 or a 1000 times to upgrade the core stats to the max, not counting all the many many times when you'll die with not enough gold for anything. Given my track record I'd probably need to play 3-4000 times to max that stuff out. What a grind!
The game is also full of cheap enemies. Enemy that will spawn out of the ground when you've already committed to a jump. Enemies that will spawn fireballs so big they literally take up 20-25% of the screen. Enemies that won't pivot to face you until the moment they fire. Enemies that sometimes will shoot through a floor, and sometimes won't. Enemies that appear to be part of the background until you jump into them. I also personally have a real problem with the concept of an enemy who both hurts you through an attack, and hurts you through contact. It should be one or the other. Touching a guy in armour shouldn't hurt me. When he swings his sword? Sure. But not when I just touch him. That's very old school, outdated gameplay in my opinion. The enemy should either be attack through contact, or attack through an animation (or a bullet), not both.
There are also some minor but annoying interface issues as well. Like when you lock down the castle, which you may do a lot, after you confirm that you want to lock it down you need to wait a few seconds for the Architect to say some more dialogue. He does this every time! In a game like this, you don't want to waste time re-reading stuff you want to get back into the action straight away. Even traversing the first room gets tedious, hitting lamp stands for a couple bucks, going backwards when your character didn't pick it up. The room should be one screen, not two three. If I'm going to keep replaying then get me back into the game straight away.
On the whole, there are some interesting ideas. And at first the idea of a game where, it's too hard at first but I grind up to get better was appealing. Then I realized the first area and its enemies were upgrading as well, and I thought to hell with it.
Can't recommend this.

The Hitman series has always been a niche series, there is not other way to state that.  However, this installment of Hitman may be unique in that it is both approachable to new players, and still satisfies the hardcore.  New players can be guided through missions using contracts and "feats", which provide a simple hint system to important cover and objectives.  Veteran/purist players can turn off all the additions since Blood Money (instinct, hints, etc).
Keeping this in mind, the first season pack and base game are excellent.  This game feels like the sandbox Hitman we've played for many years now, and it really is fun to play.  What will harm this game the most both now and in the long run is the episodic release schedule.  However, if you are a fan of the previous Hitman games (besides Absolution), and love a tactical and sandbox assassination game, this is for you.
PRO/POSITIVE
-Game feels like a return to form.  The classic series is all here.
-Game has new features like "feats" which give new players hints and guides them through levels.  Veterans and pursists can turn it all off, making for a classic Hitman experience.
-The overall presentation and interface is clean, objectives and mentions on screen easy to follow.
-The content currently there is sparse, but excellent.  Never before have there been so many actual ways to kill targets.
-As opposed to previous games, Hitman has a lot of extra social capabilities, such as guiding targets to rigged testing sites, or actually playing a model on the catwalk instead of just dressing up like one.  It really increases the immersion.
-AI is Hitman esque, which is to say, feels like classically good AI.  Don't expect perfection, but what is there is good.
-The base mechanics and game feel and play excellent.  The basis is here.  Now IO just needs to deliver content.
-All maps are very customizable with entry points, starting costumes, and many options that allow personal tweaking that did not exist before.
CONS/NEGATIVE
-The game's performance is terrible.  At the time of review/launch I am running an overclocked i7 at 4GHZ, 16GB of RAM, and a GTX780TI.  In other words, a powerful rig that is placed at the top 2% of Steam.  It's lagging and unable to push me beyond high/average settings.
-The release schedule makes no sense.  Content in terms of story and actual developer content is sparse.  It's good, but sparse.
-The AI are mostly good, but especially their aim is terrible.
-Options to disable helping features are hidden under layer and layers of menus, a strange constrast to most of the UI.

Early "Review" to help those who can't access Paris on launch day.
If you're having trouble accessing Paris with the Intro Pack or Full Experience, try this:
1. Right Click the Hitman game entry in your library
2. Click on Properties
3. Click on the DLC tab in the Properties menu
4. Be sure that the install check box next to Paris is indeed checked
Steam should begin installing the map soon after
As for the review, the game seems great so far. I can't vouch for the entire game, but I can tell you that if you're at all interested you should at least try the Intro Pack. The tutorials alone are tons of fun.

This felt magical again! Like "Risky Boots Revenge" - the first Shantae game I played. Transformations are back, the graphics feel more HD (the previous games were made for the Nintendo DS and thus had a way smaller resolution), and familiar faces in every direction.
Stages are set up "Select Screen" style again. I preferred the way they did it in Risky Boots Revenge - the world map I mean - and thought it was a downgrade to the game world as a whole when it went from that to a simple stage select in The Pirate's Curse - which they kept for this. It's not the worst thing in the world though.
The puzzles weren't hard until the final level. Most of the stages weren't set up with puzzles.  There were some here and there (avoiding laser beams, climbing a maze before time is up, the entire final level) but most levels were based around exploration or simple advancement from point A to B through a horde of enemies.
A lot of the transformations completely outclassed other transformations. I enjoyed using them anyway - and I felt a bit more lenient about there being forms that were less useful when I found out some of them were just tossed in as extra rewards for the players to enjoy.
While the graphics themselves were enhanced the animations for the characters seemed a little less amped than the previous games in the series. I mean I still enjoyed them and they still came to a point I feel keeps WayForward of the "We care about the animation quality" mentality, but they were clearly a little less ambitious than previous games on that specific detail. There's only one dance animation for example when everybody was amazed at her dancing in
. I can totally understand
though: they added several times more transformations so waiting for a cycle of 20 dances to roll through would have been unintuitive and probably aggravating after a bit.
I played with the transformations like toys. I
the transformations. I did what I could to try and beat every stage I reasonably could as each transformation (which I'm still in the middle of doing). Ultimately I feel the transformations are what make a Shantae game a Shantae game.
I feel like the game lost
about it that was there in the earlier games but I can't put my finger on it. It also added more
. It still feels like a Shantae game. Just somehow with a little more and a little less "something". The key to enjoying this game is using / understanding mouse movement.
When I read about this game I just about burst. If lack of Sid Meyer's Pirates has left a hole in your gaming soul, GET IT. BUT, I was initially frustrated with movement. This will help immensely:
I had my controller ready, prepared to catch winds and sail to ports unknown, re live my pirates dreams. Then my♥♥♥♥♥♥sat there. I tried to turn to catch the wind like I would have done in SMP. Nope. Saw that I could use the mouse at the same time. Moved a bit. More nope.
Here's how to make this game FEEL good, so you can enjoy the trading and battling and everything else.
Use the mouse, with mouse movement activated in the setting. Use ONLY the mouse. And there's a very important thing to understand about it: ***The Left Mouse Button = Increse Throttle --- The Right Mouse Button = Decrese Throttle***
I know this sounds incredibly weird, but after an hour plus of fumbling around, wondering if I needed to hold down left mouse to move... or what the heck was going on, that was when I discovered it functioned like a throttle. Once you are going in the direction you want to go, you will keep going. And, you can throttle-down for tight turns and so on. Enjoy. Love the game!

tldr - I like it. Maia shows great promise, and has a very low chance of succumbing to Early Access Syndrome.
Your base is built into a mountain (the atmosphere of the titular Maia is toxic). If your colonists need to go outside (to build solar stills for water, wind turbines/solar arrays for power, collecting researchable things like non-sentient alien creatures and plants, or meteorites, etc) they will use the airlock. The suits they use outside are cumbersome and slow.
Inside the mountain-base you designate (much like Dungeon Keeper) areas to be mined out. Once empty areas can have rooms (such as a workshop, a research room, a living area, a hydroponics room, etc) built into them. You must then place a door, and other context specific items (for example workbenches and 3D-printers in the workshop, or beds/couches and toilets in the living area).
Once a game starts you must quickly build a workshop, and add a workbench. Once that is done you must build a power system (wind turbine/solar array, or a geo-thermal power plant as well as a "fly-wheel" energy storage (battery). Once a power system has been built you must place atmosphere generators. That all takes care of your urgent needs. You must however secure a food source (hydroponics, or animal farms) and continually satisfy the needs of your colonists.
You do not directly control your colonists.
The devs of this game have stated from the outset that they don't want to 'spoon-feed' players to much information, and have designed the game in such a way that players must work for information. There is no "emotion bubble" that floats above your colonists, only biometric data like respiration rate, perspiration rate, heart-beats per minute, etc. This is just one example of a system that promotes player interaction and investigation as opposed to unrewarding spoon-feeding. All the information you'll need is there, you just have to find it.
Maia is still in Early Access (As I write this, Alpha version 0.51) which poses several problems with a recommendation. When it comes to Early Access many promising games are either; abandoned by their developers halfway through development, developed in such a way that early-adopters are angered, or have their developers react angrily from criticism. I believe that Maia, although not immune from such problems, is certainly free of them for the foreseeable future.
Maia has received regular updates, both small 'hotfixes' and major updates. The two latest major updates, Alpha 0.50 and Alpha 0.51 were deployed on the 3rd September 2015, and 22 October 2015 respectively. Each update adds a lot of new content, and fixes bugs.
The developer, Simon Roth, is also very active on Twitter and happily answers questions.
Some Early Access games have started out promising but developed along different lines than what was promised. I don't think Maia is at risk of that as it's clear from development and the content of updates that Simon and his team have a clear plan and is sticking to it. Hopefully this will protect against feature-creep, and I have seen no evidence that it isn't.
Some strong games have been let down by their developers being taking criticism very badly and being rude - which does sometimes make people shy away from their games and makes adapters regret supporting such devs and their games. Simon and his team do not appear to be the type to do any of this though, as Simon is quite open on Twitter and I have never seen or heard any complaints regarding his behaviour.

I never really got into the Trackmania series... A friend of mine made me buy it years ago (he loves it). I didn't like racing with keyboard, I disliked the casual arcade style, I disliked the very short races.  I found a whole bunch of things to dislike and noted them in order of priority (that list has been lost now, perhaps thrown away inadvertently).
2015 is drawing to an end, and having recently purchased an Oculus DK2: I downloaded the demo of Trackmania Stadium.  I can tell you that Trackmania with Oculus is a whole new experience! The graphics are beautiful in stereoscopic 3d. The visuals are very sharp, beautifully lit and it all looks very real. Not even the slightest hint of judder (running in extended mode 6.0.1. runtime windows 8, Nvidia 680).
I think HMD VR has the unique ability of being able to reveal to you the beauty of a particular game you couldn't fully appreciate without it.
When playing games the conventional way through a TV or monitor - you're seeing that game world from a distance (through a small window). With VR you are projected into that world - everything is life size. You tend to notice things and feel immersed to a degree not possible even with the best 4k monitor or large screen TV.
Control-wise it's nice to see Trackmania automatically detect my Saitek X52 Pro so I can use the joystick for racing (I haven't had to configure anything!). Much nicer than key-presses.
Racing in 3rd person with Oculus is mind-blowing (3rd person was also on my dislike list in the past).  You get to see all of the detail in the game and the tracks are jaw-dropping. I find myself looking up at the sky or at the intricate scenery. I would say this is one of the best VR experiences you can have.  In an instant I have converted from someone who didn't like the game (previous versions), to someone who thinks it's stunning and hopes Nadeo convert their entire series to VR. Yes, for every Trackmania game released with VR support: I will buy and recommend to others.
Trackmania is a great example of a game that reveals its true beauty through VR...
Nadeo should be very proud of this creation.

A fantastic rogue-lite where dying doesn't mean a hard reset. In death your character is succeeded by one of their offspring and all of your earned skills, talents, equipment and gold are passed down from one generation to the next, ensuring that even the weakest of players can still make progress. After each death you are given the choice of three characters that are randomised from a pool of three to eight classes (depending on how many you unlock) who are given randomly drawn traits and abilites; some good, some bad. The castle itself is also randomised keeping the game fresh despite there only being four environments.
All in all, I found it a thoroughly addictive game despite minimal experience in the genre beforehand and would recommend it to anyone who merely thought "that looks interesting" as they skimmed over the Steam store page.

Dear Valve employees,
Please fix the review submission system. It is very annoying to have to post a short review and then edit it into a long review instead of being able to post a long review directly like we used  to be able to do.
Sincerely,
A Steam user with way too many games who is trying to write reviews for games as I finish them.
And now onto the review...
I'm not sure why all the game reviewers were so hard on this game. Sure, it has some issues, but I had a lot more fun playing this game than many other games that reviewers couldn't say enough good things about.
The biggest thing this game has going for it is the exploration factor. The game world map is quite large with lots of points of interest to explore, both on foot and in your car. It actually has one of the more interesting game worlds I've seen in terms of exploration, which is impressive given that the whole world is pretty much a desert wasteland. There's also a good balance between time spent driving and exploring on foot. The customizable and upgradeable vehicle was also a great decision, rather than limiting Max to the interceptor.
The camps are well done, with each one being actually unique and interesting rather than just a cookie cutter layout. I enjoyed exploring them (and parking my car outside and using the harpoon to pick off as many enemies as I could before getting out of the car).
That said, this game, as much fun as it is, could have been so much better with a few changes. Hopefully someone will take note and we'll get a sequel someday with some major improvements.
The story is forgettable and ultimately ends up being a giant diversion for Max. The game ends exactly like it began. If the opening cutscene had played out slightly differently, the game could have ended right there and the ending cinematic would have fit perfectly. While that might fit the Mad Max theme, I would have much preferred a story and ending that took into account the effect that Max had on the inhabitants of the world. It was also kind of strange to see characters killed off at the end of the story resurrected after the credits like nothing had happened (although they were likeable characters so I wasn't too sad, just slightly confused).
I would also have appreciated it if the world map included all three major wasteland locations from the Mad Max lore (the Citadel and Bullet Farm in addition to Gastown). That could also have lent itself well to a better story with various warlords vying for control of the wasteland, instead of Max simply trying to get a V8 to build a new car (seriously, that's his goal for almost the entire game). The game difficulty is easy throughout, especially if you keep up with your upgrades. Unfortunately, there's a few very annoying difficulty spikes throughout the game (the first top dog boss enemy before you really have the upgrades to properly deal with them, and the death race to get the V8) that can be pretty frustrating.
I also wish that the game had more shooter and less brawler. As it stands, this game barely qualifies as a shooter given the short range of the shotgun. The brawling has its place, but the QTE block/punch that works for other WB games (this game is using the same engine as the Arkham games and Shadow of Mordor) feels overwrought here. Sure, Max punched a lot of guys to death in the movies, but he also shot just as many and with a much larger arsenal than what is available in this game. If we get a sequel, make it a proper 3rd person shooter (the Just Cause guys made this game, they have plenty of experience with this) without skimping on the melee. The lack of some kind of portable explosive besides bulky jerry cans (grenade, demo charge, whatever) is also quite annoying given how many times you need explosives to blast open a door but there aren't any gas cans nearby so you have to drive somewhere else to pick one up. Plus, given how often you get swarmed by enemies, they would be quite useful in a fight.
The vehicular weaponry is much more robust than on foot, but I would have liked to see a game mechanic that allowed Max to jump onto and hijack other vehicles (again, Just Cause comes to mind), especially since the NPC enemies can jump on your car and attack your health directly. Also, given how prominently War Rigs were featured in Fury Road, I was quite disappointed to see how little presence they had in this game. They would have been a perfect fit for convoys and vehicle boarding mechanics, and could have been neat challenges in line with the camps rather than the turkey shoot (at least once you have an upgraded thunderpoon) that the convoys are now. The fuel mechanic also feels like a bit of a waste, vehicles don't use much fuel at all unless you're using side burners so you don't generally need to fill the tank very often at all. The only reason to carry a gas can in the back is because for some points of interest, it's the only way to get the explosion you need to open a door.
The whole dog and minefield thing feels like a gigantic missed opportunity honestly. I would have much rather seen the dog implemented similarly to how it was done in Fable 2 and 3, where the dog assists you in melee combat and helps you find easy to miss collectibles. The minefields should also have been part of camp defenses or general area denial (like a real minefield would) rather than uselessly spread out where you wouldn't normally drive anyways. Right now with the current game mechanic, the minefields are just another thing you have to find to reduce threat, with the added caveat that they can be quite annoying to even find and you have to use a defenseless vehicle to do so rather than putting the dog in your awesome car you use for everything else. Plus half the time you end up driving over the mine about the time the dog reveals it, wrecking the buggy so you have to fast travel back to a stronghold to fix it, but then you can't fast travel with the buggy so you have to drive an often significant distance back to where the minefield was to finish clearing it.
Despite my long list of grievances , I did enjoy my time with this game overall and can easily recommend it if you enjoy open world action games and exploring large environments. Hopefully someone will make a sequel and we'll be able to play a really great Mad Max game. As always, try to get it on sale.

Been a while since I've reviewed something and I feel this game needs more positive PR.
Maybe that sounds like I have an agenda or some ulterior motive off the bat, but the long and short of it is this game is f*cking fun.
This game is what I picture the video-game child of Rage and Batman: Arkham Knight to look like. A strange combination of games, but they share some elements. Character development parallels your vehicle development, which thankfully is entirely customizable, and there are so many upgrades for both the Magnum Opus and Max it's ridiculous. Open world, free-roaming gameplay, auto-saving persistent progression: it also has some Assassin's Creed feel. Most open world games do nowadays, but I actually felt like I was part of the living wasteland when I rumbled past a scrap settlement, scouting camps to raid, scavenging for parts, water, and fuel.
I can understand some people may find the gameplay repetitive after some time as the story leaves quite a lot to be desired. It's a typical Max story from the movie series and writing has never been the strong suit. If intense vehicle action moments, Arkham style combat system, character progression and collectibles are your jam, then look no further.
Also, if you like the Mad Max movies at all, this game will still be right up your alley. It has all the high-octane, sawed-off, wasteland weirdness that inspired games like Borderlands, Fallout and Rage. It is not directly tied to the Fury Road movie either, but it does have some crossover characters and obviously is in the same universe.
If you've never seen a Mad Max movie, start with Road Warrior and go straight to Fury Road. Thank me later.

What can I possibly say that has not been said already?
Most people have made up their minds about this game already, but if you are one of the few who are on the fence, perhaps you have mixed feelings like: "It seems really popular, but people won't tell me WHY it's good, and some of the fans are just insufferably annoying!"
I feel you. I know where you are coming from. Let me try to help.
This game has a charming feel to it that is very story-driven. It is occasionally silly and funny, and at other times, deep and dramatic. In my opinion, the characters are developed extremely well. They all really seem to POP out of the background as far as having distinct personalities.
There are parts of it that remind me of Earthbound, Chrono Trigger, and Secret of Mana, not due to any overt reference, but because of the general feel of this variety of story-driven RPG. The music, for example, is absolutely wonderful at helping to craft the mood.
There is, indeed, a morality system in this game. You may have played games like Mass Effect or Fable that also allowed the player to make choices based on different moral frameworks, but this is different. I have never seen a game handle morality the way Undertale does, and I do not wish to go into more detail about it than that, because I feel that it is best experienced by playing through the game multiple times oneself. The game has an intriguing and unique method of presentation for it, and I want everyone to be able to experience it that way.
Your choices MATTER. Things REALLY change when you try to play the game in a significantly different way. Endings can be VERY different, depending on how you handle various situations. Undertale only allows one save slot, and this is by design. It would undermine an aspect of the story-telling and the tension around the importance of your choices if you could easily save multiple simultaneous branches of the story. I found it a tiny bit frustrating, at first, but now that I understand why it is there, I appreciate it more. I encourage you to bear with that restriction. At any point, including after you finish the game, you have the option of resetting to start over and try things differently, and this feature helps make that a bigger deal.
Now, I am a bit obsessed, so take what I say with the appropriate grain of salt. Even the creator, Toby Fox, said of the game in his Undertale anniversary tweet that it was an 8/10 niche game. Of course there are those who will never like this game, and that is just fine. If you hate this game, I do not think that you are wrong. We simply like different things, which is normal. I recommend it, though, to anyone who is curious to know what it is all about and who enjoyed the old story-driven RPG's from the previous millennium.
The fandom is, indeed, massive and passionate. Though I have seen many complaints about the fandom in general, I personally love the fandom as a whole. I understand how they may be a bit annoying to non-fans who do not know what they are blabbering about, and, of course, as with any fandom this big, there are always going to be elements of it that take it too seriously, no piece of fan-made content is going to be well-received by the whole community, and no member of the community is going to like every piece of fan-made content. The flip-side to that is that there is SO MUCH content that it is easy (for me, at least) to ignore the stuff for which I do not care and actually find more GOOD content I love than I can ever have time to experience! Truly, with the fandom as active as it has been, I can continue to enjoy Undertale-related content as much as I want without ever running out!

I came across a word today, Sensucht, which is German for "longing and nostalgia for a far-off home one has never visited,". This and the original game, Life is Strange, invoked such intense feelings of Sensucht in me, which is such a remarkable thing for me, as someone who is not American, and grew up influenced by a different culture entirely.
The somewhat lack of realism in the graphics department is overcome by the stylish art direction, and very strong story, supported by characters who are genuinely human.
Despite being developed by a third party studio, not by the original developers, Dontnod, this iteration of LiS serves an experience that really lives up to the standards set by the original game, which was amazing.

Given the fact, that Before the Storm wasnt able to use a key element of the main game - the rewind feature - and only tells the story of Chloe (without the presence of Max), Deck Nine (and the very different voice crew) did a pretty good job.
The first two episodes were great, because they focused on the emotional relationship between Chloe and Rachel. Leaving this trail in the third part und focusing on another narrative stays an arguable decision.
But for the ones out there, who love the character of Chloe Price (like I do) and the life she has to deal with, this game is definitely worth playing.

Surprisingly, I like this game even more than the original. After finishing "Before the Storm", I went back to play the original "Life is strange" again, and I have to say, I couldn't really like Chloe anymore - at least not as much as in "Before the Storm". I wouldn't ever have thought that a different studio could improve upon the original vision. Not having time powers actually made the game a much more enjoyable experience.
There are downsides - especially the [walking] animations. Basically, most characters move like they had to endure catastrophic damage to their bodies. Nothing about the animations looks remotely realistic. To be honest, I found that quite off-putting - but not enough to keep me from wanting to move on with the story. Which is where the second nuisance comes in. You know, I love slow takes in movies. I love Tarkovsky movies; I can't get enough of his "The Sacrifice". But in "Before the Storm", we're dealing with almost grown kids of our times - and nobody at that age speaks as slow and with so many pauses. At times it feels like the development team realized it needed to stretch the gameplay and just inflated the dialogue with pauses and turned the speed dial down two notches.
But even that could not keep me from playing the whole thing in one session. It has a lot of awesome scenes that just stick in your mind for a long time.
Absolutely recommended.
Edit: Clarified that the most horrible animations occur whilke walking.

- So you should treat anything I say as biased, untrustworthy, probably composed of festering garbage.
Maia is a unique, captivating game. It explores the possibility of a human colony on an alien world. Even in its present unfinished state, Maia is worthy of purchase and full of potential for enjoyment and delight.
I first encountered Maia at a
Being fascinated by space exploration, I was immediately sucked in. Maia 'gets' space exploration in the same way DayZ 'gets' zombies: The story is not the zombies, it is the
In Maia, people are at the heart of the experience. They do what the want. They interact with each other. They may follow your orders, or they may laze about and die of starvation. They might threaten each other, become sad, grow happy, or develop relationships. They are truly a group of colonists, going about life on an alien world.
Interaction with Maia is indirect. The player never builds structures, or conducts research. Instead, requests are placed in the world and colonists then react to those requests. I use the word 'request' rather than order, because colonists will not always carry out instructions.
At first, their ambivalence to a placed Atmosphere Generator may be interpreted as a bug in the game. With more play time it becomes apparent that the colonists have a sense of what is important, and what is required. Already have too many Solar Arrays? Colonists might simply choose not to build them.
There are no centralised mechanisms for managing colony power, food, and water requirements. Instead, individual stores must be inspected, and observations taken around the world. This quirk can sometimes be frustrating, but that frustration can give way to fulfillment - Balancing a power grid is very hard, and more rewarding for being so.
Often I see Maia referred to as a 'God Game.' Having never played 'God Games,' and not being familiar with the genre, I can't speak to the accuracy of that description. I would not, however, describe Maia as a god game in the first instance: The player is not god, they are a companion. Not omniscient, omnipresent, or all-powerful at all. Instead, the player is limited, flawed, and often ineffectual - A reflection, perhaps, of the colonists pottering about on the planet surface, and all the more enjoyable for it.
Generally, I am about as artistic as a pencil sharpener, so I'm not the one to judge Maia's aesthetics. But I think it looks fantastic.
The use of a custom renderer means the game does not express the intangible 'feel' of a commercial solution such as Unity or Unreal. Instead, it gives of a vibe of bespoke craftsmanship. Models are of a consistently high quality. Animations are well weighted and engaging - Though they are often blatantly disconnected from the gameplay their are supposed to be related to.
Early Access games come in various flavours of 'bugginess,' and Maia has tended to hover towards the 'very buggy' end of the spectrum through much of its development. Because Maia does not offer many explicit clues to the player about what is happening in the world, bugs can be insidious. A colonist sitting on the floor of a room may be bored and recalcitrant: Or their AI might simply be stuck in a buggy loop of doom.
Recently, the
has brought fresh stability and consistency to the experience. If Stardystopia is a foundation upon which Maia grows in future updates, then it has the potential to leave its challenged technical past behind.
Judging the character of Maia's development is perhaps the act in which my conflict of interest is most likely to manifest itself. It is also the area of which I am most critical.
An Early Access game must be open. To be on Steam Early Access to not just invite, it is to require the interaction of customers with the development team. It has been difficult for Maia's customers to find information about development. In the last few months, the team has made strides towards pulling down the fourth wall and letting information flow out to customers. This process must accelerate.
The pacing and content of development updates are strong. Most especially since around March this year Maia has received consistent, high quality updates that have steadily improved the game.
Most importantly, Maia's development team has authentic soul and character.

Maia is a unique, captivating game. It explores the possibility of a human colony on an alien world. Even in its present unfinished state, Maia is worthy of purchase and full of potential for enjoyment and delight.

Rogue Legacy is not quite a rogue-like, but neither is it just a platformer or an RPG. Yet it hits the exact right notes right for each of those genres in unision, creating an addictive experience with much to offer.
The game plays very much like an 2D action adventure game. Coupled with the castle environment, with its chandeliers, and even some of the weapons, the game is certainly reminiscent of Castlevania in both style and substance, but what it does differently is what makes the game. The castoe is procedurally generated, but with a general layout with four different areas, each with their own enemies, bosses and difficulty.
But what really makes every playthrough different, is the unique legacy system; instead of playing as a single charcter, you play through generations, picking from one of 3 choices each time who retain some of the qualities of their ancestors. Add to that the 9 classes, differing abilities and special weapons and the numerous (and often hilarious) traits, and you don't feel like you're chained to a certain style of play. Maybe you enjoy being a walking tank Barbarian most of the time, but sometines you might want to gain more money so you choose a relatelively weak Miner and fit it with appropriate abilities and gear for maxium effect.
The upgrade possibilities in the game are enough to help you feel a general sense of progress, even during times when the difficulty tests your patience. The game is not merciless but it certainly has sufifcient challege. With one upgrade, you gain the possibiltiy to visit the same castle that you did before for a certain price, still starting from scracth but knowing what's ahead and where to go. The runes for the Enchantress (abilities) and Blacksmith gear blueprints you find throughout the castle can be only found once, but there is enough to discover that it can take a while. While the equippables are beneficial, it's really the sum of the equipment that counts, no single rune or gear is a gamebreaker. The skill tree is quite important and help you with every aspect of the game, and deciding where to use your hard earned gold next will be constantly on your mind.
The controls in the game are very natural. The game plays and looks nice, and all in all gives you seemingly ever-lasting, addictive fun worth the price. The full price of 14,99€ is just right for a game of this caliber, and if you manage to grab it during a sale, definitely don't hestitate to go for it. I'm on my second playthrough of the game, with 53 hours of playtime under me, and I still get the occasional craving to just play for a little while.

I typically don't like Rogue-like games. Initially, they're enjoyable...like a novelty...but, soon, devolve into a monotonous playthrough of the same series of levels with a lot of randomized luck intertwined to make it seem like leveling up. Rogue Legacy flips the concept on its head...for the better...way better. It introduces the better looking and more coordinated Rogue sibling - the one that the original, orthodox Rogue games always pined to be. It eliminates perma-death (kind of), and cleverly integrates a true RPG-feel leveling regime through an heir system by which, when a character dies, the following character iteration is an heir of the dearly departed ancestor with all the previously earned stats still intact. The game still remains true to the procedurally / randomly generated level boards following a reincarnation, but it smartly rids itself of giving a shadowed perception of leveling up within a life by lucky pick-ups. You are in control, and you will love it.
Rogue Legacy cleverly combines the mechanics of an action platformer with elements of Rogue and Castlevania. It can be difficult to start, as it is the most Rogue-ish at the beginning when your stats are near-nil. But, that heir system kicks in with lots of deaths (rarely a meaningless death), and you start building your character with all the neat perks, weapons, spells and more. This game may have single-handedly changed my outlook on the Rogue genre. If you were sheepish to engage in a Rogue-type game for the aforementioned reasons, pick this little indie gem up, and it may just change yours too.

I don't usually review games that I play, no matter how exceptional or horrible they are, but this game changed the way I think about games, and as many people as possible need to play it.
This is a game that made me think, for once, about what I did in video games. This game puts weight behind everything the player does and makes the player realize that what he has done in other games in the past, say Call of Duty or Battlefield, is so horrible and evil that the player feels awful about themselves. And, that is amazing. I have never played another game that has effected me this much emotionally.
Lets break down the game into sections to review:
Graphics: The game is gorgeous. It is actually stunningly gorgeous. It has color where you wouldn't expect, wonderful lighting, the sand looks amazing and the destruction and dynamism of the world looks fabulous.
Sound: The sound is very well done. The soundtrack sets the moody tone fantastically, and plays at the exact right volume without adjusting the options at all. Effects sound meaty and full, and voice acting is fantastic.
Gameplay: The game is boring to play. Normally, that would be a fault. However, in this case, it is GENIUS. It makes the player ask, why am I playing this game? What am I doing? And that is integral to how this game knocks down all precedents that the player has from worse, emotionless games. This is not to say the gameplay is bad. The cover system works very well and the weapons are nice and easy to control. There is nothing wrong with the gameplay that makes the game hard to work with.
Presentation: The UI and menus are very nice, minimalistic, and unobtrusive. The main menu is a gorgeous dynamic menu that changes throughout the game.
Note: The game comes with coop and noncoop multiplayer. Both of these are dead and should only be considered if you have a group of friends you want to play with. Otherwise, discount them entirely. This game is about the campaign.
This game made all of it's characters feel like genuine human beings who were going through the campaign's awful situation, and you feel just as connected to what they are going through as to what you are going through playing it. The game is a triumph of storytelling and is a masterful piece of interactive art. The game will make you question everything you do without thinking in other games and will make you put more stock into story rather than gameplay for the first time ever (second time ever if you have played Shadow of the Colossus). Everyone who plays games needs to play this, and anyone who questions whether or not games can really be art/literature just need to be pointed this way. It is one of the greatest games of all time and will stick with you forever.

This is basically PTSD: The Game.
As a game, it's pretty standard.  You get into cover.  You shoot guys with guns.  Run to the waypoint to continue getting into cover and shooting guys with guns.  It feels fairly clunky to actually get into cover.  I felt like I had to hit the space bar a specific way to actually get into cover.  There are a handful of weapons in different categories like rifles, shotguns, small arms, snipers and heavy weapons.  Everything feels fairly generic with a few exceptions like shooting a part of the environment to dump sand on your foes and that's about it.  You can give orders to your team, but some orders only pop up at specific times and I could never seem to be able to use the attack order.  I was able to beat the campaign on the hardest availible starting difficulty in under 7 hours.  Again, as a game, it's pretty generic.
As an experience, it's a completely different beast.  Never in my life have I played a military shooter that was this shocking.  If you thought the nuke scene and "no russian" from Call of Duty were hardcore, then you haven't seen anything yet.  It's really something you have to see for yourself and I wouldn't dare spoil it.  If I had to compare the story to anything, it feels a lot like the movie "Apocalypse Now" and if you've seen that movie then you should be aware of the levels of shock you are getting into...but even the story here goes above and beyond that.   Again, as an experience, it's quite unique.
If you can get it cheap, do not pass it up even if you don't like cover shooters.  This is one game you need to see to the end...

This game is a monster that devours time. Be warned.
The unique feature that differentiates it from most other games in the genre is the deep simulation, and the emergent gameplay that results from it. You have to manage deadly gasses, boiling water, and supercooled ice. Different gasses build up in your base and layer on top of each other. Gas pressures can change, causing the other layers of gas to expand or contract. Gas pressure effects plant growth and temperature conductivity. Operating machines in a vacuum can cause them to overheat and meltdown. Badly placed machines can raise the air temperature enough to scald and eventually kill your poor colonists.
During play, you have to manage farming (and food spoilage/refrigeration), water (pumping, piping, filtration), oxygen (and a dozen other gasses), heat (and cold, both of which can kill you), diseases, electricity, even stress levels in the base. There is a ton of depth here, and it can be kind of frustrating keeping all those plates spinning at times, but if you manage to create a balanced base, it's a great feeling.

REVIEW OF 0.49:
I just had a look at the 0.49 and regrettably I must say I wouldn't recommend this game. I bought it around 0.47 because it looked so good on paper but here is why you actually shouldn't get it in my opinion, at least in its current state:
- the updates have been increasingly rare
- the updates that it does get add new functionality that seems random while it doesn't improve the (lack of ) core game play
- there is no sense in the game of what you are supposed to be doing - e.g. how much material / food / colonists in total you have. They just added reports on power which is great, but every game like this has an overview window that shows you your resources so that you know what you need to be getting next. That, to me, seems more important than adding weapons, for instance.
- there is no sense of why accidents happen - e.g. all my atmosphere generators exploded all at once - I have no idea why! And the colonists don't seem to care, they just walk around. You would expect major panic if something like this happened in the real life (the game is supposed to be a simulation, right?)
Before you all start accusing me of not knowing what alpha is - I know very well. I'm a dev myself.
In my opinion, the devs here should stop adding more functionality that create more breadth and isntead focus on improving the gamer's experience to create depth. Make a game out of this. Because at the moment, it seems like bunch of functionality stitched together. Give us a reason to play! Experimenting with new features is great, but wears off after you've built everything. The game is not interesting after that.  Give us a sense of what we are doing and why we are doing it!

This is for me a difficult game to review – this was the first game I ever kickstarted back in the misty past of 2013, and I never believed for a moment that a 2D platformer would take three and a half years to materialise. With such a long time in development, backers’ expectations were high – Wayforward have a pedigree, and I’ve enjoyed every game they’ve ever produced. The Shantae games in particular are blessed with excellent production values, level design and waifus that are frankly off the hook.
It’s clear to me that those years in development were not spent productively. I completed the game with 100% items in under six hours, and I’m fairly certain that it could easily be completed in half that. Of course length is not necessarily an indication of quality, as ur mum will attest – but the levels here are short and linear, so much so that there is no map screen. Some levels don’t even feel finished, and considering the small number of them and the extensive development time that’s pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥poor. Most of the levels need to be revisited to find items crucial for advancing the story, which is a transparent way of lengthening the dismal play time. Backtracking is of course a metroidvania staple, but here it feels forced and unnecessary.
In terms of abilities, transformations are back after an absence in Pirate’s Curse. There are certainly a wealth of transformations compared to previous games (each beautifully rendered and animated), but some of them barely have anything to do, and there’s a surprising degree of redundancy. The level design also feels very flabby and under baked – certain abilities borderline break the game at the point they can be acquired, like the bat that allows you to pretty much skip half the desert level.
Outside of the amazing visuals and music (and they really are best in class), Half Genie Hero is entirely inferior to Pirate’s Curse, and if I’m being honest it doesn’t even hold up particularly favourably to Risky’s Revenge. Looking at Half Genie Hero in a vacuum, it’s a fun little platformer, and I can’t deny I enjoyed my (short) time with it - however, compared to both its immediate predecessor and the stiff competition in the metroidvania market on Steam, it just isn’t worth the fifteen quid.

Shantae:  Half-Genie Hero is a competent platformer, but it gets too many things wrong for me to recommend it.  There are 6 stages in all, including the final stage which holds no secrets and another stage that holds only a couple that you'll visit maybe three times.  As you play, you accumulate more abilities and forms for Shantae which enable you to visit previously inaccessible areas and acquire more items and powerups.  But because the final stage has no secrets and another one has only a couple, you'll spend most of the game visiting the same 4 stages repeatedly.  To pad the length of the game and make up for a lack of content, you are occasionally given strange, lengthy fetch quests to complete to advance the story.
I'll be blunt:  Half Genie Hero doesn't feel like a complete game.  It isn't just the lack of stages.  A few of the transformations--like bat and spider--have no real part to play in the game.  You use them a couple of times to collect optional items and nothing else.  Half Genie Hero was funded on Kickstarter and I suspect the developer may have hoped to be funded for more stages that would make use of things like the bat and spider transformations.  And unlike a traditional metroidvania game, there is really no variety or sequence breaking to be had.  You either have the right upgrade or you don't.  And since the game is so small, there really isn't any sense of progression.
The game starts out at an average difficulty, but once you start buying some of the items in the shop and upgrading your life the difficulty soon vanishes.  You'll have so much health and take so little damage from attacks that you can literally just walk through normal enemies.  You can even buy an invincibility spell which further reduces the challenge.  There are a couple of places where the difficult absolutely skyrockets.  One is an area where you must climb quickly to avoid instant death, and another consists of a long path of one-hit kill spikes that you must fly through with extremely awkward controls.  It's like the developers struggled to balance the difficulty and then decided they needed some areas with serious challenge.
I really like the style of the game and its characters, but the game just doesn't live up to its potential and I can't recommend it.  If you want a platformer, grab Shovel Knight or Freedom Planet instead.  If you'd like to play a game specifically like Castlevania, I'd recommend Valdis Story.  If you like games like the classic Metroid (or just good games in general) check out Axiom Verge.  If you're set on playing Shantae because it looks interesting, I'd recommend checking out the previous game in the series instead.

Besides the terrible optimisation and the♥♥♥♥♥♥poor decision of splitting the game up into 'seasons', this is the complete Hitman experience I have longed for since the release of Blood Money in 2006. It's a near-perfect blend of Absolution's solid shooting and steath mechanics coupled with Blood money's non linear level design. It's clear from the outset that the best elements of it's predecessors have been cherry picked and neatly placed into this game. For example, Silent Assassin's expansive level size, Blood Money's broad range of options to carry out each mission with pinpoint precision and  Absolution's dark, gritty narative.
Pros
+Great story introduction
+Best elements are kept from the previous games
+Non-linear gameplay makes a welcomed return
+Believable, realistic, living, breathing environments
+Voice acting is superb
+AI has recieved some heavy treatment
+Surprising amount of variety in missions
Cons
-Poor optimisation (Wait a few months for it to be fixed)
-Episodic release
-Graphics are mediocre at best
-Lack of missions
-Controls can be clunky at times
-60fps cap
Ultimately, is this the Blood Money 2 we've been looking for? Short answer, yes. This is the right to Absolutions wrong. Well worth the price tag.

Like snow or Christmas decorations, Call of Duty shows itself by the end of the year. Like every year since Modern Warfare. This time, it's the turn of Call of Duty: Black Ops 2, developed by Treyarch. Call of Duty: Black Ops 2 brings players back into the shadows for another Black Ops mission assignment. Rooted in near-future fiction, Black Ops 2 propels players into warfare in an epic single player campaign highlighted by branching storylines and non-linear missions. A re-imagined multiplayer suite introduces players to some of the most cutting-edge weaponry and equipment that 2025 will have to offer. And on the outskirts of the campaign is an all-new Zombies experience running in the multiplayer engine. Unlike its predecessor, the story sets in two distinct eras, the 80's and the year 2025. Two viewpoints which allow the game to offer many side roads in the story, and 8 different endings. This is a first for such a mainstream series. Of course the game's core remains the same on the basics: cinematic action, epic scenes and a percussive score. Even if Black Ops 2 reuses old recipes, it does it really well and remains a great experience.
