Okay, so, I have to warn you before I begin this review. I am biased. Against TM2 (Track Mania 2) and towards TMU (Track Mania United). Let me tell you why.
So, before I begin delving into the depth of deprivation, let me tell you that this is essentially "Track Mania United - Stadium". Except TMU came with 6 other areas, which are essentially "themes", you could play in.
Price Comparison:
TMU - Star Edition --> 29.99€ (seven areas + some small extras)
TM2 - Stadium       -->  9.99€ (one area)
TM2 - Stadium + TM2 - Valley + TM2 - Canyon --> 39,99€ (three areas)
I am a little speechless. And in order to prevent myself from getting a headache, I will treat the rest of the review as if that is not a giant rip off.
A fair reviewer treats games independently. The 6th iteration in a series need not necessarily be worse than the 1st. And I would give TM2 - Stadium the benefit of the doubt, if it weren't for the fact that it is an exact copy of the TMU stadium area. The size of the stadium, the pieces that are used to build the tracks, even the color of the grass if it isn't stuck on a darker shade again for a couple of blocks because screw unified grass colors. That would be silly, right? I could of course just be a giant doof and missed the "Unify grass colors again" button, but I believe there is none. There is but a single set of road pieces that got added from the last iteration of TM.
Maybe I should have expected that, when I bought a TM game with the name "Stadium". But I didn't excpect a company to be as cocky as to sell an area they sold before for another 10 bucks and call it "Track Mania 2". But Nadeo just laughs a "Think again!" in my face.
Track Mania is about driving on courses built with an open level editor. It is about driving a course over and over and over again until you can beat that sweet gold medal time. It's about building your own tracks, and watching your friends drive into walls you placed at inconvenient locations.
Track Mania is a racing game with essentially infinite levels, built with the same +100 pieces. It is fun, it is competitive and it is exciting.
For those of you who don't know the TM Series yet: It's not a game where you can crash into other people. You'll be always driving against their "ghost". TM is about finding that ideal path through a course, not about pushing other people off the track.
The controls are as simple as you can get. Arrow keys to control your car, backspace to respawn at the last checkpoint. These are rebindable, of course. You can also use a gamepad which allows for precise driving with the analog stick. I personally prefer the keyboard, because the TM tracksusually are about trying to find the ideal path in a course, and analog input is hard to repeat perfectly every time you try again. It seems to me that the game engine and car physics have been tweaked to accomodate analog input more, which makes the cars drift a lot when using digital input i.e. the keyboard. That is more of a problem with the other areas and not so much with stadium, so I will not consider that as a disadvantage for this game.
There is no split screen option, as far as I am aware. Local players have to take turns. There never has been a split screen option in any of the TM games. I don't know why, because it is a fun game to play against friends locally; racing games in general are.
To conclude all of the above: The gameplay is solid. The game executes what it wants to do perfectly.
People say, TM2 has really nice graphics. Be prepared to drop some frames on crowded tracks though if you crank them up to the highest setting. In addition to that arguably small flaw, I had to consult the internet to find a way to change graphics settings in the launcher. Apparently, pressing "Customize" does not allow you to change graphics settings. Setting the preset to "None" does. Again, a small flaw. Overall the games graphics do not have to hide from the big players.
Conclusion: Great graphics, small flaws in the execution.
I felt like this needed an extra category. While the game has a "singleplayer" campaign and unless you have friends who also play the game, the real fun comes in beating other peoples times. Of course there is no lobby system, since you only every try to beat their time or drive against their "ghost" if you will.
The single player campaign is slightly flawed in my eyes. Gold Medal now actually means "Gold Medal", even on the first track of the first part of the campaign. There is no increase in difficulty when it comes to the times you have to beat, they will always be tough. There will be an increase of the skill you need to traverse a track though, which in my eyes is just about enough for a racing game single player campaign. Of course there is no story or anything apart from the tracks, but in a game like TM2 I did not miss that.
Conclusion: Single player is solid and demanding. Multiplayer in the classic meaning does not exists, but you will be comparing your track time to other peoples time constantly.
I don't see anything that TMU does not provide. TM2 might not be a bad game, but in my eyes it adds nothing the the TM "Genre" as a whole. If you like the slightly better graphics get TM2 over TMU. For anyone else I recommend buying TMU, especially since you get more bang bang bang bang bang bang bang for buck.

What can I possibly say that has not been said already?
Most people have made up their minds about this game already, but if you are one of the few who are on the fence, perhaps you have mixed feelings like: "It seems really popular, but people won't tell me WHY it's good, and some of the fans are just insufferably annoying!"
I feel you. I know where you are coming from. Let me try to help.
This game has a charming feel to it that is very story-driven. It is occasionally silly and funny, and at other times, deep and dramatic. In my opinion, the characters are developed extremely well. They all really seem to POP out of the background as far as having distinct personalities.
There are parts of it that remind me of Earthbound, Chrono Trigger, and Secret of Mana, not due to any overt reference, but because of the general feel of this variety of story-driven RPG. The music, for example, is absolutely wonderful at helping to craft the mood.
There is, indeed, a morality system in this game. You may have played games like Mass Effect or Fable that also allowed the player to make choices based on different moral frameworks, but this is different. I have never seen a game handle morality the way Undertale does, and I do not wish to go into more detail about it than that, because I feel that it is best experienced by playing through the game multiple times oneself. The game has an intriguing and unique method of presentation for it, and I want everyone to be able to experience it that way.
Your choices MATTER. Things REALLY change when you try to play the game in a significantly different way. Endings can be VERY different, depending on how you handle various situations. Undertale only allows one save slot, and this is by design. It would undermine an aspect of the story-telling and the tension around the importance of your choices if you could easily save multiple simultaneous branches of the story. I found it a tiny bit frustrating, at first, but now that I understand why it is there, I appreciate it more. I encourage you to bear with that restriction. At any point, including after you finish the game, you have the option of resetting to start over and try things differently, and this feature helps make that a bigger deal.
Now, I am a bit obsessed, so take what I say with the appropriate grain of salt. Even the creator, Toby Fox, said of the game in his Undertale anniversary tweet that it was an 8/10 niche game. Of course there are those who will never like this game, and that is just fine. If you hate this game, I do not think that you are wrong. We simply like different things, which is normal. I recommend it, though, to anyone who is curious to know what it is all about and who enjoyed the old story-driven RPG's from the previous millennium.
The fandom is, indeed, massive and passionate. Though I have seen many complaints about the fandom in general, I personally love the fandom as a whole. I understand how they may be a bit annoying to non-fans who do not know what they are blabbering about, and, of course, as with any fandom this big, there are always going to be elements of it that take it too seriously, no piece of fan-made content is going to be well-received by the whole community, and no member of the community is going to like every piece of fan-made content. The flip-side to that is that there is SO MUCH content that it is easy (for me, at least) to ignore the stuff for which I do not care and actually find more GOOD content I love than I can ever have time to experience! Truly, with the fandom as active as it has been, I can continue to enjoy Undertale-related content as much as I want without ever running out!
Don't let the fanbase bother you, it's the game that matters.

Many games are "adult" because they have violence and sexual themes, though children still play and enjoy them. This game is adult because it's got mature themes and will make you think.

Play this if you want something that questions the MMS genre.
Play this if you want to play something that makes you feel awful and think.
DON'T play this if you want a pro-USA shooter where you kill the terrorists and stop World War 3.

This is basically PTSD: The Game.
As a game, it's pretty standard.  You get into cover.  You shoot guys with guns.  Run to the waypoint to continue getting into cover and shooting guys with guns.  It feels fairly clunky to actually get into cover.  I felt like I had to hit the space bar a specific way to actually get into cover.  There are a handful of weapons in different categories like rifles, shotguns, small arms, snipers and heavy weapons.  Everything feels fairly generic with a few exceptions like shooting a part of the environment to dump sand on your foes and that's about it.  You can give orders to your team, but some orders only pop up at specific times and I could never seem to be able to use the attack order.  I was able to beat the campaign on the hardest availible starting difficulty in under 7 hours.  Again, as a game, it's pretty generic.
As an experience, it's a completely different beast.  Never in my life have I played a military shooter that was this shocking.  If you thought the nuke scene and "no russian" from Call of Duty were hardcore, then you haven't seen anything yet.  It's really something you have to see for yourself and I wouldn't dare spoil it.  If I had to compare the story to anything, it feels a lot like the movie "Apocalypse Now" and if you've seen that movie then you should be aware of the levels of shock you are getting into...but even the story here goes above and beyond that.   Again, as an experience, it's quite unique.
If you can get it cheap, do not pass it up even if you don't like cover shooters.  This is one game you need to see to the end...

I am confused as to what went wrong. Looking back at the previous installations of this series, all that needed some refinement was the minimap and maybe enemy combat. However, Way Forward tries to solve the navigation issues by making all levels linear, completely debilitating a lot of the established core design patterns, and we can see the consequences of this: the game has a mere six levels, yet there are eight transformation abilities, each of which can be further upgraded. The game's world is too small to bring all these abilities to life in a meaningful manner. What follows is the tedious kind of backtracking: Revisiting previous levels to find that one block you could not previously break, that one spot you could not previously climb, that one platform you could not previously reach, all while traversing exhausted content that has lost its meaning by the time you come back with your bag full of upgrades that allow you to fly past everything, just so you can get some thing using some other thing you just got, which, afterwards, you won't be using again, except maybe once in some later puzzle, deliberately designed to make you use the thing, all in order to feign the presence of meaningful choice; but there is none. This design decision spawns further problems, but I'll refrain from emphasizing. By reducing the world to linear levels selected from one central screen, Way Forward has placed an obstacle before themselves that they could not deal with.

That game is disappointing gameplay wise. While the universe is brillant, the characters are adorable, the music is great and the controls are close from being perfect, the game requires you to do an incredible amount of backtracking.

You may even say that the backtracking is overall brillantly implemented since everytime you have to go back you would be able to do it way faster than before thanks to your new power. The game is also fairly short. Count around 6 hours to finish it. Maybe a bit more if like me you got stuck somewhere at one point. The fact that the game is short makes all that backtracking even more frustrating and give the feel that all of this is just made to give the feel that the game is longer than it looks. EDIT (Gameplay) -  In the review, there wasn't much talk about the actual gameplay offered by this game. The game itself plays very well, the Paris map is extremely open and their are so many Oppurtunities to approach killing a target. The gameplay feels a lot like a HITMAN game should, and whilst in game you do not feel 'pressured' to get a lot of points like Absolution did. Once you start a mission, you are able to roam a large part of the map freely, yet there are still a lot of out of bounds areas which mean you need to be extremely stealthy or in disguise.
The mechanics such as instinct are much better now, they are a lot more balance and they can be switched off entirely allowing you to customize the difficulty of the level to match your skill. The gameplay does actually make the game worth playing assuming you can deal with the poor port/ lack of FPS this game offers.
EDIT 2 (30/09/16) -
Since the game has now had a few new updates/levels added, I thought it was worth doing another review after looking back.
I have since had a new PC that has a i7 6700k, GTX 1080 so I'm not sure I can rate the performance as quite honestly I'm yet to find anything that runs bad, so I would ignore this review if you need a performance based review.
As for the gamplay and everything else they have added to this game, I have changed the rating to a Yes for its recommendation, based purely on the gameplay itself. Each level they have added has its pre-set "Oppurtunities" that allow you to approach the mission in a pre-designed way, however you are able to ignore these and free-roam the map whilst gathering "Intel" so that you can approach the target in your own way.
I prefer to play without having my hand held, meaning I have the majority of the UI (minimap, hints etc.) turned off, which makes the game a lot more interesting and makes you think more about what it is your doing and how to plan a kill on your targets.
Overall, the game still has room for improvement (as expected), however this is a lot better than at its launch back in March. Would definately recommend, especially if you can get it on the cheap. .

After nearly 5 years in development, DayZ has added an abundance of new towns, guns, and pieces of clothing... but has still not fixed game-breaking issues that have been present since its days as a free mod, mainly erratic/teleporting zombies that can hit you through walls and have directional audio that is not synched with their actual location.
In lieu of fixing the most basic aspects of zombie behavior and clipping, the development team seems to have re-focused on making the game unrealistically hard in terms of the survival aspects around procuring food, water, and shelter. Some moments before my last play session today before deciding to permanently uninstall the game: "I've eaten two whole cooked chikens in the last hour, how on earth is my character still starving to death if I don't find food in the next 3 minutes?" ; "I am now so dangerously damp from doing 10 minutes of running on a sunny day that I pass out from hypothermia in a field?"
As much as I love WHAT THIS GAME COULD HAVE BEEN if Bohemia put resources behind its development that were commensurate with the insane amount of money they raked in based on its promise, the game is still not even remotely playable 4-5 years on. It's just punishing to even attempt to enjoy. You play for 5 hours to collect gear, converge with your friend(s), and get your character's basic needs met, and then you die from a teleporting zombie one-hitting you through a wall, or from hypothermia due to standing in the rain for 5 minutes, or from an undercooked chicken breast that you were forced to play the guessing game on because of the shamefully ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cooking system that requires you to guess the "done-ness" of meats based on vague changes to the item's tiny thumbnail image that change after an indeterminate amount of time being held over a fire. It's an abandoned game property that has been left in aboslute shambles after years of promises around follow-through that never materialized. That they are still taking people's money for it is an absolute disgrace. Everyone involved should be permanently shunned from the world of game development.

Like snow or Christmas decorations, Call of Duty shows itself by the end of the year. Like every year since Modern Warfare. This time, it's the turn of Call of Duty: Black Ops 2, developed by Treyarch. Call of Duty: Black Ops 2 brings players back into the shadows for another Black Ops mission assignment. Rooted in near-future fiction, Black Ops 2 propels players into warfare in an epic single player campaign highlighted by branching storylines and non-linear missions. A re-imagined multiplayer suite introduces players to some of the most cutting-edge weaponry and equipment that 2025 will have to offer. Two viewpoints which allow the game to offer many side roads in the story, and 8 different endings. This is a first for such a mainstream series. Of course the game's core remains the same on the basics: cinematic action, epic scenes and a percussive score. Even if Black Ops 2 reuses old recipes, it does it really well and remains a great experience.

What can I possibly say that has not been said already?
Most people have made up their minds about this game already, but if you are one of the few who are on the fence, perhaps you have mixed feelings like: "It seems really popular, but people won't tell me WHY it's good, and some of the fans are just insufferably annoying!"
I feel you. I know where you are coming from. Let me try to help.
This game has a charming feel to it that is very story-driven. It is occasionally silly and funny, and at other times, deep and dramatic. In my opinion, the characters are developed extremely well. They all really seem to POP out of the background as far as having distinct personalities.
There are parts of it that remind me of Earthbound, Chrono Trigger, and Secret of Mana, not due to any overt reference, but because of the general feel of this variety of story-driven RPG. The music, for example, is absolutely wonderful at helping to craft the mood.
There is, indeed, a morality system in this game. You may have played games like Mass Effect or Fable that also allowed the player to make choices based on different moral frameworks, but this is different. I have never seen a game handle morality the way Undertale does, and I do not wish to go into more detail about it than that, because I feel that it is best experienced by playing through the game multiple times oneself. The game has an intriguing and unique method of presentation for it, and I want everyone to be able to experience it that way.
Your choices MATTER. Things REALLY change when you try to play the game in a significantly different way. Endings can be VERY different, depending on how you handle various situations. Undertale only allows one save slot, and this is by design. It would undermine an aspect of the story-telling and the tension around the importance of your choices if you could easily save multiple simultaneous branches of the story. I found it a tiny bit frustrating, at first, but now that I understand why it is there, I appreciate it more. I encourage you to bear with that restriction. At any point, including after you finish the game, you have the option of resetting to start over and try things differently, and this feature helps make that a bigger deal.
Now, I am a bit obsessed, so take what I say with the appropriate grain of salt. Even the creator, Toby Fox, said of the game in his Undertale anniversary tweet that it was an 8/10 niche game. Of course there are those who will never like this game, and that is just fine. If you hate this game, I do not think that you are wrong. We simply like different things, which is normal. I recommend it, though, to anyone who is curious to know what it is all about and who enjoyed the old story-driven RPG's from the previous millennium.
The fandom is, indeed, massive and passionate. Though I have seen many complaints about the fandom in general, I personally love the fandom as a whole. I understand how they may be a bit annoying to non-fans who do not know what they are blabbering about, and, of course, as with any fandom this big, there are always going to be elements of it that take it too seriously, no piece of fan-made content is going to be well-received by the whole community, and no member of the community is going to like every piece of fan-made content. The flip-side to that is that there is SO MUCH content that it is easy (for me, at least) to ignore the stuff for which I do not care and actually find more GOOD content I love than I can ever have time to experience! Truly, with the fandom as active as it has been, I can continue to enjoy Undertale-related content as much as I want without ever running out!

Okay, so, I have to warn you before I begin this review. I am biased. Against TM2 (Track Mania 2) and towards TMU (Track Mania United). Let me tell you why.
So, before I begin delving into the depth of deprivation, let me tell you that this is essentially "Track Mania United - Stadium". Except TMU came with 6 other areas, which are essentially "themes", you could play in.
Price Comparison:
TMU - Star Edition --> 29.99€ (seven areas + some small extras)
TM2 - Stadium       -->  9.99€ (one area)
TM2 - Stadium + TM2 - Valley + TM2 - Canyon --> 39,99€ (three areas)
I am a little speechless. And in order to prevent myself from getting a headache, I will treat the rest of the review as if that is not a giant rip off.
A fair reviewer treats games independently. The 6th iteration in a series need not necessarily be worse than the 1st. And I would give TM2 - Stadium the benefit of the doubt, if it weren't for the fact that it is an exact copy of the TMU stadium area. The size of the stadium, the pieces that are used to build the tracks, even the color of the grass if it isn't stuck on a darker shade again for a couple of blocks because screw unified grass colors. That would be silly, right? I could of course just be a giant doof and missed the "Unify grass colors again" button, but I believe there is none. There is but a single set of road pieces that got added from the last iteration of TM.
Maybe I should have expected that, when I bought a TM game with the name "Stadium". But I didn't excpect a company to be as cocky as to sell an area they sold before for another 10 bucks and call it "Track Mania 2". But Nadeo just laughs a "Think again!" in my face.
Track Mania is about driving on courses built with an open level editor. It is about driving a course over and over and over again until you can beat that sweet gold medal time. It's about building your own tracks, and watching your friends drive into walls you placed at inconvenient locations.
Track Mania is a racing game with essentially infinite levels, built with the same +100 pieces. It is fun, it is competitive and it is exciting.
For those of you who don't know the TM Series yet: It's not a game where you can crash into other people. You'll be always driving against their "ghost". TM is about finding that ideal path through a course, not about pushing other people off the track.
The controls are as simple as you can get. Arrow keys to control your car, backspace to respawn at the last checkpoint. These are rebindable, of course. You can also use a gamepad which allows for precise driving with the analog stick. I personally prefer the keyboard, because the TM tracksusually are about trying to find the ideal path in a course, and analog input is hard to repeat perfectly every time you try again. It seems to me that the game engine and car physics have been tweaked to accomodate analog input more, which makes the cars drift a lot when using digital input i.e. the keyboard. That is more of a problem with the other areas and not so much with stadium, so I will not consider that as a disadvantage for this game.
There is no split screen option, as far as I am aware. Local players have to take turns. There never has been a split screen option in any of the TM games. I don't know why, because it is a fun game to play against friends locally; racing games in general are.
To conclude all of the above: The gameplay is solid. The game executes what it wants to do perfectly.
People say, TM2 has really nice graphics. Be prepared to drop some frames on crowded tracks though if you crank them up to the highest setting. In addition to that arguably small flaw, I had to consult the internet to find a way to change graphics settings in the launcher. Apparently, pressing "Customize" does not allow you to change graphics settings. Setting the preset to "None" does. Again, a small flaw. Overall the games graphics do not have to hide from the big players.
Conclusion: Great graphics, small flaws in the execution.
I felt like this needed an extra category. While the game has a "singleplayer" campaign and unless you have friends who also play the game, the real fun comes in beating other peoples times. Of course there is no lobby system, since you only every try to beat their time or drive against their "ghost" if you will.
The single player campaign is slightly flawed in my eyes. Gold Medal now actually means "Gold Medal", even on the first track of the first part of the campaign. There is no increase in difficulty when it comes to the times you have to beat, they will always be tough. There will be an increase of the skill you need to traverse a track though, which in my eyes is just about enough for a racing game single player campaign. Of course there is no story or anything apart from the tracks, but in a game like TM2 I did not miss that.
Conclusion: Single player is solid and demanding. Multiplayer in the classic meaning does not exists, but you will be comparing your track time to other peoples time constantly.
I don't see anything that TMU does not provide. TM2 might not be a bad game, but in my eyes it adds nothing the the TM "Genre" as a whole. If you like the slightly better graphics get TM2 over TMU. For anyone else I recommend buying TMU, especially since you get more bang bang bang bang bang bang bang for buck.

In my opinion, the writing is much better than in Life Is Strange, and the characters, despite knowing what happens to them if you've played the original Life is Strange, still cause you to feel and agonize over each and every choice. Despite the fact that you can no longer rewind, this likely adds to the game, and as it is only three episodes instead of five (a shame, but it works out), if you've got a day to spare, you can probably quickly go through any choices you want to try other outcomes for.

When "Before The Storm" was announced, I was afraid it would be pointless and just an excuse to justify fanservice. Instead, Deck Nine graced us with a prequel that was faithful to its predecessor, both in the representation of their characters, and the essence the characterizes Life Is Strange. They gave us the opportunity to finally meet Rachel Amber, a character I always wondered about, but honestly never paid much attention to. As soon as I met her I understood why everyone seemed so obsessed with her. She was funny, intelligent, witty, wild, adventurous, and insanely pretty. In one word: she was magnetic. It’s no wonder Chloe felt drawn to her from the start. I think that was something very relatable: how you meet someone and your life changes completely. Being a teenager comes with that feeling that everything is going to last forever, and time possesses a relativity beyond that of quantum physics. It’s also an age in which we say and do strange things that seem to be pointless or even rash. That’s something I think the game nailed perfectly, just like the first Life Is Strange.
In my opinion, the first two episodes were nearly flawless: the ambiance was great, the decisions mattered, the characters were complex, and the experience overall was amazing. The new characters were a nice addition, and the return of old ones welcomed, even if some appearances seemed pointless to the story. We all knew the story was going to be focused on Rachel and Chloe’s relationship, and I liked it that we could choose how to act and how far we were willing to take things. It was nice to see more of Chloe, and to finally understand her reasons for acting like she did in the original game. The first two episodes did a great job telling the story and driving it forward, even if at times the pacing felt strange. There were indeed some inconsistencies (Warren being a student at Blackwell, for instance), but overall, I think they did a great job.
Episode three, however, undid everything they worked so hard to create. By rushing to meet an impossible deadline, they ruined the game, providing a conclusion that was unsatisfying in many areas, and felt incomplete and lifeless. I know they planned for things to be different, but the reality is we got a rush product, one that answered none of the questions left from the original game, nor the ones that arose from this very story. We only had two major choices, whereas in previous episodes we always had at least four. There wasn’t any time to tie up loose ends. Many choices were removed (leaving us with the ‘friendship route’ regardless of our previous choices, for example), as well as important dialogues that would’ve given side-characters an actual reason to be there (Steph and Mikey are a clear example of this). Many events felt wrong simply because it didn’t align with what one would consider the characters would do. David giving Chloe the picture, and Rachel’s dad doing what he did felt forced to me, as if they didn’t know how to give the player closure so they decided to rush something and call it a day. The episode’s final resolution made no sense, and it left the player with a feeling of emptiness, proving that their previous decisions didn’t really matter in the end, which is quite funny, since the butterfly effect and the consequences of our actions is a major pillar of the series.
In conclusion, I would say that if you are a Life Is Strange fan and have the opportunity to play the game, then go ahead. I think Rachel is a character worth knowing, and playing the original game will feel a lot different knowing who she was and the effect she had over Chloe. It’s also a good opportunity to understand our little punk better. However, if you aren’t familiar with the series, or simply cannot afford to pay for the game, then don’t buy it. The first two episodes might have been beautiful, but the third one is so disappointing it ruins the atmosphere that had been built up until that moment.
I know Deck Nine planned for things to be different, and I think it would be great if they could somehow undo the damage they caused. Maybe releasing an extended cut. I believe they should give us the content we deserve and paid for. They should do justice to the story and give Rachel and Chloe the ending they deserve.

While there's obviously a lot left to add (I mean, I hope so because I want tons more stuff because I'm a greedy gamer), even the alpha was extremely fun and engaging to play. While other games of this type have held my attention for a while, this one is especially captivating due to its engineering systems based around transportation of fluids and gases and the different way these different fluids can intermix and fractionate.
Can't tell you how irritated I was when I realized the bottom third of my base was full of carbon dioxide, while the top third was full up with hydrogen. My little guys had nowhere to sleep, and couldn't get to all the pumps and whatnot on the lower decks!
. That's exactly the type of thing I like to contend with when playing a game of this type, since it's always a little bit different.
I found out that you can actually cool gasses enough to make them condense into their liquid state, which is super cool (HA! YEAH! BEST PUN!) and useful when you have a large quantity of a non-breathable gas that you need to get out of your atmosphere: Just filter it out, then pump it into a coolerator room of some sort that will bring it down below its specific condensation temperature, and watch the liquid start to form in the bottom of the "tank".
Geek stuff aside, I also love the graphics and animation of the duplicants and the various machines. It really makes for a great atmosphere, which is wonderful, given that within fifteen minutes of play, your dupes will be living in "Polluted Oxygen" of a pleasant brown color.
The sound is also very good, but I find the sound of the dupes sleeping rather grating, and the "break stuff when I'm angry" dupes hit things with a wrench, which also makes a very annoying sound. Luckily, both issues can be resolved by turning off the sound, but it is unfortunate that I have to do that.
Overall, excellent game so far, and I've been waiting for the day I could get this out of my head and onto Steam as a review. I look forward to the future development with high hopes.

First Impression Gameplay:
Take "Rimworld", "Don't Starve", and "This War of Mine", stick them in a blender, and you'll get a delicious puree called "Oxygen Not Included."
I really enjoy base building/management type games, and from what I've see so far, "Oxygen Not Included" will be a nice addition to my collection.  You start off with 3 "settlers" who find themselves transported inside a giant asteroid.  It feels deceptively easy in the beginning, but quickly ramps up in difficulty as resources start to dwindle.
I really enjoy the comical art-style, and the soundtrack is great; but where this game really shines is the gameplay.  I really just love how this game plays: from managing oxygen flow, to routing poop pipes, to simply carving out a living quarters.  I can find myself losing many many hours to this.  Even in the current early access state, this game is well worth $20.
-Really solid gameplay.  Very fun.
-Art-style is attractive and whimsical
-Sound track is very good
-Gas/Liquid management system works very well and is a unique twist
-No performance issues, bugs, glitches, etc
-Price feels on point
-Hoping to see more content added into the game
-May be a bit of a learning curve to those not familiar to the genre

A great addition to the Shantae line of games that have become big favorites of mine. To start off, 2D animation amongst 3D shaded backgrounds looks sharp! I was a little surprised at first, because I had played Shantae so much in it's pixel art form, but this new style WayForward has adopted for the series is fantastic and I got used to it fairly quickly. That also including the control scheme which is very snappy and responsive! Shantae has become a living realtime cartoon and it is a major factor that I'm so glad the series now has.
Major and minor characters are back including Bolo, Uncle Mimic and Rottytops and they all have great dialogue and look great in the new style. The character interactions and text are all very funny, even including some fun unexpected moments where the characters will speak automatically, used a bit more here than in Pirate's Curse. I also really like how townsfolk give you hints and small clues, which comes in handy for dummies like me in those moments where I'm stupid and can't put 2 and 2 together.
Music is great as always, Jake Kaufman bringin' it down with more sick remixes of Scuttle town and Burning Town. The new song sung by Shantae (Cristina Vee) is awesome when you first hear it on Main Street. Absolutely a major factor that makes the game stand out and goes along great with it. Though I will say I take more of a liking to Pirate Curse's tracks, these orchestral songs are great and are very dance worthy.
The transformations are back from Shantae's earlier games, being staple powerups. They are used awesomely in this game! Very quick to transform and each stage uses different transformations for key areas to find secrets and other essestial items for achievement hunters and casuals alike. For Pirate's Curse of course, I did like how snappy and fast it was to use the pirate items for the corresponding buttons, but each key feature of the chosen transformation helps out greatly in areas, not just to get around the level, but also to find secrets. And hey, it's all worth it just to see Shantae dance again!
Oh man, the bosses are pretty good too this time around. They all have some cool attack patterns and look great all while the kickin' battle them is blasting from your headphones. They're all varied and some do bring out great fun. Whoever thought up that rad giant mermaid needs a big ol' smooch.
If I had to bring up any cons at all or stuff that just irked me personally, there's nothing that kept me from enjoying the game majorly. But the story is a biiiiit more straight forward this time around, and each world is sort of broken down into tiny subplots that don't really show up again, such as with Holly Lingerbean, the new kid on the block who's sort of just kicked out in a few minutes. But the small stories are essential for getting items back into the main plot.
Some characters also felt kinda weird in this game, there's not a lot of ongoing character development carried on from past games. Risky in Pirate's Curse was Shantae's arch nemesis doin evil stuff as always,  but when the pair had to work together, she became a sort of hothead with a short temper while she worked with the good guys compared to Shantae's upbeat goofiness. She also came with a backstory where she used to have a powerful master. Here's she's just kind of the generic main baddie. Don't get me wrong, I know they kinda want the games to be accessible in any order, but for me it was just kind of a shame to see characters who have been sorta fleshed out in other games back to their plain old selves. Though it was kinda just a thing for me with Risky upfront.
Something I noticed was that some aspects can make the game feel too easy, flight abilities can have you skip entire sections of levels, you can rack up gems like nobody's business though who's ever complained about free coinage?? And with enough gems, armor and hearts, getting hit every once in a while is really no problem.
But hey, I love Shantae, and overall, this is a dang fun Shantae game with lots of great powerups, funny writing, a sweet new artstyle once again and a great soundtrack. It's just that compared to Pirate's Curse, it felt a bit more compact. While I would rate that game my favorite in the series, trust me, Shantae Half-Genie Hero is definetely my second. A great effort to everyone at WayForward and another definite step in the right direction. Can't wait to see that future character DLC!

This game is a great step forward for the series, and the previous entry was already pretty good. The new semi-3D graphics look awesome and are put to great use. Shantae gets a lot of forms and they all feel more organic and useful than they did in Risky's Revenge (probably thanks to the level design). Zelda-dungeons have been replaced with more megaman-style linear levels, which you could go either way on; my feeling is that the levels are much more fun and tightly-paced, and they have much better setpieces.
There is a lot of mandatory backtracking, but it's not any worse than the previous games (especially if you get the warp dance). Usually by the time it wants you to return to a level a few new enemies have been added you have new forms to find hidden items in it.
The only criticism I can think of is that the story is kinda all-over-the-place. Instead of pursuing an overarching "gather X plot coupons" goal you jump back and forth between unrelated plotlines that each last one level, while occasionally fetching an item for your uncle's machine from a previous level. But it still has fun characters and cute dialog, so it's ok.

It's been a while since I played a platformer worth it's salt.  Thankfully, I decided to purchase Shantae: Half-Genie Hero entirely on a whim.  I hadn't heard about the kickstarter otherwise there's a strong chance I would have backed it.  I've since rectified that mistake and bought the game when Steam suggested it to me.
Shantae is a game with great artwork, and incredibly catchy sound track, and a plethora of unlocks to get you through your quest.  The levels are designed incredibly well which is great since you'll be revisting them multiple times to get any new items you can find as the game progresses.  Bosses are humorous, animated well, and sometimes challenging.
Shantae isn't without it's flaws, though those are incredibly minor.  Really.  While the next bit sounds like a lot, I'm being incredibly nit-picky.  A few animation glitches occur during the opening sequence when Shantae first gets out of bed and in the mid-level save sequence.  Jumping can be a bit stiff but if you've played enough platforming games, you can quickly adapt.
One of the coolest parts of Shantae is also one of the most disappointing parts.  On your first go around in a level, you'll see many details that bring the stage to life.  These are usually tied to the story of the level and once you clear it, they go away.  Future vists see the level altered slightly to reflect what you've already accomplished.  For example, in the second level, a number of fair maidens are being carted away in a factory.  Once the issue is resolved, the women are obviously gone seeing how you saved them, but it kind of ruins the atmosphere a little.
Again, nitpicking and critiqueing classical art.  Shantae is worth a playthrough.  It's a tad on the short end but don't let that detract from the quality of the game you get.
TL:DR If you're still♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at Mighty No. 9 and need a platformer to scratch the itch that disaster promised, then Shantae: Half-Genie Hero is here to fix you right up.

An excellent prequel to the widely praised and tear-jerking source material; Deck Nine have done a superb job of capturing the essence of raw 'teen-angst', drama, and emotion that we experienced in the original series developed by Don't Nod Entertainment. That said, it's not without its faults. I would preface this by stating if you enjoyed the original five episodes, it is indeed a must-have. If you are a newcomer however, you may feel slightly confused or jilted as to why there is such a following for 'Before the Storm'. Allow me to indulge (without spoilers)...
The simplistic yet still surprisingly beautiful painted art design carries over to this new series, and undoubtedly remains gorgeous to look at despite only needing to gently brush the tip of a standard GPU. Without the unique rewind-time mechanic owned by previous protagonist Max Caulfield in the original series, 'Before the Storm's party-trick is instead substituted with an argument/backchat function. Though nowhere near as fun, this still naturally suits 'follow-up' protagonist Chloe Price's rash demeanour quite well. It does frustrate toward the latter end of the series however, with less opportunity to rectify an incorrect dialogue selection and thus leaving the player to deal with their consequences quite abruptly. To be fair though, Life is Strange has always been fairly lenient when it comes to player choice affecting any significant detriment to the plot, so any panic induced by picking a 'wrong' choice is generally outweighed by the overall experience you'll have.
The characters as always are on point, though lacking in depth and numbers compared to the game's predecessor. Before the Storm is focussed primarily on Chloe and Rachel's relationship; in addition Deck Nine were also restricted to three episodes compared to the five we've been granted before, so there was bound to be some caveats in character development this time round. Rhianna DeVries does an excellent job of portraying a slightly younger Chloe; taking up the mantel from Ashly Burch who quite rightly took a step back to make a stand for the exhausting conditions voice actors are put through. Moan all you like, but being told to shout or scream down a microphone for hours every day does take its toll physically. Kylie Brown voices Rachel Amber and seamlessly brings to life the mysterious character that was absent, yet quintessential to the plot of the first series. It is fair to say that Chloe's character is somewhat over-played, with 'ugh's, sighs, and snide remarks frivolously grating a lot of the time. Easy to breeze past if you're playing the game casually, but for purists who want to click on every point of interest to get Chloe's opinion on something, it's certainly an issue. While Chloe's obnoxiousness was charming in the first series, it can be insufferable in this installment. The text messages on the other hand (which are mostly overlooked), retain the bare bones of thought and desire between the characters outside of the gameplay and cutscenes. The texts between Chloe and her mother - Joyce - are of particular note, and will likely chime with those who have doting family members they choose to ignore, but should probably give a call once in a while.
The soundtrack? Limited to fewer artists than the first series; 'Daughter' occupies most of the soundspace, though it remains a chilled vibe that wouldn't be out of place on a Spotify playlist to cosy up to on a cold night with a respective/potential loved one. The licensed tracks are certainly crowd-pleasers, and there are plenty of gems to discover and engross yourself in outside of the game. Brody Dalle was a nice surprise.
There's plenty more positives I could say about this game; including the fantastic Dungeon's and Dragon's segment, the re-enactment of Shakespeare's Tempest, the intense end scene of episode two which wouldn't be seen out of place in a Netflix drama, and the obvious devotion of Deck Nine to please a small, but devoted, cohort of gamers. It's a shorter and perhaps less satisfying experience than the first series, but still has a lot of heart, and envokes a few more tears from what is an incredibly beloved franchise.

I felt this is the place to share a pancake recipe so here we go.
INGREDIENTS
2 cups all-purpose flour
2 teaspoons baking powder
¼ teaspoon salt
1 tablespoon sugar, optional
2 eggs
1 ½ to 2 cups milk
2 tablespoons melted and cooled butter (optional), plus unmelted butter for cooking, or use neutral oil

Step 1
Heat a griddle or large skillet over medium-low heat. In a bowl, mix together dry ingredients. Beat eggs into 1 1/2 cups milk, then stir in 2 tablespoons melted cooled butter, if using it. Gently stir this mixture into dry ingredients, mixing only enough to moisten flour; don't worry about a few lumps. If batter seems thick, add a little more milk.
Step 2
Place a teaspoon or 2 of butter or oil on griddle or skillet. When butter foam subsides or oil shimmers, ladle batter onto griddle or skillet, making pancakes of any size you like. Adjust heat as necessary; usually, first batch will require higher heat than subsequent batches. Flip pancakes after bubbles rise to surface and bottoms brown, after 2 to 4 minutes.
Step 3
Cook until second side is lightly browned. Serve, or hold on an ovenproof plate in a 200-degree oven for up to 15 minutes.
Enjoy!

Spec Ops: The Line, at first seems like any other (decent) third person shooter, the cover system is great, the AI is good, (until you keep dying in a chapter and you notice every enemy is scripted), though despite playing on FUBAR difficulty, this was only noticable late game.) the setting and story is different, and a good different, there is no wars, or no robot armies taking over the world, it is a simple search and rescue mission in Dubai, where cataclysmic sandstorms have caused the once shining luxurious city to become a wasteland.

There are few times in your life when you will have the chance to experience something as outstanding as Spec Ops: The Line.
The setting is the city of Dubai, a few months after it has been hit by a devastating sandstorm and an evacuation operation has apparently failed. The focus is on three US Army soldiers sent to find out if there are any survivors and getting caught right in the middle of a conflict between the 33rd Infantry Battalion and local CIA operatives. The story shows the atrocities that the protagonists have to commit during their mission and the descent of the main character into madness, as he realizes that there are no redeeming choices in his reality and he can't cope with his own actions. The plot contains parallels from various horrifying situations of real-world war zones, particularly the use of white phosphorus mortar bombs on civilian populations in Iraq and Gaza. At its core, Spec Ops: The Line explores the concepts of PTSD, cognitive dissonance, escapism and the idea that the main character is not the player's avatar but instead, the player is the main character's super-ego.
The story is amazing and it is delivered superbly by all aspects of the game. The cutscenes, the direction, the characters' models, the tone and content of the voice acting (not only during scripted sequences, but even in the way the main character addresses his companions during battles), the animations (most notably the executions of dying enemies), the level design and even the loading screen text snippets - everything in the game shifts and transforms in order to serve the story and highlight the increasingly obvious psychosis of the main character, his increasingly violent tendencies, his inescapable and growing guilt, his detachment from sanity (and reality) and his companions' gradual loss of respect, trust and faith in him, as one of the premises of the game is revealed and confirmed ("Ιt takes a strong man to deny what's right in front of him."). The game embraces literally everything at its disposal and raises every expectation regarding what we should accept as character development from modern works of art.
The graphics are decent, including realistic and detailed shaders, rich well-crafted animations, just the right amount of post-processing and destructible environments. It is one of the best uses of the Unreal Engine that I've seen to date. When you are inside the extravagant but deserted buildings of Dubai, the art style is often reminiscent of that of the original BioShock.
In the sound department, the game performs excellent - the voice acting is simply outstanding, while the soundtrack consists of a post-rock soundscape that blends perfectly with the environments and the psychological state of the characters, coupled with a plethora of known pieces from various artists, ranging from Deep Purple and Jimi Hendrix to Björk and Giuseppe Verdi.
The gameplay is that of a typical third-person cover-based shooter, with the right balance between cool (to keep you interested), surreal (to underline that something isn't quite right) and repetitive (to make you feel even more desensitized before it hits you). The levels often seem open but the level design is actually quite linear. The game's idea of tactics revolves mostly (though not exclusively) around finding a good cover, adapting by changing your position, drawing enemies out of their covers and some micromanaging with weapons, bullets and grenades. At no point do you get to choose where you are going to fight your enemies and stealth tactics, wherever applicable, don't make a lot of difference compared to just charging in. You can, however, drown your enemies using tons of sand that's trapped on glass roofs and other places.
Where the gameplay shines is in choices: instead of presenting choices with a bland menu that's disconnected from the rest of the game, Spec Ops: The Line embraces them tightly and features them exclusively as part of the gameplay. In many occasions, the game organically recognizes the intent behind your actions without having previously made the choice (or all of your options) explicit. This not only helps maintain the cinematic feel of the game, but also forces you to ponder your choices as real actions with real consequences (rather than items in a menu) and, most importantly, it makes you question your previous actions and constantly reevaluate situations retrospectively, highlighting another premise of the game, the idea that apparently you had choices all along ("There's always a choice!"), but you kept going ("None of this would've happened if you'd just stopped."). There are four endings for you to discover and they are all well-made and perfect epilogues to what your actions say about the protagonist (and you) by the end.
Some final things:
-The campaign is 6-12 hours long depending on your pace, not particularly difficult once you get used to the gameplay.
-After you finish the campaign, a variable portion of the game's events are left open to interpretation. Almost all possible interpretations have at least some plot holes or unconvincing details. For me, they are forgivable but your mileage may vary.
-There is a multiplayer mode that I simply won't consider in this review, because this game is essentially its campaign mode and the very existence of a multiplayer mode defeats the point that the story is trying to make.
-Some people have said that there are bugs (particularly sound-related ones, which can be overcome, as they say), but I can't comment on those because for me it worked flawlessly.
And that's it. This is an extraordinary game and every developer should take notes, because Spec Ops: The Line demonstrates what games should aim to be.

A lot of the enemies were the same, the bosses were the same, but overall, the game-play was just so enjoyable. I feel that this game was a perfect example of what makes Mad Max Mad Max.
This was one of the few games that made me think about what life would be like if our world ended up like that. It was raw and gritty, just the movie The Road. It makes you question existence and surviving when all of humanity has been reduced to barbarity.
The cars, and having the ability to mod some of them, was a great feature... though, I was really looking forward to mod all of them. I'd have loved to mod the Twin V6 Hot-rod. Or, putting the mine-layer on my vehicles...
Tracking down convoys and finding the ornaments was awesome. Though a bit more variety in the types of convoys/vehicles would have been better.
Overall, the graphics and sound effects were insanely good. The story was also great. The game did drag on a bit, with it's scrap/fortress beautification missions. Helping the thirsty desert wanderers could have been explored a bit more, giving the player cooler missions/gear.

If you're a fan of the Mortal Kombat franchise this should be considered Canon.
Absolute required viewing for any serious MK devotee. Call it the most awesome
homework assignment ever given. Rated R, (18+) Mature Audiences.
Pro's:
------
1.) It's Free.
2.) MK live-action movie/videos. (I love Mortal Kombat: Conquest the series too, I love live-action MK.)
3.) A lot more language, brutal fight violence than MK:Conquest. (That was rated PG, this is Rated R)
4.) A very "Realistic" view of the MK Universe. "Based in Reality as opposed to Fantasy" ~ Fxcking Brutal! Hardcore.
This could go PRO or CON:
5) Interestingly enough... the episodes are mini short-stories. That a took a moment for me to "grasp/get over." They go quick, maybe too quick, only about 10 minutes on average. However, they are a QUALITY ten minutes. If you only get 10 min to tell a quick story about a MK character, then: "Here it Is." ~ xD~ One for Sonya, one for Johnny Cage, one for Raiden, etc. All individual episodes completely independent of each other. It's not a linear story line like MK:Conquest. *Granted: I have not finished the entire series and it may have a few plot twists and turns. Hopefully the story will evolve (Legacy II, III) into incorporating everyone at some point near the conclusion of the series.  However, at this point, judging by the way it's configured in the video list and the way it's been presented so far, each episode is completely independent. I.o.w. Cons:
------
1.) Length of the Episodes. (Could be a Pro, but I wanted more content. It's Cool. Glad I got what I got.)

Check out my Steam Curators group (Minorthreatt Gaming Reviews) and hit "FOLLOW" for more of my reccomendations:
The Short of it: A hugely entertaining base-building / survial game that puts you in complete control of a colony located at the center of an asteroid. Fantastic art and presentation, lots to learn and lots to do.
Reminds me of: If you liked Don't Starve, or Rim World, you'll probably like Oxygen Not Included.
Pros +
- Awesome updates fairly often, breathing new life into an already polished game.
- Visual style is just fantastic, I #$%&ing love Klei games and their art style.
- Replay value for years
- You actually learn things about how electricity and oxygen work, and it's FUN. Crazy.
- User Interface is PERFECTION. Wouldn't change a thing about it, love it.
- Too many other giddy things to even list. Get playing!
Cons -
- A bit of a steep learning curve, with no real difficulty settings. New players could really use some in-depth tutorials to understand how and why some things work. Perhaps in the future?!
Other Ranting: I've been a bit obsessed with this game for months. It is utterly, UTTERLY worth the money. There is so much you can do with it, and it really scratches that itch for base building, organization, tech, and survival. It's so open ended on how you play it - I've probabley attempted 40 bases, and every one has been different in one way or another. If you like Rimworld, or Terreria, or Don't Starve, or anything else like those, Oxygen Not Included is a fantastic, growing mix of those and much more. Klei is a great company, and they make great games. Suggesting this game to anyone even mildly curious about it, is a no-brainer to me. It has huge replay value, it makes you think, and it has a huge amount of depth and entertainment. Money SO well spent.

Were you disapointed by Mighty Number 9?  Well look no further then Shantae: Half-Genie Hero for an example of how both kick starters and platformers can be done well.  I didn't much care for the original Shantae, and thought Risky's Revenge was only just okay.  I did love Pirate's Curse, but when I heard this Shantae was going back more to its roots with the dance transformations I admit to having been concerned.  I was also worried about the art style, which looked much more cartoony then the previous games, as well as all the 3d elements which felt unnecessary in a 2d platformer.
I'm VERY happy to say all my fears were unfounded.  This game is FANTASTIC.  You can really tell these developers are learning from each of their releases, with each one taking the best of the previous games, dropping the bits that no one cared for, and then just further expanding and refining everything people liked.  S:HGH has the speed and creativity of Pirates curse, while making the transformations finally into something fun, something I looked forward to getting.  The music is as fantastic as ever, while the art, while admittedly more cartoony, looks incredible and really feels like it fits.  Even the 3d is used in just the right proportions such that it actually feels like it adds instead of takes away from the experience.
Wayforward has officially gone from a little developer I wanted to see succeed, to one whose legitimately earned my trust and support going forward through top notch quality content that.  If you like platformers at ALL, you owe it to yourself to give this game a chance.  If you didn't like Pirates Curse, I'm not sure this game will change your mind, but if you felt the original and Risky's Revenge were over hyped, I strongly urge you to give this one a chance.

PROS:
- Amazing artwork, and the animations as always are fluid.
- The dialogue and character interactions are pretty funny.
- Jake Kaufman provides another great soundtrack.
- Good platforming challenges
- Controls are snappy and responsive, the best in the series so far.
CONS:
- The overall length is a bit short. I finished my first run in around 6 hours.
- I missed the dungeons that were in previous Shantae games. The levels in 1/2 Genie Hero are more similar to Megaman stages.
- Some of the transformations are just a pain to deal with. Looking at you, mouse.
- The checkpoints are few and far between, which is made more frustrating with the inclusion of bottomless pits and instant-kill traps.
- *Added 8-10-17* There is a bug where the audio levels are maxed out until you get to the file select screen. I don't appreciate having my eardrums blown out just because of an obvious oversight. Way Forward should have fixed this bug a while ago, but I guess over half a year just wasn't enough time to fix it.
It's a good game, you should consider getting it. There will also be more characters added that will drastically change (or so we're told) how you play the game (*Edited 8-10-17* The DLC characters are only free if you backed the kickstarter, how disappointing.)
Fans of platformers will surely enjoy this game.

When I first decided to look up "Roguelike" games (after realizing that no, in fact, they are not like "Thief"), I decided they weren't for me.  A "procedurally generated perma-death labyrinth" just wasn't what I thought I needed in my life.
When it comes to Rogue Legacy, perhaps I was wrong.
Your progression in this game is based on your growing skill, as well as the temporary gold coins that you use to permanently improve your skill tree, equipment, and runes.  I did not expect to pour as many hours into this game as I did.  I just kept trying, and kept getting better.
This game has tons of variability.  From the character classes, spells, and equipment, to traits that can help you or hurt you.  (Being gigantic gives you better reach, but makes it hard to dodge spikes; and there are so many more traits than that one!)
This game makes me feel nostalgic for two games:  Castlevania, and an amazing old iPhone game called Solomon's Boneyard (fans of Rogue Legacy may want to check that one out.)
If I were to give them some advice on improving this game, I would say the most tedious part is trying to pick out your next character - quickly recognisable symbols or differing text colours may help to expidite this process.
I'm really excited to finally progress past the castle into the more difficult areas :)

Really good rogue-lite. Each playthrough you play as a knight of a family in a randomized castle. Everytime you die the next member of the family can upgrade the castle to improve all future generations with the money you find. Every generation has unique buffs, debuffs, and skills (High damage but maybe "near-sighted" so enemies not in the middle of the screen are blurry)
Also great soundtrack

That might be an overstatement since I haven't played every game on steam. Regardless, Rogue Legacy is a fantastic game. It has all the right elements to make a great roguelike and includes personal touches that make it a truly unique game.
- It's different every time you play. Seriously, you pick a new character every time with a class, a spell, and several traits (irritable bowel syndrome hehehe). Additionally, the map is scrambled every time, forcing you to explore the castle over and over again.
- They also include an option to lock down the castle, giving you the option to continue exploring the same map you had before you died. BUT you are slightly punished by doing so (only receive 60% of gold loot). This is a fantastic option because it gives you an advantage at a price. Let's not make things too easy.
- Teleporters (thank you).
- Simple responsive controls.
- Enemies and traps follow specific patterns - learn them!
- The combination of the previous two points makes this game very fair. It is purely skill based. Did you take damage? It was probably your own fault.
- Enjoyable music.
- Different segments of the castle have different themes and enemies.
- Lots of collectables scattered around the castle.
- Option to level up stats and diversify the genepool.
- Different armour, weapon and rune options that you can customize before entering the castle.
- First play through is a challenge (especially the two last bosses, those took me a long time).
- Great replay value.
- You can have up to 3 different profiles at one time (start a new game without overwriting your previous save).
-
- Many enemies are just reskins of older enemies (but they have new abilities and patterns).
- Blob boss is very difficult.
- Attacking downwards to open platforms can be difficult.
- You will die a lot in the beginning - try not to get discouraged.
- Over time you will figure out which kind of character you prefer playing, leaving the other ones almost untouched. Personally I almost never played the mage.
I am fairly certain that you will know whether or not you will like Rogue Legacy based on the trailer. It is exactly as it seems: fun, fast-paced, rewarding and punishing. If the trailer tickles your fancy, I would definitely urge you to get it.

Spec Ops: The Line.  Oh, where to begin...
If you are a hardcore CoD 'leet quickscoping FAZE member, who goes through the campaign slamming the "skip cutscene" button, go back to your clan.  This game will chew you up, spit you out, chew you up a bit more, spit you out again, and take a p*ss on whatever's left over*.  (*On the easiest difficulty)  This is a TACTICAL 3rd person shooter, where moving out of cover at the wrong time will get you killed, every time.  Now that we have that out of the way, let's talk about the game!
It is beautifully designed in the ruins of Dubai, with shiny skyscrapers and amazing sunglint and lots of sand.  In the first cutscene, you meet the 3 main characters.  A hardcore squad leader, some campy white guy who carries a sniper and cracks a few jokes, and the quintissential black guy with a SAW LMG.  But do NOT be influenced by the first scene.  This is one of the few games that gets it's Mature rating for something more than a few naughty words and marijuana references.  It gets it's Mature rating because it would seriously screw up any 12 year old who plays it.
Normally, you get into a helicopter, or an AC-130, or whatever to blow some sh*t up, while you have absolutely no chance of dying.  And once you're done, you get a pat on the back and a shout of "Look what you did!  You REKT them Ruskies/Nazi's/Cubans/generic-bad-guys-who-deserved-to-die-and-definitely-didn't-have-a-family-or-wife-or-kids-or-a-puppy-or-dreams-of-opening-a-flower-shop-on-Martha's-Vineyard.  And you get the feeling of acomplishment, the feeling of success, and you want to keep playing to feel that way again.
This game takes this standard and rips it's d*ck off.  You will get to shoot-em-up with all the big guns, but when you're done you don't poof away to the next spot.  You get to SEE what you did.  And let me tell you, it is the opposite of what you're used to feeling.  I don't want to spoil the game here, but there was one point where my eyes got watery.  If you are looking for a "realistic" experience, then buy this game now and find out what war is really like.
The pros of this game?  Unbelievable story.  You go into this game expecting some "this guy with a Deagle is a jerk and you must kill him at any costs" kinda story, then get knocked out of your socks. The character development is also great, as well as a very big joke around the middle of the story(if you pay close attention).  The graphics are great for it's age, and it has a dynamic start screen that represents what is going on in your campaign (very cool).  And if the game chews you up one too many times, it gives you the option to tone down the difficulty!  That was very kind of them, but a little necessary...
Cons.  Controls are ugly.  More than one time I am sitting behind cover and randomly vault over to meet the incoming sniper round, or crazed knife rusher, or shotgun soldier just before reaching a checkpoint.  Friendly AI is also atrocious.  Rushing across 70 feet of open ground to get to some cover, and having your squadmate take it when you are about 5 feet away is the worst feeling.  This game is out to kill you.  Not often is the time when you aren't surrounded on at least 3 sides by enemies.  Much like Dark Souls, you must learn to embrace death, and try to figure out where the hell you can stand to pick off tangos without getting pumped full of copper-plated lead.  Ocassionally you will get stuck with a checkpoint where you are surrounded on ALL sides with only a Desert Eagle with 5 rounds in it.  And you will get angry and groan and scream at this game for having such terrible balancing.  But remember: IT'S REALISTIC for this scenario.  The targeting mechanic for your squadmates to expend their limitless ammo on enemies is a little finicky, but only when you are fresh out of bullets.  Also, some gameplay that should have been cutscenes realllllyyyyyyyyy sucks when you need to run from a chopper and get stuck on a planter that is 5 feet away from where you are running.   Finally, giving us the illusion of a choice is digigng up a dead horse to put a saddle on it and ride it back into the ground (but the choices may be one of the best parts of this game, even if they have no effect on the story.  oh yeah, that might be a spoiler :|  )
The Skinny:
This game is amazing, for it's story.  The gameplay is broken, but still playable.  CoD fans beware, you need to stay in cover as much as possible.  Prepare yourself for a game that will question your morals, standards, and make you look at the military in a completely different way.
BUY IT NOW,  If for no other reason, play it on easy just to experience the story.
Did I mention how great the story is?  Because it's pretty cool.
"To kill for yourself is murder.  To kill for your country is heroic.  To kill for pleasure is harmless."

Gameplay-wise, this game shares a lot with games like Call of Duty or Battlefield. However, while those games are about gunning down black people with a gun you've balanced on your giant America-boner, this game is about madness, and the horror of wartime.
You play as the commander of a squad of soldiers, sent to evac Dubai after a series of disasters. However, you arrive to find the people being oppressed by rogue US soldiers. What follows is a long, hard journey, punctuated by brutality, anger, insanity and blood. In this regard, The Line could be described as a parody of CoD, except no-one's laughing.
A little pre-warning for this game: you will feel evil. Certain events in the game involve doing things that no sane man could do, and you will hate yourself. The more famous example of this is the infamous White Phosphorous scene, but what stuck with me more is the scene at the very end, when you have time to reflect on just what you have done.
This game will abuse you, smack you around for a bit, and light you on fire. But hey, after playing hundreds of games where you stomp all over the innocent, maybe we deserve our punishment.

Were you disapointed by Mighty Number 9?  Well look no further then Shantae: Half-Genie Hero for an example of how both kick starters and platformers can be done well.  I didn't much care for the original Shantae, and thought Risky's Revenge was only just okay.  I did love Pirate's Curse, but when I heard this Shantae was going back more to its roots with the dance transformations I admit to having been concerned.  I was also worried about the art style, which looked much more cartoony then the previous games, as well as all the 3d elements which felt unnecessary in a 2d platformer.
I'm VERY happy to say all my fears were unfounded.  This game is FANTASTIC.  You can really tell these developers are learning from each of their releases, with each one taking the best of the previous games, dropping the bits that no one cared for, and then just further expanding and refining everything people liked.  S:HGH has the speed and creativity of Pirates curse, while making the transformations finally into something fun, something I looked forward to getting.  The music is as fantastic as ever, while the art, while admittedly more cartoony, looks incredible and really feels like it fits.  Even the 3d is used in just the right proportions such that it actually feels like it adds instead of takes away from the experience.
Wayforward has officially gone from a little developer I wanted to see succeed, to one whose legitimately earned my trust and support going forward through top notch quality content that.  If you like platformers at ALL, you owe it to yourself to give this game a chance.  If you didn't like Pirates Curse, I'm not sure this game will change your mind, but if you felt the original and Risky's Revenge were over hyped, I strongly urge you to give this one a chance.

CONS:

- Some of the transformations are just a pain to deal with. Looking at you, mouse.

- *Added 8-10-17* There is a bug where the audio levels are maxed out until you get to the file select screen. I don't appreciate having my eardrums blown out just because of an obvious oversight. Way Forward should have fixed this bug a while ago, but I guess over half a year just wasn't enough time to fix it.
It's a good game, you should consider getting it. There will also be more characters added that will drastically change (or so we're told) how you play the game (*Edited 8-10-17* The DLC characters are only free if you backed the kickstarter, how disappointing.)

A few years ago, I was browsing the virtual console games on 3DS and found a game called Shantae, which was originally for Gameboy Color. I played it and found it clunky, but the characters and world were very charming, so I picked up the next game. Risky's Revenge was solid and improved a lot of the gameplay, and I became a bit excited when I heard that Shantae and the Pirate's Curse was coming out. Shantae and the Pirate's Curse was absolutely one of the best games I've ever played, so when I found the option to kickstart a new entry to this series which I've become really fond of, I absolutely did.
And it delivered.
Shantae: Half-Genie Hero is an incredibly solid entry into the Shantae series. While the pixel art of the previous games was amazing, I really do like this new art style, and I'm a sucker for 3D backgrounds with 2D characters. The game is really pretty, keeps up with the silly quirky story and characters I've come to love, has great platforming, and is absolutely a worthwhile sequel.
The game improves upon a few things from previous entries. One of the biggest problems in the first two Shantae games was how long transformations took for the amount of times you needed to use them. Transformation dances took a LONG time, and really took you out of the moment. To be completely honest, the best part of Pirate's Curse was how there were no transformation dances. The Metroid-style pirate items they used as a replacement made the action smoother and more enjoyable. Half-Genie Hero did take a page from this to an extent, and made transforming MUCH easier and quicker, especially with the optional Metronome item that increases the speed further, but the best thing they did was triple the amount of dances Shantae could perform. This gives the player many options on how to tackle a puzzle, and while I think some could have been utilized further than they were, I really appreciate having so many creatures to transform into! I really feel like they hit the sweet spot of Shantae having her signature transformations while keeping the gameplay smooth.
In terms of music, Half-Genie Hero has definitely gone more electronic than its predecessors, but in a good way. It's very lively and really gets your heart pumping. It makes you feel good to play while listening to it. I think good music is a very important component to making a game enjoyable, and the Shantae series has always delivered on this. I love the track for Mermaid Falls especially!
There are a few negatives, of course. I feel that some of the unlockable items are utterly useless except for achievements (a lot are just attacks for your animal forms, which generally are very weak and serve little purpose). There are also times where I would get stuck in an area after a puzzle and need to exit the entire level just to get out of that room, or going into a new room would totally screw up my camera requiring exiting the level as well. I also really miss dungeons, which were a Shantae staple up to this point, but the new level-based design really wouldn't have allowed for them the same way, so I can give them a pass on that.
In terms of gray areas, things that some people might like and some people won't: There is a LOT of backtracking through levels, and its really hard to avoid some enemy attacks. You're going to get hit and need items to restore your health. Both of these are really common in all Shantae games though, so they're just kind of expected at this point. I didn't mind backtracking in this game as much as games like Pirate's Curse or Risky's Revenge, though, where you have to go back through entire dungeons to find stuff you might have missed. I also really don't like the TOTALLY CAPS YELLOW TEXT that appears in a lot of dialogue. I just feel it shows up way too often, but it's really not a dealbreaker to a lot of people.
Overall, I think I would still consider Pirate's Curse to be the better game. I think its puzzles, bosses, and levels were more fun, and it had a really good story as well as some interesting bombshells, whereas Half-Genie Hero's story falls a little flat as far as these games go. That said, Half-Genie Hero is no slouch, and has been an overall great game that I had a really good time playing.
Whether you're a fan of the series or just want to try it out, I recommend Shantae: Half-Genie Hero as a very solid platformer with wonderful visuals and music, and I recommend checking out the other games in the series if you can!

CONS:
