It's a Shantae game, in both the good ways and the bad ways.
The good ways are that Shantae looks and sounds better than ever, and that the characteristic good writing is present, along with all the characters you know and love(or love to hate).
The bad ways are in the sense that every Shantae game is, to some extent, experimental. Some aspects and mechanics recur, but every single game is made up of those "classic" elements mixed evenly with the developers tossing new ideas up into the air and seeing what sticks. But it feels like they rarely test these things(except to avoid bugs), as long as nothing's outright breaking the game, it stays in, and the final test of whether it's actually fun or functional, is left for the game's buyers to figure out.
For instance, we've got the shapeshifting from Risky's Revenge back again, this time with even more forms. But there are a couple of forms that you'll never actually use(outside of their mandated one or two applications for gaining bonus items or quest items), because their uses are either extremely niche(elephant, spider and mouse, looking at you) or heavily overlapped with another form. Some also feel like they weren't tested much, since the Bat allows you to trivialize large parts of some areas(sky bridge in the desert, hello to just flying past all those platforms).
Boss fights also still feel spastic rather than tactical. I'm sure I'm going to get the usual "git gud" comments for this, but in some platformers, I can go into a boss fight, and after screwing up one or two waves, I can go: "Oh, okay, this is what they want me to do." And then sure, I may lack the brains or dexterity to actually do it, but I can always see the IDEA. In HGH, there are some attacks where I just can't see HOW to dodge them, some bosses where I just can't figure out their mechanics(what actually triggers the Tinkerbrain popping up its canisters?) and the game also suffers a bit from some things that look good being a bit counterproductive.
In the case of boss fights, circular boss arenas are VERY neat, since they basically give you "infinite" horizontal space without any screen scroll, but it makes it hell to judge the distances of something rolling towards you, and when there's a LOT of stuff in the middle of the circle, like in the final battle, it can be hard to see projectiles spawned on the other side of the circle before they're all the way past the clutter and way in  your face.
In general, the improved graphics also feel like they make things a bit more vague. It's less "sharp" where spikes end and where they begin, or what parts of a heavily animated flame projectile actually burns you. I mean, it looks GREAT, not denying that, but it feels like if you're gonna do that in a platformer, you should be a bit more forgiving about hit areas.
It also feels like there's no "good" difficulty in the game. Like, again, I enjoyed it, but I never really felt challenged except by instakill spikes in a couple of areas, and that's not the sort of challenge that appeals to me(seriously, WayForward, the final dungeon of Pirate's Curse was a mistake. PLEASE don't try to recapture any of that. Ever.). But unless you intentionally avoided upgrades and heart holders, it just feels like you can brute force your way through most areas, chugging a few consumables when necessary, and the same for the boss fights.
On the one hand, a bit more challenge would make it feel a bit more satisfying when beating an area, but on the other hand, I appreciate that if I really get stuck on doing something "right" I can just power through it with potions.
I'm also not sure how I feel about the new approach to travelling, with the world map and warp dances. It makes everything feel easier, backtracking is considerably less of a pain, but it also makes Sequin Land feel less like a world, and more like a series of levels. But that's probably a personal thing.
Finally, there are a few technical issues, mostly related to some animations "chopping" a bit, sometimes characters flicker partway through animations, etc. but it's pretty rare. It's almost completely isolated to the world map screen where Sky, Wrench and Shantae sometimes behave a bit oddly.
So ultimately, the verdict is: It needs polish, and in some cases issues that have been showing up in Shantae games since Risky's Revenge need to be recognized as issues and addressed, but it's got so much heart that I can't pretend I don't love it. This was money well-spent for me, and it will be for anyone else who likes the Shantae games. Because like me, I bet you've spent half an hour listing all the things that could be fixed about Risky's Revenge and Pirate's Curse, but then you finish by going: "I loved the game anyway. How did they manage to make a zombie so cute?"
You know, unless you have no taste and don't agree that Rottytops is best girl.
When people ask if I prefer Metroid or Castlevania, I just say Shantae and walk away.

This isn't a game folks. It's a doorway into your soul. You will learn things about yourself that you would never have noticed having not entered the world of Arcadia Bay. I'm not even joking. This series is an RPG where you can make choices that have consequences.  The devs originally anticipated the player base's tendency to save/load to get the best outcome, and built a time warping gimmick into the game to account for that.  This time, no such benefit.  The safeties are off, there is no rewind, and it actually makes it more intense.
The original Life is Strange is truly something else.  I checked out my review of it, and I apparently only have 15.7 hours on it, yet nearly 3 years later I still sometimes think about it, it's characters, the choices I made, what else could have happened if only I'd had just a little bit more control over the details of my character's actions.  When I saw that a new Life is Strange was out, I didn't even have to think, I bought.  And I wasn't disappointed.
The good:
-the characters:  once again, they brought out good characters.  They are well developed, believable people who I care about.  Sure they frustrate me sometimes with their mistakes, but they are believable, human mistakes.  At no point did find myself disconnected, as I often do with horror movies, because "nobody would ever do that!"
-the story:  It's interesting, it has depth, and again, it's plausible.  While fictional, this story could have happened.
The bad:
-The graphics:  while not that important in an RPG, I can quite enjoy some 8-bit myself, they're not up to the standard they need to be for the style of presentation they are going for here.  I get that they are going for an "animated drawing" style here, but sometimes it is distracting.  For example, in the opening scene, you are on a path in the woods, with some rocks that look like construction paper cut outs from South Park.  I know it's petty, but it's bad enough to be distracting, which breaks the immersion.  They lip syc was also, once again, pretty bad.  Again, petty, but distracting.
Final verdict:  I loved it!  Absolutely get it!

Spec Ops: The Line is a very difficult game to give a binary "Yes" or "No" reccomendation to. This is mainly because it doesn't provide what many seek from a video game. The gameplay mechanics are average at best, with very few thrills to speak of. It's just not very fun to play.
However that's kind of what makes the game special, as these mechanics inform the story in both compelling and disturbing ways. Spec Ops: The Line is less a video game and more of an interactive art piece, with its main focus being on you, the player. It disects the modern military shooter in a very damning fashion and questions whether we should be feeling catharsis from carrying out acts of violence on our fellow man. It takes a scalpel to our power fantasies and makes you uncomfortable for having them. It's a thought provoking narrative, expertly constructed to deliver gut punch after another and is an experience that will leave you drained and probably much more cynical towards the next installment of "Call Of Duty".

This game, in terms of gameplay feels like Shadow of Mordor, for the ground fights at least. Unfortunatly the fights aren't really well designed and you often end up just mashig the left mouse button and occasionnally the right one when the game tells you to do so. There is some contextual actions, like shield-bashing, disarming, etc, but those actions are basically just pressing a button at a precise time (with a rather weird time window). The survival system, relying on keeping water to healk you, and fuel for your car, is a good idea but works poorly, because far too permissive.
Now, about the car, which is a main part of the gameplay, well, it's not bad, but not good either, the car does not feel really good, but car battles are something quite fun, if a little boring in the end. The customization, sadly, is pretty poor and consist of just upgrading each part of your car without having real choice to do, and it just seem too artificial. It's even worse for max, where the only possible choice is levlling up each items he wear, to just make them better (using scrap, kek). And the customization via levels feels really poorly designed.
The story isn't really crazy, and suffers from some lazyness in some character designs, which are poor (hello top dogs recolors) or not developed enough. The main feminine char is really cliché and her story with max is telegraphed as♥♥♥♥♥ (The two others you can meet aren't that bad, tho).
Where the game really stands out, for me, is that the world around you is quite well thought and graphically really nice (in terms of art), There is really some beautiful views, and tons of good screenshot to make for sure. The camps you have to destroy in order to progress and the stonghold you can rest in are not bad, but sometimes (especially for camps), feels just like a lazy attempt to create a maze, while some others are pretty well thought.
Overall :

-Good World Design
-Car Battles
-Beautiful Areas
-Some background to discover thoughout the game about the world.
-Technically Working. (Yes I'm looking at you, XCOM 2)
-Explosions.
Cons :
-Car Driving could have been better
-Sound Design (really boring in the end)
-Upgrade System (no real choice)
-Survival System (not evry deep)
Meh :

This is a very good open world adventure game overall, with one major flaw.
I really liked Mad Max when I began to play it, and the more I played the more I liked it. I enjoy open world games and I like grinding out all of the collectibles, locations, side missions, etc., that come with games in this genre. Mad Max's graphics are great, the voiceover work is excellent, and overall the gameplay is very solid.
HOWEVER, when it comes to open-world adventures I'm a completionist. I wanna see that 100% on my screen at the end. Unfortunately, some of the timed driving missions require an absolutely flawless run to complete, which can be near impossible when you're driving a vehicle with poor handling capabilities. 1. Nobody like sleeping with snooring people, so avoid those loud sleeper (negative trait), except they got awesome stat & you know what you are doing.
2. Watch their expected decor, try to get the lowest decor when you start picking your first 3 dupes.
3. Learning, Digging, and Construction are pretty useful for early game. Another good attribute to consider are Athletics (they move faster, can easily be trained but still useful if they are high from the start) & Strength (currently you can't train this, so definitely has its own value)
4. Stress Response. Try to avoid Binge Eater if you still learning and you know you won't do well.
5. Start digging (shortcut G), get those sandstone, algae & copper (metal).
6. At early in the game, you might think you have enough algae. But
.
7. The first thing you need to build is restroom (Outhouse), your dupes need a place to pee and poop. or they will make a mess.
8. Build Research Station ASAP (research farming first). It need to be connected with electricity, so enjoy looking at your dupes running on the hamster wheel
9. Dupes breath oxygen in and emit Carbon Dioxide (they can fart too). O2 are light blue & a bit transparant, CO2 are black. CO2 can stack up pretty fast, be careful with it. They are heavier than O2, so they will fall at the bottom of your colony/base. (they also tend to go right)
10. Oxylite produce oxygen, try to open area that have them (you don't need to dig them).
11. Watch for warning notification, dupes are not the smartest creature in the asteroid, sometime they can kill themselves in the most unpredictable (stupid) scenario.
12. Exploring is good, but be careful not to expand too much or open a big vacuum area when your oxygen production is still low.
13. There is Priority Tools in the bottom right panel. 1 lowest, 9 highest (avoid using 9 for all your job order, setting all to 9 means no 9). You should probably check the other tools too, and overlay (top right). They are useful.
14. Hatch & puff are useful. Rule of thumbs, just don't kill any creature before you actually know what they do (good or bad).
15. Taking new dupe is okay, but be very careful with your oxygen & food supply.
16. You might think mealwood will be your stable food supply. But
17. Don't freak out with unfriendly/toxic gases, but you should start worrying when they are getting out of control.
18. Electrolizer spit out lots of oxygen but they also spitting out hydrogen. (they are lighter than O2, so they'll go upward)
19. Some resource are more scarce than the other, be very careful. Some example: Algae, clean water, and metal (copper, gold) at early game. Sands and coal at mid-late game.
20. #DupesLivesMatter, remember to take care of your dupe. When stress hit you hard, it will be a snowball effect and your colony is doom before you realize it
21. Watch your decor, some building have bad decor and it is bad for your dupes. (use decor overlay)
22. Watch your building temperature, some building emits heat and can be overheated (break & need repair, cost time & resource. again, use overlay to check)
23. Watch your own necessity, like dupe, your life matter too. You need food, drink, and sleep.

This Call of Duty is a very good Call of Duty. The campaign was fantastic and the implementation of varying story lines based upon the player's decisions was a fine touch. Unlike past Call of Duty's, I, as the player, was able to choose the equipment that I would bring into battle. For the time that I played it, the campaign was a fine spree of action and violence spanning from the 1980's all the way to 2025.
Zombies I enjoyed immensly, and I played through every zombie map with random players whom I encountered through the matchmaking system. The Versus mode of zombies I was not able to play through merely because of the lack of players playing it. Zombies is, in this game, what it has always been since its beginning in Call of Duty World at War. I will admit that minor to major changes have been made to the formula to keep it fresh throughout these years. However, the primary concept is still there and it is still fun as ever to hold out with your friends or complete strangers throughout infinite hoards of zombies.
I have spent around 170 hours on multiplayer. I must say that, while I understand why people play it and why they enjoy it, it is merely not my taste. Weapons that I find entertaining to use were not avalaible until the latter part of the unlock system. Maps are varied in their atmosphere and visuals, but are lacking in their variety of paths available for the player to use to get to the objective. Maps such as Yemen and Downhill have only set paths for the player to use. I would prefer to have more paths, both known and unknown, to use in order to get to the objective. I would also like to be able to climb the evironment. I find, while playing, that there are a lot of oddly placed invisible walls that hinder my ability to hide and sneak attack my enemies. These type of features, multiple secret paths and being able to climb most of the evironment, I would like to see in Black Ops III when it releases.
In the end, here was what I liked :
- Great campaign with branching story paths that allows the player to choose the equipment that he brings into the mission.
- Zombies is great with varying maps and in game concepts. Puts great effort into creating wonderful and rewarding easter eggs.
- Multiplayer has a lot of weapons, while the most powerful and entertaining to use may not be available until later in the unlock process.
Here was what I did not like :
- Lack of varying paths to use in the multiplayer maps.
- Invisible walls that rob the player of his ability to transverse throughout the evironment.

I should probably say that I’m newcomer to the series and Half-Genie Hero is my first game in the franchise.  I liked the game, which seems strange considering my final vote on it – my final feelings lie somewhere in the middle, but Steam doesn’t have neutral score, so I cannot use this.
The game certainly looks polished when you play it – characters look beautiful, music is fantastic and animation fluid. Game plays smoothly and responsively (usually, we will talk later about some forms...). The level design is good and most of the levels are blast to play. Transformation are fun and open a lot of new ways to move though levels, other power-ups and spells make fight interesting and give players a lot of options to dispatch enemies.
So far it seems like very nice platformer, doesn’t it? However, the longer you play, the more cracks start to show. There are only few (hub, five main and final) levels, which wouldn’t be a problem – game doesn’t really have to be very long to be good and leave nice impression, but you can see that creators saw short length of the game as big problem and were afraid that it seemed to short. Most of my problems stems from methods they applied to combat this problem.
- First, that five main levers? They are very interesting first time you play though them and nice second time, with some small changes in monster or trap placement. However, you better hope you will really like them, because you will be playing them over and over trying to find that missing upgrades necessary to progress your story. At this point I just cannot look at beautifully designed and interesting creepy factory level considering how many times I have to beat it. When you have to give players spell to skip parts of the world to get instantly to next level (you get that and this is immensely helpful, but still doesn’t  eliminate main problem) you really should think if amount of backtracking isn’t too big. At some point it just stop being fun (and I’m a completionist type of player) and start to seem like artificially padding the game’s length.
- Instant death traps spanning entire sublevels. Well, they are not exactly instant death (you only lose some energy after failing and are moved to the beginning of challenge), but they are rather long with no checkpoints in the middle. It wouldn’t be that bad, but they are designed for you to fail at least few times before you can play them from memory. Two of them remove most of your special skills and make you fall down slippery slope while jumping over chasm and avoiding barrels (don’t know, maybe it is series tradition? Doesn’t really seem fun), with some jumps timed in the way that you cannot really succeed on them without inhuman reflexes or precise knowledge coming from failing them before – and if you will, you will have to replay entire segment from the beginning.  Another one is “lava rising” type of the level – you need to climb tower while instant kill condition rise from the bottom. This is classic platformer design, however even in Ninja Gaiden series it was clear where you should jump – Shantae sublevel is long and have tons of blind ends, making you constantly fail until you progress to almost the end and can play sublevel from memory where you should move to avoid moving into blind end.
- These instant death trap type of sublevels? One of them comes just after final boss. It’s extremely fun to have do trial and error long gameplay segment when you have just won final fight and want to sit back and relax while story unfolds ;-)
- There is instant death sublevel build entirely on how unwieldy and full of inertia is one of the transformed Shantae’s forms. I know that controls of that form are bad, you don’t have to show me that so much ;-)

- Lots of upgrades seem like afterthought – for example, special power of bat transformation is used exactly once and only to get relic that allows another (not really useful for combat) almost optional form to attack.
- There is an upgrade late game (I think you get it for unlocking entire art gallery? Not sure) that gives you unlimited mana allowing for endless casts of spells. Doesn’t seem too bad, strong bonus for completionists, until you realize it means unlimited instant full life heals, unlimited healing items spawn and unlimited invulnerability bubble spell.  Because of that final level consist mainly of instant kill spikes, while final bosses are a joke.
- For the end – characters. They seem fun and interesting. They seem to know Shantae, but I have no idea how and why. If you don’t know them from previous installments, there is pretty much zero explanation who they are, how they know Shantae and why are they friends/enemies.
To sum up -  I enjoyed most of this game, at least until more annoying parts came up, killing my enjoyment each time. It is a very nice game and I hope there will be next game in the series that will polish problems this one is full of – but at this point, my opinion is a little more negative than positive (I would really like to be able to choose neutral opinion in Steam review options).

Trackmania 2 Stadium is an arcade-like racing game with loops, jumps, and ridiculously fast speeds. I picked it up  on a Steam sale for around $2.50 along with Trackmania Canyon for me and a friend because it was so cheap. There's a stripped down single player version: No story, no opponents (Except for the predeterminded time goasts), no collision. Just you and the road.
The multiplayer is the real reason why you would buy this game, though. The basis of multiplayer is that you have at set amount of time to finish the track and get the fastest time possible, while others are doing the same. There's a "place" in that it's how you match up against other player's fastest times. It has an extensive server list, modding community, and track creators, and they're friendly!! Some actually say hello and strike a conversation when a new person joins. Because the game relies mostly on skill, professional racing teams have been created. I must say, server admins have a very good taste in music.
On the visual side, it looks very good, and because it's a reletively light game, you'll be running a pretty high FPS most of the time. You can also design your own vehicle skins, either the default car, or something from the Steam community. The modding community can let you race around the track as Sonic if you want.
The game itself can be pretty hard, to be honest. Many tracks require split second reaction time with very low margin for error. Don't be discouraged if you crash off the track a few times or if the pros get a faster time than you. Happens to the best of us. The more you play a track, the better you naturally get at it.
Overall, try to get it on a Steam sale. You might like it.

Life is strange before the storm does a good job at filling in some gaps left by the first game, as well as further developing one of the original games most beloved characters. The gameplay is very similar to the original, though it features many different tones due to being told from Chloe's perspective rather than max's. These differences are noticeable in many different ways, one of the most notable being the choice in music throughout the game. But perhaps the most glaring difference is the fact that you don't have rewind powers in this game. Some will find the lack of rewind powers to be irritating and possibly dislike the game for this fact. It could be argued however that by excluding rewind powers from this game it provides choices with far more weight since you can't just rewind if you get a result you dislike.
I consider this game a must buy for any Life Is Strange fan, and a very good game overall, definitely a story worth your time, and a unique one that poses interesting questions throughout for the player.

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

Space shooters or shoot em ups are not exactly my favorite genre. It takes a lot to impress me in this genre. This game didn't impress me, but I was pleasantly surprised that the game was actually good. I was initially very turned off by the visuals, the menus, and the UI... but the game is fun. When it comes down to it, a fun game is better than a pretty game.
The game is very simple to learn and easy to control. While the controls could be tightened a bit, there isn't too much to complain about there. The core gameplay is very fun. The autofire is a nice feature for those of us who don't want carpal tunnel injuries! Something other games in the genre could learn from.
The way the entire game is played on the mouse just makes sense in this game. You steer with the mouse, you use skills with the mouse. It just works. The skills are one thing I really loved about the game. The combo of offensive and defensive skills made the game feel strategic, which was unexpected.
The game could use a visual upgrade. As it is, it really just isn't much to look at. There's no character to it visually. It just looks bland and generic. Pretty much the same thing can be said for the music. Although, the music is not too bad. That being said, I actually liked the voice acting. The voice acting in these sort of games is normally non-existent or absolutely terrible. The voice acting in this game is actually pretty decent.
One particularly nasty thing about this game is the fact that the multiplayer is totally dead. That's not really a fault of the developers. The multiplayer is only dead because nobody is playing it. That's likely due to the game being fairly unknown, not because the game is bad.
My last complaint is that the game feels lacking in content. I'm not exactly sure what I would change as far as that goes, but it's just something I feel is worth pointing out. Maybe some more unlocks and just more visuals in general.
I know I've listed a lot of complaints, but the game is really pretty decent. I'm giving it a recommendation. The amount of content in the game is low, but if you like these sort of games you will likely enjoy this one.

I love the idea of this game... it also looks really great. The weather effects are awesome. That being said, I have purchase several games in alpha and beta stages. I have been in invite-only beta tests also. I know what to expect and what not to expect from games in early stages, and this one is terrible. The developer clearly has little idea of what he's doing from a procedural point of view. In the time i've owned this game here's what's happened: several patches have been released, but the big problems haven't been resolved... neat new little content has been added, but with the game unplayable it makes little difference. This game is sure to disappoint over and over again. I waited so long to write this review because I wanted to see if some progress would be made, but it hasn't. The worst part of it is that the developer has had to go off steam (on kickstarter) to continue to raise money. Please save yourself the headache of downloading this game. If you do try to play, here are a few tips.
1) Save often. F5 saves and F9 loads... the icons at the top right also save and load, i'll let you try to figure out which is which
2) The AI is always getting stuck in stupid loops or just shutting down. This happens every few minutes like clockwork... you must save, exit the game, and restart it to continue playing.
3) Things don't update like they should... if you mine ore but can't figure out why it isn't being moved to storage... it's probably AI to blame again... another reload should help.
4) Sometimes things stop working inexplicably, If the airlock breaks and cannot be repaired, you must start a new game. some things can be repaired though, so who knows.
5) Always place two doors on rooms... if the door breaks and needs repair, but your people are inside of the room, and the guys outside the room are too tired to do it and the door that's broken leads to the sleeping area... they might decide not to repair it and instead die from lack of sleep... leaving the others trapped inside to starve
6) Just get in the habit of restarting the game every few minutes
7) Don't bother with research, it causes bugs which basically cause the game to crash beyond a certain point... meaning you'll never get past that point without starting yet another new game.
8) Use windows 7 or vista, and make sure you have the latest drivers for your graphics card (and by that I mean have a graphics card that uses newer drivers) The dev doesn't like helping with bugfixing if your computer doesn't use the latest drivers, despite the fact that some older cards (like the ones in my windows 7 machine) have old drivers (even if they are the "most up to date" they are still like 2 years old) and that still others (like on my windows 8 acer machine) require the use of special drivers provided by the OEM which may not be the "latest and greatest".
9) Don't expect too much, this way you won't be disappointed.
Edit: still... don't buy this game. It's on sale, but seriously... you wouldn't play it more than 30 minutes, even if it were free.
UPDATE: 21 May 2015... I'm not sure how it's even possible, but the game is even worse now than it was before.
UPDATE: 1 Sep 2017... Still going to be a negative on the recommendation. I advise staying away from this one a little while longer. The dev has continued on pretty much the same trajectory. New features, new bells and whistles, and failure to address very long-standing issues with the game. It still has graphical glitches everywhere. Sometimes a door will be stuck closed because of power outages, but it will never update. It looks open, but noone can get inside. Upon reloading you'll go "oh, that's why they weren't building anything... they couldn't get to the workbench". Sometimes colonists become unresponsive but seem to still be standing around. AI has improved, but not by much. Resolution problems and graphics problems. None of my OTHER games require disabling overlays or nvidia share. None of my other games are affected so horrendously by UI scaling (if you go fullscreen and can't click the buttons, that's probably why... this game hates UI scaling). None of my other games break horribly when my gpu drivers are a couple weeks out of date. The dev is better at writing exuse posts blaming the flaws in his code on everyone else's setup than he is at writing code to fix problems and address issues. The game is not as awful as it was, but at this rate it'll never be a thumbs-up game. In the past couple hours I've only had one crash-to-desktop.

TL;DR: For grinders and people who want to keep their hands busy.
Rogue Legacy is a grindy game. I have played a touch on PC and quite a bit on Vita and it has proven to be a slog in a lot of ways.
This is a game that has good ideas but at every turn it asks you to invest time over and over to get over specific walls. Damage is heavily scaled so later areas are disproportionately hard for early runs which means that you have to die and restart just to get the stats to make your attempts easier. Bosses favor specific character traits and classes which means when you finally start running bosses, you can sometimes get stuck dying repeatedly till you pick up a better character to make things work.
It also lacks meaningful variation to break up this monotony. Tile sets can get rote and enemies don't have interesting attack patterns to master. Change in locals also brings reskinned enemies most of the time with some exceptions.
I can recommend Rogue Legacy but only to a specific crowd, those who appreciate a long grind or need a brainless game. Other than that you may want to steer clear.

After almost 150 hours on this game, I think it's time to review.

Pros:
*Controller Support!
*User generated maps.
*Great community.
*Fun and frustrating, yet strangely addicting.
*Everyone has the same stats, no matter what car "skin" they have.
Cons:
*Dry times for servers.
*There are people that are better than you.
*"Planets" as a currency system could use some work for the later game.
*Lacks some individuality-per-player.
Overall: 8/10 Pretty solid racing experience!

Why so much time on what looks like a pretty basic, arcady, and completely unrealistic racing game?
Well, after 3k+ hours, there are probably about 3k+ reasons. Let me try and pick a few.
First off, this is very much skill-based. Even on the 'silly, luck' tracks (which I'll come to in a moment). Play online, and you'll find pro-level gamers showing almost unbelievable levels of skill and achieving the seemingly impossible. But it's not impossible - this is a very fair game. Any cheating is caught and eliminated pretty quickly. All the cars have the same spec, there is no car-to-car collision to mess up your times. It's (mostly) just you, and a track, and your level of skill that determine how well you do.
Next, the variety. The track creator provided allows an almost limitless tracks, and the community has produced masses of content. This obviously varies enormously in both style and quality, but since you are generally only on any given track for 4-5 minutes, if you don't like one you just wait it out and see if the next is more your kind of thing. And probably, in those 4-5 minutes you'll try it anyway and still get sucked in to try and beat your own times at the very least.

For anyone unfamiliar with Trackmania, here's a quick overview:
- Tracks are built out of prefab pieces, kinda like lego (but obviously with race track shapes instead of rectangles).
- Cars cannot collide with other cars.  You cannot run other players off the road in this game.
- In multiplayer, you're in a simultaneous time-trial competition with the other players, but sometimes there are other goals... such as simply being able to finish a very difficult track or a specially crafted stunt-oriented track at all.
Generally speaking, this is a game for perfectionists, speed seekers, and stunt lovers.
The main benefit of this game over other racing games is that you can jump into an already-running multiplayer server at random, encounter new tracks that you've never seen before as well as ones you've mastered, and have people to compete with, pretty much any time you want.

FINALLY ! I'm done with this game after 66 hours. Well, I didn't even complete it 100% honestly, I scavenged the first two territories, completed the stronghold of the 3rd one, and then rushed to the ending, which was not the ending, and continued to the true ending, which was awesome.
It's really too bad that they've put 60+ hours of grinding and fetch quests. The game starts with a cinematic where you see the main baddie Scrotus, and then you don't see him until the end. Between that cinematic and the final part of the game, all you have to do are fetch quests to liberate and upgrade strongholds, so the leaders can help you upgrade your car. And that, until you get to Gastown, where things finally start getting interesting. From there you'll have a few hours of "real" missions with characters and dialogues that feel like a real game, and not just filler content.
Of course you're not forced to do all the grinding, but then you won't unlock upgrades for the car, or bonuses from the strongholds ( replenishing your ammo, health, water, gas, etc ). You also need thousands of scraps to unlock those upgrades so you better do the secondary missions and capture the camps, which in return will give you a lot of scrap.
Anyway, if you played games like Batman ( same combat, but "simpler" ), Far Cry ( lot of capture-the-camp ) or any open world with filler content and liked them, this game is definitelly for you.
Don't expect a happy ending though, this is not Fury Road...

The game is simple:
Build your car
Gather scrap
Improve car with scrap
Gather more scrap
Improve more
Gather more
...
It's practically a giant collectathon for scrap.
But the thing is, I'm okay with that. Even though the whole world is filled with the same camps and objectives to complete and the repetitiveness sometimes gets a bit much, the game is well crafted with some actual love for the Mad Max franchise behind it, which is more than I can say for other movie-based games.
Everything in this game in the area of mechanics and gameplay has been done before, the game brings nothing new to the table but what it does bring is a refined formula, if a tad dated.
I will say though that my largest gripes were with the music and the story:
The music is practically nonexistent except for very particular moments, I just expected a lot more after coming off the back of Fury Road with all those drums (and I'll be adding that kick♥♥♥♥♥♥flame guitar to my wishlist for Santa) and with this I either didn't pay much attention to the soundtrack or my expectations were too high. Either way, I always enjoy hitting up a convoy with the Fury Road ost playing in the background, adds a hellava lotta umf to the game.
Storywise, it was pretty bland for the most part. After the beginning Max just feels like a very average character when compared to the dialogue of everyone else. Maybe this was done on purpose to make him stand out, I don't know, but either way I didn't really care about the story or Max until the second last mission of the storyline, but boy did it feel like a proper Mad Max ending. Left a real bitter taste in my mouth it did.
All in all, 7/10. A solid game even if its mechanics have been done before. Definetly one of the best movie-games to come out in the last few years.

I should probably say that I’m newcomer to the series and Half-Genie Hero is my first game in the franchise.  I liked the game, which seems strange considering my final vote on it – my final feelings lie somewhere in the middle, but Steam doesn’t have neutral score, so I cannot use this.
The game certainly looks polished when you play it – characters look beautiful, music is fantastic and animation fluid. Game plays smoothly and responsively (usually, we will talk later about some forms...). The level design is good and most of the levels are blast to play. Transformation are fun and open a lot of new ways to move though levels, other power-ups and spells make fight interesting and give players a lot of options to dispatch enemies.
So far it seems like very nice platformer, doesn’t it? However, the longer you play, the more cracks start to show. There are only few (hub, five main and final) levels, which wouldn’t be a problem – game doesn’t really have to be very long to be good and leave nice impression, but you can see that creators saw short length of the game as big problem and were afraid that it seemed to short. Most of my problems stems from methods they applied to combat this problem.
- First, that five main levers? They are very interesting first time you play though them and nice second time, with some small changes in monster or trap placement. However, you better hope you will really like them, because you will be playing them over and over trying to find that missing upgrades necessary to progress your story. At this point I just cannot look at beautifully designed and interesting creepy factory level considering how many times I have to beat it. When you have to give players spell to skip parts of the world to get instantly to next level (you get that and this is immensely helpful, but still doesn’t  eliminate main problem) you really should think if amount of backtracking isn’t too big. At some point it just stop being fun (and I’m a completionist type of player) and start to seem like artificially padding the game’s length.
- Instant death traps spanning entire sublevels. Well, they are not exactly instant death (you only lose some energy after failing and are moved to the beginning of challenge), but they are rather long with no checkpoints in the middle. It wouldn’t be that bad, but they are designed for you to fail at least few times before you can play them from memory. Two of them remove most of your special skills and make you fall down slippery slope while jumping over chasm and avoiding barrels (don’t know, maybe it is series tradition? Doesn’t really seem fun), with some jumps timed in the way that you cannot really succeed on them without inhuman reflexes or precise knowledge coming from failing them before – and if you will, you will have to replay entire segment from the beginning.  Another one is “lava rising” type of the level – you need to climb tower while instant kill condition rise from the bottom. This is classic platformer design, however even in Ninja Gaiden series it was clear where you should jump – Shantae sublevel is long and have tons of blind ends, making you constantly fail until you progress to almost the end and can play sublevel from memory where you should move to avoid moving into blind end.
- These instant death trap type of sublevels? One of them comes just after final boss. It’s extremely fun to have do trial and error long gameplay segment when you have just won final fight and want to sit back and relax while story unfolds ;-)
- There is instant death sublevel build entirely on how unwieldy and full of inertia is one of the transformed Shantae’s forms. I know that controls of that form are bad, you don’t have to show me that so much ;-)

- Lots of upgrades seem like afterthought – for example, special power of bat transformation is used exactly once and only to get relic that allows another (not really useful for combat) almost optional form to attack.
- There is an upgrade late game (I think you get it for unlocking entire art gallery? Not sure) that gives you unlimited mana allowing for endless casts of spells. Doesn’t seem too bad, strong bonus for completionists, until you realize it means unlimited instant full life heals, unlimited healing items spawn and unlimited invulnerability bubble spell.  Because of that final level consist mainly of instant kill spikes, while final bosses are a joke.
- For the end – characters. They seem fun and interesting. They seem to know Shantae, but I have no idea how and why. If you don’t know them from previous installments, there is pretty much zero explanation who they are, how they know Shantae and why are they friends/enemies.
To sum up -  I enjoyed most of this game, at least until more annoying parts came up, killing my enjoyment each time. It is a very nice game and I hope there will be next game in the series that will polish problems this one is full of – but at this point, my opinion is a little more negative than positive (I would really like to be able to choose neutral opinion in Steam review options).

I'm not normally one to write reviews, but I really want to write my thoughts on the game somewhere. It's like 4AM though, so I'm not sure how coherent this is going to be, but uh, here we go.
First of all, I love the direction that they've taken the art style. The visuals are absolutely gorgeous. The hand-drawn characters over the 3D backgrounds look very nice. Speaking of the characters, I feel that the more chibi-style is really cute. All in all, it's just a great game to look at.
The soundtrack is fantastic as usual. A couple of tracks really reminded me of Mighty Switch Force!, which y'know, makes sense considering Jake Kaufman composed the soundtrack to that too. I don't think he's ever produced a track I haven't liked.
Now in comparison to the previous titles in the series, I do feel like Half-Genie Hero takes a couple of steps back in places, particularly the level design. I wouldn't really call the game a Metroidvania. The more exploration-based dungeons are gone and have been replaced with much more linear levels divided up into a few sections each followed by a boss. If I had to draw a comparison to something similar, it'd probably be Mega Man. (This certainly doesn't mean I think Mega Man has bad level design or that I think the level design in this game is bad. Really, it's just different.) The scale of the worlds also feels a lot smaller, especially in comparison to Pirate's Curse. I was a little surprised at how short they all felt, even on my first playthrough. I also feel like the game doesn't utilize all of the transformations enough. There are a couple that are really only used once and then never again. There are also a few that don't even really need to be used at all. Most of those are optional though, so it's not a huge deal.
I've got a few small issues with the story, too. I'm sure others have said this before, but the game is sort of a soft reboot. There were some character development moments in Pirate's Curse that I was interested to see possibly get expanded upon, but the game kinda just ignores them. It's not really that big of a deal, though. It was just something I was kinda hoping to see. Something that does bother me though, is how disjointed the story feels at times. The events of the game never really feel all that connected and are more like random tasks that are just there to move the plot along. It doesn't really feel all that much like an adventure. The dialogue is great, though. I did enjoy the references to previous games and I laughed at most of the jokes.
I know it probably sounds like I'm being too critical, but I really enjoyed the game. It just feels a little weaker compared to the rest of the series, in my opinion. On its own, it's a really great game and a hell of a lot of fun. If you've never played a Shantae game before and you're interested, this is a great place to start. I feel the game does a good enough job of introducing the characters and the world to newcomers. If you do pick it up and enjoy it, then I strongly recommend you check out the others as well. It's a great series and it's really a shame that it's still so relatively unknown.
To sum everything up, I feel the game takes some steps forward in certain areas and some steps back in others, but it's still a great experience. Give it a try if you're interested!
There's probably more I would like to say, but it's really late and I'm tired so I think I'm about done here.

TL;DR: Good game, but a step back from the previous title. Initially downvoted because of lack of content, and even now I feel like the base game only barely meets the $20 asking price, especially since there will be paid DLC in the future (unless you were a backer in which case it's all free). If you're looking to get into the franchise, I would VERY strongly recommend Pirate's curse instead, or even Risky's Revenge: Director's Cut since Pirate's Curse is a continuation of that story.
PROS:
-Platforming is fluid and satisfying.
-Absolutely amazing soundtrack. Less tracks here than PC, but what is here is golden. My only critique is that the first run of the first level had vocals which I found distracting, but that same track is also played during the credits which is perfectly fine.
-Transformations are more fluid than previous games, and there are many more of them.
-New art style isn't bad (chibi isn't really my thing personally, I prefer pixel sprites and Inti Creates' art style from Pirate's Curse).
-Humorous dialogue. I laughed out loud on multiple occasions.
CONS:
-Easily my biggest issue is the switch from the metroidvania playstyle. There are no dungeons, no save stations and no open world. HGH plays more like a Megaman game. You have stages divided up into a few areas that give you a save option between them. Stages can be replayed from the beginning to collect upgrades/items previously unattainable, and later on you get the ability to warp ahead to the next area of a stage if what you're looking for is in that area, but there is no backtracking to the previous area in a stage. If you miss something in the previous area you have to restart the entire stage (warp is handy here).
-Overall less content than PC, as stated before.
-Story is severely lacking. Rather than an overarching plot, HGH consists of several mini-plots, none of which are very interesting.
IMO, the game feels like less effort went into building the game and instead that effort went into creating new assets and engine. Probably the reason Pirate's Curse was so awesome was because it reused so many assets from Risky's Revenge, and so much more effort was able to go into the game itself. If so, then I can only hope that the next game turns out to be at least as successful as PC was by reusing assets from HGH.
Also, I would absolutely LOVE to see the return of Inti Creates artwork for the next game.

I recommend this game for anyone looking for intelligent immersive storytelling that delves into the ambiguities of war. Throughout the game I found myself questioning, as did the main character, who was really friend or foe, what really was going on in Dubai, and what purpose the many different factions in the game had and why they were fighting eachother. The game also delves into the psychological stresses of war, and you will notice your character suffer from symptoms of shell shock / PTSD, or some type of psychological trauma caused by extreme stress.
Spec Ops has an amazing story with many twists and turns, coupled with intense brutal modern combat, some moral dilemmas and even some dry humour to cut the tension at times. The characters and personalities are rememberable, for example the eccentrics, and the morally ambiguous characters you will meet.  I also found my team increasingly becomes lovable as we went through all the hardships together and their psychological states and personalities showed through.
The voice acting is superb, the AI is smart and challenging, the graphics are amazing, overall the game is extremely solid.   Even the music seems to fit, although it's not the type I would generally listen to or enjoy, it seems to somehow convey that you are on an intense 'special operation mission'. Maybe because it isn't the music that I would listen to in order to mellow out to, but it seems to fit the stressful situations the main character and his team will get into.
Definetely not a game for children. But highly recommended.

Spec Ops: The Line is a terrible game. As a person who shuns the big budget FPS and TPS copouts of today, I never expected it to be so bad. It grabbed me from the very beginning, and took me on one of the worst experiences I’ve ever had as a gamer. As I ventured through, I couldn’t help but keep shaking my head at what was going on. You know what? Terrible doesn’t even work. NOTHING fits as a description for what I went through in Spec Ops: The Line. And for that sole reason, it’s one of the best games I’ve ever played……..oh, what, you thought I was gonna say it sucked? As if.
The campaign puts us in the role of Captain Martin Walker. He and his two squadmates, Lieutenant Alphonse Adams and Sergeant John Lugo, are sent on a rescue mission to Dubai; a Dubai that took a devastating hit from a record-breaking number of sandstorms. It seemed as if it was going to be simple: go in, get the survivors, and get out. However, part-way in, they find dead American soldiers. Now their goal is to get survivors and find out what happened here.
Because I had known what the story was about beforehand, I knew exactly where it was going to go: ♥♥♥♥♥own. I’m not going to spoil anything (at least, not yet), but these men go through some tough, TOUGH stuff throughout the campaign. All kinds of bad decisions of made, and all kinds of consequences happen as of a result. It made me feel something I’ve never felt when playing a game like this: guilt.
I honestly wish I couldn’t reversed some of the things I did in the game, but the thing is, it was the game telling you what to do, not you. With a few exceptions, you were forced to comply with what the game wanted you to do. You were not in control, the game was. Any shooter that tries to evoke this kind of emotion *cough* Modern Warfare 2 *cough* doesn’t have anything on Spec Ops’ story. I’ve had the honor of reading through some of the best video game tales of all time, but Spec Ops is definitely gunning for the top.
And a good thing, too, because the rest of the game is rather unmemorable. Spec Ops’ is a third person shooter, and a cover-based one, at that. Most of the gameplay boils down to, “Run here, shoot, run here, shoot, run here, shoot, keep shooting, you’re almost there!”, and it’s exciting, but doing that over and over again during the six hours you’ll spend in it gets dull. The fact you can command your squadmates to do certain things during battle, like healing a downed partner or sniping an enemy from far away, is a nice addition, but because the game says it makes the shooting tactical, it comes off as shallow.
It also doesn’t help that the game is hard as hard can be. I’ll admit, it’s mainly because I’m not into games like this and for that I have no skill, but I’m pretty sure that even veterans of the series and genre would find this difficult. Many of the enemies take more than a few bullets to go down, and because there’s a wide variety of guns and weapons, ammo can get scarce. You, on the other hand, are not quite the bullet sponge your foes are. If you stay out of cover for more than three seconds, you immediately get the sensation of the colorblind, and any more time out in the open brings death. Still, even when the game asked if I wanted to change difficulty, I didn’t switch to an easier mode. I dread what the hardest mode is like: you probably die after one bullet and everyone else takes 50 bullets to even flinch.
I do have a few other complaints. The game does looks really, really good, even if it’s running on an extremely outdated engine that people still use for some reason, but the pre-rendered cutscenes look surprisingly bad, with compression up the wazoo and a really bad framerate. The other problem involves a few spoilers, so head on down to the last paragraph if you don’t wanna listen. The story is very, very, very, very good, but for some reason, I felt that the multiple endings at the end dulled the impact a touch. They all suck, in the sense that you’re still a bad person, which is good, but I believe a story like this should have a definite conclusion. It’s not necessary, and again, the four endings they outlined are perfect for what the player feels when they play, but I would’ve appreciated it.
Nonetheless, Spec Ops: The Line is still worth playing because of its engrossing tale of the human being. Even when I died or got tired of the monotonous shooting, I kept going because the story was so freaking good. This has never happened whenever I played any other FPS or TPS campaign. Usually, I slug through half of those campaigns and then stop. Thankfully, that’s not the case for Spec Ops.
- Even Luck

Spec Ops: The Line is one of the only games I would ever recommend putting on the lowest difficulty on the first playthrough.
This is not a game you play for the amazing gameplay, although it's nothing worse than generic. I liked it. Different strokes for different folks.
Were it to be judged purely on its design and mechanics, Spec Ops: The Line would be pretty forgettable, but it has an ace in the hole. And it's a bigg'un: a story so out of the blue in its direction and message that it's a miracle, a major publisher put this game out at all. What you think you're getting- particularly if you only play the demo- is another gung-ho gun-wielding slice of Americans saving the day by killing all the brown people. What you actually get is a slow, spiralling descent into madness of one man, that wears its Heart of Darkness/Apocalypse Now inspirations proudly and uses them to forge a modern-day commentary on the type of video game you thought you were going to play.
Captain Walker is no tiantic Call of Duty avatar who can murder a thousand people and walk away- he falls apart mentally, visually and audibly as the game continues, his professionalism is stripped away and raw ego left exposed. "Tango down" becomes a more chilling, "Kill is ♥♥♥♥ing confirmed" as the game confronts you with issues of culpability and responsibility. It's incredibly unsettling and so out of the ordinary for the modern gamer that to most people, this might be thrown aside in disgust.
This is no Gears Of War/Army Of Two clone. This is the story of one man who loses himself to the brutality of war.
To the open minded and for someone who wants a great story mixed with an unsettling message, this is a MUST OWN.

There really is no episodic game out there that can be compared to Life is Strange as its arts and visuals along with the sounds that includes a incredible taste in music and lyrics that immerses you into the story where you really feel drawn into it and it captivates you; almost every episode leaves you feeling astonished which I couldn't say for other games with the same genre.
The only downside is that the main character who is Chloe can be overly obnoxious with her prejudice thoughts of sexism and amongst other adolesent nonsense that spews from her mouth, but it is tolerable and it is part of her character which leads one to overlook it; she is still developing into an adult after all. As much as there are to dislike about Chloe, there are good traits to her as her best friend Max from the first game definitely had left her marks on her to being a better person and she holds a very strong will to do what is best for her new found best friend, Rachel who becomes Chloe's "everything."
There are also episode endings that are hardly cliff hangers which makes the wait for the release of each and every episode much more relaxing. Life is Strange actually gives the player a sense of closure in every ending and it all simply feels perfect for me, it is a story that results in one feeling complete in the end and as well as takes one's breath away with the songs that are chosen to play at the end.
The final thing I have to say for the game is passive aggressive behavior put into a video game is very tacky. If the devs can keep their moral standards intact, they can be flawless. Nonetheless, Life is Strange to me is a very highly reccommended game.

FINALLY ! I'm done with this game after 66 hours. Well, I didn't even complete it 100% honestly, I scavenged the first two territories, completed the stronghold of the 3rd one, and then rushed to the ending, which was not the ending, and continued to the true ending, which was awesome.
It's really too bad that they've put 60+ hours of grinding and fetch quests. The game starts with a cinematic where you see the main baddie Scrotus, and then you don't see him until the end. Between that cinematic and the final part of the game, all you have to do are fetch quests to liberate and upgrade strongholds, so the leaders can help you upgrade your car. And that, until you get to Gastown, where things finally start getting interesting. From there you'll have a few hours of "real" missions with characters and dialogues that feel like a real game, and not just filler content.
Of course you're not forced to do all the grinding, but then you won't unlock upgrades for the car, or bonuses from the strongholds ( replenishing your ammo, health, water, gas, etc ). You also need thousands of scraps to unlock those upgrades so you better do the secondary missions and capture the camps, which in return will give you a lot of scrap.
Anyway, if you played games like Batman ( same combat, but "simpler" ), Far Cry ( lot of capture-the-camp ) or any open world with filler content and liked them, this game is definitelly for you.
Don't expect a happy ending though, this is not Fury Road...

Vehicles are more diverse, but there arent big trucks or War Rigs. There are static globes, but no gyrocopters. What a surprise! The best action post-apo game since "Rage".The game is great on so many levels. The game is simple:
Build your car
Gather scrap
Improve car with scrap
Gather more scrap
Improve more
Gather more
...
It's practically a giant collectathon for scrap.
But the thing is, I'm okay with that. Even though the whole world is filled with the same camps and objectives to complete and the repetitiveness sometimes gets a bit much, the game is well crafted with some actual love for the Mad Max franchise behind it, which is more than I can say for other movie-based games.
Everything in this game in the area of mechanics and gameplay has been done before, the game brings nothing new to the table but what it does bring is a refined formula, if a tad dated.
I will say though that my largest gripes were with the music and the story:
The music is practically nonexistent except for very particular moments, I just expected a lot more after coming off the back of Fury Road with all those drums (and I'll be adding that kick♥♥♥♥♥♥flame guitar to my wishlist for Santa) and with this I either didn't pay much attention to the soundtrack or my expectations were too high. Either way, I always enjoy hitting up a convoy with the Fury Road ost playing in the background, adds a hellava lotta umf to the game.
Storywise, it was pretty bland for the most part. After the beginning Max just feels like a very average character when compared to the dialogue of everyone else. Maybe this was done on purpose to make him stand out, I don't know, but either way I didn't really care about the story or Max until the second last mission of the storyline, but boy did it feel like a proper Mad Max ending. Left a real bitter taste in my mouth it did.
All in all, 7/10. A solid game even if its mechanics have been done before. Definetly one of the best movie-games to come out in the last few years.

Call of Duty: Black Ops II is certainly one of the franchise's more notable titles since Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare's massively critical & commericial success.
I unfortunately cannot give an accurate review on the Multiplayer & "Nazi-Zombie" co-op mode, as Call of Duty's multiplayer has ceased to be of any interest or enjoyment to me, nor do I have the company to provide me the optimal Nazi-Zombie experience. What I can say is this is one of the few respectable PC ports in the franchise, and it's single-player attempts some rather interesting new tricks to provide a new spice of life into the Call of Duty games.
Firstly, the PC port.
You are given a wide number of options for Graphics & a particularly wide number of options for Audio. An especially welcome addition to these options an FOV Slider which provides a range from 65-90, which also increases the viewmodel FOV with it.
Now, the Single-Player (The favoured mode of play I know).
To sum up the story set-up, it's the third entry into Treyarch's story arch that began in Call of Duty: World at War, where you'll fight in two different time periods of the 1980s & 2025. I say anymore, I'd potentially spoil what little there is to find otherwise. What I will say is it does try to deliver a more detailed story whilst trying to add more development to it's characters, especially it's antagonist. Whilst I personally wouldn't say Treyarch succeeded, it was a step in the right direction, which I hope more are made in the future.
What makes it more interesting than it's predecessors is not only it's futuristic setting & RTS-like Strike Missions, but also it's branching arcs. There are periods of the game where you can fail a mission or make a choice and it can alter the game's conclusion in up to 4 different endings. These are not always obvious to detect, either making the experience more unpredictable or simply being replayability incentive for the player to replay the story to find a better outcome. I personally think the latter as the various endings would seem to rank from worst to best in certain regards. But it does allow for a more varying experience with the single-player.
The Strike Missions, an all-new feature to Call of Duty: Black Ops II, are optional missions in the single-player campaign. What's different about them is that they're a mixture of RTS & FPS gameplay, allowing the player to command units such as a trooper squad, ground & air combat drones & "CLAW" tankbots whilst being able to take manual control of each individual unit and continue to provide commands from the first person perspective.
Whilst this was actually a very interesting mode to play, the RTS side of things was somewhat unreliable, especially during the more fast & tense moments, with the AI sometimes a little difficult to tame or on occasions a little slow to respond to commands. I cannot recall if drones & "CLAWs" are limited in number or not, but human soldier units seem to be unlimitedly replenishable, which comes as a relief as they can be killed pretty quickly, even if you've taken control of one of them and giving them a hand.
And probably one of my favourite attributes that hasn't received much discussion is Single-Player Loadout Customisation. Each mission starts you with a recommended loadout of weapons & attachments, grenades, perks & equipment. However, as you progress through the campaign or complete various single-player challenges, you can unlock the entire arsenal of weapons & attachments (3 can be used at once), grenades, equipment, perks & camoflague to customise your loadout before a mission/chapter, providing a vast wealth of loadout variety & potential replay value. Although you're probably gonna want to stick to the "Access Kit" perk, which will allow you to access secret doors, chests, etc for secrets or pickups which tip the gameplay in your favour. Another thing to note is that when unlocked, you can take all of the Future Arsenal into the past missions, making for a little immersion-breaking fun (aswell as an achievement to encourage it).
So after that babble, would I recommend it? If you enjoy Call of Duty, then Yes I would. It's a good PC port & Treyarch applied a fair number of new ideas to provide improvement & breathe some new life into the franchise. Whilst they may not have all been significant enough or completely successful in my eyes, they were a step in the right direction, and with a franchise where any amount of change causes fright for developers & publisher and dedicated fans alike, I can only give words of encouragement to Treyarch to try again!
Otherwise, there are a number of other shooter games I would consider to be more realised experiences such as Wolfenstein The New Order, BioShock Infinite & Spec Ops: The Line.

Of all the games in my library, this is my go-to when I don't have much time, but I want something fun to play for 10-15 minutes before I need to move on to homework of one kind or another, or as a stress reliever when I need to unwind from work. Its proceedurally generated rooms and halls keep it from ever getting dull, and it always seems to keep the challenge just hard enough to require some genuine skill from you.
However, beyond the proceedural generation, one of the most unique additions is where this game gets its title from: the legacy portion. A basic perma-death system means that each time you die, you must choose one of your heirs in order to re-enter the castle. Each one of these heirs often has specific traits, some funny, some adventageous, and some which are downright frustrating. These two key elements of Rogue Legacy hold up what would otherwise be just another Metroidvania/Kirby game with a retro style. Could there be improvement here? I think there could. For example,
-I'd like to see maybe a little more story than the simple and often downright vague journal entries you collect as you make your way through the castle, although to be fair to it, I have not yet "completed" the game and found all the journal entries.
-Also, while many of the bosses and minibosses feel challenging, it's not always in a "git gud" kind of way, but in the Dark Souls, "We're going to hurt you and you're going to like it" kind of way, which in my opinion ruins the kind of game this feels like: a light arcade game that you pick up and play as filler, not as an immersive experience.
Despite these nitpicks (and they are nitpicks), this game is a great one for those with a couple of minutes to spare/waste, and will probably be that one game that you'll always come back to for "just one more quick run."

Most shooter games set out to make the player feel like a hero as they mercilessly gun down their enemies. Spec Ops: The Line turns this idea on its head, and makes you hate yourself for the same thing by the time you make it to the fantastic ending.
The 3rd person shooter mechanics are solid for the most part, but is nothing groundbreaking in that category. The storyline is the true star of this show. The player is placed in horrible situations, sometimes with no real "right" or "good" way out. The moral shades of gray challenge the player's emotional fortitude far beyond what is seen in most mainstream shooters today.
I can't possibly recommend this game enough. It's one of those pieces of entertainment I found myself thinking about long after the credits rolled, and I couldn't wait to begin another playthrough. Yager knocked this one right out of the park.

This is probably one of the best games I've ever played.
Why?
The gameplay is pretty standard fare for the shooter genre, with some somewhat interesting squad dynamics thrown in. I've heard the multiplayer is terrible, if you can find anyone still playing it at all.
So why is this game so amazing? The story in the campaign. It plays on your psyche, messes with your head, and makes you question why you even play games like this. It's a critique of the entire genre, one that desperately needed to be made. Why do we, as gamers, typically like to shoot things for fun? Is killing people in a video game truly harmless? If so, should we still enjoy it as much as we do?
The story draws from some classics for inspiration (most notably Heart of Darkness, by Joseph Conrad), but it takes what it needs and expands on the rest. It takes some classic conventions, and finds a way to use that to tell its own story, and tell a completely new and fresh message.
"To kill for yourself is murder. To kill for your government is heroic. To kill for entertainment is harmless."

I have to say, this is a game I want to like. Its a great concept, but the execution is very poor.
I've been patronizing this game's early access since it was available for early access, and while some bugs have been fixed, numerous game-breaking bugs still remain. Its pretty-much unplayable still, despite several months development since its initial release.
Glitches in character AI get them stuck in routines that eventually lead to their deaths. For example, eating and sleeping, repeat et infinitum, while not working on the hyroponics bay. The AI seems to get deadlocked quite a lot. Since the characters start running to the food and then eating, I assume that the value for hunger isn't being reset properly.
There are also animation problems that seem to somehow reflect character position. Character position in the world should not be a function of the 3D engine. The location of objects should be purely data, which is then rendered. The reason why I suspect this isn't the case in Maia is because characters "jump" back, particularly after a collision with a wall. Yes - they walk into walls and then teleport back a few steps. So the pathfinding is bad too. I think this is because the objects in the world are not on a real "grid" system. While rooms might be, everything else seems to be kinda "free-floating" and placable anywhere in the room / outside. While this would be cool, it doesn't work right, so its not cool.
Also the object rotation system is very annoying. It would be much better if there were a "spin by increment" key prior to object placement. And objects can intersect eachother, which makes no sense.
Additionally 6 mo after launch there's still no save / load system. The game still starts with invalid start conditions (breaches in the base start point to the outside world makes colonists unable to move around in the cavern without space suits, and the airlock is on the other side of the base). There is no way to make a new game without exiting to desktop and starting the game over. The settings are very minimal, and there are enormous problems with resolution. You click and it changes, in a cycle, rather than selecting from a menu. This is terrible because it saves the last setting, and there's no "does this resolution work for you?" dialog. This means you can get yourself into unusable settings and be unable to get out.
Also the game performance is really quite bad.
Meanwhile the creators are adding content while there are still problems with the fundamental mechanics of the game. I wonder if they understand how unusable the game is right now....

Mad Max is an action-adventure video game developed by Avalanche Studios. It offers a unique gameplay experience, but it is not flawless.
Pros:
1. The game itself looks very good graphically. It also runs smoothly on many PC setups, so don't be surprised if you can run this game at 60fps smoothly. The draw distance is also rather impressive (you can see certain structures across the map)
2. The in game world is quite large, and each region differs from the others, aesthetically. It takes a fair amount of time to drive from one side to the other.
3. The car combat, coupled with a very volatile physics engine, is very enjoyable. You can also upgrade your vehicle in various ways, like improving the suspension, engine and ramming capability. The weapons available to you, like a harpoon, sniper rifle and "thunderpoon" can also be upgraded as the game progresses. Seeing the enemy cars explode is glorious, and the amount of ways in which you can dispatch them is very nice indeed.
4. The characters in the game are, in my opinion, memorable, and each has their own view on the post apocalyptic world. The lore is also respectable; history relics, collected from scavenging locations, allow you to have a glimpse at the past.
5. Death runs, which are essentially races, are also enjoyable. There are three different "modes" and you are rewarded for clocking in a good time.
6. A major part of the game involves destroying camps. These camps could contain oil pumps, storage camps, or could simply house a horde of enemies. These camps are all unique, and are generally quite fun to dismantle.
Cons:
1. Certain resources are way too abundant. At the Stronghold of each region, you can build a fuel tank, which, if visited, replenishes all of your fuel. Even though there is a twenty minute cooldown, because there are 4 Strongholds, you can fast travel to one every five minutes to restock.

The same applies to ammunition, water and health. This somehwat detracts from the feeling that you are struggling to survive in the Wasteland, and I feel the benefits need to be toned down significantly.
2. I have previously talked about the camps. There is, however, another type; Top Dog Camps. Here, your objective is to reach the "Top Dog", the leader of the camp, and kill him. Although there is nothing inherently wrong with this-in fact, it starts off as rather fun-all of the Top Dogs are the same, and use the same weapon.

Even though each one has a "weakness" such as shivs or the shotgun, it is still easy to kill them regardless of which weapon you use. This makes it easy to learn when to dodge and strike them. It would be nice if each Top Dog utilised a different weapon-maybe one uses a heavy weapon, while another uses a ranged one.
3. Another issue arises when you look at the upgrade system for Max. The premise will be familiar to you-as you progress, you gear gets better. But, once you are "Maxed" out (See what I did there?) your character is, quite frankly, unstoppable. As there is no difficultly setting, if you want to have a challenge during fighting, then you will want to use the gear you get near the start of the game.
Personally, I feel like they could have gave the improved gear different benefits, other than making you a killing machine-maybe increasing your sprint speed, or something other than reducing the damage you take by X%, or increasing melee damage by X%.
4. Mad Max offers you many ways in which to collect things. For instance, you will need to collect Stronghold parts, for things like fuel tanks or maggot farms. Also, there are scavenging locations, in which you can find scrap (the currency of the game) or a history relic.
The thing is, there are about 200 of these places. As you can imagine, going to each scavenging location and looting it becomes extremely repetitive, especially since they are all very similar. Although going to these places is not compulsory, you have to in order to 100% the game. Some even contain Stronghold Project Parts, which create very useful resources in the Stronghold, as mentioned.
If you do not enjoy games which require a LOT of looting, raiding a ridiculous amount of locations, then this game may not be for you.
Overall, though, I would recommend Mad Max, but only consider buying it when it is on offer. The car combat is very fun, and it looks amazing, but it becomes very repetitve towards the end. The abundance of resources is also rather annoying, but the sheer wealth of potential upgrades is staggering.
