Ugly as hell? Yes
Buggy? Yes
Wonky controls? Yes
Fun as hell with friends? Hell yeah
That said, there's tons of bugs in this game.
It feels unoptimized which is especially strange since it isn't graphically demanding.
Sound will cut out every now and then, multiplayer is a pain, you'll clip through walls and floors occasionally and the controls are atrociously laggy. There isn't even a tutorial or practice mode for you to get used to them and the UI looks like a flash game from NewGrounds. Stages the devs put in the trailer for the game are nowhere to be seen, such as the sausage factory.
However, this game is a goddamn riot to play. The first 2 hours I played it I couldn't stop laughing and its even better with friends when you're all trying to throw each other off platforms and knocking each other out.
With friends this game is great and its better if you're not expecting anything competitive; just go in looking for a good time. The bugs in this game are very distracting though and its a bit surprising that this very unpolished game has been in development since 2014.

I enjoyed this game a lot. Sure, it could be cringy at times with its teenage angst narrative, but the story touched me and I was engaged at every point of the gameplay. It was a joy to play this game, revisit things I'd loved about the first game, explore more of Chloe's past, and enjoy the (in my opinion) far superior soundtrack this game had. Futhermore, despite it being very hammered in at times, I really appreciated the overarching theme of this game. There were some pretty deep moments in this game and I often had to pause to reflect about what had been said and contemplate things (I was going to say contemplate life, but that would sound pretentious/ over-the-top). However, despite my great enjoyment of this game, my review is going to focus mostly on the
I personally found.
1- For one, it lacked the awesome supernatural element the first one had. I didn't mind the realism of this game, but the absence of the supernatural element that made the original game so unique somehow made it less... fun? But, at the same time, doing that made this game a lot more serious, which is also a good thing.
2- Secondly, this game only had three episodes (honestly, a very minor complaint of mine -- I guess I just wanted more!)
3- Furthermore a lot of the 'important' choices you are given are often seemingly inconsequential while smaller choices sometimes end up being story-changing, with the final 'very important' choice leading to a pretty weak and disappointing ending, in my opinion.
4- Another complaint I have about the choices given were that they often didn't give the option of very differing opinions. I for one often found myself
disagreeing with all the choices given in conversations or actions and wishing they would have considered that certain people might think differently.
5- Most importantly though, while I felt greatly connected to the characters in this game, I did not feel nearly as emotionally invested in the events unfolding this time. Somehow, the stakes did not feel as important.

6- Something else that disapointed me was how little was revealed in this prequel as to certain unanswered questions we may have had, contrary to what I'd expected.
Although, I could attribute the lack of revelations or connections to events in the first game as being because this game was set
before Life is Strange. This, however, doesn't really excuse some of the inconsistencies (plot holes) between both games and some of the things ommitted in this game alone that make it a bit illogical at times.
Overall, despite all the negatives I pointed out here, I loved this game very much and wish there were more of it. To give a comparison, I'd rate the original Life is Strange a 9.5/10 and Life is Strange: Before the Storm a 8.5/10. I just wanted to focus this review more on the negatives, but I could just as well have focused on the positives. I 100% recommend that everyone who loves a good story-focused game play both this game and the original as they are both very good (the first one being excellent).

Rouge Legacy basically plays like if Mega Man was near constantly melee, with some magic attacks for some range. The story is mostly put to the side until later in the game, so if you're looking for MGS kinds of stories, maybe the story isn't quite for you. The combat is a jump and slice game, like Mega Man or Shovel Knight. Your sword is your standard weapon, with a magic spell for each child you choose. Yes, child. While your character is actually a knight in their mid-thirties, when you die in this game, that knight is dead. Actually dead. You're then parted with a gameplay tip, you're sent to the title screen to then choose one of three children who have special quirks that are real-world traits, such as ADHD, Near/Far-sighted, Gay/Lesbian, the list goes on. Each have their effects in game that make each child special. To sum it all up, play this if you like platformers, jump and shoots, things like that.

I normally don't like to review games this early on because I really don't think it's fair to either the consumer or the devs to do so at this stage.  However I think a good number of the of the reviews have been a bit unfair.  A lot of the reviews aren't taking into account how early this game really is in development.  Yes that is the fault of the devs for jumping the gun, and putting it on the market, however the game does show a lot of progress, and it's a really good concept.  It is extremly buggy at the moment but that's to be expected of any early access game.  That's why I'm not considering the bugs in this review but I'm focusing on the content.  The devs have done a good job of keeping this game as a more realistic survival/ managment game, and that's nice to see, since it's not really something that has been done that much.
HOWEVER! I don't write reveiws for the sake of the devs, but for the sake of the customer.  This game is a big risk!  It's very hard to tell how this game is going to turn out at this stage since it's in such a raw state.  I myself think that it's going to turn out well, and that's why I'm giving a positve review.  However unless you're a risk taker I would advise that you hold off for a little while before you buy this game, and keep an eye on it from afar.

WayForward did a good job working out this game.  In comparison to previous titles in the Shantae series, this one has the least "clunkiness" feel to it.  The game feels better streamlined.
I will also say, the game will feel easy.   Once you are decently equipped with pick-ups and upgrades, the game and boss fights do get easier.  This game is built around the same premises that keeps Super Metroid in the spotlight.  Super Metroid has good replayability and is as challenging as you make it.  Shantae: Half-Genie Hero, all the same.  This game is as challenging as you make it.  If you don't want the last fights too easy, don't collect everything or put everything to full use.  Find your own challenges.
The story is great and worth reading through, even though you can skip through it for a speed run.  I find the story is well balanced and fun.
All being said, previous games had a Metroidvania feel.  This game is more like the Mega Man X series where you replay levels to pick up items hidden in each level.
I fully recommend playing this game and the other 2 Shantae games available on Steam.  The original game is Shantae for the Game Boy Color, and WayForward has not ported or remastered it for a modern console or PC.  And this game is also the 4th game in the series, not a reboot.

Half Genie Hero plays more like a Mega Man game than a Metroidvania. Mega Man X to be precise. If you're looking to scratch a Metroidvania itch, this game won't do it for you. It's a trend that has been happening with the Shantae games. Risky's Revenge had a large world that was entirely open, but Pirate's Curse broke the world into islands containing a dungeon. Half Genie Hero only has pure levels.
The levels are mostly linear, with a few side areas you can explore if you have the right transformation. The transformations while fun, are too abundant and have the obvious consequence of having their roles overlap. Their usefulness depends on the player. If you care about optimizing your movents, all the transformations can help you blaze through levels and collect items. For regular and casual players, half of them will probably never see any use.
Other than that, everything else is what you'd expect from a Shantae game. The character art is beautiful and animates nicely. The platforming is very fluid and flows really well. There is also an option to turn off items you collect. Don't want Level 3 Fire? You can turn it off and enable Level 1 if you want to use that. It's not a major thing, but I appreciate it's inclusion.
Just keep in mind that this isn't a Metroidvania. It's a Mega Man game. And it's good.

This is probably one of the best games I've ever played.
Why?
The gameplay is pretty standard fare for the shooter genre, with some somewhat interesting squad dynamics thrown in. I've heard the multiplayer is terrible, if you can find anyone still playing it at all.
So why is this game so amazing? The story in the campaign. It plays on your psyche, messes with your head, and makes you question why you even play games like this. It's a critique of the entire genre, one that desperately needed to be made. Why do we, as gamers, typically like to shoot things for fun? Is killing people in a video game truly harmless? If so, should we still enjoy it as much as we do?
The story draws from some classics for inspiration (most notably Heart of Darkness, by Joseph Conrad), but it takes what it needs and expands on the rest. It takes some classic conventions, and finds a way to use that to tell its own story, and tell a completely new and fresh message.
"To kill for yourself is murder. To kill for your government is heroic. To kill for entertainment is harmless."

tl;dr: Fight, trade, and move people; expand, capture, or play peacefully (opt out of non-pirate conflicts with your white flag).  If you like casual gameplay you can have it; if you want something harder you can configure it for that.  A good cooperative game which doesn't force much fighting onto you (and you can set it up to pretty much avoid it).
If you've played Anno  1707 or Dawn of Discovery (Anno 1404), you could be forgiven for thinking of this as the "Anno trade ship simulator".  For a lot of it, it will be.  You are a trade vessel responsible for moving goods from place to place, or a military vessel responsible for sinking pirates, defending territory, and reclaiming towns; you are, in essence, the fleet of your particular trading company.  But it's more than that.
This game starts off as a relatively slow, steadily paced, single player game which allows friends to drop in and out of your world.  Your objectives vary from trading to fighting, and a handful of things inbetween (like shipping around drunk civilians of cities on "sight seeing" trips -- who say some ridiculous things which you get to read above your vessel).  You might be a glorified taxi, or you might try to stabilise the economic values of the region (making a tidy profit along the way); but you will almost never be a true warmonger -- the factions are neutral to one another unless you've enabled permanent war.
There are a few things worth noting: worlds and captains are persistent.  You can change your captain or your world, or both; your experience (and items) carry between games as long as you use the same captain.  This applies to cooperative and single player (as well as the "PvP" multiplayer -- which is the same as cooperative, but you pick an enemy faction from another player, or change your flag).  Now for the nitty gritty:
1. PvP combat (including singleplayer "war") is achieved by removing your white flag (open inventory while in a dock, then unequip -- simple);
2. You can "bundle" equipment into sets so you can swap your focus from diplomacy (useful for trading) to some sort of war type (e.g. range, accuracy, etc.);
3. The "endgame" is crazy, and I'm not even close to it yet.  The more you play with others the crazier it gets; the more they can help you.  You have the option to force "scaling" in a world (though it can't be turned on or off); if you want a world with a level 10 town (for ship swapping) get a friend who has good ships (or a good captain and gear) to help you.  Let them come into this world to help you up the town so you can play with ships.
4. Ships are unlocked by killing ships of the type.  Pirates typically "gear up" in lower regions.
5. Yes, two ships fly.
6. Cargo is limited, inventory is limited, and this is beneficial (otherwise I'd do insane things like carrying 20 people) -- the largest cargo capacity is 5 items (though it can still net you a very tidy profit at times).
7. Items go from white to orange (legendary), and at the end (the legendary) you can continuously upgrade with talent points or gold to keep getting stronger.
8. Worlds can be designed/edited or be played as they come out randomly (they are seeded) -- in saying that you can also set a minimum and maximum level for challenge, allowing you to force ships to spawn.
9. The easiest way I've found to "level up" is by trade-spamming and quest-spamming (typically as yellow, the Exchange).
10. You can edit all factions before a world is setup to gain more XP (harder to play) or gain less (much easier to play).
I'd say it's suitable for just about every approach; it's a fun game, simple to play, and can be played while half-asleep if you're just looking for something relaxing to help you unwind.
Oh, and it's less than 100MB download, so there's that ...

I find this to be a very pleasing and enjoyable game and is one I'm still playing on a nearly daily basis. The gameplay is simple, but can still be a challenge. The graphics are vibrant and change based on the different climate of whatever region you visit and with day/night cycles. The music fits the game very well with a cycle of simple, but unobtrusive melodies. The sound effects are just right, from cannon fire to the ship creaking as you change direction to catch the wind.
Windward is a casual trading/city building game where you complete quests such as ferrying passengers to nearby town or hunting down pirate well as buying and selling goods to raise money to buy your next big ship.
It also has exploration and conquest where you have to squash the pirate threat when you enter a new territory. You won't be able to trade or gain quests until the pirates are driven out. You engage in ship to ship combat using you cannons and then as the game progresses other abilities such as throwing barrels of fiery oil, poisonous barrels of rotting fish, the fog of war to mask your position and the old standby of just ramming into your enemy.
When you start, you're a lone buccaneer who must put together other ships in your fleet. The most direct way is to either capture the other pirates or bribe them to join you. Once you have a crew, they will come to your aid when you're attacked as well as engage pirates on their own and work to secure ports. Once a region is secure, you can trade between the cities to build up money and skills or you can move on to the next region and engage more pirates.
As you explore you can dives for treasure amongst the wrecks or pick up flotsam that is washing ashore. This can contain gold, wood, iron, sails, cannons, and even crew members. You then keep building up your attack fleet to engage the enemy. You will also gain XP which can be used to increase the skills of your crew in attack, defense and negotiation.
People say the game is slow and there is a lot of grind. If you prefer endless hordes in an FPS, then yes, this is mild by comparison. If you expect to do something once and move to the next level, then no, it doesn't work that way. You will have to trade goods to make money. You will have to buy bigger boats to trade more goods to make more money. You will need to make money to buy bigger boats so you can defeat the bigger ships the pirates will have. In essence, you will have to trade. The progression makes perfect sense to me and the game has a mixture of both easy, moderate and difficult regions on the same playing grid.
This is a great game at the retail price, but is a downright steal at $5. There has been a nice stream of updates and new features and bonuses have been added, not to mention Steam Workshop integration.  I think this is a great blend of action and adventure and can provide hours of enjoyment.

Windward is an enoyable take on the naval combat and exploration genre, with a great sense of naval combat and interesting abilities. However the slow down in the latter stages of the game and an unrewarding trading system make it a real grind. 8/10.

Trackmania² Stadium is classed as a Racing game, but as I see it, it's more of a puzzle and strategy. With the single-player mode, you get a set amount of tracks split into five groups of skill level, White being the easiest and Black being the most difficult (a bit like the karate belt system) and within those tracks, there is no room (as I know) to download other tracks and play them alone in single-player.
Multiplayer is a whole different story, however. As you get more used to a server and it's map rotation (if there is one) you'll be able to remember the tracks as you play them within the five to ten minute time limit per map, and shave off those precious few tenth's of a second, sometimes even making it come down to the hundreth's of a second, truly making your mark in the track's leaderboard. A bit like Formula 1 in that matter, as it really comes down to the skill of the driver, and the knowledge of the track that you're on.
But don't let that deter you if you aren't into that track-precision stuff, as there as many other fun-orientated maps which don't focus as much on your time taken, albeit there are less people on those servers.
Story = -/10 (no story)
Multiplayer = 9/10 (amazing community, great maps in general, easy to get along with)
Graphics = 8/10 (when maxed out, the game can and does look stunning)
Graphics Perfomance = 9/10 (runs very smoothly on older pc's and laptops)
Controls = 10/10 (personally, I play with a keyboard, but controllers are supported too, and again, how you drive your car really makes the difference)
Total = 36/40
Final Comments - Please, if you can, pick up Trackmania² Stadium when you can, or even Canyon or Valley. If you have to wait for a sale, then so be it, but if you can buy it at full price, then please support the developers behind the amazing game(s) that is Trackmania².

This is a cover based regenerating health over-the-shoulder shooter that has you roaming the desert city of Dubai with 2 other soldiers under your command. The game has a lot going for it, gorgeous vistas, licensed music, a villain that blurs the line of who is the villain, story choices, but the real thing Spec Ops: The Line can hang its hat on is the engrossing story. I'm not a story person, but this would make a great movie watching the story unfold. There are brief cut scenes here and there, but nothing that gets in the way of the action. You are even given choices, so there is some interactivity to the story, but the choices don't have any real impact on the story.
The story is simple, subtle and deep all at the same time, you are sent in to find what happened to a group of soldiers in the 33rd and you quickly discover in the first 10 minutes they've gone rogue. You're not just fighting inhabitants of Dubai, but US soldiers and other factions that I can't name since spoilers. Dubai itself is in a post-apocalyptic state, because it has been hit by a major sandstorm destroying the city except for pockets of civilians and soldiers. You'll come across both. There are elements where you can use the sand to defeat your enemies, such as destroying glass will send sand oceans burying enemies. There are blinding sandstorms. The game makes good use of the environment and city. You'll be in the sand oceans full of wrecked yachts, on top of towering skyscrapers, inside falling buildings and junkyards, this game has a great variety of areas. Each area is gorgeous, no matter how depressing and shambled they are. When you execute enemies at close range, you'll see the detail on their faces. A lot of detail was put into this game beyond the gorgeous scenery.
Since this is a cover based over-the-shoulder shooter, it feels extremely familiar to others especially Uncharted, especially when the main character is voiced by Nolan North who played Nathan Drake in the Uncharted series. Left stick to run, right stick to aim, left trigger to aim, right trigger to fire, left button to throw something, left and right on the D-pad to cycle through your grenades, Y to change weapons (between two, but you can pick up others), X to reload, B to melee, execute downed enemies and leap over cover. Up on the D-pad will let you alt fire weapons, but its mostly forgotten about. The only unique touch to this game is the right button will command your followers. Tap the right button and Lugo will send out a flash bang that on the PC seems virtually useless. I rarely see it even effect people. Holding the right button and aiming at an enemy will have your sniper take out a long range foe, but really when I'm aiming with the right button I can literally just shoot someone myself if I'm aimed at him. On top of that, it seems like commanding your sniper doesn't work on PC when it does on PS3. The final button is of course the all purpose A button that tap it to run, hold it to run and slide to cover, standing next to cover will make you stick to cover, but really this needs a lot of work. I find my character running in and out of cover or sticking to the cover behind me instead of in front of me. It is quite frustrating and results in most of the deaths I had while playing.
The enemy AI seems smart enough and they will flank you, just like you can flank them with your squad. The enemies are similar for the most part, but with AI so good, that means every enemy can kill you. They boil down to standard soldiers, snipers, shotgunners that come to you, bladers that will run at you to knife you and heavy soldiers that walk slowly at you and take a lot of bullets to kill. Its a lot like playing the Uncharted series. You and your allies get put into big open areas with a lot of cover and you need to stay there until everyone dies. Your allies feel competent enough and will take out enemies on their own and call out things to warn you.  They will need to be resuscitated if they take too much damage, but that rarely happens and you can command the other one to bring the fallen back to life. Your teammates serve as guides without seeming too overbearing. The voice acting in the game is great and its probably an unseen high point in a game full of amazing highs.
For the most part this feels like a fun game with an incredible story, despite frustrating cover and run buttons being the same. I can't say the game is worth $30 and I'm really surprised that its not $20 yet. Get it on sale. Its worth it for the single player.

==EARLY ACCESS==
The only way you are going to succeed in playing this game is for you to know what you are doing. "Prison Architect" has a lot of built in features and all sorts of tools for you to build and maintain a prison. You can bring in four types of prisoners, minimum security, normal security, maximum security, and death row. Not all of these prisoners are equal, you will need to build your prison in a specific way to handle these inmates. Just remember that this is a sandbox game, it depends on how good your building and micromanaging skills are and how much you care about your prisoners. If the prison can run itself from day to day without incidents, then you can pat yourself on the back as a reward for building a functional prison.
When you start off building a prison, it is best to centralize specific rooms to efficiency satisfy the needs of the general prison population. A large canteen for each security level of prisoners, a single large laundry room to handle the entire prison's clothing needs, a protective custody wing for snitches and former police officers and prison guards, a supermax wing for locking up your absolute worst prisoners, and 'staff only' corridors for guards and staff to easily move throughout the prison. Make sure your armory is locked down tight or is a seperate building outside the prison, and be sure your reception room and delivery sector is near the main road. Your administrators' offices should be kept away from shared corridors and be built in a safe place, especially the warden and the chief guard. Everything that promotes reform and takes care of the needs for your prisoners should be centralized within a main corridor for ease of access.
Once you get everything set up, you will need to prepare the entire prison in case of an emergency. People who play this game will complain of legendary prisoners, snitches, and ex law enforcement. Legendary prisoners will slaughter anyone who stands in their way, sometimes without warning. Snitches and former police officers will be frequent targets for murder. You will need to build separate cell blocks for them, preferably you should build a prison within a prison for these guys and fill them with more guards than usual. You must designate the legendary prisoners and their specialized cell blocks as "supermax" while designating all the prisoners marked for death as "protective custody". These two security wings must be similiar in construction. You want to keep prisoners from breaking into the protective custody wing and prisoners from breaking out of the supermax wing. You will find armed guards appropriate for defending the only entry ways to these wings.
There are a lot of things you will need to figure out, and you will be micro-managing a lot of stuff. But if you build and design your prison right, it should run itself without any problems. Unless, of course, you have the intention of stiring up a riot.
==ALPHA 35 UPDATE==
A lot of things have updated, so I liked to recap on what has happened since my previous review. An economy system has been installed into the game, prisoners working for any assigned job will be payed $0.50 an hour. They will then use that money to buy things at the shop to cover for their needs, the average price for items in the shop costs around $5. Since visitors can give money to inmates, you can make a small profit off the shop each day.
Gangs are now a force within Prison Architect. As of this update, there is a 15% chance of normal and maximum security inmates coming into the prison to be a member of one of three gangs. Once all three gangs have a minimum number of ten members, a gang leader will come in through prison intake. These gang leaders have legendary reputation, they will go around the prison and recruit non-gang members and occasionally promote one into a lieutentant. These lieutentant carry out the works of the leader, organizing "plays" to capture territories such as Common Rooms and Yards. Once captured, rival gang members are banned from entering. Non-gang members can still use the facilities within the common rooms, but they will be charged $1 an hour. The gangs will then use the money to buy smuggled weapons to defend the territory. Now anything owned by gangs cannot be modified or dezoned, but you can evict the gangs. However, this can have grave consequences. If successful, guards will now control the zone. Obviously guards are not a gang, but they are a faction in their own right.
Notable bugs:
- There's an "X & Y" bug where an error occurs for items being transported. This can be fixed by dumping the items and then cancelling out the order. However, there is no fix for bodies. Guards will just pick them up and literally try to carry them off the map, or they don't carry them off at all. This bug are mostly prevalent in pre Alpha 35 saves.
- Death row inmates no longer sign up for appeal. No fix.
- Inmates are no longer interested in carpentry. You can fix this by dezoning the workshop and rezoning it, but you'll need to do this everytime a class is finished.
==FULL VERSION==
Yes, now there is a campaign and a new mode: Escape Mode. The first mission of the campaign is the standard introduction, the next few chapters will touch upon riots and the treatment of prisoners. I will not try to give too much away since the campaign is not that long, but it holds some familiar prisons seen in IVSoftware's update videos.
Escape Mode is found in the extras, any prison you or others had built will be turned on its head. It completely reverses the concept of the game. Instead you are in prison, one you have personally built or otherwise. The goal is to escape, and the reward is anti-climatic. It is so much the method of the escape than the final result. Your results may vary from your given prison, but it should be fun in the end.

Half-Genie Hero is my first venture into the Shantae series, and it is always kinda difficult to review a game in an objective way if said game is part of an established franchise. I went out of my way to look at other people's opinions on the game and reviews of the previous titles in the series, as well as look over the wiki a few times, all just to make sure I knew what exactly what I was talking about. Without further ado, here's my review (oh hey it rhymes !)
Half-Genie Hero is fun, really, really fun.
The gameplay is just great, with super smooth controls, rapid transformations that open up new paths, magic powers to use and abuse, and despite the level design being on the weaker side, levels are a joy to play over and over again, collecting all the things you can find, and speedrunning is just the icing on the cake. It is a shame the levels are completely disconnected from the main hub, it makes the world feel rather disjointed. A shame for an entry in a series that is usually praised as a good example of Metroidvania (and god knows I'm a sukker for Metroidvanias).
Graphically, the game is gorgeous, pure eye candy (and i'm not saying that for all the lovely Jigglypuffs, IYKWIM). The lovely art direction is only an added bonus on top of some of the smoothest animations I've seen in my life. Every level is a joy to explore thanks to the clever mix of 2D and 3D. It's just a shame that most of them are rather generic, with a port, a jungle with waterfalls, a desert, a volcano...the real standout level was the magic carpet ride, which isn't something you see everyday.
Musically, it's also great, with many catchy tracks that don't feel the need to venture into 8/16 bit territory to be good. Jake Kaufman's the man when it comes to making great music, and I'm happy to say he delivered big time with his work on Half-Genie hero. The mermaid factory theme has to be my personal favorite, along with the boss fight theme. Sound design is also neat, it's very satisfying to fight enemies and hear them burn or get crushed.
The story is pretty weak, however. It's kind of all over the place, with mini-plots that don't go anywhere, and no real big narrative to string it all together. Characters get introduced only to be ignored or forgotten, and it doesn't make a strong impression. For what it's worth, the writing is funny and the interactions between characters are great, and the whole thing can be ignored, but it's a shame that a game like this couldn't give its story more attention. It's all over pretty quickly, as is tradition with games designed with speedrunning in mind.
Overall, I'd definitely recommend this game, even if you're not a fan of the series like me before playing it. I'm going to give Pirate's Curse a look one of these days, and I'm definitely looking forward to the extra content coming to HGH in the future.

I'm a big fan of simluation and management games and Prison Architect scratches both of those itches very well.
While the game is not complete, it is very playable, with solid mechanics, and the devs are very active, posting update videos along with an update, every month.
Pros:
Great simulation/management including prisoners, staff, confidential informants, reform programs, parole, even death row if you want.
Fantastic tools including a planning tool that allows you to draw out walls, objects, and pathways before you build. It's amazing how useful that is in a game like this, and PA has spoiled me in that respect - I'll never look at another builder game the same without a planning tool.
Interesting mechanics including different risk levels for prisoners, which poses challenges for managing different regimes (schedules), housing, and public spaces in order not to have fights or riots break out.
Cons:
Disclaimer: the game is still in development, so some of these may get fixed.
Planning tools could use some refinement - such as allowing you to define rooms while in plan view, as well as selecting specific objects to place in plan rather than relying on you memorizing the size of objects or flipping back and forth between plan and build modes to determine size. It's even worse if you haven't unlocked the object as then you can't even select it to see the size, and the tooltips don't tell you either.
In general, there is a lot of tutorial or tooltip work needed. Right now, you have to rely on guides, the wiki, or forum posts to really learn the deeper mechanics such as confidential informants, deployments, how many of certain items are required for a given population, etc.
Conclusion:
Don't let the cons put you off - if you like builder/simulation/management games, you will NOT be disappointed. This, even in this early stage, is a very solid, very enjoyable game. And it will only get better as the devs continue updating it.

A stellar game that it's backers should feel proud to have supported.
Shantae: Half Genie Hero excels in just about every category. The level design is superb, the music is fantastic, the visuals are gorgeous, and the characters are likable. Add those with one of the most unique and well-designed protagonists in gaming, and you get one of the finest games of the year. Unlike the previous installments, Shantae travels via map rather than a connected overworld. Keep this in mind if you were expecting more of a Metroidvania style game. Each area of the map counts as a chapter, with each chapter having a seperate plot, making it somewhat akin to Kirby Super Star. Assuming the player is a completionist, the game shold take roughly around 6-8 hours. Some may feel this is too short, but for me personally, I think it's fair for it's price. I do wish, however, that Risky Boot's story was availabe at purchase, and that Hero Mode gave the player access to ALL of Shantae's transformations and transformation attacks. Other than that, I find it hard to find any notable criticisms with the game itself. What I think this game really did well at was achieving it's own identity. For me, it didn't feel like "a Mega Man game" or "a Metroidvania" game. It felt like a SHANTAE game, which is something that Risky's Revenge and The Pirate's Curse, as good as those games are, felt like they were lacking in my opinion.
Buy this game. It's great.

While this review will be mostly opinionated, I would like to point out first and foremost the lie that is the claim that this is "A full movie split into 9 parts!".  This statement is simply not true.  At best, these are 6 scripts turned into mini-movies, and thrown together under one title.  While you could say that they make references to each other with the MK tournament and such, bear in mind that this is part of the lore.  Nothing else is tying these episodes together.  Now I know there is a Season 2, and they are making a season 3, but what you get here with these 9 episodes is not much.  No bigger underlying story or motivations besides what each character is up against.  Jax and Sonas ordeal with Kano has no correlation to Kitana, or Scorpion.  Example:  In the first two episodes, Kano sells cybernetic parts to the Lin Quei and gets his cybernetic eye.  When he shows up in episode 9, his face is full human, but they are still making robots.  Is this in the past, before the first episode?  Why have it out of order like this?  Why can't you tell us?  Why is Kitana/Mileenas story mostly artwork?  WHY ARE THE CREDITS 2 MINUTES LONG?!?

Anyway...
Do you love Mortal Kombat?  Have you been a fan your whole life?  Do you want to see a modern take on all your favorite characters?  Then, sadly, I must tell you that this isn't it.  I remember watching this on Youtube a few years ago.  First there was a 10 minute trailer, which I wasn't a big fan of due to their attempt to make the backstories super realistic and super gritty.  Reptile was a harlequin-baby that grew up to eat heads, and Baraka was a serial killer who did surgery on himself.  Then they made these short films, and while they toned down a lot of the super-realism, it didn't quite jive with me.  I remember thinking that it was a nice fan film endeavor, but not much more.
Now, with the release of Mortal Kombat X on the horizon, steam adds these videos.  I understand that this is to get more hype for the game, but the story here, and the story presented in the games themselves, are so utterly different that I am shocked.  I would definetely recommend the games story over this.  In MK9 we got an idea of every character, the basic story, and how they all came together.  And while I want to call this a prequel, I can't do that either.  In the Raiden episode, he spends 90 days in a straightjacket before he gets an icepick lobotomy and dies.  Then he just pops back up alive in Chinatown and strolls along.  And while the basic premise was ok, there are glaring issues.  If he is the God of Thunder and Protector of Earthrealm, why is he so weak he gets beat up by two fat guards and made null by a straightjacket?  He absorbs the electricity from the tasers, but there is no teleportation or lightning powers used at all.  He spends the entire episode being beaten up and powerless.  And the worst part is, the episode GOES OUT OF ITS WAY TO TELL YOU THAT THIS EPISODE IS THE CLOSEST TO THE DIRECTORS VISION FOR MORTAL KOMBAT THAN ANY OTHER EPISODE.  What?????
In conclusion, if you want to watch several fan films about Mortal Kombat that are well done with decent acting but lack any well written scripts or loyalty to the established lore, then watch these.  But while I am ok with people reimagining certain franchises with their own twist, this is so far off base that its a wonder why this is getting so many good reviews.  If you want a good story and the classic characters, then just play the game.
PROS:
Good Editing and Camerawork
Decent Acting
Promising Premise
CONS:
Bad CGI
Use of pictures a-la slideshow when they don't want to act something out
No underlying story to connect the episodes
Character reimaginings that either go nowhere or make the characters useless
No connection to the games
5/10.  Not terrible but definitely not clamoring to see more.  Just play the games and watch the original movie instead.

I'm not a huge Undertale fan, and the fandom bothers me just as much as the next guy, but... heck, it's still a good game. It may not deserve QUITE as much hype as it gets, but I'd say it's definately still worth playing.

Can you imagine a world where we're all represented by a font? Huh, I wonder which one I would be? sees Arial Too straight. No! Not in that way! Just, straight, as in unexciting. sees Badaboom Too.. uh... Deadpool.... BROADWAY! Now that's the one! Now THAT'S the one! Hello Internet, welcome to GAME THEORY, where instead of putting a joke here I want to ask you a question. If your personality were represented by a font, what font would you be? Take a moment and put your font in the comments. I'm really curious to see what everyone has to say. Maybe find a couple new cool fonts to use. I'm getting bored with ol' Calibri 11. And with that out of the way, it's time to talk UNDERTALE. Now I don't think I've ever gotten this many requests to cover a game. Well, except for FNAF. And I suppose FNAF 2. OH and there was FNAF 3. Wait a minute, should I be worried about something here? Anyway, across the board on YouTube, Reddit, and Twitter, you all have wanted Undertale. And honestly, I'm glad you brought it to my attention. True loyal theorists will know that Earthbound is my favorite game of all time. So a self aware RPG in a similar style, WHOA MAN, it's like a gift from the indie gaming heavens. Undertale is a game where every character, from goat mom to grind fodder has a sympathetic design and a unique personality, motivations, goals, fears. Whether you're saving or slaughtering them, the game makes you feel something every time you enter an encounter. But to me, one character stood out amongst all the rest. SANS. A skeleton named after the font, Comic Sans, hence all the font references at the beginning of the episode. If you haven't played Undertale I'm sure that was a really weird opening. ANYWAYS, Sans is, well, there's a lot of mystery around this guy. And before we get into it, let me put up a very special spoiler warning: UNDERTALE is a game best experienced blind. So if you haven't played it, pause the video and come back after you've finished. I PROMISE YOU, I PROMISE you won't regret it. Alright, so everyone out of the pool and ready for the adult swim? Good. Because I'm feeling pretty determined to get to the bottom of Sans' mystery. So just to recap for those of you who haven't played the game and ignored the SPOILER WARNING, or just need a refresher, Sans is one of the two skeletal brothers who appears in the game. His partner is Papyrus, a loud, goofy trap lover also named after a font. But in the world of Undertale their origins are a big question mark. All you really know is what's given to us by a shopkeeper in Snowdin, who explains that Sans and Papyrus, quote, “just showed up one day and asserted themselves.” Weird, right? What's more is that, well, Papyrus is just kinda the goofy sidekick. Sans is much more complex. He likes fart jokes, but he's also incredibly powerful and deadly serious. Not only is his boss battle the hardest in the game, he's one of the only characters who has knowledge and power over space and time. He can take shortcuts around the world through ridiculous routes. Even is walking through walls. He also acknowledges that he's only one of infinite versions of himself, making self-aware commentary of the various timelines that you've played through in the game. He can even count the number of times he's killed you. He acts like an arbiter of this world, passing out judgements on the player's actions in the game, even explaining the secrets of EXP and LOVE, or EXECUTION POINTS and LEVELS OF VIOLENCE, just to clarify. In short, he just doesn't quite fit in with the rest of the world of monsters. But then, what, or who, is he? Well, the idea that he doesn't belong in underworld seems to be correct. The evidence seems to point the fact that he WAS, in fact, formerly a surface dweller. In the true pacifist ending of the game, as the group looks out onto the horizon, Papyrus asks Sans about the giant ball in the sky. Sans says, quote, “we call that the sun.” This is important because A, the usage of the word WE, and knowledge of the sun shows that Sans has a kinship or knowledge with other humans, and B, that despite he and Papyrus both being skeletons, or, supposedly, brothers, and apparently appeared in underworld at the same time, they clearly-- uuuGGHH take two CLEARLY have two very different histories. Why would Papyrus not know the name of the sun but Sans would? We get further clues to Sans' origins as we hear him say multiple times he wants to "go home" or "go back." He says as much during his dinner date scene at the Mettaton hotel. He notices that the player wants to go home and says, quote, "i know the feeling." He then continues, "maybe sometimes it's better to take what's given to you." As though he ended up in the underworld by accident. AND in a genocide run during his boss fight he says, quote, "look, i gave up trying to go back a long time ago." End quote. And before you say he means going back to the surface world, that's clearly not the full story. His very next line of dialogue is, "and getting to the surface doesn't really appeal anymore either." Key word here, is EITHER. Yes, he seems to hail from the surface and wants to go back, but based on his dialogue he no longer considers it his home. It's as though the surface world he once knew is gone, as though he's from a different time. It's pretty intriguing. So we're left with a being that appeared out of nowhere, presumably from being from the human surface, but from a different time period, who seemingly has the power to teleport. That's a lot of questions and not a lot of answers. But here's where things get REALLY interesting. Sans has a hidden workshop that takes a fair amount of searching to find. You could say it takes a lot of DETERMINATION to unlock. Anyways, obligatory determination references aside, as you start to look for this easter egg Sans gives you a key to his room and says "it's time you learn the truth." After some searching you find the workshop which contains items that leave even more questions. A photo album featuring Sans and a bunch of smiling people you don't recognize, a badge, blueprints with illegible handwriting, and a broken machine hidden behind a curtain. In the latest update, one more detail was added. A handdrawn picture of 3 smiling faces with the words “don't forget.” so what does it all mean? Well a lot of Undertale theorists have been linking these details to a feature to a character named W.D Gaster. A ghostly character who never truly appears in the game. Honestly, covering him is a theory all unto itself, and probably one best saved for another day. Even still, none of the Gaster theories I've seen have been able to explain all the details. In particular, the photo album, and the badge. And that's what kept nagging me as I researched Undertale. A badge? That one in particular really stuck out to me. Why would such an oddly specific item to be hidden in the huge easter egg of a room? Something that supposedly reveals the truth about Sans? Badges just aren't important in Undertale. Then it hit me. What if this badge isn't from Undertale? What if this badge is from a completely different game? And was, in fact, the most important badge in the history of gaming? The Franklin badge. Now, for those of you wondering what I'm talking about, the Franklin badge is a pivotal item from the Mother series. You know, the one with Earthbound. Or, maybe you don't know that one either. Uh, you know, the one with Ness from Super Smash Bros? Yeah well, Ness is from Earthbound, and Earthbound is the second part in this larger Mother trilogy. Alright? Good. Anyway, the Franklin badge is a really important part of that series. It gets its start in the very first game and carries through the whole trilogy, saving your life multiple times in the process. Mad Max could have been a lot of things, but what they ended up going with was something that weirdly, feels more like a medieval fantasy game than the companion to the completely gone-mad world and king hell, razor's-edge speedfreak high we get from the films. Most of the time, you'll feel vaguely like a knight riding out to quest against evil and protect the weak. Gunplay is rare since the game outright tells you the Bullet Farm is far away- shotshells are one of the rarest resources in the game, until you start setting up shop in various strongholds where the locals will pay you tribute in the form of 12-gauge handloads. NPCs talk about becoming serfs to secure food (every resource, even beetles, has been used up to a ridiculous degree) and safety. Hell, your starting area is a castle.
Thankfully, this medievalism doesn\'t extend to what's probably the real core of the game, which is building your car. EVERY modification has a seriously cool-looking visual element which fits the gas-guzzling Mad Max look perfectly. While not crazy-deep, each mod tends to carry a tradeoff. Racing slicks or offroad tires? Speed or armor? You can change your parts with whatever you have unlocked, whenever you want. Up to you whether that makes it better or worse. The driving itself feels VERY fast, even before you've really souped up your machine, and rams are damn satisfying. Driving around the wasteland is seriously beautiful- the vistas are sweeping and desolate without being dull, while the lighting really stands out, especially around dusk and dawn. You're gonna be doing a lot of that, as the map is pretty damn large. While surviving bandits and even war parties can be enjoyably challenging, raiding convoys lets you turn the tables a bit and just pick off enemy vehicles one by one, however you like. All the action is perfectly fluid too, with a smooth 60FPS.
On foot though, things are a little less shiny and chrome. The combat system is pretty much Arkham Asylum, with the addition of some satisfyingly brutal finishers you can dispatch Warboys or other raiders with. One of the many, many things to do in the game is clearing out Warboy outposts. It can be a nice break from the driving, but after a while all these little forts start to blur together in a jumble of yellow paint and scrap metal. This is one of the mixed aspects of the game- there are a ton of things to do, but they can get pretty samey after a while. Most egregiously, the mini-bosses are literally pallette swaps of the same model, same AI, and same weapon despite the handbook giving them varied and interesting bios.
The characters and story in general are pretty mixed. Max himself is much less likeable, and ends up looking and acting like a Standard Issue Game Protagonist. A lot of the side characters are more memorable, though weirdly there's probably only one important and developed female character and no, it's not the one you think. Even the wretched wanderers throughout the wasteland are decently compelling- the biggest impact it had on me was when I'd just given the last of my water to less-fortunate travelers, hoping they'd find some measure of safety, before seeing them run down out of nowhere by warboys. It's a totally unexpected moment, but it and my ensuing nitro-fuelled vengeance rampage felt more like Mad Max than anything else.

This is a rather lengthy review, but I think it gives you everything you need to know.
XIII Century is a double-edged sword. On one hand, it has cool battles and requires you to use some clever thinking to win tough fights. On the other hand, it only works when it wants to. I played several battles, but then the game decided I've had enough and refused to work properly. Every time I try to load a campaign battle, I get an error and a black screen. The sound and narrative play, but all I get is a frozen screen. I think there is a way to fix it for some people, but for me personally, I'm stuck.
So how can I review a game that won't let me play? I'll base this review off of my experiences in the few battles I actually played.
First off, the graphics are decent and the sound design is solid ( though the battle sounds of swords clashing and arrows falling are a bit bland). The music is nothing to write home about, but it serves its purpose and is okay. The maps are well-designed and allow for strategic play. You got hills, rivers, marshes, etc. All of these come into play when you are commanding your army.
The AI is rather decent. I've seen it counterattck, flank, keep reserves, and press forward when I am weak.  It's not perfect (it's easy to exploit and crush AI units using cavalry archers), but it is aware and will challenge you. At times it can even be relentless and clever, forcing you to really pay attention.
I never had a moment where I was totally relaxed. I was concentrated almost all the time - managing my units, picking off lone enemy sqauds, and positioning my army so that I could best face the enemy. In that respect XIII Century succeeds. The game requires thinking and good unit management. Terrain must be taken seriously and the AI is not one to be underestimated.
However, there are certain downsides. As mentioned before, I get an error before every battle and the screen freezes and goes black. Aside from that, the camera is awkward. It has weird angles and is odd at times. I recommend taking it off the "free camera" mode and putting it on either "horizontal" or "normal" settings. That helps out a lot.
So what do we end up with? We have a game with great potential that falls flat on its face. With decent graphics and a stong dose of strategy mixed in with bugs and some awkward camera angles and controls, XIII Century is a game that I would recommend getting only on a big sale. If you don't experience technical issues, then you'll have a blast with this game, but wait until it's on sale in order to avoid spending a lot of money on a product that won't even work.
Do not buy this game! Under any circumstances...

Guards is a simple turn-based strategy game in which you have to pick 4 out of 8 heroes (Peasant, Healer, Archer, Witcher, Rifleman, Amazon, Knight and Assassin) to fight hordes of monsters. Basically, there are 10 levels (the last one being the boss fight), and in each level you have to eliminate x monsters before proceeding to the next level. At the beginning of each turn, you have to swap the position of two of your heroes : the 3 on the front line attack, while the one in the back regenerates and prepares his special attack for the next time he'll go back to the front line. Once you defeat the boss in normal difficulty, you'll unlock the Nightmare mode ; then, if you manage to beat the game again, prepare yourself for the Hell difficulty. There are also quests to complete during the game for extra rewards.
But here is the thing : when one of your heroes dies, it's game over. You'll acquire some skill points and mithril to upgrade your heroes and buy items from the shop, depending on how many levels you finished. And then, select your heroes and inventory and start again - you'll have to go over and over again through the same levels until your heroes are strong enough to defeat the endboss.
That being said, despite the grind, the game is actually not bad at all. The graphics may well be simple, but I find it cute and original. The soundtrack is also a plus, it always puts me in a fighting mood. It even requires some tactics : team composition, hero upgrading, skill tree, choice of limited items you can pick per game, good moves during the fight and clever use of special abilities. Hell difficulty is in fact quite challenging.
Guards is definitely a game to get on sales if you can and if you are into strategy / tower defense / turn-based combats. Even if it seems incomplete at first, it gets addictive and is a well-conceived game.
For it's price it's really something special. I'd call it a strategy simulator since there is very little actuall gameplay, which isn't that bad considering the pricetag. Chess with guns basicly.

Can you imagine a world where we're all represented by a font? Huh, I wonder which one I would be? sees Arial Too straight. No! Not in that way! Just, straight, as in unexciting. sees Badaboom Too.. uh... Deadpool.... BROADWAY! Now that's the one! Now THAT'S the one! Hello Internet, welcome to GAME THEORY, where instead of putting a joke here I want to ask you a question. If your personality were represented by a font, what font would you be? Take a moment and put your font in the comments. I'm really curious to see what everyone has to say. Maybe find a couple new cool fonts to use. I'm getting bored with ol' Calibri 11. And with that out of the way, it's time to talk UNDERTALE. Now I don't think I've ever gotten this many requests to cover a game. Well, except for FNAF. And I suppose FNAF 2. OH and there was FNAF 3. Wait a minute, should I be worried about something here? Anyway, across the board on YouTube, Reddit, and Twitter, you all have wanted Undertale. And honestly, I'm glad you brought it to my attention. True loyal theorists will know that Earthbound is my favorite game of all time. So a self aware RPG in a similar style, WHOA MAN, it's like a gift from the indie gaming heavens. Undertale is a game where every character, from goat mom to grind fodder has a sympathetic design and a unique personality, motivations, goals, fears. Whether you're saving or slaughtering them, the game makes you feel something every time you enter an encounter. But to me, one character stood out amongst all the rest. SANS. A skeleton named after the font, Comic Sans, hence all the font references at the beginning of the episode. If you haven't played Undertale I'm sure that was a really weird opening. ANYWAYS, Sans is, well, there's a lot of mystery around this guy. And before we get into it, let me put up a very special spoiler warning: UNDERTALE is a game best experienced blind. So if you haven't played it, pause the video and come back after you've finished. I PROMISE YOU, I PROMISE you won't regret it. Alright, so everyone out of the pool and ready for the adult swim? Good. Because I'm feeling pretty determined to get to the bottom of Sans' mystery. So just to recap for those of you who haven't played the game and ignored the SPOILER WARNING, or just need a refresher, Sans is one of the two skeletal brothers who appears in the game. His partner is Papyrus, a loud, goofy trap lover also named after a font. But in the world of Undertale their origins are a big question mark. All you really know is what's given to us by a shopkeeper in Snowdin, who explains that Sans and Papyrus, quote, “just showed up one day and asserted themselves.” Weird, right? What's more is that, well, Papyrus is just kinda the goofy sidekick. Sans is much more complex. He likes fart jokes, but he's also incredibly powerful and deadly serious. Not only is his boss battle the hardest in the game, he's one of the only characters who has knowledge and power over space and time. He can take shortcuts around the world through ridiculous routes. Even is walking through walls. He also acknowledges that he's only one of infinite versions of himself, making self-aware commentary of the various timelines that you've played through in the game. He can even count the number of times he's killed you. He acts like an arbiter of this world, passing out judgements on the player's actions in the game, even explaining the secrets of EXP and LOVE, or EXECUTION POINTS and LEVELS OF VIOLENCE, just to clarify. In short, he just doesn't quite fit in with the rest of the world of monsters. But then, what, or who, is he? Well, the idea that he doesn't belong in underworld seems to be correct. The evidence seems to point the fact that he WAS, in fact, formerly a surface dweller. In the true pacifist ending of the game, as the group looks out onto the horizon, Papyrus asks Sans about the giant ball in the sky. Sans says, quote, “we call that the sun.” This is important because A, the usage of the word WE, and knowledge of the sun shows that Sans has a kinship or knowledge with other humans, and B, that despite he and Papyrus both being skeletons, or, supposedly, brothers, and apparently appeared in underworld at the same time, they clearly-- uuuGGHH take two CLEARLY have two very different histories. Why would Papyrus not know the name of the sun but Sans would? We get further clues to Sans' origins as we hear him say multiple times he wants to "go home" or "go back." He says as much during his dinner date scene at the Mettaton hotel. He notices that the player wants to go home and says, quote, "i know the feeling." He then continues, "maybe sometimes it's better to take what's given to you." As though he ended up in the underworld by accident. AND in a genocide run during his boss fight he says, quote, "look, i gave up trying to go back a long time ago." End quote. And before you say he means going back to the surface world, that's clearly not the full story. His very next line of dialogue is, "and getting to the surface doesn't really appeal anymore either." Key word here, is EITHER. Yes, he seems to hail from the surface and wants to go back, but based on his dialogue he no longer considers it his home. It's as though the surface world he once knew is gone, as though he's from a different time. It's pretty intriguing. So we're left with a being that appeared out of nowhere, presumably from being from the human surface, but from a different time period, who seemingly has the power to teleport. That's a lot of questions and not a lot of answers. But here's where things get REALLY interesting. Sans has a hidden workshop that takes a fair amount of searching to find. You could say it takes a lot of DETERMINATION to unlock. Anyways, obligatory determination references aside, as you start to look for this easter egg Sans gives you a key to his room and says "it's time you learn the truth." After some searching you find the workshop which contains items that leave even more questions. A photo album featuring Sans and a bunch of smiling people you don't recognize, a badge, blueprints with illegible handwriting, and a broken machine hidden behind a curtain. In the latest update, one more detail was added. A handdrawn picture of 3 smiling faces with the words “don't forget.” so what does it all mean? Well a lot of Undertale theorists have been linking these details to a feature to a character named W.D Gaster. A ghostly character who never truly appears in the game. Honestly, covering him is a theory all unto itself, and probably one best saved for another day. Even still, none of the Gaster theories I've seen have been able to explain all the details. In particular, the photo album, and the badge. And that's what kept nagging me as I researched Undertale. A badge? That one in particular really stuck out to me. Why would such an oddly specific item to be hidden in the huge easter egg of a room? Something that supposedly reveals the truth about Sans? Badges just aren't important in Undertale. Then it hit me. What if this badge isn't from Undertale? What if this badge is from a completely different game? And was, in fact, the most important badge in the history of gaming? The Franklin badge. Now, for those of you wondering what I'm talking about, the Franklin badge is a pivotal item from the Mother series. You know, the one with Earthbound. Or, maybe you don't know that one either. Uh, you know, the one with Ness from Super Smash Bros? Yeah well, Ness is from Earthbound, and Earthbound is the second part in this larger Mother trilogy. Alright? Good. Anyway, the Franklin badge is a really important part of that series. It gets its start in the very first game and carries through the whole trilogy, saving your life multiple times in the process. Somewhat conflicted over this one. Half-Genie Hero is a good game in its own right, but IMO it's a big step down from Pirate's Curse. The transformation dances from the original game and Risky's Revenge are back, but many of them feel shoehorned in and don't serve much purpose outside of getting an item here and there. The level design is much more linear and straightforward compared to the previous entries, and dungeons with maps and keys are completely absent. Even so, there are still plenty of secret items that you can go back and find throughout the levels.
The bosses are a lot of fun but also pushovers, it's true that these games have never been particularly difficult to begin with but I think even by the series standards this game stands out as being the least challenging one yet(Hardcore mode update rectifies this). As far as story goes, it still retains the charm and humor from the previous games but there's not really any continuation from Pirate's Curse, as if all the character development and events that occurred never took place. The game acts more like a soft reboot.
Despite everything, I still think it's a good and very fun game, I definitely recommend it if you're a fan of the series. Music is top notch, controls are tight, the game looks great and DLC is coming in the near future that'll let you play through 4 additional campaigns as other characters, so that may alleviate some of the issues.

The gameplay is also a bit too easy this time with a very easy puzzle and easy bosses... (especially if you go for 100% completion)
But still overall, even though this is not the best of the Shantae series for me (so far the best is still the Pirate Curse IMHO), the game is still highly enjoyable nonetheless.
Hopefully next time, Wayforward can come out with a better Shantae game series with longer story, challenging puzzle, platformer and bosses but with the same charming aesthetic of 1/2 genie hero. :)

A very good Mad Max game, with some excellent bits but also some issues. The setting is great, car combat is incredibly fun - there's a good sense of freedom and the main missions are pretty good, but the story is quite flat (even though the ending is great), the fighting system is nothing more than decent and the optional stuff becomes pretty repetitive.

This game isn't very good. Take Saint's Row, sprinkle some Assassin's Creed and Arkham on top, and throw the whole thing into the desert, and you've got Mad Max.
The hand to hand combat is a clunkier, less intuitive version of the Arkham combat system. The only thing this game adds to it is a "timed" counter mechanic, which would honestly be pretty cool if the entire system didn't feel like trash. Whereas Arkham combat is very smooth and responsive, Mad Max's combat just feels like a complete slog.
The gun play is abysmal. You aren't really allowed to freely aim, just sort of scroll between targets directly in front of you. This leads to a lot of "checking" for enemies that you can lock on to, which slows the pace of combat sequences and makes them more of a hassle than they should be.
The game does not benefit from being an open world sandbox. The world is full of useless distractions for you to drag yourself through which detracts from the gameplay experience as a whole. You'll quickly tire of these distractions by the way, as there are only about 6 unique ones, and they're going to make you replay them more times than you'll care to.
The one thing Mad Max did get right was the cars and vehicular combat. Your car in this game is completely customizeable to suit your playstyle, and vehicular combat is pretty damn satisfying, at least for a little while. The challenges stop rolling in once you get to the second half of the game, and by that point vehicular combat becomes more of a chore.
The story is very decent, and the overall voice work is pretty good, barring a few edge cases. However you won't be experiencing the meat of the story until you're about halfway through the game, as the rest feels like useless fluff.
I could gripe about a few more things, but I'll just leave it with this: Overall, the game doesn't have enough depth with ANY of its systems to keep players engaged long enough to see everything. It makes you wonder what kind of game this would have been had they focused on one area of the game (like the cars) and just made a game based around that. The game feels very skeletal, like they just had to ship a product so they copy pasted a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of content together and called it Mad Max. This game is bad, but it is worth checking out if you're a die hard Mad Max fan, or are just in the mood to power through another open world sandbox title. If you aren't either of those cases though, it's safe to pass on this one.

Complete and utter garbage by mediocre developers, that was clearly rushed out. Take every trope from every Ubisoft open-world game, but then make every single thing you ripped off x10 worse and you'd have Mad Max.
If you buy this game for more than the equivalent of $5, then you're a bigger jackass than I was. Did I also forget to mention I have never played a game with as noticeable input lag as Mad Max? Oh, and the balance of the game is utterly screwed. Hand-to-hand combat you can sleep through and not even lose a sliver of health, while car combat is pure glasscanon nonsense. You can go out of your way to build the most defensible car in the wastelands, yet it'll explode as soon as you grace a dune buggy; but it ultimately doesn't matter as you'll just kill everything from a distance with your car RPG.
Don't be an idiot like me who spent over 40 hours and way too much $ on this open-world garbage.

I met one of my greater friends on rust. Let me explain: I was raiding with another friend, she got stuck in room and had to log off. So while we were off, the owner of the base decided to build her in, as a prisoner. So he stripped her naked and made a prison cell. So I decided to go get some explosives, I crafted a ton of beancan grenades for a simple solution.  I blew myself into a ladder hatch and jumped down ( As stupid as I was ). Surprise surprise, I had gotten stuck as well... There were about three doors left from rescuing my friend, so I made an attempt to get through with my remaining beancan grenades. I did not succeed. And of course I had brought my most precious gear, and an ak. So I was in no mood of killing myself.
The dude that owned the base was kind of a mascot for our time on the server. His name was something along the lines of ¨SharkSlayer¨ or something. So we called him Sharkie-Boy, and we had secretly been stealing from him. ( I stood outside talking to him, while the other one ran into his base and stole some loot, as he always left his doors wide open when he went out ). Haha reminds me, he even gave me loot after we had stolen from him... Poor guy, I truly felt bad, but it was hilarous of how lost he was. He had no clue.
So he had trapped my friend, and I was stuck three rooms away with a hole in the ceiling. I remember thinking ¨F*ck. I'll never get this damn loot out...¨ But to my surprise I heard footsteps outside his base, and I knew it wasn't Sharkie, because he had been off for a while ( Checked server list as well ). So I listened, heard the person running around the base, inspecting the missing stone walls. He called out ¨ Uhm, hello? I'm kind of new to this game, can someone help me out?¨. I took the chance and answered ¨ Hey uh, can you come inside? I'm stuck and need help to get out. If you just follow the walls, *explained how he had to parkour to get up* then you can come in and help me up. I'll shoot you in the head, so you don't need to be trapped too. I'll place you a sleeping bed in my house that you can later spawn in. We can be buddies? Alright? I just need to get my stuff out.¨
And to my surprise this convinced him, and be boosted me up. I looked him in the eyes and said ¨ Are you ready? I'll pull the trigger, and then I will see you in a while buddy¨. He nodded and I pulled the trigger.
My other friend was still stuck inside, and she starved to death. So she came back to our base as well. This new dude spawned in my base, and I taught him everything he had to know about the game. I moved my base, and let him construct the new one. And now we are great friends, he has surpassed me in hours and is a great Rust player. And also, he introduced me to a clan, so I have made new friends there.
So Rust is really shines when it comes to the social aspect. Making stories, talking to people... Killing people... Stealing from sharks...

I would give this a neutral or mixed rating rather than a positive one If I could, but I don't feel like this game deserves a negative rating, so I'll just rate it up instead. So anyway, If I had to describe Rogue Legacy in three words I'd call it "Roguelike The Game." Because the only really original thing in Rogue Legacy is the descendant system. Instead of respawning as the same character or choosing from a list of pre set character every time you die, you instead choose one of three randomly generated descendants. These descendants all have different classes, traits, and even some character model differences that do play into the gameplay. It doesn't do enough though. Sure the characters all have different strengths and weakness, but besides height and some weight traits most of the traits just make the game harder or have such small bonuses that they really change gameplay. No matter what, you'll always be running around whacking things and collecting as much gold as you can. The only thing that changes is how easy or difficult it becomes. Honestly, I feel like this system would be more impactful if you couldn't choose a descendent because it would mean that you couldn't just negate the system by picking the character with none or the least negative traits. Even if it might've come off as unfair I feel like it would've made death more meaningful because if you had a really good character then you might play more defensively because you could never be sure if the descendent the game would next time would be any good, and that would really help build tension and make you more hesitant to taking risks for loot.
Besides that mechanic though, It's pretty much everything you've come to expect from a Roguelike side scrolling action platformer. On each run you'll play through a new set of levels with varying sizes and layouts, enemies and traps are randomly placed within these levels and use projectiles and attack patterns that are difficult to memorize and avoid, and the game's difficulty curve starts off hard and only gets harder the farther into the castle you get. Even with tons of upgrades, loot, and experience you can die very quickly if you get too cocky (or simply bored with replaying the same types of levels every time you die) and stop paying attention. Even though the game has a similar appearance to, and references Castlevania, notice that I didn't call this a metroidvania game. That’s because when you get down to it Rogue Legacy really isn’t one. You have access to pretty much every area and boss in the game right from the start. The only things blocking you from accessing them is the ever increasing difficulty of the enemies and traps in each new area, how many upgrades and items you’ve acquired, and how good you get at avoiding projectiles. Sometimes it even just comes down to whether you get a good castle layout or not. If you're really good at the game though you can get through the entire thing with just a starting character and the default equipment.
Now you might be expecting me to tell you about the faults of the game, and while there's obvious things like the jumping feeling somewhat floaty and the hit detection being off at times, everything else is entirely subjective. I feel like while the random generation of the game keeps it from getting stale too early, it lacks the refined and well designed structure that something with set levels and characters has. As a result the experience of Rogue Legacy simply has none of the longevity of a well designed Metroidvania, even though it references them. I also feel like the game subscribes to the notion that a hard game equals a good game. At many times Rogue Legacy well simply fill a room with tons of enemies that use tricky attack patterns and shoot fast and hard to avoid projectiles, traps that make you constantly have to move and put yourself in danger, and makes the rooms chaotic messes that have no flow or gradual build up to anything and calls that finished. You pretty much just get bombarded with cluttered rooms from the start and this never changes. Simply making a game hard or random does not mean it's well designed.
Take a game like Dark Souls for example. Dark Souls is a hard game, sure, but if that's all it had going for it then it wouldn't have become the smash hit it eventually ended up being. It had great level design, an interesting combat system, was surprisingly forgiving and easy on the player at times when it could’ve been much harder, and had a mysterious world and setting filled with strange and eccentric characters who went through their own arcs without the player’s input. Rogue Legacy simply doesn't have any of that, and unfortunately it just isn't a very memorable experience as a result. Even the potential story elements which could’ve been fleshed out more, like the diary entries of the ancestor you find or the fact that you the player are throwing members of your own family into what is essentially a meat grinder for personal gain go nowhere. In the end, your enjoyment of Rogue Legacy will simply depend on how much you enjoy Roguelikes as a genre. Because if you're going into it thinking that it will change your opinion of Roguelikes, or because you think it will have really innovative and original elements or design not seen before, then unfortunately you'll just end up being disappointed.

XIII Century Is a Real Time Tactics (RTT) game set in the thirteenth century A.D.. It has 5 single player campaigns, each camaign is a series of Historicall battles. There is also multiplayer mode but I cannot review it because I can't find anybody online to play with.
The main gameplay of XIII Century is playing historical battles. The scale of the battles is huge, it is comparable to the scale of battles in Total War games. The battles have great depth so they offer great challenge and fun. Also due to the battle mechanics the use of tactics is totally neccessary in order to win battles, moreover any wrong move can drive your army to it's total annihilation. The UI is prety much simmilar to the the UI of Total War games and it's quite simple and functional so it doesn't cause any issues to the player during battles. As for the AI, it knows how to use it's units and combined with the battle mechanics it offers  a lot of challenge and fun. The battle mechanics, the AI and the UI combined offer a great gameplay, but it would be better if there would be any conquest campaign with a map like in total war games.
The visuals of XIII Century are pretty good. The models are not as detailed as in the Total War games but they offer some visually impressive battles. Also, there is variety in the soldiers appearance so they don't look like clones. As for the animations, they are a little awkward but there are some of them that may impress. For example the soldiers draw their swords only when the enemy is near which may be something minor but it's an eyecandy that I like. The particles are just ok, when the soldiers are running there are some dust effects and also there are blood effects and gore which make the battles sort of gritty. Unforunately there is one objection that I have, the HDR makes everything to look too bright. Visually the game is great in comparison to many stategy games and it runs with high framerates.
The sound of the game is not anything special, it just fulfills it's purpose. There are descent sound effects and the music just fits with the atmosphere of the game. It is not anything imressive or bad, it is just ok.
XIII Century is an underrated game which has been overseen by gamers . It is a game that I highly recommend to Medieval II Total War fans.
