Okay so making a sequel/prequel to a big success game/movie/book/etc... is always a tricky thing. When confronted to this problem, most of the times the makers of said prequel/sequel go for the "Bigger, longer, better" approach. Sometimes it works out incredibelly well (look at The Witcher 3, Assassin's Creed II...) but a few more times it just create something that feels a bit less alive or even just plain garbage (Mass Effect Andromeda, Assassin's Creed Unity or even The Hobbit trilogy or The Dark Knight Rises). Well Deck Nine chose the exact opposite approach with Life is Strange : Before the Storm, and I love it.
Why? Well because every story doesn't have to have a giant a storm and hundreds of lives at stake for me to care. They just need good characters and a coherent story in which they are forced to choose, grow and resist to whatever they're facing. And I'm pretty sure most people who played and liked Life is Strange would feel the same, in that the storm and the lives on the line are not the core of the game, merely a context that brings desperation and urgency.
So, what about LiS : BtS as a game? Well it's pretty much what you can expect gameplay-wise. A product, closer to an interactive movie than to actual game, with very-well written dialogue (even though sometimes there can be a lack for a 3rd/4th option when choosing a response), simple graphics, that are a bit smoother around the edges compared to the first entry and a great soundtrack.
Story-wise, well this game blew my mind. Not because it is complex, but because the Rachel/Chloe duo feels so right, their interactions so genuine and their evolution so interesting and natural that I started caring for anything that happenned to them, minutes after I first started the game. To the point that when confronted with the finale, the impact of it was even greater than that of LiS, simply because I gotta admit, Chloe is a much more charismatic protagonist than Max was, no matter how much I loved everything about LiS.
The last thing I want to address about Before the Storm is the disparition of the rewing mechanic, which, in the end, didn't bother me merely as much as I thought it would. This feature was great in LiS, because it brought contrast between real and fantasy, showing how dark the world is, even when facing a semi-magical storm, and created a true sense of helplenness and uselessness when it stopped working. But here, the plot is not about any of this anymore and so the return to a much more traditionnal style of linear dialogue trees felt coherent, be it a bit less new and original.
All in all, I never thought I'd say this when I bought this game, but I think I like Before the Storm just a bit more than Life is Strange.

Life is Strange Before the Storm is a story about Chloe and Rachel's relationship before the events that happened in Life is Strange. While this may seem like a prequel to the first game, in reality its not. It tells the story of Rachel's troubled life with her parents instead of offering you a clearer picture of what happened before Life is Strange, so be sure to recheck your expectations.
Being a story adventure game, the story and voice acting have to be the most important aspect of the game and in light of the extremely positive reviews and people saying this is better than the first game, I have to make a reality check. It is far from being amazing or better. The voice acting is incredibly average throught the entire game with some minor exceptions. The story is okay but dont expect anything near the original one. Its cheesy, generic, boring and honestly irrelevant to the series as I've mentioned above, not being a true prequel. Some will find it interesting just to know a bit more about Rachel's life but I didnt. I'm also not a fan of the "rebellious" soundtrack that they were aiming even though it fits.
Theres not much to talk about the gameplay and graphical style of the game. Its as you'd expect, almost nonexistent and inferior to the original, since the original had a cool time mechanic which made things more interesting and offered real consequences, well at least better than Before The Storm.
Overall considering the positive buff and overly praised reviews its getting on steam, I will have to not recommend this to anyone looking for a true prequel to LiS and to those who just want to know a bit more about the protagonists, make sure you lower your expectations, as the voice acting and the story is hella average. 6/10

tl;dr: If you really liked Life is Strange and you want more: Get Before the Storm. If not: Look forward to Life is Strange 2.
It's really hard not to recommend Before the Storm. More content from one of my favorite video game franchises? YES! PLEASE!
Before the Storm offers insights on Chloes' past and how she and Rachel met. In Life is Strange Rachel is mentioned basically everywhere, Chloe searches for and talks about her, there are missing person posters all over the place, which is why you really start wanting to know more about them both. Especially the first but also the second episode deliver, showing the beginning of their friendship, but the more the game focuses on the imminent personal problems of Rachel the more uninteresting it gets. Episode 3 and its finale is pretty disappointing and compared to the first game really anti-climactic. And what's most disappointing I'm still left wondering
Still, having the chance to dive into the universe again and getting to know the characters more is great.
Additional rants: The "talkback mechanic" is useless compared to Max' rewind powers. There are 3 dialogue options you can choose, but there is no way to figure out which is the right one. It's just unfair try and error. Dialogue options make basically no difference whatsoever and often enough Chloe ends up saying something completely different than the prior selected option suggested. Character animations and facial expressions feel wooden, some of the voice actors sound like they're having a stroke and talk with 0.5x speed as if the animators didn't know how long the voice line is going to be (e.g. Rose Amber in the kitchen).  Character models often glitch out, snapping necks 90° at the end of cutscenes, putting character models in other character models, teleporting characters around. From a technical and production standpoint there is loads of room for improvement. Deck9 is either an inexperienced team or was just out of time due to the episodic nature of the game. Also there clearly was no notable game testing involved.

Playing this game is rather like watching the proverbial train wreck: you'll be horrified, but you can't look away. This is in no way a bad thing. Spec Ops wants to tell a story about soldiers in war. But unlike games such as Call of Duty, it doesn't want you to feel like an awesome, unstoppable killing machine that's fighting terrorism FOR 'MERICA!!!' or whatever; it wants you to see that war is not glamorous, awesome, fun, or desirable. It wants you to see the terrible toll that combat can exact on those who experience it. And above all, it wants you to see that in real conflict, there are no "good guys" and "bad guys," and the world is full of gray areas. War is hell, and anyone who goes in will either join the fortunate dead...or have to live with what they've done to survive.
While I enjoyed the storyline, I felt sad, very sad at parts. The graphics are amazing, worth getting. Because this game tells a story. A sad story about war.

This game may be slightly pretentious, but ultimately it's heart is in the right place. It attempts to bring a sense of moral conscience to the player in a genre drowned by bro shooters without any sense of ethical ambiguity.
The gameplay has you fight your way through the most generic enviornment's, someplace in the middle east, moving forward from one shooting gallery to another. Mowing down soldier's, rebel's, and civilian's alike. Then it begs the question of looking beyond the polygonal wall of indifference, and consider the violent actions you've taken, as if they were real people! I believe, had I been contemplating over the feelings of every A.I. I've killed in a videogame, I would've joined a human rights organization by now. As opposed to sitting here twittling my thumbs up my bum while I right this review.
I don't mean to criticize Spec Ops so harshly, but I have to when it's setting itself up as such an ambitious, philosophical, game. Trying to raise the bar in any industry is hard enough as it is, but the developers obviously had a tight production budget which shows when actually playing the game.
Which brings me to my next gripe, gameplay and controls. It plays out like any other cover-based shooter, which isn't a genre you can particularly build upon, just look at the Gears series, but you can refine it. And refinement is something this game lacks. You move your character forward, he does so with a rigid animation. You want to sprint efficiently around the battlefield? Too bad you'll be stuck with this robotic, gears inspired, camera wobbling,♥♥♥♥♥♥animation. That's mapped to holdin down the "A" button on a 360 gamepad and has horrible amounts of sensitivity. It's like trying to guide a raging bull towards a specific area. Then there's your a.i. partners who are suppost to add a level of tactical options in order to outsmart your opponent, but they're dumber than a bag of bricks, and you frequently have to go save their♥♥♥♥♥s after they've been downed.
The one redeeming value of this game has to be it's ending which wasn't unexpected after the 6 hour acid trip of a campaign but welcome nonetheless. The amount of variations is just enough to place you into the shoes of the main protaginist, and sell the illusion of, "I made those decisions, and this is my Walker."
Ultimately if you want a standard cover based third person shooter, but are feeling a bit brave that day, then this game is worth the money for the shock value alone. If you happen to find any life changing virtue's from its story that you weren't already aware of from common sense, then I suggest you book into an insane asylum.

It was pretty good. I had a lot of fun playing it and I'm glad to be adding it to my Shantae collection. It's a little bit expensive for the length, but I think it will be much more worth the price when all of the rest of the Kickstarter-promised features get added in. Like I said, I recommend it on sale and mostly to fans of Shantae.
If you own previous Shantae games, you should probably get it. If you haven't played a Shantae game before, I recommend you get Shantae and the Pirate's Curse much more.
Warning: My review perspective will involve a lot of comparisons to Risky's Revenge (RR) and the Pirate's Curse (TPC) since I played all three this year.
It also has a lot of gripes and may come off as slightly negative.
Gameplay:
The main way it deviates from the previous two Shantae games is that the levels are much more linear. Each level is divided into 2 or 3 separated sections that you have to sift through to get the collectables. It's much closer to TPC's island levels than RR's single connected overworld. No more dungeons, which is a little disappointing because I really like the previous games' dungeon designs. I think it completely loses its status as Metroidvania, even though TPC wasn't very Metroidvania. But that's fine.
I felt that the platforming suffered. Shantae runs slightly too slow and jumps slightly too short to be satisfying. Platforming only felt good in monkey form. And unfortunately, transforming from human to monkey repeatedly was not great. It was much more jarring compared to RR's dance transforms because it requires more complicated inputs and briefly pauses the game. The platforming with Risky's items in Pirate's Curse can't be outdone.
The dance system felt sort of "crowdfundy" with a bunch of transformations thrown in just because they could. However the transformations were generally really fun to use once you got used to it, even if some were a bit too niche. My favorites were the monkey and crab mechanics.
Combat was solid. The character hitboxes and attacking animations were super smooth and fluid. The max attack speed upgrade surpassed my xbox button pressing abilities, which is kind of absurd.  It also added the spellcasting system back from RR which is fun, but pretty much optional for most of the game. Upgrades allow you to become completely overpowered very quickly.
Boss designs were pretty good, all had pretty cool designs and unique mechanics. However, I did not have very much fun with the final boss, or the final level design in general.
The overall difficulty is pretty low. It was the easiest of the three Shantae games I played.
Story:
I think it was almost a soft reboot?
The story was okay. I felt like it was clearly "crowdfundy," meaning it was kind of garbled to fit a desired checklist. I had no idea what my main storyline motivation was for the first 80% of the game and I had to get invested in these little villain-of-the-week episodic stuff. But the episodic stuff was fun and amusing, so I was able to roll with it, even though some of the subplots weren't fleshed out enough. Shantae has never been known for its gripping story line, but I didn't think it was as good as the last two games.
Characters:
As with every Shantae game, the characters are super appealing. They are as endearing, flirty, and ridiculous as I expect out of Wayforward. The dialogue writing is clever and funny. My one big gripe is that all of the Sequin Town NPCs are just there to bombard you with hints for progression, which feels wrong. Also, some of the great characters don't get a long enough exposure because the story is so scattered.
Music:
Virt's work is godtier. No exeptions. I downloaded the OST (free on his Bandcamp!) immediately.
Artstyle:
The art is great overall. The character and world designs are top notch, and together with the music it makes a very pretty package. Sometimes the 2-D/3-D mix is a little jarring.
So far soo good. The graphics are good, the music is great, and it plays like a dream. Kind of like a tounge-in-cheek Symphony of the Night.

==EARLY ACCESS==
The only way you are going to succeed in playing this game is for you to know what you are doing. "Prison Architect" has a lot of built in features and all sorts of tools for you to build and maintain a prison. You can bring in four types of prisoners, minimum security, normal security, maximum security, and death row. Not all of these prisoners are equal, you will need to build your prison in a specific way to handle these inmates. Just remember that this is a sandbox game, it depends on how good your building and micromanaging skills are and how much you care about your prisoners. If the prison can run itself from day to day without incidents, then you can pat yourself on the back as a reward for building a functional prison.
When you start off building a prison, it is best to centralize specific rooms to efficiency satisfy the needs of the general prison population. A large canteen for each security level of prisoners, a single large laundry room to handle the entire prison's clothing needs, a protective custody wing for snitches and former police officers and prison guards, a supermax wing for locking up your absolute worst prisoners, and 'staff only' corridors for guards and staff to easily move throughout the prison. Make sure your armory is locked down tight or is a seperate building outside the prison, and be sure your reception room and delivery sector is near the main road. Your administrators' offices should be kept away from shared corridors and be built in a safe place, especially the warden and the chief guard. Everything that promotes reform and takes care of the needs for your prisoners should be centralized within a main corridor for ease of access.
Once you get everything set up, you will need to prepare the entire prison in case of an emergency. People who play this game will complain of legendary prisoners, snitches, and ex law enforcement. Legendary prisoners will slaughter anyone who stands in their way, sometimes without warning. Snitches and former police officers will be frequent targets for murder. You will need to build separate cell blocks for them, preferably you should build a prison within a prison for these guys and fill them with more guards than usual. You must designate the legendary prisoners and their specialized cell blocks as "supermax" while designating all the prisoners marked for death as "protective custody". These two security wings must be similiar in construction. You want to keep prisoners from breaking into the protective custody wing and prisoners from breaking out of the supermax wing. You will find armed guards appropriate for defending the only entry ways to these wings.
There are a lot of things you will need to figure out, and you will be micro-managing a lot of stuff. But if you build and design your prison right, it should run itself without any problems. Unless, of course, you have the intention of stiring up a riot.
==ALPHA 35 UPDATE==
A lot of things have updated, so I liked to recap on what has happened since my previous review. An economy system has been installed into the game, prisoners working for any assigned job will be payed $0.50 an hour. They will then use that money to buy things at the shop to cover for their needs, the average price for items in the shop costs around $5. Since visitors can give money to inmates, you can make a small profit off the shop each day.
Gangs are now a force within Prison Architect. As of this update, there is a 15% chance of normal and maximum security inmates coming into the prison to be a member of one of three gangs. Once all three gangs have a minimum number of ten members, a gang leader will come in through prison intake. These gang leaders have legendary reputation, they will go around the prison and recruit non-gang members and occasionally promote one into a lieutentant. These lieutentant carry out the works of the leader, organizing "plays" to capture territories such as Common Rooms and Yards. Once captured, rival gang members are banned from entering. Non-gang members can still use the facilities within the common rooms, but they will be charged $1 an hour. The gangs will then use the money to buy smuggled weapons to defend the territory. Now anything owned by gangs cannot be modified or dezoned, but you can evict the gangs. However, this can have grave consequences. If successful, guards will now control the zone. Obviously guards are not a gang, but they are a faction in their own right.
Notable bugs:
- There's an "X & Y" bug where an error occurs for items being transported. This can be fixed by dumping the items and then cancelling out the order. However, there is no fix for bodies. Guards will just pick them up and literally try to carry them off the map, or they don't carry them off at all. This bug are mostly prevalent in pre Alpha 35 saves.
- Death row inmates no longer sign up for appeal. No fix.
- Inmates are no longer interested in carpentry. You can fix this by dezoning the workshop and rezoning it, but you'll need to do this everytime a class is finished.
==FULL VERSION==
Yes, now there is a campaign and a new mode: Escape Mode. The first mission of the campaign is the standard introduction, the next few chapters will touch upon riots and the treatment of prisoners. I will not try to give too much away since the campaign is not that long, but it holds some familiar prisons seen in IVSoftware's update videos.
Escape Mode is found in the extras, any prison you or others had built will be turned on its head. It completely reverses the concept of the game. Instead you are in prison, one you have personally built or otherwise. The goal is to escape, and the reward is anti-climatic. It is so much the method of the escape than the final result. Your results may vary from your given prison, but it should be fun in the end.

I'm a big fan of simluation and management games and Prison Architect scratches both of those itches very well.
While the game is not complete, it is very playable, with solid mechanics, and the devs are very active, posting update videos along with an update, every month.
Pros:
Great simulation/management including prisoners, staff, confidential informants, reform programs, parole, even death row if you want.
Fantastic tools including a planning tool that allows you to draw out walls, objects, and pathways before you build. It's amazing how useful that is in a game like this, and PA has spoiled me in that respect - I'll never look at another builder game the same without a planning tool.
Interesting mechanics including different risk levels for prisoners, which poses challenges for managing different regimes (schedules), housing, and public spaces in order not to have fights or riots break out.
Cons:
Disclaimer: the game is still in development, so some of these may get fixed.
Planning tools could use some refinement - such as allowing you to define rooms while in plan view, as well as selecting specific objects to place in plan rather than relying on you memorizing the size of objects or flipping back and forth between plan and build modes to determine size. It's even worse if you haven't unlocked the object as then you can't even select it to see the size, and the tooltips don't tell you either.
In general, there is a lot of tutorial or tooltip work needed. Right now, you have to rely on guides, the wiki, or forum posts to really learn the deeper mechanics such as confidential informants, deployments, how many of certain items are required for a given population, etc.
Conclusion:
Don't let the cons put you off - if you like builder/simulation/management games, you will NOT be disappointed. This, even in this early stage, is a very solid, very enjoyable game. And it will only get better as the devs continue updating it.

I know that regardless of all of the Steam reviews of this game, a number of people have almost nothing good to say about this game. While I can see why some people don't like certain aspects of this game, I ultimately feel like this game was better than the first. While the end was a bit underwhelming, and the final episode was the worst of the three, the rest of the game was phenomenal.
The first episode was by far the best, and I believe it was the most well written of the three. Although some voice actors are missing from the original game, I can't help but feel like the characters are more human in this game than the previous, to a certain degree. The interactions between Chloe and Rachel seem way more genuine than those betweem Max and Chloe, and it gives the story a bit more meaning to it when you see these interactions unfold. Though I still prefer Ashly Burch over Chloes new voice actress.
The story did seem to kind of lose track of itself later down the line, namely in episode 3. Some plot points were either glossed over, or inserted for the sake of what felt like extending the length of the episode. As a result, it glossed over a major plot point that pertains to the end of the game. Honestly I'm not too surprised, given that this game was made by another studio, but overall I'm impressed with how well this game turned out in the grand scheme of things.
I must say that I was epecting this game to be more about what happened right before the first game, and I was a bit disappointed that there was such a huge disconnect between this game and the events that led up to the original. I really wanted to know how Rachel fell into the problems that we knew she faced before the first game, nut unfortunately we didn't see even a little bit of that. None of it is mentioned, at all.
One thing I cannot praise enough is the absolutely fantastic music by Daughter. I felt like I was watching Friday Night Lights again with that post rock style of music, which fit the setting marvelously. I've always felt that music can complete a story, because without it, I feel certain points wouldn't hit you emotionally the same as they would without music. Just like the last game, I am walking away from this experience with a whole new library of incredible music.

I had little expectation that Mad Max would amount to much, as all of the gameplay videos I had seen felt a little lifeless and repetitive.  The first few hours, as I had feared failed to impress and I found the whole experience a little dull and underwhelming.  However, I persevered and something pulled me back in for another try.
It's frustrating in the first few hours, and you will die a lot.  You'll be punched to death/fall off a ledge/get ran over repeatedly while your car is slowly repaired.
Yet if you give it a chance - and the mood takes you, and you can get into Mad Max it really is a fantastic, criminally overlooked game, which looks gorgeous, is fantastically optimized and addictive as anything you have played.
In a nutshell, the game is split into regions (all completely open after an early mission, with no load screens or barriers inbetween, at least not that I came across) and you need to perform tasks such as destroying an enemy camp, in order to reduce the threat level, which in turn unlocks upgrades for Max and your car the Magnum Opus.  If you've played Far Cry/Assassins Creed/Shadow of Mordor you know how this type of game mechanic works.
There is something strangely satisfying and addictive about leveling up in this game.  It has a certain old school flair, whereby nothing ever feels impossible, even if you fail at the first few attempts.  To me, that was always the mark of a great, well balanced game - you always have a shot of accomplishing your goal the first time around, and it never takes more than two or three attempts should you fail - including the racing challenges which are optional, thankfully.
It captures the spirit of the films nicely in terms of the character names and bizarre, twisted traits found in the bosses and main personalities found throughout the game.  Mostly inspired by Fury Road, much of the game will seem familiar if you have watched the movie, and there are plenty of nods to the original trilogy as well.
The voice acting is good, the landscapes are bleak and beautiful, and the Magnum Opus feels suitably powerful.  There are character bios (all of which are in keeping with the tone of the films) and a wealth of information and tidbits about the world available from the menu screen.
Mad Max is a rarity for an open world game - given it's enormity, it almost has a linear feel to it, and you have very limited options as to how you can approach the game - once you've done it, it's unlikely you would ever consider a replay, but in the near fourty hours I have played I have enjoyed it tremendously, and often found that sitting down for twenty minutes to destroy some oil pumps or tackle a convoy turned into an obsessive three hour stint, being unable to tear myself away chasing that next upgrade or hood ornament.

After beating so many New Game +'s, getting all the achievements and defeating all the Obol bosses, I think I am in a position to finally review Rogue Legacy to it's fullest.
First of all, Rogue Legacy is possibly one of the hardest games I've ever played, mentally and physically. Continuously grinding to get better equipment and money was always a psychological thing, and if you didn't have the willpower to do that, you would slowly fall to the game's relentless ability it crush and punish any mistake you make.
And that's the brilliant thing.
Rogue Legacy is a game that I would only recommend to the people who are willing to put in hard time and be crippled by the game's difficulty over and over again.
Lots of time to be spent
Very fun hack and slash
RPG elements to add that slow but steady progession
Enemies that fit the area and level, and can show players the path they should take
Lots of upgrades to be unlocked and purchased
Tons of different classes to choose from
Bosses are interesting and unique
Random layout every time you enter the castle
Story is interesting
Enemies can be redundant, as reskins will be found as progession continues
Not forgiving and very punishing to beginners and players not very good at platformers or hack/slashers
May find grinding to be very boring and not a lot of time fighting bosses
Progession is slow and tedious
Insanely difficult Obol bosses (I'm looking at you, Alexander the 4th.)
Overall, Rogue Legacy is a difficult hack and slash RPG game that will punish you for every mistake that you make. It is a brutal ride and is very discouraging at times, but when you finally beat the final boss, the bittersweet taste of satisfaction will stay with you (at least for a while).
Purchase this game only if you are willing to grind and die and grind and die over and over again.

Do You Feel Like the Hero Yet?
What are your expectations when you start a military shooter? What are you willing to do just because the game tells you to? Do you think killing countless people will somehow lead to a happy ending? Why are you still playing? Do you think this is fun? Spec Ops: The Line forces you to think about these questions.
Let me begin by saying this is NOT a normal military shooter. Spec Ops is easily one of the darkest games I have played in years. It causes you to think about what you’ve done rather than just letting you mindlessly complete objectives. No, not a military shooter, but the opposite. This is a game about the horrors of military shooters.
Spec Ops is unique. It’s not about “fun” how we usually think of it. The story is where this game shines. Sure, you shoot things and hide behind cover just like every other third person shooter out there, but that’s not the point. The point is to make you think. The point is to make you question “Why am I still here?” While falling short in several areas, the narrative is what keeps you playing. You need to play this game.
*Please note, this is only a review for the single player portion of the game. Multiplayer will only be mentioned once, right now.*
GAMEPLAY
Spec Ops may not have the most polished gameplay, but it works well enough. The camera perspective is third person over the shoulder, which works well for this type of game. You feel more connected to the protagonist rather than him just being an empty vessel for you to possess. The gunplay is edgy, and the shooting mechanics are solid. The level design keeps things tense while providing for interesting ways to finish each area. The environments can frequently be used to your advantage, which is a wonderful addition to the gameplay.
Sand is your best friend and your worst enemy. If sand has blown against a window, shoot the window to drop it all on your enemies. However, sandstorms show up from time to time and make combat very difficult. Having the environment be a part of the gameplay is genius, especially considering how vicious the AI is. If left alone, they will murder you. Be prepared for some annoying sections where the pesky guy with a shotgun repeatedly flanks you.
The area where Spec Ops falls short is the controls. Having melee be the same button as vaulting over cover is annoying. There were several times when enemies were flanking me, so I went to hop over cover, but I just ended up punching it instead. That’s frustrating. However, the rest of the controls are mostly what you expect from shooters nowadays. It’s definitely not the worst control scheme I’ve ever seen, but it’s also not incredible.
VISUALS
Spec Ops: The Line is a pretty game. From the moment I started the game, I could tell I was in for some eye candy. I wasn’t disappointed. Beautiful scenery, excellent detail, and horrifying deaths, this game has it all. However, the character models could have used some work. If you showed me a lineup of characters and told me to pick the protagonist from this game, I wouldn’t be able to do it. His personality makes up for his bland appearance, though. Nolan North’s performance as the protagonist is excellent, just like everything else he’s ever done.
Spec Ops’ aesthetics are fantastic. Set in Dubai, you wouldn’t think there’s much to see besides buildings and sand. You’re right! Yet somehow, they manage to keep it interesting. From giant billboards to war torn villages, it manages to keep your attention. One part that really stood out to me was when you reach the top of a skyscraper, you look out over all of Dubai. Off in the distance, you can see your ultimate goal, and you realize just how far you still have to go. This is great. It shows you how far you’ve made it, yet it also shows how beautiful the landscape really is.
Expect to be shocked by how brutal this game is. They will show you things you wish you hadn’t seen. Without spoiling anything, there’s a scene in the middle that is painful to see. They show you that your actions have consequences. Without these visuals, it wouldn’t have had the impact that it did.
SOUND
Nolan North. Does anything else need said? It probably does, so I’ll continue. All of the sound is very believable. The gunshots have punch, and the sandstorms are terrifying. The banter between characters helps the world feel real. Your two friends will always let you know when someone is trying to flank you, and they’ll tell you when they kill a target you’ve told them to kill. This sort of feedback is excellent, and I want to see more games incorporate it on this sort of level. Also, the soundtrack is appropriate and well implemented. Overall, excellent sound.
STORY
Now for the good stuff. The narrative is the greatest in any game since Bioshock. Seriously. I won’t spoil anything, but it needs to be played more than once to fully grasp just how deep it actually is. This is the most well-paced shooter I have played in years. Some shooters leave me worn out after a few hours of playtime, but Spec Ops always gives you a breather after you get through a tough section. Partly the writing and partly the level design, but it’s worth noting. If I say any more, I’m afraid I’ll spoil something, so I’ll close with this: play this game.
CONTENT
Player discretion is advised. Be prepared for some very shocking visuals. You will see things you wish you hadn’t. It’s not pointless, though. It is essential to the narrative. Occasional language, including the “F” word. Not nearly as much language as GTA or Saint’s Row, but about as much as The Walking Dead. Don’t let your children play this game. The visuals are disturbing, even for adults.
THE VERDICT
I highly recommend this game. Probably wait for a sale on Steam since the campaign is only six hours long. However, you will probably want to play it through more than once. Be prepared to be shocked, but also prepare to be amazed. This isn’t the game we wanted, but this is the game we needed. “Fun” is not in its vocabulary. Spec Ops: The Line sheds some light on the gaming industry itself, and it proves that a military shooter can truly be original.
SCORING
Gameplay: 7.5
Visuals: 8.5
Sound: 8.5
Story: 9.5
Overall*: 8.5
(Scale of 1-10. 1 being terrible, 10 being perfection.)
*(Not an average. This is the score I give to the overall product, not an average of certain aspects. This score is my recommendation for whether it should be played.)

This game is the one I'm going to use to determine whether people are really aware of what they are doing in games, or if they still view things as 'just a game' and brush off the consequences of their actions.
This is a game that is engaging, but paradoxically NOT FUN. I'm constantly struck by how there are two different levels to the game. If you chose to focus on the raw gameplay, to block out all the talking and the changes in plot and just play... it's not fun. It turns into a trudging mind-numbingly boring game that really FORCES you to pay attention to just what you're doing. The enemies, the things your character yells in combat, the situations you face, all of them come together to force you to think very dang carefully about just what the heck you're doing. You are put in the same place as you would be in any other Modern shooter a-la COD or Battlefield, but you really never feel comfortable completing your objectives.
If you're payin attention, this game won't make you happy. If you're not, you really weren't paying attention.

Brilliant storyline. 10/10 for that. Immersive, shocking. Several moments that really highlighted the horrors of war, especially knowing that it ws you that pulled the trigger. This game will make you hate yourself.
Gameplay, however, holds back this otherwise amazing experience.
1. As a tactical shooter, cover plays a very important role. The cover mechanics in this game, however, are laughable. Often, the only way to get from cover to cover is to stand up and fully revealing yourself to the enemy. The game enters and exits cover in very counterintuitive ways, which, again, often means you will be stainging up in full view of the enemy.
This shouldn't be a problem. Cover mechanics are nothing new. Mass Effect, Deus EX: HR, etc all have done infinitely better.
2. The squad commands are limited to "kill this guy". Not even "hold back", which means your two vulnerable squadmates will sometimes rush, then require medical attention deep into enemy lines.
Other than that, the game is amazing.

I did not like this game. Let me tell you why.
Nice graphics, but the lack of options is too bad. For isntance, the game would benefit from antialiasing greatly. Also you have to note that there is no FOV option to change it.
For the sounds, well, if you have 5.1 and a headset, then sometimes you won't be hearing jack since the wrong output is used. It is the case during some cinematics (they are video files). Other than that noises spacialization and stuff are great, but speeches are often only heard from the rear speakers. Weird. Voices are okay, but dialogs sucks. It is basic military stuff and has no depth. Don't expect much humour either.
A basic linear TPS that plays pretty much like a FPS. Move to area, waste tangos, take cover, move to next area, repeat. Your health regenerates, and combat is all about cover. Run, and hide behind a crate, low wall, whatever. Then aim, so your dude raises above the cover, shoot quick, and release aim to get back behind cover. Now, wait safely for your health to recover.
Lame. No tactics, nothing.
Mouse sensitivity is super high even when setting the stuff to zero. I had to lower my mouse DPI in order to play. Keybindings now. Well, it must be a console port: keys are screwed.
To take cover your have one key. To jump over stuff another key. To sprint, it is the same cover key. Uhg... how many time did I die, holding shift to sprint... but no, it was space. And rebinding space to shift is no good since it makes you take cover as well when near an object. Also, sprinting continues when you release the button.
Awkward game to play that's for sure, but not impossbile.
The AI is half scripted. Some tangos will always go to the same spot, other will react to your actions.
Same for your buddies that will go to the same initial cover. You can command your grunts, and tell them to focus on a specific target. It worked well at the beginning of the game. A far away tango will get sniped by Lugos, and a close one will be taken care of by the support dude.
But near the end, the map is not as open as previously. So issuing an order will make your goons move out of their cover and have a little stroll on the battlefield, not dodging lead of course. They will end up incapped near a swarm of tangos.
You cannot issue moving or throwing a flash orders. The throwing a flash command seems to be scripted when certain tangos spawn in groups. Not cool.
Also, your buddies have infinite ammo, and pretty much never die. If they 'die' you can revive them with what it seems to be an adrenaline shot.
Actually, the best part of the game. At first, it looks like total generic crap. But listen, I realized it was not total shït at the end of the game. Pay attention to details, I mean it, it will increase this game's story awesomeness.
Now, some scenes during the game are horrible on purpose. There were no controversies, and that is surprising since some stuff are much worse than in the CoD airport mission. You will have to kill civilians and US soldiers. Even though choices are offered to you, the outcome will always be the same. The story will try to put the blame on you, and make you realize how horrible war is.
But unfortunately, these gruesome scenes are there for the violence/18+ rating only, they do not IMHO deepen the game's story nor the main character's mindset. It is weak and not subtle.
Life is not black and white.
There is a twist though, you will feel it coming, but you won't know what exactly. It is not bad, but not great either.
You can pick weapons from dead enemy. SMGs, rifles, snipers, and handguns.
You also have an alternate fire button that will do special action depending on the weapon you are carrying. For exemple, the SCAR will switch to nade mode. Some rifles like the AK47 or FAMAS will switch fire mode. However this is not done well, like a hint comes and tells you the burst fire is recommended for stable sniping... WTF.
3-Burst fire is used in CQB, that is what it has been designed for. None of the weapons have a single shot mode suitable for stable firing, except for sniper weapons and a HK417.
Also the AKs are full-auto and 3-burst shot while in real life burst shot doesn't exist on AKs. I would totally prefer to have single shot instead of burst; most areas are open you see.
Aside from these minors innacuracies, ammo is weapon specific. You would expect some weapon to share their ammo since they have the same caliber. But instead it is magazine specific.
Accuracy is decent and correct. Handguns are too accurate though, like the .44 that can snipe tangos and put them down in one single shot :/

I was a backer of this "Daniel David" in the credits (should have been Daniel David Kelly but it seems they acknowledge that some names got messed up), but theres no bias here, the game is good. I'll go into some details on the game however because its not flawless, no game is.
Shantae managed to make a game many times better than Mighty No. 9 on a fraction of the budget, beautiful artstyle with solid gameplay with a feel of a Saturday morning cartoon. This really was a kickstarter done right.
Shantae is not without its problems however, the main thing to point out in these flaws however is they've been persistant throughout all Shantae, so if these are a problem for you its more a problem with Shantae in general instead of this specific game:
1) Game is linear compared to the past..... I guess? The past Shantaes were no Symphonies of the Night as far as exploration goes either, I don't know why it suddenly becomes a huge thing for this game. And in all honesty while they don't have alot of screens, theres still alot of stuff hidden in them for you to find using your powers which kind of ties right into the next major complaint.
2) Alot of backtracking and fetch quests as "content":  I got no counter for this, its absolutely true. Even if the fetching is comical and corny on what they make you find, a spade is a spade. They do make you backtrack alot as playing in Hero mode proves. Most every shantae I've played however used this formula so its more a knock against Shantae than this game specifically.
3) The game is short: my first play through was 6 hours, and has only gotten shorter in replays and hero mode.... once again however this is something Shantae has almost always been known for (I mean hell Risky's revenge you can 100% clear in 2 hours X minutes) Platformers are rarely epic 60 hour games unless they are a castlevania where most of that time is grind.
What should be made important here is the game is put together very well and solid, while its a short experience its one that is great from beginning to end and is colorful and fun. I also sort of liked the format of this one that really felt like playing an old Saturday morning cartoon, as in each "level" feels self contained like an episode out of a show that all contribute a small thing that the last level feels like the conclusion of a season arc, it added to the over experience and made it fun.
If the game is a bit too pricey for you, just wait for a sale, but if you love platformers this ranks up as one of the best ones.

Windward is lacking in some large areas though. There is no ending, just ever more sections to conquer or petty missions to complete. Brilliant storyline. 10/10 for that. Immersive, shocking. Several moments that really highlighted the horrors of war, especially knowing that it ws you that pulled the trigger. This game will make you hate yourself.
Gameplay, however, holds back this otherwise amazing experience.
1. As a tactical shooter, cover plays a very important role. The cover mechanics in this game, however, are laughable. Often, the only way to get from cover to cover is to stand up and fully revealing yourself to the enemy. The game enters and exits cover in very counterintuitive ways, which, again, often means you will be stainging up in full view of the enemy.
This shouldn't be a problem. Cover mechanics are nothing new. Mass Effect, Deus EX: HR, etc all have done infinitely better.
2. The squad commands are limited to "kill this guy". Not even "hold back", which means your two vulnerable squadmates will sometimes rush, then require medical attention deep into enemy lines.
Other than that, the game is amazing.

I did not like this game. Let me tell you why.
Nice graphics, but the lack of options is too bad. For isntance, the game would benefit from antialiasing greatly. Also you have to note that there is no FOV option to change it.
For the sounds, well, if you have 5.1 and a headset, then sometimes you won't be hearing jack since the wrong output is used. It is the case during some cinematics (they are video files). Other than that noises spacialization and stuff are great, but speeches are often only heard from the rear speakers. Weird. Voices are okay, but dialogs sucks. It is basic military stuff and has no depth. Don't expect much humour either.
A basic linear TPS that plays pretty much like a FPS. Move to area, waste tangos, take cover, move to next area, repeat. Your health regenerates, and combat is all about cover. Run, and hide behind a crate, low wall, whatever. Then aim, so your dude raises above the cover, shoot quick, and release aim to get back behind cover. Now, wait safely for your health to recover.
Lame. No tactics, nothing.
Mouse sensitivity is super high even when setting the stuff to zero. I had to lower my mouse DPI in order to play. Keybindings now. Well, it must be a console port: keys are screwed.
To take cover your have one key. To jump over stuff another key. To sprint, it is the same cover key. Uhg... how many time did I die, holding shift to sprint... but no, it was space. And rebinding space to shift is no good since it makes you take cover as well when near an object. Also, sprinting continues when you release the button.
Awkward game to play that's for sure, but not impossbile.
The AI is half scripted. Some tangos will always go to the same spot, other will react to your actions.
Same for your buddies that will go to the same initial cover. You can command your grunts, and tell them to focus on a specific target. It worked well at the beginning of the game. A far away tango will get sniped by Lugos, and a close one will be taken care of by the support dude.
But near the end, the map is not as open as previously. So issuing an order will make your goons move out of their cover and have a little stroll on the battlefield, not dodging lead of course. They will end up incapped near a swarm of tangos.
You cannot issue moving or throwing a flash orders. The throwing a flash command seems to be scripted when certain tangos spawn in groups. Not cool.
Also, your buddies have infinite ammo, and pretty much never die. If they 'die' you can revive them with what it seems to be an adrenaline shot.
Actually, the best part of the game. At first, it looks like total generic crap. But listen, I realized it was not total shït at the end of the game. Pay attention to details, I mean it, it will increase this game's story awesomeness.
Now, some scenes during the game are horrible on purpose. There were no controversies, and that is surprising since some stuff are much worse than in the CoD airport mission. You will have to kill civilians and US soldiers. Even though choices are offered to you, the outcome will always be the same. The story will try to put the blame on you, and make you realize how horrible war is.
But unfortunately, these gruesome scenes are there for the violence/18+ rating only, they do not IMHO deepen the game's story nor the main character's mindset. It is weak and not subtle.
Life is not black and white.
There is a twist though, you will feel it coming, but you won't know what exactly. It is not bad, but not great either.
You can pick weapons from dead enemy. SMGs, rifles, snipers, and handguns.
You also have an alternate fire button that will do special action depending on the weapon you are carrying. For exemple, the SCAR will switch to nade mode. Some rifles like the AK47 or FAMAS will switch fire mode. However this is not done well, like a hint comes and tells you the burst fire is recommended for stable sniping... WTF.
3-Burst fire is used in CQB, that is what it has been designed for. None of the weapons have a single shot mode suitable for stable firing, except for sniper weapons and a HK417.
Also the AKs are full-auto and 3-burst shot while in real life burst shot doesn't exist on AKs. I would totally prefer to have single shot instead of burst; most areas are open you see.
Aside from these minors innacuracies, ammo is weapon specific. You would expect some weapon to share their ammo since they have the same caliber. But instead it is magazine specific.
Accuracy is decent and correct. Handguns are too accurate though, like the .44 that can snipe tangos and put them down in one single shot :/

I want to like this game.  I really do, but it has a few seriously major problems:
The game plays very slow.  Ordinarily, this wouldn't be an issue, but as an action RPG, the game needs to feel a little more arcadey and not so simulating.  The game literally becomes a timesink of your real life time to achieve virtual progress, and at that, it's not that much.  You just upgrade your ship and develop skills while expanding your faction's control of the map.  It'd be a better use of one's time to make this a turn based game where you make career or campaign decisions instead of having to actually wait to do things.
On the other hand, for all the game is a timesink in the name of realism, sailing in the game isn't very realistic.  You don't have to adjust your sail for the right point of attack to catch the wind.  Yea, you sail faster with the wind than against it, but that's it.  The game also doesn't make much difference between fore-and-aft versus square sails in how fore-and-aft sails are supposed to sail fastest at a 45 degree angle away from the wind while square sails are supposed to struggle much more with either sideways or backwards wind.  A square sail ship shouldn't be able to move at all in many currents since the sail doesn't turn.  Fore-and-aft ships don't have to use tacking to get from point a to point b, and weather doesn't change.  Yea, the wind changes direction now and again, but there are never any choppy seas to sail through.
The singleplayer game has no narrative at all, so the quests you do are literally just sailing from point a to point b in exchange for points.  This sort of mechanic works well in a multiplayer aspect where you're competing over efficiency and strategy to control the map among your friends, but in singleplayer, it's a pointless grind.  On top of that, friendly AI boats bump into you all the time.  There's no understanding of "right of way" between smaller and bigger, slower and faster, forward and backward, or other different positions of ships.
The multiplayer game has a very small community, and is already dominated by elites who took charge with the Valiant faction.  The other three factions have no chance of success unless you spend a ton of time developing your singleplayer profile and import it.   Keep in mind that I've spent 15 hours by now just to reach level 34.  The regions that Valiant doesn't control for you to start on the public server go into the 90s.
Also, understand that combat represents the climax of the game.  Once you explore and trade a lot, the only thing left to do with your experience and money is spend it towards combat skills, bribing pirates or recruiting allies, and upgrading your ship and getting equipment.  The Valiant faction succeeds in the climax.  The other three factions are supposed to grow faster than it one way or another to reach their climaxes before it does, so once Valiant climaxes, it's pretty much game over for the other three.
Yes, you can host your own private game with friends or host your own server, but that's not something the game deserves credit for.  It's an extra effort you have to make.
Also, yes, it's advertised that you can customize your own maps, but that doesn't mean anything beside choosing which tiles to deactivate in a square grid.  Also, the public server isn't customized at all.  It simply left every tile activated which means there's no direction in which way to expand.  This wouldn't be a problem if the archipelagos had some real diversity to them, but they don't.  Therefore, it just adds more monotony into the grind in order to secure your faction's borders.
Instancing in the game is what the game should be in general, but it's boring to instance on your own, and nobody really does it in multiplayer... unless they're importing their own superclassed ships.
All and all, the game is just passive-aggressively out of control.  I don't expect the community to ever thrive because while the combat, trading, and exploration mechanics have potential, it just isn't handled very well.  If the game played in 30-120 minute instances between 5 on 5 teams where everyone starts at the same level (like a MOBA), then the game would be great, but it doesn't.
Alternately, the game could be played in monthly seasons so people can have some sense of saved progress, but if the game doesn't reset periodically, then it will constantly alienate newcomers from joining while oldtimers dominate (which is exactly why I advise you, a newcomer, to not buy this game).

I'll keep this brief. The newest game in the Shantae series is a sure winner. Wayforward has outdone themselves in many ways with this game.
The visuals are fantastic. They're clean, crisp and colorful, and the animations are really smooth for virtually every character onscreen.
The audio is amazing. The compositions by Jake Kaufman are perfect to get you in the proper mood for the level and the challenge ahead. Sound effects are well done and avoid being annoying. What little voice acting is here is well done and makes me wish the voice acting stretch goal was met.
Controls are spot on. Rest assured that if you get hit by an enemy or if you fall off a cliff, it's 99.9% your fault and not the controls acting up. Playing on a keyboard is alright, but a bit annoying, so I recommend using a controller for this game.
The game structure is different from previous Shantae games, as it is level-based instead of metroidvania style. This allows for stronger platforming, but somehow makes the unavoidable backtracking a bit more annoying that previous entries.
Using Shantae's abilites is way smoother and faster than in past games. No longer is it a chore to, for example, transform into a monkey, climb a wall, transform back into Shantae to fight an enemy, transform back into a monkey to climb more walls, then back to Shantae, then to an elephant to break a wall, then back to Shantae. The various upgrades and special powers also make the gameplay varied and more fun for all.
Shantae: Half-Genie Hero is more platformer than metroidvania. It loses on fun exploration, but gains better platforming challenges. It doesn't feel as cohesive as Pirate's Curse, and the individual stories don't get enough time to develop, but it's charming to see these new, individual sides of the world. Maybe in a future game we will see a better story, but as a whole package, I found it completely satisfying.

My review may contain minor spoilers, you have been warned.
Many other reviewers are going into the specifics of why this game is a great buy, I pretty much agree with all of them so I'll save you time on that. I'll just talk about what I would have liked to have seen instead:
- Closure on who's Shantae's mom (I have a feeling about who her father is)
- Closure on Rottytops and her brothers finding out about their pasts (cliffhanger from previous game)
- I would have liked to have learned more about Sequin Land's Sultana, but as of yet there isn't even concept art of her.
- Boss Rush mode (I know the DLC for bolo, sky and rottytops weren't successfully funded, so I'm not worried about that)
This is really nitpicky stuff, I'm honestly grasping at straws to find any flaws with this one. If this isn't wayforward's last Shantae game, you can pretty much ignore this review, I'm treating it as though it is.
Other than that, this is easily the best Shantae game in the series to date (I've been playing since GBC, still have my tinkerbat transformation!), the visuals are outstanding, the soundtrack is out of this world, the writing is still funny. Definitely worth a buy if you liked Pirate's Curse.  I will definitely be replaying for 2 heart runs, speed runs and mono-animal runs in hero mode.

I really, really wanted to like this game.
Mad Max Fury Road was an exceptional piece of art that brought me to a level of obsession never before seen. I saw the video game, and realizing it wasn't strongly correlated, made a slightly hesitant purchase. My first impression wasn't great, but after a couple of hours of gameplay I began to enjoy myself. I let the story go to the wayside as I drove around wreaking havoc on convoys and boosting myself off of cliffs. I upgraded my car, and did it all over again.
After about 20 hours, though, it lost its fun as it became reptitious to an extreme. I thought that maybe if I added the story element back into it, it might make things more enjoyable.
How wrong I was.
The story for this game is absolutely awful. It's short, only accounting for maybe 6 hours of gameplay. Worse than its brief duration, though, was the plot. Thinly constructed and with no redemption, I finished it up feeling a little sick inside and very upset. I decided I won't be touching this game again for months, at least.
Pros:
It's pretty
Things explode
LOTS of things explode
Wonderful engine sounds for all you car lovers
Cons:
Surface-level game with absolutely no depth
A story that is both laughably short and sickeningly repulsive in its finale
Repititious gameplay
Absolutely nothing in this game is balanced in a healthy way.
If you really feel like spending good money on a game that will keep you entertained for 20 hours at most, feel free. I'd consider recommending buying it on sale, but it would need to be at least half off for me to heartily get behind that idea.
Overall score:  5.5/10

What can I tell you about Maia? I can tell you that it has sat on my wishlist for quite some time before I bought it during the sale. I have watched with some interest as the game has developed. Having now, albeit briefly, played it for myself I can say that - in it's current state I cannot in any good conscience recommend this to my friends in its current state.
That's not to say that Maia hasn't got potential, it certainly has. But the fulfilment of that potential is a long, long way off.
The most glaring shortfall here is the staggeringly poor optimisation. All early access excuses aside, this is a game that is charging almost £20 to get players to poke around at what is currently available - the scope of which is very limited, and in my opinion, not especially fun either - for that money I would have expected that the game engine would be in some sort of state that was reasonably optimised for the very broad range of system builds that comes from PC customers. Whilst the game is not unplayable, it's always irksome when a system that vastly exceeds the recommended spec splutters along at 12 frames per second, like some elderly man with a cold.
The second issue I had was with the minimalist UI. This is subjective and some people will like it, but for whatever it's worth, I didn't. Having to blindly cycle through construction options using 1-9 and B and V felt unintuitive and was something I can't ever see myself getting used to. That being said, I liked the way I could place items pretty much wherever the hell I wanted in a room, that felt smooth and comfortable to get along with.
Another thing that struck me was the very sparce tutorial. Alright, alright, so it's not rocket science this and for the majority of people, there isn't much that is going to need explaining, you can figure stuff out just by playing around with the game, plus it's an alpha, I have yet to see a game in it's alpha state that has a fully fleshed out tutorial. Nonetheless, I feel that the areas covered by the tutorial were hastily put together, and not especially informative.
Whilst i'm on the subject of tutorials, the dialogue. Being British myself, I 'get' that whoever wrote the tutorial was attempting  to create the lofty humour of a smug, arrogant ai. However. At the early stages of the game, it's a bit jarring, and doesn't lend itself well to imparting knowledge. Those of you who played Frozen Synapse may remember the tutorial and it's deeply condescending dialogue. That worked for two reasons: 1. It was offset by a more pleasant dialogue as a counter and 2. It was voice acted so it felt like a infinitesimally intelligent ai and not, in the case of Maia, simply the developers quietly sneering at it's customers. In this instance it comes across as not only churlish, and dare I say, a little rude, but also because of it's delivery, entirely misses the target of being funny.
Another bone of contention was that there was no feedback to see what was being worked on. Not being one to build one thing at a time, I slapped down a load of stuff and waited. It was hard to tell whether people were working on something, or just running around like lunatics. Another thing is that I had very little feedback on what it was that my colonists needs were at any given time, it would be nice to be able to see a general overview of that at a glance.
Maia might be a good game one day if it's devs stick to the plan and don't get too lost in the woods on the way, but it's a long was off that chequered flag, and at this juncture there really is no guarantees that it will be good in the end. My enthusiasm has certainly been significantly dowsed by playing the game in it's current state, and I have to say, I regret paying the money, but you never know, maybe i'll have gotten a good deal in the long run, only time will tell at this point. Only really worth investing if you really have an overwhelming desire to support the developer or have an incredibly optimistic disposition. Elsewise, wait and see.
TL;DR --- One for management/stategy fans to stick on their wishlist and check in on every so often.

A racing game that that fully embraces and embodies the "Arcade Racer". The tracks all feel unique, range wildly in difficulty, and are short enough that it doesn't feel like a chore to replay a level to shave off a few milliseconds (as opposed races that take upwards of three minutes, where you may have to drive through the same few kilometers time and time again to get to the one corner you're focusing on). It ends up feeling like a condensed version of other racing games, where the races can take less than a minute, the tracks are full of interesting bits and concice, and the controls are very tight.
Additionally, the game looks great. It has a unified asthetic and looks smooth and polished, even on my sub-par labtop. The sound and music are not outstanding, but they serve the game well. It also has local multiplayer, which is always a plus in my books.
Finally, the track editor is excellent. It's not hard to make a good level, and the level editor makes it easy to make good looking games as well. I've only made a few low-quality tracks, but even then the ability to build>test>tweak>test>tweak>test makes the proscess enjoyable in itself.
Would recommend, especially if you've been turned off other racers in the past because you find them tedious.

I very rarely pay full price for games if I can. And I almost never preorder a game. This was one of the exceptions, and I am very glad that I did so. Deck Nine managed to capture the essence of Life is Strange, from the weirdness of Arcadia Bay down to the (accurately) cringy teenage angst. And, instead of the rewind mechanic (which matched up quite well with the indecisive Max), Deck Nine decided to throw in the Backtalk mechanic which keeps gameplay interesting and fits the ever sassy Chloe Price
I admit, one of my fears going into the game was that Rachel Amber, who the original Life is Strange had put upon a pedestal, would be... disappointing. I am glad to say that they have managed to show us why the characters in the original and placed her there, and why Chloe would come to love her.
My only gripe isn't really Deck Nine's fault, and that is that Chloe Price is not voiced by Ashly Burch, but instead voiced by Rhianna DeVries due to the SAG-AFTRA strike. Now, Ms. DeVries does an excellent job in delivering Chloe's lines, and everything she says feels like the character, partially because her lines were written by Ms. Burch. It's wasn't immersion breaking for me, but it doesn't feel quite the same. Again, this is not the fault of the developer nor is it the fault of Ms. DeVries or Ms. Burch, and Ms. DeVries does an excellent job. There's just the lack of a certain je ne se quoi.
But beyond that gripe, this is an excellent game that is worth both your money and your time. I highly encourage you to play it. And if you haven't played the first Life is Strange, this can also be an excellent jumping-off point as there aren't any spoilers for the original. Most games, I'd recommend you buy during a sale. This game, I recommend that you buy it when you can, even at full price.
TL;DR: It's a great game. Buy it.

Maia shows promise, although in the way of being so little more than a bare-bones engine, that anything is possible in the end. It could be that (judging by the progress speed that makes continental drift seem fast) in half a decade it will evolve into the most amazing colony sim ever. Or not. Who knows?
But at the moment, it's NOT a good use of your money. As was said, it pushes the limit of what is acceptable to release as "early access". It's just a bare-bones graphics engine, with some minimal and BROKEN animations, a non-functional AI, and no save and reload either, so your progress WILL be lost each time you exit.
And by "non-functional AI" I don't mean "might not prioritize right", but as in "doesn't even work, or not for long." Colonist AI routinely craps itself and either stops building anything any more (lucky version) or you just get a colonist going catatonic in the airlock and never moving any more (more usual version.) And when you do get it to work for half an hour, it will prioritize the hilariously wrong thing, like everyone keeping repairing the doors instead of building the air purifier.
Now that might be palatable (not really) in a game where you can direct them around, like in The Sims, and the AI only keeps them alive in between. But here you can't direct them, and the WHOLE premise is that they do their own thing, a broken AI just means a broken game.
Etc.
Really, it has no excuse to be released at this early and dysfunctional stage. It may eventually be worth playing. Save your money for then.

The kind of gameplay elements that the final mix will have can just as well be what you like, or what you hate, and there's no way to know which it will be, as there doesn't even seem to be any plan.

I had little expectation that Mad Max would amount to much, as all of the gameplay videos I had seen felt a little lifeless and repetitive.  The first few hours, as I had feared failed to impress and I found the whole experience a little dull and underwhelming.  However, I persevered and something pulled me back in for another try.
It's frustrating in the first few hours, and you will die a lot.  You'll be punched to death/fall off a ledge/get ran over repeatedly while your car is slowly repaired.
Yet if you give it a chance - and the mood takes you, and you can get into Mad Max it really is a fantastic, criminally overlooked game, which looks gorgeous, is fantastically optimized and addictive as anything you have played.
In a nutshell, the game is split into regions (all completely open after an early mission, with no load screens or barriers inbetween, at least not that I came across) and you need to perform tasks such as destroying an enemy camp, in order to reduce the threat level, which in turn unlocks upgrades for Max and your car the Magnum Opus.  If you've played Far Cry/Assassins Creed/Shadow of Mordor you know how this type of game mechanic works.
There is something strangely satisfying and addictive about leveling up in this game.  It has a certain old school flair, whereby nothing ever feels impossible, even if you fail at the first few attempts.  To me, that was always the mark of a great, well balanced game - you always have a shot of accomplishing your goal the first time around, and it never takes more than two or three attempts should you fail - including the racing challenges which are optional, thankfully.
It captures the spirit of the films nicely in terms of the character names and bizarre, twisted traits found in the bosses and main personalities found throughout the game.  Mostly inspired by Fury Road, much of the game will seem familiar if you have watched the movie, and there are plenty of nods to the original trilogy as well.
The voice acting is good, the landscapes are bleak and beautiful, and the Magnum Opus feels suitably powerful.  There are character bios (all of which are in keeping with the tone of the films) and a wealth of information and tidbits about the world available from the menu screen.
Mad Max is a rarity for an open world game - given it's enormity, it almost has a linear feel to it, and you have very limited options as to how you can approach the game - once you've done it, it's unlikely you would ever consider a replay, but in the near fourty hours I have played I have enjoyed it tremendously, and often found that sitting down for twenty minutes to destroy some oil pumps or tackle a convoy turned into an obsessive three hour stint, being unable to tear myself away chasing that next upgrade or hood ornament.
Overall Mad Max is an excellent game I find it difficult to fault, other than in terms of replay value.
Oh, and one thing - there is a glitch with one camp - you'll know it when you get there - whereby waves of enemies keep on coming at you, and the doors don't open, and you'll Google Youtube videos of the wall trick to complete it.  Take note - remove all accessories from the Magnum Opus, blast up there, and DON'T AIM  - JUST AUTO FIRE!  Camp complete.
Sole glitch in an otherwise awesome game.  8.5/10

I really, really wanted to like this game.
Mad Max Fury Road was an exceptional piece of art that brought me to a level of obsession never before seen. I saw the video game, and realizing it wasn't strongly correlated, made a slightly hesitant purchase. My first impression wasn't great, but after a couple of hours of gameplay I began to enjoy myself. I let the story go to the wayside as I drove around wreaking havoc on convoys and boosting myself off of cliffs. I upgraded my car, and did it all over again.
After about 20 hours, though, it lost its fun as it became reptitious to an extreme. I thought that maybe if I added the story element back into it, it might make things more enjoyable.
How wrong I was.
The story for this game is absolutely awful. It's short, only accounting for maybe 6 hours of gameplay. Worse than its brief duration, though, was the plot. Thinly constructed and with no redemption, I finished it up feeling a little sick inside and very upset. I decided I won't be touching this game again for months, at least.
Pros:
It's pretty
Things explode
LOTS of things explode
Wonderful engine sounds for all you car lovers
Cons:
Surface-level game with absolutely no depth
A story that is both laughably short and sickeningly repulsive in its finale
Repititious gameplay
Absolutely nothing in this game is balanced in a healthy way.
If you really feel like spending good money on a game that will keep you entertained for 20 hours at most, feel free. I'd consider recommending buying it on sale, but it would need to be at least half off for me to heartily get behind that idea.

Spec Ops: The Line is a third-person shooter with a cinematic game play style.
The graphics are very impressive. Highly detailed, highly colourful depending on the filter you select and the beginning. It appears to runs very smooth throughout. There is the odd time the graphics will pause to update your save file or load part of the game but this is rare.
The sound effects are great and brings the environment and the game to life. The sound of the weapons are good on release and impact. The ringing in the ears after a grenade explodes close by is effective. The voice acting is good and brings the reality of war to life through the character you are playing.
The story is immersive and told through a cinematic style game play with queues for gun battles. This does make the game very linear and not much scope to explore the interesting environment of Dubai after a devastating sand storm.
There are time where you can make moral choices that will play out differently within the chapter but does not effect the end of the game. Within the last chapter, it has its own moral choices for you to choose from, which will determine the end of the game. The choices you need to make are not clear cut but are somewhat abstract which fits into the story nicely.
I highly recommend this game for the storyline. The game maybe a bit too linear for some, but it is a well made linear game.

I'm sure there are other reviews outlining the plot of the game, so I won't regurgitate things that have been said elsewhere, save a brief, brief synopsis. You're a Captain leading two more men into a buried Dubai, and the♥♥♥♥♥♥has hit the fan for that city. People are killing each other, men and women are dying and so on, and a simple recon mission turns into a quest to save the city from....well, who knows?
Now, this is a 3rd person cover shooter. And maybe it's because I'm bad at shooters, or maybe it's because the mechanics are a little flawed here and there, or maybe it's a bit of both, but I died. A lot. Thank god this isn't a rogue-like game. Anyways, it's all about cover, cover, cover. And while the cover system does get a little wonky here and there, and many of my deaths were due to slipping out of cover when I didn't want to, or being unable to break cover to avoid a grenade, I had fun. That's what's most important. I had fun.
But, again, the story is what makes this game so incredibly strong. The story is so shocking, and the choices you make aren't clear cut good and bad. Most of the time, it's a lesser of two evils. By the time you finish, you will love the game.
But you might hate yourself.
