Shantae: Half-Genie Hero is Shantae's newest game, Kickstarted by the fans. Updated for the modern age and brought to Steam, the game is in full color (big shock) with a wonderful "indie" feel. Is it any good? Let's find out!
Shantae's story in this game is fairly straightforward. It's definitely an indie-written story, but it wears that designation on its sleeve. The story itself is like the game: Quirky and fun. However, its pacing is somewhat awkward. It's not bad, but it seems to have some sections that drag on from a lack of direction (Thankfully, "Bathroom Angel" can fix that somewhat) and some that blow by.
There's also some funny references and 4th-wall-breaking. The writing itself is fantastic, giving everyone personality and charm. I just wish the story itself was paced a little better and the initial directions you're given at the start of each quest were clearer, but nothing in the story has made me consult a walkthrough yet.
OK, I have to gush about the writing for the characters. There is so much charm and personality to the characters, ESPECIALLY Shantae. Shantae is a mixture of a straight-woman to the weirdness, a generic hero-type (played with), an airhead (without being a motor-mouth), and a bit of thickness. (She's not dense by any means, she seems pretty smart, just naive.) I like all of the characters and their dialogue is all great.
Shantae is evocative of the old-school Nintendo platformers, including some Metroidvania elements. You jump around like a maniac looking for platforms, look for every tiny hint to a secret/easter egg/new power-up, and some Castlevania-like brawling.
Shantae's also bringing some tricks to help make platforming better and uncover more secrets. She can use her Belly Dance (which has an adorable animation) to transform into different Forms, each with their own unique traits, jump height, attacks (or lack thereof), and special abilities. Most Forms have an upgrade to unlock a new attack, which is, unfortunately, not that interesting. (Mermaid Form gets a bubble, Crab Form gets a quick snap that clips through seaweed, Mouse Form gets a spammable-low-damage bite, and so on.)
The platforming itself is highly refined, practically to a science. The controls are tight and intuitive, Shantae's movement and jumping is consistent and controllable (You can adjust and correct your jumps mid-air, thankfully), and it's usually clear what you can and can't jump on. My only real complaint lies with a couple of her Forms, mainly with Harpy Form, where the controls become extremely floaty and nigh-controllable. Sometimes, the hitboxes can be a little iffy, especially with Mermaid Form where I've taken damage while close to (but not touching) an enemy that only damages you by touch because my TAIL got near it.
The brawling is very simple: One button makes Shantae slap a short distance in front of her (your generic Hair-Whip Attack) and another uses your Magic. It's very simple one-button combat (technically, two-button, but w/e) and works well.
I think my current major complaint with the gameplay is just the insane amount of backtracking you have to do. This isn't anything new if you've played a Metroidvania-style platformer in the past 10-15 years, but it really drives the pacing into the ground sometimes as you run from place to place, running the same levels at least 2 extra times each just praying you'll see the one thing different you can do with a new Form or upgrade. Granted, I'm not huge into Metroidvania, so take this with a massive grain of salt.
One more minor complaint I have to get off my chest is the inventory. There's no quick-use keys, so if you want to use something, you have to go into the Inventory screen, select it, and Use it. This is a very minor complaint, considering this actually HELPS, since the Inventory screen pauses the game and can let you get your bearings.
The music in this game is fantastic. It has that indie quirkyness to it without being grating. My only real complaint is that the music can get a LITTLE repetitive due to the Metroidvania nature of the game, forcing you to backtrack a ton and hear each track plenty of times.
The art style in this game is absolutely awesome. It's 2.5D (meaning, gameplay on a 2D plane, but 3D models) with a very anime-esque style. In fact, this whole game looks like a playable anime. Everything has this cute-quirky style to it and just drips with personality. It's an absolute treat to look at, combining an old-school 2D game with a 3D art style flawlessly.
Any the animations are just...AAAAAAAAAAA I LOVE THEM! Everything has this bouncy energy that brings the game to life. Shantae's idle animations are fun to watch, her Belly Dance is playful, just everything is beautifully animated.
Simply put, Shantae: Half-Genie Hero is a fantastic game. I'm rarely a fan of platformers, but Shantae has me absolutely entranced. I can't stop smiling at this game. Its fun old-school gameplay, energy-filled art and animations, just everything about the game oozes charm and personality. This was clearly made by developers who love their craft and wanted this game to be fantastic. While I haven't played any of the previous Shantae games (Nothing against them, just wasn't interested), this game seems to fit perfectly with the rest of them, but with some excellent modernization.
It's an absolute STEAL at $20. I can't wait to see how the developers will follow up to this fantastic platformer.
Maybe a Squid Baron standalone with $0.99 Shantae DLC is in order too. ;)

I met one of my greater friends on rust. Let me explain: I was raiding with another friend, she got stuck in room and had to log off. So while we were off, the owner of the base decided to build her in, as a prisoner. So he stripped her naked and made a prison cell. So I decided to go get some explosives, I crafted a ton of beancan grenades for a simple solution.  I blew myself into a ladder hatch and jumped down ( As stupid as I was ). Surprise surprise, I had gotten stuck as well... There were about three doors left from rescuing my friend, so I made an attempt to get through with my remaining beancan grenades. I did not succeed. And of course I had brought my most precious gear, and an ak. So I was in no mood of killing myself.
The dude that owned the base was kind of a mascot for our time on the server. His name was something along the lines of ¨SharkSlayer¨ or something. So we called him Sharkie-Boy, and we had secretly been stealing from him. ( I stood outside talking to him, while the other one ran into his base and stole some loot, as he always left his doors wide open when he went out ). Haha reminds me, he even gave me loot after we had stolen from him... Poor guy, I truly felt bad, but it was hilarous of how lost he was. He had no clue.
So he had trapped my friend, and I was stuck three rooms away with a hole in the ceiling. I remember thinking ¨F*ck. I'll never get this damn loot out...¨ But to my surprise I heard footsteps outside his base, and I knew it wasn't Sharkie, because he had been off for a while ( Checked server list as well ). So I listened, heard the person running around the base, inspecting the missing stone walls. He called out ¨ Uhm, hello? I'm kind of new to this game, can someone help me out?¨. I took the chance and answered ¨ Hey uh, can you come inside? I'm stuck and need help to get out. If you just follow the walls, *explained how he had to parkour to get up* then you can come in and help me up. I'll shoot you in the head, so you don't need to be trapped too. I'll place you a sleeping bed in my house that you can later spawn in. We can be buddies? Alright? I just need to get my stuff out.¨
And to my surprise this convinced him, and be boosted me up. I looked him in the eyes and said ¨ Are you ready? I'll pull the trigger, and then I will see you in a while buddy¨. He nodded and I pulled the trigger.
My other friend was still stuck inside, and she starved to death. So she came back to our base as well. This new dude spawned in my base, and I taught him everything he had to know about the game. I moved my base, and let him construct the new one. And now we are great friends, he has surpassed me in hours and is a great Rust player. And also, he introduced me to a clan, so I have made new friends there.
So Rust is really shines when it comes to the social aspect. Making stories, talking to people... Killing people... Stealing from sharks...

A racing game that that fully embraces and embodies the "Arcade Racer". The tracks all feel unique, range wildly in difficulty, and are short enough that it doesn't feel like a chore to replay a level to shave off a few milliseconds (as opposed races that take upwards of three minutes, where you may have to drive through the same few kilometers time and time again to get to the one corner you're focusing on). It ends up feeling like a condensed version of other racing games, where the races can take less than a minute, the tracks are full of interesting bits and concice, and the controls are very tight.
Additionally, the game looks great. It has a unified asthetic and looks smooth and polished, even on my sub-par labtop. The sound and music are not outstanding, but they serve the game well. It also has local multiplayer, which is always a plus in my books.
Finally, the track editor is excellent. It's not hard to make a good level, and the level editor makes it easy to make good looking games as well. I've only made a few low-quality tracks, but even then the ability to build>test>tweak>test>tweak>test makes the proscess enjoyable in itself.
Would recommend, especially if you've been turned off other racers in the past because you find them tedious.

I own this on PC and PS4/ Vita and I absolutely love it, fantastically addictive game. You play as a member of a family whose sole ambition in life is to infiltrate the mysterious castle, I won't give too much away in terms of story but each time you die you return s an heir to the previous family member. You can choose between 3 heirs and each will have their own class, strengths and weaknesses. This game is incredibly underrated, and it actually annoys me a little that it hasn't gotten the attention it deserves. It starts off like a typical action/war-game would. You are on a mission and you have a task or a goal to achieve. Once you progress through  the game, you will encounter some tough desicions and some seriously tough outcomes. This game has an incredibly deep story which totally blew me away, because I seriously didn't expect it. I haven't played the game for a long time, but I finished the storyline, and it made a huge impression on me.
I will not spoil the game's story, but it has a crazy turning point and some serious mind♥♥♥♥s beyond measure, that I never expected when I bought the game. If you decide to play through the story, make sure that you listen carefully to the dialogs and pay attention to the details. Seriously, it's worth it. This has been one of my best gaming-experiences in a long time. The game is very emotional, especially towards the end. It represents war in a realistic way, and shows the outcome and damages it causes. It's not just a typical action game where you kill  the bad-guys and save the day. It's so much more than that. It makes you really reflect over your choises and it's outcomes. The game has four possible endings, and you have the option to chose towards the end. You pick the one you want, and the one that you feel  is the correct one. Because as i said earlier, this game includes a massive mind♥♥♥♥ as you progress, and people would have different opinions on what they feel is the proper ending.
One of the things I'm not a great fan of, is some of the awkward controls. They are not bad, but it is not something I'm used to in a game within the genre. But you can of course mess around with key-bindings till you find something that works alright for you. The graphics are good and the voice-acting as great.
The game is also fairly cheap. But even if the game was more expensive, it would still be worth every cent. Very deep and very emotional game. The game is not perfect, but it is truly a great gaming-experience.

Just completed my second Shantae game. The guys at WayForward really now how to make a great game. I have no cons other than the game is a bit on the short side but there is still two more campaigns to go through. Can't wait for Risky mode!
Wayforward made a great shantae game, they really knocked it (and the dlc's for the most part) out of the park.

It's still a good game but I feel like the kickstarter model didn't do too much good to the game because it's a step back from Pirate's Curse. Personally I'd say Risky's Revenge is even a little bit better.
On the bright side they did progress from pixel art and have what I think is a great engine for the game. So perhaps there's some great potential in the future. The graphics, music and general movements are on point, although there are some minor bugs causing the game to stop for me from time to time. So overall it still plays great like a Shantae game. You get a lot of dances and the typical magic, which is very fun.
Where it gets insufficient and I suspect may be due to the kickstarter forcing them to implement so many elements to the game and thus not having enough time left, is the content and the story. The writing, first of all, seems a bit off. Shantae isn't a story focused game by any means but I thought this game story wise is especially shallow and did not portray the main characters as well as they can. Content wise you have so many powers and forms but there is very little content specifically designed for them, in some cases only one zone or none at all. Also, to inflate the content the devs added a lot of backtracing the the zones and since this game is no longer metroidvania style that's also not as good an experience as in previous games where revisiting zones and doing challenge dungeons can be so much fun. Another issue is boss difficulty tuning-- the later bosses are a joke unless you restrict yourself to not using any magic or item at all.
I think if this game was a bit more polished story wise and had 50% more content (that's not backtracing) it would have been great. As it is I still can't hate it because it's still Shantae but I don't regret not joining the kickstarter either.

15 Minutes of Gameplay:

I recieved a key as a promotion, (most of my other games have been humble bundles for my kids) but here is my honest review and overview.
8/10 A solid little turn based arcade strategy game. Expect a game session to take 15-30 minutes or more once you've progressed.
5+ hours of game play including leveling time for normal, plus 2 more challenging difficulties of nightmare, followed by hell. 10 rounds of play per difficulty, plus an endless survival option if you beat all ten. Each round takes a couple minutes, the later rounds generally taking more time.
Unfortunately there is no save (arcade style) during these attemps to beat all ten levels, but you do keep rewards earned for how far you make it. The rewards you keep are mithral for leveling characters and buying items and stars for using skills. Once mithral is spent it is gone, but the stars can be reassigned at any time before starting combat for differnt skill choices. Mithral is earned for every round beaten and many quests (completed milestones of progress) while stars are based on your total progress across all difficulties and survival rounds, i.e. beating the same rounds you've beaten before don't add stars.
A third reward type is used only during a specific playthough. Gold is used to level your characters total health, normal attack damage, and special attack damage for that playthrough only.
Game play is simple, you choose your 4 characters you want to play with - you start with 4 and the other 4 can be unlocked with mithral - they will be randomly assigned to the front or back column. The three in front use their normal attack while the back row may heal, or be moved to the front performing a special/super move switching places with one other hero of your choice. The character moved to the back then heals some instead of attacking. Your turn plays as soon as you switch two characters then the enemies attack and advance. If you want to keep your current three in the front column, you may switch two of them and their normal attacks will fire in their new position. You never move outside these two ranks, the rest of the 3x7 grid is used for enemies. Each class has a different set of super and normal attacks. The healer for example has a ranged normal attack and a heal when moving forward. All the characters except the witcher have a ranged attack either in the super or normal attack. This is important since the ranged enemies don't seem to advance into melee range. As you advance through the game your enemies become both more numerous and diverse in the strategies necessary to defeat them. Luckily your team also gains new powers and potency as they level, and new skills and items become available to you.
Every level your characters gain is a different upgrade, subtly changing the challenge as you advance. You have character progression locked after a certain number of upgrades until you beat the current difficulty level, so you always have to put some thought into total victory for each of the 3 difficulties and not just grind your way there.
8 character classes with unique strategies for each.
6 special "skills" of three levels each to aid your heroes and their options, such as improved healing in the rear position, or extra inventory slots.
12 expendable items to use, limited by your inventory spaces (2-6 depending on skills) and up to 2 of a type per inventory spot. these include items to revive a charcter (otherwise it's a loss on that round), extra attack damage for a number of rounds (3-4) or increased defense etc.
Moderate replay value, not quite diverse enough for high replability.
I hope for those interested the game gains some traction for my own sake cause I'd like to see additional characters to be added. That will depend at least in part on the success, or lack thereof, of the game going forward. Even new development teams can't live on aspirations alone after all.
I like it and I hope I've helped inform you whether or not you will.

+ 8 upgradable unique heroes
+ a variety of magical items to help your heroes survive longer
+ extra difficulty levels
+ nice soundtrack
+ steam achievements and trading cards
The game is funny and simple but still addictive and in my opinion is a nice time-killer for a couple of evenings. I'd recommend this game to people who like casual strategies and turn-based tactical games.

first off, this game isn’t bad. its actually very good.
it’s the grind that made me give this review a thumbs down.
so, the game starts off with you selecting a nation to start with. from what it seems like, they are mostly colour variations with slight differences to the stats.
and you have all the basic archetypes: the ones who love to trade, fight, explore and some other stuff.
then they put you in the game and it’s utterly gorgeous.
the water effects on maxed out settings are on the level of assassins creed black flag’s water effects.
and the soundtrack is filled with piratey goodness.. only there are 4 tracks in total, so you might want to google some pirate themed music and ‘alt tab’ the game now and then to play it.
the gameplay is also quite good. you move your ship by left clicking the mouse. the more you hold it down, the faster the ship will move.
to slow down you either right click or press the space bar. this makes your ship drop the anchor (you don’t see anything happen, though) and it brings you to a complete stop.
add to the fact that your ship will auto fire its cannons when the enemy gets in range and you have a wonderful and fulfilling combat experience.
however,  even with all that going for it,  the game is still far to grindy.
after getting out of the first zone (the dead easy one),  I spent 2 hours trying to kill the same pirates and their bases on a single map.
as another user said in their review,  the pirates will respawn much quicker when they only have one base, as it is the only place they can come from.
I thought I was going to blast them off the planet when I got the 3rd ship, but I was wrong.
even after playing long enough to get 8000 gold (you usually get 25 per ship killed) I barely did more damage then I used to.
even though the game gives you the option to recruit friendly ships and have them follow you, doing so takes away from the number of ships fighting the pirate threats.
and I’ve heard of another review, that once you get your own faction you are attacked by a never ending stream of pirates.
so to sum it all up: I would love the game but it gives me a pirate/grind overload.
Unless you really want to play multiplayer, better off playing Sid Meier's Pirates.

"If you clicked on this game to check it out, it's almost certain you'll like it."
Written April 2015, updated July 2015
April:  Since I've gotten a lot of enjoyment and hardly any frustration from this game, I figured it was worth writing my first game review.
July: The last couple updates added additional content that has made a good game more enjoyable, and I decided to expend additional...effort...praising the game.
Pros:
-Good interface - not perfect, but very useable and generally pain-free.
-Crisp, simple graphics - I'd like to see some tweaks to item placement though.
-Fun systems to play with - and many are optional.
-Replayability - Automation?  Miserable / nice conditions?  Max security inmates?
-Difficulty / challenge is easily determined by the player, essentially on the fly.
Cons:
-Some things take a bit of experimentation / quick internet search to figure out, but a builder like this is kinda all about experimentation anyway, so no biggie unless you're a terrible spoon-fed halfwit.
-I'd like to see a few more objects and, in some cases, things like more object rotation options (ironing boards can only be oriented 2 ways, not 4, same with doors)
Wall o Text:
It's deep for a casual game, which is perfect for when you want to do some thinking and designing, but aren't looking for pressure.  The depth comes from the clever systems the devs came up with, and you can choose to play around with them / ignore them at will.  I built a few prisons without remote door control, and now I'm enjoying the process of implementing remote doors into my plans.  It's fun to tinker with "zoning" which areas prisoners can go and which cells are assigned to min / max security inmates.  Designing good traffic flows, schedules (regime), guard stations, and secure buildings is satisfying.  And finally, it's downright awesome to see a prisoner hopping around like a madman, crapping all over a cell, desperate for drugs.  That never gets old.
Notes on Recent Additions:
The devs continue to add cool, well integrated features in a timely and logical fashion.  Every time I'm ready for another playthrough, there's something new.  Executions were a good addition.  Cell grading and gangs were in the late June update, and they add a welcome bit of challenge and depth to the game.
TL/DR:  Turn your money into fun.  The developers obviously have a sense of humor.  Alpha?  Sure, whatever you say.  Currently it's $30, and worth the investment.

One of those games that tugs at your mind long after you've walked away from it. And I couldn't wait to get back and try new ideas.
I like "systems games." Games where one designs a complex mechanism or system and then watches it go, usually to the point of failure, and then modifies and tries again. Prison Architect did this handily.
There are some aspects that were either unfinished (Early Access) or beyond my reckoning. E.g. I found myself ignoring the prisoner dossiers, partly because I wasn't sure if it mattered.
However, my wife and I spent hours poring over the layout, predicting movement patterns, course-correcting, and scrapping to try again. We would chuckle about "checking in on our prison" while away from the computer.
I may have put it down for now, but I'm anxious to see where it goes next and pick it up again!

As a die-hard Lis franchise fan, I had to buy this game. I loved the first two episodes and loved the way D9 portrayed the relationship between Chloe and Rachel, I felt like there was finallly going to be -to put it simply- something nice and soft for us gays (I was somewhat wrong). I really liked the new characters as well as the music. But during the second episode I was already wondering/worried about how they were going to fit in the answers to all the questions we still had, in just one episode.
I was right, episode 3 felt rushed and was shorter than the other two episodes, or at least, there were more cutscenes and there was less actual playtime. It seemed that the lesbian relationship (depending on what your choices were) between Chloe and Rachel was quite different from what it was in the first two episodes: What happened to the affection between the two? Where did all the scenes with them go? There was barely any interaction between the two of them. It seemed as if D9 decided to make the relationship 'less gay' (?) all of a sudden. It was just hopping and transporting from scene to scene, and one useless and odd 'BackTalk' moment. The thing they pulled after the credits was not very fair either. It was an unnecessary addition to an otherwise soft and sweet ending. Apart from that I heard there were quite a few bugs in the Third episode (not in 1 & 2 or in my game though). And there are some inconsistencies regarding the original game as well. There are still some questions left unanswered after the last episode.
Anyhow, I would still 100% recommend this game if you're a LIS-fan and want to spend as much time in Arcadia Bay as you can. It can also be a very nice game for people who seek gay representation (you gotta get what you can get). I enjoyed playing it, I just thought the last episode could have been way better, I'm pretty sure they cut a lot of stuff out.  But I'm still very glad this game came out and that I got to be in Arcadia Bay one last time, and I liked the end choice you had to make. I'm looking forward to the Bonus Episode with Max.

I have put a lot thought in whether or not I like Life is Strange: Before the Storm. Is it worth recommending? Can I see pass my own personnal biases to see the game objectively ? Probably not, but I will try never the less. SPOILERS AHEAD
Whether you are new to the series or if you have already dealt with Max`s Reality altering shennanigans you will soon find yourself in control of Chloe Price:  A traumatized teenager who has lost her father, is in state of clinical depression and feels abandoned by her best friend and her mother. Quite tragic
You see, I try to never enter a game about teen angst expecting said teen to be a wholesome individual, but there are aspects of CHloe that result particulary unsavory, even if you are already acquainted with her from the original game: Not even ten minutes the game , you are given the option  to thrash some dude`s car, steal clothing from him in addition to his cash. Not bad enough? How about using the cash to buy you some drugs? Charming. I get the angle is to represent how hurting Chloe is, but this perpetual state of toxicity does not make CHloe a plesant protagonist, maybe that`s the point, but it railroads the narrative into a certain direction: Its really hard to feel your input as meaningful when most options will always feel into the sphere of CHloe`s Toxic Angst. In case, it felt borderline frustrating: Always having to oscilate into self-compassion and confrontional selfishness . I know that CHloe is hurting, and all in the game is supposed to reflect that but, I simply just couldnt grew too like her: I already felt antagonism towards her when she killed a man and his dog for info a about the whereabouts of her gal-pal, but this showcases another problem.
Chloe was never better than that. Is hard to see her as a wounded child worthy in emphathy when you see her in context
Then , there is the Strange Case of Rachel Amber: To be quite honest, the first time I interacted with her...She gave me the creeps. In the first episode there was something truly uncanny about her (again, maybe intentional) but not in a misterious or charming way, I was expecting her to get a jump and CHloe and then sacrifice her to Old Gods or something ¬¬U...
About her character? Well...If get to the nitty-gritty of her personality there isnt really that much to say, Perfect Girl Archetype: Beatiful, Intelligent, Passionate, Determined. Quite boring if you ask me. But comes with a twist, her father had hidden from her the fact that her biological mother, a woman named Sera, abandoned her after a long period of neglect(Did I mention Sera was a drug addict?)  This however promps some sort of psycological self-destruct mechanism what leads her to take some very questionable choices which lead to:
*Getting stabbed by a criminal.
*Causing a guy to get stabbed to buy her and Chloe some time to escape
*Manipulating CHloe into breaking into the DA`s office to find Sera
*Getting Cloe to be assaulted by the aforementioned criminal
*Putting the life of the aforementioned guy in risk again
There is a sense of ambivalence about Rachel`s actions, which might Before the Storm`s greatest narrative achivement, but at some times are so contrary to common sense (Remember, we are talking about an allegedly brillant young woman here) that baffles me. At one point I remember yelling at the screen "Rachel, by  f***s sake stay put and keep you damnable mouth shut" Which further oumpounded into my sense of frustration with the game. There were time in which I truly wanted to feel symphaty for Rachel but the fact she has proven to be a manipulative succubus and I cannot ensure her words or actions are genuine I simply couldnt.
And thats the problem(or at leats my problem): I do understand the fact that even the most intimately made games which include narrative choices only offer the illusion of choice, but between Chloe`s perpetual state of angst and Rachel almost parasitic (?) companionship I feel little in the way of meaningful choosing in the game and makes the relationship between CHloe and Rachel feel less organic. I would have loved an ending in which they end in Bad Terms, even if they are reconcialed in the end sequence because otherwise impregnates Rachel with aura of Dominance over Chloe
I get that we only can make choices that Chloe would make, but then again, whats the point of playing if nothing we will ever make will make a dent on Chloe`s actions or personality? In that regard, the game did feel as an exercise of fuitily for me.
Then there is the secondary cast of characters: Some are recurring from the first game, some others are new but they both equal in regards to their relevance to theplot, which is none. They ried infuse some personality into some of them: some are geeky, some are compassionate, some are in-debt with a drug-dealer, but all of this felt like an after thought given the narrative tendecy to orbit the Rachel-Chloe axis. I didnt feel as if there was something to loose if they were to be removed from the story. Perhaps with exception of Rachel`s father, but he is portrayed so comically villainous (including the goon hiring) that is hard to say he is "complex character", there is some depth in his love for Rachel, but the devs decided to scratch that notion by making him even more evil. And his wife Rose , the woman who raised Rachel, might aswell not be there, and that`s a shame, because she a lot of potentional given the context of the story.
All and all, I cannot truly recommend this game given how "railroady" it is: in the first game you could at least act in such a way that gave the impression that Max can think and act in the best interest of of Chloe and not be reduced to a thrall of hers. Polarazing descisions might labelled as unrealistic and gamey, but I felt they would have done a favor to this game in particular
My advice? Watch some playthrough of it without comments in Youtube, you wont be missing  much in the interactive aspect I assure you,  if you are a die hard Life is Strange fanboy and you need to scratch that itching , stay determined and wait for a sale

For a long time now have I been obsessed with scenarios concerning the twilight of human civilization, whether entirely fictional or somewhat probable. Yet the Mad Max world  appeared on my radar only alongside Fury Road. Due to its close match to the themes that I enjoy, it managed to score bonus points on top of my already lenient, easygoing approach to reviewing, where I tend to focus on the positives. But don't get me wrong, there's much more to this recommendation than the bias induced by my personal tastes - this is just a great product. I'm also a big fan of almost anything paranormal, supernatural. And the complete lack of such elements exhibited by this game would normally be a turn off, but here it instead adds a delicious glaze of knowing that man and man alone could inflict such things on himself. For the record, I filed the scenario depicted herein under "somewhat probable".
The graphics are nothing short of glorious. The sky and clouds, in their myriad colours, are beautiful and form an enchanting contrast with the harshness of the Wasteland. And the Wasteland is also surprisingly pretty despite its limitations - nowhere will you find any greenery, all vegetation is dead and dry. Just the various shades of dirt and sand and rock, and the occasional black of oil. Yet not once - in almost 80 hours - was I tired of watching this landscape. Not sure how they pulled this off, but it's impressive... even more so considering my past encounters with the Fallout series, where the colours of
wasteland have always been turning me off and away. The animations are smooth and the bullet time in combat can create some downright cinematic scenes. When driving, you can either stay with the default third-person camera, which is best suited to relishing the views, or switch to a faux-fps view for enhanced realism and immersion. It's a difficult choice but I wish all choices in life were this kind of difficult. And then the storms... and the experience of fighting a convoy inside of a storm... it made me regret not having a VR headset yet.
There is a huge amount of stuff to do, but some may see the content as repetitive. I, for one, was pleased. The scavenging and debris sites follow a clearly discernible design pattern, yet each was sufficiently unique to keep me interested; I liked imagining their stories based on what little information was conveyed through these locations. Similarly, the History Relics are a huge treat - little glimpses into the lives of strangers through which we can learn of the Fall. The look and feel of the world, its inhabitants and their lives is just right - hopeless in the long run, somber and grim without plunging
deeply into grotesque or pulpiness. There is food for thought here, but the game is smart about it and does not jam it down ones throat (most of the time, at least).
I suppose almost everyone starts to run from their past once they're old enough. Max seemed to be doing well at it, right up until he wasn't. Chumbucket was an endearing sidekick, right up until he wasn't. I admit I got completely blindsided by the twist in the second-to-last story mission, although the whole plot leading up to that point was predictable - but still majorly entertaining. While we didn't get to meet any characters from Fury Road other than our protagonist himself, the game does a good job of tying itself to the world it is based on - I kept getting the feeling that Bullet Town and the Citadel can't be far away. The voice acting is stellar and within you can hear and differentiate the personalities of Max and the cast. The rest of the audio is above average as well; I appreciated the subtleties of how different engines sound even though I know next to nothing about cars.
There are bugs, yes. I was going to sum them up by saying "nothing too terrible", but as time went on my patience wore thin. Menus randomly locking up, forcing me to alt-f4 the game, which in turn usually caused some progress loss because of how the autosave system works. Cars and enemies despawning (disappearing) before my face, sometimes mid-swing. The Magnum Opus's wheels often being half-buried in the ground after fast traveling (nitro fixes this). All kinds of physics shenanigans that come with depicting an open world as large as this. Very heavy, non-toggleable aim assist... I agree with it for vehicular combat, else the "cinematic scenes" mentioned earlier would've been hard to come across. But in ground (on-foot) combat it can conversely create some cringeworthy moments, particularly when it comes to sniping. Or you're trying to throw a lit explosive in between two fuel tanks (which happen to be targetable objects), but the game "helps out" and throws the payload directly at one of them (not where you were aiming).
I feel that more could've been done with the Wasteland wanderers - sometimes I don't have any water to spare but I'd like to give them a recently "liberated" car instead, or a lift to a stronghold. Some challenges are aggravating, especially Unstoppable; I still remember the feeling of liberation after finally completing it. The combat is... well, you know. It's a WB game, so maybe that is why it's Batman combat. It's very good though, I enjoyed it massively. However, the damage dealt to Max by snipers, by explosions, by being rammed by cars at full speed makes him look superhuman by way of how low it is. An experienced gamer will find the overall difficulty below average - you can tell they were aiming for the more casual crowd, the kind that perhaps might not play many games but would get this one because of the movie. And yet it's not as absurdly easy as Stick of Truth ended up being while chasing that audience - on the way down Avalanche stopped in a perfect place in terms of difficulty. Wholeheartedly recommended - this is the open world genre at its finest.

After the thrilling vehicular chaos that graced the silver screen last year in
, the time to translate the vast possibilities of exploration within the wasteland into a sandbox videogame couldn't have been anymore perfect. While not directly based on the film, this adaptation is a beast of its own with an original story and new characters that somewhat borrow from its cinematic predecessors.
Gamers take control of Max as his teams with a hunchback mechanic in order to rebuild his stolen chariot of death, and bring down the heavens against those who stole it and left him for dead. The wasteland is large and full of surprises that will certainly distract players from the main story for hours. Various locations contain collectibles, different enemies to bring down, and hidden camps to raid in a quest to level up Max, his vehicle, and of course, survive.
Gameplay revolves around fast paced action in hand to hand combat that controls very well with a fantastic counter system. Each chain of attack is never the same as leveling up unlocks further satisfying bone crunching, or eye gauging deaths. When not on foot, much of the action will take place in car combat flying off sand dunes while shooting out tires, or better yet, opposing drivers in mid air. The lock-on target system works exceptionally well with a few camera twitches every so often, but overall, it cannot be stressed enough the variety of ways one is allowed to create mayhem with Max. Whether on foot or in a buffed, post apocalyptic hell ride, the action never stops.
As expressed earlier, side quests include a variety of tasks that include scavenging smaller enemy camps, competing in death races, strengthening strongholds, seeking and destroying wasteland snipers or towers, collecting vehicles, infiltrating enemy headquarters which all have their own unique boss, taking down enemy convoys, or simply exploring in search of collectible history relics. The game is absolutely stunning in ultra settings, and each time an electric or sand storm erupted, I couldn't help but want to abuse the Capture Mode which allows players to undertake the role of a film director, and capture mini reels  and stills of the on-going aesthetic destruction.
While most will get lost within the numerous activities within the world of
, be warned that often times many of the challenges can become repetitive, so it is highly advised to balance out the free roam and main story progression.
However, with the exception of a few annoying glitches (none that were game breaking), a somewhat short main story, and a subjective opinion of what can be considered repetitive,
is an absolute blast that any fan of the George Miller films should experience. It is a stellar post apocalyptic experience, and overall gaming gem of 2015.

A bit of an adventure game ala prince of persia, with pits you need to jump and ropes you need to zip-line mixed with a bit of gearhead simulation, fortress building (or more, improving. Max scours the wasteland looking for scrap and interesting pieces that can be combined into improvements for your car, for max himself, or for the various fortresses that shelters him while adventuring in the region.
Building and improving on a new wagon that will carry Max across the Silent Wasteland, you run into warlords, bands of villains, interesting exotic locations, and you find hidden caches of scrap and ammo. Water is essencial since it replentishes your hitpoints, so you learn to keep your canteen full at all times.
Your hunchbacked sidekick Chumbucket keeps your car repaired and delivers one-liners when need be. He also acts as a spotter, warning you of warboys and buzzards and other dangers.
And sand storms. Big, red flashing sand storms that will impale you with electricity if don't find shelter or drive like hell.
I was afraid the game would anonymize the villains too much. The warboys in the movie were all given personalities and names and you could see them several times thoughout the heated action scenes. In a sense, you "witnessed" all of them go either under the wheel of a tractor or explode as they sacrificed themselves.
In this game, the warboys are mindless cretins that only need to be pummeled down. The more important npcs however have personalities, decent voice-actors and wonderful scripts.
The fighting mechanics is easy to get a hang of, and the incremental build-up of "rage" in a fight that makes you ever more powerful for every successive hit you land, gives you a feeling of being really bloody good at what you're doing and a proper badass.
I got bored within the first hour...

Well, as a start I'd like to say that I didn't want to play this game for a fairly long time, I bought a deluxe edition in June 2013 (It had belt buckle, OST disc and Nukecity DLC). I installed it only around November of the following year and got to actually play it somewhat in beginning of May.
And, yes, I underestimated it.
The game itself looks better than its ancestors in fact, it is clearly seen at points, faces show expressions and the characters don't look like robots...The graphics did become better as well, comparing to MW3, it's made a decent leap. Everything, looks better, somewhat like Mirror's Edge especially to the end of the game when things start exploding (YEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEAH).
The story is divided into three parts. Let me tell about every of them in short:
First story:
As usual, flashbacks of Woods, who did survive in Laos (or it was Vietnam?..) Anyway, this looks pretty interesting, has some stupid moments, some ridiculous twists, but to be honest, I liked this part the most. It ends at somewhat middle of entire game
Second story:
The main part, protagonist of which is son of Alex Mason, who follows old foe of his father and so on and so forth. This part takes place in 2025. it has some futuristic features, but all in all, the gameplay is pretty sample to first. I didn't like this one too much, even though it has a pretty charismatic character named Harper, and that it has the most conscious plot...The thing is that this part looks a lot like Crysis because of those future weapons and stuff. I know, that it hardly would look any different, if you want to make some close-future shooter, but still.
Third story:
Is kinda the ♥♥♥♥♥iest for me. You command a squad that goes all around the world, defending different places from the main villain's troops. It's made as a tactical part of game, you have around 10 soldiers and machines under your control and you can control every of them on your own, but as tactics it's pretty useless...Choose all your troops and command to attack enemy, not a big deal. I finished it as well, so there.
The thing I did like about the game is the variety of endings. The thing is that the only two things you're going to care for are Woods and Harper, so that doesn't matter way much, but in game it is pretty exciting, to choose things, knowing it may affect the game
Sound is good, I really liked the ending, even though not fan of A7X, but yeah, pretty cool
I hardly played multiplayer, but it looks pretty fun too, a lot like MW2 which I did like
In the end, would I recommend this game? Yes, if you're afraid to waste your time on one more "CoD ♥♥♥♥♥♥ shooter omg", then leave your fears, it's pretty decent even though pretty easy (played on hard difficulty, died only 7 times throughout the game, the squad was lost only once)
In the end, I'd say 8.4/10. Would have been better if not that stupid tactical feature

Once again, I wish Steam had a neutral review option.  This game isn't really bad, it's just not any fun if you play single-player like I do.  If there's anything to really describe it, imagine an endless game of Call of Duty or Battlefield where there are 10 capture points, and the game is only over once every one of them is captured. Then, you move to a functionally identical new map and do it all over again... Except it's not first person, it's overhead with poor line-of-sight, it's MUCH slower, and the controls are frustrating because clicking to shoot an enemy at the top-right corner of the screen instead opens up the map.
I went into this game wanting to really like it, but I just can't help but feel like it lied to me about what it really was...  EDIT: The game's developers have since rewritten the game's description to say, essentially, it's not even meant to be played single-player, but since that's the only way I would really care to play, it's more clear what it is to potential new customers, but doesn't change how I look at the game.
For example, the game says that you can trade, and it even offers a trading faction, but then, trading doesn't really DO anything.  The game only helps you understand what trades are available within one small map which usually only has 4-8 towns, and all of which generally use the same commodities.  Also, to get better trade ships, you need to sink ships, which means that to play a "peaceful" trader role, you need to perform combat.  Combat gains you experience/upgrades, but trading doesn't, meaning that trading is basically an invalid way to play.
You can name your own towns, but as soon as you've colonized an area, and kicked out anyone else trying to take control of it, there's basically no reason to stick around, and it's time to head off to the next area, completely forgetting all those areas you tried to build up, before.  You COULD found your own town, and work on growing it by hand for hours on end... or just take over a fully-grown town for a hundredth of the effort.  Towns have zero customizability past what they are named and where they are located, so there's zero investment in any of them.
It's hypothetically capable of being played single-player, but there's very little reason you'd want to do so.  You move into an area, conquer it, then rinse and repeat the next island down the road.  Also, playing single-player, the instances, especially the combat instances, are nigh-impossible to win solo, as your side is outnumbered, the enemies tend to be stronger than your ship, so they respawn faster than you can sink them, and the main way to win is to simply grab what are overglorified capture points.  Without the coordination or intelligence of a human team, any time you grab a few towns, some others are lost, and any time you defend what you have, it's just an unlimited stream of the same enemies coming at you again and again until you get bored and quit.
Obviously, some people are capable of having a good time being in some clans and fighting competitive games, but there's very little enjoyable gameplay for someone like me who actually wanted to play the trading and exploring aspects this game pretended it had, but really didn't have.   This game is only meant to be played as a nautical-themed DOTA MMO, and any other playstyle is invalid.

"If you clicked on this game to check it out, it's almost certain you'll like it."
Written April 2015, updated July 2015
April:  Since I've gotten a lot of enjoyment and hardly any frustration from this game, I figured it was worth writing my first game review.
July: The last couple updates added additional content that has made a good game more enjoyable, and I decided to expend additional...effort...praising the game.
Pros:
-Good interface - not perfect, but very useable and generally pain-free.
-Crisp, simple graphics - I'd like to see some tweaks to item placement though.
-Fun systems to play with - and many are optional.
-Replayability - Automation?  Miserable / nice conditions?  Max security inmates?
-Difficulty / challenge is easily determined by the player, essentially on the fly.
Cons:
-Some things take a bit of experimentation / quick internet search to figure out, but a builder like this is kinda all about experimentation anyway, so no biggie unless you're a terrible spoon-fed halfwit.
-I'd like to see a few more objects and, in some cases, things like more object rotation options (ironing boards can only be oriented 2 ways, not 4, same with doors)
Wall o Text:
It's deep for a casual game, which is perfect for when you want to do some thinking and designing, but aren't looking for pressure.  The depth comes from the clever systems the devs came up with, and you can choose to play around with them / ignore them at will.  I built a few prisons without remote door control, and now I'm enjoying the process of implementing remote doors into my plans.  It's fun to tinker with "zoning" which areas prisoners can go and which cells are assigned to min / max security inmates.  Designing good traffic flows, schedules (regime), guard stations, and secure buildings is satisfying.  And finally, it's downright awesome to see a prisoner hopping around like a madman, crapping all over a cell, desperate for drugs.  That never gets old.
Notes on Recent Additions:
The devs continue to add cool, well integrated features in a timely and logical fashion.  Every time I'm ready for another playthrough, there's something new.  Executions were a good addition.  Cell grading and gangs were in the late June update, and they add a welcome bit of challenge and depth to the game.
TL/DR:  Turn your money into fun.  The developers obviously have a sense of humor.  Alpha?  Sure, whatever you say.  Currently it's $30, and worth the investment.

However, my wife and I spent hours poring over the layout, predicting movement patterns, course-correcting, and scrapping to try again. We would chuckle about "checking in on our prison" while away from the computer.
I may have put it down for now, but I'm anxious to see where it goes next and pick it up again!

Guards is a 2.5D turn-based strategic RPG game with simple low poly graphic and nice heroic music in background. From the beginning the game will set your mood right with an interesting fighting technique and with the offer of eight different classes. Naturally you have to progressively buy and upgrade new characters for obtained Mithrils (in-game currency). Before you start your adventure you have to choose a lucky team of four. Each hero has different abilities and can be deadly dangerous in combination with other team members. Every journey has 10 levels and 3 difficulty levels, which are progressively unlocked if you have vanquished the easier level.
The fight takes place on the chessboard of size 3x7. Each character has given field of activity and the number of possible targets. To play your move, it is always necessary to swap the positions of two of your characters. Your heroes are placed into 2 rows – 3 in the first one and one in the second one. If you move a hero from the front to the back, he/she will be healed every turn that he/she stay there. But when you move a hero from the back to the front, you will activate their special abilities.
Is it too hard for you? Is the final boss permanently kicking your♥♥♥♥♥ You can boost your heroes and turn the score! You can buy different boosts for Mithrils in the shop – potions, stone slabs of time etc. To be able to use more useful things on your road, you have to conquer as many levels as you can or complete as many quests as you can – in order to get stars. With those stars you can upgrade your passive skills (e.g. more inventory slots, better healing, more coins for upgrades).
There are 2 different types of upgrades in this game – permanent (for Mithrils) or temporary (for coins). After each successful level, you can temporarily upgrade your heroes (more hp, better attacks…) for the collected coins and if you lose, the effect disappears. Usually you can’t buy all the offered improvements, so you have to decide and tactically buy the best ones.
Guards was an interesting experience. I enjoyed the competition which this game caused in me, but at this moment I have vanquished all levels of difficulty and most of achievements. The game does not attract me further on and maybe I will come back to it after a larger update patch.

Guards is a colorful 3D TBS and I have to say it’s one of the better ones I played in quite some time. I enjoyed the seemingly simple combat system which encourages pacience and while it does involve some grinding eventually, I never felt bored or compelled to stop because of its increasing difficulty. I welcomed it with open arms, but perhaps for some newer players to this genre, this might represent a hindrance. The art style in Guards is reminiscent of cel shading and I enjoyed the ragdoll-like appearance of characters and units within the game. The presence of items and hero skills, does spice things up and offers plenty of strategic variety on its own. The soundtrack was pleasant enough, though nothing out of the ordinary. Still, the game looks and plays great for most strategy fans out there who don’t  mind some degree of repetitiveness. Guards received recently a hefty patch and I for one never encountered any glitches or bugs. Any recently released indie title which already gets patched to this level, deserves praise since we’re getting more and more used today, seeing  big-budget games fail miserably from a stable gameplay perspective. So Battlecruiser Games made a stallar job at providing and updating a very well polished game, their first project released on Steam. The price tag is fully justified.

Incredibly fun game engine, some top notch voice acting. Sound and visuals are excellent. Sadly the game itself lacks depth.
I would love to have seen a little more detail. The interior and exterior locations are beautifully designed and varied enough while still fitting into a wasteland environment. Sadly, you are almost strictly collecting 'scrap' which is the currency you use to upgrade your car and yourself. Would have been nice to see some variance in items (collecting wires, sheet metal, finding actual parts instead of amorphous 'scrap')
The NPCs you encounter in the wasteland serve very little point. Share your water with them, feel better about yourself? Good because it doesn't really seem to do much else. You can listen to them mumble and sometimes point you in the direction of scrap because there isn't already tons of it littering the countryside.
Exploring the interior levels was fun and they are gorgeous, but I was never 'discovering' anything. There were no surprises or secrets. It counts down how much more scrap you have to find and tells you when you've found it all. For all the work that obviously went into designing the levels, they seem sterile and missing personality. The incentive to explore new locations ran out when I knew all I could get was more scrap and already had plenty.
I still enjoyed all 50 hours that I played, and I can see myself going back and visiting my hunchback friend in the future just to make life miserable for the bad guys of the wasteland.

For a long time now have I been obsessed with scenarios concerning the twilight of human civilization, whether entirely fictional or somewhat probable. Yet the Mad Max world  appeared on my radar only alongside Fury Road. Due to its close match to the themes that I enjoy, it managed to score bonus points on top of my already lenient, easygoing approach to reviewing, where I tend to focus on the positives. But don't get me wrong, there's much more to this recommendation than the bias induced by my personal tastes - this is just a great product. I'm also a big fan of almost anything paranormal, supernatural. And the complete lack of such elements exhibited by this game would normally be a turn off, but here it instead adds a delicious glaze of knowing that man and man alone could inflict such things on himself. For the record, I filed the scenario depicted herein under "somewhat probable".
The graphics are nothing short of glorious. The sky and clouds, in their myriad colours, are beautiful and form an enchanting contrast with the harshness of the Wasteland. And the Wasteland is also surprisingly pretty despite its limitations - nowhere will you find any greenery, all vegetation is dead and dry. Just the various shades of dirt and sand and rock, and the occasional black of oil. Yet not once - in almost 80 hours - was I tired of watching this landscape. Not sure how they pulled this off, but it's impressive... even more so considering my past encounters with the Fallout series, where the colours of
wasteland have always been turning me off and away. The animations are smooth and the bullet time in combat can create some downright cinematic scenes. When driving, you can either stay with the default third-person camera, which is best suited to relishing the views, or switch to a faux-fps view for enhanced realism and immersion. It's a difficult choice but I wish all choices in life were this kind of difficult. And then the storms... and the experience of fighting a convoy inside of a storm... it made me regret not having a VR headset yet.
There is a huge amount of stuff to do, but some may see the content as repetitive. I, for one, was pleased. The scavenging and debris sites follow a clearly discernible design pattern, yet each was sufficiently unique to keep me interested; I liked imagining their stories based on what little information was conveyed through these locations. Similarly, the History Relics are a huge treat - little glimpses into the lives of strangers through which we can learn of the Fall. The look and feel of the world, its inhabitants and their lives is just right - hopeless in the long run, somber and grim without plunging
deeply into grotesque or pulpiness. There is food for thought here, but the game is smart about it and does not jam it down ones throat (most of the time, at least).
I suppose almost everyone starts to run from their past once they're old enough. Max seemed to be doing well at it, right up until he wasn't. Chumbucket was an endearing sidekick, right up until he wasn't. I admit I got completely blindsided by the twist in the second-to-last story mission, although the whole plot leading up to that point was predictable - but still majorly entertaining. While we didn't get to meet any characters from Fury Road other than our protagonist himself, the game does a good job of tying itself to the world it is based on - I kept getting the feeling that Bullet Town and the Citadel can't be far away. The voice acting is stellar and within you can hear and differentiate the personalities of Max and the cast. The rest of the audio is above average as well; I appreciated the subtleties of how different engines sound even though I know next to nothing about cars.
There are bugs, yes. I was going to sum them up by saying "nothing too terrible", but as time went on my patience wore thin. Menus randomly locking up, forcing me to alt-f4 the game, which in turn usually caused some progress loss because of how the autosave system works. Cars and enemies despawning (disappearing) before my face, sometimes mid-swing. The Magnum Opus's wheels often being half-buried in the ground after fast traveling (nitro fixes this). All kinds of physics shenanigans that come with depicting an open world as large as this. Very heavy, non-toggleable aim assist... I agree with it for vehicular combat, else the "cinematic scenes" mentioned earlier would've been hard to come across. But in ground (on-foot) combat it can conversely create some cringeworthy moments, particularly when it comes to sniping. Or you're trying to throw a lit explosive in between two fuel tanks (which happen to be targetable objects), but the game "helps out" and throws the payload directly at one of them (not where you were aiming).
I feel that more could've been done with the Wasteland wanderers - sometimes I don't have any water to spare but I'd like to give them a recently "liberated" car instead, or a lift to a stronghold. Some challenges are aggravating, especially Unstoppable; I still remember the feeling of liberation after finally completing it. The combat is... well, you know. It's a WB game, so maybe that is why it's Batman combat. It's very good though, I enjoyed it massively. However, the damage dealt to Max by snipers, by explosions, by being rammed by cars at full speed makes him look superhuman by way of how low it is. An experienced gamer will find the overall difficulty below average - you can tell they were aiming for the more casual crowd, the kind that perhaps might not play many games but would get this one because of the movie. And yet it's not as absurdly easy as Stick of Truth ended up being while chasing that audience - on the way down Avalanche stopped in a perfect place in terms of difficulty. Wholeheartedly recommended - this is the open world genre at its finest.

After the thrilling vehicular chaos that graced the silver screen last year in
, the time to translate the vast possibilities of exploration within the wasteland into a sandbox videogame couldn't have been anymore perfect. While not directly based on the film, this adaptation is a beast of its own with an original story and new characters that somewhat borrow from its cinematic predecessors.
Gamers take control of Max as his teams with a hunchback mechanic in order to rebuild his stolen chariot of death, and bring down the heavens against those who stole it and left him for dead. The wasteland is large and full of surprises that will certainly distract players from the main story for hours. Various locations contain collectibles, different enemies to bring down, and hidden camps to raid in a quest to level up Max, his vehicle, and of course, survive.
Gameplay revolves around fast paced action in hand to hand combat that controls very well with a fantastic counter system. Each chain of attack is never the same as leveling up unlocks further satisfying bone crunching, or eye gauging deaths. When not on foot, much of the action will take place in car combat flying off sand dunes while shooting out tires, or better yet, opposing drivers in mid air. The lock-on target system works exceptionally well with a few camera twitches every so often, but overall, it cannot be stressed enough the variety of ways one is allowed to create mayhem with Max. Whether on foot or in a buffed, post apocalyptic hell ride, the action never stops.
As expressed earlier, side quests include a variety of tasks that include scavenging smaller enemy camps, competing in death races, strengthening strongholds, seeking and destroying wasteland snipers or towers, collecting vehicles, infiltrating enemy headquarters which all have their own unique boss, taking down enemy convoys, or simply exploring in search of collectible history relics. The game is absolutely stunning in ultra settings, and each time an electric or sand storm erupted, I couldn't help but want to abuse the Capture Mode which allows players to undertake the role of a film director, and capture mini reels  and stills of the on-going aesthetic destruction.
While most will get lost within the numerous activities within the world of
, be warned that often times many of the challenges can become repetitive, so it is highly advised to balance out the free roam and main story progression.
However, with the exception of a few annoying glitches (none that were game breaking), a somewhat short main story, and a subjective opinion of what can be considered repetitive,
is an absolute blast that any fan of the George Miller films should experience. It is a stellar post apocalyptic experience, and overall gaming gem of 2015.

So far it is my favorite game on steam. It's truly a game where you write your own story, you make both friends and enemies as you go along.
I met one of my greater friends on rust. Let me explain: I was raiding with another friend, she got stuck in room and had to log off. So while we were off, the owner of the base decided to build her in, as a prisoner. So he stripped her naked and made a prison cell. So I decided to go get some explosives, I crafted a ton of beancan grenades for a simple solution.  I blew myself into a ladder hatch and jumped down ( As stupid as I was ). Surprise surprise, I had gotten stuck as well... There were about three doors left from rescuing my friend, so I made an attempt to get through with my remaining beancan grenades. I did not succeed. And of course I had brought my most precious gear, and an ak. So I was in no mood of killing myself.
The dude that owned the base was kind of a mascot for our time on the server. His name was something along the lines of ¨SharkSlayer¨ or something. So we called him Sharkie-Boy, and we had secretly been stealing from him. ( I stood outside talking to him, while the other one ran into his base and stole some loot, as he always left his doors wide open when he went out ). Haha reminds me, he even gave me loot after we had stolen from him... Poor guy, I truly felt bad, but it was hilarous of how lost he was. He had no clue.
So he had trapped my friend, and I was stuck three rooms away with a hole in the ceiling. I remember thinking ¨F*ck. I'll never get this damn loot out...¨ But to my surprise I heard footsteps outside his base, and I knew it wasn't Sharkie, because he had been off for a while ( Checked server list as well ). So I listened, heard the person running around the base, inspecting the missing stone walls. He called out ¨ Uhm, hello? I'm kind of new to this game, can someone help me out?¨. I took the chance and answered ¨ Hey uh, can you come inside? I'm stuck and need help to get out. If you just follow the walls, *explained how he had to parkour to get up* then you can come in and help me up. I'll shoot you in the head, so you don't need to be trapped too. I'll place you a sleeping bed in my house that you can later spawn in. We can be buddies? Alright? I just need to get my stuff out.¨
And to my surprise this convinced him, and be boosted me up. I looked him in the eyes and said ¨ Are you ready? I'll pull the trigger, and then I will see you in a while buddy¨. He nodded and I pulled the trigger.
My other friend was still stuck inside, and she starved to death. So she came back to our base as well. This new dude spawned in my base, and I taught him everything he had to know about the game. I moved my base, and let him construct the new one. And now we are great friends, he has surpassed me in hours and is a great Rust player. And also, he introduced me to a clan, so I have made new friends there.
So Rust is really shines when it comes to the social aspect. Making stories, talking to people... Killing people... Stealing from sharks...

Then after a while I had this game that went well, I just finished building a max security facility for my violent prisoners, when 6 prisoners managed to escape by digging below the administration building and out to the road.
And there was the time we did construction in the max security block, and two prisoners had drills on them.
You eventually discover that planning is key, and spend time using the planning tools to scheme out the complex or a new cell block. Everything can fall apart pretty badly in this game with careless construction.

Nothing is labeled well enough to navigate menus, build correctly, or do anything. Spent 25 minutes laying down foundations and building your mess hall? Oops, the game forgot to tell you that your mess hall needs a specific piece of furniture or it won't count! Also, this piece of furniture must be oriented in a specific way for prisoners to access it, but we won't tell you which way! Yep, you guessed it correctly, but now it's blocking the door and you can't actually change the location of the door because the builder AI is broken, and the builders will never dismantle stuff that you've clearly told them to dismantle so god forbid you misclick.
So after restarting literally a dozen times (because the prisoners show up so quickly the first day that you don't have time to change  your mind at all) you finally get things oriented correctly and labeled and the builders managed to build it all on time and you didn't accidentally place an impossible-to-remove door somewhere. Oops! Your mess hall must be 5x8 tiles large or else the game arbitrarily decides that it doesn't qualify as a mess hall... and the game thought it would be fun to just let you discover that bit of info on your own.
"Prison Architect" is actually a great name for this game. It's telling that it's not called "Prison Builder" or "Prison Warden" or anything like that because "Prison Architect" describes exactly what you do! You create designs for prisons and tell the computer AI what you want it to build... and then your job is over because the prison won't ever get built and you'll never actually be able to run it.

I can't believe I'm saying this, but Life is Strange: Before The Storm sucks. The original Life is Strange was amazing - interesting and logical plot, many likable characters, hard choices (in which I really needed some time to think about). What do we have here? A romance. That's basically what the entire game is - the relationship between Rachel and Chloe. And don't get me wrong, this idea doesn't seem bad at all, but Deck Nine somehow managed to ♥♥♥♥ it up...
First of all, as I said, there's only one plot: Rachel and Chloe. In the previous game, we had: Rachel's kidnapping, Max Cauffield's rewinding time power, Max and Chloe's relationship, Prescotts and a few more. Here, you pretty much won't find anything except Rachel and Chloe's love. That's an obvious fan service; they fall in love basically the first day they meet, and from that day on they suddenly know everything about each other and are willing to sacrifice themselves in order to save the other one. I'm not a big fan of rushing things like that, but okay, it's still pretty fun. Then you get to see some familiar faces, like Frank or Nathan, but they are present for maybe five minutes tops, and don't play any important role in the game. Episode's 2 ending was supposed to be a big wow moment I guess, but I was totally indifferent. But then, episode 3 came out... and it turns out that it's possible to make the game even worse.
I'm sorry, as much as I love both Chloe and Rachel, this entire game just sucks. I think that Deck Nine thought that if we get a lesbian romance, then nothing else really matters, so ♥♥♥♥ the plot, ♥♥♥♥ the logic, give them a nice kiss and let's get this over with. ♥♥♥♥♥♥ move. If I wanted a romance, I would buy myself a Barbie Date Rush.
So, to sum up: rushing Chloe&Rachel relationship, lack of logic, very easy choices (and only the last one really matters), pretty much ignoring the existence of characters other than Chloe and Rachel almost the entire game and uninteresting plot made me hate this game. I'm not sure if I'll buy the next one.

Spec Ops: The Line is set in a war torn Dubai in the aftermath of an unprecedented sandstorm that left the city engulfed in sand. You take up the role of Captain Martin Walker, leader of a Delta team alongside Lieutenant Adams and Sergeant Lugo. Together, you've been sent to Dubai after a strange radio transmission was reported and your objective is to search for any remaining survivors. Dubai, (meant to be completely uninhabited after the sandstorm) is discovered to home many civillians and the group known as the 33rd. As the story progresses, you discover that the 33rd are not who they were thought to be and with that, you're forced to go through many different moral choices to help decide the fate of Dubai and your squad. By the end of the game though, everything isn't what it seems and you discover who the true enemy really is and it will leave you wanting more.
TL;DR Edition:
Pros:
+Shooting mechanics are fun and simple to use
+Squad members actually help out in fights, when compared to other games
+Amazing Story
+Had to Google what the ending meant
Cons:
-Most decisions decided in the game doesn't really affect the ending
-Once you die, you cannot be revived, unlike your squad members
