You ever been driving your car and see a car wreck on the side of the road? You shouldn't let it distract your driving, but you can't help but stare at the car that flipped over onto its roof as you drive by?  That is this game - no matter how much I know I really shouldn't be playing it, I just can't help but finish the storyline.
Why shouldn't I be playing it? Because of how annoyingly frustrating and even sometimes mundane it can be.  Now this game isn't all bad, I'll cover that soon.  I am just shocked out how a fundamentally good game is marred by horrible rage-inducing mechanics.
Let's cover the good things.  If you're a fan of Mad Max universe, you'll like this game.  They really did a good job mirroring what you'd see in the movies.  The voice acting is well done, the graphics do a great job replicating the universe in great detail.  The sound will shake your desk (or headphones) with satisfying bassy booms (and there will be lots of booms!).  There's a lot to explore in the open world.  Once again - the graphics and sound are just excellently done it's a shame all the other crap brings it down.
The mediocre things?  Story is meh.  I can't say I could write a better story, but compared to the movies, it was just your typical turn-off-brain and watch the movie unfold and then you're done.  The combat is pretty cool and grungy at first, but just like Arkham Knight - gets super repetitive and you'll do the same thing over and over again to the same type of enemies and same boss strategies.  The handling of the cars is pretty decent, and you can feel differences when you upgrade the cars.  Storms are fun at first, but can be annoying when you're just trying to knock out that one last thing... Vehicle combat will get repetitive too - but it was fun for the first half of the game at least.
The bad things? Ohhhh boy...the controls + cameras, unlocks, upgrades, and a specific set of minefield clearing tasks.  First, the controls are a mess sometimes.  Sometimes they are just downright unresponsive and completely random.  I was dodging a boss in a fight and Max decided to roll into flames and then proceed to get hit by the boss, even though the first 3 times it work perfectly fine!  The camera will try and kill you every chance it gets - you will miss many melee weapon reversals because the enemy came at an angle you couldn't see from the camera and you had to do a basic parry.  In tight spaces with low light you will find yourself cursing at the screen as the fight pursues.
Unlocks and upgrades are only mildly exciting.  When you unlock the V8 it barely feels faster than the V6, and the funny thing is it actually sounds worse - almost muted (probably the only sound fault in the entire game!).  The upgrades are blocked by certain tasks you must complete, and the most infuriating and mundane of them all is minefield clearing.  I have no idea why you would ever consider putting this in a video game, but it was completely uncalled for.  This is by far the worst experience in a video game I can remember in the past 10 years.  I'd rather grind to level 100 in WoW via mobs than clear another goddamn minefield in this game ever again.  And I couldn't unlock a final weapon upgrade until that was done in one territory!  No matter how much of a scrap lord I was.  Of course, the other territories are also riddled with these minefields, and the only way to reach them is to drive a weak, crappy buggy to them.  You cannot fast travel with the buggy either! WTF?!
Sometimes I played the game and actually enjoyed it - sometimes, and most of that was in the first quarter of the story.  For the most part, I found myself cursing and getting annoyed farrrr too often, it felt like I was doing chore after chore all while struggling with crappy controls and an annoying camera.  I forced myself to complete the game just to check it off my "to do" list.  I'm glad it's done, and I doubt - if there actually is - I will even be remotely interested in playing a sequel - time to right-click>delete, yay!
Summary:
Great graphics, great sound, great environment, ok fighting, ok story, infuriating controls combined with camera, terrible minefield clearing missions absolutely ruins the game.

Nothing good ever happens to anyone in Spec Ops: The Line. It starts with a rescue, a rough situation destined to get worse, and unravels in a downward spiral where only bad things happen to good people. By the end, physical, mental, and moral disruption leave each character in a very different place than they started. You almost expect it to have been written by Game of Thrones author George R.R. Martin. This isn’t a good thing for Captain Martin Walker, our intrepid hero whose will weakens with every enemy encounter. He transforms from a cheesy cliché to someone you sympathize with, and then develops into something despicable. How he gets there isn’t up to you -- what it ultimately means, though, is entirely your call. Story is Spec Ops’ strong suit, and while the inconsistent combat isn’t ideal, the gameplay does a great job of facilitating that narrative between intense encounters. In fact, The Line accomplishes something most shooters don’t bother with: It makes violence meaningful. Every firefight ends with Walker and his Delta Force squad regretting what they've done. The Line puts them in the precarious position of fighting their brethren. Rogue American soldiers who’ve abandoned their duty in Dubai attack on sight, and not without reason. The city is a wasteland, the environment is as hostile as the refugees, and surviving requires aggressive self-defense. Dubai hosts a civil war between multiple factions trying not to die. The Deltas are just one of these groups. As Walker, you’ll discover dark and disturbing things about Dubai and the people stuck within it. In your mission to save civilians and make contact with a former commander, you’ll make tough decisions that aren’t like other video game choices. Morality isn’t a feature or mechanic in Spec Ops: The Line -- each ethical quandary Walker confronts are subtle story beats dealt with by in-game action rather than a separate yes/no mechanism. You project their meaning and importance onto your character without seeing substantial in-game consequence. Deciding which of the bickering, increasingly angry teammates to side with, or who lives and dies, doesn’t affect the outcome of your rescue mission. In fact, the finale has a greater effect on the six hours leading up to it. Choice changes what it means to be this man. He makes the inevitable bad call and deals with it, nothing more. On the other side of every door and dune are conspiracies, betrayals, and mysteries waiting for Walker. The battles on the way to each one strengthens The Line's constant tension. Walker is just a man, and bullets rip him to pieces. He’s vulnerable and his enemies are aggressive, which encourages intelligent tactical combat. The Line introduces new variables in each fight. Sometimes sandstorms, sunshine, or objects obscure your vision. Fast-moving melee specialists, heavy gunners, and grenadiers force you to stay mobile and risk exposure. Destroying walls to drown enemies in sand is as viable a tactic as taking a turret, popping out of cover with a SCAR, or commanding squadmates. Marking targets keeps you safe while slipping from one unreliable cover point to the next, and issuing commands to stun soldiers with flashbangs keeps them from suppressing you. Walker’s commands are simple and few because he doesn’t rely on them. When they’re not shooting at walls, Lugo and Adams -- Walker’s left- and right-hand men -- are capable of dealing with waves of attackers. They saved me from dying multiple times when Spec Ops’ mechanics failed me. On multiple occasions, Walker didn’t slide into or sprint out of cover properly. Half the time I tried protecting myself, my character stopped dead before dropping dead. Vaulting over objects is an issue as well because its input is the same as the melee attack, meaning Walker would sometimes punch the air instead of hop over a barrier. With no evasive roll to dodge effectively, control problems hung me out to dry. Unpredictability and variety are the saviors of Spec Ops’ standard stop-and-pop formula, and neither exists in its online multiplayer. The adversarial side of The Line is an empty experience that relies on your lust for unlockables without presenting a reason to care. Getting new guns, protective gear, perks to boost stats, and cosmetic apparel is fun, but playing eight-player deathmatches on large yet cluttered maps is hardly a thrilling method to earn them. The reward system itself is a letdown, too. The prizes for leveling up are similar weapons with minimal improvements and too-familiar ballistics. The beacon of hope in multiplayer is the objective-based Buried mode, which tasks two teams of four to sabotage the enemy HQ while defending their own. It’s a tense tug-of-war full of panic and planning -- it’s a shame such a smart game type is trapped in the shell of an unremarkable online afterthought. Multiplayer lacks the aesthetic spirit of the single-player campaign as well. What begins as a drab, brown desert shooter suddenly develops a gorgeous, colorful personality. The purples, blues, greens, reds, and golds of the campaign's incredible interiors leave lasting impressions; you'll associate red and green with different but equally unsettling events. Color certainly exists in the multiplayer maps, but it isn't spotlighted or emphasized in a meaningful way. Meanwhile, the rock music of the early game gives way to somber acoustic melodies as the Delta crew deteriorates, further establishing the unforgiving tone in and out of combat. When all's said and done and the dust has settled, Spec Ops puts players in an interesting position. The endings -- whichever one you get -- are open to interpretation while still offering closure. The new information shines new lights on various spots in the story that warrant a second run through the campaign. The depth of these convincing characters is clearer when you know the fate you're responsible for. You see Dubai and those left behind in a new way. Most importantly, you finally understand Walker, which could well change the way you act on his motivations. What you regretted the first time could eat you alive when it's done differently. This is why Spec Ops is a daring experiment worth celebrating. For the first time, a game with guns doesn't want you to be the hero -- it wants you to feel terrible about trying to be one.
THE VERDICT
Spec Ops isn’t about a war, protecting the world, or defeating some evil threat -- it’s about you, the effects of your actions, and events that are out of your control. The sum of Spec Ops’ unexpected story is an army shooter that makes killing people mean something. This, along with its thoughtful aesthetic and intelligent enemy encounters, defies the standard established by low-aiming action games. Multiplayer can’t muster up the same courage, though, and while the hollow online experience doesn’t detract from the single-player campaign’s accomplishments, its reliance on convention doesn’t do anything to elevate it.

I will leave you guys to read the synopsis yourselves rather than going over the same thing various descriptions have said. So I will jump right into my review of the game:
Spec Ops: The Line is a 3rd person shooter based upon the post apocalyptic ruins of Dubai. It follows a squad of 3 Deltaforce soldiers on a rescue mission into the vast yet empty city - or is it?
After completing this game within the space of 24 hours it is hard not to admit that I thoroughly enjoyed the storyline of this game. Everything about this game is spectacular. The storyline (though dark and gritty at times juxtaposing to the vibrance of the desert atmosphere) the graphics. Wow, the graphics. This game was great for its time. Although it was only 2 years ago, it looks next generation - plain and simple. And the action side of it was amazing too. With many different weapons to choose from in combat with a pretty good melee and execution system. Though my only gripe would be being stuck in a firefight with no ammo and having to beat the crap out of a dude with your fists in the middle of a gunfight. But it adds a sense of realism to the game given the fact it is based heavily off of the feral survivors of the sandstorm upon Dubai, meaning ammo and any resources would be scarce.
The story goes on and the game becomes all the more dark and almost scary as it progresses. It affects the protagonists (though the player is the main one) begin to experience the horrors of war, which is realistic to war heroes in real life. I think it was a completely justified move for the writers to do this in the campaign, as we do not often see many war games such as Call Of Duty or Battlefield experimenting with this, but rather just mindless killing on the field without the after effects of the people who kill. Though they're good at what they do.
I am yet to try any multiplayer modes/ DLC but if they are anywhere as good as the campaign was it won't be long before I am gearing up for the streets (or rather skyscrapers) of Dubai once more.
Overall, this game is a great experience for anybody in the mood for a third person war game with a twist.
10/10 - a fairly Linear 3rd person playstyle spiced up with an epic storyline. Perfect for anybody who likes Gameplay and/or Graphics and/or Story.

One of the best games I've ever played, and one that was created by a single developer.
I would definitely recommend this game. It has a wide range of playstyles and can suit any mood. The game is not system intensive at all and the visuals are stunning. The audio is wonderful and gameplay feels fluid and fun. The controls are good and you can choose between mouse and keyboard. Shortly after purchasing this game it quickly became on of my favourites. It offers many playstyles for any mood. You can spend hours exploring new regions in beautiful Procedurally-Generated worlds, you can battle pirates or other ships for loot and glory in battle, or you could play the entire game as a passive trader and never see battle. The game is designed to be played with friends or in a group, but I often play in a solo world just trading. The multiplayer is well set up and fun, you can fight in Heroic worlds with other players against the most ferocious pirates, or you can engage in PvP Battleground combat. If you'd like, you can just join a server and chat. Playing with your friends is simple, they can join your world at the click of a button or you can find a nice public server to join together. Whether you are a casual trader or a fearsome warrior, if you come for plunder or exploration, Windward is the game for you. Tasharen has created a masterpiece, and a solo developer no less. Be very proud of what you have created, sir. I look forward to playing your next creations. Personally, I give this game an easy 9/10. Absolutely love it. I'll see you all on the high seas.

Maia is sci-fi strategy simulation game by Simon Roth. The game is currently in Alpha however it seems to be very pre-alpha at the moment. The game has a lot of potential but is lacking a few features right now. One of the biggest issues I have seen is the ability to save, right now there is no saving feature. With that, it doesn’t matter how far you have progress, in the end you have to start over again. There are a few glitches where your Colonist and Robot worker will ether stop working or would not complete tasks assign to them. The tutorial of the game is very limited but having them pop up is the annoying part.
The good thing is that if they brought out updates and improvement it might become a great game. However, so far it has been 22 days since the steam launch and it has had zero updates so far. If that changes or the game get better I may have to come back and change my review. This review is based on what is available during this stage of the alpha.
In a word... terrible.

In it's current format, Maia is not a playable game. I would say that it is currently in VERY early Alpha stages. Graphics are up and running (for the most part), but that's about it. The actual gameplay is not really implemented, and the parts that are there are not easy to figure out. There's no way to change the settings, no way to look at the key mapping (a critical thing in any new game), and it's really just trial and error.
I'd advise putting Maia on your Wishlist and waiting for about 6 months or so. It looks like it has a lot of potential, but it has a way to go before it's even in an Early Access playable form.

From the sales blurb: "The current sandbox build (0.38) allows a basic level of colony building, colonist interaction and base simulation"

I hope this will someday become a good game but right now there is absolutely nothing in it. I only wasted my time trying to figure out what I was doing wrong but turns out you can't do anything right because there is no "right".

Maia's ambitious and intends to inherit/borrow from some of the best. Given another year or two of updates it may actually become a good game.

Nothing good ever happens to anyone in Spec Ops: The Line. It starts with a rescue, a rough situation destined to get worse, and unravels in a downward spiral where only bad things happen to good people. By the end, physical, mental, and moral disruption leave each character in a very different place than they started. You almost expect it to have been written by Game of Thrones author George R.R. Martin. This isn’t a good thing for Captain Martin Walker, our intrepid hero whose will weakens with every enemy encounter. He transforms from a cheesy cliché to someone you sympathize with, and then develops into something despicable. How he gets there isn’t up to you -- what it ultimately means, though, is entirely your call. Story is Spec Ops’ strong suit, and while the inconsistent combat isn’t ideal, the gameplay does a great job of facilitating that narrative between intense encounters. In fact, The Line accomplishes something most shooters don’t bother with: It makes violence meaningful. Every firefight ends with Walker and his Delta Force squad regretting what they've done. The Line puts them in the precarious position of fighting their brethren. Rogue American soldiers who’ve abandoned their duty in Dubai attack on sight, and not without reason. The city is a wasteland, the environment is as hostile as the refugees, and surviving requires aggressive self-defense. Dubai hosts a civil war between multiple factions trying not to die. The Deltas are just one of these groups. As Walker, you’ll discover dark and disturbing things about Dubai and the people stuck within it. In your mission to save civilians and make contact with a former commander, you’ll make tough decisions that aren’t like other video game choices. Morality isn’t a feature or mechanic in Spec Ops: The Line -- each ethical quandary Walker confronts are subtle story beats dealt with by in-game action rather than a separate yes/no mechanism. You project their meaning and importance onto your character without seeing substantial in-game consequence. Deciding which of the bickering, increasingly angry teammates to side with, or who lives and dies, doesn’t affect the outcome of your rescue mission. In fact, the finale has a greater effect on the six hours leading up to it. Choice changes what it means to be this man. He makes the inevitable bad call and deals with it, nothing more. On the other side of every door and dune are conspiracies, betrayals, and mysteries waiting for Walker. The battles on the way to each one strengthens The Line's constant tension. Walker is just a man, and bullets rip him to pieces. He’s vulnerable and his enemies are aggressive, which encourages intelligent tactical combat. The Line introduces new variables in each fight. Sometimes sandstorms, sunshine, or objects obscure your vision. Fast-moving melee specialists, heavy gunners, and grenadiers force you to stay mobile and risk exposure. Destroying walls to drown enemies in sand is as viable a tactic as taking a turret, popping out of cover with a SCAR, or commanding squadmates. Marking targets keeps you safe while slipping from one unreliable cover point to the next, and issuing commands to stun soldiers with flashbangs keeps them from suppressing you. Walker’s commands are simple and few because he doesn’t rely on them. When they’re not shooting at walls, Lugo and Adams -- Walker’s left- and right-hand men -- are capable of dealing with waves of attackers. They saved me from dying multiple times when Spec Ops’ mechanics failed me. On multiple occasions, Walker didn’t slide into or sprint out of cover properly. Half the time I tried protecting myself, my character stopped dead before dropping dead. Vaulting over objects is an issue as well because its input is the same as the melee attack, meaning Walker would sometimes punch the air instead of hop over a barrier. With no evasive roll to dodge effectively, control problems hung me out to dry. Unpredictability and variety are the saviors of Spec Ops’ standard stop-and-pop formula, and neither exists in its online multiplayer. The adversarial side of The Line is an empty experience that relies on your lust for unlockables without presenting a reason to care. Getting new guns, protective gear, perks to boost stats, and cosmetic apparel is fun, but playing eight-player deathmatches on large yet cluttered maps is hardly a thrilling method to earn them. The reward system itself is a letdown, too. The prizes for leveling up are similar weapons with minimal improvements and too-familiar ballistics. The beacon of hope in multiplayer is the objective-based Buried mode, which tasks two teams of four to sabotage the enemy HQ while defending their own. It’s a tense tug-of-war full of panic and planning -- it’s a shame such a smart game type is trapped in the shell of an unremarkable online afterthought. Multiplayer lacks the aesthetic spirit of the single-player campaign as well. What begins as a drab, brown desert shooter suddenly develops a gorgeous, colorful personality. The purples, blues, greens, reds, and golds of the campaign's incredible interiors leave lasting impressions; you'll associate red and green with different but equally unsettling events. Color certainly exists in the multiplayer maps, but it isn't spotlighted or emphasized in a meaningful way. Meanwhile, the rock music of the early game gives way to somber acoustic melodies as the Delta crew deteriorates, further establishing the unforgiving tone in and out of combat. When all's said and done and the dust has settled, Spec Ops puts players in an interesting position. The endings -- whichever one you get -- are open to interpretation while still offering closure. The new information shines new lights on various spots in the story that warrant a second run through the campaign. The depth of these convincing characters is clearer when you know the fate you're responsible for. You see Dubai and those left behind in a new way. Most importantly, you finally understand Walker, which could well change the way you act on his motivations. What you regretted the first time could eat you alive when it's done differently. This is why Spec Ops is a daring experiment worth celebrating. For the first time, a game with guns doesn't want you to be the hero -- it wants you to feel terrible about trying to be one.
THE VERDICT
Spec Ops isn’t about a war, protecting the world, or defeating some evil threat -- it’s about you, the effects of your actions, and events that are out of your control. The sum of Spec Ops’ unexpected story is an army shooter that makes killing people mean something. This, along with its thoughtful aesthetic and intelligent enemy encounters, defies the standard established by low-aiming action games. Multiplayer can’t muster up the same courage, though, and while the hollow online experience doesn’t detract from the single-player campaign’s accomplishments, its reliance on convention doesn’t do anything to elevate it.

I will leave you guys to read the synopsis yourselves rather than going over the same thing various descriptions have said. So I will jump right into my review of the game:
Spec Ops: The Line is a 3rd person shooter based upon the post apocalyptic ruins of Dubai. It follows a squad of 3 Deltaforce soldiers on a rescue mission into the vast yet empty city - or is it?
After completing this game within the space of 24 hours it is hard not to admit that I thoroughly enjoyed the storyline of this game. Everything about this game is spectacular. The storyline (though dark and gritty at times juxtaposing to the vibrance of the desert atmosphere) the graphics. Wow, the graphics. This game was great for its time. Although it was only 2 years ago, it looks next generation - plain and simple. And the action side of it was amazing too. With many different weapons to choose from in combat with a pretty good melee and execution system. Though my only gripe would be being stuck in a firefight with no ammo and having to beat the crap out of a dude with your fists in the middle of a gunfight. But it adds a sense of realism to the game given the fact it is based heavily off of the feral survivors of the sandstorm upon Dubai, meaning ammo and any resources would be scarce.
The story goes on and the game becomes all the more dark and almost scary as it progresses. It affects the protagonists (though the player is the main one) begin to experience the horrors of war, which is realistic to war heroes in real life. I think it was a completely justified move for the writers to do this in the campaign, as we do not often see many war games such as Call Of Duty or Battlefield experimenting with this, but rather just mindless killing on the field without the after effects of the people who kill. Though they're good at what they do.
I am yet to try any multiplayer modes/ DLC but if they are anywhere as good as the campaign was it won't be long before I am gearing up for the streets (or rather skyscrapers) of Dubai once more.
Overall, this game is a great experience for anybody in the mood for a third person war game with a twist.
10/10 - a fairly Linear 3rd person playstyle spiced up with an epic storyline. Perfect for anybody who likes Gameplay and/or Graphics and/or Story.

Spec Ops: The Line is a 2012 third-person shooter video game developed by Yager Development and published by 2K Games. It was released on 26 June 2012 in North America and 29 June 2012 internationally for Microsoft Windows, and the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 consoles.
n Spec Ops: The Line, the player controls Captain Martin Walker, who is sent into a post-catastrophe Dubai with an elite Delta Force team on a reconnaissance mission, where they find dead American soldiers. Upon the finding, Walker declares that the team's mission has changed, and that they will search Dubai for survivors
Spec Ops: does so many good things right, but falls short from a masterpiece. While the game is a brilliant set-piece of PTSD and the true horrors of war, it falls short as a game in whole. While the story, soundtrack, voice acting, visuals and overall quality is amazing, it's gameplay is just so generic and boring. Nothing new will be seen here, unfourtunately. The game is a third-person cover shooter game, with no originality. The cover system and gunplay are mediocre at best, and this is a real drawback from it being an amazing experience in all sectors. But, I really don't want to get too much into such details, it's just something you've played in a hundred other games, let's focus on what's so amazing about this underrated game.
The story. It may sounds like something trivial, because people have high standards these days, amazing gameplay, amazing graphics, amazing this amazing that, you get my point. This game is narative driven game, and that's it. Multiplayer is shallow and unstatisfying, but this isn't the point of Spec Ops. It's a game that sets one goal, and one goal only. To trully showcase the
of war. War is a gruesome experience that really scars the human mind, and while me and you won't probably fight in one, this game has a trully shocking way of showing us just how brutal things can get between the gunfire. It will surely have a last impact on you, it did on me at least. The game starts pretty standard, a turret section that's pretty
and
, nothing too over the top here. But once the game kick off, things start to get heated. We start in the shoes of Cpt. Martin Walker, voiced by Nolan North. The game starts off with you and your squad mates being sent to the new destroyed Dubai, to investigate and search for survivor, call for reinforcements and get back home. Those are your only orders, nothing more. But things get out of hand once Walker gives to order to
. This thing will become more relevant down the line, since this game has set out to question one simple thing,
. And it will teach you that thing, once you complete it.
Being developed on the Unreal 3 Engine, the games shines mostly. Dubai is a super showcase of glowing sand, vibrant interiors and a feel of depth and complexity. But it's all just a shell to hide all of the horros that lay ahead of your journey to destruction. The game will soon present to you the brutal, and extremely graphic violence of when
when people mentally breakdown and can't tell the difference between good or evil. It's amazing, especially since this game breaks once and for all the trope that all enemy's in video games must be shot down immediatly without question, and because they are
or russian/middle eastern. It's superb, to be honest.
In the end, since I could talk about this game for hours and hours, even though it's a short, but it's an intense ride, and filled with guilt. Never, ever I have felt such guild after playing a videogame. Like, really. Videogames that make you feel guilty?
One might ask. Well, it's quite easy. This game does not reward you for shooting everyone in a 100km radius at the speed of Clint Eastwood, it will break you down as fast as the protagonists. It's amazing how well the story is crafter, considering at the end of the day, it makes you feel human, it makes you question so many things. Superb. Honestly, superb.
In case you don't want to hear all of my rumbling, I will list the things that I enjoyed and disliked about this game and give it a rating.

The game is fun but has too many flaws and repetitive tasks to be of any fun after the the first area (Jeet's).
+Great graphics and world design. It really feels like a wasteland.
+Optimization. Everything runs great and smooth on most rigs.
+Explosions and destructions. Cars driving into each other and the thrill of destruction.
-Repetition and grinding: Most unlocks are locked away behind achievements that require you to lower a territory's "threat level". This means taking over camps, destroying scarecrows and (killing) snipers, destroying convoy routes and clearing minefields. The minefields are the worse since it requires you to switch to a god awful vehicle and drive around while the dog barks in whichever direction the mine is in, you then disarm or destroy the mine. That's it. You'll have to do this in every territory to get the upper level upgrades.
-Base takeovers: As mentioned. Repetition. Take out the watchtowers and perimeter defences, then walk into the base until you move into an open area and fight warboys (this might happen more than once in certain bases) OR fight warboys and then destroy Oil Tanks or Oil Rigs. That's pretty much it. Just add in a mini boss at the end if there's one in that camp.
-Combat: Simplified version of the Batman Arkham Series combat. It actually feels sloppy. Left click to attack, right click to counter. You can use a shotgun for extra effect and a shiv for finishers.
-Miniboss and enemy variety: Same guy wearing the leather mask just with a different skin. You fight in an arena type area where there's some type of contraption spewing flames and you avoid those while taking out the boss. It rages and you dodge then attack it. The scrubs you fight are all pretty simple too, some of them will have an unblockable attack but you can easily roll and avoid those then proceed to wail on them.
-Vehicle handling: This is a 50/50. It's terrible at street handling but decent enough at open spaces. Once you upgrade the Magnus Opus (Max's car) it gets a little better but does still get wonky and floaty at times. The game boasts vehicles for goodness sake, at least be competent at it.
There's really not much else to do after Jeet's territory. You'll wind up doing the same things over and over again just to get the upgrades and the story mission itself isn't too interesting or varied. It just sends you to pickup someone, make contact with someone or kill/ destroy someone or a base.
I'd wait for a sale. It's hard to hold any interest in the game after the first couple of chapters. It's too basic as it is but again it runs great though and you might have fun driving around the wasteland while chasing down war parties.

Well, here's to a monkey paw wish. For the record, I was a Kickstarter backer.
Shantae: Half-Genie hero is a big step forward visually from its predecessors... and a smaller step back gameplay-wise. In general, the game looks gorgeous. Though Crybringer's redesigns are jarring compared to the the previous game, they hold up well animated. The animations are fantastic, though there's less variety than there was in Pirate's Curse, perhaps owing the new engine.
In terms of speed and flow, this game feels like it's slightly slower than Pirate's Curse. There are more transformations, but many are just so situational you won't find yourself using them widely - most are just keys to open locks, with only a few serving as general use, and another few literally just existing to generate powerups or the like. Magic has been nicely expanded, with a third level for most of the spells. However, one issue is that it simply overdoes it in terms of upgrades - even early upgrades can trivialize things like health loss, whether it's just reducing damage or being able to generate health and healing items on a whim. One even lets you generate cash, leaving your ability to purchase upgrades down to your patience. Worst of all is the item you get for collecting all the gallery keys, which may as well have "CHEATING MODE ACTIVATED" in big red letters, making a number of the final boss battles trivial. If you want challenge out of Half-Genie Hero, it's only self-enforced - the menu at least lets you switch off most of the upgrades if you like.
Enemies are no longer of the "stop-go" nature from previous reviews, and in general the enemy design is nicely varied, with a number of really great boss fights with varied styles... save for the final boss, which was an annoying slog for me. In general, though, fighting enemies is pleasant and there's more use for the varied spells against them than previous games (which mostly boiled down to "spike ball or nothin'").
Collecting is, of course, a core element, and it teeters between reward and annoyance. I found myself revisiting levels a lot to get this or that geegaw or power, and the game enforces it a bit to pad its relatively short number of levels. While most of these trips aren't too laborious, towards the end I started to resent having to dig for the last few chunks. There's a lot of keys for various locks to open up Metroid-style, and slightly too many in my estimation.
The story is almost episodic, reflecting the varied plots promised in the kickstarter, and a lot of the side stories are much more clever than the main plot. The dialogue is often genuinely funny and sharp, and does make me wish for voices on account of it. The climax, however, is cliched to the point of being painful. I understand they probably wanted to get back to basics... but it features a twist you'll likely see coming from the very start of the game, and a pretty bad one at that.
It should be noted that the extra playable characters aren't finished yet. Presumably they'll be DLC to non-backers in the future, but it's not clear. In general, the game isn't long - it took me about 9 hours to do 100% completion without any guides or tips at all. It doesn't overstay its welcome, and I didn't mind that at all. Presumably when the extra characters / modes are completed, they'll add to the length of the game for better or worse.
Ultimately, despite my criticism, I really enjoyed my time with Half-Genie Hero, though I don't feel much of a need to revisit it. It's a pretty fun ride over all, with a very appealing look, solid controls and innovations... but also is the sort of step back you often see with a new engine like this. As such, go into it expecting some flaws, but it's worth getting into if you've enjoyed the previous games or want a light, colorful platforming adventure. Just bear in mind it's got a few kinks.

Half genie hero is a great game, in terms of platformers and metroidvania games it is up there as one of the best, but as a Shantae game, it feels more like Shantae 2.5, which is puzzling seeing as we have a true Shantae 3 (pirates curse).
Pirates curse was always going to be a hard act to follow, pirates curse became a 10/10 game by abandoning a lot of what made Shantae and replacing it with a new system that was much better, the dancing transformations are for sure unique, but even as fast as they are here it still unnaturally broke up the gameplay whereas the pirate gear in the previous game flowed in seamlessly.
Compounding the issue is the story, pirates curse was a much grander tail that did a lot to build out the world and its characters, a lot of big elements are introduced in pirates curse such as Shantaes farther, the history of rottytops and her brothers, the humanising of risky, hell buy the end of pirates curse Shantae had seemingly developed feelings for risky, I was sure that would all be built on here but it's not, instead we get a more episodic day in the life of Shantae style story, which works on its own especially for first timers, but as a sequel to pirates curse, the lack of continuity is maddening.
Before I played this game I didn't know if it was a prequel or a sequel, and the fact I still don't know is a bad sign.
But despite that, I had a blast, if you like platformers or metroidvanias this is one of the best, but just don't expect it to be better than pirates curse.

So, since i played the first Life is strange and often wondered what made Chloe so obsessed with this girl i can finally kinda relate to her.
But lets start slowly: If you haven't played Life is strange [LiS] all by yourself prior to buying this game - do it. Play it all the way through,
If you however have played the first game
then welcome to Life is strange: Before the storm
I had high expectations in this game. Some were satisfied, some have been left unpleasured. But why?
The first Life is strange had some cringy moments, but was overall good to play and not too emotional
. But now Life is strange: Before the storm sometimes just tries too damn hard to trigger your emotions. I sometimes caught myself rolling my eyes.
Its sometimes hard to relate to the "mental" problems some of the characters in this game have.
The worst thing for me is partly the best thing, i know it sounds twisted, but to be real here for a sec: You play a game, because you want to achieve something. You play for the satisfaction of completing something. In the first life is strange, we all wanted to know what happened and in the end everything kinda tilted back to the original question of what happened to Rachel Amber.
In this game(since this story is happening before the first game) you know from the start, not how it will be, but how it will end.
So you feel kind of powerless, helpless, since you know with every decision you make: "It wont make a difference in the end"
So you still play the game, and you kinda like it anyway, but you always have the first game in the back of your mind telling you how irrelevant your choices and decisions are.
So as you may see im not completely for or against buying this game. But it just could have been done better.
Okay, i still think this game is a great explanation of how the characters in the first game came to what they are. I think im going to have to play the first game again, just so i can relate to any references or clues the devs might have put in there.
The sad thing is....i already know how it will end. And that no choice i make will change any of that.

I don't even know where to begin with this game. I was so excited when they announced it. I mean I loved the first game even though it had some problems, but the story was great. I loved the characters, the plot, and I wanted to know so much more about Rachel, she was always so interesting to me. Honestly they did this way better. Having actually finished Before the Storm (all 3 episodes) I can say I am SOOOOOO incredibly happy we got to meet Rachel. She is probably my favorite character now, and for good reason. I couldn't have asked for a better Rachel than the one we got in BtS, truly. They did a phenomenal job with creating her character. She is so intriguing and amazing to get to know, and her and Chloe make such an amazing couple. They compliment and go with each other so well. The way they mix music with this game is unreal. They nail it everytime. The music mixed with the scenes make the atmosphere so captivating and beautiful. To explain better my favorite part is in episode 3 after the whole junkyard knife incident and Burn it Down starts to play. The music and the way they edited it with the scenes is just so crazy I wanted to honestly just watch it multiple times. The soundtrack is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing 10/10. I didn't excpect the story to unfold like it did, and I am not dissapointed at all!  Rachels story with her family hit really close to my heart and it was done so well. I also instantly loved Sera. I have met, and known a lot of people like her in her position and so it hurt me even more when you finally speak to her. Her whole conversation with Chloe made me so emotional because I geniunely understood where she was coming from and why she was saying it. LiS does an amazing job of making characters so grounded and real, and Sera's story was just too real that it got me almost harder then the rest. So let's just say I got her the happy ending, the one she deserved. And seeing it made me break down in tears of joy, even for those few moments. It was literally all I wanted to have happen since we became aware of who Sera was, and I am so happy I ended it the way I wanted to. I could literally go on forever, about how I loved playing tabletop games with Steph and Mikey, how Frank is such a ♥♥♥♥ing MVP like holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ how amazing Chloe's dream moments with her dad were, the themes of lying and protection, ect. But I don't want to ramble forever. I just really love this game so much, and I am so sad It had to end. It was great seeing how Chloe and Rachel met, and how close they became... I mean being together for three years.. damn it hits you even harder when you know their fate in the end. This was truly such a beautiful experience and I loved every part of it- except when it had to end... (I'll be waiting for the Farewell episode)

I would say this game is overall very good. It was a tough task to follow up the Pirates Curse, and I didn't expect a masterpiece.
First of all, the music and graphics are simply great. The trailer gives you a pretty good impression of what this was going to be in that regard and I'm really loving it. The gameplay feels smoother overall than previous entries and they improved on the transformations, making the process less time consuming.
That said, the transformations are my first big negative. We get a mix of old and new, but really they  break the flow of the game. That's an issue previous games had already, but it feels a lot more pronounced in this one. If you want to move efficiently through levels you will change forms a lot, and that can be a bit annoying at times. Not terrible, but I would say the older games handled this better, probably because this one has more transformations, and quite a few aren't really that useful.
Similarly the backtracking feels worse in this one, probably because you only have 5 leveles plus Risky's Hideout. Going back to the same level, with minor changes when you enter the 2nd time, over and over just doesn't feel satisfying. Even worse every level basically consists of 2 main screens with secrets dispersed in between them plus a boss battle.
The biggest issue for me is that everything feels so segmented. The stories of the bosses don't really have anything to do with the main plot, the levels, due to the select screen, feel just like that: levels and not a connected world. I just feel like they could have done a lot better by connecting the villains and give us pointless connection roads. Yes they take more time and can be annoying, but they make the gameworld feel connected.
The levels themselves are absolutely great. They just feel well designed and fun to play, if you weren't forced to play them quite as often (if you want to get 100% of course). The bosses are also very creative, and some kind of boss rush at the end would have been really fun.
Overall, I would certainly recommend this game to anyone who likes fun platformers. It's a little too easy for my tastes and could be better, but it's fun and that's what matters the most.

SPOILERS ALERT
Like almost everyone here, I was eagerly waiting for the release of this game.
I played every Shantae game in the series and and had many expectations for this last one,
I was drooling when reading goals on Kikcstarter achieved one by one and naturally an ideal game picture was
drawn in my head, a picture of a game that at least does not give in to it's previous incarnation, the brilliant
Shantae and the Pirate's Curse. A game with the budget of almost 800,000 USD.
I have never been so wrong...
Graphics
From the very first time I played Shantae, I loved the concept and dreamed it to become an HD.
Partially my wishes became true in RR and PC but that only involved sprites, not the actual universe.
I like the graphics in HGH, it looks refreshing, though somewhat lacking in magic previous games had.
I especially like the the job devs did on some of the Shantae's forms such as Mermaid and Spider, they look adorable.
Some of my complaints lie in character animations, they are almost noexistent. Whatever happens during a dialogue,
Sky is smiling happily, Risky dances, Bolo remains pokerface etc. It especially strikes your eye during a scene when Shantae turns dark and they come for help. I don't think it is a very difficult job to change a facial expression since it's HD and it would contribute greatly to a scenes' emotional impact.
Music
Music is wonderful. Kaufman knows his job well.
Plot
This is what actually disappoints me and what makes me give the game a thumb down.
During the whole course of the game an impression stuck with me that devs had some great ideas which they failed (or didn't want) to implement for some reason. The plot seems rushed, teared and incompleted. No character development at all.
New charactes appear to be tossed away right after their debut. Main Shantae friends could have more impact on the story. I'll give an example.
- In the very first stage - mermaid falls, Bolo catches up to Shantae and complains he is always left out of her adventures.
It was a great reference to the previous game but unfortunately it didn't go anywhere.
There is a couple of funny moments with him in this episode, but after that he doesn't play any significant role at all.
- The same thing with Rotty, I have an impression the devs had no idea how to insert her into the plot and just got away by giving her some nominal role. Abner and Poe are introduced and forgotten.
- An episode with Shantae taken over by dark magic just cried for a fight with her dark self or an extra level "inside her",
don't get me wrong, the thing her friends coming to her rescue is great but still a lot of potential is lost.
- The new "villain" Holly was downright pathetic. Her reasons ridiculous, dialogues far-fetched, character - bad guy cliche. It was a real challenge to beat the boss with a palm on my face.
- Moreover I was negatively suprised when I discovered it was actually a "bonus chapter" (along with the cape crustacean) inserted in the story because the kickstarter goal was achieved.
Would would be left of the game without those? Bonus chapter should be BONUS and usually after you BEAT the game or can be completed optionally, but here it is an integral part of the story. I don't oppose this approach, just don't call it BONUS. Call it: "Initially we planned to make the game 4 hours long, but since you funded it we will make it 8".
- The game has two endings and they differ by a couple of lines. If the whole genie realm was destoyed, Shantae will say something like: "Well, that's a bummer." and Mimic like: "Well, maybe it wasn't".
Yes, I know it is a kind fairy-tale and there is no place for heavy dramatic moments but this very ending should motivate a player to search for a better one, but it doesn't.
Difficulty
Too casual. It does give you some challenge in the beginning, but once you have a bikini and 4+ hearts you dont really care to avoid attacks at all. Some people complained the last boss to be very difficult, but when you have invincibility magic what difficulty are you talking about??? I really like easy games, when I don't have to smash break the gamepad and just enjoy the gameplay, but there must be balance between difficulty and enjoyability, which this game definitely lacks.
Conclusion.
I, as a fan of the series, am very disillusioned because the potential the series had was destroyed by this game.
Maybe the DLCs will brighten things up a bit but we'll have to pay for them which highlights the desire to only earn money, not caring much about their product.
I'll repeat myself, as I was going through the game it seemed to me the devs had great ideas but right after the beginning they decided to save budget, which I don't understand. They raised twice they pledged + income from release, did they only care to make it "ok" but not "great"?

Well, it was just my personal opinion, there are tons of positive reviews, so I probably just dramatized a lot.
Agree or not? Comments are welcome.

Short version: Sleeping Dogs in the Mad Max Universe. If you like either, go for it.
I got this as part of Humble Monthly, which is the primary reason I played it since I wouldn't have picked this up on my own, but I'm incredibly glad I did.
The game players entirely in third person except for a few short parts, and doesn't really suffer from any big camera issues in my opinion. Most of the controls are fairly responsive, although I had some issues with parrying sometimes not responding, and difficulty with finishers during combat, although that could have been a positioning issue on my part.
Melee combat is very strongly flavored as Sleeping Dogs - with more than a couple of enemies, you're far better off parrying if there isn't a ton of space, especially once melee weapon enemies are introduced, but against non-boss groups you can easily overpower them as you unlock more upgrades.
Upgrades are handled via an in-game currency, "Scrap". Conquering enemy camps will earn you steady scrap income to either upgrade Max ( fists for attacks, wrists for blocking / parrying, jacket for defense, bandolier for ammo, skills, appearance, shotgun, and the jimmy bar accessory ), or the vehicle you spend the game with ( engine, ram, wheels, suspension, armor, etc ).
There are several "gates" where you are required to reach a minimum level of upgrades before you can proceed, to ensure that you aren't completely outclassed.
Gameplay itself is varied - there are races, base conquering, zone control, collectibles, and a series of side missions that reward you with extra vehicles, scrap, or unlocks like side burners or the final sniper rifle upgrade.
As far as the plot goes, it was pretty decent, although this essentially being a move tie-in leads to a heavy case of plot railroad towards the end.
Overally, I think the game is pretty great, but very similar to Sleeping Dogs, which may be an issue for some.
Combat is interesting for a while, but as a single player game it becomes boring after you get the largest ship.

This is a fun little metroidvania-type title. It's not an especially long or difficult game, but the different abilities are cool and add new dimensions to traversing the levels (except Spider. I like the design but I'm not really sure how useful it is outside of one instance where it's necessary). I also like that it's fairly short because it makes backtracking to use those new abilities much less tedious than it could otherwise have been.
It controls well, the art direction is charming, and the songs are all nice. The voice acting is good although there isn't much of it, which is fine; it's not something I need in every game and I would have been fine without it. I also like the fact that you can 'adjust' the difficulty in-game by turning on or off your different power-ups; for example, something you can unlock later is unlimited magic as well as an invicibility spell which can make the last few bosses rather trivial, but if you feel like challenging yourself or 'doing it right' you can just turn off the relic and activate one of the lesser forms of the spell.
In short, I recommend it.

Pros:
+ HD graphics put this game way ahead of its predecessors visually.
+ OST is awesome and includes remixes of songs from previous games in the series.
+ The game allows you to unequip purchased upgrades if you want more of a challenge.
+ More transformations than all the previous games combined; and a well-implemented dance menu.
+ The bath lady gives free hints so that you don't get stuck for too long.
+ The whistle and warp dance make it very easy to either leave a level or skip a certain part so you don't have to do the same platforming over and over each time you revisit a level.
+ Giantess mermaid boss with "plot" to spare! (Did I mention she's chained up too?)
Tossup:
+/- You can purchase invincibility magic and later on get unlimited magic to effectively make it last forever. This makes the game (and especially the final boss) brain-dead easy as long as you are competent at platforming.
Cons:
- No dungeons: a big departure from the series' norm.
- Too many types of collectibles and not enough worlds to really do all that collecting justice.
- Spider transformation, Spider Venom, and Bat Sonar are barely used at all in this game.
- Story is a bit shallow with no serious conflict and little exposition until the very end.
- Boss designs could be a lot better
It appears that Shantae and the Pirate's Curse, the game that preceded this one, set the bar juuuust a little too high for WayForward. Half-Genie Hero may have gotten some negative reviews for not living up to it's predecessor, but I'll give it a pass since I enjoyed it anyways.

This game is very easy to speed run. The time limit for any% is around 3 hours and 100% is probably around 4 hours. Hero mode makes both of these extremely easy, but I've also seen some more dedicated runners get both achievments in a single playthrough on regular mode.

The next two phases are really boring and are super easy to beat. The "Harpy Gauntlet" heading up to those bosses was a much more satisfying challenge. This game is really fun, but if the developers could fix the immersion-breaking bugs and add a few of the features that Classic has, then this game could be incredible.

I fully support indie development. I buy just about anything indie that pops up on Steam (that isn't 2D). So I saw this, the premise sounded interesting, so I grabbed it. I immediately got into the game and was presented with a VERY early release game that really shouldn't be on Steam at all.
The game menu starts with "Launch", "Settings" and "Abort". Settings consists of... "Toggle Fullscreen"... that's it. Nothing else. No keybinds, no graphics, no sounds, NOTHING. The other two menu options are self explanatory.
In-game you're presented with a couple tutorial tasks, but it throws you into the world with no real understanding of how to build, what each item does, and what's really needed.
I found myself being frustrated with some of the game functions like building a couch for example. If I hover a section of the room, it gives me the build for the couch. If I move around and accidently touch a wall or door, the build option turns into a door and I have to cycle back through the build items again (using V and B keys). Annoying.
I branched my outpost out with additional rooms and my characters refused to venture into it. I was left with having to cheat build to get the rooms to finish. Then, after I did that (having waited minutes for the NPC's to do it), my characters ventured that way by walking through walls.
I felt pretty disappointed with this title. That's not to say that with patches and updates it wont be decent. It's one of those early releases that I'm left scratching my head wondering why this was accepted by Steam, let alone at a price tag of $25. I just missed by 5 hours, a 25% off sale which is also quite disappointing.
All in all... wait this one out. Give it time to really get fleshed out, and turn into a solid title before you give it a try. You might regret it now. I know I did.

Old School Simulation style Prison Builder. Although there are some things that need to be added or tweaked for a better more enjoyable game play experience I rather enjoy playing this game.
One of the greatest downfalls this game presents is a lack of an informative tutorial. The tutorial provided is entertaining and presents a couple of issues you'll encounter later in the game but fails to provide grass roots. I found myself floundering for the first couple of hours to build a basic starter prison. Once you have a basic idea of how a base prison should be laid out its gets easy to start over, expand or destroy parts of existing prisons to make way for new ideas. I don't suggest destroying too much however as money is a precious commodity early to mid game.
The Planning tool is a helpful addition when adding on to or starting your prison but other than walls and pathways it lacks detail. While the lack of detail is purely aesthetic, and may just be personal preference on my part, I think it would only add to the games charm. As this game is currently in Alpha with a possible release by the end of this year (2015) I still remain hopeful that Introversion will add more detail to the tool.
Later in the game, when the prison population starts to expand greatly, you wind up getting prisoners that kick off for no particular reason. Inmates and staff alike often get stabbed and can and will end up dying. Before Patch 31 there was nothing you could really do about it other than escalate them to Max or Super Max and change the daily routine to minimize the damage they can cause. Now you have the option to place them under permanent lock down. The prisoner still kicks off daily but with minimal damage to the staff and other inmates.
One of the things I think could be added is periodic updates, perhaps with animated or semi-animated cut scenes similar to the tutorial. Anyone who has played SimCity or Sid Meier's Civilization or anything similar will be familiar with periodic updates that appear every so often to tell you how your doing in the game and where you need to improve. These could be inserted at pre-designated landmarks, like say after completing a grant. They should provide valuable information that is readily available throughout the game but is often neglected by most gamers and have the option to skip or turn off at any point in the game. Sometimes you just need to know how bad you are doing before you know enough to improve.
If your Still reading this than these are my final thoughts on the game so far. This game is in early access but it pretty much feels like a full game already. With a few tweaks and a couple of add ons this could be one of the best Sim games I've played in a long time. Although the price, currently set at $32.99 CAD, may seem a bit steep for most, if your a fan of Sims and aren't too concerned about flashy graphics and over the top fancy animations I recommend this game to you.

It almost goes without saying at this point, but Undertale is one of the most exciting things I have played in a while. I'll skirt over the game's well-known-by-now unique and punishing take on in-game morality and analysis of killing-as-wish-fulfillment in games, and focus on the other stuff.
The writing is extremely smart and the characters are universally endearing. The dialogue does lean a little heavy into the internet culture references, video game and anime references, and so on, which can feel a bit cringey right now and will likely date the game a few years on.
The gameplay, particularly the combat systems, is often repetitive and a tad clunky, but of course they are there in service to the story and theme and in that sense are functional enough. The game does make an effort to put spins on and subvert the combat mechanics later on, which can be refreshing.
The graphics are simple and workmanlike, bordering on ugly, even considering the game's status as something of a retro throwback to NES-era RPGs. One does get used to them after a time, and again the game subverts its graphical style a couple of times toward the end to clever effect.
Even if you are going in knowing the sort of game Undertale is (which is likely by now), it will still manage to surprise you.

Ahhh..... I feel the cold Alaskan morning wind in my face and  smell the characteristic smell of spruce in my nose as I make my way downhill to my favorite spot for Moose. That said, there’s no such thing as the perfect game and neither is HCOTW. I wish the devs would have put as much effort into the game mechanics as the have in the landscape and sound environment. It lacks in weapon variation and customization, but maybe that’s something they’re planning to add with dlc’s IDK? Also one thing I really miss is a trophy room to show off your achievements in the wild. Anyhow, if you think you would enjoy the great outdoors from the comfort of your PC this is the game for you!. The Hunter: Call of the Wild is a (mostly) true to life hunting sim. As such it is a curious game in that it exists in what is a fairly niche genre. There used to be quite a few hunting titles out there. I remember EA's ultimate hunt challenge pack, Cabela's Big Game Hunter and Dangerous Hunts. Yet the audience for these games is anything but niche. There are plenty of folks (like myself) who enjoy hunting. For example, my home state of Pennsylvania makes much of it's revenue from the sale of hunting and fishing licenses and the sales of equipment.
I began hunting when I was 12 years old and have continued to hunt ever since. I enjoy hunting Whitetail, Turkeys, and Rabbit Hunting with my beagles. I've even shot a coyote or two.
Why do people hunt? Ask any hunter and you may receive a different answer. A break from the daily grind at work? Or maybe to just enjoy the outdoors with friends and family and make memories.
The reasons people may play this game are probably just as varied, and the game allows for those same kind of experiences albeit in a virtual space.
Visually the game is very nice looking and the Apex engine creates very nice vistas and environments.
The game is one of the most robust hunting sims I have seen. It offers complex believable AI for the wildlife. Deer can pick up your scent if a wind is blowing over your back towards your quarry. They can also detect noise and will give warning calls, perform mating calls/grunts. On top of that there are areas where animals may feed, rest or drink water.
The game comes with a full day and night cycle as well as some impressive weather effects. Rain can range from a light drizzle to a hard driving rain. Fog can move in and cloak the surrounding area with a haze. Wind can blow heavily through the trees and as noted earlier either work for you or against you as in real life.
You can hunt a wide variety of wildlife with several species of deer (whitetail, blacktail, moose, elk), bears, coyotes, foxes, bison, lynx, and more. Your approach to hunting any of these is your choice. You can opt to hunt with rifles, shotguns, pistols or a bow, though some of these need to be unlocked by progressing a given skill.
Yes that's right, the game does have a progression system. The more game you harvest, the more XP you gain which allows you to allocate skill and perk points. These can make you more effective, like reducing wobble while looking through the scope for instance.
You can stalk your quarry trying to be quiet and patient, or perhaps you would like to opt for huting from a blind, or spending some cash to build an elevated stand.
When you hit an animal, one of three things can happen. You down it with one shot and don't have to track it. You make a solid hit and it runs a short distance. Or in the worst case you only cause a flesh wound only resulting in 'very low' blood loss. This can mean an exhausting effort to try and recover the animal. When you first start the game, you are given a .243. Nothing really wrong with the caliber. It's a solid caliber and I've shot many deer with it in real life. The problem I think comes from the ammo type. The default ammo is absolutely rubbish as it is a type that has 'rapid expansion'. What this means is the round will typically fragment on impact rather than penetrating which is crucial for taking game like Deer. In real life, I use a 100 gr. core lokt round and I have never had any problems with deer getting up and running away as they do in this game. That being said, the game places great emphasis on shot placement. Aim for the neck, or other vitals like heart and lungs.
Another thing the game does well is to simulate hunting pressure. The more deer or game you harvest in an area, the less likely they are to continue frequenting that area until the pressure lowers. It's a neat mechanic that keeps you from getting too accustomed to one particular area and it encourages further exploration.
While the core of the game is primarily about hunting, there is a good deal of exploration with various things (like shed antlers that reward cash) to find. You can even try and get close enough to wildlife to snap a photo if you so choose.
There are missions to complete as well but can be done at your own leisure. It gives you considerable freedom to play the way you want to play. You can even play co-op with friends as well.
Finally how is the price? For $30, I think the game is fairly priced for what is on offer. I prefer this model to that of the previous game (Hunter Classic) which had some pretty restrictive microtransactions. This game instead is a one time fee and you get everything minus the DLC which is also pretty reasonable. The game is a solid foundation and hopefully the devs continue to add new content.
I would like to see more reserves, perhaps an African one. Other additions I would like would be bird and rabbit hunting with dogs, fishing, turkey hunting, more rifle and handgun calibers. No 30-06? Might be nice to see a flintlock as well at some point. More modes of transportation like a truck/jeep, boat, float plane, snowmobile etc. would be welcome. I think the game would benefit from more fast travel points as well.
If you enjoy hunting and can't help but think about it even during the off season? I think you will find a lot to enjoy in this game. If however walking sims arent your cup of tea or if you lack patience, this may not be one for you. This is a game where patience is ultimately rewarded.

SUMMARY: A fun, colorful metroidvaina-esque platformer with a lot of personality.  Though heir to a fan favorite series, it stands out pretty well on its own and shows a lot of crafting.  There's a few issues of polish and levels of difficulty, but the overal experience is very enjoyable.
I Kickstarted this game.  Not because I was actually into the series, but as a lot of friends were, and were thrilled to see it returning.  I figured "what the heck" and tossed some money into the pot.
Fast forward to now, and the results of a non-fan of the game?  Pretty damn good.
Shantae is a platform-heavy metroidvania type game.  Start in a town, go to various areas on missions.  Complete missions, find new abilities, return to other areas to find stuff and use abilities, repeat.  Unlock new areas and new treasures.  It's a standard formula we all love.
So let's see how it breaks down.
PRESENTATION: The game is colorful and fun, with great graphics and soundtrack.  Characters have plenty of personality.  The game's look and feel is excellent.
GAMEPLAY: Gameplay is very old-school and there's a heavy emphasis on exploring the environment and platforming timing. If you're not ready for it, it may be a bit of a shock.  When you "get" it then the game really comes together.
CHARACTER GROWTH: Shantae basically A) finds new dances to transform into things, B) Buys spells and some combat upgrades, B) gets increased health.  It's not exactly complicated - the dances are the important part as they give you access to new areas.
PUZZLES: Though the need to re-return to areas can be annoying,the different abilities you unlock make them easier to navigate, and help you access hidden areas.  A few times you'll have an "aha" moment and figure out how to solve something and get a real rush from it.
STORY: The story seems to be more of a "Shantae's greatest hits gets the band back together" so you're not getting Game of Thrones or Dragon's Age here.
If there's a flaw to the game, its some of it feels a tad disjointed, from varied difficulty to a grand adventure suddenly turning into a fetchquest that feels like it should have been optional.  It's a minor concern, but it did stand out for me.
So do you buy it?
1) If you're a fan, judging by the game's quality AND the fans I know you either should or already did, and I'm shocked you read this far.
2) If you like colorful old-school patformers you'll probably enjoy this.
3) It'd make a GREAT gift for a friend who liked old-school platformers.
Who shouldn't buy it?
1) If you don't like platformers, really, don't.  This game will make you angry.
2) If you're not up for a game that involves repeating levels several times and poking around in their corners.

I enjoyed this game a great deal.  For me...
Pros:
Good platform jumping game play. (Somewhat challenging at times but always fun.)
Smooth controls. (Every death was my own fault and I never felt I was fighting against the controls.)
Excellent art style/graphics that felt vibrant and immersive. (The world that I saw seemed deep and detailed.)
Enjoyable/Whimsical characters and a tongue in cheek story line. (It IS silly but it has an infectious cheerfulness to it.)
Very good music throughout the game.  (Some of the stages have really decent scores.)
Cons:
Short.  (I milked as much as I could out of my first time and only got to about 9 hours. Others will do that in half.)
Easy Bosses.  (Although creative and fun they are not going to be much challenge to seasoned players.)
Few Stages. (Couple this with "Short" above but the world itself is crying out for places for Shantae to visit.)
Summary:  I would recommend this game to anyone who likes a good 2D platformer.  I enjoyed it very much and had a smile on my face while I played it.  And for its price I'd say its worth it.

Overall a very fun game with solid controls in which you start out really weak and get exteremly broken by the end of the game...so much so that you feel invinicbile (i dont think i ever died in this game and came the cloest to dying on the first level due to how weak shantae starts out)
unlike most games of this genre, when you beat a boss you get a new transformation then usually you have to backtrack through a level you beaten again to find more upgrades (and this isnt optional the game halts and forces you to do this to continue the story and it happens every time)...this may sound like a negative but since you just got a new transfomation and became even stronger, it wont seem like backtracking through a stage and you might find optional upgrades to make the rest of the game even easier...
and thats the charm of the game, you really feel the progression of the main character who starts out super weak with very traditional moveset you will see in most platformers then slowly start breaking the mold once you start finding upgrades and start going back to levels that gave you headaches in the past and just watch them get broken apart due to your new abilites.
Also you eventually get a warp spells so you can skip unneccary parts of a level to find that 1 upgrade or part you need in a level you already beaten and you can leave the level at anytime you want if you gotten everything you need...
it does become super easy at the end when you can go invinicbile at will, fly over the whole stage, and have so many heart containers that theres no way the enemy can kill you but ya you sorta earned that right? though hard work and upgrading yourself...its not a hard game in the slightest but its so much fun when you are so strong at the end of the game and it feels justified with all the time you spent on making shantate stronger...
Lastly this game is getting dlc to extend the gameplay later on...and its not just skins...its new playable characters with unique gameplay styles and their own storylines so you have something to look forward too...and this game rewards speedruns so if you thought it was so easy by the end...try going for the achivements, some requiring you to speedrun the game...

In 2015 I decided to play Life is Strange completely on a whim. It had good reviews, I recognized a bunch of songs off the soundtrack, it had "time travel" and "story rich" in the popular tags. So I gave it a chance... and I loved it. Life is Strange hooked me with its loveable cast, captivating mystery and suspense, brilliant voice acting and storytelling moments that still weigh on my mind 2 years after. I was truly enamored with the game, but still I'm a cynic and I had low expectations for Before the Storm. I thought "oh a cashgrab" and "it's just gonna be fanservice without any of the quality I want from a new Life is Strange story". Boy was I wrong.
Before the Storm is a worthy addition to the Life is Strange universe without a doubt. It has less mystery but makes up for it with sharper wit and genuinely funny humour. I definitely laughed more in Before the Storm than in Life is Strange. Not to say that BtS is not without its gut-wrenching and heartwarming moments. It's got that in spades. It deals with heavy themes including grief/loss, addiction, love, angst... if you've played the first game, you know what you're getting into here. I feel as though the first season hurt me because I cared so much about the characters (especially Chloe and Max), whereas BtS hurt me more personally.
That was difficult to stomach for me because I can relate so heavily to those themes and the uncertainty surrounding them.
So yeah, Before the Storm ♥♥♥♥ing hurts. But it hurts in a good way. It hurts because it makes you care. There are moments here that are so joyous, so heartwarming, touching and loveably blunt. There are moments that are crass, painful, disturbing, even infuriating. But it's a story crafted with love, depth and development that is rare to find in such stories. Before the Storm keeps the trend of fantastic voice acting, great writing, interesting characters and moves with grace and dread towards its most important plot-points. But there is still a beauty to the quiet parts of the game. There's a reason many scenes give you the option to just... sit down and take it all in. Let Chloe think about things. Let yourself think about things. Like Samuel says... "It's okay to be not okay".
If you have not played either Life is Strange games, please go ahead and do so now. I've loved everything about it so far. Awkward writing and divisive endings all inclusive. If you've played Life is Strange and are hesitant to give Before the Storm a chance... just say ♥♥♥♥ it and go buy it now. You might love it! You just never know. Life is strange that way.

I have just finished the game and I must say it was quite a wild ride.
Advantages:
- LIS BtS managed to retain all the best elements of the original game. The characters, that no one is as easy as they seem from the first look, that there are always layers and layers of complexity for every single person you meet.
- Amazing voice acting. Just, hands down, amazing.
- Storyline was truly interesting. I admit I wasn't the biggest Chloe's fan after original LIS, but LIS BtS showed me things I didn't see, failed to see or was determined not to see. Getting to know what Chloe was going through in the time after WIlliam's death and Max's departure was a good experience. It was even greater to get to meet Rachel and learn her sad story. Things to appreciate!
- Music arrangement was again done fantastically well. This soundtrack will join my favourite playlist, because it's so chill and so very Chloe.
- Graphics was as good as LIS had it.
Disadvantages:
- Though the story was good, chapter 3 felt very-very lacking. Strange plot holes, like literally, Chloe waking up to sit with Sera. Did I miss something? There were many other points like this, and they left me wanting and somewhat disappointed.
It is more my own wish rather than a game's disadvantage, but I lacked a driving force in the entire game. Maybe, to me it just didn't held up high to the original story, where Chloe's life was Max's main goal, as well as finding out what happened to Rachel and the origins of the storm and her powers. It felt... more complex and actually driving.
Beside that, I do wish there was a bit more lead up to the original LIS's events.
Overall, however, I do think this game is incredible and worth playing for every single fan of LIS.
