After 3 years in development, the fourth installment of the Shantae franchise has finally been released. Is Half-Genie Hero worth the weight? Well, let's find out.
Shantae: Half-Genie Hero is the fourth game in the sassy and charming Shantae series and now in high-definition. The visuals in this game are fantastic to say the least. The game mixes colorful and nicely textured 3D assets with high-quality 2D sprites. The animations on characters are also excellent and gives the game some life. Game also ran very well at least for me it did. No crashes either.
Unlike Pirate's Curse, Half-Genie Hero brings back the transformations from the first two games; however, they made some more changes to the system in this one. The way transformations work now is that you go into dance mode and the game goes through a menu of transformations automatically and you use the d-pad (if you played it on a controller which I did) to select your transformation. Additionally, there is now a grand-total of 14 transformations (2 of them can be swapped) with some being more useful than others. The transformations are fun to use but they are not as good as the Pirate Gear from the previous game due to having to pause and wait to select the transformation you want to use which can ruin the flow of the gameplay. There is an upgrade that increases Shantae's dancing animation speed which helps somewhat.
Now for the most important part, the gameplay. Is it any good? Absolutely. It controls nearly as well as Pirate's Curse and using the transformations is still fun despite not flowing as well as the Pirate Gear. The game is more linear than its predecessors but the metroidvania elements are still there as you will be doing a lot of backtracking in earlier levels to go into areas you wouldn't have access to before. The levels are fun to explore but the lack of dungeons is really disappointing. The Shantae games always had really fun dungeons to explore and the lack of them in this game is a crime. I don't know why they removed them but hopefully they will bring them back in the next game. Also, there is no map in this game which is odd considering that Risky's Revenge and Pirate's Curse had maps. The game seems to be quite shorter than the other entries but there will be new character modes that will be coming up later on which should increase the length of the game.
The music is composed by Jake Kaufman once again and I must say, some of the tracks in this game are the best in the whole series. The soundtrack of this game consists of high-quality remixes of songs from previous games and new tracks. There is one track from the previous games that gets reused but is only used for one section. Overall, the soundtrack does not disappoint and Jake Kaufman has done an amazing job once again.
Now for the story, I know the story isn't really the main focus in these games but Pirate's Curse did a pretty good job on that aspect and this game seems to ignore some of the character development from that game. Risky just goes back to her "LOL IM EVIL" self without any explaination and a few characters from the last two games don't make an appearence in this game. Speaking of Risky, there is a lack of Risky in this game as she only appears in the beginning and the end of the game. The story feels pretty unfocused throughout the majority of the game as each level in the game feels more like an episode of "Shantae beats the bad guy from doing bad things". The rival Half-Genie that appears early on in the game would have made for an interesting story but they just conclude her story shortly afterwards. Despite the story being unfocused, the dialogue is still very funny and charming.
Overall, Half-Genie Hero is a very polished and well made game that will not disappoint any fan in the series. It may not be as good as Pirate's Curse but it's still a great entry to the franchise. Let me just say it first: yes! The game is pretty good.
However, when you played Pirates Curse before, then may not expect a direct sequel to that. I mean, yeah, Storywise it is the continuation of the Shantae francise, but when it comes to gameplay, it's kinda more like Riskys Revenge and the first game on the GBC.
And even then it is quite frankly less of a Metroidvania then before. There are no Dungeons anymore for example. Instead you got regular levels who seems more linear at the first sight, and play suprisingly more like the old Mega Man games, with focus of challenging levels with plenty of obstacles to avoid instead of the open nature with a lot of exploration what Shantae used to be (yeah, the old Games had also a lot of tricky platforming, but in this game there are way more bottomless pits and instant death Spikes like in Mega Man as I already mentioned).
However, when you unlock more and more transformations (and there are a lot of them, much more then in the old titles) and revisit old areas, which the game forces you on a repeatedly routine, then you realise that there are more and more open areas hidden inside of these levels where you can find new Items and upgrades and such. And because you can buy a move which can warp you through revisited levels and later even unlock a transformation with that you can fly and skip hard platforming, backtracking isn't even that much of a problem anymore. However, there is no more Map that help you to orient, but too be honest, it isn't needed, since the levels are still quite linear.
So yeah, the gameplay rocks, but sadly, the Story doesn't. Instead of a fully fletched Story, we got more like a Saturday Morning Cartoon approach with small stories that surround every level and a tiny, tiny main plot that got it's focus at the end of the game, and is pretty predictable to be honest. It's not bad, but kinda dissapointing since Pirates Curse felt more massive beause it was one big story (and the Story in that game was really good!).
But that aside: It is really a good game, the second best in the series too be honest. and while I had my problems with the Story,  the gameplay, the really excellent humor and awesome Soundtrack made me forgive this one particular flaw. If you are a Shantae fan: buy this game! If this is you are a newcomer to the francise, hmmm, try Pirates curse first, or even Riskys Revenge so you can tell if you like this Gameplaystyle. But at the end it is indeed a good game!

Your typical platforming experience, with gorgeous graphics and full of charm. You jump around to get through levels while whipping some fools using your hair as a weapon. The usual.
The most notable aspect of the game is that Shantae, the protagonist, transforms into different animals, each with their own abilities that'll be necessary at specific moments to reach all sorts of secrets or progress-related key items. There are also a lot of upgrades to these transformations that increase their capabilities to deal with both enemies and the terrain.
Every level has a very distinct theme and gameplay focus. Each of them feels original and engaging.
The only possible problem with this title is how much backtracking it puts the player through. I personally didn't have a problem with it, but I'd wager some people did. It's probably done to extend the durability of the game, since it's quite short. The silliness involved in the many NPC interactions that occur during these backtrack experiences made them totally worth it to me.
Overall, it gets a hearty recommendation. It's fun, it's charming, it's funny, excessive backtracking being the one thing to be aware of before you get this title.

If you want reference for how good or bad the series is as a whole, it's good, read my other reviews of the previous 2 games:
This time around, they went for a more visually stunning but shorter game, to be expanded with lots of replay value thanks to the upcoming DLCs.
So right now it has the same problem as Switch Force: It's cool, and fun, it's pretty in graphics, but once you've done the 2 modes you're basically done with it. Wait for DLCs.
As it is, and considering how the game's supposed to be expanded, it's good, it's really great. Most importantly, the graphics are really well done and don't even get close to straying off of the style the game usually goes for: Toonish, charming, colorful, vivid, and with noticeable details and tweaks. I believe it's the first time WayForwad does 3d models on one of their IPs, and they did it great for a first time. Characters are still well-put sprites in a 3d-2d parallax world. Really comes together as a modernized classic way of doing things.
60FPS engine, but animations aren't all 60fps. It still looks consistant and doesn't really bother. Also, yes, it comes with chest jigglies. As it's obvious. I mean, WayForward? Fanservice? Isn't that the same thing? /joke
This however doesn't stop the game from being fun and really great. As always, the prime 3 aspects i like about this company are on point: Decent difficulty (questionable here but whatever) and fun gameplay, great artstyle and personality, absolutely rocking synth muslc from Jake Kaufman AKA Virt.
game's a bit short, you can get 100% in the base game mode in 5-6 hours approx, considering how the other games took up to 8 hours for that (all of those are player-dependant times, might take longer if you're not familiar with the games or genre).
The game's very iconic and takes everything positive from the other games, such as returning gags, levels, enemies, bosses, transforms and abilities, while still refreshing everything really well.
On the minus side, because of how short the game is, some features fell under the "situationally helpful" cape of negligence, but at least they get used once. There are a few annoying mechanics that were uncalled for, overall for the very stupidly placed pauses inbetween the action (Why is the level start Ready! screen a thing, and why can't you move while it's playing?), but for the most part it still is a great game.
Buyer's advice: Play the other games before. Some of the content might go unappreciated if you haven't played the other games, or just watched a full gameplay. Any works. But still, playing is much more fun than watching, at least for me.

For some strange reason I was given a large peice of land and a $30,000 grant by the government. They never told me what to do with this land and lump sum of cash, so I did what anyone sound-minded person would do.
We started with the foundations, an apocalyptic HQ was constructed with the bare minimums and our executives came to the decision of using our resources to enter the lumber industry.
We layed out the land that would be used to grow trees, it was a little much for our current small operation capacity, but we were looking to the future.
After a few months we had a steady income.
I wanted more.
After some thoughtful think time, the executives at Lazy Lumber Inc. had made the decision to take the company to the next level.
With some research we found that by sawing the lumber into planks, we can multiply our profits.
To ensure that these profits are maximized; we would be using a system of labour that not only provides us free labour, but even pays us in return for less than comfortable housing.

Life is Strange: Before the Storm (which I will from now on refer to as BtS for convenience) is the prequel to the 2015 game Life is Strange (LiS). The focus is now not on Max Caulfield, the protagonist from the first game, but her sidekick Chloe Price. BtS is set three years before the events of LiS: Max lives in Seattle and Chloe is left behind. She feels alone and without any reason to live. That changes when she meets Rachel Amber.
A prequel will inevitably be compared to the original it was based. The first thing that becomes apparent is that BtS has completely different themes and setups to it, but still feels like the original. The rewind ability from the original is gone. In fact, the most supernatural occurance you get is a bunch of creepy dreams Chloe has of her deceased father. And that’s not a spoiler, because that’s the entire premise of the game. Chloe feels alone because Max left her, her dad is dead and her mother finds a new boyfriend while Chloe still hasn’t accepted her dad is really gone. Through this setup BtS explores the themes of loneliness, depression and ultimately finding a new purpose in life, in Chloe’s case by her friendship with Rachel. In that sense it hits very close to LiS because it also delves into the more emotionally wrecking stuff and focuses entirely on placing characters in difficult positions. Except now its Chloe Price, not Max Caulfield and the whole missing person mystery, the storm and time travel from the original are also gone.
That said, the removal of a lot of extra plot points that were in the original does offer a story that feels a lot more personal. You really get to know Chloe and Rachel and you really feel bad when something bad happens to them. Plus, BtS really managed to nail the feeling of loneliness and abandonment and that magic moment of finding someone to live for. While the original LiS did a reasonably good job of balancing the various storylines, it did never have the opportunity to dig deep into them the way BtS now allows to. A downside to that is most side characters are just background extras or cameos but perform no role in the story. A shame because the original game did such an amazing job of creating a world that felt alive and immersive through the amazing side characters and set pieces. BtS cuts it down to Chloe and Rachel, some minor characters here and there and mostly the same locations throughout the three episodes. But in the context of the new, more focused story it does work. BtS does however tumble down story wise during the last half of episode 3. Mainly because it made the mistake of trying to put in a whole new storyline which it didn’t focus on before and so has no time at all to develop it. That while it was a genuinely interesting plot point. The ending is…weird. It’s not bad but I felt this game’s story would have been better if it was spread over 5 episodes and not 3. That said, the ending does a really good job of setting the stage for LiS and both possible endings feel equally satisfying for different reasons.
Graphics and audio wise, BtS hasn’t changed much compared to LiS. It uses the same graphics engine, though slightly updated the lip synch but then decreased the quality of the character animations. It has some nice cinematography of the American northwest and the town of Arcadia Bay, Oregon, even if these moments aren’t as frequent as in LiS. But anyone that knows LiS remembers the franchise’s amazing soundtrack. And in my opinion, BtS’s soundtrack surpasses the original’s. LiS used mostly soft, quiet guitar music. BtS uses more loud and energetic tracks which perfectly fit the type of person Chloe is. But the songs are incredibly fitting and well chosen. To give an example, in one scene Chloe thinks about how her life has spiralled out of control while
by Speed Ortiz plays. The main chorus of ‘I was better off just being dead. Without my old friend’ fits so perfectly with the scene and the situation and also reference back to LiS. The only downside is that while the songs are amazing, the ambient music is very lacking or sometimes not even present in certain scenes. This is a shame because good ambient music in a scene between two songs can really do a good job of setting the scene. The iconic theme of
(IMO one of the best music tracks in any video game) from the original LiS is a great example of an ambient theme that made every scene it was played it much better. But song wise, BtS does a tremendous job.
Overall I feel BtS is a decently competent prequel. It tells its own story while staying true to the source material it was based on. It doesn’t get as brilliant as the original LiS, but it’s still a good game for newcomers and fans alike.

One of those situations where you could really use a 'meh' option, Mad Max is wrong on many levels (this is the most activity-packed wasteland ever), but as a toy box it is undeniably fun. It hits all the usual open world tropes as you clear camps, wear down factions etc. The voice acting is ropey as hell and there's no real sense of the broken nomad of the films. The fighting is sub-Arkham. But the driving is great, it looks amazing, and you can achieve a lot in 20 minute bursts. Treat it like Shadow of Mordor - as a mindless non canon spin off - and revel in the playground.

Depending on what you are looking for, Mad Max will bore you to tears or entertain you for 50+ hours.  The game blends popular elements from other games into a post-apocalyptic open world with a focus on driving.  Fans of Assassins Creed, Shadow of Mordor and the Batman Arkham games will feel instantly at home.
You have the Batman combat, but surprisingly more brutal and less "smooth", which I think works pretty well as you aren't a superhero!  You have an enormous map, which is probably the biggest I've seen in a game like this.  Finally, you have an abundance of collectibles and that satisfactory feeling when you completely clear an area  and have it marked as 100%.  The game certainly is repetitive, but fans of collectibles and upgrading will enjoy this game and that part of the game appealed to me more than the lacklustre story on offer.
What makes Max Max stand out from the open world crowd is the use of the "Magnum Opus", a car that you will do battle in, upgrade and race over the entire course of the game.  There's plenty of choice when it comes to upgrading weapons, making the car faster, getting the armour upgraded and adjusting the parts for the task at hand.  I enjoyed this part of the game immensely and I don't even enjoy driving games.
A slightly boring story and repetitive gameplay will turn a lot of people off, but the game does shine when it comes to its driving mechanics and how it gives you so much to collect and explore in its enormous map.  Graphics aren't the most important thing, but I have to say that the game is gorgeous and managed to make a game that is mostly sand look breathtaking at times.  I highly recommend this game to people who like the games I have mentioned and perhaps those who were intrigued by the driving sections in Rage.

Mad Max has the most small, repeated annoyances out of any game I have ever played. Every time you have to interact with something, get back health or refuel your car the animation is 5 to 10 seconds longer than it should be. And you will see each of these animations hundreds, if not thousands, of times.  This game's exploration and world are great, but I wish it didn't remind me every 60 seconds that watching this animation is more important than actually playing the game.

This game was over-hyped, and frankly it fell short of my expectations by a couple of miles. There is literally nothing good I have to say about this game.
BAD THINGS ABOUT THE PLOT:
When you first get shot at by the 33rd US Army, your character yells a few things about "friendly fire" and "stop shooting" which is what normal people do. Then, when they don't stop shooting, you and your squad just mow them all down and continue butchering your way through your own side for the rest of the game. A highly trained Delta operative would and could shoot to incapacitate and or minimise loss of life when shooting at people on the same side.
When you get to the bit when you use the white phosphorous, in the thermal imager you see the humvees that you "have" to blow up, and the soldiers shooting at you that you "have" to blow up. Then, after destroying all of the military targets, I found myself stuck and unable to exit the mortar shooting section. Right in the corner, is this little blob of white. I can tell that it's people, they're not shooting at me, they don't have humvees; but the game won't let me progress until I've blown them up as well............SURPRISE THEY'RE INNOCENT PEOPLE!!! AAAARGH HOW COULD YOU DO THAT YOU EVIL PERSON SITTING BEHIND A COMPUTER SCREEN!!!! AAAARGH, THIS WILL PLAGUE YOUR CONSCIENCE FOREVER!!!!!!
No, game, you made me do it, and you executed that little moral section really poorly.
Now, Conrad has a little bit of an argument with his team, and then the mindless slaughter of American soldiers continues. At some point, both your team members die and I don't even remember when and I don't care because they had no human characteristics, they were just one dimensional distractions. Skipping to the next 'moral' point is when there are two people tied up and snipers point their guns at the two of them. Then, you "have" to make the choice over which one to kill. I just shot the snipers, and I think the two people just automatically die, or maybe they still live; either way you don't have to choose which one lives, you can just shoot the snipers. The whole plot point where you blow up all the water and cause some death isn't a choice, it's how the plot progresses so I'm not going to lose any sleep over that. Skipping over some utterly stupid next sections of the game, I'll rant and rave about the multiple endings of the game. "Hmm, should I shoot the mirror or let the mirror shoot me?" What kind of stupid choice is that? The whole point of a video game is to live and shoot everyone else and then in some games a cutscene makes you die for some reason. "Hmm, should I shoot the friendly soldiers come to rescue me?"   If you shoot the soldiers and then go back inside, then how are you going to survive? You blew up all the water remember?   If you put the gun down, then you get to go home and live happily ever after, THE END!
BAD THINGS ABOUT THE GAMEPLAY
I played it on the hardest difficulty, and yet I could still blind fire with perfect accuracy? Who can get headshots crouching with a pistol upside down over the top of their head and hit someone that they can't see in the head? STUPID!
Why could I only get extra ammo by 'executing' fellow American soldiers? Why was I executing fellow American soldiers anyway? (see rage up above)
Why didn't the guns jam all of the time if you're constantly in sandstorms?
Why after your support gunner gets shot in the leg as part of a plot point does he make a big deal of it and when in gameplay he gets shot all of the time and doesn't notice?
OVERALL SUMMARY
Bad gameplay, bad plot, stupid choices, and whoopdedoo nobody has done "morals" in a game before, lets make the rest of the game bad and base our entire selling point on a flimsly poorly executed moral thing to draw people into buying the game. I know that's me suckd in right there, I payed $7.50 for this game, and I regret parting with every single cent.
If you have high or even medium expectations for this game, then don't buy it.

I brought this on the recommendation of the story; the premise being that the largest sandstorm has engulfed the entirety of Dubai. You control Walker from Delta Squad, who is sent in, to recon the situation after an entire US Army battalion went to save civilians over a month ago and didn't come back. It obviously doesn't turn out well else you'd not be sent in the first place.
The setting is sublime - a post apocalyptic-like mess, it stands out heads and shoulders as the most intriguing part of the game - much more so then the army personnel and your squad are.
However I was both fascinated and frustrated by the game; on one hand the story unfolds at quite a pace (with no spoilers here, but just go with the flow even with the plot holes, it's interesting, although I'd have loved more backstory with such a setting), on the other hand the game is frustrating gameplay wise - with constant dying and not the best cover mechanics with the same tired "two weapons, limited ammo for you but not everyone else", and a lack of gameplay choices - even if some of them are "the point" and "making me think", bah to most of the forced choices!
However due to the short length of the game I eventually succeeded past the waves of "You've died too many times, want to lower the difficulty?" messages. Even if some of it wasn't enjoyable I almost took it to heart that the game, as a whole, was better for being that bit more rough then I had expected; war isn't nice after all and it led some gravity to it. I'd say it's well worth a play, especially if it can be nabbed for a fiver or under.

While this game is visually superior to previous games in the series, in other areas it appears to have taken one or two steps backwards.
Gameplay is as good as it's ever been, though perhaps a bit stale given how little has changed. Same spells, same upgrades. Even the transformations are largely recycled from previous games. In fact there are probably too many transformations. It sometimes felt contrived how the level layout required certain transformations to progress.
This game can't seem to decide whether it's aiming to bring in new fans, or pander to old fans. The game is more simple and linear compared to previous games, but spends next to no time on character introductions, expecting you to already know who everyone is. And while the old transformations do look great in HD, they lack personality. In particular, I really miss the monkey's idle animation from Risky's Revenge.
The pacing is also kind of messy. As with previous games, to progress you need to find the relevant collectibles in levels you've already cleared. This creates a sort of slow, leisurely "scavenger hunt" type of game, during which you jump around and fight enemies set to an exciting soundtrack. This structure was also in previous games, and is not a problem.
What I'm talking about is the "in-between" segments, when you talk to NPCs to get hints and hand in quest items. There's very little dialogue before you're onto your next task. So you might spend half an hour finding the item you need, and then you get less than a minute of plot before you're onto the next level. The game felt really short, too.
While we're at it, boss battles. This game's bosses are pitiful. I'm not talking about difficulty, I'm talking about buildup. Risky's Revenge had actual dungeons in which the bosses resided, and you would know their name before meeting them.
Pirate's Curse was longer, so didn't do this for each boss. Those it did build up, though, were well done.
Then we get to Half Genie Hero, and there's practically no build up for any of them, least of all the final boss, which is only introduced when the battle begins.
The final bosses are the most irritating example of this. RR had the boss take something the player themselves had come to cherish, and turn it against them. PC had a deliberate repeat of this, but getting the right collectibles adds a twist to the ending which turns everything upside down. HGH has the boss show up and fight you. And... that's pretty much it. If more effort had gone into developing the plot or characters, the stakes might have felt higher, but as it was, it was just a moderately more difficult boss battle.
If you've read this far, you might be wondering when I get to the reason this is in the positive reviews section. And that reason is that despite all its flaws, this is a good game that I enjoyed playing, and I think it is well worth the $20 USD pricetag.
The other games are better though.

This is my first real attempt to try a rogue-like. I had a cup of tea with The Binding of Isaac a couple of years ago but thoroughly disliked it. See, my problem with rogue-likes is that I feel that they inherently waste my time, if I die then I lose all of my progress and have to start from scratch. As an adult with a full time job and limited free time to play games, this experience is not enjoyable to me. I do not like the feeling that my time is being wasted, and when I played BoI this is exactly how I felt. Yes, I know that part of the rogue-like experience is learning new things about the game each time but this is essentially just trial and error. Again, if I had all the free time in the world this wouldn’t bother me nearly as much. Thankfully, Rogue Legacy mitigates this concern a great deal.
Rogue Legacy is a rogue-like with progression. What a novel idea! It takes your standard 2D sidecrolling platformer and ingeniously adds a family legacy mechanic: each time you die, you pick a family member as a successor giving you a sense of history and context for your playthrough. Each successor you pick will have specific traits as well that affect the game: this might be colorblindness (the game is black and white), glaucoma (blurry screen), ADHD (you move faster) among countless others. This smart addition makes each run through the castle seem fresh and interesting.
Another aspect that carries over from run to run is the gold that you accumulate. Any gold collected during a run can then be used to permanently upgrade your family tree (HP, mana, damage) or buy new gear for your heirs. This added progression, for me, fixes my biggest problem with rogue-likes, I always feel like I’m chipping away at a goal. So even if I died quickly during that last run I can grab a new helmet that will help me from there on out. In addition to this carry over, you can also lock down the dungeon so the layout is no longer procedurally generated. Just had a long run and loved the layout? Lock it down! This, of course, comes with a reduction in the amount of gold you earn though.
So while I may not be very good at Rogue Legacy and will almost assuredly never beat it, I appreciate what it has done for rogue-likes. It has taken a genre that I have never cared about and given me pause to explore it a bit more and see what variations are out there.

The best way to describe this game is that it wouldn't be a stretch to say the ship combat from Sid Meier's Pirates inspired this 17th century based sea action based multiplayer sandbox. And 17th century means Sloops, Galleons and Frigates.
You control one ship as you fight pirates and other factions for dominance in cells in an overall map. Capturing all towns and defeating all enemies pacifies the cell and allows you to proceed into the next harder one.
Progression is marked by skill tree, equipment and ship variety.
Skills are seperated into defence, offence and support. Defence involves defensive buffs and abilities such as damage resistance, in combat repairs and speed. Offence involves attack buffs and abilities such as AOE attacks and damage buffs. Support involves accuracy, diplomacy and miscellaneous abilities and buffs.
Friendly towns have quests which involves transport, trade, creating new towns and structures, town defence and hunting enemies. A large basis of the game is completing quests and trading which not only will reward the player with resources and currency but also will improve the prosperity of the town and raise the quality of equipment and ships on sale.
The gameplay and control are straight forward and all information is provided to player. No hunting through wikis for essential knowledge of game.
Being a sandbox, you can customise the layout of the map (the cells themselves are procedurally generated so you cannot create you own custom landmasses), the factions themselves and names of towns.
Now, there are set backs to this game.
Windward is clearly designed for multiplayer in mind, but the online multiplayer scene is lacking. Windward needs a group of friends willing to play for a night or two. Hypothetically you could play this single player (and I have) but it will get dull real fast.
Windward is 100% sandbox. The game goes on for as long as you play. There is no plot or main quest. You make your own goals and fun.
The act of taking over a cell without human opposition will get dry very quickly. Once again, a mark against the lack of online scene. I cannot stress how much of a shame it is that this is not popular enough to have a large online presence because I would think a wide scale sea warfare in a map is incredibly capable but hasn't been made possible.
The game also implies that there are non combat routes to this game. Not realistically possible. I would like to see more of a variance in the scope of offensive capabilities as the entire diplomacy/support tree is not supported by how the game actually operates.
The late game ships choices essentially ask if you want more damage or more health and that's all the variance you will get and the early game ships are just moderate improvements on your previous one.
And lastly, I made reference to this being inspired by Sid Meier's Pirates. To clarify, this game is definately not Sid Meier's Pirates. The way the ships handle and how combat operates is a reasonable comparison as well as the 17th century ships, but the entire game and how it operates is entirely different.
It's a neat game. Worth a bunch of friends passing time and maybe possibly one day, a server could get popular enough to get the true nature of the game fleshed out. Because then it would be promoted from neat game to great game.
It's fun for a few hours, but gets repetitive. There needs to be more to it.

Got this game as a gift right before I attempted to get it for myself.
This game is cute as hell with wonderful animation (already a huge motivator for any animator or artist to get it. I might be a bit biased because of this, lol.)
The gameplay is fairly straightforward as a platformer, but even if it's a little more on the simple side it's very polished. Most of the game involves platformer puzzles and exploration, greatly expanded by how the transformations affect your ability to move through levels.
Some forms unfortunately only see use for one or two puzzles and don't have any practical use outside of that, which is a little disappointing, but far from a dealbreaker.
The soundtrack is absolutely killer, and just to stress again the visuals are great. I haven't seen a non-pixel 2D game look this good in a very long time.
The only other gripe I have would maybe be some of the fights are underwhelming or overly simplistic: wait for enemy to use X attack, then attack back a few times. Rinse and repeat many many times until dead. The AI for the fights is more based on patterns rather than reaction--enemies won't do anything different depending on what you're doing, they'll just go through their own motions and soak up what damage you output. There also doesn't feel like there's a lot of randomness in the fights--when a boss uses a move, it operates the same way every time.
It's a little short and a bit easy--leisurely playing will take maybe 5-6 hours to beat, but the game also is only $20, so it's hard to complain about length considering its cost. Plus it's a game that has a decent bit of replay value with speedrun achievements and alternate modes (including a few upcoming and DLC ones). It's also worthwhile going for a full clear.
Overall though it's also a game with a focus on its art, soundtrack, characters, and writing, all of which are good or better, without being held back by elements such as length, difficulty, and mechanics which are 'adequate'.

I ran forward through the castle complex, but no matter how hard I squinted, the world outside the small bubble of clarity around me remained blurry and out of focus. “Damn this short-sightedness,” I muttered before hacking at a beast in my path. Nothing. The damn blade passed right through it. Oh great, I’m seeing things again. Dementia’s a ♥♥♥♥♥.
Welcome to Rogue Legacy, a game quite unlike anything else I’ve come across. Looking for all the world like a 2D action-platformer, behind the charming pixel art presentation is a consistently surprising experience, packing a dizzying array of variables.
It’s all anchored by robust Roguelike game design, which means a procedurally generated world and perma-death. Each time you enter the castle, its layout and the challenge ahead will be different, and if you die, well, that’s the end of that hero - it’s time to send one of his heirs in to try and finish the job. Thankfully, the meta-game lets you spend any gold earned during the last run on your family’s fort, which means unlocking new classes and perks, and upping your stats for the next attempt.
Caption
The core sword and spell action-platforming is tightly designed.
And boy, there’s going to be a lot of attempts. When you first start playing Rogue Legacy you might last a minute or two before succumbing to one of the ghouls, undead, or other nasties that lurk inside the castle complex. It’s a classic 30-second gameplay loop – hacking, slashing, running, jumping, dashing, evading, and spellcasting, repeated until you die. This core gameplay is compelling in and of itself - Rogue Legacy is wonderful to control provided you have a good gamepad - but to make true progress you’ll need to boost your stats, get better equipment and activate perks. Gradually your runs will get longer and longer. Then you’ll wander into a higher-level area and die almost instantly.
The cycle of life, eh?
It’s an excellent way to structure the challenge, and really puts the fear of god into you. You may be kicking♥♥♥♥♥in what amounts to Rogue Legacy’s foyer, but boy, you’re not ready for the forest yet, or – god forbid – the dank dungeons underneath the castle. This is a game where your best option is to turn and run away if you enter an area you’re not ready for. This is a game where it may be several hours before you beat the first boss – despite being able to reach it in a matter of minutes - and many more before you’re ready for the next. Good thing the bosses stay dead after you die, otherwise beating Rogue Legacy would be an even more distant prospect.
Caption
The bosses can be next to impossible with the wrong character, but as you'd expect, learning their attack patterns is key.
Now, levelling up is all well and good, but Rogue Legacy has one very unique trick up its sleeve in addition to this. I’ve already mentioned that you send an heir in to continue the fight after each death, but you actually get a choice of three, and each has a random class, random spell, and random traits. Traits? Yup, and they’re glorious, surprising and bewildering. Ever played as a hero suffering from vertigo and OCD? How about a colour blind protagonist who also has Alzheimer’s? ADHD and dementia anyone? Tunnel vision and irritable bowel syndrome? The list goes on and on.
The really clever part of this system is that many of these traits have significant gameplay ramifications: ADHD means you move faster, far-sightedness and near-sightedness leave areas of the screen blurry, and characters with dementia will hear things and see enemies that aren’t there. Dwarves, meanwhile, are so light and small they don’t activate spiked floor panels and can access areas no other characters can.
Of course, some traits really have been included just for fun. Dyslexia, for instance, means any in-game text is garbled, while a character with coprolalia (Tourette’s syndrome) will swear any time he or she gets hit. Heroes with hypochondria, on the other hand, will have much larger numbers pop up any time they take damage, while you’ll probably avoid vertigo at all costs – unless you’re a masochist – because who wants their world to be upside down? Getting your head around the traits system is all about working out what comes with meaningful changes to the world and how that factors into your play style.
The world near long-sighted heroes is out of focus.
Cool, right? And that’s really just a taste – there’s plenty more for you to discover when you play it yourself... which you absolutely should. The traits are just one facet, too. Once you factor in the ten classes and all the spells characters can have, the list of potential combinations is incredibly long.
It really is pot luck, and no matter how far through the meta-game you are, you will never know exactly what to expect. Of course, the further in you are, the more you’ve honed your skills and come to know how best to use each class, trait, and spell, and – crucially – how to select the random character that you can best utilise.
The learning curve is right on the money, and almost every run has something to teach you, whether it’s an epic boss-killing mission with a heaven-sent character that’s able to survive a wide-roaming journey through the castle, or an abject, miserable failure with the best of a bad bunch. Mind you, the random nature of Rogue Legacy won’t be to everyone’s tastes - getting a series of dud characters can definitely feel punitive at times, as opposed to a learning experience.
Caption
Every class differs in core stats and special ability, while equipment and enchantments are class agnostic.
Thankfully, the mix of enemies is quite compelling. Each area introduces new enemies - ninjas in Hannya masks, headless horses that charge the player - as well as fresh variants on old designs. Juggling a set of monsters with their own disparate attack patterns is a big part of the challenge. The five bosses represent a good mix of bullet hell and precision platforming too, whether you’re facing a huge flaming skull or a gigantic gelatinous blob.
The castle holds more surprises than just rooms full of enemies. Special rooms abound, including carnival games, shrines, mini-boss battles, and plenty more. Perhaps the most interesting, however, are the fairy chest rooms. Each has a very specific challenge for you to beat. Kill everything! Get to the chest without jumping! Don’t fight! Don’t take damage! You get the idea.
Unlocking a fairy chest will net you a rune that can be equipped for specific perks, like air-jumping, dashes, limited flight, extra gold, reflecting damage taken back onto enemies, gaining health/mana from kills, and so on. Best of all, these runes stack. So if you want to, you can spec your character with highly customised ability sets. Multiple air-jumps? Don’t mind if I do!
While some of the fairy chest rooms can be conquered by almost any character, others require particular traits or sets of runes. Thankfully, you can use the Architect - one of three characters unlocked via your fort (alongside the Smithy and Enchantress) - to lock down the layout of the castle for successive attempts. He’s a great inclusion, and indicative of Rogue Legacy’s ability to balance random elements with tight, fair game design.
In fact, if that balance was wrong, this game wouldn’t be anywhere near as compelling. It’s a testament to Cellar Door Games that the team was able to juggle so many elements and make it work.
It’s one hell of a meaty undertaking too. The most adept players will be able to beat it in about 15 hours, whereas I sunk in considerably more time than that. It’s a lot of gaming for only $15 (USD $17 on PlayStation), and once you’ve finished your first play-through, New Game + awaits, which lets you keep all your stats, weapons and runes, but gives you a much harder variant of the castle to beat.

To put this in the most basic sense, Assassin Creed 4's ship combat put in a single game.
That isn't bad, nowhere near it. In fact, they improve on the concept a whole lot.
The long version is this. Windward is a ship exploration game where the goal is to take your randomly generated world in the name of your faction. You can pick from 4 current factions on the start, and later join 2 more later on. The factions are pretty straightforward with what they do with their experience bonuses and ship discounts.
The Valiant are pure combat ships, so they get experience bonuses from battles and they get a discount on the heavy combat ship.
The Sojurn are exploration based, and get bonuses from discovering new places. They also get discounts on the fastest ships in the game.
The Exchange are merchants at heart. They get the best bonuses from trading and profit, and their ship discount is the one with the biggest cargo.
The Consulate are diplomatic, and get bonuses in questing. Their discount are with the jack-of-all-trades ship.
Now, for the meat and bones of this game. Plot-wise, there's really no plot. You're a captain and you have to make the best of it.
So, you're on the reverse end in Assassin's Creed 4, of sorts. Now YOU'RE the merchant ship fighting off pirates! And the combat is great. You have to make sure your cannons are lined up right, some factions can fire volleys of death, among other things. You can also conquer and plunder towns, take down pirate captains, and other things.
So my final verdict, this game has a real appeal to me personally. I say get this game if anything I said got your interest.

If you liked the sailing in Sid Meyer's Pirates, you'll love this game.  Rather than a large, open world, everything takes place on a series of maps and, if you desire a bit of privacy for yourself and friends, instances.  You can even host and play the game in a LAN party locally, or by direct-connection to a private server.
In gameplay, you choose a faction to start with, are assigned a basic ship, and can quest/trade or hunt down pirates to fill your own personal coffers and increase your experience level, which unlocks more difficult areas and provides talent points that increase your capabilities.  Higher areas = more money and experience.  Towns can be leveled up through a combination of trading and questing, which unlocks access to purchase and then choose between new ships.
If you like a peaceful game that can be played at your leisure, then this game is for you.  If you like teaming up with friends and blowing the competition away, this game is also for you.
Cons: some content is still being worked on, and the end game can be a bit sparse.  Definitely a game to be savored and not rushed through.

Before we get into the actual review lets establish a baseline. There isn’t a story in this game, you just do quests, combat and trading to acquire gold and experience so you can level up, get better items and better ships. With that being said, once you discover multiplayer servers you will never do anything single player again. Multiplayer servers have much more experience and gold than anything you will do in single player from early on in the game. I am writing this at the start of the review so someone actually reads it and doesn’t waste their time grinding out single player – like I did. It took me a few days of single player to reach level 20 and buy a handful of ships. It took me one day of multiplayer combat instances to reach level 50 from 20 and unlock all of the ships. My first impressions were that the game was really slow because I was playing it alone and offline. This view gets completely flipped on its head when I discovered multiplayer.
You can log into a multiplayer server, join a heroic combat instance and just collect items in the sea that sell for a ♥♥♥♥ tonne of gold. While people who are of the appropriate level fight the pirates and you just soak up the map-wide experience. It’s pretty cheesey but a lot less dry than playing the game offline, alone. Also, the items you collect to sell take up your inventory rather than your cargo spaces which means you can collect a lot of them. I’ll address this point later on, but just be mindful of this – it’s huge. Once you get enough levels, gold and items from this scavenger type of play you can actually assist in the combat and drive out the pirates – which is good fun. Heroic combat instances are group oriented content so you can’t solo the ships very easily. You’ll need to work with the others on the server to defeat the pirates.
The combat is actually fun and quite strategic. If you have a fast ship, you can position yourself in the enemy blind spot while you pepper them with your broadside cannons. You can also just zip around pirates and capture unprotected towns. If you have a defensive, slow ship, you can ram pirates or just be supportive and protect the more fragile ships in your fleet. If you’re a low level ship and clearly under levelled for the instance you’re in – you can still play a role. You can scout the fog of war and locate towns that need to be captured and sometimes capture a town yourself while the pirates are distracted elsewhere.
With each level you get a talent point to spend on passives/abilities but the talent choices are pretty♥♥♥♥♥ A lot of abilities share cooldowns with each other so you’ll mostly use the same ability over and over again because they’re not particularly balanced. In addition to this, it’s easy to get levels so you never really specialise. You’re only ever a support/offensive/defensive ship in the early game when you don’t have enough talents to fill out everything.
Overall the game is really fun. I’ve found that the online community are willing to help people who have just started and get them to a point in which they can contribute to big combat instances and be useful – which is when the game peaks for me.
From this point on, I’ll talk about the single player but the above is the best part of the game and if you’re debating whether or not to pick up the game – base it on the above. Multiplayer servers are fun and so much faster to get gold, experience and items that you’ll will never need to or want to play solo at all.
==================================================================================
Solo Play
These are your options for solo play:
Quests
You can do quests to get experience and gold from each town dotted in the regions. Doing quests levels the town in which you got the quest (up to a max of level 10). Level 10 towns sell better items, more ships and reduce prices of the goods. When you start a quest you get given an item that occupies a space in your cargo hold – so in the early game you can probably do around three quests at a time. It takes a mountain of quests to upgrade a town, so, if you have a small ship with three cargo spaces you’re going to be questing for a really long time before you get a level 10 town.
The quests are pretty run-of-the-mill: deliver this, collect that, and kill this guy. They are fun while you’re learning the game but after a while they get stale. I think we can safely assume that if you’re questing it’s because you want a level 10 town. It’s a big grind. Alternatively you could just join a multiplayer server that already has level 10 towns and use those to save yourself a headache and a few hours.
Trading
The trading was alright. You visit each town and it presents you with a list of what goods they have in excess and what they need – then you rearrange good between towns accordingly by sailing back and forth. We come back to this point, but the goods occupy the cargo hold (max of 5 spaces late game).
The Problem with Quests and Trading
Overall they’re slow, make less gold/experience than multiplayer server combat instances and are less fun. Quest items and trade goods occupy your cargo hold, in which you can have a maximum of 5 slots. Items found from multiplayer combat instances occupy your inventory which has 25 slots, no matter what ship you have.
I am level 64 currently and each quest gives me about 500 gold and a good trade can earn me 1k-2k gold after a lengthy bit of sailing and working out which town needs which material/item. So this means I can earn around 5k from a full cargo-hold, from quests and trading. Each item in the cargo hold is very unlikely to be destined for the same town so I’m going to be sailing for a while, back and forward to different towns.
Combat instances regularly drop items worth between 2-5k and I can hold 25 of them. This means I can have an awesome time fighting pirates and conquering the region alongside friends before I sail to one town and vendor all my spoils and earn my payday. I can acquire items used for my ship or just sell them. I can pick up aesthetic items to change the way my ship looks or just sell them and make bank. The questing and trading isn’t fun enough to warrant losing that much gold and experience. Whereas multiplayer combat instances are great fun, great gold and great experience so I’m not sure why you’d play alone.
Exploring
You never explore in this game. Each map is made up of tiles that are covered by a fog of war. You sail around to reveal the fog of war and then take over the towns by sitting in them while pirates contest your actions. Each region is this, over and over again with a different spread of land masses. It gets dry pretty quick.
The Review
Join a server and never play alone.

No, game, you made me do it, and you executed that little moral section really poorly.
Now, Conrad has a little bit of an argument with his team, and then the mindless slaughter of American soldiers continues. At some point, both your team members die and I don't even remember when and I don't care because they had no human characteristics, they were just one dimensional distractions. Skipping to the next 'moral' point is when there are two people tied up and snipers point their guns at the two of them. Then, you "have" to make the choice over which one to kill. I just shot the snipers, and I think the two people just automatically die, or maybe they still live; either way you don't have to choose which one lives, you can just shoot the snipers. Skipping over some utterly stupid next sections of the game, I'll rant and rave about the multiple endings of the game. "Hmm, should I shoot the mirror or let the mirror shoot me?" What kind of stupid choice is that? The whole point of a video game is to live and shoot everyone else and then in some games a cutscene makes you die for some reason. "Hmm, should I shoot the friendly soldiers come to rescue me?"   If you shoot the soldiers and then go back inside, then how are you going to survive? You blew up all the water remember?   If you put the gun down, then you get to go home and live happily ever after, THE END!

I played it on the hardest difficulty, and yet I could still blind fire with perfect accuracy? Who can get headshots crouching with a pistol upside down over the top of their head and hit someone that they can't see in the head? STUPID!
Why could I only get extra ammo by 'executing' fellow American soldiers? Why was I executing fellow American soldiers anyway? (see rage up above)
Why didn't the guns jam all of the time if you're constantly in sandstorms?
Why after your support gunner gets shot in the leg as part of a plot point does he make a big deal of it and when in gameplay he gets shot all of the time and doesn't notice?
OVERALL SUMMARY
Bad gameplay, bad plot, stupid choices, and whoopdedoo nobody has done "morals" in a game before, lets make the rest of the game bad and base our entire selling point on a flimsly poorly executed moral thing to draw people into buying the game. I know that's me suckd in right there, I payed $7.50 for this game, and I regret parting with every single cent.

However I was both fascinated and frustrated by the game; on one hand the story unfolds at quite a pace (with no spoilers here, but just go with the flow even with the plot holes, it's interesting, although I'd have loved more backstory with such a setting), on the other hand the game is frustrating gameplay wise - with constant dying and not the best cover mechanics with the same tired "two weapons, limited ammo for you but not everyone else", and a lack of gameplay choices - even if some of them are "the point" and "making me think", bah to most of the forced choices!
However due to the short length of the game I eventually succeeded past the waves of "You've died too many times, want to lower the difficulty?" messages. Even if some of it wasn't enjoyable I almost took it to heart that the game, as a whole, was better for being that bit more rough then I had expected; war isn't nice after all and it led some gravity to it. I'd say it's well worth a play, especially if it can be nabbed for a fiver or under.

For those of you who used to play it waaay back when, it's like TrackMania: Nations Forever.  Except it's better.
TrackMania is widely known as being one of the most difficult racing games ever - to beat the different achievements ("medals") on each track, you need to clock some seriously freaking amazing times.  And then there's the so-called "Author Medal" - the medal you can only achieve by beating the best time set by the track's
.  I've played this game and TM:NF for years and I've only ever earned about three of them, at best.
The visuals of this game are absolutely stunning, bringing the cars, tracks, and of course the stadium itself, truly to life.
The amount of content in the game is virtually limitless, from user creations in the Workshop to tracks you can put together yourself.  The map creator gives you literally as much flexibility as the game's creators had, and is super easy to use.
The multiplayer is a lot of fun too - connecting to servers and racing live with other players, or even having everyone individually clock their own best times, with a time limit to see who can clock the best time the fastest.  It's very easy to set up a server of your own too!
And I also like the "Official Time" function - that's something they didn't have before in TM:NF.  It's solo-play, except that you can observe your best times and how they stack up to other players across your state, country, or across the globe.
The music, as it was in TM:NF, isn't amazing (it's not bad, but not great either), but then again, it's the gameplay we're after, right?
The only real gripe I had about the game is this: I noticed very quickly going through the White-level (easiest) tracks that a number of tracks were re-used from TM:NF, just adapted to the new graphics engine.  Really?  If I wanted to play those again, I would have just gotten the free download of Nations instead.
But all-in-all, I recommend that you go for it, especially if you love racing and you love a challenge.  After all, it's only $10, and it comes with the free demo of ShootMania Elite.

I don't usually write reviews. To be honest, I usually don't even rate the games I buy. But this series is just special to me.
Both Life is Strange games are my favorite games ever. Not my only favorites, mind you, but still my favorites with no doubt.
Surely not everyone's cup of tea, but if you really get into the game, immerse in the atmosphere and care about the characters, you might see how much of a masterpiece it really is.
Since the first episode of Life is Strange, I've actually changed. These peaceful moments with relaxing music and great scenarios to look at made me see beauty in tiny things, not to mention how it affected my music taste.
My recommendation? If you like story based games and don't mind a little bit of cheese (like my comment, for example) then I totally recommend. It might steal your heart if you let it.
If you only like realistic stuff and expect characters to act or react the way you imagine people would - In other words, If you can't suspend your disbelief - then maybe this is not for you.
My only criticisms are:
1-Choices should make more difference;
2-The last episode of both games felt like they went a little too long on some things and too short on others;
3 (or 2.5)-Not enough interactions between main characters. In the first one, not enough between Max and Chloe, and in this one, not enough between Chloe and Rachel. Everytime they're not together, I wish they were.
In conclusion, I bought the Deluxe version in pre-order before even bothering to check what was the content of them because I knew this game would be worth every cent regardless, which it totally did. I just wish it was longer. But, to be fair, I can't get enough of this so i'd ALWAYS wish it was longer. I still give it a 10/10. It wouldn't feel right to me to give less than that. Nobody will read this since it's just another positive review among thousands, but thank you, Square Enix, Deck Nine and everyone involved.

It's a sandbox game with a whole lot of sand, a great atmosphere, visual design taken straight of Fury Road and made by fans of the whole series or at least people who really documented themselves, with lots of details and easter eggs about the three first movies. As a fan of the Mad Max universe myself, I had a blast.
However, just as in a real sandbox, it's mostly up to you to make your own fun. The story is a bit weak, and while there are a ton of locations (over 250 I think), all of them unique, all you do is drive and fight, either in a vehicle or on foot with a Batman Arkham clone system which is very brutal and satisfying and offers quite a bit of different possibilities once you've unlocked skills. You can upgrade your vehicle to make it tougher and meaner, get a few weapons for your car and unlock fighting skills for Max, but the core experience stays the same. If that appeals to you and you like to explore every nook and cranny in a game to find stuff (it's always scrap, but you need it for everything), go right in. If you need to be poked every five minutes by narrative to stay interested, it isn't the game for you.
There a over 16'000 reviews already, so there isn't much I could say that you can't find elsewhere. I'm just going to say "watch the trailer", for once it isn't just an empty cinematics showcase filled with buzzwords but it shows you most of the gameplay and really shows you the game and what to expect.
Disclaimer: I am a fan of the Mad Max universe since The Road Warrior, back in the days where there was no videogames and where it was the only post-apocalyptic experience around, so I'm probably biased.

I wasn't positive on Rogue Legacy from the beggining - at one point while playing this game I absolutely hated it. I thought grinding was necessary since I kept dying without getting a sense of advancement, and I absolutely despised the idea of a game that involved grinding in its gameplay. After some time playing I realized I needed to adapt to the game, which meant actually dodging enemy attacks and attacking safely. Before long, I was doing room clears and beating bosses all to the final boss. In that, my initial disgust with the game was based on a misunderstanding on my part.
All this is to say Rogue Legacy is the same formula of any hard-as-nails game: there's no grinding involved if you git gud. You can finish a first playthrough without grinding at all, just dying once in a while to spend all that gold from bosses and room clears. At that, the game's design is quite inclusive, since you can either turtle your way in by using the architect to reach and beat the bosses, or you can become aware of the enemies' patterns and dodge like a ballerina while hitting fast - either playstyle is valid. A lot of people might hate the first style (rightfully), so to fully enjoy Rogue Legacy you either have to be quite skilled or have the patience to creep your way up. You could say it's a gitgud or gohome kind of game, and maybe that's its greatest fault.

I mean he built a game intended for LAN play that somehow supported 300 simultaneous players in a single game instance running on his home server via cable modem!  That is nutz!  He added server limitation code after that to ensure more managable numbers since this was not intended as an MMO, but it shows the quality of his code work that it worked at all.  How many other 1 person dev teams could put out a game that allows 50 + users enaging in battle simultaneously?  Seriously... Let's get this out of the way: if you like to turn off your brain and shoot other people on the internet, Black Ops 2 is probably the thing for you.
Now, I don't think anybody buys a game from the Call of Duty franchise thinking: "Oh, boy, I can't wait to play the campaign! I bet there's gonna be some awesome character development, and a solid storyline." However, this game does have a campaign. I have been playing it on Veteran mode, which is the highest difficulty, and the biggest challenge I have encountered so far is a ladder. I can't get past it, and according to Google, a myriad of people have the same problem I'm having, and the only solution that MIGHT work is to redo the entire mission from the start.
This game won't reward you with the simple joy of progression if you don't do things exactly the way it wants you to. If you like to think before taking action, go play Arma or something, this is a run n' gun bonanza. If you're interested in this game's single player content, please do yourself a favor and don't buy it at full price. Hell, don't buy it on sale. Don't even borrow it from a friend, don't accept it as a gift, and if someone is willing to pay you money to play it, keep your dignity and politely refuse.
Having said that, the multiplayer is probably fun, but I didn't care enough to find out yet.
If you see me playing Black Ops 2, it's because I am a masochistic idiot, and I'm trying to get my money's worth from this hemorrhoid of a game.

This game is what every military shooter that tries to focus on war attempts to be but doesn't reach it.  The gameplay is solid, sticking to being a TPS with cover mechanics. But while the gameplay doesn't offer too much, the story more than makes up for it. The painful choices of war, the violence you're forced to witness in times of desperation, all become in sync with each other, making you realize what war truly is. As you progress through the story, you (not the character, but the player) will question why you are forced to do such things. Why must you kill all these people? Then it hits you, sometimes you truly have no choice. As the game progresses, the executions and killings you perform become more gruesome, reflecting on the leading character's declining sanity.
If you're looking for a brand new style of gameplay, don't expect anything new. But, if you're tired of a typical military shooter story, this is worth everything. Hell, if you want a real story, get this game. There is also replayability due to the multiple endings that are based on your choices. Not as cryptic as Silent Hill but still very strong choices.

Beats anything Telltale has done for the past several years. Hell, I didn't expect anything of it since I didn't enjoy Life is Strange Season 1 that much (done by a different studio, although I felt the atmosphere and the emotions), however this... is so much more. 3 Episodes instead of 5, beats the original in every single aspect. I wish Deck Nine would do Season 2. Everything was on point of perfection here - the music, tracks, authentic charaacters and their problems, dreams, voice acting. Although I agree lots of questions were left unanswered after Episode 3, but that's because Before The Storm was cursed with being better than the original. People were expecting it to link to and give us answers about Rachel's disappearance and her unlikely love story with Frank, but it was never a story about that - it was a story about Rachel and Chloe's relationship.

. I am entirely sure that if the original Life is Strange's story was made AFTER Before The Storm, it would be different and better, as I agree that a lot of things that happened in the original didn't make sense after Before The Storm and were extremaly unlikely.
I bought the whole season about 2 days after Episode 3 came out and I was immediately hooked, despite not expecting much of it, just a time filler with a good story. It proved to be so much more. A beacon of hope, a reminder that there is beauty in this world, and love is true indeed.
After deciding that, as an actor, having a tattoo wouldn't be a smart choice for my career, now I'm seriously hesitating about getting Chloe's tat done. Being a punk and a rebel already, it would certainly mean a great deal.

I thought that leaving a review after playing the first episode will be a great idea. So after playing the first episode I can say that I have never felt so sad eventhough I played the original Life is Strange. I hope that the last two episodes will be the same as the first and won't dissapoint me.
I like that I can change my reviews. So after playing through the whole game I can say that it was better than the first version of this game. I like that they gave us the opportunity to see what happened between Chloe and Rachel. I liked the connection between them. I knew what will happen to Rachel because of the first game, but still I felt sad for the rest of the day. Looking forward to the special episode.

It was hard, but I fought myself to wait for all episodes to release and I did played all of them at once- without food, without sleep without anything. It is truly the masterpiece, the jewel, the second best game I played in my life (the first best is the original LiS). Actually I wouldn't call it a game, it is an expirience: visual, musical and emotional experience.

If you're going to play this game after watching the newest Mad Max movie, you're going to be sorely dissapointed.
Even if this game doesn't follow the storyline of the movie, it is quite a game.
FILLED with adrenaline, you ARE Mad Max, the titular anti-hero, who's trying to get some peace and redemption, but, to go to the light, you need to embrace darkness.

I played Mad Max like a Mad Man after I picked it up on sale. I'm torn on this game, on one hand the Batman style combat is tried and true,(I have to add that after replaying Batman Arkham Asylum, the combat is a lot more responsive and fluid than batman) and the car combat is pleasant enough, on the other hand this is the majority of things to do in this game.The story what little of it there is left me wanting . There are certain choke points in the story where you are bottle necked into doing the highly repetitive "side missions" to reduce the threat level in each goofy dumb-asses territory you need to proceed through to the end of the story.

The main content consists of shooting snipers off perches,with a very poor shooting mechanic only available from the back of your car. Blowing enemy convoys up with your car, which is the one of the better realized components of the game but becomes trivial after some of the late game upgrades for your car thus removing replay-ability.  Pulling down towers with your cars harpoon, also trivial but required to progress, but I had some of my most enjoyable time in the game just driving around the games world. The vehicle handing is fun once accustomed to it.The game has very few fast travel points compared to most open world games. But it can be exciting driving your death machine around the wastes.
The most time consuming part of the game is going into enemy camps where section by section you use the before mentioned batman style combat to achieve a small set of simple and repeated goals. Although it is similar to other games combat it has its own unique touches that brought glee at times. The tools at hand in combat are gruesome and useful allowing the above mentioned fluidity to combat, making combat the most pleasant part of the game and consequentially the game play is what helped me push through to the end of the story. Although upgrading Max's abilities brings more tedium to the game, you are forced to drive to a roaming shaman-esque character in order to spend a skill point.Halfway through I found myself dreading the proceeding the bored cut scene pushed every time you visit this "shaman". So I took the route of letting five to ten points build up before i took the time to search out the shamans newly relocated position on the map. Which seems odd because my garage i.e the way to upgrade the car is simply in the game menu?....
I found the game to be getting too tedious around the hour twenty mark, so hey I got twenty hours of funish game play out of it before i could take no more and just mainlined the story as fast as i was allowed. I decide to lean positive due to the fun I did have but fair warning, the game is VERY repetitive and i was disappointed when it was all said and done that the game gave me to compelling reason to play after completing the story.

Avalance studios is well known for their Just Cause series, a huge open world sandbox with wonderful mechanics and much to do. This pedigree holds true for the Mad Max "movie tie-in." The reason it's technically not a movie tie-in is because it has nothing to do with the story of the 2015 movie Fury Road. Instead, it has a different villain and a more australian Max.
Avalance did a good job applying their open world-ness to the game. It's a huge map split into different sectors with each having a set of objectives to do to lower Scabrous Scrotus' influence in that region, much like in Red Faction. Each part of the map is different from the others but still has the dry post apocalypse tone to each. These objectives range from taking down Scarecrows, defeating convoys, killing snipers, and clearing very intricate and varied "dungeons" full of War Boys. Basically, in Mad Max, there's a lot to do, and explaining them all would take a long time.
The combat comes in two flavors: hand to hand combat, and the very well done car combat. On ground combat is very similar to the Arkham series. Enemies surround you but it's a simple task to get rid of them with coordinated punches and timed counter attacks. The enemies have different classes that need to be taken out differently. Some have shields, some dodge your attacks until he is killed with a counter, some brandish a knife with impossible to counter slashes, and my favorite: the war crier who hangs from a crane with a drum and buffs the rest if you don't take them out. Some drop weapons upon death you can use. Combat is enhanced further with the use of your upgradeable shotgun and rare shivs that do massive damage. The second form of combat is among vehicles with your car the Magnum Opus and with the help of the one called Chumbucket. There are so many different upgrades to the car there are presets called Archangels that change the stats of the car. There are a few ways to do battle with the many wheels you find in the wastes. You can ram the sides of cars with a heavy car with high damage, you can use exploding harpoons like in the movies, you can use a grappling hook (It's Avalanche, you HAVE to have a grappling hook) to rip the drivers out of the car, or you can even make them fight eachother with clever dodges.
The game is a 10/10 for the above reasons already, but my favorite thing is the picture mode. Max has the Instagram app... somewhere, and he can take very good pictures (you can see the extent of the mode in my screenshots).

theHunter used to be a mediocre and way to expensive "f2p" title. With Call of the Wild they finally decided to use their skills to make a decent game. The "f2p" version already had a great atmosphere and mechanics but this game heavily builds up and improves on them. Of course not everthing is perfect! The UI is a bit clunky and needs some getting used to. I do miss the mini games on the Huntermate but thats not cruical.

In my opinion, though it might just be me, this game can be best enjoyed in Multiplayer which to this date lacks some features. You cannot play any missions together which means that hunting itself is your only income. The Multiplayer is hosted on dedicated Servers which apparently are located somewhere but not in my country. 100-80 Ping is a bit too much for shooting in my opinion. It's great that there are Servers but you should be able to host one yourself.
The search and filter options for Multiplayer games also need a lot of work.

Thats not inherently a bad thing but way sooner than later your character gets so strong it becomes laughable how you breeze through the stages. Magic spells are incredibly strong and in general, power-up items are really easy to get, you can pretty much start breezing through the game after the first hour of playing. Bosses are incredibly easy (with the exception of one or two, but not by much tho) and stages are pretty to see, but easy to traverse once you start getting one or two items and power-ups.
Outside of the game being way-too-easy for its own good in general what it offers is great. The levels are pretty and intersting, the music is insanely good and, even if it easy, it will provide you with a handful of hours of great fun.
Again, its only sin(?) is just that its way too easy for its own good but that might be a plus to some, not so much for the more hardcore of players tho.

As a longtime fan of the series I eagerly anticipated this game (and in fact I backed it on Kickstarter).  Well now that I've finished a playthrough I'd like to give it a good, honest review.
For those of you unfamiliar with the series, Shantae is a half-genie who protects a tiny little town called Scuttle Town that sits along the coast of a place called Sequin Land.  She defeats enemies by whipping them with her hair, and can eventually transform herself into multiple different forms that are useful for accessing hidden parts of the map (Some of these you'll unlock as the game progresses. Others you'll have to find on your own).  If you've played any other Metroidvania-style platformer, you'll have an idea what you're meant to do. Jump on often shaky platforms, defeat enemies, find lots of hidden items.  The platforming works well--the controls are quick and responsive and everything feels really good.  The game's story is pretty light fare, written cleverly.  It's not laugh-out-loud funny but there are a few good lines scattered about.
Graphically, the game is a treat.  It has a very cartoony art style, full of vibrant colors--it's a welcome relief from all the brown, gritty reality of most of today's games.  The game's audio is well done too. Voice acting is limited (only a few characters have any lines at all, and most of their lines aren't voiced).  This is easy to overlook, however.  The soundtrack is provided by Jake Kaufman (you may know him as virt) and the music in the game is up to his typical standards--it's mostly a combination of dance-pop and 70s funk with a light Middle Eastern vibe that fits the game really well.  Most of the music in the game is either new, or arranged versions of tracks from previous games. I don't think any of the music is carried over from previous titles, but there are a few that will sound familiar to anyone who's played older games.
If you are looking for a hardcore platformer, this isn't your game.  The difficulty curve in Half-Genie Hero is pretty mild, and even a novice player should be able to complete their first playthrough in about 6 hours or so. The challenge to this game comes in finding all the collectibles scattered throughout the world, or in attempting speed runs.  Some collectibles are hidden in plain sight and it's just a matter of unlocking the right power to get to them. Others are hidden deep in barely-accessible parts of a level and require some serious searching to locate.
So would I recommend this game?  Overall, yes.  It's not too expensive, and there's a lot of fun to be had playing it even if it's not incredibly hard.
