I hesitated in playing or writing a review for Life is Strange: Before the Storm until the entire game was released, as I personally hate episodic style games and don't like waiting for new episodes to be released. I did the same in the original Life is Strange, which I thoroughly played and loved.
I can definitively say that I enjoyed playing Life is Strange: Before the Storm. This game is a great prequel to the original Life is Strange that provides more insight into Chloe's character. It has a great initial plot and setting development that draws players right into the world. The players feel like they know (or can learn about) every character.
Every decision you make
like it will make an impact, even if it doesn't overall. Thus, the weight and tensions of your decisions resonate with you throughout the game.
The game deals heavily with love, family, companionship and loss, and plays these aspects strongly into the game's overall narrative. What Deck Nine has done with these themes is extraordinary. Most remarkable to me is how they have created essentially another reality in which the relationship between Chloe and Rachel can exist. As well, Chloe's loss,
is
thoroughly shown to the player, adding depth to their characters and making the player feel empathy for them. A person's hardships cannot be truly experienced unless someone else sees the world through their perspective, and Deck Nine does a good job of making sure the player knows the hardships Chloe endures. She becomes a very likeable character in this regard, despite her flaws.
While there are plenty of positives for this game, there are also a couple of negatives. (That's your queue, haters)
As much as I liked Life is Strange: Before the Storm, I felt a stronger surge of "the feels" at the end of the original LiS. Meanwhile, the majority of the emotion from this one hit at the end of the first episode, not the end of the game. After the second episode, the plot somewhat deteriorated and became more choppy. There were gaps in the story that often didn't make sense or justify the characters' actions. At points throughout the game, the characters even seemed unrealistic by their actions. It seems as if there was much more planned for this game that didn't make it into the final version. These plans may have provided more closure.
There were so many elements to this game that could have been told, used, or expressed better than they were in the final cut, and it disappoints me that this potential was not used to it's fullest.
I understand this game isn't much for gameplay, and I accept that. However, in the original LiS, Max's rewind power felt more powerful and influencial in the overall gameplay. Max's rewind seemed more useful to me than Chloe's backtalk. While the backtalk feature was fun, there were very few instances where the feature was actually used. When I originally heard of this game, I had thought that this mechanic would be used in nearly every conversation. (It's a fair assumption; rewind was used in nearly every room in LiS.) Oh boy, I was wrong. Too many times I was telling myself "I really need backtalk right now," not have the option.
Conclusion:
The first and second episodes, while lacking some plot details, were very well put together. The two episodes draw the player in, and make them want to play long enough to find out what happens. The player expects a big finish. Then, in the third episode, the plot begins getting 'strange.' Overall, the majority of the game was fantastic, but it died down in the end.

This game is what every military shooter that tries to focus on war attempts to be but doesn't reach it.  The gameplay is solid, sticking to being a TPS with cover mechanics. But while the gameplay doesn't offer too much, the story more than makes up for it. The painful choices of war, the violence you're forced to witness in times of desperation, all become in sync with each other, making you realize what war truly is. As you progress through the story, you (not the character, but the player) will question why you are forced to do such things. Why must you kill all these people? Then it hits you, sometimes you truly have no choice. As the game progresses, the executions and killings you perform become more gruesome, reflecting on the leading character's declining sanity.
If you're looking for a brand new style of gameplay, don't expect anything new. But, if you're tired of a typical military shooter story, this is worth everything. Hell, if you want a real story, get this game. There is also replayability due to the multiple endings that are based on your choices. Not as cryptic as Silent Hill but still very strong choices.

This game has ruined the "Modern Military Shooter" subgenre for me.
This is not because it is by any means a bad game, or does a bad job of presenting the subgenre. Rather, it is because Spec Ops: The Line does what Don Quixote did to the chivalric ballads of old, or School of Rock did to inspirational films about schoolteachers: it eviscerates the subgenre so thoroughly that it will be impossible for me to take any earnest attempts seriously ever again.
At first glance, Spec Ops: The Line comes across as generic shovelware, and the name certainly doesn't help. But it only takes an hour before the plot starts to twist, the line starts to blur, and the black and white starts to become a uniform grey. (Until a certain scene which I dare not spoil, at which point the grey starts to take on a much darker shade.)
This is not a "rah-rah, America saves the day again" video game. This is a game with content that you really should expect after seeing a character named "J. Konrad". This is a game that pulls no punches in its depiction of the horrors of war, or your participation in them.
This is a game that shines like a giant red beacon, burning forever in the night, proclaiming for all to see that videogames can indeed be art.

An underrated gem, Rogue Legacy is a surprisingly difficult game which has tons of replay value thanks to it's wide array of upgrades you can obtain and also the unique traits that each of the combatants you play as possess.
My video review:

Rogue legacy is one of the most fun, rewarding and challenging games I've ever played. First, the "magic" attacks (AKA throwing daggers, axes, fireballs, and swords) are very well done, since they all do the same amount of base damage, but each have different movement patterns to allow players to hit enemies as many times as possible with one shot. It also prevents the player from always choosing the class and magic abilities they are most comfortable with, since that is randomized every time you die. Each boss is also unique, having it's own custom arena and requiring custom strategies. Each boss also has their own section of the castle to them, with different enemies, meaning you get to experience almost entirely new gameplay leading up to all the bosses. I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who likes not just roguelikes, but action platformers in general.

Very decent rogue-lite, though it has its ups and downs. Its simplicity is in certain ways good and bad, good in being easily accessible and bad in being... well, fairly basic. It's pretty hard, but in the sense that stems from Super Meat Boy's difficulty in that the player's mistakes are what costs them. That is, when gameplay doesn't revolve around luck. (AND WHEN THE BOSSES DON'T FEEL A BIT UNBALANCED.) And this difficulty also encourages a leveling system that is fun to explore through. There are a handful of abilities, but I found myself just favoring the standard sword attack for some reason. Can't really say if it's the game's fault; I think I just prefer swords over magic. Rogue Legacy is often criticized for unoriginal enemies (in how many of them are virtually the same), and I can't say I disagree. The first hours of this game are fantastic, learning all these cool concepts. But the well runs dry eventually, and what we're left with doesn't have much of a legacy at all. At the end of the day, it's worth the enjoyment. But even though I expected further playtime to not grow stale, that's exactly what happened.

2. I can barely hear people while playing.  Their voices are extremely quiet in the voice chat when the volume is at 100%.
3. There is this strange sound bug that happens gradually while playing.  First, the sound is fine.  However, as you keep playing, the SFX start to deteriorate, before going away altogether. It starts with the music starting to cut out, and then the punches, and then the only noises left are the ones from the map.  I get music in the menu/scoreboard screens, but as soon as I enter a game it stops again.  You need to restart the game for this one.  People have reported this bug for a while, and the devs have responded, but I still have yet to find a solution.
4. Turns out the input lag is due to connectivity.  The game already has a bit of input lag built into the engine, and that's fine.  However, when I join an online server, even one that I myself and hosting, I immediately notice a huge delay between a keypress and the action.  (Not sure about controllers, I don't have a receiver/wire for mine)  This is a huge problem because the servers that I join have 20 ping at most.  That's almost nothing in most games but in this one it causes input lag.  When I join a local server for survival, the controls are much snappier and quick.
5. If you've ever seen old footage of this game, you will know what I'm talking about with this one.  Remember when people would get knocked down for 1+ minutes when they get hit hard?  Or when a leg would snap to a head from a mile away?  Well, none of thse happen anymore.  When somebody gets hit by a train, you better act fast with that input lag because they are getting right back up like the train was a goddamn feather.  No more stupid launching physics either.  A bummer for me, but some people might feel better about that.
I still don't think this game is worth $20.  It seems like I'm not the only one getting these issues.  It's up to you to decide if you want to risk it or not.  Come on, Nintendo.
Update #2: I've decided to get a refund. There are much too many bugs too make this game worth $20 and fun for me. I'm just going to save up for a different game that I wanted. Give this a shot at a discounted price, or wait until it gets fixed.
Update #3:  Steam thinks that 5 hours is too much playtime for a refund.  Oh well.
UPDATE #4: I figured out the issue. The game just isn't optimized at all. It runs with 100% cpu usage. It's 32 bit. It only uses one thread. Yet it somehow works on my friends Macbook Pro. I EVEN TRIED MY OWN MAC AND IT STILL DOESN'T WORK, MAYBE THE GAME JUST HATES ME?
I emailed support and linked this review. If they respond and have any more questions / solutions I will respond and update again.
final update: i give up.
UPDATE #5: I DONT GIVE UP, IM JUST AN IDIOT.  They got back to me on May 2nd, 26 days ago, and I never saw it.  They think it could be a memory leak in the engine or game.  Thanks support!  Sorry for being an idiot and not seeing it!
Update #6:  They did it!  They fixed the CPU!  Now my pc doesn't lag during this game!  Now, there is still obvious input lag and the sound does still cut out, but one of my main problems is gone.

I played Mad Max like a Mad Man after I picked it up on sale. I'm torn on this game, on one hand the Batman style combat is tried and true,(I have to add that after replaying Batman Arkham Asylum, the combat is a lot more responsive and fluid than batman) and the car combat is pleasant enough, on the other hand this is the majority of things to do in this game.The story what little of it there is left me wanting . The main content consists of shooting snipers off perches,with a very poor shooting mechanic only available from the back of your car. Blowing enemy convoys up with your car, which is the one of the better realized components of the game but becomes trivial after some of the late game upgrades for your car thus removing replay-ability.  Pulling down towers with your cars harpoon, also trivial but required to progress, but I had some of my most enjoyable time in the game just driving around the games world. The vehicle handing is fun once accustomed to it.The game has very few fast travel points compared to most open world games. But it can be exciting driving your death machine around the wastes.
The most time consuming part of the game is going into enemy camps where section by section you use the before mentioned batman style combat to achieve a small set of simple and repeated goals. Although it is similar to other games combat it has its own unique touches that brought glee at times. The tools at hand in combat are gruesome and useful allowing the above mentioned fluidity to combat, making combat the most pleasant part of the game and consequentially the game play is what helped me push through to the end of the story. Although upgrading Max's abilities brings more tedium to the game, you are forced to drive to a roaming shaman-esque character in order to spend a skill point.Halfway through I found myself dreading the proceeding the bored cut scene pushed every time you visit this "shaman". So I took the route of letting five to ten points build up before i took the time to search out the shamans newly relocated position on the map. Which seems odd because my garage i.e the way to upgrade the car is simply in the game menu?....
I found the game to be getting too tedious around the hour twenty mark, so hey I got twenty hours of funish game play out of it before i could take no more and just mainlined the story as fast as i was allowed. I decide to lean positive due to the fun I did have but fair warning, the game is VERY repetitive and i was disappointed when it was all said and done that the game gave me to compelling reason to play after completing the story.

Avalance studios is well known for their Just Cause series, a huge open world sandbox with wonderful mechanics and much to do. This pedigree holds true for the Mad Max "movie tie-in." The reason it's technically not a movie tie-in is because it has nothing to do with the story of the 2015 movie Fury Road. Instead, it has a different villain and a more australian Max.
Avalance did a good job applying their open world-ness to the game. It's a huge map split into different sectors with each having a set of objectives to do to lower Scabrous Scrotus' influence in that region, much like in Red Faction. Each part of the map is different from the others but still has the dry post apocalypse tone to each. These objectives range from taking down Scarecrows, defeating convoys, killing snipers, and clearing very intricate and varied "dungeons" full of War Boys. Basically, in Mad Max, there's a lot to do, and explaining them all would take a long time.
The combat comes in two flavors: hand to hand combat, and the very well done car combat. On ground combat is very similar to the Arkham series. Enemies surround you but it's a simple task to get rid of them with coordinated punches and timed counter attacks. The enemies have different classes that need to be taken out differently. Some have shields, some dodge your attacks until he is killed with a counter, some brandish a knife with impossible to counter slashes, and my favorite: the war crier who hangs from a crane with a drum and buffs the rest if you don't take them out. Some drop weapons upon death you can use. Combat is enhanced further with the use of your upgradeable shotgun and rare shivs that do massive damage. The second form of combat is among vehicles with your car the Magnum Opus and with the help of the one called Chumbucket. There are so many different upgrades to the car there are presets called Archangels that change the stats of the car. There are a few ways to do battle with the many wheels you find in the wastes. You can ram the sides of cars with a heavy car with high damage, you can use exploding harpoons like in the movies, you can use a grappling hook (It's Avalanche, you HAVE to have a grappling hook) to rip the drivers out of the car, or you can even make them fight eachother with clever dodges.
The game is a 10/10 for the above reasons already, but my favorite thing is the picture mode. Max has the Instagram app... somewhere, and he can take very good pictures (you can see the extent of the mode in my screenshots).

<Full Disclosure: This game was provided for free by Greenman Gaming as part of a contest they held in 2015.  Full-er Disclosure: I'm a huge Avalanche Sweden fanboy, mainly because of Just Cause 2, but Mad Max plays a big role in that as well.>
While my time with Mad Max was severely shortened due to a crappy computer getting in the way a good eight hours after starting, I'd be lying if I said I didn't enjoy every moment of it.  No, I'm serious.
The world of Mad Max is actually interesting to explore.  Sure, it's all sparsely populated desert regions, but it's a damn interesting one at that!  The world has a whole lot of detail, the way your car interacts with said environments is packing plenty of detail itself, and overall the world acts like a desert should, rather than "here's some brown fields of nothing, go crazy."
On top of this, when you're exploring, it's fairly common that warboys will attack you, and both the car combat and hand-to-hand combat in this game is exceptionally fun to use.  The hand-to-hand combat has been compared to Batman: Arkham often, but in reality it takes a much more brutal approach with weapons and environmental objects (like walls or railings) often affecting the combat.  As far as cars go, they pretty much nailed it-- the controls are slick, the visuals are amazing, and the weapon variety is really something.  When you slam another car, the visuals do nicely in representing that as sparks fly, junk scatters, and the target goese a good 50 degrees in the wrong direction before you skid around the windshield to give him a shotgun shell in the face.  If you think that's somehow not enough, then just take the car combat for a spin yourself and see the crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥you'll do.  When you've got to pick between rare shotgun shells and a fold-out sniper rifle, or a harpoon, thunderspear, spiked bumpers, and fire spewing out the sides of your car, I'm sure you can think of ways to take down warboys in style.  If you want to stick to hand-to-hand, though, just find a way to get their car cornered, step out of your vehicle, and begin suplexing your foes.
Built into the mechanics of this game is progression, in three main trees: Max's own skills, special perks from Griff (the Australian apocalyptic equivalent of a hippie or stoner), and of course, your car.  As you progress in the game, you're going to be working your way towards better gear that can open up more areas, make combat a little easier, and give Max a beard so that warboys know not to ♥♥♥♥ with you.
The story is great as well.  The main actors do a great job, and the opening scene alone screams that Avalanche knows how to make a Mad Max game.  The characters are all interesting, especially Chumbucket, and it follows through a completely new character arc for Max rather than going with what Fury Road established.  If you had any fears of this game being a crappy movie tie-in, set those aside and burn it with the rocket fumes of a v6 engine.
This is hardly a perfect game, and when it hits a snag (mostly because of WB Games), this game REALLY trips up.  At many points, the scrap system makes very little sense, the fuel collection can feel a little too forgiving at times given the setting, and WB Games' commitment to loading screen advertisements and other complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t is a serious issue.  Still, once you've unchecked the "free content" from your DLC tab, the game will act as it should, completely free of WB's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.  My points about scrap still stand unchanged, though.
A cash-in videogame for a movie reboot, a very short deadline, and WB Games-- the end result should have been a trainwreck, but it wasn't.  Instead, the game we got in the end was not just enjoyable or serviceable, but excellent.  There's a reason developers like Monolith and Avalanche Sweden deserve your respect; they rarely disappoint their fans, and when they're involved in a game's development, they mean business.

As a longtime fan of the series I eagerly anticipated this game (and in fact I backed it on Kickstarter).  Well now that I've finished a playthrough I'd like to give it a good, honest review.
For those of you unfamiliar with the series, Shantae is a half-genie who protects a tiny little town called Scuttle Town that sits along the coast of a place called Sequin Land.  She defeats enemies by whipping them with her hair, and can eventually transform herself into multiple different forms that are useful for accessing hidden parts of the map (Some of these you'll unlock as the game progresses. Others you'll have to find on your own).  If you've played any other Metroidvania-style platformer, you'll have an idea what you're meant to do. Jump on often shaky platforms, defeat enemies, find lots of hidden items.  The platforming works well--the controls are quick and responsive and everything feels really good.  The game's story is pretty light fare, written cleverly.  It's not laugh-out-loud funny but there are a few good lines scattered about.
Graphically, the game is a treat.  It has a very cartoony art style, full of vibrant colors--it's a welcome relief from all the brown, gritty reality of most of today's games.  The game's audio is well done too. Voice acting is limited (only a few characters have any lines at all, and most of their lines aren't voiced).  This is easy to overlook, however.  The soundtrack is provided by Jake Kaufman (you may know him as virt) and the music in the game is up to his typical standards--it's mostly a combination of dance-pop and 70s funk with a light Middle Eastern vibe that fits the game really well.  Most of the music in the game is either new, or arranged versions of tracks from previous games. I don't think any of the music is carried over from previous titles, but there are a few that will sound familiar to anyone who's played older games.
If you are looking for a hardcore platformer, this isn't your game.  The difficulty curve in Half-Genie Hero is pretty mild, and even a novice player should be able to complete their first playthrough in about 6 hours or so. The challenge to this game comes in finding all the collectibles scattered throughout the world, or in attempting speed runs.  Some collectibles are hidden in plain sight and it's just a matter of unlocking the right power to get to them. Others are hidden deep in barely-accessible parts of a level and require some serious searching to locate.
So would I recommend this game?  Overall, yes.  It's not too expensive, and there's a lot of fun to be had playing it even if it's not incredibly hard.

The main offender for this happening is how easy and quick it is to obtain powerups in this game that basically breaks your character. You will find that you are practically invincible after the first stage, once you obtained 2 health powerups and the armor that reduces all damage taken by half.

Great soundtracks. Having played the mobile version of "Lit", WayForward did it again.

There are a handful of abilities, but I found myself just favoring the standard sword attack for some reason. Can't really say if it's the game's fault; I think I just prefer swords over magic. Rogue Legacy is often criticized for unoriginal enemies (in how many of them are virtually the same), and I can't say I disagree. The first hours of this game are fantastic, learning all these cool concepts. But the well runs dry eventually, and what we're left with doesn't have much of a legacy at all. At the end of the day, it's worth the enjoyment. But even though I expected further playtime to not grow stale, that's exactly what happened.

Alright so this is first impressions on the game Rogue Legacy. I will state the thoughts of the game during the first hour of playing the game.
First thing I'd like to say is that if you don't like games that frustrate you, don't get this game. You are not going to beat the game with Lee, you are going to die! This game like many rogue games involve the player dying multiple times and improving as they continue to play the game.
But there is a twist to Rogue Legacy that make it different then games like the Binding of Issac for example. Each time you play the game, you improve in game as well. If you get a certain amount of gold when your character dies, you can upgrade stats, armor, abilities, and more! These upgrade stay with you for the rest of your career so you can play further/longer the next time! Till I realized you can have double jump, dashing, and more; the game just felt like a generic Rogue game. But with these upgrades, it's definitely not.
The next thing I want to talk about is bosses. I have played an hour and I have found the boss once. The boss is in a random location due to the random generation and I love it. I got destroyed by the first boss and the desire to get stronger so I can wreck him is high. The fact you can't beat the boss easily makes this game have a purpose which some Rogue like games don't have. In Issac, I can beat the bosses without getting hit but in this, I'd be lucky to avoid getting hit every few seconds.
This is all I have for the hour thoughts of the game and I got to say it's worth full price. The only real complaint I could have about the game is the fact that when I had my controller plugged in I couldn't see keyboard controls (and I can't validate if it ever shows keyboard controlls at this time). I also have a problem with the platforms you create by stabbing towards the ground. 90% of the time when I downstab or whatever you want to call it, I go in an angle and platforming that SHOULD be easy isn't. Maybe it's just me but I really feel it's the game, but I guess it could also be the controller. But that is just my insight on it.
I recommend Rogue Legacy and if you like games that make you want to tear out your hair, get it. With the inheritence from your parents as they die one by one to this castle adding to the game, I got to say it's much different. But WHY does the child always throw away their cash inheritance to go into a dungeon where every generation of their family tree threw away their lives!?!? xD

One of the most underrated games of all time.  The campaign has one of the best stories of any shooter from the last ten years. I had no idea what I was getting into the first time I played this one.

The visual presentation of Windward is great, and the combat doesn't require too much of the play but is still very fun. I spent a lot of time being a merchant, buying goods in one port and selling them in another port, or ferrying passengers. And while that's exactly what I wanted from this game, I can see others becoming bored since there are very few quests with any kind of storyline attached. There isn't much in game reason to push into pirate controlled regions other than seeking more gold to buy better ships. You are questing and selling goods to have more gold and more experience to upgrade your ship or buy new ships, and that alone has been enough of a hook for 20 hours of gameplay, but there isn't any personality to the captains or crew, and no overall story to keep me emotionally invested. Still worth a buy at this price point, but I'd love to see a sequel that is fleshed out with a storyline, day/night cycle, stormy weather, crew boarding, and dialogue.

This is a fun game.  Even better with friends.  The physics and the fights make it perfect for laughs.  My problem is, it doesn't want to run.  I launch it, and it immediately starts lagging right off the bat, in the menu.  My computer starts to get slow and freeze up, apps like Discord stop creating audio and nobody can hear me, and the game just takes forever to do anything.  Hell, even right now as I am writing this without the game open, my computer is being a bit slow.
I have a GTX 1070, Core i5 6600k computer.  This shouldn't be happening.  I know it's early access and all, but all other games run buttery smooth and this one refuses to do anything.  Not to mention the input lag that I am getting, and it's frustrating to see a game that I've wanted for so long and do actually enjoy go down the drain.  This is something that I might actually get a refund for.  It's unplayable.
Whether or not this will happen to you, I don't know.  My friend plays fine on a MACBOOK PRO, yet my computer can barely handle it.  I can't find a solution and might resort to a refund.  This game should not be $20 right now.
Update:  I've noticed a few things while playing.
1. The weird lag seems to have stopped.  It went on the first and second day, then just suddenly ended.  It still lags from time to time, and has the mic bug still, but seems to be fine with it now.  The mic bug seems to fix itself when I join an online game though, and then I can hear other people and then can hear me.  Sometimes it randomly happens during games.
2. I can barely hear people while playing.  Their voices are extremely quiet in the voice chat when the volume is at 100%.
3. There is this strange sound bug that happens gradually while playing.  First, the sound is fine.  However, as you keep playing, the SFX start to deteriorate, before going away altogether. It starts with the music starting to cut out, and then the punches, and then the only noises left are the ones from the map.  I get music in the menu/scoreboard screens, but as soon as I enter a game it stops again.  You need to restart the game for this one.  People have reported this bug for a while, and the devs have responded, but I still have yet to find a solution.
4. Turns out the input lag is due to connectivity.  The game already has a bit of input lag built into the engine, and that's fine.  However, when I join an online server, even one that I myself and hosting, I immediately notice a huge delay between a keypress and the action.  (Not sure about controllers, I don't have a receiver/wire for mine)  This is a huge problem because the servers that I join have 20 ping at most.  That's almost nothing in most games but in this one it causes input lag.  When I join a local server for survival, the controls are much snappier and quick.
5. If you've ever seen old footage of this game, you will know what I'm talking about with this one.  Remember when people would get knocked down for 1+ minutes when they get hit hard?  Or when a leg would snap to a head from a mile away?  Well, none of thse happen anymore.  When somebody gets hit by a train, you better act fast with that input lag because they are getting right back up like the train was a goddamn feather.  No more stupid launching physics either.  A bummer for me, but some people might feel better about that.
I still don't think this game is worth $20.  It seems like I'm not the only one getting these issues.  It's up to you to decide if you want to risk it or not.  Come on, Nintendo.
Update #2: I've decided to get a refund. There are much too many bugs too make this game worth $20 and fun for me. I'm just going to save up for a different game that I wanted. Give this a shot at a discounted price, or wait until it gets fixed.
Update #3:  Steam thinks that 5 hours is too much playtime for a refund.  Oh well.
UPDATE #4: I figured out the issue. The game just isn't optimized at all. It runs with 100% cpu usage. It's 32 bit. It only uses one thread. Yet it somehow works on my friends Macbook Pro. I EVEN TRIED MY OWN MAC AND IT STILL DOESN'T WORK, MAYBE THE GAME JUST HATES ME?

Borderlands2 is a First Person action adventure shooter game developed by Gearbox and released 2012. Borderlands2's story takes place on the planet Pandora... Pandora is a very violent war-torn planet where no one in their right mind would visit, except for the insane... being bandits, local inhabitants who can't get off world, and vault hunters.
Story: You're a vault hunter, you've been lured onto Pandora in attempts to find the mystical place known as “the vault”, in the vault you gain unimaginable treasure... should you succeed in finding the vault; there's no telling what wonders you will encounter.
But wait, before you run off and try to open the vault yourself, there are many enemies who wish to claim the vault as their own prize! Not to mention monstrous beasts that protect the vault. You don't even know where to go! To find the vault you will need friends, cue “Handsome Jack”...
...okay, okay, by now most people actually know how this story goes, the Story telling in Borderlands2 is excellent, a nice blend of cinematic, voiced dialogue.
Borderlands2 is played in the first person view, initially there are only four playable characters/classes (with mods you gain 2 more), you have different types of weapons, elements, many different types of NPC's to fight, 3 skill tree's for each class.
The playable characters/classes are: Axton (Commando), Maya (Siren), Salvador (Gunzerker), Zero (Assassin), and with purchasing the appropriate DLC you gain access to Gaige (Mechromancer), and Krieg (Psycho). If you want to know more about a specific character/class I would recommend checking out online guides.
It's important to note that there are about 6 different classifications of weapons (Assault rifles, sniper rifles, pistols, shot guns, 'ya know – the normal gun you expect) it's even more important to note that each character/class can use any weapon... however some characters are better at certain weapons because of skill builds. (meaning, Zer0 (the sniper/assassin) is better with sniper rifles, but you can pick one up with Salvador (gunzerker) and use it, but you probably won't be as accurate as Zer0 is.
In addition to various weapons, are there many different special perks a gun can randomly roll, including different elements (Incendiary, Corrosive, Shock, and Explosive) which are more effective against different types of enemies. The point is, that the same gun can drop twice and have completely different stats.
Borderlands2 has 69 achievements in total, 50 achievements are available on the core game, the 19 other achievements are spread out across 4 DLC items you'll need to purchase to get 100%. All of the achievements are very obtainable, however, some require some grinding and luck (like, Challenge Accepted, Tribute to a vault hunter, and a number of other circumstantial achievements) Lastly, there is at least one achievement per class, the rest can be obtained with one character.
Borderlands2 is priced at $19.99 The game of the Year edition is priced at $39.99. I personally suggest purchasing the game of the year edition so you can get the DLC for the whole game. With the release of Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel the chances of picking up a copy of Borderlands2 on sale is dramatically increased, so it's worth noting that you could wait for a 75% off sale.
Borderlands2 is hilarious, fun, has morbid-humor, insane people, guns, guns and more guns! I have little to nothing negative that I can say about the game. The graphics for the game itself are more cartoon-styled in nature, increasing the life of the game (It won't take back seat to high end graphic games as fast, because they're trying to replicate realism, they're implementing their own style and art).
All in all, I loved playing Borderlands2, I played the heck out of the game, it's more fun to play it with a friend, but it's one of those games you can spend a lot of time playing just to blow up bandits. I recommend this game for FPS gamers, and people who enjoy Adventure/Action games.

Avalance studios is well known for their Just Cause series, a huge open world sandbox with wonderful mechanics and much to do. This pedigree holds true for the Mad Max "movie tie-in." The reason it's technically not a movie tie-in is because it has nothing to do with the story of the 2015 movie Fury Road. Instead, it has a different villain and a more australian Max.
Avalance did a good job applying their open world-ness to the game. It's a huge map split into different sectors with each having a set of objectives to do to lower Scabrous Scrotus' influence in that region, much like in Red Faction. Each part of the map is different from the others but still has the dry post apocalypse tone to each. These objectives range from taking down Scarecrows, defeating convoys, killing snipers, and clearing very intricate and varied "dungeons" full of War Boys. Basically, in Mad Max, there's a lot to do, and explaining them all would take a long time.
The combat comes in two flavors: hand to hand combat, and the very well done car combat. On ground combat is very similar to the Arkham series. Enemies surround you but it's a simple task to get rid of them with coordinated punches and timed counter attacks. The enemies have different classes that need to be taken out differently. Some have shields, some dodge your attacks until he is killed with a counter, some brandish a knife with impossible to counter slashes, and my favorite: the war crier who hangs from a crane with a drum and buffs the rest if you don't take them out. Some drop weapons upon death you can use. Combat is enhanced further with the use of your upgradeable shotgun and rare shivs that do massive damage. The second form of combat is among vehicles with your car the Magnum Opus and with the help of the one called Chumbucket. There are so many different upgrades to the car there are presets called Archangels that change the stats of the car. There are a few ways to do battle with the many wheels you find in the wastes. You can ram the sides of cars with a heavy car with high damage, you can use exploding harpoons like in the movies, you can use a grappling hook (It's Avalanche, you HAVE to have a grappling hook) to rip the drivers out of the car, or you can even make them fight eachother with clever dodges.
The game is a 10/10 for the above reasons already, but my favorite thing is the picture mode. Max has the Instagram app... somewhere, and he can take very good pictures (you can see the extent of the mode in my screenshots).

<Full Disclosure: This game was provided for free by Greenman Gaming as part of a contest they held in 2015.  Full-er Disclosure: I'm a huge Avalanche Sweden fanboy, mainly because of Just Cause 2, but Mad Max plays a big role in that as well.>
While my time with Mad Max was severely shortened due to a crappy computer getting in the way a good eight hours after starting, I'd be lying if I said I didn't enjoy every moment of it.  No, I'm serious.
The world of Mad Max is actually interesting to explore.  Sure, it's all sparsely populated desert regions, but it's a damn interesting one at that!  The world has a whole lot of detail, the way your car interacts with said environments is packing plenty of detail itself, and overall the world acts like a desert should, rather than "here's some brown fields of nothing, go crazy."
On top of this, when you're exploring, it's fairly common that warboys will attack you, and both the car combat and hand-to-hand combat in this game is exceptionally fun to use.  The hand-to-hand combat has been compared to Batman: Arkham often, but in reality it takes a much more brutal approach with weapons and environmental objects (like walls or railings) often affecting the combat.  As far as cars go, they pretty much nailed it-- the controls are slick, the visuals are amazing, and the weapon variety is really something.  When you slam another car, the visuals do nicely in representing that as sparks fly, junk scatters, and the target goese a good 50 degrees in the wrong direction before you skid around the windshield to give him a shotgun shell in the face.  If you think that's somehow not enough, then just take the car combat for a spin yourself and see the crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥you'll do.  When you've got to pick between rare shotgun shells and a fold-out sniper rifle, or a harpoon, thunderspear, spiked bumpers, and fire spewing out the sides of your car, I'm sure you can think of ways to take down warboys in style.  If you want to stick to hand-to-hand, though, just find a way to get their car cornered, step out of your vehicle, and begin suplexing your foes.
Built into the mechanics of this game is progression, in three main trees: Max's own skills, special perks from Griff (the Australian apocalyptic equivalent of a hippie or stoner), and of course, your car.  As you progress in the game, you're going to be working your way towards better gear that can open up more areas, make combat a little easier, and give Max a beard so that warboys know not to ♥♥♥♥ with you.
The story is great as well.  The main actors do a great job, and the opening scene alone screams that Avalanche knows how to make a Mad Max game.  The characters are all interesting, especially Chumbucket, and it follows through a completely new character arc for Max rather than going with what Fury Road established.  If you had any fears of this game being a crappy movie tie-in, set those aside and burn it with the rocket fumes of a v6 engine.
This is hardly a perfect game, and when it hits a snag (mostly because of WB Games), this game REALLY trips up.  At many points, the scrap system makes very little sense, the fuel collection can feel a little too forgiving at times given the setting, and WB Games' commitment to loading screen advertisements and other complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t is a serious issue.  Still, once you've unchecked the "free content" from your DLC tab, the game will act as it should, completely free of WB's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.  My points about scrap still stand unchanged, though.
A cash-in videogame for a movie reboot, a very short deadline, and WB Games-- the end result should have been a trainwreck, but it wasn't.  Instead, the game we got in the end was not just enjoyable or serviceable, but excellent.  There's a reason developers like Monolith and Avalanche Sweden deserve your respect; they rarely disappoint their fans, and when they're involved in a game's development, they mean business.
It's a real shame that I only came 8 hours into the game, because I desperately want to finish this one.  The moment I have a proper i7 4790, this very well may be the first thing that gets queued for download.

Life is Strange is one of my favorite games of all time. It impacted me in a deeply personal way that very few books, movies or other media has ever done. So great anticipation and expectations awaited LiS:BtS. While it's not quite as good as its predecessor, it is still an excellent game.
I was somewhat concerned that playing a series before Max and Chloe wouldn't work. After all, we shape our opinion of Chloe in LiS. How could a game set before meet those opinions? Well, they did with a mostly spot-on tone. We get to meet Chloe at the nadir of her life, the moment she meets Rachel Amber in the events that lead up to LiS. While it wasn't voiced by the same voice actors it's still very well done, with that familiar neat art style and a decent soundtrack that fits the tone of the game. You can expect somewhere between 9 to 10 hours of gameplay from this title if you play it through once.
The story is the thing here and it's mostly pretty good. The first two episodes are quite outstanding in both tone and storytelling. The last one feels a bit uneven, lagging at times while rushed at others. It seemed like there may have been too much to try to put into Episode 3 or that it needed a better editor to tighten things up. Areas like the main story involving Amber's father, Eliot popping up for an unneeded and momentum-derailing scene and a couple of others didn't quite work. But even with Ep 3 not quite living up to the series standard the rest of it carries through.
If you didn't play LiS then I wouldn't get this one yet. I think you have to know Chloe before this would make any emotional impact. But if you have played the first then get ready for an emotional roller coaster. Knowing what faces Chloe (and Rachel) in the LiS series makes the emotional highs and lows here all the more effective. There are a handful of real gut punches, like in Ep1 where you get to see the car (if you play you'll know what I mean). She turns the corner and *boom* there it is. I literally felt my breath taken away at that moment. There are a few others, especially if you look closely. Another one is seeing Amber in a paritcular shade of clothing. But by and large the emotional impact is really due to knowing what happens later, so in essence this story borrows the much more poignant moments from the first game. Just because it doesn't carry the weight of the first story doesn't mean that this is bad though. It's still entertaining.
So is it a buy? If you're at all a fan of this series then it most certainly is. If you didn't like the series, then no. This is more of the same. If you're new to the series, go buy the first game and play that one before considering this. Me? I still love this series and bought the special edition. TL;DR: It's an excellent game. It has its shortcomings, but its strengths far outweigh its weaknesses. 9/10
From the studio that brought Booty Genie, Booty Genie 2, and Booty Genie 3: Booty Pirate, comes a new installment in the Booty Genie franchise, this time with full animated HD jigglies.
Now for my serious review.
-----------
GAMEPLAY: 8/10
It's a platformer, and a very good one at that. The jumping feels exactly as you'd expect, and Shantae's movement speed is at a very comfortable pace.
I very much enjoyed the amount of transformations available in the game, but at some point there were simply too many, and as a result, there were some transformations that ended up not being used at all. For example, I think there were 2 areas total where bat form was required, whereas every other area could have been covered by harpy form much more quickly and easily. If not for the fact that you don't get harpy form until later, I don't think I would have used bat form at all.
Shantae: Half-Genie Hero follows the same formula as the games before it, in which you collect items for people in different areas to unlock the next. Every now and then, you have to return to a previous level with new powers in order to access areas you were previously unable to. Now, this works extremely well in Pirate's Curse, where you only really have to go back maybe 3 or 4 times. In this game, however, I ended up going back to Main Street maybe 6 times, and because of how linear the levels feel this time around, it seems a lot more tedious than it really is. Gone are the exploratory corridors and branching pathways in this game. Seriously, where are the dungeons?
While it may seem tedious, the overall game feel, I think, makes up for the tediousness of the game. These were minor inconveniences at worst. The game still plays exactly as it should, and it feels amazing.
-----------
DESIGN: 10/10
Wayforward strikes out of the park once again with this game. The art design fits the style of the characters and the tone of the game so well. It uses a mix of 2D graphics on 3D environments, and still manages to fit the series as well as the old pixel art style, almost better even. Backgrounds were memorable, and really popped out, to the point where you could tell what level you were in just by the lighting. The new 2.5D approach to this one got a little bit dizzying in Scuttle Town Square, but it was something that I got used to very quickly.
The music, as usual, is a major high point to the game. The retro vibe mixed extremely well with the Middle Eastern tones, especially in Main Street. Virt, applause to you.
-----------
OVERALL: 9/10
Shantae: Half-Genie Hero is most definitely a Shantae game. It's got great controls, great gameplay, great art design, and amazing music, and I am excited for the upcoming DLC. Can I recommend it at $20.00? You'd probably wait for a sale or something, unless you plan on replaying this game a lot. It's no Pirate's Curse, but it's definitely one of the best in the series.

Rust is a monster of its own. After you first boot up the game and spawn into this new world, you're immediately pressed to find food (and perhaps water), otherwise it takes about 5 minutes to start starving. Hitting trees and rock "nodes" will allow you to construct tools to replace your frail starter rock, hunting animals is essential to eventually crafting a furnace, allowing for access to guns, high-grade armor, and more, and defending against the massive and highly aggressive playerbase makes for an incredibly difficult beginning, but it's by all means feasible.
You'd be hard-pressed to find someone who won't KOS (Kill on Sight) in Rust because of how hard it is to gain enough momentum to get a base up and sustain it until it's upgraded and secure, but once in a while there's a few nice people that crop up that won't start shooting or insulting in the first two seconds of contact.
Rust is almost a permadeath game in a way. In-game there's a "sleeping bag" that allows the player to spawn at its location, but if you die without a base, bag, or supplies, that's game over and you start all over from scratch. This makes for a lot of rage and frustration, so always bear in mind that patience and persistence are the only things that will get you a base, guns, and armor in the end.
All that being said, Rust's learning is exceptionally high for a sandbox/survival game. Its design presents a challenge that I personally haven't found in all the games of this calibre I've played, and that's saying a lot. It takes a bit of luck, a lot of skill, and plenty more persistance to succeed in Rust (unless you join a zerg like some weak sucker), but when wins are had and firefights are won, this is one of the most satisfying games on Steam.

Friendly AI- This is probably the game's biggest weakness in terms of a specific gameplay problem. When attempting to conquer the high-level territories in the center, the friendly AI become increasingly useless. They continuously patrol the entire map, while the pirate AI always go directly towards capturing objectives. This can become incredibly frustrating when you continue to be the only ship challenging 2-3 pirates at a time that spawn from pirate-controlled towns. You can have ally ships follow you, but as soon as you die, your allies often wander off if they haven't been destroyed too. This is something that isn't as big of a deal in multiplayer, but has a big impact when you play your single player world.

Well, it's been a while since I've played a CoD game; and World at War was the last Treyarch CoD game I played. This one however, I feel, could be the pinnacle of the series - but I'm a sucker for Near-Future (but not Tom Clancy near-future, that's too close to present for my imagination at times).
At the moment, it is fairest that I stick to multiplayer, as that's what I've had the most experience with, although the campaign looks good, although it's definitely reliant on spectacle. This is only a thinking man's game if you make it that way: don't expect to have your mind opened to the Akashic realm, but instead expect your eyes to be burnt from their sockets from the action and badassery.
So, back to multiplayer, where this review should stay. The format is the same as usual, no surprises here. There are some changes though to the formula and metagame aspects though that freshen things up and make it a far more inviting experience than previous iterations of the series. In-game-wise, the art direction and setting are intriguing, creating a familiar world full of strange new things. This provide stimulus to the player, so that the game isn't just 'memorise map > check corners and shoot'. When things do inevitably fall into that cycle though, when one's "in the zone" so to speak, the actual aiming, shooting, and panic-firing of rockets into things 5 feet away is tighter than ever.
So far, if you have been abstaining from CoD games since, say, MW2 or similar, this is a good spot to jump back in if you're pining for a polished version of the same basic game, but with completely new assets, environments, and ambience.
A final word though on price: I can't recommend this game at the Steam store price - sorry Activision. For people in other countries, you might be confused (if you're lucky). To explain, this game costs $89.99 on Steam at the moment in Australia. For comparison, for about $10-15 extra I could use all that money to get two brand new PS3 games. While prices are rising again for new games, with the introduction of next generation games (don't expect consumers to follow this though), $89.99 for a now last-iteration PC game is a bit of a joke, and Activision are pricing themselves out of the market, however decent I think the game is.
Luckily, elsewhere, and accessible for Australian buyers, the game can be found at much more affordable prices, like the $20-30 range. So I can recommend the game, but unfortunately not with Steams current Australian price.

If you liked the original Life is Strange, there's no reason why you wouldn't like this. It's a pretty good prequel to the main game, albeit a bit short - but that's not a complaint, as it delivers the story extremely well and is paced accordingly. It's nowhere near as intriguing as the main story from the original, but you can't expect anything on that same level in a prequel. If you're interested in the characters, then it's definitely intriguing and will definitely keep your intererst throughout it's entirety.

I still recommend it and firmly believe that everyone should try this game out, ESPECIALLY if you haven't played the original one. But below there is going to be a bunch of criticism. The main 2 points I can point out are:
1. Its much less interactive compared to the original. By a lot. Even when it is, all choices basically lead to the same outcome. You never feel like anything you do matters. The narrative is linear, however you try to dress it up. I noticed that when I was in the exploration mode or whatever it is called and just for the fun of it tried different dialog optons. It was all the same. It looks like the hope here was that you only play the game once and never come back to it gain to explore different options. That's quite a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥approach.
2. In a game which is so story oriented prequels like that are a terrble thing. You literally know where everything leads to.
When I played it I had the feeling that major story points that we know from the original were unexplored. Basically leaving a gap between Before the Storm and the original. But then it occured to me that I was looking at it from the perspective of knowing whats going to happen and that this gap is something that is supposed to be explored in the original game, something that is a major focus of it. That agan just re-confirms my second point - prequel is a♥♥♥♥♥♥idea story wise for this game.
I am 100% positive that I would have enjoyed it a lot more if I played it first. But what are you gonna do. When they finally invent the memory wiping technology one of the first things I am going to do will be erasing my memory about these games and playing them in the order they are supposed to be played.

I bought this game on a whim, I was looking for another age of sail game that would scratch the itch Sid Meier's Pirates left.  Now this is nothing like Sid Meier's Pirates, in fact, there's very little actual story outside of the lore of each faction.  It drops you into the random world you crate, gives you a basic tutorial on how things work, and then lets you go.
The art style is simple and beautiful, it's top down.  The controls take a bit of time to get used to, I ended up using both my mouse/keyboard and controller but it was completely playable with either.  I love the music, it's calm and relaxing but ramps up for combat.  The combat is where I feel the game falls a little flat.  It's simple, your cannons auto-fire a broadside when the enemy ships are close and you press two buttons for your special abilities.  Most of my combat ended up either sitting in one spot turning my ship to make sure I could always fire or going in a circle to keep them in line of fire.  The trading is simple as well, each town produces certain goods, and if they have an abundance, you can buy it and sell it for a profit at another town.
The quests are also very simple, they range from hunting down pirates, to building towers, settling a new town, defending a city, or bringing people or cargo to another city.  Completing quests levels up the towns which gives you access to better ships and items.
The worlds are randomly generated from a map you can design yourself if you choose, the map is broken down into sections, each section is it's own little map to be explored.  At the beginning of the game, most of these sections are controlled by pirates and you conquer them for your faction.  There are also instances that you can create.  These are simple maps where you can choose it to be all out combat or a trading/quest hub.  You can use these to get loot, money, and experience  and once they are complete, you are put back in to the regular world.
There are 4 factions you can play as, each with their own preferred ship type and bonuses.  When you create a map you can have all 4 on it, or just one, or any number in between.
Overall, I enjoy this game, it does have issues that I have listed above and the developer is active on the forums.

But upon recent review, I'm sincerely disappointed in the tutorial that the devs added for two major reasons. 1. The graphic detail that has been added which turns the game rather uncomfortable, while likely increasing the rating as well.
The tutorial was a great idea, and I get that they want to make it obvious that these guys are bad guys, not people you should pity. But the graphic sex scenes and graphic violence are not necessary in a game that otherwise doesn't really focus on those things so much.

Rogue Legacy is a trial and error game at first. Once you begin getting stronger by grinding, the game becomes easier. Once you get to a point where you start one shotting most enemies, then you should New Game +. I've done a New Game + twice. The problems with the game are, the random generation of rooms, is very limited. You'll find yourself remembering rooms, and eventually you'll know how a certain layout of an area will be, regardless of how many times you play it. After New Game + the second time, I found myself needing to use the Grace Rune (I believe thats the right one) to lower the enemies levels, so that I'd get second tier and a few third tier enemies as well as a few mini boss enemies, as opposed to all third tier and mini boss enemies. Even though I only descaled the enemies with one rune, I was able to one shot them, but without it, it took several hits, and with as many enemies and projectiles on screen at once, I found the game unenjoyable due to difficulty. There's no in between. After you become strong, it's either too easy, or too hard. After you beat New Game + the first time, you automatically unlock all the runes. After traversing the areas, unlocking blueprints, etc. you'll find yourself wanting more. But once everything is unlocked, there's nothing else to do. Aside from beating the superbosses with preset characters (Who suck), which unless you're a good player (I'm mediocre at best), you'll probably be unable to do. I've unlocked pretty much everything, and aside from the superbosses, I've completed the game. And I don't feel satisfied, I want more. But there is no more.
For the S15 price tag, you'll find a gem of a game, that will hold your attention until you've done everything. Decent replay value. I can only hope the devs make a sequel.

This game was a pretty good experience overall. A great story and enjoyable shooting made for a nice experience, and the moral choices the game presents you with made me question my own morality as well as further immerse me in the story. It is certain that the main reason you should buy this game is to experience the story, with its interesting plot, immersive setting and well-written dialogue. This game also reminded me of Gears Of War, and not just because they are both third person shooters. This game gave me the same experience of being powerless in the face of impossible odds - and it certainly is impossible on the highest difficulty. Throughout the game I also felt a constant sense that what I was doing was wrong. I was fighting for my life - and yet I didn't want to. This was only because I was mercilessly slaughtering U.S. soldiers - my allies. At times I found it difficult to shoot people. One striking moment was when my squad had sneaked up behind two soliders who were chatting together. The dialogue reminded me of their humanity, and made me pause before putting bullets through their heads.
In terms of gameplay, the game is a fairly solid third-person shooter. Shooting feels good, and the gore is well done. Blowing up several soliders at once with a grenade launcher and watching their disintegrated bodies coat the floor is far more rewarding than it should be. The cover system however feels very clunky, and I often found myself moving in a way I didn't want to, and being quickly killed afterwards. This may be down to the fact that the game uses a one-button cover system, so control is lost as the game has to guess what you want to do. However, you have the ability to hold down spacebar and slide into cover from a couple of metres away. This feels very slick and polished, and it works very well. Not only does it feel good, it is also very useful to evade enemy fire. Without it, I feel that the cover system would be a nightmarish experience. Overall, the game plays well, with some enjoyable moments, but the gameplay is nothing special. This game is saved from bad reviews by its story.
One extreme irritation I have with this game is the lack of gameplay options. There is a good graphics menu with lots of options, and rebindable keys (although not as rebindable as I would have liked; many of the buttons do multiple actions clearly designed with a console in mind. For example, left shift both melees and vaults over cover. This is extremely annoying and there is no way to change it). However, there is also noticeable mouse acceleration and motion blur, neither of which can be turned off in the options menu. FoV also cannot be changed in options, although the 65-70° angle that it is locked at is reasonable for a TPS. In order to change these things, you have to somehow get into the encrypted INI files for the game. I was fortunate enough to find a decrypter online, and it was simple enough to disable  motion blur and mouse acceleration. However, the fact that these were unchangeable in the options menu is unacceptable for PC.
In summary, this game is a fairly solid third-person shooter. It is worth buying this game for the experience, but the short (6 hours on the second-highest difficulty) campaign has little replayability because the major strength of this game is the story. Do not buy this game if you are playing for the gameplay. The multiplayer is uninspired and dull, the only original aspect being the sandstorms that occur randomly in multiplayer games and make it harder to shoot. The real problem with the multiplayer is that you die so quickly that kills and deaths are mostly down to luck and positioning. However, the fun in this game lies with the story, and I recommend it for that alone. For me this game scores 7/10.

In my opinion call of duty black ops 2 is one of the best iteration of the entire COD franchise so far. I bought this games Digital Deluxe Edition a while back on a Steam sale and I do not regret it. it's no secret that Call of Duty is getting very very old and that it's being milked to death by Activision, but I'm glad that at least Treyarch can still bring some new interesting things to the table. this game is literally broken down into three separate parts. campaign, multiplayer and zombies and I'll go over each of them separately.
CAMPAIGN: Black Ops 2 campaign is by far one of the best Call of Duty campaign to date. it has one of the most epic and in depth stories of any of the CODs so far. most of the newer CODs (ghost and AW) have a absolutely ridiculous plot with an absolutely ridiculous amount of explosion and special effects that looks like it was directed by Michael Bay just to keep little 12 year old kids amused. Black Ops 2 actually takes time to explain itself and go in depth on its story and elaborates itself. there's also multiples choices throughout the campaign that leads to multiple endings giving you incentive to replay the campaign more than once. overall I found the campaign to be very enjoyable :)
MULTIPLAYER: the multiplayer in black ops 2 is pretty standard to all the other call of duties besides a few tweaks to the load out system and a new score streak system in place of the kill streak one and the return of the custom emblems from the originally Blacks ops. but overall it's still your standard Call of Duty multiplayer. so if you're not into Call of Duty multiplayer you're probably not going to like this one either but if you do like them then you should feel right at home with this one.
ZOMBIES: what can I say... zombies is the crown jewel of this game xD but personally I don't find this iteration of zombies as fun as black ops 1. transit is definitely an interesting mode and is very fun and difficult but it's no replacement to the traditional zombies we know and love. if you get the DLC I think you'll get more traditional zombie maps and that may fix it for you but i for one am not spending $40 on a bunch of DLC for a game that is nearly three years old... the closest map you get to a traditional zombies map in this game is "town" and even that doesn't feel like a complete zombie experience :/ like I said I liked transit but I don't feel it's a replacement for traditional zombies. overall it was still fun though especially if you're playing with your friends.
so overall Black Ops 2 is still a very good game and is still a lot better than most call of dutys out now a days *cough cough* ghost *cough cough*... sorry i must be coming down with something xD lol anyway I would recommend this game to anyone that enjoys playing fast pace shooters, games with deep stories or just wants to relax and kill some zombies. either way you can't go wrong with this one ;)

The original TrackMania games were damned amazing and had a great following with tons of servers full of thousands of players at any given time of day. For the last ten months, the new TrackMania games have been dead. I paid full price for all three titles, expecting to have an even better time with the new games, because why not?
Well, as the days turned to weeks, I realized the folly of my wasted money as almost all of the servers remained dead across the planet and it continued to be impossible to find a choice of heavily populated servers. Whether it was the dumb choice to milk the players of their cash by splitting the game up into three separate releases (one for each environment) and requiring separate servers for each or if it was the decision to charge money for the new games, at all, the result remains the same -- nobody plays these.
If you reference
for Stadium, you'll find that the average number of players at any given time through all of 2013 was between 90 and 190. Across the entire planet - and most usually seem to be overseas (Germany, France, Russia, Spain, the UK), so if you're looking for a populated low-ping server in your region and you're in North America, you're going to have a bad time.
It's a very unfortunate situation. The game looks better than ever and it has a lot of enjoyment to offer if you like this style of game. It's a fantastic time waster when you need a break here and there. However, you ultimately need a player-base for a multi-player game to be enjoyed. Their business and release model for this series of games completely failed in this way, this time around.
Here's to hoping they give the franchise another shot in a couple more years and they correct their mistakes.

The average third-person shooter with a really good storyline.

This game was a pretty good experience overall. A great story and enjoyable shooting made for a nice experience, and the moral choices the game presents you with made me question my own morality as well as further immerse me in the story. It is certain that the main reason you should buy this game is to experience the story, with its interesting plot, immersive setting and well-written dialogue. This game also reminded me of Gears Of War, and not just because they are both third person shooters. This game gave me the same experience of being powerless in the face of impossible odds - and it certainly is impossible on the highest difficulty. Throughout the game I also felt a constant sense that what I was doing was wrong. I was fighting for my life - and yet I didn't want to. This was only because I was mercilessly slaughtering U.S. soldiers - my allies. At times I found it difficult to shoot people. One striking moment was when my squad had sneaked up behind two soliders who were chatting together. The dialogue reminded me of their humanity, and made me pause before putting bullets through their heads.
In terms of gameplay, the game is a fairly solid third-person shooter. Shooting feels good, and the gore is well done. Blowing up several soliders at once with a grenade launcher and watching their disintegrated bodies coat the floor is far more rewarding than it should be. The cover system however feels very clunky, and I often found myself moving in a way I didn't want to, and being quickly killed afterwards. This may be down to the fact that the game uses a one-button cover system, so control is lost as the game has to guess what you want to do. However, you have the ability to hold down spacebar and slide into cover from a couple of metres away. This feels very slick and polished, and it works very well. Not only does it feel good, it is also very useful to evade enemy fire. Without it, I feel that the cover system would be a nightmarish experience. Overall, the game plays well, with some enjoyable moments, but the gameplay is nothing special. This game is saved from bad reviews by its story.
One extreme irritation I have with this game is the lack of gameplay options. There is a good graphics menu with lots of options, and rebindable keys (although not as rebindable as I would have liked; many of the buttons do multiple actions clearly designed with a console in mind. For example, left shift both melees and vaults over cover. This is extremely annoying and there is no way to change it). However, there is also noticeable mouse acceleration and motion blur, neither of which can be turned off in the options menu. FoV also cannot be changed in options, although the 65-70° angle that it is locked at is reasonable for a TPS. In order to change these things, you have to somehow get into the encrypted INI files for the game. I was fortunate enough to find a decrypter online, and it was simple enough to disable  motion blur and mouse acceleration. However, the fact that these were unchangeable in the options menu is unacceptable for PC.
In summary, this game is a fairly solid third-person shooter. It is worth buying this game for the experience, but the short (6 hours on the second-highest difficulty) campaign has little replayability because the major strength of this game is the story. Do not buy this game if you are playing for the gameplay. The multiplayer is uninspired and dull, the only original aspect being the sandstorms that occur randomly in multiplayer games and make it harder to shoot. The real problem with the multiplayer is that you die so quickly that kills and deaths are mostly down to luck and positioning. However, the fun in this game lies with the story, and I recommend it for that alone. For me this game scores 7/10.

Half-Genie Hero feels and plays like an HD 2.5D Shantae should. The animation and music are, as usual, incredible. The dialogue is hilarious and it's great to see all the old favorite characters return. This entry has more in common with Risky's Revenge than Pirate's Curse, as you'll be dancing to take animal form, INCLUDING THE TRIUMPHANT RETURN OF THE ELEPHANT! It feels rock-solid right from the start and you'll be hair-whipping mermaids in no time.
Two very minor, very patchable gripes though: my natural instinct is to use Escape to get out of/go back in menus, and that doesn't work here. Two, monkey controls for climbing might take you a bit of getting used to, as they're not what you'd think they'd be (pressing toward the wall does nothing, pressing away from the wall holds you still, can't remember if it felt this sticky in Risky's Revenge).
Overall though, I am loving the game and am very happy with how it turned out! Worth picking up if you enjoyed the previous games or are in the market for a fun, colorful, and actually fairly challenging Metroidvania platformer!

Gameplay is fun. There's lots of items to collect if you want to get the 100% clear rating! Revisiting the stages with power-ups you've collected since is rewarding, occasionally expanding into areas you didn't expect. The upgrade shop is a nice idea, but could do with a bit more stuff in it. The difficulty curve starts a bit higher than average - it might be a bit difficult for a beginner player - but it peters out towards the end as it doesn't scale well to match all of the upgrades you've amassed. The bosses are okay, but some of them are quite boring, especially
. Controls are nice and responsive (as they should be!), but I'd recommend using a gamepad.
The visuals are great! Shantae definitely benefits from not being on a tiny handheld screen! They've built upon the techniques they learnt while making
- bright 3D environments with 2D animated characters. The characters are really well animated, and share a nice, consistent style.
Music is on point as well! It's been done by the wonderful Jake Kaufman (who also appeared on previous WayForward titles). Definitely some very catchy songs in there, my favourite being the
stage.
Luckily the story isn't the focus of the game, because it's an afterthought at best. I'm not familiar with the series, but it seems clear that they tried to squeeze every single earlier-established character into the game. They also introduce a new character... only to have
. Overall, it doesn't really make much sense.
The writing is terrible - it definitely tries way too hard to be funny. It seems like it was written by a four-year-old; I remember one of the worst offenders being "
". Unfortunately, you need to read some of the text to know what to do next; if you don't want to read it, try skipping through the main text, then talk to the NPC characters afterwards to get them to repeat the important details.
Overall, it's a good platforming experience! It suffers from being a bit short - it took me 7 hours to 100% it at a rather leisurely pace - but I'm aware that there's more content coming in the future.

I backed this game during the Kickstarter campaign both due to the fact that the Shantae series has had some excellent games, and WayForward have yet to disappoint with any game they've made. I received the code for it approximately a week ago and basically marathoned my through it.
If you've played many platformers, or even more relevant, many metroidvania style platformers, you will find an enjoyable but somewhat short experience in Shantae: Half-Genie Hero. In about 10 hours in-game time I had completed everything the base game had to offer. This includes achieving 100% in the main story and in the New Game+ style mode known as Hero Mode. That being said, the experience was a thoroughly enjoyable one. There is DLC content on that way the will no doubt add several dozen more hours of play time to the game for me. I'm actually half-considering learning to speed run it, that's how much fun I've had with it.
The sprite work in the game is phenomenal, animation that is both smooth as butter and full of personality. You can tell just from first the level alone that a lot of hard work and dedication went into producing this game. With all that said, I highly recommend the game to anyone who is a fan of the genre.
