I am a father of two boys, ages 3 and 6 and hold a BA in Game Design (although I work as a database admin - tough to leave a job of 15 years to pursue the "dream" of game design with a family to support.) That aside, we use a HTPC with Steam in Big picture Mode launched from XBMC. With a wife and two young ones, everything has to be remote and controller friendly. The games also have to be kid-friendly. If you find yourself in a similar situation and trust the opinion of a trained game designer (but not professionally working at it) - then read on.
edit: since I bought the Trackmania three game pack, I am posting the same review in the other two titles as the pros and cons are the same for all (except for Valley, which has a Con unique to itself.)
-- The game was cheap. $20 for three games (Stadium, Canyon, and Valley) during the Steam winter sale made this something worth trying out.
-- Despite not having an ESRB rating (that I could find anyway), the games are kid friendly. Physics are loose, no bodies are flying out of cars, you can restart at a spawn point on the track, facing the right way (important for the three year old!) at any time you get stuck. I can start a split-screen game and choose a "playlist" for the kids to race at the same time. They're happy, I'm happy.
-- The game is fun. Stunts, fast cars, loose physics, respawns, tricky tracks, loop tracks, various difficulties, time trials, medals, rankings. And I haven't even tried actual online multi-player yet. I'm not too interested in that part so I won't review that part of the game at this time.
-- Game runs smooth. I've experienced no crashes (the game software, not cars!), no jerkiness, graphics are decent, controls on a 360 controller are easy enough for the three year old to win races against his big brother occasionally.
-- The interface is severely lacking. Poor design choices abound. To launch the games, Steam launches another launcher (ManiaPlanet). In this new launcher, you see all three games you purchased (after you installed them all). However, if I click on "Stadium" from Steam, then decide to play "Canyon" in the ManiaPlanet (MP) launcher, it says I have to restart the game I want from Steam. What's the point of this extra layer of launcher then? Stupid design.
-- The MP launcher is not controller friendly. This means I have to get the keyboard out just to be able to arrow down to the "Start Game" button. You can't hit it with ANY button on a controller. Once that's done, you can use the controller in game, but not in this MP launcher.
-- Selecting items using the controller is poor design. Blue text turns a bit "more blue" or slightly brighter. Arrows that are white turn slightly brighter when selected. The wife and kids can't tell what the heck they're navigating. I know about this and I can barely see this on a 42" screen. It's clear the interface is designed only for mouse. The controller does work, but it's not easy to see the navigation. This means I have to setup the game for the kids. I have to get them into the tracks, I have to change playlists (or games if they want to play Stadium for instance.)
-- Kids can't get their own profile. I tried setting the game to use "multiple profiles" but the feature is nigh-useless. I attempted to create a profile for my eldest so he can have his own rankings or even just his own car model when playing split-screen. I didn't want him to access online so I created a local profile. Now none of the games launch. They say "You must connect online to launch the game." I did say LOCAL account didn't I? Again, stupid. So I tried to create a new profile using my already created online account (cause I couldn't get the games to run even by myself before doing this.) The game wouldn't let me do that. Only one key per account it says. I tried creating a new account to the same effect. They want you to buy the game again just so you can use multiple profiles. So to recap, you can't create a local profile without connecting it to an onlne account and you can't create multiple users under one account and you can't create multiple online accounts without buying additional licenses. Stupid.
-- Due to the above, the simple feature in almost any racing game, choosing a car skin, can't be done except by the online profile. So my kids playing in split screen have to settle for the plain gray cars and my eldest can't keep his own records and scores.
-- Car engine sounds disappear when you select High quality Audio (you have to keep it at normal).
-- Some of the tracks are way too difficult for really little ones (not a knock on the game, just something to be aware of.)
-- Controls are not consistent between solo play and multiplayer. For example, the respawn button by default is the yellow Y button in solo play. In split screen, you push down (click the button) on the left analog stick. I'd like to remap it as the respawn button on the steering control leads to accidental respawns However, it doesn't seem to "take" as it looks like it's tied to profiles, which as mentioned above, I can't create.
-- the in-game HUD is awful. Everything is so small it's pointless on a big screen from across the room. Thankfully the kids don't care about this info, they just want to race. Worth noting.
There is just too much stupidity in design to overcome for me. So if you find yourself with a media center that also serves as a game machine for the kids and are looking for a fun racing game the little ones can enjoy. I'd consider this title at rock-bottom prices otherwise I'm recommending you go elsewhere. You simply can't do simple things other racing games can, nothing is intuitive, the interface is awful (both menu and during racing). Despite that, once you get a race going, it is fun for the kids. So the core gameplay is ok, it's all the design elements, the spit and polish that surround the game that is severely lacking good design. If you want fun big-screen family room entertainment, local split screen multi-player, racing game - go get Sonic Transformed.
If you read this far and are just looking for a single-player or online, match-making, stunt racing, beat the clock game - why did you read my review? Didn't I write at the start this wasn't the perspective? Go check out other reviews that are more your demographic. Since you're still here, all the flaws mentioned above still irk me as a designer, so I'd look for a more realistic racing game than this one if it weren't for my kids and split screen wasn't a factor.
Get it on sale, avoid it otherwise.

I bought this because it looks like Sid Meyer's Pirates! but ended up having way more fun with it because of how straightforward it was. Single player drags on a bit at first and it's a pretty nice experience, but heading online to a populated server will yield greater rewards, like faster level gain and better loot. Learn the ins and outs with single player, then once you get it, head online, and join instances. There's an excellent community and the devs are always helpful, in the forums. They also play themselves as I've heard, although I have yet to run into one. The sea battles are a lot of fun, and the trading and questing adds a different flavor to it too, but the meat of the game is online. Windward is wholly enjoyable especially if you like seafaring games. It's pretty much a game made up of the sea battles from Sid Meyer's Pirates! except with added abilities and flair. Don't miss out.

Exploration, sea battles, territory control, questing, trading, PVP, and loot! Leveling your ships and the equipment they use is a lot of fun, there's always rarer loot out there to bump your stats up a little higher.
This game is fine in single player but really shines when you've got one or more friends on your side. Create an instance and the game will generate a single map for you and your friends to drive out the pirates. Or create a world and take it over map by map. Or join a server and battle for territory control with other players. You can also observe other people's instances and take control of the pirate faction ships they're battling.
I look forward to seeing what else this game has in store.

I've really enjoyed Windward so far (25 hours).  Sailing, combat, quests and trade are right in my wheelhouse.
The sailing mechanic seems simpler than Pirates, but the combat is richer, with a number of skills to throw along with cannonball.   The way I play, I spent a lot of time in each zone, including the starter zone, so moving to the next levels I had access to better ships than some might if they like to play through quickly.  If you have enough speed and can 'cross the T', you can hold out against powerful ships.
One does need to be 'OK' with trade 'grinding', as that seems to be the only way to grow cities and subsequently get better ships.  Personally I've liked this kind of mechanic since Elite, and after that Privateer  (though both of those are first person flight, and Windward is top down looking very much like Pirates world).
It is a sandbox game, and in its current form, it might get too repetitive for some who aren't really into the premise.  For me, though its a great find.
There have been a couple of updates already in the week since I got the game.   I'm curious where the dev might go.
All in all this is something I'll keep installed and probably come back to like I kept going back to Pirates for 10 years.

This game feels a little bit like a puzzle game, a little bit like a shooter (duh, guns), and a lot like a very massive open-world adventuring game.
There's a sense of accomplishment when you track a large buck down for 20 minutes and get within bow distance and send an arrow right through his heart. You feel like you really earned the kill. The game does a good job of not just handing the kills to you. Although I have encountered situations where shooting at a deer would not send the others into a panic, so I managed to bag 3-4 before the rest scattered. Not so sure that is realistic.
There are a handful of bugs so don't be surprised when you see teleporting bears, or a clear broadside lung shot results in a 25 minute chase only to reveal the game thinks you hit a tailbone, but I don't think it detracts from the quality of the game.
Visuals are amazing. If any other game in any other genre made a world experience like this one, it would be GOTY for that genre. Simply stunning how real some of the environments feel.
Shooting is eh. Most of the time I feel like this is a simulator of an out of shape man going hunting. Holding your breath to steady a shot should easily last more than 0.5s and should definitely not result in a maximum heart rate. (This is bad at least in the early levels, you can get perks and skills to mitigate this)
ATV DLC is quite honestly a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t charge, but I got the game on sale so it was well worth it.
I recommend it if you have any interest at all in hunting or just want a nature-walk simulator.

For those who have never played a Shantae title, the premise is fairly unique: You play a half-genie bellydancing heroine who fights enemies using her magical prehensile hair and magical dances that allow her to transform into a dozen-odd different animals.
The game, unlike most previous Shantae titles, is split into distinct levels, which vary between being fairly linear to fairly open-ended, though both sorts allow for a fair amount of exploration and discovery. This division does make getting 100% much easier, as the level select lets you know what's left to find in a given level, so rather than having to hunt through the entire overworld you just have to explore on level, which is rather nice.
It's not flawless, the story is largely an afterthought, the jokes can fall flat, and some of the transformations see essentially no use, but the game is definitely fun and very much worth a look.
It took me about 7 hours to 100% the Shantae campaign (an additional campaign where you play as her arch-nemesis, Risky Boots, is being worked on), so this isn't going to occupy you for months, but that does make it comparable to Super Metroid for the amount of content, which is fine by me.

Honestly surprised this game hasnt droped off the face of the earth.
Devs seem to want to make a good dayz experence but they fail to see that it requires a strong and healthy player base for that to work. No matter the current state of the game the fans will never really be pleased, and can you blame them?
2013 is when they started raking in money from overly ambitous player base that really just wanted more content that they had come to love from Arma 2 mod, What we got was far from that. while the OG dayz mod was slowly dieing newer mods focusing more on the pvp and less survival become more popular over the years intill you couldnt really find a decent pop dayz server unless you like people driving around in tanks. Mean while everyone who grew to love the mod for what is was put their eggs in the standalone basket myself included.
Needless to say its the end of 2017 coming close to 4 years since this game was put up for sale and we are still in alpha. I cant say it bothers me much. I realized awhile ago that dayz is gonna die, even if the devs did push beta out this year would it make a difference? How many players have moved on? Do we really think a beta update with more bugs than content will bring this dead IP back from the grave?? Dayz has now become an example of what happens when the hype train runs out of control, indeed its almost all the player base fault for setting themselves up for disapointment. At the same time the devs need to shoulder the weight and critisims from fans because without the fans you have no game.
Even tho i gave into the hype I never really encouraged others to purchase this game nor would I have ever said this game was in a decent playable state. I feel sad to write this because seeing talk of going into beta did respark my intrest in the game but after seeing how the community has reacted to yet another obvious delay I cant see this game taking off.
Im not bashing the devs or telling the players that they are wrong for being upset over not getting what they expect.
Instead i would encourage anyone whos been let down by this game to remeber this, dont just jump into early access games expecting everything to work out on your time. Early access is a risk both for the devs and the consumers and im honestly sick of seeing the market flooded with them.. I enjoy suporting things I love but there can only be so much trust we consumers should have for devs. At the end of the day its a job for them, these guys just wanna sell copies so they can live. sometimes that means stretching truths and breaking promises because sales are the bottom line.
So the next time you see some early access game that looks so good and you want to support it and get all your friends to buy it. Remmeber what happened here... and what will keep happening intill consumers educate themselves about what they buy instead of mindlessly buying things cuz they are on sale,friend told you to, looks good.. etc
At the end of the day its your choice to vote with your dollar, the more game devs see this kind of behavior get rewarded the more they are gonna do it.

Ignoring a few nights of tabbing out, I think I've played Windward for about 20 hours and discovered that the boat combat genre is something I need in my life. Being a big fan of the rogue-like genre, Windward plays like a shallow Diablo/Torchlight/Path of Exile with the restraints around boat combat mechanics. I only say shallow as I wished there was more variety in the in-game activities.
It is obvious that the developers spent the brunt of their effort on combat, and it shows in how smooth(mostly) it plays out. Fights can be very simple 1v1 focusing on positioning, or they can be chaotic brawls with narrow escapes. There is some variety in ship configurations, with "tank and spank" and "hit and run" being the two successful configurations I went with. However, in my opinion there is so much more potential for other combat mechanics. Boarding ships, tethering via harpoons, mines, disabling weapons and steering(more than the existing rigging shredding), and better skill shots could enhance combat.
Outside of combat, the game economy could provide a nice non-combative way to advance with a bit of engineering effort. Add a low-key city builder, enable trade route formation, and things of this nature. Outside of online instances and heroic instances, I found manually moving goods around to be an acceptable means to generate enough gold for the zeppelin, but grinding that 1m gold left me wanting more variety in gold generation.
All the above points however would just be a wishlist for another installment or another game. At the pricepoint that Windward is sitting at, it is interesting enough to keep the player engaged for 10-20 hours. Online play is fun, solo play is fun, and the gameplay is simple yet rewarding.

The only con I've run into was not being able to view my first intel after having picked up the second; I didn't listen to it initially because there was a cutscene happening, and I didn't realize the game would pause for intel. The ability to pause at any time, regardless of whether a cutscene is happening, is a huge plus. Having a log with articles for later retrieval would be nice, but the lack thereof isn't a dealbreaker.  I looked up what I missed on YouTube.

I've played this on a console before and it is safe to say this is one of the best shooter of this generation.
Spec Ops does not reinvent the wheel in any way in terms of game mechanics, graphic engine nor brings up action sequences never seen before in the history of gaming. The gameplay is pretty much your usual shooter. The controls are good, the graphics are decent, but it does nothing different tech-wise from other action games, really. So how can I think so highly of such a "generic" game?
Well, there's the game's plot and what it stands for. It is a reimagination of Josephs Conrad's 1899 short novel "Heart of Darkness". Don't worry, I won't spoil anything. While the game kicks off as a standard "military squad vs the world", as the game progresses it gets darker and darker and what appeared to be just a shalow story turns into a very deep critique of violence, human mental health and even the own game industry tendencies. There's TONS of articles out there the discuss the importance of this game's plot, but you'll have to play first.
TL;DR: the game "disguises" itself as a generic game (and in its mechanics, it really is) but there is so much more stuff going on in this plot that turns Spec Ops in one bizarre phenomenon of the game industry. I dropped the game a few times because he was just "OK" but I'm glad one day I had the motivation to finish. It really is worth it if you're into good stories and some grim stuff.

Dear lord, I just finished Spec Ops: The Line. A masterpiece of a game. It is a military third person shooter, but if the gameplay doesn't chase you off, don't assume anything else. The story is a major deconstruction of the standard views, and deciding what is right, what is necessary, and are they really either of those things. It also has rather excellent use of color, balancing against the common browns and grays.
Now it's not perfect, the game tends to increase the challenge by simply adding a lot of enemies, and they can (even early on) shred through you pretty quickly if you are in the open. Coupled with infrequent checkpoints this can easily ruin the narrative and flow of sections. In addition while stealth is sometimes suggested, it is intensely difficult to do in practice.
However I can't tell you how important of a game this is, both for the general plot, and the emotions it leaves you with. If you can stomach the gameplay and theming, PLEASE give it a shot.

I am proud to have backed Shantae: 1/2 Genie Hero, and along with games like Shovel Knight stands as evidence to the usefulness of Kickstarter in delivering the game developers wanted to make to the players who wanted to play it. From the onset to the credits, its a delightfully colorful and vibrant platformer, that happens to be well written and funny on top of its mechanical excellence. I consider it a treat for returning fans and I'm sure, for newcomers as well.
As the first title in the series built for home consoles and PC, the graphical improvements are immediately apparent. We have come a long way from Game Boy Color, with vastly more fluid sprite animations over pleasing 3D backgrounds. It has notably lost none of the magic of its predecessors, as well as its reputation for charmingly attractive character designs that have just enough appeal to not be tacky. The controls are spot on, and should be familiar to anyone to has played SNES or Genesis era titles with a keyboard.
I must give special consideration to the soundtrack, which I coughed up extra for during the Kickstarter. If you're at all familiar with Jake "Virt" Kaufman and his work on the previous Shantae games, Shovel Knight, Contra 4, Scurge: Hive and many other projects, you'll know what to expect. He's really outdone himself this time.
The transformation dances that are a hallmark of the series return, including at least once dance that hasn't been seen since the very first game. This one has by far the most dances and other upgrades, enough that collecting all of them makes you virtually indestructible, in particular making the final boss fight rather trivial. This would require you to actually FIND everything, but it's not the hardest Metroidvania to explore. In fact, it's structured more like the Megaman X games. It also has some harder platforming segments then Pirate's Curse.
The few negative reviews of the game all talk about the difficulty, or rather, the lack of it, and the afforementioned backtracking. At no point in the game did I find either of these things aggrivating. Having recently completed a solo playthrough of Bloodborne, I can tell you that there are hard games out there. And there are cheap ones, overhyped ones, and ones that value leaderboard scores over anything resembling fun. Shantae: 1/2 Genie Hero is none of those things, and that is fine. What it is, is a diamond in the rough, a game that made me feel good just to be alive to play it. I think it will do the same for you, and in the end, that's what gaming is really about.

A game with beautiful, energetic aesthetics and unadventurous design.
+ Aesthetics in general are sharp, cartoony and juicy. The animations with Wrench are particularly fun.
+ Factory stage has a nice narrative progression.
+ Stage progression is more arcade-style than metroidvania-style, which is a fun change for the series.
+ New-form-containing genie rooms remind me of Rayman (PS1), and make understanding the basic utility of new forms very easy.
+ The writing is fun and self-deprecating. Most of the dialogue has great gameplay utility as well, guiding the player with hints (though the bolded text takes some of the fun out of parsing dialogue for the important bits).
+ VO is sprinkled throughout the game and contributes to the personality of the characters and dialogue. It seems like a clever (and budget friendly) way to equip our imaginations with a little more material.
- The megaman-style disappearing blocks are played out, and a little overused in some of the level designs.
- The dance selection screen is colorful, but has an odd timing-element that automates the cycling of menus. More than once I mis-selected as the menu switched at just the wrong time.
- Stages tend to introduce a new mechanic, but they don't seem particularly novel so far. This level features something you can climb / hang from (Donkey Kong Country). This level features wind that pushes you (Megaman). This level features...enemy spawners? Levels don't feel surprising after the novelty of new visuals wear off.
- The monkey form feels weirdly sticky when climbing on walls. It can feel awkward when I try to climb up over the side of a wall, or transform back into human form. The time lost performing attempting these acts often leads to cheap damage in combat situations.
- projectile-wielding enemies tend to shoot from off-screen, which can lead to cheap damage when playing an area for the first time.
- The Wilbur worm escape features level design that essentially dooms the player if they proceed up the wrong path. The choice is arbitrary the first time a player sees it, so these deaths are very frustrating.
- Game over screen should have more character in a game as colorful as this. Players may see it several times, so why not try some arkham-asylum-style flavor dialogue?
- The hitbox of Shantae's human form seems a bit large. Shrinking it a bit within the actual sprite raises the odds for a daring, exciting dodge. Players who get used to the smaller hitbox can use it to make combat faster, more risky, and more showy
- Characters often animate during cutscenes and dialog, but without any zoom, this easily goes unnoticed (some dramatic zoom wouldn't seem out of place in a story this goofy).
- Monkey form seems to have far more general utility than the crab form.
- I wish there was an overarching villain to give the story a visible destination. As it stands, the magnet contraption ties things together a bit, but the player isn't even told how many pieces remain, or what the final design looks like (unless I'm missing something-- perhaps there was a way to look at the blueprints before handing them to uncle).
- The liberal use of VO really gives the characters...character, but we don't need Shantae revealing the high-level strategy to each boss phase. It takes away the fun a bit, and most are simple enough to simply not need it.
- There seems to be little difference between a fall-death and a game over. The latter should be a more impactful fate than the former, yet the latter typically places the player at the exact same location as the former, but with full health! Often, it is the better option, as being forced to restart an area without having health replenished sometimes sets the player up for quick, highly-probable (and frustrating) failure.
- Bosses don't seem to emphasize new abilities much, in the way a Legend-of-Zelda boss would. While LoZ bosses may go overboard with the way they require stage-specific abilities, the bosses here feel a little rote-- all they seem to require is a bit of hair-whipping and jumping, for the most part. Mechanics never really come together, or combine in interesting ways during these fights, and they never really feel exciting as a result.
Thank you for your effort on this game, and best of luck moving forward!

This Shantae’s first HD adventure along with her returning genie powers, and it is excellent.
Story/Graphics/Music:
Like the previous entries, this is a very light-hearted story, not as great as Pirate’s Curse, but still fun. The cute style and great humor is all there, but in HD. You can probably tell from the screenshots, but this game looks beautiful and set a very high standard for future Shantae games to come. I also don’t know how Jake Kaufman did it, but the soundtrack is even catchier than the last. I’d also like to note that I really like how many older animations were carried over such as the butt wiggle as well as both the bouncy Shantae and Rottytops idle animation, because it wouldn’t feel right without them.
Gameplay:
We’re back to regular movement with genie transformations. I thought I'd miss the Pirate items, but transforming is quick and each one serves a good purpose. Levels are pretty big and while there is a decent amount of backtracking, it really feels like you’re exploring the map a lot more than previous titles. So while it is technically backtracking, it doesn’t feel like you’re going back to levels just for the sake of padding. Most of the time you’re looking for more items, if not you’re at least compelled to because finding secrets in this game is fun. Some of the secrets don’t blatantly stick out either so you’ll have to use a bit of brain power to find everything, which I perfectly welcome. Much of the annoyances some people had are also gone, such as being able to leave a level at any time and skipping any parts that you’ve already clear for free (once you receive the ability to). This means more playing and less waiting.
The combat is quick and satisfying like an old school Castlevania game. You get access to spells and upgrades that generally help you do more damage and take less damage. One of the great things about every one of these upgrades is that they can be toggled off. This is great because after fully completing the game I started a playthrough with minimal upgrades as a challenge. Bosses are generally fun, with a few that are the “wait for your turn” variety.
Some gripes:
I really only have two issues with the game, the first one being the missing dungeons. If you’ve played the previous Shantae games, you would consider these dungeons a staple in the series. You could say they’ve made up for it with bigger, more explorable levels, but fans have shown that they are missed.
My second gripe is the difficulty, way too easy this time around. I actually died being careless once or twice on the second level, but once you clear this and you get access to some money, you can reduce your damage by half. On top of that, you start to gain access to a lot more health upgrades so you’ll have tons health. Another issue is that most enemies will not knock you back when getting hit like you would a lot of the time in Pirate’s Curse. Because of this, I normally just ran through levels taking damage for the sake of speed. Most bosses can also be brute forced before you need to use items, however I will admit I had to use healing items for the last boss. If you really wanted to, you could also fully nullify damage by end game which is a very questionable balance decision. I mentioned earlier I'm on a limited upgrade playthrough thanks to being able to toggle off upgrades. Again, I'm glad this is something you can do.
Final thoughts:
This marks the beginning of some great Shantae games. They have the engine and everything they need to make a great game now. I see this game as a little reboot to the series so I’m hoping for many more to come. Some people might call this game too short. My first 100% playthrough was about 5 ½ hours, about 1 hour shorter than my first Pirate’s Curse run. I would say the amount of content is just a little under the last game because you save so much time with the new features I’ve mentioned before, such as skipping beaten sections. Another thing that saves time is that the town NPCs actually give you hints on where to go so you more or less always know what you have to do. Regardless of the short time, I loved every minute of it and I’m still re-playing the game even with all the achievements. I can’t wait for Risky’s campaign and any more content to come. If you’re into these types of games, there’s absolutely no reason you shouldn’t own Pirate’s Curse and Half Genie Hero.
Edit: And now the added content/DLC (received free for being a kickstarter backer)
Hard mode: It's actually pretty hard. There is smaller limit to useable items and enemies not only do more damage, but are faster too. Definitely harder to brute force your way through.
Pirate Queen's Quest: Fun alternate story where you play as Risky. Has altered levels tailored to the returning pirate items you receive throughout the story. It rewards you for looking for the extra collectables by using them make your abilities stronger.
Friends to the End: Tag-team control Shantae's 3 friends each with their attacks and abilities. A decent challenge too since there is shared health and very limited healing. Similar to Pirate Queen's Quest, the levels are tailored to the abilities, which are all available from the get-go. There's also an interesting mechanic where your characters do more damage the more gems you collect, but you drop some upon taking damage.
The extra content altogether can easily extend the game for another 4-10 hours depending on how much of a completionist you are. If you want really want extend your stay in Sequin Land, I'd say pick them up, but maybe wait for a sale as it is a little pricy.

I have never been the biggest fan of platformers at the best of times, and to be honest I tried this game a few times and couldn't really get into it, but after having a good go for a couple of hours I have reached the "Just one more run and then I'll leave" mentality.
The platforming mechanics are super solid, the enemy variety is fantastic and the rogue-like elements work really well in the context of the game.
There are a several classes to choose from, which can be upgraded as you play through and heaps of equipment/runes to find. Sometimes the procedurally generated levels can be unforgiving but ultimately it's up to luck. If you have trouble with a particular castle setup, the next run will probably be completely different.

Rogue Legacy is a roguelike-platformer hybrid: in layman's terms, you make your way through a castle and realms beyond while jumping and fighting monsters. Also, character death is permanent, and the layout of the levels changes each time you start a new character. Think Castlevania, but where you get a different castle every run. As an additional mechanic, each new character is randomized to an extent -- they have a random class, subweapon, and a selection of mutations that may or may not be helpful. Mutations include being really large, being really tiny, having difficulty seeing, seeing in sepia or black-and-white, regaining mana by breaking furniture, inability to see your health bar, immunity to spike traps, random farting... the list goes on.
The game revolves around getting as far as you can with each character, so you can unlock stuff (like better armor, special abilities, better stats, etc.) so your next character can (theoretically) get a little bit farther. It's an okay concept, but I would only recommend it if you're already a fan of difficult roguelikes and platformers. And I mean the really, really hard "keep trying and trying and trying and trying and maybe you'll get one step closer to beating this game" roguelikes, because that's what's going to happen.
I personally find this game's progression too frustratingly slow -- the amount of gold you need to unlock things gets pretty ruinous fairly quickly, and since the price of everything rises as you unlock things, really the "best" way to play the game seems to be to just beeline straight for anything that helps you make more gold and ignore everything else, *including* unlocking things that make it marginally easier to survive without insane platforming skills. (Hint: unlock things on the right side of the castle first -- that's where you'll get the miner class, which gives you +30% to all gold pickups.) Maybe I'm just bad at the game, but I have a hard time collecting enough gold before getting killed horribly to really make any significant progress -- usually I'll scrape together maybe a few hundred, die, and then have to start all over because anything less than at least 600-ish just doesn't cut it after the first few unlocks. The fact that you can't control when you get traits that help you explore more efficiently (like getting a miner or somebody with dwarfism) just makes things that much more frustrating, in my opinion.
I've put a bunch of time into this, and, while I've had fun, I find this game too difficult to keep playing (maybe if the prices didn't keep rising, I could actually get somewhere). Go ahead and try it out if you're really confident in your platforming skills and willing to deal with having to start over countless times for miniscule gains. If that's not you, then maybe give this one a pass.

Probably one of, if not the, best licensed movie game.
PROS:
+ Awesome car combat.
+ Awesome driving AI. The raiders will boost out of the way of your ramming runs, group up on you and sandwich you.
+ Satisfying ground combat. Great Arkham-like melee, and probably the most challenging out of the Arkham clones because health is harder to recover via water and food.
+ Optimization. Runs great on my computer, easily hit 60 fps.
+ Graphics. The variation of the wasteland is very surprising. The devs could have made one big desert and called it a Mad Max game, but they included different regions which all have their own unique take on the wastes.
+ Story. While the plot is very simple (as it should be in Mad Max), the interaction with the weird characters is great.
+ Audio. There is very little music in the game so as not to distract from the overwhelming roar of the V6 and V8 engines.
+ Theme. If you thought the opening of Fury Road where Max is chased by the horde of War Boys was cool, expect to be outnumbered constantly. While you may be a martial arts master on foot, you will be not be able to destroy multiple cars with ramming alone. Use the harpoon to rip drivers out of their cars, shoot their gas reserves to explode their car, and pull off doors and tires to disable the vehicle. I often found myself driving away from war parties, resulting in a tense chase.
CONS:
- Repetitive tasks. The meat of the game is the driving and melee mechanics, so expect to drive and melee things. Collect scrap, upgrade, rinse and repeat. Any other game that did this would be uninstalled within an hour, but I play Mad Max to drive around the wastes and punch people, nothing more.
- Very little music.
- Upgrading your engine can make it louder. I lowered my volume and played without troubles.
Conclusion: This game goes on sale often, both through Steam and Bundle Stars. Buy during a sale and enjoy.

If you think of buying this game for the pc and you don't have a powerfull desktop pc, think twice. Multiplayer is very demanding and incredibly laggy. Multiplayer population is inconsistent and depending of your country you will have a hard time getting into servers. Mainly you can either choose TDM or Search and Destroy, as the rest is pretty much abandoned. The game seems more balanced (excluding Kap 40), but netcode is a mess. If your host has any small change in their network, everyone gets flooded with lag until the time it goes back to normal (if the server room does not crash). Bad optimization for pc is the only word that could be said about it. Nowadays seems impossible to play a game without having lag, crashes and mistical ghost shots from bad connection (happens to me and my cousin, other people might have it differently).
Zombie also suffers from low server populations. It's hard to find a game, even harder to find good players that won't leave the room just after it starts or after they die one time. If you can have some friends instead of strangers changes the experience completely. But, as the multiplayer, it also suffers from horrible connections, you will get lucky if the server does not crash and freezes your screen until wave 20. Me and some friends played zombies a lot, but aroudn waves 17-21 it ALWAYS crashes. It's so bad, that's it's not even worth after all.
Singleplayer does not suffer from a lot of problems the rest of the modes do. It's the safest mode to go for. For the players that want to play the campaign, you won't find any troubles around here, some framerates drops, but nothing major. Not the best of campaigns, but not so bad either. By this time and day, you will probably know what to expect from a COD campaign. Some new adds are weapon customization and you can pick whathever you want for any mission. You can also get to some alternative places and machines using a perk that opens some possibilities. Multiple endings and a few choices.
Overall, not really worth it for this price. If you have x360 or Ps3, choose to buy a copy in this systems if you want the game.

It's good. It's not the pinnacle of outstanding platforming like, I dunno, Mario, but it's still a very solid game with good jokes interwoven with it, much like the rest of the series. Ultimately the whole adventure is maybe six to eight hours long.
There are some downsides, though; it's plainly obvious some content was abandoned during development. A lot of various abilities to pick up over the game or even series staples like the destructible blocks only serve to, straight up, get one thing before becoming useless again. This one thing could actually be plot demanded or just a health upgrade. It's very strange in that regard; time was spent on giving Shantae a spider form, yet it's used for A Puzzle and then never so much as useful again.

Half-Genie Hero is a triumphant return of the Shantae series. The art style and animation is so fluid and detailed, there are times when I'm honestly not sure if what I'm looking at is a sprite or 3D model. I've NEVER had a game make me question this, and it's a testement to artists and animators who brought Shantae to life.
The game is equally a blast to play. Controls are fluid and responsive, even the seconds needed to cycle between Shantae's animal forms don't take too long to break flow. Combat with Shantae's equally detailed and expressive foes is challenging, without being too frusterating. The platforming never gets so pixel-perfect as to want to break your controller, especially with Shantae having multiple ways to progress through challenges. I am also happy to say I never needed to go Googling for the answer to any puzzles or platforming challenges.
The game is relatively short, I finished in about 3 days, spending 2-3 hours each run. Despite being metroid-vania in structure, the game is spread over different stages you chose to travel to, akin to Shantae and the Pirate's Curse. However, every stage is PACKED with secrets, and I found myself going through each stage again whenever I gained a new ability. The stages themselves visually change after the boss is defeated, making return trips feel fresh. Plus, there's new characters that will be added to the game for free with their own campaigns in the future, and I am eager to play them!
The boss fights themselves are amazing. Many even zoom out to make room for the massive boss on screen. Each one is intense and satisfiying to fight, though none proved to be so difficult that I could not defeat on the first try.
Like most of the Shantae games, the plot is fairly standard, and you can probably see all the twists a mile away. Though, like most of the Stantae games, the story is more defined by the characters and their dialogue, all of which is cleaverly written. Shantae and her friends are utterly hilarious and witty, and it's worth playing the game just to see them bounce quips off one another.
My only serious complaint is the relatively weak finale, especially compared to the previous games. The final battle is disapointing, as is the conclusion, at least compared to the last 2 games. For less serious complaints, the story overall, especially in terms of character development, isn't quite as good as Pirate's Curse, though still good. There's also an issue of balance, as most of Shantae's animal forms are pointless to use in combat. You even wind up finding upgrades that enable them to attack too late in the game for them to be of any use. Shanate my actually have too many attacks, spells and abilities, most of which can't match her standard hair attack. And by the end of the game, I was stuffed with so many healing items and restorative abilities, I could brute-force my way through anything.
None of these issues make me regret Kickstarting this game. The greatest testement to its quality, is the longing I felt to play more games like it, and seeing nothing in my steam library that match it.
If you enjoy platformers, quality indie titles, metroid-vania, or just want a enjoyable tale about a beautiful and witty Half-Genie, Buy This Game!
*Note: Was a backer on the Shantae: Half-Genie Hero Kickstarter.

The game is fairly simple but a lot of fun. You start off with a small, slow, ship without much in the way of equipment. You'll  begin doing some simple quests, trading, light combat against single pirate ships and such as you try to upgrade your little dinghy. You'll be able to customize your hull, cannons, sails, crew, captain, and more with a Diablo-esque loot system, as well as custom paint and decals for your hull and sails to make your ship uniquely you.
Before too long however, you'll be invited into your first combat instance, which is basically a region at war with a fleet of endlessly respawning pirates. The combat instances I can only describe as something out of Star Wars Battlefront, or Dynasty Warriors, with two (or more) fleets of ships competing to control all of the towns on the map. To win, you need to capture every town on the map. The more towns under your control, the more allied ships will spawn to help you finish the job.
Once you've finished your first combat instance, you can either choose to continue a more peaceful casual game of trading and questing, or maybe try to take over the entire single player world map. At any time, you can invite steam friends into your game, and they can even bring their own custom ship.
The real "meat" of the game in my opinion, is playing on the public servers, which can have hundreds of players populating the world. In the frontier regions, you'll experience particularly insane pvp and pve fleet battles which you can initiate simply by sailing into another faction's region and clicking a button. Pvp is purely optional however, and you can raise a white flag to "opt out" of it if you're not interested in player vs player.
At this point, you've done just about everything you can expect from the game, aside from the extra challenging "heroic" missions that you'll unlock at a higher level.
Pros:
- It's really REALLY fun if you like the sound of large-scale battles with pvp factions and pirate lords.
- Diablo-like loot system where finding "that perfect" new item can be really exciting.
- New abilities and custom builds add exciting strategies to combat as you rise through the ranks.
- A quick message on the global chat, and you'll VERY quickly get invited into multiplayer coop.
- The combat is engaging. Strength in numbers, as well as good sailing usually win out against higher level ships.
- Combat has a perfect level of difficulty. Sinking an enemy ship is just hard enough to feel satisfying.
- The humor is amusing, it's not not uncommon for enemy pirates to shout things like "THE CAPTAINS ON FIRE!!"
- The game doesn't force anything on you. If want to play a more casual trading/questing game, you can.
- The online community, while very competitive in pvp, is friendly and welcoming to new players.
Cons:
- The game is VERY simple. If you're not having fun by the end of your second or third combat instance, the game isn't for you.
- There's not a ton of content. You're either trading commodities, going on quests, or fighting in fleet battles.
- Combat instances can be really tough to do alone, highly recommend playing online.
- There's not a ton of different music tracks.
Summary:
I really, really enjoy this game. It's a bit too simple for some people, but there's something really great about taking part in the massive online battles. I recommend looking up some gameplay footage on Youtube. I do hope this game gets some new content at some point. (Ghost ships? Sea Monsters?)

This game has a great history, better than the previous Life is Strange. I thought that the lack of moving through time would make the game worse, but it made it better, because you know your choice matters.

At first I wasn't interested in this game because it was a different developer and didn't feel all that interested in a Life is Strange prequel but they really nailed it. If you loved Life is Strange you owe it to yourself to play Before the Storm.

What can I say about this game?
On the one hand we have the first two episodes which to me were just as great as Life is Strange. I really enjoyed that the suprernatural elements were really muted and the entire plot is rather mundane, which in my opinion strengthens the characters. Like LiS where the focus was the relationship between Max and Chloe, in BtS the focus is on the relationship between Chloe and Rachel, only this time without the looming threat of an all consuming storm.
As Chloe and Rachel fall in love, you as a player fall in love with them and if you don't wish you never knew about the events of LiS by the end of the Second Episode I don't even know why you're playing this game. And up until this point I can wholeheartedly recommend Life is Strange: Before the Storm.
But then comes the third Episode and everything kinda falls apart. I hope it does not become a common thread of these games that their last episodes disappoint. As I was playing I had the feeling that connective tissue between some scenes was missing and that others felt incomplete. Not to mention that absolute gut wrencher of a post credit scene, which honestly was just cruel and absolutely unwarranted.
Do I recommend it? I don't know. Episode 1 & 2 where beautiful, emotional experiences I wouldn't wanna miss.
Episode 3 felt really rushed and poorly thoughtout. It was lacking in decisions, those fun little backtalk segments and weirdly enough Rachel Amber by comparison. Plus that devestating "post-credits" Scene leaving an overall bad taste in my mouth, which is why I'm leaning towards a "No Recommendation". I didn't expect some kind of happy-retcon ending, but I expected better.

- Context regarding Rachel Amber and the love between them.
- The perfectly well written storyline
- The also perfect soundtrack that makes us company during the Story.
- This could easily be a movie that You are a part of.
- Extensive character depth and building, that respond to your choices.
- Your choises matter in this game.
- Everyone that has experienced loss in life can relate to many of the feelings Chloe has, and therefore the game creates an emotional connection with the Player.
- The tempest scene ( no spoiler ), is one of the best scenes ive seen in a game!

Cons: - Other then the ending, specially the part we are all wondering about regarding the first game, it largely unexplained, offering only half a minute segway into this.
Final review : The creators of Life is Strange: BTS hit again the nail on the head, by delivering a second masterpiece that is successful in connecting with the players, making them cry, laugh, a hurt with the characters and their life stories. For me it hit deep, and it will remain like its Predecessor, one of my top games ive ever played. A definite 10 in my book. Totally worth the buy if you are into sentimental, adventure, singleplayer games.

It forces you to improve with Charon taking your money every time you go through the castle and the amount he takes from you can be reduced should you get enough money in the first place (this is a problem I will get to in a bit) so you can't just get a chest or two, die, then rinse and repeat. I respect this a lot. But the problem with improving is that it's really ♥♥♥♥ing hard to do. Of course, it's SUPPOSED to be hard! It's a rogue-like, I don't want a stupidly easy walk-in-the-park session. But this is way too difficult, and not designed-in-a-good-way difficult, I mean the difficulty is COMPLETELY RANDOM.
And this is where my problems with  the game explode.
Randomness keeps the game fresh, and although this is a good concept, the way this game uses it can be a bit... flawed. The randomized family tree is nice as it sort of gets you doing multiple different play styles, but random enemy placement can, at times, be ABYSMAL. You'll be in such a mad rush to get past a series of traps (Say, a spikey floor and some projectiles shooting downward at you) that you won't have enough time to get close enough to the end to check for an enemy, such as a zombie who only appears when you're literally a foot in front of it, as doing so would get you hit by the trap, causing damage when health is hard to replenish in this game and knocking you into the trap and likely killing you. And  if you don't check for an enemy as you're so focused on avoiding the trap and you DO make it to the end, SURPRISE ZOMBIE OUT OF THE NOWHERE! This can hurt you immensely, and will probably kill you.
There was one placement in an empty treasure room where the room was devoid of all but a few statues and a chest at the end and there was a zombie in the middle to trick people who rush right in there, and I love this placement. It's rather hilarious and well-designed and something you can STRATEGIZE FOR. But the placement I just mentioned before is NOT ideal. Enemies you can't even see will float through the wall and attack you while you're busy trying to kill that one magic attacker that deals so much damage with so many projectiles. This game is more a difficult and stupidly grindy randomized platformer than it is a genuine rogue-like.
Enemy patterns are hard to learn as a result of this constant death and random enemy placement, and this makes it hard to get gold which you need to upgrade yourself in the first place, so it turns into a constant grind of "Am I going to get even DECENTLY kind-ish spawns," getting a couple of chests and then dying a swift death. You only got 600 gold? Well too bad, it already costs over 1000 for most of the practical upgrades! Here, have this upgrade that you CAN buy now and it'll make everything more expensive! The random enemy patterns and room placements make it almost impossible to use proper skill and strategy as it's based mostly on some ridiculous reflexes (and me, having some hand-eye coordination issues this doesn't help one bit) and luck.
But none of this would be so bad if you AUTOMATICALLY TURNED TO FACE AN ENEMY. I might be really close to an enemy and about to attack it, but in a panic I accidently press the other direction to move away first, then attack. Not only does this cause me to miss my attack, but as I'm thinking "oh wait, I need to turn around to hit this guy now," "This guy" will hit me and again, most likely kill me or at least severely wound me so that I'll die a horrendous death in the following room. Compare this to say, the Huntress character from Risk of Rain, where she is designed to kite enemies. Because that game is not a dual-stick game, she automatically turns and faces the nearest enemy to her once she starts shooting with her bow. But in this game, which may I remind you is a rather DELICATE PLATFORMER involving VERY TOUCHY MOVEMENTS PAIRED WITH INSANE REACTIONS, it's really hard to actually hit anything when you're trying oh-so-very hard not to die, but you're gonna die anyway if you don't ♥♥♥♥ing kill the buggers!
So basically, I don't like this game. Whatever. I'll stick to Magicite and Risk of Rain if I want an actual fun rogue-like. Maybe I'll find some better games along the way.

Sent to the ruins of Dubai on a rescue mission captain Walker and his squad find themselves embroiled in a war between the survivors and are forced to take increasingly ruthless and desperate decisions in order to survive. Despite the fact that the promised decisions available to the player are just 3-4, with the rest of the uncomfortable decisions being made for the player, the narrative of the game manages to be particularly haunting as it explores the horrors of war and the damage they can do to the human psyche.
The game isn't particularly deep gameplay wise. It's a standard 3rd person action game with a few tactical elements thrown in. Most battles play virtually the same and it can get a bit repetitive. But thanks to its short length, its gripping story and beautiful setting it manages to remain interesting. The setting does deserve particular mention. The ruins of Dubai are very very beautiful and unique. With all its magnificent buildings and supertall skyscrapers abandoned and in disrepair it creates a thick atmosphere that further stresses how haunting the narrative feels.
I recommend this game. It might not be great, but it is interesting and brief. If on sale it's a definite must. I just can't believe the UAE banned the game for depicting Dubai ruined. If anything the game made me want to visit Dubai one day.

First, when I saw the game on Steam, I wasn't sure if I should buy this game or not. I did a little bit of research, and I saw many reviews and YouTube videos that showed only some aspects the singleplayer game. In this review I will try to answer some of the questions I had when deciding if this game is worth the money.
The game is a sandboxed naval Action-RPG. In essence, ignoring the naval part, it's pretty much Diablo III, but:
- with cool loot;
- with 100+ players multiplay (not 4 like in Diablo III; OK there are instances which are limited to a handful of players, but WoW has this too, and that's a MMO);
- real procedural generated world.
I won't be speaking much about things that you will obviously find in every review or gameplay video you find. With that in mind, here are a few things I wanted to know about the game before the buy, and couldn't find a fast answer to:
-
You create a user name that has an unique ID (I guess) associated with it. The user information is saved locally on disk (as a backup), and also on Steam Cloud, so basically, you can never lose your progress.
-
When you log to a server, or even your own game instance, that can be shared with your friends, you will use the same user name already created by you. Your progress will be saved on Steam Cloud. You can switch to any number of servers you want, you will still have the same XP and loot as before.
-
The servers are independent, you can make one of your own, the developer shared all the info you need to create a dedicated server on the community forum. Each server is not related to another, and all your progress, as mentioned before, is saved on the Steam Cloud. Each server can be configured to have admins. Admins can ban players for cheating or for breaking any of the rules that may govern the server. The ban is server-based (it's an important factor, as I though cheaters could be banned forever from any servers, but there is no Steam ID ban unfortunately).
-
Yes, they are, and the people using them can mess up your fun a little bit, but there are ways to get pass these issues:
1. The world maps has many zones, so one cheater can't being all the zones;
2. The admin can ban the cheater;
3. One night, many servers were hacked and some players got respawned a few times and levelled up fro 100+ levels, and some wanted to go through that levelling process doing trading quests, killing pirates, capturing zones from other factions (yes, there are a few factions, you can find all about it all over the Net) or by doing combat instances with other people. In this case, you could revert using your local backup (everything is documented on the community forum).
Final words on cheating: there will always be people which will try to cheat or hack, the important thing is that, in this game, those people are rare, and it can be dealt with them.
-
There were in the past. Most bugs that appear these days don't affect your progress, but may affect some actions you do in an area; usually there is a workaround. The important thing is that the developer is very involved into this project, and replies to most of the feedback he receives. He didn't abandon the game like others do with their game.
I played the game in singleplayer mode for the first 10 levels. It was nice, but I could feel like it will get boring soon. I jumped into a multiplayer Internet server, and never look back on singleplay.
In the multyplayer mode, players chose different factions and can conquer areas of the map controlled by others or the pirates. So the areas change all the time, and may not be the same from your last login. Also, some servers do resets, which may change the way the worlds look. You can also do multiplay combat instances where you coop with others to remove all the pirates on the map, get the loot, level up, get new cool items and spend points on actions. You can also get flags that you can use to switch factions (there is even a pirate flag, Arr!!). There are many of things you can do to keep you entertain for a couple of hours or more each day, I won't spoil your experience by talking more about them.
Probably, there is a point in time where you can say you are bored, but I didn't find it yet. So, YES! For me, THIS GAME IS PRETTY FUN! And for ~13 euros / 15$, it's one of the best investment in a game I ever made.

Why I bought the game:
After having read several positive reviews on the game (in which many comparisons are made to my old favorite pirate game: Sid Meier's Pirates) I decided to give this game a go hoping it would be all the reviews said it would be. The game is often described as Sid Meier's Pirates without the sword fighting bit.... Sadly this aint so. Other then a Pirate theme and the same isometric perspective this game has nothing in common with the old classic. Any comparisons to the the old classic are therefore misleading.
The game looks great but in its current state offers little content other then grinding for loot and xp for leveling, so I very soon grew bored with the game.
Pro's:
- Great graphics and an intuitive UI
- dynamic map / world builder when starting a game
- ship customization offers a nice touch
Con's:
- Its basically just a mindless grinding game.
- no gameplay depth whatsoever, quests and and trading are pritty much pointless side activities to the main grinding and offer no challenge.
- no land or tactical combat whist capturing cities
- no crew morale/ ship capture or ship loadout options
Although the game has great potential to become a worthy successor to the old classics: Pirates, the game in it's current state is anything but. So if you're looking to relive the Pirates experience, i'dd suggest to buy the original and put this game on interesting games to follow.

Disclaimer: I'm a kicstarter backer and I was able to play this game early. I completed my first playthrough on December 19th. There are no spoilers in this review.
I have been a long time fan of the Shantae series, the unique charm of the protagonist combined with the world the stories are set in made it for a fun and unique experience every time. The series falls into what qualifies as a Metroidvania. All games encourage backtracking and exploration as you gain more powers and mobility, the rewards being more story and of course, a higher completion. To my knowledge the latest two games even have multiple endings determined by your completion rate.
Some history:
---------------
The first game in the series called "Shantae" came out late in the Game Boy Color's life (2002) and was a superbly animated game for the time. In my opinion it is also the most difficult game in the series so far as the first hour or two before you gain more abilities can be brutal. In this game, Shantae was set out to stop her ever present rival, the pirate called Risky Boots and her horde of Tinkerbats. The physical version of this game is quite rare nowadays. Thankfully, if you own a (New) 2/3DS/XL you can play this game via Virtual Console.
The second game "Risky's Revenge" came out much later (2010) for the DS/DSi and was a worthy follow up that saw Shantae once again facing off against Risky Boots as the pirate lady sought revenge for the events in the first game. This game is still available for the DS series of portables and a PC version has been released as well, available right here on Steam.
The third game came out in 2014 and is called "Pirate's Curse". This is the first game in the series to provide some voice acting, but also features a plot where Risky Boots seeks Shantae's help in defeating a foe more dangerous than her. Nevertheless I think this is the best game in the series so far. This game came out on a lot of platforms, including PC. The 3DS version has some nice depth effects as well.
----------------
Does it mean that Half-Genie Hero is an inferior game? Not at all! From a personal perspective I think Pirate's Curse has a better story and higher stakes (although even that could be argued as there is a lot at stake in HGH too, plot wise). But the gameplay, graphics and music are superb as expected from the experienced team at WayForward as well as the designs of Matt and Erin Bozon (who created Shantae) and the music of my favourite games musician, Jake "Virt" Kaufman.
That said, in HGH, Shantae is once again out to face off against Risky Boots who seeks to abuse the knowledge she gained during "Pirate's Curse".  The controls are good and the storytelling is funny in the right places. Transformation magic returns once more (it was absent in "Pirate's Curse") but has been simplified to speed up game play.
If you wonder if you should play all games in chronological order...that depends on you! While each game can be played on its own without knowing the earlier stories, there are some small nods here and there to events from previous games. Even so, HGH makes sure you are introduced to each character and immediately know what they are like.
There were some problems in the version I played and I expect they will get ironed out after the game is released tomorrow. While not breaking, some powers can be exploited to make sections of the game extremely trivial. If you happen to find such a way, consider challenging yourself!
All in all, it took me the listed time as of this review (11.7) hours to finish the game first time through. I had to peruse some youtube videos to find some items I missed, but the game does clue you in . I recommend talking to everyone after each plot event!
-----------------
TL;DR: Great game, as polished as expected from the creators. Personally I think the story in the previous game was better, but that's my opinion and doesn't detract from the gameplay enjoyment.

Shantae: 1/2 Genie Hero is exactly what it was initially intended to be: a shined and polished Shantae title that offers a fourth helping of exactly what made the previous titles so well-loved. While it still has a lot of growing to do to live up to everything WayForward has promised (in the form of DLC and other bonuses), the core game is ret-2-go, and for the most part, it's pretty wonderful.
As with previous installments, Shantae: 1/2 Genie Hero follows a policy of "if it ain't broke, don't fix it," retaining the same core gameplay mechanics it's always had while further refining the way extras like items and transformations work.
As always, Shantae runs, jumps, and attacks enemies with her hair, exploring (and occasionally backtracking through) five main worlds, each chock full of secrets and surprises, and as with the first two titles, earns (or discovers) new transformations that enable her to navigate her world in different ways.
While the immediate predecessor (The Pirate's Curse) temporarily did away with transformations in favor of new abilities that blended seamlessly with Shantae's standard controls, reverting to the transformation mechanic is handled tastefully. Shantae can now choose from a palette of up to 12 "dances," which are accessed via a single button press and subsequent single directional command, enabling Shantae to transform in and out of forms hastily to suit the occasion. Many of these dances are optional, hidden, or available for purchase, and a few are actually mutually exclusive- players must decide if they'd rather hold onto, say, a convenient teleportation dance, or a form that spits out free money. Players are free to change their mind on these choices, but only via trade with the merchant who sells said optional dances.
While a few of these forms are combat-capable (or can be made so via hidden upgrades), few if any are ever more viable for combat than Shantae's base form. Though Shantae can no longer pick up hand-to-hand secret techniques or upgrade her arsenal with pirate weaponry, her trusty battle-ponytail can be upgraded as in previous titles do deal quite a bit of damage. If this seems duller than integrating projectiles and blades into your fighting style, fear not. Series mainstay items like the Pike Ball and Storm Puff have been given a very welcome upgrade- rather than consumables to be purchased and used at the player's discretion, these magic items now manifest as permanent upgradeable skills in Shantae's arsenal, swapped out as sub-weapons and usable for as long as Shantae has the magic power to deploy them (think Mega Man). Thus, players can now hurl flames and thunderbolts at will, or protect themselves with barriers and damaging satellites. While not quite as seamless as the previous title's pirate powers, this is a fun system that puts the series' classic quirky weapons on full glorious display.
This is largely a welcome change, but I couldn't help but notice that sometimes the extra powers made things *too* easy. The fully upgraded bubble shield, for example, makes Shantae completely invincible for as long as she has magic remaining. This synergizes very well with items that expand Shantae's mana pool, to the point that by the game's final challenge, I found I was able to remain invincible indefinitely. I'm not sure if this was an oversight or simply poor judgment, but I hope to see it fixed in the near future- I'm not opposed to letting players enjoy some casual godmoding, but I feel like offering it to players just before the last boss is in poor taste.
Indeed, the difficulty of the game is perhaps its weakest attribute. While the game has a few sections that new players are very likely to need to repeat again and again (an aspect soothed tremendously by the introduction of frequent autosaves), I often found myself sufficiently geared and upgraded to pass most challenges on my first try, not from skill, but from simply having so many health items and defensive upgrades at my disposal. The game does offer players the choice to turn off any specific upgrade at will (which is, honestly, a fantastic option to provide), but offers no real incentive to do so- after facing the odd gauntlet of instant death two or three times, I falsely presumed the rest of the game would match that challenge and prepared accordingly, only to watch the rest of the game crumble before my seemingly-bottomles well of force fields and monster steaks, and before I knew it, it was over.
After three years in development, I'm a little surprised. True, the worlds are enormous and the powers vast, but five main worlds? Just five? I confess I'm a bit disappointed by the shortness. I completed this game with 100% progress in exactly the same amount of time as I took to complete the previous title. DLC promises new levels and modes, such as the ability to play as the other main characters in their own separate stories, and as much as I did truly and consistently enjoy my first playthrough as Shantae, I do welcome the chance to do it all again differently. Still, until those new modes arrive, I must say, the game feels a little scant for all the work that's clearly gone into it.
And to speak of that work- my goodness is this game ever gorgeous. The characters are presented as hand-drawn faithful recreations of their old sprites, and if one recalls just how fluidly-animated those sprites were, one can correctly assume the degree to which this title absolutely gushes charm. The visual style of lively 2D characters against lovingly-rendered 3D backdrops works marvelously here, and unlike other 2.5D titles there's no question of where obstacles begin and end.  Shantae: Half Genie Hero is without a doubt the tightest 2.5D game I've yet experienced.
As for the story, it's a bit less compelling than its immediate predecessor, but every bit as hilarious. Shantae has really found its essence in humor and awkard charm- I caught myself laughing out loud once or twice, and my heart lept to see certain characters reappear. Still, while I was never bored by the dialogue or story, I don't feel that this game has yet managed to outdo itself in terms of weaving a truly epic narrative. Pirate's Curse opened the characters up to a measure of depth not previously seen- we saw a powerless Shantae, a vulnerable Risky, a lost Rottytops, a successful Bolo and a terminally misfortunate Sky. None of this is present in Shantae's latest adventure, and while it does tell a pleasantly lighthearted story, we've seen WayForward do better.
After so much time in development, Shantae: 1/2 Genie Hero feels solid, if surprisingly sparse, and is over long before it has a chance to wear out its welcome. With the promise of expansive DLC on the horizon, I feel hopeful that WayForward will gradually flesh this game out into the epic adventure we imagined it becoming. Perhaps future stories will introduce us to new sides of beloved characters, offer us the chance to approach the world from a new perspective, or simply expand upon an already successful formula. For now, though, it's another short yet fantastic romp through Sequin Land, and well worth the price of admission.

Cute characters and light-hearted humor elevate this tiny indie gem of a game.
True to the series roots, Shantae combines a liberal amount of classic Megaman-esque run and jump platforming with a bit of exploration and backtracking ala Castlevania/Metroid. As you beat bosses and explore the mostly linear levels, you will earn upgrades to open up new pathways through levels and discover secrets in previously completed areas.
While relatively small in scale, it matches the length of the previous installments in the franchise (about 6 hours for my first time to 100%) and certainly lives up to the legacy of its lavishly illustrated predecessors, trading in it's former pixel art for hand animated characters and brightly painted textures. Level design is clean and concise, making up for a lack of quantity with a density of quality content for the price. This game maintains the series focus on light-hearted humor and cute characters, with a strong soundtrack to tie the experience together.
Some upgrades curiously seem superficial and under utilized in the level design (i.e. the Bat Sonar ability is only use-able in one side room and the room can still be navigated using visual cues from other light sources), but most content in the game is well utilized throughout the game.
The storyline feels much more segmented than previous titles, probably due to the fact that each level was a different "stretch goal" when the game was being kickstarted. This makes the plotline and characters feel much more episodic and less developed than previous entries (especially comparing it to Pirate's Curse), but overall tone maintains a sort of "Saturday morning cartoon" feel that remains consistent across the entire game.

If you haven't played the original series yet, just stop reading this and play it first. You can come back later and feel glad you have another chance of visiting Arcadia Bay once again with the exact atmosphere and familiar characters that Deck Nine have taken such great efforts to recreate.
I know that the original Life is Strange has gotten a lot of flaks from those who have such weird ideas, like that video games are all about taking up challenges and getting achievements, or that it's somehow more becoming of a man to be utterly incapable of feeling emotions or sympathizing with any fictional character unless he's some badass hero, and so on.
I understand that if you've purchased this game, there's little chance that you actually fall into that category. However, I have to warn you that this game relies even more on your ability to appreciate such subtler and more intimate forms of emotions and a relationship between more or less flawed, angsty characters than the original game did - there's no mystery to solve, no supernatural powers. All you have is an impetuous and intense relationship between two teenage girls and how they deal with a loss, but depicted in such a depth and subtlety that few other games have tackled before.
The pacing and direction seem to have been improved compared to the original series, which means in place of drawn out fetch quests or even a stealth sequence you can expect more well directed and memorable scenes, like a truly magical moment during a performance of Shakespeare's play.
Storywise, the only complaint I have is that the last few minutes of the final episode progresses rather abruptly, relying on a bit of 'Deus Ex Machina' element to resolve a crisis which leads to the ending sequence in a rather forced manner. And even though I felt the final cut scene to be a quite appropriate one to bridge the two series, it might upset some people, depending on what they expected from the prequel.
As a big fan of the franchise, I'm so glad to have purchased and played this game, and feel grateful that Deck Nine has come forward to take such a tremendous task to continue the story of Life is Strange.
It's not hard to imagine how difficult it must be to build upon such a masterpiece with a huge established fan base, especially when the original game was developed by a different company with different set of voice actors. I had my own reservations when I first heard about the attempt, but the dedication and love the developers have shown to the franchise, and such a great performance from Rhianna DeVries, the voice actress for new Chloe, have soon erased any doubts from me.
Granted, I'm not saying that Before the Storm is superior to Life is Strange in every aspects. It does not compete with, or contradicts but builds upon the established characters, atmosphere, plots of the original series, and I believe that's what a well made prequel is supposed to do which this game exactly delivers.

I haven't written a little thing on Rogue Legacy yet?
Okay.
Let me summarize the gameplay for you. It's fun, by the way.
You go into a castle. You get gold. That's pretty much the only goal. Just get that dank cash. Then die, eventually! Then you pick a new hero, with a few randomly selected disabilities (which aren't always a negative) and a randomly selected class based on what you've unlocked, and then do it all again (after spending that hard earned gold on upgrades, stat boosts, equipment, etc...)
It's a simple, but very challenging game. And one where you need to be able to adapt readily to your new disabilities and class. Playing as Hokage can make the game insanely easy once you nail down dodging as a super fast, hard-hitting glass cannon of a ninja. Then you have to play as a Lich. See, you have to adapt right then and there to your new abilities.
Dodging is key. Learning to get out of the way of every single attack that comes your way is the big challenge of this game. You generally will not have enough health to take many hits, and health pickups can either be common or won't ever drop, depending on your luck, so sometimes you'll have to make it through rooms at a time if you screw up here or there.
Like Castlevania, you get one spell. And that's your spell. You use mana to cast this spell. It's not even that useful of a spell, most of the time, but it can come in handy at times - your sword is going to be your primary weapon.
Mastering the tight controls and your melee weapon in a game where touching any enemy will deal significant damage to you is the key to success.

I must say after playing the Hunter Primal I was very reluctant to buy this game...as a matter of fact it took me a long time to even consider trying it but I must say this game is just great.
