I like turn based RPG or RPG in general. I like Shin Megami Tensei (SMT) games and also Touhou series. It should be out of the question that Undertale, a game that is basically a fusion of SMT and Touhou, will be right in my alley. However, after I played this game, I would not recommend it for anyone with the same interest as me.
This game rely on the deconstruction/subversion of the genre of RPG games. The problem is that it heavily rely too much on this, to the point that if you remove all the subversions, it will left behind the most generic premise. You play as a human who are stuck in monster world, now you have to go back to your world by adventuring the monster world. If you have played any fantasy RPG game, then you have played this premise many times before.
Next, you get the bullet curtain/bullet hell battle system that lacks of the depth of actual bullet hell mechanics. All you do is dodging the pattern that are thrown at you. There is no bomb, no focus/slow down, no dash, and no way to destroy bullets. Dodging the pattern is not even challenging, unless it is boss battle because it often ends too quickly.
Lastly, this is the biggest problem that I have with this game; how it handled the Meta and 4th wall breaking joke/content. A surprise element has a big role in presenting a meta and 4th wall breaking joke. If you plan to do it more than once, then you have to increase the scale from the first meta presentation. Unfortunately this game did not, it repeats meta joke several times, resulting it get stale very quickly. By the 2-4 hours mark, all the meta presentations come off as annoying and obnoxious. Not to mention, the condescending “got ya” and “didn’t see that coming, did ya?” attitude that the game present after the meta content. It is just appaling if you have seen/guessed what the game is going for.
I beat the game and it expected me to do a second run, I tried, and that made me dislike the game even more. I cannot get past all the 4th wall breaking skeleton puns the second time, I do not want to re-experience all the stale meta content again. Thank you for making me realize how much I hate meta and 4th wall joke.
In conclusion, Undertale tried to mix many game mechanics and elements with the goal to create a diversion in mind. I do not think it worked so I will suggest games that do each of those elements better than Undertale.
- If you like being able to take side in the plot, making a choice that result in endings that contrasts each other, and  being able to negotiate with enemies, play Shin Megami Tensei games
- If you are looking for a proper bullet hell battle system, get Furi or Touhou games.
- If you want a game that presents meta and 4th wall breaking content so much better than what Undertale can dream of, experience Nier: Automata.

Original Life is Strange absolutely caught me off guard by how freaking amazing it was. Does Before the Storm live up to it's crazy high standard? For the most part, yes.
This game is just as beautiful as the original game in terms of style, atmosphere and storytelling - and trust me, it will change the way you approach original game quite a bit, especially when it comes to Chloe and Rachel. It gives original game a bit more emotional weight - yes, that's right, original LiS will be even more thrilling to play through once you know this origins story. I would also love to give props to developers for technical direction - they switched to Unity and the game looks almost just as good, even better in some aspects (way better facial expressions and lip movements), and runs waaaaaaaay better, especially on low-spec hardware.
However, I belive this game falls short in certain aspects, at least when compared to previous game:
1. Three main-story episodes simply isn't enough, the first two work mostly as introduction and character developing, and the last one is kinda meh for the most part, and then out of nowhere drops a few heavy moments on you. Whilst in original game you were investigating and working stuff out, in BtS you don't really get to do any of it, the game just kinda drops big story twist bombs out of nowhere. I really wish devs just dropped the idea of bonus episode with Max and developed 4 main-story episodes instead.
2. Developers advertised Chloe's banter minigame as if it is good enough replacement for Max's powers from the original game - it really isn't. And it seems like developers themselves realized that as in third episode there was only one instance when it was being used (unless I missed some other dialogue).
3. While the game expanded on many characters of the franchise, it didn't really give us as many main-story related answers as I was expecting from it. I don't want to spoil anything from either game, so I won't go into specifics... but yeah, I think the game could have done a bit better job at this.

Three favorite parts of the game:

3. Ending is intense and will hit you even harder if you know what happened in original LiS.
So in conclusion - not as good as original game, but since original LiS is 10/10 material... there's no shame in that. Solid 8/10 and if you consider yourself a big fan, it's even higher, hitting the 9/10 territory.

I want to start off by saying this is in my opinion one of the best games that I've played in the last couple of years.
It does not take a long time to get used to the gameplay, it's mostly self-explanatory and the most important parts get explained at the beginning when you start a new game.
The graphics are stunning and I am able to run it at smooth 60fps at 1080p (MSI GTX 980, i5 4690K). The two available maps are huge (although I have only played in "Hirschfelden" so far, but I guess the other one is equal in size) and there is a third map available for DLC (8$ should totally be worth it).
As for the hunting itself I am not in a position to tell if it is really realistic since I have never hunted animals before, but from what I can tell it looks to be very life-like with very precise hitboxes for the animals. The in-game store has a lot of different weapons to offer, from bows over shotguns, handguns and riffles, as well as the corresponding types of ammunition. Also available in the shop are different kind of lures, binoculars and additional backpacks.The rating system for kills seems to be pretty solid and it is nice that one is able to see where they hit their prey, although the colors seem to be a bit too bright sometimes which makes it hard to see where exactly you hit.
You get provided with a lot of different questing lines, each one getting a bit more difficult over time.
There is also two additional DLCs, one for tents and one for vehicles, which seem to be worth it for 4$ each if you do not want to walk for long times.
I do not have much in terms of critique, one of the main points being that the game sometimes can be a bit buggy. I have had wounded animals disappear right in front of me on different occasions, which can be frustrating because your "consecutive harvest" score will again start at 0%. I have also noticed weapons, binoculars and lures not being displayed and usable, unless fast travelling to the next outpost to fix it.
I hope I have touched a bit of every aspect of this game with this review. If you would ask me I would give it a solid  9 out of 10 and could only recommend to anyone asking me.

Right, so...Windward. *Deep Breath* Where to start?
Ah, right. Let's get this review rolling by getting a few things out of the way from the git-go.
1) This game is billed as an adventure-sandbox title.
2) This game relies upon repetitive, simple tasks.
3) This game has some beautiful scenery and aesthetics.
Okay, with that out of the way, you're going to fall into one of two camps. Those camps are the 'I love this game!' and the 'I tried to like this game and I ended up wasting a handful of hours trying to like this game,' And that's fine. You have your tastes and your preferences. I'll be writing this review from the aspect of the latter camp, having tried to be a member of the former camp.
What Windward tries and (arguably) fails to present you with is an in-depth naval combat/economy simulation, top-down with nice graphical appeal. Where it fails is the 'in-depth' aspect with its 'bounce your ship back and forth between towns for hours' mentality, you may begin to ponder the value of your time. Unfortunately, because of this, it's not a game that I would say is fun if you want to just 'jump in for a few minutes' but instead is probably a far more playable game from the sphere of 'play a few hours at a time and save your game progress'.
Each and every faction tries to offer a special ability or focus that, after the first couple of hours, you don't even really think about anymore. And that is because each faction does the same things, with the same ships, but with one of four different color options. In the end, you may decide to restart simply because you want to play as your preferred color rather than for any 'faction specialty' reasons. In fact, one of my biggest problems with this game is that your sail embroidery is stuck as the color of your team. Frankly, that just pisses me off.
All this being said, I did play the game and I may continue to play it, and since I work a decent job the price tag isn't a deal-breaker either (especially on sale!).
But let me bring up another point, the game's aesthetics; they're pretty damn cool. I like the wind and sunlight effects. I like the way my sails creak and the mast groans and the wind buffets my ship around. That's cool stuff right there, and that little detail here and that other little detail there--that is what makes me want to play this game, and makes my little voice in the back of my head say, 'This game sure is neat--but we've been bouncing back and forth in this same square block of the map for hours now...'
Trust me. It'll happen, if you're any sort of gamer with an adult life and an adult schedule.
Interestingly enough about the 'sandbox' descriptor...is it? I mean it's got that basic random-map-generator thing right? But what does it honestly matter, when you're going to essentially be setting up some variety of chess board squares, slowly trying to build up the first block so you can move to a second block and begin again, grinding and bouncing around inside the map block of various islands/waterways in an attempt to stymie the flow of rabbit-like spawning pirate ships. (Oh god, the pirate ships...)
The game seems to aim big. It's got a lot of polish. But it's shots fall short of their target. In fact, now that I think about it...
...the game designer(s) have a lot in common with the in-game crew of my Sloop-O-War.

...Uhm, oh. Hi there! You are probably looking for a review, right? Well, then:
Before buying a game I usually look for gameplay videos first. Trailers are great to convey the story, but they often don´t say much about the in-game experience. Luckily, the store page already featured a gameplay video with the Dev explaining.
This game has a lot of potential to become a large MMO, as it is very unique and currently the only one of this particular genre. The scaling of players (scaling lower players up in higher-lvl areas, and higher players down in lower areas) allows for co-op play without restrictions, e.g. in combat-instances.
I´d tag this game as RPG/Action/Strategy/Tower-defense. To get an in-game experience I recommend watching the gameplay video.
You control a ship, sailing on shallow waters around chains of islands, fighting pirates, questing or trading. When starting you can choose any of four factions, each with its own benefits and penalties. The gameplay can be whatever you like it to be - peaceful questing and trading, PvE, or even PvP. You can play either alone, starting your own instance with nobody able to enter except by invite, or play on the regular map where you will cross paths with other players.
As you progress and level up, you will find better loot, more gold, buy better ships, equip better gear/crew/captains. You can also join more factions, one unlocking at level 50, another at 150, as well as the option to join the pirates.
The large server-map consists of multiple area-maps, with each having different difficulties the further they are to the factions spawn point. Once you reach a certain level, you will have outgrown the regular map content. To progress further you will have to join or create yourself an instance.
Instances are private area-maps that are generated according to your level. Nobody can enter your instance unless invited by you. You can also team up with others and try to finish a heroic (much harder) instance, which will give you much better loot.
The game can be played in single player, local co-op, internet multiplayer. You can also host games yourself, available in the online serverlist. The game is moddable.
The only problematic thing about this game is: It is terribly addictive.
Valiant: Combat
Consulate: Trader
Sojourn: Explorer
Exchange: All-rounder
Start by doing quests. Trade as soon as you have enough gold. Buying every ship is very expensive, check which one you want. Team up and join instances for better loot.

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Ok Mad Max... what do we get here?
(TL;DR below)
Well it's an Openworld Singleplayer Action Adventure, set in a postapocalyptic World playing as Mad Max.
So what do we do?
The game is focused on customizable cars, customizable Max and lots of "Sidequests", and the Game starts like this:
You find yourself in a desert and some scrap building/forts here and there, you go from area to area kill, destroy and loot everything. Sometimes you do some actual Sidequests or do the Mainquest or just roam around in your car and kill people.
All in all sounds like a good and solid game right?
Yes well while it is solid you'll soon notice that the game is way too solid. You'll just find yourself roaming in the big, beautiful, wide and monotonous desert to get an upgrade for your car or for Max. And the upgrades aren't even that great it's just a bit more damage here a bit more defense there. it's not like these upgrades enable anything gamechanging except for the harpoon and thunder cap but you'll just get these 2 relatively early anyway. Also if you have ever played a WB game before you might notice that the "on-foot-fight-mechanics" have a certain similarity with other games from WB. I'm not saying that the fight mechanics in itself are bad but people who played lots of other games from WB might just get bored...
Furthermore there are no checkpoints, when you die you respawn in a stronghold and from there you can just kill,destroy and loot again.
TL;DR
The game does make fun... for 15-20 hours imo then it just gets repititive, dull and idunno slouchy?
I recommend this game for people who like to drive customizable cars with weapons and WB fans, else well invest your money in something else then I guess...

Spec Ops: The Line is the hidden gem of 2012. FTL would be my "hidden gem," but after the whole massive Kickstarter success thing, it was obvious FTL was going to be good in my point of view. Honestly, I used to play Call of Duty and Halo. There. I said it. However, after Black Ops 1, I quit the Call of Duty series and haven't played any of the games since MW3. Halo Reach was the Halo that I played the most, and was the only Halo game (Halo 3 and Wars were good though) that I loved and played often. However, above all of these games, Spec Ops: The Line has one of the best stories of all time. It isn't like Call of Duty how you're fighting as some American soldier running around solo armed to the teeth with weapons and murdering terrorists and in the end "saving the world." Not at all. Some people believe there are "good guys" and "bad guys," but this game is solid evidence that war is just opinions being decided to the death, sometimes costing one's sanity, social health, emotional health, and physical health. Spec Ops: The Line proves war in no way is enjoyable, cool, or humorous in any kind of way. War is horrific, and this game is enough to prove that.
The visuals are absolutely outstanding. The environments look beautiful, and the atmosphere is bright on the outside, but dark and horrific on the inside. The characters look amazing, and it's rare you can actually see the sweat of a character in the middle of combat. This game is able to do that. If I were to compare these visuals to The Last of Us, Spec Ops: The Line would win by a mile. These graphics are extremely realistic, but the only con to this is that the facial animations can look weird. For example, when Walker is talking to Lugo or Adams when it isn't a cutscene, it looks like he's gaping every time, like he's shocked at everything for some reason. During cutscenes though, Walker looks fine and doesn't gape like that when he speaks.
The gameplay is suprisingly the weak point to the game. Although this game is a shooter, Spec Ops is more for people who want a story based game, rather than a gameplay based one. The AI is suicidally bad and the difficulty spikes at times and the awful gunplay ruins it even more. My squadmates keep bumping into me and I die, one enemy shot 3 RPG rockets in a row without reloading for some reason (He had an RPG, I saw him with the weapon, I swear!) and the AI prefer running toward me like overconfident barbarians. However, the game understands the meaning of "limited" unlike other games *cough* Call of Duty *cough* *cough* and makes ammo a bit more difficult to get, so that's something few games did that aren't in the zombie survival genre.
The story is the reason Spec Ops is highly praised. Like I said before, it proves that war is a terrible thing and (quoted from Fallout 3) "never changes." Lugo, Adams, and Walker's bond with each other was strong, like they were old friends, then all of a sudden, Lugo and Adams part away from Walker, realizing that he's gone insane, but Adams is still merely following orders, while Lugo wants to make a stand. You realize that Walker is in no way a hero, but calling him a villain is illogical. The plot twist around the midst of the game was amazing and blew my mind. I'm going to do another quote, but this time from one of my favorite songs: "This ain't no place for no hero, this ain't no place for no- better man, this ain't no place for no hero, to call home." -"Short Change Hero" by The Heavy. It perfectly describes the story, mixed with the atmosphere, and how the characters develop over time in the destroyed and now insane city of Dubai. I assure you, this game has one of the finest stories in gaming. It seems like 2012 was the year for gaming, since games like this and The Walking Dead came out and wowed us with their storytelling. In the end, the story for this game is simply outstanding.
The audio is also amazing for this game. The voice actors did an amazing job with their roles, and all showed personality. They  weren't androids and were kind of like the Mass Effect characters, in a way you grow attached to them because they feel like real, breathing humans. But you still gotta hate Walker. Then, hate yourself while you're at it for doing all the harsh decisions. Name me a few other games that truly make you want to hate yourself that much. The music is similar to those found in a zombie apocalypse game, like the recent ones State of Decay and The Last of Us. It's usually a guitar backed up by a few other instruments or the guitar playing solo. It sounds beautiful and fits in perfectly. The audio in this game is some of the finest in recent gaming.
It's a bit more difficult to provide replayability to a game like this, unfortunately. However, you could go back and get all the endings. The multiplayer is pretty dead, so I haven't had any chance to try it yet. Either way, I suppose the replayability in this game is determinant.
In conclusion, Spec Ops: The Line proves war is terrifying and that it's not fun at all. However, the horrible gameplay holds it down significantly, along with a dead multiplayer and the jaw drops that happen when Walker talks while playing (Not in a cutscene) hold it back. Either way, Spec Ops: The Line is a must have for any story based game buyer. I highly recommend this gem.

After gaining almost 1,200 hours on the game, I'm finally ready to write a review on it. When I first played the game back in legacy, the game was great for the time and still a classic today. Now with the work from the undisputed great developers in the Facepunch team, the game recieves weekly updates and content wise, continues to flourish. By no means do I ignore the issues the game has, but in my experience these can be overlooked by the amazing things you can achieve regardless.
+Great concept for a survival game with an amazing variety in game styles through different servers
+Spectacular graphics
+A great PvE and PvP System which could be tweaked but regardless is extremely fun
+Community driven developers who take account of requests and complaints in every update they release
+Great workshop content fueled by a creative community
+The forced wipes keep the game fresh and refresh server populations very well
-Some concepts within the game remain unbalanced (for example the high quality metal costs and large crafting times)
-The community is rather toxic and unfriendly, especially to new players, but obviously that's something you'll get on any game.
-Optimization remains an issue for many users with lower end PC's, work is being done to combat this but it's by no means swift.
-The process of server creation is rather tricky and takes an element of skill to manage effectively.
All in all, the game itself is great and considering it's an Early Access Game, you couldn't ask for more. I would encourage you to take a chance and try it out for yourself. Just keep in mind that no game is easy at first, and you may want to consider watching a few YouTube tutorials or videos to get yourself the boost of knowledge at the start. Another important thing to consider is your PC, make sure you're able to run the game before you complain you cannot. The minimum system requirements are stated but these in my opinion should be raised as with those, you'd be seeing extremely low FPS.

As a huge fan of Uncharted Waters, Sid Meyer's Pirates, etc., I really wanted to like this game.  I had fun for the first few hours, but then I hit a wall where it was obvious that a boring and repetitive grind was the only way forward.
I went for a trading-based character to start, but trading in this game is too limited to be a viable strategy as far as I can see. Not only do the first AND second ship only have 2 cargo slots, with profit on all deliveries on the level of 20-100 gold (for comparison, the first ship with THREE cargo spaces costs 9,964 gold), quests take cargo space.  That's right, if you take a quest to kill a pirate, it takes one of your two cargo slots.
Trade routes are also impossible to create, because in order to sell something, you have to find a port that wants one, and selling it may erase the demand altogether.  I ended up with a piece of cargo within the first hour I simply could not sell because no port would buy it any more.  I then had to play with only ONE cargo/quest slot until I died or threw away a piece of cargo equivalent to a third of my wealth.
After venturing out a bit more, it became obvious that combat specs were really the way to go.  I respecced into combat abilities and upgraded my ship the best I could and went to town conquering the next two maps, which was pretty fun.  I still don't have enough money to buy the next ship, though, and the fourth map is beyond my level so I am having to rely on NPCs to fight my battles and hope I get some gold and xp... or else I'm going to have to go back to trading/questing for 20-90 gold at a time until I can upgrade enough to win a fight on my own again.  If the grind is this bad at the beginning of the game, I can't imagine how bad it is in late game.
There are things that are promising about this game, but it feels as if the devs thought that a grind was a substitute for content.  Maybe it is more fun in multiplayer, but for single player I can't recommend it.

I like the game, so you're probably wondering why I can't recommend it. It's pretty simple. It's very repetitive, grindy and trying to capture zones from the AI without help is like a re-enactment of the first landing on the bug planet in Starship Troopers. Also, loot is only really obtained via combat, specifically farming/grinding your butt off. Some loot is so ridiculously over-powered that you will be blown to bits in no time flat in PVP even if you manage to get your hands on the two most powerful ships in the game (outside the special design ship). That brings me to the other sore point: PVP itself.
If you play on a public server, you can be attacked even if you have the no-PVP special item (which you don't start with, by the way, you need to find it) by players who farm up the Black Flag that lets them join the Pirate faction. You are not safe anywhere from these people. These people have joined "instances" I've been in and proceeded to farm everyone in it driving everyone else out. They can also sail into newbie zones with near impunity killing everyone in sight. The reason is because of the item imbalances and the fact that the insane farming needed (I'm told) to get the special item that lets them join the Pirate faction in the first place has given these people pretty much every skill unlock, tons of gold, every ship they want and probably Legendary quality everything. It's like in World of Warcraft, having a person in full top-tier PVP epics walking into a newbie starting zone and start slaughtering except there are no NPC guards to worry about.
Not really much fun to be fodder for the e-peens of angry adolescents in a game where PVP is supposed to be consensual if you have the item that gives you that option. I watched for months and months on end, as bugs were ignored throughout repeated patch cycles, only to see some new pistol or new hat added. It puzzled me for quite a while, I wondered why they had the time to be coding hats when there were so many game-breaking bugs going unattended. Then I realized the reason. I've already paid for it. The devs don't really need to care if I'm happy or continue to play. But new hats and guns trucks and towns and whatnot being added all the time might entice some new guy to pay up more than random bug fixes he hasn't even experienced. There's no monthly fee for me to pay, no DLC to get my money flowing their direction. As far as the devs are concerned, once I've bought the game, I do nothing more for them. There's zero reason for them to do anything in the way of veteran player retention. And it showed, month after month, bugs left completely and totally ignored.
So at that point, I decided if the devs don't really care if I keep playing, maybe I just don't need to keep playing. I wouldn't suggest you start playing either. For a game with such potential, development has been haphazard enough to be a massive disappointment. Maybe some or most of those bugs have been handled now, I can't really be bothered to check.

Let me start with the rating: 9/10 - GO BUY IT ASAP!
This game is an amazing trucking simulator, that let you live the life of a trucker with your own company. You start out with having to drive for other companies, because you don't have money, to buy your own truck yet. From here your goal is to earn money, and buy your first truck, then later expand your fleet of trucks, and hire drivers to work for you. It might sound simple, and it is, but it's bloody brilliant! As you drive and complete deliveries, you'll earn XP, and rise through driver levels, which helps you unlock more trucks and customization options for your trucks.
There is a wide selection of truck brands: DAF, MAN, Mercedes, Iveco, Renault, Scania, Volvo.
No American trucks? YES! You can download mods that adds american trucks to the game! Kenworth, Peterbilt, Mack? Yep! you can find them on mod pages (Just google it). You can even download Russian trucks if you want!
Talking about mods. This game is so mod friendly, even the developers are making modding, and managing your mods easy! and there is a ton of mods out there, ranging from trucks, trailers, maps, and tuning parts, and so on!
What about music? This is very cool! You can add your own music to the game. You can even listen to REAL internet radio from various European contries. So you can cruise down the German Autobahn listening to Rock'n'Roll! That's the dream, right?
Controlls? You can use your keyboard, if you want. However, i would recommend either using a controller (PS3, or Xbox), or a steering wheel (i recommend the Logitech G27)
Pros:
- Great selection of trucks. (DAF, MAN, Mercedes, Iveco, Renault, Scania, Volvo. Even more with mods!)
- Trucks are very detailed.
- Mod friendly. (The developers encourage modding, they even released a modmanager!)
- Good Graphics. (Even though the game is a couple of years old, it's stil beautiful)
- Lot of customization options for the trucks, and even more for modded trucks.
- The driver levels, makes you want to keep playing for ever!
- You can add your own music or listen to internet radio. (You can listen to BBC radio, while cruising down the M3!)
- Great support for the Logitech G27 steering wheel. (It's easy to setup and easy to use)
- Big map. (even without the DLC's, the map is huge! With the DLC's you'll get most of Scandinavia, and Easteren Europe
Cons:
- The AI traffic (Just acts stupid sometimes. Not yielding when changing lane of motorway)
- The cities in the Scandinavian DLC makes your framerate drop. (I don't know why, they just do)
- Weather. (There is not a whole lot of weather effects. Not much variety! No snow or winter weather)
- Limited details in the cities. (You'll see some landmarks, but don't expect to recognize your home city!)

In Prison Architect, you build a prison with a constant income of prisoners that forces you to keep expanding while keeping your existing prisoners happy and healthy and incarcerated.
Pros
-very addictive
-non-sandbox mode is very challenging
-funny bios for lots of prisoners, general silly feel about the game.
Cons
-pretty steep learning curve. It took me a few prisons to maximize my efficiency with building placement/guards and stuff.
-not much micromanagement of workers/guards

A lot of gamers these days have grown tired of sequels. Of constant rehashing of the same ideas, of the same characters and the same worlds constantly pushed in your face in exchange for your precious money. We want new faces, new worlds, and new experiences. The idea of sequels has definitely been worn thin by big publishers and developers. It's a safe way to cash in with gamers. And to an extent, gamers tend to flock to sequels because they know what they're getting themselves into. If you liked one Call of Duty, chances are you'd like another. Unless it was Ghosts.
Making actually good sequels is a tricky thing. It requires more than just a new coat of paint and some changing of menus around. A video game sequel should show improvement in mechanical and conceptual design. It should build on the themes present in its predecessor, not just rehash them. Being able to get it all perfect though, that can be tough. Especially if the first game could be considered a masterpiece itself. Going from Megaman 1 to Megaman 2 was a big jump in quality, but Megaman 1 was pretty rough around the edges to begin with. But that's really what sequels are about. A second chance, to smooth out the kinks of the first game and improve it. While some say sequels are never as good as the original, there's one game in particular that was practically made by its sequel. Borderlands 2. Now wait, wait. Before you say anything, just here me out. Steroid-infused midgets. Eh?
The original Borderlands was a pretty decent game. It wasn't perfect by any means, no. It was pretty repetitive, the side-quests could get pretty dull, and it wasn't balanced all too well. The world definitely had an interesting hook to it, but it was really just a one-trick midget. Just "here's some sand and♥♥♥♥♥♥ Have fun. Stay out here, your mother and I have to... uh... give grandma her sponge bath."
But grandma moved to Florida three years ago, and we're all pretty sure she's dead by now.
Borderlands 2, however, improves on literally everything Borderlands did in some incredibly impressive ways. Everything that Borderlands did, its sequel has done significantly better.
Most notably, there's more than just sand now. Yes, that's right. There's still plenty of sand to go around, but now there's snow. And grass. And cities. It's like you really are on an alien planet, not just lost in Afghanistan somewhere. There's still plenty of crazy people trying to shoot you and blow you up though, so I guess it's still kind of like Afghanistan.
You know what they should do, they should get the Taliban to film a new Mad Max movie. That'd be pretty crazy, you know? It'd add a nice touch of realism to it I think. Or just have a constant "Allahu Ackbar" playing during all of the high action scenes.
Borderlands 2 picks up a little after where Borderlands left off. There's a strange new substance called "Eridium" popping up everywhere now, and people seem to really like it. It's purple. Can't go wrong with anything that's glowy purple. That's why strip club neon signs are usually purple. Or pink. Or red. But you get the idea, people like purple.
With all of these purple glowy things everywhere, this big bad guy from an evil corporation thinks that there's a lot of strip clubs opening up on this planet. So he decides to take it over to have all of the strippers for himself. Makes sense, right?
Borderlands 2 carries on the FPS-RPG formula from its original. Shoot something in the face, and suddenly there are numbers. Numbers mean pain.
The general Borderlands theme is still present as well. Though you'll adventure through many different areas, they'll all have that same desolate feel to them. Not to mention the Borderlands sense of humor, which is as dark and perverse as ever. It still feels very Borderlands-y.
But everything feels better developed. The environments are more diverse, the guns and classes are better balanced, and the writing is superb. It manages to run an incredibly fine line between ridiculously zany, dark, perverse humor and dramatic, serious moments. And not only that, it takes the only okay plot of the first Borderlands and adds so much depth to it. Where Borderlands had a few extremely memorable characters, Borderlands 2 has an entire cast of them. It fleshes out the world so well, adding a surprising amount of lore and character depth.
Borderlands was a game about rednecks, guns, and sand. But Borderlands 2 isn't just rednecks and sand anymore. The same sci-fi Mad Max-esque world is there, but it feels like it truly found its own identity as well.
Like the original Borderlands, it's much more fun as a multiplayer game. I definitely recommend getting a group of friends together to play with you. Go make some. Trust me. It helps. Not just for playing the game either. You need to get out and socialize more. Your mother and I are worried about you. You spend too much time on the internet.
It really feels like the game gives you so much more purpose. Instead of wandering the desert, following whatever missions that have been thrown at you, Borderlands 2 gives you a much more personal motive in the form of a real villain. Though the original Borderlands had all manner of villains, they were all over the place. Random gangs of bandits, mercenaries, and a few big characters with very little time on screen. Borderlands 2 throws the game's big bad at you seconds after you start. And not only is he a major antagonist, he's a pretty damn fine one too. They really don't make villains like him anymore, I'll tell you what. It doesn't take too long for him to genuinely get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at him. And he just doesn't stop. The writing and dialogue is so perfect for him, it makes for the most satisfying boss fight.
The endless slew of side-quests is given a similar treatment. Rather than heading to a mission board and stocking up on dozens of missions to do, you'll get most of them from major NPC's in the game. Giving a face to each mission, as opposed to just being given a to-do list from a generic board, is something of an improvement. Also aided by the inclusion of more entertaining dialogue for each side-quest. There are less generic fetch quests and killing quests. Still plenty of them, but the way they're presented makes it less noticeable.
While Borderlands 2 could still use a few improvements here and there, like how it's still a tad bit repetitive at times, the changes already put it way ahead of the first. There's a massive amount of content as well, meaning that it's entirely possible to sink hundreds of hours into it. And most importantly? Everyone's favorite crazy circus stripper is back in all her trashy, bouncy glory. It's great, because♥♥♥♥♥♥
She's no longer tied to DLC, as she was in the first game. Though I feel it'd be a little more fun if she was tied to something. However, there's still a massive amount of DLC. Most of it is fantastic, adding so much more to the game. It has definitely been well-supported after release. I'd definitely recommend going for one of the Game of The Year editions. Lots of new areas to explore and characters to meet and play as.
With how utterly fantastic the jump was from Borderlands 1 to 2, I can only imagine how great the next game will end up being. It's not like they could possibly mess it up, right? See, the secret to telling how good a Borderlands game will be is to see how many really bad Gearbox games came out recently. How many Duke Nukem Forevers and Aliens: Colonial Marines... Marineses came out. If a bunch of really bad games come out, that's when you know something big is coming. Borderlands 3 could easily be right around the corner. We should all look forward to it.

What was still the same? Well, everything else. Vaulting and key recognition, still buggy. Performance, still garbage with stuttering and hugely inconsistent FPS. No loot to be found anywhere. Now you run around for 40 minutes and find barely any clothes, tools, or food. Don't even think about finding a decent weapon, even if you run clean across the map to the military areas. Manage to avoid starving to death due to the complete lack of available resources for 10+ hours and finally found a gun with ammo to get into a firefight with someone? Save your time, save your money. This game is a joke. The devs are a joke. The playerbase is dead and dropping further everyday. SO:TL is at its heart a tactical military cover shooter, simlar to games like Rainbow Six: New Vegas 2 and Brothers in Arms.  Perspective is 3rd person and you have two squadmates who can receive simple orders like "focus attack here"... generally they will advance as enemies are cleared.  Levels are mostly confined space, although later in the game the field opens up giving you a few path choices.  The setting is something unique to this genre: Dubai, following a series of catastrophoc sand storms that have decimated the city.  The US military has moved in to assist with the evacuation... however something has gone wrong and your small team has been sent in to investigate.  The story feels predictable at the outset but then becomes very surreal as you progress... with a fantastic ending.
As a shooter the game is challenging in spots without being oppressive and provides the standard occasional over the top action sequences.  The control system takes some getting used to, but is easily customized to suite your style.  Graphically the game uses the Unreal engine which is quite responsive but somewhat dated.  Weapon assortment is typical... you have 2 weapon slots and can freely pick up those dropped by enemies.
What really stands out here though is the story, which explores the impact of killing on the mind of the killer.  Having played through the game I can say that there are parts of the game where decisions seem murky at best leaving you feel a bit unnerved.  You can only imagine how our soldiers must deal with these decisions in the field and through the rest of their lives.  An eye opener.

Do not expect a new Sid Meier's Pirates! from Windward. Yes, it has ships and towns and cannons, but the game works totally different.
Essentially, this is a standard MMO (with over 100 players on one server possible), where you happen to control a ship and not a character. You level by gathering experience through combat or quests. You get points to spend on your skill tree of choice. Likewise, you get gold doing the same activities (add trade).
If you do that on your own, you will likely get bored after a few hours, because the grind is harsh and fighting against the same NPC ships becomes pretty boring after a while.
But then Windward shines when it comes to PvP, where you battle other players over the control of regions. There are also coop-missions in "Heroic Instances" (WoW anyone?) for Epic Loot.
While the game mechanics remain repetitive, fighting against or alongside other players makes the game so much more fun.
Graphics, sound and music aren't exactly pretty, but they are not too ugly as well. Other than some minor glitches, I have not experienced any bugs, too.
Verdict:
Solo play: 5/10
Multiplayer: 8/10

This review is only in regard to the single-player campaign.
COD: Black Ops II was the most enjoyable FPS experience I have ever played.  The campaign was not overly long, but it was long enough, intriguing, and dynamic enough to keep me interested to keep me coming back for more.  I loved the fact that players get to revisit characters from the original Black Ops and meet new ones in the futurisitc side of the story, with both timelines working together to push the narrative along.
A welcome and cool addition to the campaign were the Strike Force missions.  In these missions, the player remotely commands troops and mechanical units during timed missions.  The player can have an overview, generally telling the units what to do or they can assume control and carry out the mission objectives directly.  These missions helped to break up the story missions and added some padding to the campaign.
The whole package is wrapped up inside a world filled with the best graphics that have ever been in a Call of Duty game.
This is the best Call of Duty game (and FPS) I have ever played.

Do not expect a new Sid Meier's Pirates! from Windward. Yes, it has ships and towns and cannons, but the game works totally different.
Essentially, this is a standard MMO (with over 100 players on one server possible), where you happen to control a ship and not a character. You level by gathering experience through combat or quests. You get points to spend on your skill tree of choice. Likewise, you get gold doing the same activities (add trade).
If you do that on your own, you will likely get bored after a few hours, because the grind is harsh and fighting against the same NPC ships becomes pretty boring after a while.
But then Windward shines when it comes to PvP, where you battle other players over the control of regions. There are also coop-missions in "Heroic Instances" (WoW anyone?) for Epic Loot.
While the game mechanics remain repetitive, fighting against or alongside other players makes the game so much more fun.
Graphics, sound and music aren't exactly pretty, but they are not too ugly as well. Other than some minor glitches, I have not experienced any bugs, too.
Verdict:
Solo play: 5/10
Multiplayer: 8/10

Overview
First, this game is basically the naval version of Mount & Blade without the battles. The trading and questing systems are the exact same. You quest and trade to purchase what is effectively new equipment to improve your stats, and eventually upgrade your base ship after grinding enough gold and quests to increase towns' populations. Not complicated but that isn't a bad thing. In fact, if you're looking for a somewhat casual game to burn time this game is ALMOST excellent particularly given the price. In fact, if not for one glaring flaw, I'd give this game a 7-8/10. Throw in a few other quick tweaks and this game would be one of the better deals on steam.
The Really Bad
However, I cannot recommend this game. The problem? The game-breaking pirate spawning mechanics are nothing short of absolutely absurd. Yes, this one mechanic alone is enough to take this game from being a solid game to borderline unplayable.
Let me explain what I'm talking about a little bit. The war aspects of the game (as opposed to the questing and trading ones) involve moving region to region liberating all the towns in each region. There's typically 40 regions or so on each map with prates controlling 100% about 30 or more of these regions are partial control of all but 4 with the four playable factions on the map. Each region has a difficulty setting. The farther from your or another faction's territory the more difficult the pirates. That's obvious, nothing new. The problem is that liberating each region requires you to essentially put half the world's supply of wood to the bottom of the sea. Pirates have anywhere from 3-5 ships active on any given region map as long as they control one town. That wouldn't be an issue if the pirates ships didn't spawn as fast as you destroyed them. I literally had map where I turned down the difficulty and attempted to liberate a town the pirates captured. Given that I had a much more powerful ship than the pirates, I camped in the port to liberate the city (as to prevent pirates from spawning in that city). I was killed after face-tanking 8 (yes 8!!!) pirate ships without a chance to repair my ship. The spawning mechanic is so ridiculous that liberating regions requires building an obnoxious number of towers, then buffing them, and avoiding pirates ships and stealing towns while the pirates are bogged down with the♥♥♥♥♥clown allied ships (that are wholly useless and love to sail around aimlessly while towns quickly fall to pirates) and your towers. The effect of this is that you end up avoiding what should be the best part of this game - the naval battles. But since the pirates spawn so quickly and actually work together, there is no such thing as a decisive battle on this game. Kill three pirate ships and the occupied towns to replace them faster than God could fiat them into existence. Early in my first game I had an awesome naval battle. All three or four of my allied ships against all the pirates in the region in pitched battle. It was great. We lost two ships but sank the pirate fleet. Victory... right? Wrong. Despite annihilating the entire pirate fleet, they re-spawned, attacked immediately, finished us off and took three towns (half the map) in the next few minutes. After resorting to the unrewarding town-stealing method, I took control of the region.
It's not that this makes the game too difficult. It's worse than that. It's merely not fun. Compounding this is the fact that any region bordering another region has has even one pirate-controlled town subjects the region to pirate raids. This raid can take half a region in only a few minutes. They'll attack from two or three sides of the map (even those not bordering the pirate-controlled region). Since your buff on your towers only lasts 10 minutes, your town-protecting tower cannot hold off even a single pirate ship very long. The result is your liberated region has to go through the same ridiculous garbage again as the pirates nap a town or two and you're forced to go town-stealing while buffing your towers in an effort to hinder the pirates' progress. Just ♥♥♥♥ing stupid.
Aside from this game-shattering flaw the game is pretty decent. You can get around this aforementioned issue by turning the difficult WAY down (it will still take you 15-30 minutes to retake a region).
The Good
Graphics - the water looks amazing and the graphics as a whole are solid. I'm a hardcore turned-based strategy guy so I don't value graphics much. This game is pleasant to look at without creating any performance issues.
Customized Ships - your ship has many different options for adjusting its appearance. The symbol on your flag, the flag color, the symbol color, and your ship's hull can all be changed with paints and sails found or purchased (for very little).
Transparency - the game is straight-foward and relatively simple. There wasn't any point in the game where something confused me, I didn't know what something did/meant, and/or I didn't know how to do something. A lot of games overlook this, but this is a non-issue. Yeah, some of the damage/accuracy/range numbers aren't readily translated into useful information, but combat isn't over the complexity that an analysis of the numbers is necessary.
The Gameplay - aside from the opening issue and some minor ones listed below, this game is actually fun and could be much more fun with some relatively small changes (a mod would do the trick). The controls are simply yet require some mastery to excel in combat by maneuvering your ship.
Difficulty - the combat and difficulty can be adjusted to exactly what you want. I like more difficult games and this game is actually fairly difficult in a good way.
The Needs Improvement
Allies - in each region that your faction controls, four allied ships patrol. Unlike the pirates they don't coordinate their attacks nor do they respond to pirate invasions unless the chance upon them really. You can solicit their aid, but since you have to avoid combat to win, there really isn't much point.
Grinding - the monetary (gold) rewards from quests and trading are a fraction of what they should be. To acquire better ships you need to spend hours doing the same quests and trading in the same towns over and over again. It's incredibly boring and a lot of it is required right off the bat. Since you need to have a least one ship upgrade better than pirates to handle the endless spawn, you have farm for probably 5 hours on your first map unless you lower the difficult significantly (and lose much of the fun of combat). The good news is your profile carries over your ships and equipment to any new map you start. If you don't want to dominate the new map, you can switch to a lower-level (and faster) ship without it costing you a thing.
Content - although the game is simple, it would benefit from some additional content. The other three factions you're not playing don't do anything. The quests and trading never really changes. There's no diplomacy mechanics to spice things up. The pirates and factions have no real distinguishing aspects apart from appearance. One thing that would greatly improve the game would be to really exploit the differences in ships' balance to make them feel unique. For example, the smaller and lighter ships are faster and more maneuverable, but lack the defense and firepower of bigger ships. One might think that this game would allow you to make a choice for the ship design you prefer. No such luck. The smaller and faster ship quickly become militarily obsolete with an upgrade of two doing 2.5-3x the damage. With a little balancing and making the smaller ships harder to hit, it could really make the ship choice vastly more interesting a fun.
I'll update this review if anything changes. I really would give this a mixed review if that were an option.

Wow, 3 hours in and I already can't help but give the thumbs up to this game. The maps are randomly generated and well drawn, the music and beautiful and thematic, the gameplay flows well, it is fast paced and engaging. While the start might be a bit slow, the game picks up big time afterwards - e.g., in your starting area you might be facing only a few enemy or pirate ships, while as the game progresses, there might be nothing BUT enemies... Wowie, those are some nail-biting engagements.
Still, one can't help but compare Windward to one of the best games of this genre, Sid Meier's Pirates (let's shorten it to SMP for convenience). So let's see what the games does well, and what poorly.
The GOOD:
1. Like SMP, you are free to do whatever and go wherever. Wanna be a goods trader? Sure. Wanna hunt down every pirate on the map? Go ahead. Wanna help your factions towns to grow, thus ensuring yourself more lucrative quests? Yep, can do!
2. Like SMP, you can still upgrade your ship with better hull, sails, armament, crew, etc.
3. Unlike SMP, you don't need to worry about food, crew morale and mutinies. This is a VERY welcome decision by the developers.
4. Unlike SMP, there is a RPG style progression. As you level up, you can unlock talent points, which can be spent on various trees governing ship strength, durability, speed, shot accuracy, cargo, diplomacy, etc. Great addition, supporting all styles of gameplay.
5. Unlike SMP, if you lose a battle on the map (and you will!), you don't get marooned on an island, rescued, and forced to start with a basic sloop. You get to keep the type of ship you last died with AND its cargo. All you lose are the active quests. In other words, you don't get to punch the screen cause you just found some OP item and lost it due to death.
6. Unlike SMP, battles are engaging and dynamic, and may easily include up to 7-8 ships, both friendly and enemy ones.
7. Unlike SMP, where you very rarely fight more than 1 enemy ship, here you could be facing a lot. At one point you are on the verge of destroying an enemy sloop, the next moment 4 more enemies converge on you and you blow up before you are able to say "oh shiiii..."
8. Like SMP, there are factions who may or may not be at war with each other. This may turn a battle into an even bigger free for all fun time.
9. Unlike SMP, your ship will fire automatically when faced with a clear shot at an enemy on any of the port or starboard sides. Like SMP, there are a few shot types, which can be manually activated - like chain shot for example, fired at close range to tangle the sails and reduce enemy mobility.
10. Unlike SMP, you can have a bunch of followers (friendly ships) who actually fight at your side and don't brainlessly tail behind you to the next port.
11. Unlike SMP, you don't get to keep the ships you capture, so no more skill-kills on stronger enemies just to give yourself some advantage. Could be considered a bad decision too.
12. Unlike SMP, the quests are way more diverse - not constricted to ferry a governor, or some grain, or do stupid things to gain the favor of a governor's daughter just for the opportunity to look at her bosom up close.
13. Unlike SMP, tactical thinking is the difference between spoils, life or death. Fight, run or tactically retreat for a while, repair and get back in? Up to you :)
14. Like SMP, you can lose and (re)capture various towns and important map positions, thus gaining more experience and reputation with the various factions.
15. Unlike SMP, hitting a shore actually damages your ship. In SMP; it used to happen only when you hit a reef or wade through a storm.
16. Unlike SMP, followers can be commanded to do stuff for you, or protect various areas.
17. Unlike SMP, you can purchase and build sentry towers and lighthouses to either give vision or defend a certain area, city or a bottleneck, which gives you time to react.
18. Unlike SMP, this game actually has a decent multiplayer. What's even better, you can switch between SP, Co-op with friends and MP at will.
19. Unlike SMP, this game can also be considered an MMO of sorts, as it has a very good number of populated servers, doing instances, fighting for sectors, and so on, and so forth.
Short comment before we proceed to the BAD: the developers are committed and have already stated that they are working to improve the single player part with more quests, content and improved friendly AI.
Long comment: At present, MP offers more than SP. Playing online will net you a better ship way faster than the do-it-yourself way. Everyone who whines and complains about SP should pick themselves a nice low-populated, built up server and go for it - why? Because it will still feel like you are doing SP, unless someone joins in. You will gain more money and you will upgrade your ships way faster.
In all fairness, the developers understand us and have said that SP will improve. However, only in SP and low-pop MP servers can you get the satisfaction of flipping a whole map all by yourself. Don't ever forget that.
Having said that, do not expect miracles in SP - it would be unfair if the devs bump up SP at the expense of MP, as any of the 3 aspects of the game (SP, Co-op, MP) must have some respect to the online part of the game.
The BAD:
1. Unlike SMP, you don't get to keep the ships you sink, unless you do a quest, which turns the enemy ship into your follower. No more skill kills on famous pirates just to capture their well-built ship... Could be a good thing too.
2. Early game requires some grinding until you buy a slightly better ship.
3. To me it feels like the game sort of forces you into some grinding to get a better ship before entering the next area, unless you like respawning a lot. Very much noticeable towards the 4-5th maps.
4. On quite a number of occasions you might get overwhelmed, especially when entering enemy-controlled territory.
5. Unlike SMP, there is no romance or siblings saving here. Could be considered a bad thing, as some people like to see some heart in a game.
6. Learning how NOT to run aground could be a huge pain, as it takes a good chunk of your ship's health.
7. Fair is fair: single player is a little lacking in content right now, and doing-it-yourself takes a good chunk of your free time. It's easily remedied if you go do some MP, but I fully realize it may not be everybody's cup of tea.
The conclusion:
With the amount of stuff the game does well, at the current 13€ price it is a really good buy. Being a MMO of sorts, you will double or triple the money spent on it as gameplay hours, maybe even do a tenfold if you get into it big time. As I said, I am three hours in and I am already hooked. I can't wait to sail the seas, capture stuff, sink pirates, haggle with merchants and... ferry passengers, I guess...

Overall, it is a good game considering it is a prequel. I would not recommend to person who didn’t play LIS but I believe you will get something out of it even if you haven’t play LIS if you have a taste of “story rich games”. Still, it would be smart choice to try out LIS first.
I was disappointed a little sometimes while I was playing the game, but overall, I am satisfied with the moments and lots of thought after completing the game. They tried deliver memories and something to consider and they presented very well.
Early concern
I was concerned that Chole won't be voice recorded by Ashly Burch, and she is going be done by another actress. Her name is Rhianna DeVries. I have to admit that when I was playing the first episode, it felt really weird to hear her voice. However, as time goes by, I begin to see that she did fine job expressing Chole’s feeling for the most of times. But there were some ‘weak moments’ and I did get the feeling that her voice is off few times. It is not that her voice acting was disappointing or unfitting but I do prefer the voice of the Previous voice actress.
Story
I found it a little dramatic but satisfactory. I found some of things are rather extreme (well maybe that’s the charming point for some other). I could go along with “extreme” so maybe it not that big of issue. Just like I said I enjoyed being there and having a great time with characters in there while everything going to crazy. They did things expected from prequel while presenting some priceless moments and pain inducing surprises.
Personally, I think they did what they can so that I can be engaged in the story but I did get the feeling the story develops rather quickly and suddenly without clues. Unlike LIS, where you can be surprised when you play it for second time, it didn’t happen with this one. But story was something to reflect on and helped me to get engaged in the game. It was really nice to uncover what happened before LIS and things that didn’t cover in LIS, though.
Gameplay aspect
I have encountered 2 performance issues throughout 2 playthrough. One is that I could not connect to the server to see the stats of the game.( I was able to connect and stay connected to the server in LIS without doing anything) Second one was quite serious, being in stuck because of a bug when I was trying to repair a car at episode 2. I could not progress no matter what I do. I had to reload and had to do it again. Otherwise, the game runs just fine.
The gameplay is still similar from LIS. Devs gave Chole a power of back talking instead of time rewinding power. It is means less brain teasing puzzle, but it requires more attentive listening and thinking. Also they did say that people will act differently if you wear some other clothes. As far as I know, they do comment on your outfit but that’s all. It’s not like you have to strategically choose what to wear. Those are only differences I managed found and otherwise it’s same LIS game: making decisions, interacting with people, being nosy and collecting graffiti (instead of pictures and selfies).
Characters
They introduced some new characters and added some new aspects to some of characters from LIS. The game offers to chance to meet with new people. They are typical to some degree, but it is really something that they reveal some other aspects. They are fun to listen and pay attention. For some of characters from LIS, you won’t look at the characters form LIS same once you have done the game.
Choice mattered?
At times, it was questionable to believe that choices did matter. After all, it is a prequel to LIS. Details will be vary, but you will get the outcome of the things just have happened before LIS. Just like LIS, you will have the chance to make a big decision at the end of the game, but other choices won’t be accounted that much for when you make a last decision, but I do believe it will bring some nice little things to the game.
Soundtracks and graphics
Just like LIs, I loved soundtracks and graphics. Graphics are pretty much same as LIS. Soundtracks are awesome and really nice to hear. I did not liked few soundtracks but I really loved others. Fitting and setting atmosphere very well, and did fine job delivering feelings. Some may disagree, but I liked new soundtracks even more than those from LIS. Searching for an artists and looking for names after playing the game is common to see if I dare to say.
Deluxe Edition
Ok, this stuff comes with 3 extra things: a bonus episode, selection of clothes that is exclusively available to person who purchased deluxe edition and, mix-tape mode.
I cannot talk about a bonus episode because it has not been released yet, but I am pretty sure it won’t be something like they are selling a “true ending” in a deluxe edition. The game has an ending without this.
Clothes that exclusively available were quite disappointing. I do expect people will react when I put these new clothes like the “normal clothes” but that didn’t happen. As far as I remember they didn’t even commented once when I put one of exclusive clothes unlike the non-exclusive ones. Maybe they wanted these clothes as pure cosmetic skins. They do look cool but that’s it.
I did love mix tape mode. It was really nice to hear the soundtrack whenever I wanted. It came with every soundtrack with artist names on it so you don’t have to wonder about those. I used to launch the game several times to just hear those.
For now, the deluxe edition is not worth if you are not fan of the soundtrack of the game but I cannot be judgemental until the episode comes out.
P.S :After playing it , I don’t know what to believe now. Pricefield or amberprice.

Rogue Legacy focuses on upgrading your character -- and these are permanent, lasting upgrades. Because of this, you don't get the satisfaction of getting better at the game.

Interessante e cativante, este third person shooter.
O jogo decorre no Dubai, após uma tempestade de areia lançar o caos e semear a destruição. É ordenada a evacuação e cabe-nos a nós com a pequena squad de 3 elementos auxiliar cidadãos a evacuar. Mas há algo macabro na forma como determinadas facções de soldados se comportam e passa a ser a nossa missão investigar o que se passa, auxiliando os civis.
Parece simples e linear, mas não é. E é isso que torna o jogo bastante interessante. O que poderia ser apenas mais um jogo de acção destaca-se pela sua narrativa, pelas escolhas que somos forçados a realizar e pelas suas consequências. Está em jogo a moral e a ética, além da pontaria e das decisões. Não é, definitivamente, um jogo para crianças, pelo conteúdo extremamente violento, tanto graficamente como em termos de história.
Na acção propriamente dita, há laivos de Gears of War misturados com Company of Heroes, cabendo-nos o papel de organizar, de forma simplista, o ataque dos nossos companheiros, enquanto buscamos a melhor posição para defender ou flanquear.
Surpreendeu-me pela positiva, uma vez que tinha ouvido falar pouco do jogo.

This beautiful 2012 third-person shooter video game developed by Yager Development & published by 2K Games was nominated for, several industry awards, including Best Narrative at Machinima's Inside Gaming Awards. Still even after it's said to have generally positive reviews it is heavily underrated.
Spec Ops: The Line may look like a normal third person military shooter but, if you delve deeper into the game, the more you will notice that Spec Ops is a game that really makes you think about the decisions you make throughout the game. The story in Spec Ops is one of the best stories I've seen in this genre's product. The characters and voice acting also make the game really come to life. The action and shooting mechanics all feel great, some of the set piece moments are really awesome. Spec Ops is actually a thinking man's game and is one of those games that actually made me feel sorry or regret some of the things I did in the Speec Ops: The Line adventure.
The cover based shooting does feel repetitive at times, but like in Gears of War it somehow doesn't feel old, adding new weapons, and new enemies just at the right time to keep you engaged. As the story progresses, it should be noted that the dialogue during combat also changes, as well as the brutality of close quarters execution moves. However, it should be said that the gameplay is very linear, and those seeking a unique gameplay experience should look elsewhere. The element that keeps you engaged the most, and putting up with linear cover based shooting is the story. Dubai is destroyed by catastrophic sandstorms, and you and your two comrades from Delta Force go in to locate survivors, then radio for evac, and go home.
Yager did a great job on this game and I hope it sold well enough so that they're possibly crafting a sequel. If you like story oriented games and a bit of good action,or kinda suberb actually & occasionally flavored with amazing soundtrack, then Spec Ops is the perfect game to play during the summer drought. This game really suprised me.  This is one of those games that would have been off of my radar completely had it not been part of a sale that I saw.  I've ended up with over 80 hours in the game up to this point to get 46/48 achievements and will continue to work on the last two.
In short, if you're a fan of the Batman Arkham series of games, this is a lot like those, just in the Mad Max wasteland environment.  A lot of criticism comes from the hand-to-hand combat system, which is a watered down version of the combat in the Batman games because the primary focus of combat in Mad Max is the vehicle combat, which is quite a bit of fun.
I tend to be on the fence about open world style games because I'm so goal oriented but this game has lots to do and lots of goals to drive those seeking achievements.  The gameplay can end up getting repetitive but for folks like me there is that constant drive to get to the next goal despite that repitition.
The game also looks amazing and I had almost zero technical problems with it, which is impressive in today's games that tend to ship and fix later.
Did I get $60 worth of gameplay from it? Yes.  Would I have paid $60 for it, probably not even though I'm making a contradiction.  The primary story can be completed in short order and the bulk of my 80+ hours comes from going after every tiny little POI and achievement in the game, which for many can get tiresome.
This game is part of the May 2016 Humble Monthly subscription and I can't recommend it enough for that.  Besides that, if you can get it on sale for $30 or so it's well worth it, or if you're a big fan of Mad Max then you'll probably feel like you got your $60 worth.

Otherwise, if you have nothing better to play just lower your expectations a bit and git it a try, but wait for some kind of discount first. An old school open world romp.

Amazing Game, well worth buying if you like sandbox style games that have an end of the world type plot.
This game reminds me in a lot of ways of Red Dead Redemption but instead of Horses you have a souped up V8 instead. The open world is very engaging and there is a lot of things to do to keep you occupied as you play through the main story.
Personally, I am a completionist and so ensured that each territory was threat free and that I built all projects before I left the area properly. Each area usually has 2 or 3 enemy camps to clear out (which vary in difficulty as you prgress through the game), 2 Minefields to clear, 5 or 6 Sniper's to eliminate and a Death Race. There are also 5 projects to complete for each stronghold which usually require you to collect 2 or 3 parts per project (they reward things like Health and Ammo when you go back to the stronghold if complete) and each Territory leader usually has 2 or 3 side missions to complete as well. There are also random wasteland encounters where a survivor will give you some small task to complete in order to obtain some precious scrap metal too. There are also a heck of a lot of cars that you can find and aquire to add to your collection if you want to. I found that I had played 30+ hours before I realized I hadn't done a main story quest since the start of the game and so I suddenly caught up with the plot. That just shows how much there is to actually do if you want to do it.
All in all; by the end of completing the main story I have played 50 hours of this game and as is usual with Sandbox titles, after the credits roll the game reverts to a moment just before the final encounter so you can tie up any loose ends or just explore if you want to. Basically, this game has literally hours and hours of good solid gameplay and so is worth the money to purchase.
The story is very well written too, and mixes just enough hope with heartache as you progress and in all honesty it ends as only a Mad Max title should end. There are also History Relics (photographs) that you find as you play which gives you more of an insight into the breakdown of society and the formation of the wasteland which is a really nice touch.
Your Magnum Opus (Car) is fully customisable and as you play through the game you can unlock different Chassis and upgrades for your engine. This is a wonderful addition to the game as if (like me) you want your Opus to be similar to the interceptor from the original trilogy, you can do it if you want to. Or maybe you would rather have a 1950's Hot Rod style car instead? Again, this is something you can do. There are many upgrades that make the game easier to play, such as extra weapons or damage increases, extra armour or defense upgrades like spikes, all of which are unlocked via either playing through missions or reducing threat in each area. Each territory also has it's own "Top Dog" mini boss that has their own unique paint style and so if you defeat them you can then repaint your Magnum Opus. I honestly had a lot of fun in customizing my car (and max as well) to be as strong as possible so I could literally tear through enemy cars as they came close to me.
During my 50 hours of gameplay I encountered only one bug and that was because I tried to refuel my car whilst standing too close to a wall. the animation made Max appear inside the wall and afterwards I could not get back out and so I had to fast travel to a local settlement. All in all, it certainly wasn't game breaking and I think the lack of bugs in this game really shows just how great the developers have done.
The world itself in this game is also beautiful in a tragic kind of way. The developers have done a wonderful job of showing the destruction of a continent and it's subsequent dissapearence into the sand. There are times where I would simply stop and admire the view which is another aspect that constantly reminded me of Red Dead Redemption. The weather effects are also very well made and the first time I goty caught in a Nuclear Storm I was very nervous as to whether I would make it back to my camp. The world builders have really excelled in creating the world for you to explore.
I would say buy this game. I can honestly think of no bad points to it, and having just completed it I am just blown away by the whole experience and can't wait to play it again. As of writing this (14/4/16) the game iscurrently offered if you subscribe to the Humble Monthly Bundle too and so you can buy it much cheaper than on steam which is an absolute steal.
It's alright, but it gets boring fast. Glad I got it 75% off, because for that, it's worth it. Otherwise, wait.

I bought this game thinking it would be a realistic hunting simulation, but it's an arcade hunting game.
Now the game is described as the most immersive, but I don't know what they mean by that.
If a game about real-life hunting isn't realistic, I can't be immersed in it very easily.
It has some pretty graphics and nice audio, but that's about it.
The way you progress in this game is by taking down animals and getting weapon score. With enough weapon score you unlock the next weapon in the category.
The cons of this game are very lengthy.
-The way you get score on your kills is based on what type of ammo you use to kill the animals.
-There are 2 variants of most ammo, being hollow-points and polymer-tipped bullets. The former do nothing to the animals unless lucky.
-The menus and the hud are a complete mess, they glitch out, become non-responsive and mess out all the time.
-The rifles and handguns seem to be ok, but the first shotgun is garbage and you have to use it to get the good one. The bows are inaccurate, but they do more damage than some of the rifles.
-The animals glitch out constantly, run in circles, the bears loop in an animation where they stand up on 2 legs, the animals teleport around the map, sometimes the animals become zombies being at 0 health, but being unkillable.
If you really want this game, buy it from sale. It is very frustrating most of the time and could possibly be an easy fix if the devs would fix most of the bugs, glitches and annoying parts of the game.
TL;DR Looks and sounds pretty, but is an arcade hunting game with lots of glitches and problems.
