This is the first review I have ever written on steam. I feel compelled to write this in the hopes that I might save someone else a couple dollars. I purchased this game after reading several very good reviews on steam and after reading about how this game came to be developed based on Sid Miers Pirates. That is a complete lie. The only thing this game has in common with Pirates is they both have ships. This game takes all the great aspects of Pirates and throws them away, replacing them with paired down, simplistic, boring(by mine and my friends tastes). Please do not expect this to be a MMO like port of Pirates. Here are some of the problems. Unlike Pirates combat in this game does not take place in a close up tactical map, imagine if in pirates all combat took place on the shipping map. Add to this the fact that your guns fire automatically, as if they are machine guns. You watch as you circle your enemy, both ships firing frantically at each other hit points ticking off. The combat is exactly like World of Warcraft low level combat. Imagine a fight with an orc, your ship and the enemy ticking off damage, every 5 seconds you click a button to do a little extra damage. Wind is not a factor like it is in pirates. You don't really need to pay attention to it. The ships operate more like tanks than ships. able to spin in place and get this, they can back up. That's right, your ships operate as if they had a motor. You can back up. I could have lived with the lack of diversity in quests and the lackluster skill tree, if they would have kept the original pirates combat. This game is a serious waste of money and hard drive space. You do not get anything remotely like a high seas adventure game. Get the original instead. If you really need the RPG type experience just play the free first 10 levels of World of Warcraft. The gameplay in WoW at least has more depth and stategy than this title does, you will also get about as much engaging play time. Do Not Waste Your Money on this title if you have ever played Sid Miers Pirates.

Windward is one of the greatest Early Access successes since the program launched. When the game was launched on Steam, I hadn't heard of its history on Desura, from which the developer, Aren Mook, had completely redone the gameplay. A game about sailing in a procedurally-generated open world and fighting pirates and trading and performing quests and just being a bad♥♥♥♥♥sailor? Hell yeah!
I never actually played Sid Meier's Pirates!, so I have no idea how to compare the two. But I did play
on the PlayStation 2, and near the end of the game there was a whole area where the player could take their pirate ship and go exploring. All I could think of was, "I want a whole game centered around this." And Windward is that game. You sail your ship between towns, trading goods, completing certain quests for each town such as defending against pirates or sending villagers to other towns, and building up your own ship as well as your faction. Eventually you will move on to the next region and continue the process to become an experienced sailor with a decked-out ship and some powerful cannons in case anyone wants to say anything to you.
There is no story mode to speak of, which is my main problem with the game. I love the procedurally-generated worlds and I love building them up, but it feels like it's lacking actual substance. There's no voice acting, and things will feel empty a lot of the time just because nothing ties it together.
But where the story lacks, the multiplayer shines. When you play a world in single-player, it's just you and AI ships. Other regions don't do anything unless you travel there, and it's all centered around you. But in multiplayer, you can have dozens upon dozens of players fighting for control all throughout one world in each of its separate regions. Everyone will be trading and questing and potentially fighting and it's insane. In my first multiplayer session, I spent more time playing than any other time I've played the game because it was that much fun.
Sound design is top notch. Everything has its own unique sound effect, and the battles sound like actual battles. Sure, there's no wood separating from wood when the cannons break in, but it's not nearly that detailed. What's there works very well. I also love the game's soundtrack, even if it can be basic at times. It's a joy to listen to.
The real great thing about Windward is the developer, Aren Mook. In early access, he periodically updated the game
since it first released. Don't believe me? Check out the change log for yourself:
This is a developer who has been listening to the community and who truly cared about what he was making. This is such a rarity and he deserves so much credit for this. Windward is a damn good game made by a damn good developer and you damn well better give it a try. I've been recommending it for months, so an upvote in a review is easy to come by. I can't wait to see where it goes from here!

Its a good little game
Pros - Lots of it... game looks nice, plays nice, loads quickly
The bad -
I'm going to harp on it a little bit but that doesn't mean I don't like it
1.) Gameplay balance - Grog cocktail and the explosive shot that enemies get can OHKO you but good... If you run into grog fire even late game in a defensive build you are pretty much sunk
Defensive skills are typically bad, with some rather obvious exceptions (speed and repair), support skills are generally bad with some rather obvious exceptions (100% luck, accuracy, range)...  Offensive is generally good,,, and completely necessary due to how much damage enemies do making the other trees a bad choice...
For special you are then forced into offensive as the others don't synergize with anything really useful.
2.) Pirates - As they get less cities they begin to spawn rapidly, when they are down to one city they can be all but an endless stream of ships...  Pro side of this is lots of exp, lots of loot, downside is it makes capturing the final city a lot harder than anything else there...  This is also the end game farming strategy... The late end game farming strategy is heroic instances and siege tower swarms.
Cities should be able to make 1-2 ships each, and they should have a cooldown as they are constructed (possibly seen being build and bombarded to stop it)
3.) Grindy - The game is quite grindy... the last ship costs 1,000,000 gold and then a bunch of materials... You can sell for 6k or so a pop of items from heroic instances, so maybe 60-120k per heroic go depending on how well you survive the mass swarm of pirates.  But its not just the last part that is grindy, most of the game is grindy...
4.) Reward balance... Non combat rewards are worthless... questing = a few hundred gold, trading = a few hundred gold... sinking ships?  6000 gold half the time.  (basically 20-50x the reward of the others and its quicker and easier)
Suggestions for improvement?
1.) Towns build ships in the docks, they can be destroyed before being built
2.) Towns have a cap of ships they can put out (the final pirate town shouldn't have access to 8 pirate ships that spawn endlessly)
3.) Growing towns needs to be re-thought... It is terrible to do now...
4.) Completely capturing regions should provide steady income to a player (more towns and level of towns more reward)
5.) War instance - Just a stream of ships decking it out from each side... give a max # that can spawn... Maybe a DOTA style one...
6.) Ships purchased and no longer used should be able to be assigned to a region to improve it... they just bounce around doing quests and trading in that area or whatever the town improvement model becomes
7.) Unstack cooldowns... Right now fog is useless because it starts grogs countdown, its also bad because it has a delay...  Defiance is bad because of the same reasons and it doesn't really provide a ton of use... Hasty repair is good because it stacks with others... poison fog is bad because it starts grogs countdown... and while useful it isn't as good
8.) Increase maps level caps (39 seems to be the max in maps, 54 in heroic instances... but I did have a 57 before it reverted next time) - Ok just clarify in game how to do this... as it isn't obvious
9.) Make factions have more use... IMO they appear completely useless as of now...  Just more ships on the map that really do nothing different than yours (or pirates if you are default hostile)
10.) Don't "Liberate" towns for other factions...  or at least allow the option... weird to help others for no reason in empire style games
11.) Add heroic enemy ships...  Something only enemies get that are massive and deadly with good rewards and skill required to defeat

I'm giving this game a soft recommendation. If you liked Chloe in the original Life is Strange, you'll probably enjoy yourself. If not, this game won't do much to win you over. In the original game, Chloe hated her stepfather, grieved over the loss of her real father, and complained about missing her best friend. In this game, she does the exact same things. Simply put, Chloe isn't interesting enough to carry her own story. I expected this game to soften Chloe's edges, make her more relatable, and redeem some of the flaws she exhibited in Max Caulfield's storyline. It doesn't. Chloe spends the whole game flipping off authority, getting into shouting matches, and going through the same song and dance with her mother that we've seen before. All the emotion centers around her relationship with Rachel Amber, the most popular girl in school. If you played the original Life is Strange, you know Rachel's story doesn't have a happy ending. Is that explored in this game? Not at all. Instead, it invents a new storyline about Rachel's family that doesn't have anything to do with Chloe's own life, or her troubles. Like I said, Chloe isn't interesting enough to carry a storyline on her own. So, if you emotionally connect with Rachel Amber, you'll probably find this game engaging. If you're like me, and you couldn't care less, you'll be bored. There are very few side stories to explore, and limited interaction with outside characters. Worst of all, Chloe lacks Max's power to rewind time. That mechanic is the entire reason the original Life is Strange was so good. Without it, this is just another visual novel where your choices don't matter, because every character needs to end up in the place where Max finds him/her later on. Color me disappointed. I expected more emotional depth in a game with this pedigree.
Pros: Good voice acting, music, cinematic atmosphere, a few funny sequences.
Cons: Random audio cut-outs, graphical stuttering (learn how to force V-sync in your NVidia control panel), storyline goes nowhere and leaves some loose ends.
Final verdict: If you really love Chloe, and you're a huge fan of Life is Strange, you'll probably have a good time. The game is definitely well crafted, and there's a decent variety of things to do. The problem is, the story is completely unnecessary. It tells us nothing new about Chloe, and doesn't even show how or why Rachel Amber was adored by so many students at Blackwell.  Someday, Square Enix will add a campaign where you play as Max again. But it’s Max as a child, which means you’ll just be watching Chloe lose her dad for the third, bleeding time. Thanks, but I’ll pass.

TL;DR:
I wanted to like this game. I thought it was going to be Shovel Knight with roguelike elements.
It's pretty, interesting, but a huge grindy time sink that fights against you having fun. Go play something else if you have an addictive personality.
PROS:
+ Funny, all the characters have these neat ailments or conditions and figuring out what they do is fun.
+ Nice sprite art
+ Interesting upgrade system, I like unlocking classes
+ You feel smart for beating some of the challenge rooms. Like, there's this moment of "How in the ♥♥♥♥ am I going to beat this puzzle", but then you realize you have (or don't have) the tools to do it or try something on a whim and it happens to work.
Cons:
- The castle lock down system is opt-in instead of opt-out. It's bad UX. When you lock down a castle it means you want to repeatedly attempt that castle again, until you don't. However, this game assumes that you'd want to do a new castle every single time, so EVERY SINGLE TIME, you have to go to the architect and say you want it locked.
This BLOWS if you FORGET and ALL your progress is ABSOLUTELY GONE.
This irritates the mess out of me because the mechanics of the game encourage you to repeat castles that you roll.
- A couple of really cheap deaths. Sometimes you enter a room and there are immediately spikes. Sometimes you enter a room, sit for a bit to try to figure it out and something off screen totally comes and messes you up.
- I feel like the upgrade system is nerfed from what it could've been to make a short game longer. Like, you get the "essentials" (NPCs, one or two classes) kinda quickly (when you're beginning and don't know what you're doing so it doesn't feel like grinding) however, once that phase is over with, you have a daunting task of getting all this gear so you can beat a boss or survive for a couple rooms in a new area.
If you've played old school MapleStory or Runescape, you know what I mean. It's when you've mastered a part of the game, or a mob of enemies, but you can't move forward simply because you're not strong enough, so you have to overtrain with things you're already used to. And grind for gold to buy the next gear.
-....which would be okayish but you lose all of your gold each run. I get that they want you to spend it, and that's liberating, HOWEVER, that means I constantly have to re-roll castles for something that gives me a bunch of gold earlier(front-loaded). If I roll and get something bad, like a monster ridden, magic spam, spike soaked room, I have to re-roll again. And as soon as I find something front-loaded and I want to lock it in(pay the Architect), I'm losing a large chunk of the gold(40%) so more than likely (unless you get really lucky), I have to re-roll again. WASH.
Once you do that, you get to enjoy the fun part of the game where you're experiencing the fights and challenges at a reasonable difficulty. RINCE.
Then WASH WASH WASH WASH WASH RINCE repeat.
- Puzzles show up regardless of whether or not you have the tools to solve them. (I think, if I'm wrong I'll come back to correct this. (I was right. They gave me a double jump chest before I had double jump.))
EDIT:
- The Legacy part doesn't seem to do anything. I thought picking a gay character would cause my other two offspring to have their traits re-iterated or something, but it seems like you just get three random characters each time. They could've done so much more.
- Holy Fried Peppered Buttplugs, the cost of upgrades goes up by 10 every time you buy an upgrade. Are you kidding me; that's stupid.
- The view area of the screen is too small. You need more space so that you can see the spikes on the platform below you or the giganto knight.
- You can't really play to a play style. You can't beat the game using spells easily unless you beat it as a Barbarian first (to maximize survivability to get gold), then buy all of the mage skills. Then play as a mage.
- All of the upgrades should've been laid out instead of you gradually unlocking them so you can know what information you'd get going down a particular skill tree (Like in borderlands or league of legends). I built a skill tree that made it hard for me early game.
- Your down attack can't be held. Makes platforming hard for the wrong reasons.
- The enemies need more knockbak and pause times.

Games with better combat:
Terraria

If you have the option, get those instead. They have their flaws (Risk of Rain has a difficulty hump, Crypt is.....I'm still looking for a problem with Crypt. )

Overall a great game, but it would not be a review if I did not tell you why I think so, let`s begin.
Rust is an amazing survival game, that turns into a survive from players really fast, when you get a base going. Animals are not easy to avoid, but not hard either, keep your distance, Around a corner, or behind a bush, might be a wolf, that you could not see, be ready to fight back. Bears are OP as hell, you will need a gun to stand a chance against one head on. The building system is gorgeus, perhaps the best in survival games like these. The servers will restart from nothing between a week and a month, depending on the server. With updates, comes forced server restarts. So that is something to keep in mind, on top of the fact, that raiding other people and their bases is one of the main aspects of this game.
Pros: Amazing graphics, great sounds, excellent controls, best building system, perfect day and night cycle (IMO), quite balanced pvp, You won`t get bored, since the servers restart, and you get to start again. Tons of fun.
Cons: Terribly optimized, WILL REQUIRE an gaming rig to play. Other people might lag on behalf of their crap internet connection, possibly screwing you over in pvp, or if they are running from you, they might stay still for a split second from time to time, letting you hit them with melee, when in reality they should be out of your reach, so a silver lining. Bears are (too op), advanced gun parts (ak, bolt action rifle etc.) Are extremely hard to find at this point, too rare IMO. Giving the players who have them, an undoubted upper hand in pvp, especially if they are in groups. You might get salty, when people raid you, and take everything, or kill you when you have too much on you.
Do not let the long con list scare you, only the optimization, hard to find parts, are something you should consider.

A series of dust storms has destroyed Dubai and a three man delta force team is sent in with the mission of locating survivors.
The games plot is loosely based off Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness (the same book that inspired apocalypse now). The story puts you in the role of Captain Marin Walker, leader of the delta force team in Dubai as he struggles with the hardship of war. Whilst many would dismiss it as another modern day shooter they couldn't be more wrong. Unlike your average modern day shooter such as call of duty or medal of honor, Spec Ops: The Line has a gripping story that forces the player to make tough desicions and begin to question whether or not you are in fact the hero. The game makes use of it's setting in order to add new gameplay mechanics for the player to utilize. There are several points where glass can be broken to allow sand to enter changing the environment, and times when a sandstorms will appear mid firefight to add a new dynamic to the combat.
Overall this is one of the best modern shooters to date with an immersive plot, great gameplay and an interesting new take on the popular genre, Spec Ops: The Line is a must have for any fan of the genre.

DISCLAIMER: This is a long review, but I've tried to cover setting, story and gameplay. If you read the whole thing, that probably confirms that you need to play this game.
This game. Oh man, this effing game.
I heard about this title a while back, noted for it's solid story and setting. I popped it on my wishlist and eventually I managed to get it at a good price (2K Humble Bundle, thanks guys!).
It was worth the wait.
Long have I dreamed of a military-themed title that forces you to confront the more horrific aspects of war, and this game does it beautifully. There is very little in the way of clear-cut, waypointed binary 'moral choices', but choose you will, because most of these decisions are organic, and because this is war, none of the outcomes will be pretty.
The setting is incredible. Dubai is a freakish juxtaposition between limitless luxury and hellish desolation; and that's just in the real world. Throw 2K's incredible vision of a city abandoned by authority, beset by brutality, and drowned in the desert itself over the top and you have possibly the best location for a game I've seen in almost a decade. They didn't just make it look good, either - much of the environment is destructible, and if you've ever wondered what crushing your enemies with a thousand tonnes of sand might look like, now you can find out.
I deeply enjoyed the story, and if you've invested any time in military/conspiracy literature or cinema you will see immediately that much of the overarching plot arc is a direct nod to the legendary film Apocalypse Now (to the point that the main antagonist's name (Konrad) is a variation on that of John Conrad, author of the film's inspirational text, Heart of Darkness). The story contains many well-known and frequently used elements of military and warfare media, but by no means does that make it formulaic. The characters are well-written and the voice acting is excellent. Your squadmates, through their words and actions, will elicit within you feelings of compassion, pride, fear, mistrust and guilt.
At times the plot twists sharply enough to make you uncertain of the details, and by extension yourself, but this really only serves to further immerse you in the chaos that almost constantly surrounds you. Factions within the game are unpredictable and rarely what they seem, their motives shrouded in blood and the chain of command; to the point where you wonder if they can be regarded as factions at all. Cutscenes are frequent, appropriately expository, and provide the right mixture of closure on the last scene and motive for the next one. The conclusion really, genuinely deserves to be discovered - but only by those who survive their way through to it, those who /earned/ it.
In terms of gameplay, the title is also top-tier. Very rarely did I feel hampered by game mechanics, although I will acknowledge that I found the default keybinds a little clunky - remapping them may be advisable. (The best example of this is the use of 'Q' to throw a grenade and 'E' to switch weapons. If you've played Source engine games much, you'll occasionally have your muscle memory revert to 'Q' for weapon switch, which results in comically lobbing a grenade without aiming, usually onto your own feet or the wall in front of you).
Weapons are similar enough to be reliable when picked up on the run and different enough to be useful in the right situation. Alternate fire is not something you'll use often, but it works well when you do. Iron Sights are absolutely essential and I didn't find a weapon that didn't do them well. The extra level of thought regarding stationary weapons, like being able to flip a fixed MG turret in the opposite direction, or crouch down and blind-fire it (inaccurate, but out of harm's way) are extra details that make such fixtures infinitely more useful.
Your NPC squadmates are well characterised and are actually useful in a firefight. Squad commands come in handy, laying down suppressing fire to cover their movements (or vice versa) is a useful tactic, combat speech is all business but absolutely an asset in a fight. Thankfully your guys won't run blindly into opposing fire, and being able to recover them if they do manage to fall in battle is no small mercy.
Combat environments are varied, or as much as they can be in a battle-scarred city of sand, glass and steel. There is some element of vertical combat as you engage with enemy combatants rappelling in from the upper levels of the building you're fighting in, snipers on rooftops, and making your way up/down staircases in towers and shopping precints. Some cover can be degraded by heavy fire and there are explosive props that can be used to help dispatch your enemies, but they are not heavily advertised, and spotting one and using it effectively to take down an opponent feels like a victory in perception and adaptation under fire. Additionally, enemies do not automatically spawn and stand mindlessly next to the red crate or barrel, waiting for you to shoot it - you'll need to flush them out or lure them in if that's how you want to obtain your kills.
The only environmental gripe I could come up with was that some static props seem to have a hitbox slightly larger than expected - leaning out to loose few shots would at times result in the bullets harmlessly striking the edge of whatever I, or my enemy, was hiding beside. This seemed to happen more often with scoped weapons, I noticed.
Ultimately I found this game to be one of the best I've played in recent memory. Tense, terse, immersive and explosive. I found myself hungry for answers, but apprehensive of what they'd be. I scrambled for ammo and lunged for cover. I grit my teeth, swore, dug in, and expended brass and blood in equal amounts. I travelled from mindless bloodlust to gut-wrenching grief, and back again, and I loved every minute of it. When you finish this game you'll be left, in a way, unsatisfied. Not because the game was lacking, far from it - but because you'll be asking yourself, over and over;
"..what if I'd done something different?"

Before I give my review, I want to start off by saying how big of a fan I am of the Original (or first season) Of Life is Strange, and how by the end of that game, I wanted more. But, it also left me emotionally depressed, and made me think about the things that went on in my life.
Unlike its predecessor, Life is Strange: Before the Storm did not give me the same emotional feeling, or any feeling in that matter. It made me feel like I was watching a TV show.
Im not saying the game is bad, the game definatly had it moments and I enjoyed the first two episodes. They were both fun, and it made me happy to be back in the world, especially with my favorite character Chloe, and I very much enjoyed the chemistry her and Rachel had. But, then we get to episode 3. Episode 3 is the worst episode in both games. It was weirdly paced, made no sense in correlation to the original (ex David being nice to you at the end but suddenly becomes a jackass again in Episode 1 of LIS), and the stupid plot of the identity of Rachel's mother.
I feel like this episode/game could have been better if they went with either 2 ideas or merged them. 1 Focusing more on thee friendship of Rachel and Chloe, and them bonding more (which was seen in the first 2 episodes but then dies in the third) and 2 Getting rid of the Rachels mother plot and replacing it with how Rachel died. This could have allowed us to see how Chloe became so broken in LIS, and lead us straight into Episode 1 of LIS perfectly. It could have also allowed us to see the bond of Rachel and Chloe even more, and how Mark Jefferson came to Blackwell.
For now I will recommend this game because it is a good time, (except for episode 3) but do not come in expecting an emotional cannon like LIS, because you will not find it here.

Here's the premise: you explore an ancient castle, but each time you die, the interior layout changes. When you die, you choose an heir amongst your children. Each potential heir has different abilities, classes, and traits. The traits sometimes affect gameplay (such as size, weaknesses, or abilities) or aesthetics (such as colorblindness, vertigo, or insanity).
The fact that you play as different characters and that the castle changes makes each run unique and interesting. There are also global RPG elements (upgrades, unlockable classes, etc.) that carry over, making the game even more addictive. Like most roguelikes (or rogue-lites, whatever), the game is crushingly difficult at first, and making any progress is really rewarding. But no matter how good you become, the game makes sure you're always challenged.
is challenging yet rewarding, brutal yet satisfying, accessible yet deep. Once you get into it, you won't want to stop.

When I look at a game, the first thing I do is check out the actual player reviews. I look for the negative ones first. Not from a bad news perspective but because, I want to know if they think a game is worth the money they paid for it.
So right now, I see Windward selling for $14.99. (Though right now it's on sale, I still look at the base price.)
I and a buddy tend to play games together, and so I look for the features of a game next, as well as if it's something that is in both our wheelhouses.
This game crossed our path after we recently took a break from a different game. (7 Days to Die)
We looked it over, the videos seemed pretty simple, it was going to be about sailing, but not a sail simulator. It was going to be about trading commodities from town to town, but not an economic simulator. It would involve quests that would bring in wealth, where you can deliver goods, pick up goods, ferry passengers, smuggle goods, capture pirate ships, defend towns, build lighthouses and watchtowers, and even build new towns themselves. That seems like it's billed correctly. There is also the exploration aspect of the game, explore new regions, find new towns, encounter pirates and other factions.
That so far, sounds like it's meeting it's advertising. Then it involves getting in and playing, and finding out how quick it is to pick up on the various aspects of the game.
What seems like grinding to those with the attention span of gold fish, can alternatively be seen as growing the region, training your crew and upgrading your equipment. There are RPG elements to the game in the leveling of captains, crew, equipment, ships and more.
Well that's a fun thing to do as we continue to strive to expand our wealth, and beat back Pirate forays into the region.
So with a good number of hours under my belt.
I can say this game is well priced for the entertainment it brings. Fun adventures exploring a map, settling towns and naming them as well.
So it's got a lot of fun positives.
Pros
Easy to learn - Principles of the game are easy to pick up and learn from observation.
Quick to play - You can drop into the game for a few minutes here and there, do some combat, or trade, or both.
Difficult to Master - The average player is used to having their hand held through everything, this game let's you understand the easy aspects, but the nuances of trade and combat and even exploration are at times complex.
Visually Attractive - Looks pretty, and there is minor ship customization cosmetically.
Pricing - Good price point for a fun casual game
Addicting - It's got that one more turn mentality baked into it. You urge to learn and explore.
Cons
Little documentation - You can go to a wiki or even read the beginners guide here on Steam. But not much explained at all. (Some actually like this convention and see it as a plus, that it lets you learn it's secrets.)
Co-Op Play - If you're used to being able to clicking on your friends who are gaming and then joining them in game. This will be an exercise in frustration. You'll need to set up either a server or do some port forwarding, and other hoo haw stuff to get a private server up and running or a direct connection. The best way I've found is go to a public server that is up frequently, and have your friend meet you there. You can then join a private instance if you're inclined or participate in the general map multiplayer play.
Special Combat Options - Others have indicated combat is a case of doing a circle of death, waiting for special buttons to pop up that you can initiate. These often do feel a bit detracting. But again it's a casual game, and millions of people planted crops on other casual games that weren't nearly as interactive as this one.
Verdict: Addicting purchase. Go for it, especially if you see it on sale. Otherwise it's still worth the $14.99 it's selling for. For some this could be a several hundred hour to a thousand hour game, from a shelf-life. (And that's not even including any future updates, or even DLC's or expansions of the game.)

I don't know what to say about this game, so here is a recipe for pancakes,
Ingredients:
4tbsp plain flour (about 100g)
1 large free range egg
½ pint semi-skimmed milk + water (about 300ml - ¾ milk ¼ water)
Pinch of salt
Butter for frying
How to make pancakes:
Sieve the flour and salt into a large bowl and make a well in the mixture.
Break in the egg and stir to make a breadcrumby mix.
In a jug add 1/3 of a pint of milk and top up with water to make 1/2 a pint (200ml milk, 100ml water) - this makes a lovely light batter.
Add the milk and the water mix bit by bit, beating constantly to avoid lumps.
Tip:*If you have a food processor just throw all the ingredients in and zap until smooth!
Pop a large frying pan over a medium heat.
Add a large knob of butter (roughly 50g) and melt.
Pour the excess butter into a small bowl and reserve it for later.
Using a ladle pour a spoonful of the pancake batter into the hot pan and swirl to get a full covering - cook for about 1 min each side (it's ready when it's easy to flip over).
Serve immediately with sugar and lemon or other exciting toppings. We love cheese and Marmite for an extra British twist! Delicious!!

Mad Max is an enjoyable game as you play the title character in the quest to cross the Wasteland. Unfortunately, your car was wrecked and Lord Scrotus, war boys wound you and left you to die on the Wasteland. As expected and cliche as it sounds, it's the classic one-man hero story taking revenge on your aggressor as you get tangled with Lord Scrotus and his gang of war boys in the tussle for power in the Wasteland. Along the way, other colorful characters and allies added some emotions to the otherwise one-dimensional story telling.
The pros;
-The main story game is packed with actions and story the first 20 hours or so.
-You get the options to modify your car, the Magnum Opus and upgrade its arsenals.
-Few different factions of bad guys and allies added some variety to the gameplay.
-Different challenges from car to ground combat available to test your skills and yes patience
Some cons;
-can be highly repetitive after completion of main story line
-allies should do more than just decorating the story, game doesn't even allow the option of calling allies to storm a camp
-top dog character design and fights are also repetitive; hit hit hit, fury mode, shiv, and rinse and repeat
-some upgrades like the last V8 engine only unlocks after completing 100% of the threats making it pointless to even upgrade in the first place
Overall, a good experience and story telling. If you choose to pick it up, do get it at a discount though.

This game is definitely an oddity. On the one hand, it is a modern military shooter with cover-based shooting and regenerating health. On the other, it is possibly one of the best story experiences I've had in a while. Sure, it falls into the shooter trap of quantity over quality of enemies and throwing random heavy soldiers at you that can take 40 shots to the head, but the gameplay is still solid. The mechanics will not blow your hair back, but they are also not why the game is great - they exist solely to drive the narrative, which is the game's main selling point. Knowing this: solid, simple gameplay was definitely the way to go.
I wish, however, they had improved the enemy AI and lowered the amount of bots (maybe add in some extra characterization to the ones we do get). It would have definitely reinforced what they were going for in the story, while retaining the challenge. Because of the nature of the story, it'd be next to impossible to recreate this, so I can only chalk that up as a "missed opportunity," a single mark on an otherwise fantastic game.

This is my first, and likely only, game review. It’s not that I'm against reviews or anything, I'm just lazy. This series though (and the following is directed at the
Life is Strange series) ...is just so damn perfect.
Deck Nine and Square Enix could do what so many games have done before them, which is focus on the fact that protagonist(s)
But they don't. Hell, I found myself forgetting about that because I'm so absorbed in the plot of both these games. Everything about them is done so damn well.
I'm 26, it's been a decade since my "angsty" teenage years but hitting play on these games is like pressing a time machine back to those days. I mean...I couldn't control time or anything, but the atmosphere, characters, plot... and the soundtrack...oh man, the soundtrack.
Both these games are so good at pulling you in. If I was having a particularly stressful day at work, coming home to these was great because you would just get lost in the world of Arcadia Bay. You remember what it’s like to have such simple problems that, as a teenager, you thought were world changing. You remember what it was like to meet and fall so damn hard for your "first love". That's where these games really shine. It uses those nostalgic moments that we all had, regardless of race, gender or
to connect with the player on such a personal level.
Next up is the plot, which they deck nine have mastered in ramping up the progression and emotional intensity. You start with episode one and those nostalgic moments and then it gets more and more intense and personal to the point where you are a uncontrollable ball of sadness and stress, just sitting in your chair staring in to your monitor, trying to wonder what the hell you just witnessed. The ending to the original Life is Strange BROKE me. Like...indescribable. I was a mess. Each time you finish an episode, you want to hop right back in, you NEED to find out what happened. Your choices have
consequences which, most of the time, you'll learn the hard way.
The music and songs are brilliant not only in their selection, but
their used, and the scenes they are used in. When I say that, I'm sure you know what I mean. They complement the emotional intensity, or sadness, or joy so well that without them, the scenes wouldn't be nearly as impactful. They convey that sense of wreckless, carelessness we all had as teenagers.
Finally, the characters. While much loved Chloe makes a triumphant return to the series, Rachel was the one who really drew me in, for more personal reasons. While not in the exact same way, I could relate to her situation. You get attached to these characters. You root for them. You want these fictional people on your screen to be happy. To me, THAT is the sign of a good game. When you quite literally put their happiness ahead of your own, or what you think is right, because it’s better for them.
Just when I thought they would let us end on a happy note, once again, your heart gets shattered. That ending scene...
That, to me, is the biggest sting of all. Having played the original Life is Strange, from the second I hit play,
While not as emotionally gripping as the original Life is Strange, Before the Storm is another fantastic entry in to the world of Arcadia bay. Buy it...but bring the tissues.

This game's mediocrity is unforgivable when it is inevitably compared to the original game. tl:dr, I do not recommend it.
As far as positives go, we get more backstory for the characters, it puts some elements of the original story into perspective and despite the original VA's not being involved, you can tell that the replacements are putting in their best effort. The backtalk mechanic feels appropriate half of the time and is probably as good as it gets without time travel.
However, there is no acting effort that can possibly fix the screaming mess of a dumpster fire behind an abortion clinic that the script is. The dialog is often times so stilted, it feels like it could be right at home in an episode of "The Office", but was rejected as too cringy. People don't interact like that in real life. It would be more or less passable if it were just the teenagers, but it's badly written for almost every actor.
The animations are bad. The original was not the paragon of realism, but it worked around the limitations of the engine in a way that created its own distinct style. Here we are treated to models that looked good when San Andreas came out.
The plot gets interesting enough at the end of the first and second episodes and the beginning of the third. It keeps you curious as to what happens while you wait for the next sequence, but sets you up for an incredible disappointment when you realise that most of the stuff that you had to do to get to the good parts is painfully boring and the strong points of the narrative are only brushed on. The stuff that does get the center of attention, however, is not enjoyable on the meta-level. The choices that are presented as important decisions don't feel as such, because you either already know that it won't matter, or it feels out of character and contradicts the story that you know to be true so far.
When I experienced the original Life is Strange, I was already spoiled on almost the whole plot and yet it still hit me like a truck because the delivery is so damn good. I went into this game's playthrough blind and all I can do is shrug.
I paid exactly the same amount of money for both games, but I sure as hell wish it all went to the original developer insted, because Deck Nine doesn't deserve a penny for their lackluster job.
P.S. what is up with the episodic formula anyway? It made sense when adventure games were dead for so long they were considered risky, or when the company does not have the budget to release the full game in one piece, but point-and-clicking seems to be coming back, Life Is Stange is an established franchise, it does not need a proof of concept and it's not an underbudgeted indie game either, so there is no reason we don't get the full monty.

This game is amazing, it's hard to put down, it has almost endless replayablity, it's difficult at first but once you learn the enemies attacks and upgrade your characters it becomes wonderful. A mouse isn't supported which can be somewhat annoying for the menu but you can bind the keys however you want allowing you to perform maneuvers you wouldn't be able to otherwise, you can use a controller though so that can eliminate the problem quite fast. If you're stuck with a keyboard try binding your spells, abilities, attack, and dashes to U,O,J,K, and L (U and O for dashes) or the numpad keys (numpad needs to be on obviously). Lets's start with your characters, after you go through the tutorial and start off with a character you will enter the castle and probably die, then you will get to choose an heir with random traits, class, and spell then you can purchase upgrades which you can return to anytime by going to the left of your screen before you enter the castle. You will be able to get armor and runes which can be applied to armor once you get the smithy and enchantress (small amounts of customization are great, too much seems to do harm to a game). The levels are randomized which is great since you can discover new rooms and challenges. There are four sections of the map, the castle, the forest, the maya, and the land of darkness, for beginners once you have cleared the castle try the forest first, then the maya, and last the land of darkness (you may have noticed dots on each section of the small map in the first room of the castle representing the difficulty and the order). Each section has enemies that are unique to them as well as some enemies you've seen before so as you progress there will be noticeable changes (there are also more difficult versions of each enemy). The bosses remid me of older games that were coniderably more difficult than the mainstream games you see eveywhere, don't worry there are harder versions of each boss too ;) The soundtracks are unique and are great in terms of variation as well as, each boss and sections of the map have their own soundtracks respectively (you may come across a juke box in some rooms allowing you to change the song you're listening to as well). The artwork and character sprites are great, love it. Be wary of the hit boxes for enemies since they may seem large at some times and small at other times, your hitbox is something you should pay attention to as well. Overall I give this game a 4.5/5 making it one of my favorite games.

This review is made after about 10 hours of multiplayer with 3 friends(4pack).
-TLDR-
Would recommend if you plan to play it with friends,4 pack is recommended
Casual enough that you could just attack pirates and trade freely
Trading can get complicated but profitable
-----------------------------------------------------------------
Singleplayer is not recommended
-TLDR-
-------------------------------------------------------------------
-Additional Notes-
After an additional 20 hours after writing his review,for a total of 30 hours. I can say after reaching "end game" it was unreplayable
------------------------------------------------------------------
It is a casual game where you could either focus on trading or battling pirates.
-Combat-
The fighting is simplistic, you point your broadside of your ship against his ship all the while trying to get behind him so he can't point his gun to you.This is your "standard attacks"but is enhanced by new abilities, such as a Fire Barrel(Grogolov Cocktail) that does AOE fire damage;A Water Barrel that does AOE Heal to friendlies.
-Combat-Items-
Items have stats that enhance your combat capabilities.There are Damage,Range,and Accuracy for hitting your targets.Then there are Sails,Hull,Mobility,and Speed to Avoid/Take Damage.
-Trading-
Trading at a new region first involves taking over towns from pirates in a region. Buying abundant resources for cheap and selling it at other towns with high demand.Occasionally you get Quests for making a new town, and you get to name it, which is half the fun of making the town.More towns increases more Demand and Supply for a region. Potentially making more Profitable runs and cities become more closer to each other.
-Trading-Items-
Important stats for trading are Diplomacy,Speed,Cargo Space,and Maybe Mobility(Turn rate of a ship).Diplomacy gives you better prices for buying and selling goods.Speed should be obvious, but Mobility is dependant on your map layout.
Cargo space are slots on your ship.The more slots you have, the more quest/trading you can do simultaneously.
-Ship types-
There are ships for Combat,Trading or Both, you start with a fairly small ship.You Progress up by buying a ship with hardearned gold. If you plan to fight pirates, a high offence and/or defence ship is good.Trading would require either a Speed Ship or a huge cargo space amount. Both is just having Average stats of Offence,Defence,Speed,and Cargo Space.
-Replayability-
When you reach the so-called endgame, there is almost nothing else to do anymore. Trying out new ships can be done in your current play through, and you can respec your skills in towns. I would say after this play through I wouldn't bother starting a new one.However it was definitely a fun game and worth my hours spent
-Ending-
The initial review made with 10 hours of gameplay has been updated with notes after playing 30 hours of gameplay.
-Ending-

A lot of gamers these days have grown tired of sequels. Of constant rehashing of the same ideas, of the same characters and the same worlds constantly pushed in your face in exchange for your precious money. We want new faces, new worlds, and new experiences. The idea of sequels has definitely been worn thin by big publishers and developers. It's a safe way to cash in with gamers. And to an extent, gamers tend to flock to sequels because they know what they're getting themselves into. If you liked one Call of Duty, chances are you'd like another. Unless it was Ghosts.
Making actually good sequels is a tricky thing. It requires more than just a new coat of paint and some changing of menus around. A video game sequel should show improvement in mechanical and conceptual design. It should build on the themes present in its predecessor, not just rehash them. Being able to get it all perfect though, that can be tough. Especially if the first game could be considered a masterpiece itself. Going from Megaman 1 to Megaman 2 was a big jump in quality, but Megaman 1 was pretty rough around the edges to begin with. But that's really what sequels are about. A second chance, to smooth out the kinks of the first game and improve it. While some say sequels are never as good as the original, there's one game in particular that was practically made by its sequel. Borderlands 2. Now wait, wait. Before you say anything, just here me out. Steroid-infused midgets. Eh?
The original Borderlands was a pretty decent game. It wasn't perfect by any means, no. It was pretty repetitive, the side-quests could get pretty dull, and it wasn't balanced all too well. The world definitely had an interesting hook to it, but it was really just a one-trick midget. Just "here's some sand and♥♥♥♥♥♥ Have fun. Stay out here, your mother and I have to... uh... give grandma her sponge bath."
But grandma moved to Florida three years ago, and we're all pretty sure she's dead by now.
Borderlands 2, however, improves on literally everything Borderlands did in some incredibly impressive ways. Everything that Borderlands did, its sequel has done significantly better.
Most notably, there's more than just sand now. Yes, that's right. There's still plenty of sand to go around, but now there's snow. And grass. And cities. It's like you really are on an alien planet, not just lost in Afghanistan somewhere. There's still plenty of crazy people trying to shoot you and blow you up though, so I guess it's still kind of like Afghanistan.
You know what they should do, they should get the Taliban to film a new Mad Max movie. That'd be pretty crazy, you know? It'd add a nice touch of realism to it I think. Or just have a constant "Allahu Ackbar" playing during all of the high action scenes.
Borderlands 2 picks up a little after where Borderlands left off. There's a strange new substance called "Eridium" popping up everywhere now, and people seem to really like it. It's purple. Can't go wrong with anything that's glowy purple. That's why strip club neon signs are usually purple. Or pink. Or red. But you get the idea, people like purple.
With all of these purple glowy things everywhere, this big bad guy from an evil corporation thinks that there's a lot of strip clubs opening up on this planet. So he decides to take it over to have all of the strippers for himself. Makes sense, right?
Borderlands 2 carries on the FPS-RPG formula from its original. Shoot something in the face, and suddenly there are numbers. Numbers mean pain.
The general Borderlands theme is still present as well. Though you'll adventure through many different areas, they'll all have that same desolate feel to them. Not to mention the Borderlands sense of humor, which is as dark and perverse as ever. It still feels very Borderlands-y.
But everything feels better developed. The environments are more diverse, the guns and classes are better balanced, and the writing is superb. It manages to run an incredibly fine line between ridiculously zany, dark, perverse humor and dramatic, serious moments. And not only that, it takes the only okay plot of the first Borderlands and adds so much depth to it. Where Borderlands had a few extremely memorable characters, Borderlands 2 has an entire cast of them. It fleshes out the world so well, adding a surprising amount of lore and character depth.
Borderlands was a game about rednecks, guns, and sand. But Borderlands 2 isn't just rednecks and sand anymore. The same sci-fi Mad Max-esque world is there, but it feels like it truly found its own identity as well.
Like the original Borderlands, it's much more fun as a multiplayer game. I definitely recommend getting a group of friends together to play with you. Go make some. Trust me. It helps. Not just for playing the game either. You need to get out and socialize more. Your mother and I are worried about you. You spend too much time on the internet.
It really feels like the game gives you so much more purpose. Instead of wandering the desert, following whatever missions that have been thrown at you, Borderlands 2 gives you a much more personal motive in the form of a real villain. Though the original Borderlands had all manner of villains, they were all over the place. Random gangs of bandits, mercenaries, and a few big characters with very little time on screen. Borderlands 2 throws the game's big bad at you seconds after you start. And not only is he a major antagonist, he's a pretty damn fine one too. They really don't make villains like him anymore, I'll tell you what. It doesn't take too long for him to genuinely get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at him. And he just doesn't stop. The writing and dialogue is so perfect for him, it makes for the most satisfying boss fight.
The endless slew of side-quests is given a similar treatment. Rather than heading to a mission board and stocking up on dozens of missions to do, you'll get most of them from major NPC's in the game. Giving a face to each mission, as opposed to just being given a to-do list from a generic board, is something of an improvement. Also aided by the inclusion of more entertaining dialogue for each side-quest. There are less generic fetch quests and killing quests. Still plenty of them, but the way they're presented makes it less noticeable.
While Borderlands 2 could still use a few improvements here and there, like how it's still a tad bit repetitive at times, the changes already put it way ahead of the first. There's a massive amount of content as well, meaning that it's entirely possible to sink hundreds of hours into it. And most importantly? Everyone's favorite crazy circus stripper is back in all her trashy, bouncy glory. It's great, because♥♥♥♥♥♥
She's no longer tied to DLC, as she was in the first game. Though I feel it'd be a little more fun if she was tied to something. However, there's still a massive amount of DLC. Most of it is fantastic, adding so much more to the game. It has definitely been well-supported after release. I'd definitely recommend going for one of the Game of The Year editions. Lots of new areas to explore and characters to meet and play as.
With how utterly fantastic the jump was from Borderlands 1 to 2, I can only imagine how great the next game will end up being. It's not like they could possibly mess it up, right? See, the secret to telling how good a Borderlands game will be is to see how many really bad Gearbox games came out recently. How many Duke Nukem Forevers and Aliens: Colonial Marines... Marineses came out. If a bunch of really bad games come out, that's when you know something big is coming. Borderlands 3 could easily be right around the corner. We should all look forward to it.

Probably the biggest disapointment I've had in a long, long while.  GRANTED I didn't expect all that much from yet another movie turned game. However they did fairly well on gameplay, and great on visuals (which don't really matter in the end but are a nice touch).
1.) This is by far, the most repetetive game I have (and I can say this honestly) EVER played. It's like they came up with a few missions to do around the wasteland, duplicated them each say 30 times, scattered them everywhere, and called it good.
2.) If you're OCD about games and do everything you can. This'll either be a hit or miss for you. There is a good amount to find, HOWEVER what you find is either scrap, or a history relic. Aside from that you have insignias to destroy at every camp, but these things are more... They feel like they were thrown in at some point to avoid emptiness. Which leads to my third fact.
3.) The wasteland. Is. EMPTY. Yes you have camps, scarecrows to find and destroy, but it's rare that you'll find just straight scrap. If you get lucky and do, chances are some enemies are gonna pop up (out of the ground?) and ambush you. This is fine... but when it happens nearly every time and becomes such scripted nonsense you expect it... stop... please...
4. Although it is advertised as one. This is NOT an open world game. However I do have to give them credit for doing fairly well making it FEEL like an open world game. By this I mean yes, you can go where ever, and do whatever.  The biggest thing for me in an open world though, and probably you as well (most people I feel like) Is that the gameplay isn't scripted. Yes have cutscenes (especially when theres a story involved). BUT, when I come around a corner and every time the same guy is running towards me ready to attack, because I stepped in a trigger box that spawns him. Completely breaks my immersion, the same thing happening every single time, is not an open world. This game has aspects of an open world, but it is most definitely not (far to linear). Yes you have the option to go wherever and do whatever, but theres no point, You'll have a total of maybe 3 different missions at once, all in generally the same area, very obviously guiding you through the map at a logical pace. Not open world.
5.) They also claim its a survival game. (I'm wondering if this is even necessary, the fact they labeled themselves that is just sad.) There is not a lick of survival game in this. The closest thing, is that you can find water. However, your genius friend Max, carries one canteen, one gas can, yet has all that room in his car. Not really open world or survival if you can't make the choice to stock up on these things I feel? On top of only getting one, the water you find doesn't effect your thirst, as you have no thirst, it refills your health, just like finding food. Survival? No. The closest it came to survival was the need for gas to drive around. However later (not far into the game at all) if you've put ANY amount of points into the perk for not using gas. You will never need to refill your gas, and it becomes a pointless feature. Aside from the project parts that cause your gas to be rifilled upon entering a compound... Gas was... sadly another wasted feature.
6.) In my opinion, I feel like they spent a week on this game. Got it to a playable state, and sold it for far more than its worth. I'm not one for early access games at ALL. This might as well be. Well aside from of course the fact that, they say it's done and won't be working on it more, and goes for the price of a full game.  That, personally disguists me. I have seen early access games that are done better than this, that you can tell the developers put effort into and cared about the eventual outcome. NOT JUST THE CASH. The way I see it, this game was thrown together as quickly as they could, and slapped into the market around the time of the new movie coming out because they knew it wouldn't sell any other way.  I have many reasons for feeling this way, but one example, this is a game BASED ON DRIVING. Yet your vehicle rotates from its physical center. not your front wheels. I currently am making a game. Small details like that, are BIG, and its like they didn't care.
7.) Coming from Avalanche Studios, I personally expected a lot more. Just Cause was a great open world game. Mad Max seems... Honesty stolen. I feel like I'm playing Assassins Creed and Motorstorm at the same time. BOTH ARE FAR BETTER GAMES (because for what they tried to do, they did right).
8.) My end summary, Yes it's a good game, great story, until they end (in my opinion, but no spoilers and you can continue playing so I won't actually complain, the writers can do what they want (sadly)). BUT (theres always a but), I have a few days of gameplay in so far, I do enjoy the game. It's great and a lot of fun, but being entirely honest. When I'm done playing it and have had my fill, I will never come back. My OCD is pushing me to obtain every collectible and whatnot, if that's how you play games, you'll enjoy this. I warn you though. REPETITION. SO. MUCH. REPETITION. Primarily though, if you have know need to collect everything and get everything done. I beat this game in about 4 hours. The rest has all been side quests. UTTERLY, POINTLESS. SIDEQUESTS.
9. ) BLUNT AND TO THE POINT. Unless you like the movies. DO NOT BUY IT. If you like the movies. It's up to you weather a mere couple days of fun, is worth the hours it took to earn 60 bucks, and are you willing to spend that much on something worth half that? (I have literally played early access games for 30 bucks, done better than this.) Maybe I expect too much from big companies, but maybe they expect too much money.

I would like to begin by saying that this is genuinely a really great game.It has a great storyline,great effects,great fighting scenes. It was definitely worth what I paid for it.(actually it was worth a lot more than what I paid cause it was like 80% off when I bought it.lol) But all jokes aside this is one of the best games I have ever played. It was the first open-world game I had played so I didn't really know what to expect. Because of this I guess I can't say it exceeded my expectations but only because I didn't have any.
Throughout the game I felt I could really sympathise with Max's struggle which I think helped me enjoy the story to the fullest. A man who has lost everything that is important to him. His wife, his daughter, his home, and most of all his peace. All that is left is his will to survive.
Anyway about the gameplay. This game has very creative car combat as I'm sure you will find out should you decide to play this game. I found both the ground and the car combat both very enjoyable. I had a lot of fun playing through all the various side/story missions.And believe me there are a lot of them, you will be kept busy. But I never found them boring or even tedious. They all had their own unique ways to keep me excited and interested.
I also liked how realistic the ground combat was. I'm sure we all know and hate the way action movie villains attack the hero one by one but I found this game never had that unrealism. In fact acting like that is the case is a excellent way to get killed. The fighting controls are fairly simple to master. Hit,block,parry etc. You will unlock more fighting moves as you progress.Also you have a cool variety array of melee weapons that you can pick up from fallen enemies although they will wear out over time.

When you fight you build up your combo meter until you will enter 'fury mode', which is as awesome as it sounds, if not more. Enemies can also enter fury mode
(of a sort). In their case it is called being 'buffed' which will occur over time. This can be undone/prevented by eliminating the war crier,located in camps(see later). A troop incapable of attacking except indirectly by buffing up enemies. However if you kill all enemies in a camp the war crier will simply hang there and apologise/plead for mercy. This has no strategic purpose, however it is very amusing.
Your car and Max himself both have a variety of upgrades with can be unlocked after completing certain requirements and purchasing them with the game's currency; scrap, which you will have many opportunities to find and collect within the game. There are many various types of enemy's and vehicles which you may study in the pause menu once you first come across them as well as all the other characters you meet who's basic history you can read if you so wish.
The game also leaves plenty of room for strategic thinking when it comes to taking down enemy camps. Wastelanders located close to the camp will inform you of secret entrances and other useful intel. It is important to eliminate perimeter defences quickly lest they become buffed, which makes attacks more powerful.
As a side note I feel I must point out that the game does have a significant amount of gore. Not so much when actually playing the game, more so during cutscenes. I would recommend avoiding this game unless you are aged 16 or older (With a possible exception if you are reasonably close to said age).
I feel I should also point out that the boss battles have very little variety from each other. This actually never bothered me for some reason so I don't recommend not buying the game solely based on that. In all honesty I really can't think of anything else that I even slightly disliked nor of any other cons in any aspect of the game.
Finally what would have to be one of the games coolest features in the game is that there is also a capture mode which can be used to pause the game at any time (except cutscenes) and take a screenshot. You can add colour filters, logos, backgrounds, and adjust camera angles which is a lot of fun especially when driving off ramps.
So in summary this game was truly an awesome experience for me with all of its cool features, terrific gameplay, great effects and excellent storyline. I assure you that if you buy this game it will be very much worth your while.
Also in case you care this is the first review I have ever made.

Spec Ops: The Line is one of those games that, every now and then, reminds you of why people keep making shooter games, and most important of all: why we must not lose faith in the genre.
Set in the current era, in a sandstorm-ridden Dubai, you play as Captain Walker, a guy leading a pair of battle hardened soldiers that are tasked with finding survivors of a previous rescue attempt and what little civilians may still be alive amongst the ruins of the buried city and retrieving them. What initially seems like a rescue op, soon goes awry, as not only they find hostile locals, but also signs of rogue elements amongst the US troops stationed there. As you traverse the game, level by level, you can't help but feel like you're losing grasp of what's wrong and what's right, as the carnage of war forces you to make ever increasing tough calls, and that's where Spec Ops: The Line's beauty truly shines: it's not an ode to war, liberty or freedom - much like other shooters nowadays are - , but a tale of how easy it is to lose one's self in the midst of war; of how easy it is to cross the line.
The story, apart from being deeply engaging and as stated, morally challenging, is deftly told by superb voice actors who make the beautifully crafted monologues and dialogues come to life with utter credibility. Also, the explosions, and effects, generally speaking, are top-notch. The music choice is SUPERB, even getting Verdi's Dies Irae in a running sequence that caught me unawares. It is worth noting, however, that for all the good this campaign is, it can be finished in about 7 hours, standard difficulty. And while the game does ask for a second playthrough to tie up some loose ends, it doesn't have much to offer in terms of further replay value.
Gameplay is great, but in a game that excels in every department it may stand out as a somewhat bland and "been there, done that" thing. Still, it never gets boring, firefights being intense all the way throughout the game by either a change of pace, weapons or availability of squadmates.
Finally, it is worth mentioning that the game features coop. It's nothing worth acclaim, but a nice plus should you have a friend that happens to own the game.
While a tad short, a gripping story, a state of the art sound and music department and great gameplay makes Spec Ops: The Line the best shooter I've played in a long while: 8.5/10.

For someone who is not really a fan of the RPG genre, this game took a whole new turn for it.
Normally, I find combat in normal rpg's to just be annoying and boring.
However, in Undertale, the combat was actually very enjoyable.
One of the things that made the game as enjoyable as it was for me was that the amount of monsters that you fight during the game is a perfect amount. On top of that, the different style of combat of dodging and attacking was super cool.
But that's only the combat...
The strongest part about Undertale is the story and atmosphere.
As you progress through the game, all the characters that you meet are never just a blank character. Almost every npc in the game has some sort of comedic value, or emotion behind them.
The story that is demonstrated between all the characters is one that I haven't seen in any game since the Earthbound series. It's truly engaging and once you start playing through the game it is difficult to stop.
To add to the story and atmosphere, the music plays an incredibly important part in it. The music in Undertale can go from super happy to super serious to super sad, but it all feels like it fits into that part of the game. The soundtrack of this game is simply a masterpiece.
Pros:
Great Music
Engaging Story
Fun Combat
Beautiful Art Style
Some replay value
Cons:
Shorter Game
If you haven't picked up the game I highly recommend it. It's one of the best games I've ever played.

Surprisingly, Before the Storm is even better than the original Life is Strange and works perfectly fine without any supernatural powers. There might be some minor flaws here and there plus some sudden convenience plot near the end, but nothing that your suspension of disbelief can't handle given the superb character drama and excellent voice acting (even without Ashly Burch). You can count the games on your fingers that are able to evoke such emotion, which is why this is a 10/10 for me again. Oh and the soundtrack (Daughter) is absolutely awesome too, if you're into this kind of music.

Deck Nine does it again! Overall: 9.0/10
Just as I expected, the Life is Strange universe delivers again with their unique take on storytelling and player choices. The developers did a fantastic job of retaining what was so good about the original - the art style, attention to detail, and soundtrack are all phenomenal. What really makes the game worth a purchase is how well the same incredible character development, world-building, and moral dilemmas are applied from the first game to a new arc. The original LiS alluded to its secondary characters having incredible potential for further development, and Before the Storm satisfies this potential excellently. Rachel is an incredibly complex character, and her interactions with Chloe fuel an emotional story of friendship and loyalty. However, side characters are not left in the background. David, Drew, Victoria, Frank and many others recieve a welcome amount of attention as well, but not too much to take away from the "main act".
As for the story itself, it really depends on the player, as to be expected. Personally, I thought everything was really well thought out; each scene had purpose, none were forced. The only "issue" I had was with the ending, which seemed a tad abrupt to me, but I will leave that up for you to play and decide!
No matter how you choose to play, be prepared for the same type of rollercoaster that Life is Strange provided. Although it's nearly impossible to beat the first game, Before the Storm is a real treat and will surely satisfy the desiring fan.

I would like to begin by saying that this is genuinely a really great game.It has a great storyline,great effects,great fighting scenes. It was definitely worth what I paid for it.(actually it was worth a lot more than what I paid cause it was like 80% off when I bought it.lol) But all jokes aside this is one of the best games I have ever played. It was the first open-world game I had played so I didn't really know what to expect. Because of this I guess I can't say it exceeded my expectations but only because I didn't have any.
Throughout the game I felt I could really sympathise with Max's struggle which I think helped me enjoy the story to the fullest. A man who has lost everything that is important to him. His wife, his daughter, his home, and most of all his peace. All that is left is his will to survive.
Anyway about the gameplay. This game has very creative car combat as I'm sure you will find out should you decide to play this game. I found both the ground and the car combat both very enjoyable. I had a lot of fun playing through all the various side/story missions.And believe me there are a lot of them, you will be kept busy. But I never found them boring or even tedious. They all had their own unique ways to keep me excited and interested.
I also liked how realistic the ground combat was. I'm sure we all know and hate the way action movie villains attack the hero one by one but I found this game never had that unrealism. In fact acting like that is the case is a excellent way to get killed. The fighting controls are fairly simple to master. Hit,block,parry etc. You will unlock more fighting moves as you progress.Also you have a cool variety array of melee weapons that you can pick up from fallen enemies although they will wear out over time.

When you fight you build up your combo meter until you will enter 'fury mode', which is as awesome as it sounds, if not more. Enemies can also enter fury mode
(of a sort). In their case it is called being 'buffed' which will occur over time. This can be undone/prevented by eliminating the war crier,located in camps(see later). A troop incapable of attacking except indirectly by buffing up enemies. However if you kill all enemies in a camp the war crier will simply hang there and apologise/plead for mercy. This has no strategic purpose, however it is very amusing.
Your car and Max himself both have a variety of upgrades with can be unlocked after completing certain requirements and purchasing them with the game's currency; scrap, which you will have many opportunities to find and collect within the game. There are many various types of enemy's and vehicles which you may study in the pause menu once you first come across them as well as all the other characters you meet who's basic history you can read if you so wish.
The game also leaves plenty of room for strategic thinking when it comes to taking down enemy camps. Wastelanders located close to the camp will inform you of secret entrances and other useful intel. It is important to eliminate perimeter defences quickly lest they become buffed, which makes attacks more powerful.
As a side note I feel I must point out that the game does have a significant amount of gore. Not so much when actually playing the game, more so during cutscenes. I would recommend avoiding this game unless you are aged 16 or older (With a possible exception if you are reasonably close to said age).
I feel I should also point out that the boss battles have very little variety from each other. This actually never bothered me for some reason so I don't recommend not buying the game solely based on that. In all honesty I really can't think of anything else that I even slightly disliked nor of any other cons in any aspect of the game.
Finally what would have to be one of the games coolest features in the game is that there is also a capture mode which can be used to pause the game at any time (except cutscenes) and take a screenshot. You can add colour filters, logos, backgrounds, and adjust camera angles which is a lot of fun especially when driving off ramps.
So in summary this game was truly an awesome experience for me with all of its cool features, terrific gameplay, great effects and excellent storyline. I assure you that if you buy this game it will be very much worth your while.
Also in case you care this is the first review I have ever made.

I grew fond of Max in this game, I admit.
I believe the strong point in the game that it might provide fun for those who are hasty and for those who like making every small detail on an open world or a mix of those (such as myself).
Having means to make your Magnus Opus a car of legend, you soon start looking for means to have the parts and the scraps to build them. Besides, you also have Fortresses where you can replenish your resources (if you build them), and make fast travels, and run for your death trying to get new vehicles.
I admit that near the ending I started getting bored with the worldly missions and got rushed up to the last missions at Gas Town, so the game ended rather suddendly (although it'll continue from there, if you want).
Car battles can be rather nice and/or extremely annoying, depending on what you have to do. Sometimes some stupid small rock you make your world an inferno. Alas, that's what it takes when driving at high speed trying to explode other cars which are trying to do the same to you.
Man-to-man battles get fairly easy in no time. You must mainly be wary of counter-attacking at the exact moment, even when you a surrounded by a dozen foes of different attack styles, it's not hard finishing them up without being hit once. Also, learning battle skills make these battles even easier and faster to finish up.
I also think that you must visit Griffa more often to learn what he has to say to Max. I used to visit him after collecting around 15 or so Griffa Tokens, so I visited him not that often and got Maxed out in all my abilities too soon, then I guess something was left 'unsaid'.
Graphically, it is a pleasing game that I need not to play in low stats. The voice casting was also nice.
Something that got a bit boring was sniffing out land mines with the dog and cleaning the maps whole, sometimes going to very far fetched places to get only a handful of scraps in which you could also get by exploding a single car in your way down there. I believe some places could be a bit more rewarding.
Story-wise the game is not groundbreaking. It does show some situations in which you ponder about how it would be if it was real, specially considering natural resources, food and the likes. Still, it has room to show a branch of expansion towards Bullet Farm, which is again only mentioned here, just like it was in the movie, so I think there's a probability to have an Expasion entitled Bullet Farm. As long as they don't simply only add a new region without any tweaks in gameplay to make the game less repetitive and more engaging and insteresting.
All in all I would give a 8.5 even a 9-10 for this game. It was fun.
